ResearchPlanTitle: Linking pollination to population dynamics and life history.
ResearchPlanAbstract: The long-term goal of our research is to link pollination ecology to plant population biology.  Our research explores consequences of successful pollination for the dynamics of plant populations and for fitness of plants measured as number of successful offspring.  This information is critical to pure and conservation-related studies of plant population dynamics, and to the studies of the evolution of plant life history and natural selection on floral traits related to pollination.  Previous workers have been forced to assume that differences in pollination success are important.  However, there are other factors that could easily swamp out the “signal” of differential pollination success among individuals. </p><p> Our study will examine whether such factors as microhabitat characteristics, seed predators, herbivores and competitors effectively mask the effects of increased pollination on reproductive success measured over multiple generations.

ResearchPlanTitle: Control of mayfly antipredator tactics
ResearchPlanAbstract:
Control of Colorado mayfly nymph behavioural responses to native and
introduced predatory fishes will be investigated.  Mayfly nymphs avoid
moving in the water column (drifting) during the day when visually feeding
fish are present to avoid a high risk of predation.  Baetis mayfly nymphs
reared in fishless water will be exposed to fish at various times in their
lifehistories to determine whether their avoidance is an acute response, a
developmental switch or learning, or is an evolutionary response.  </p><p>The
predation risk presented by two introduced and the one native trout species
will be estimated by measuring consumption of mayflies in experimental
tanks.  
</p><p>
Comparison of relative risks with the magnitude of predator
avoidance will determine the importance of evolutionary history with a
predator and the predation risk the predator presents.  Also, the predator
avoidance behaviour of five species of mayfly nymphs will be compared to
 their vulnerability to trout predation to evaluate the selective forces
producing different antipredator tactics.  This research will determine how
prey develop antipredator tactics, how long it takes, and the important
selection forces.  Thus, it will contribute toward better understanding and
management of introduced predators.  It will also increase knowledge of the
importance of predation in stream communities.

ResearchPlanTitle: Slowly-changing soil properties and long-term biological reserve design
ResearchPlanAbstract:
The motivation behind this Ph.D. dissertation topic is my aspiration to see soils become a more integral and rich aspect of the nature conservation agenda.  In this spirit I propose to conduct empirical research that will speak to and complement </p><p>a. an analysis of the historical and cultural context of soil science and soil valuation and a </p><p>b. (re-) evaluation the role of soils and soil diversity in promoting biological diversity, ecosystem processes, aesthetic pleasures, and pedagogic functions.  The questions my field work will be designed to address are:  </p><p>Does soil particle size distribution (texture and rockiness) matter to plant community structure now?
</p><p> and </p><p>Can this parameter be expected to modulate plant community response to climate change?
</p><p>1  Here I sketch an experimental design that will primarily address the first question (which I expect will constitute the core of my dissertation work), whilst also leading to the development of hypotheses addressing the second question.

ResearchPlanTitle: Effects of plant population fragmentation on pollination: effects of local density on pollination and reproduction in Delphinium nuttallianum and Aconitum columbianum
ResearchPlanAbstract:
In an era of increasing habitat fragmentation it is important to understand how pollination and reproduction respond to plant population density. Compared to dense populations we might expect sparse populations to experience declines in pollination service and in seed set. We explored these effects in 1997 in natural populations using the larkspur Delphinium nuttallianum and monkshood Aconitum columbianum. The quantity of pollinator service (pollinator visitation rate and pollen deposition on stigmas) to both species was unrelated  or weakly related to density. In contrast, seed set declined by one third in sparse populations relative to nearby dense populations. This loss of fecundity may stem from receipt of more inbred pollen, or sparsity indicate poor environmental conditions that lower seed set  for reasons unrelated to pollination.  
	</p><p>This summer we would like to test these hypothesis using experimental manipulations of density and of availability of self pollen to disentangle the contributions of pollen quality and of resource availability to density effects on fecundity in both species.

ResearchPlanTitle:
“Evolution in a plant hybrid zone”
“Pollination, plant fitness, and population dynamics”
ResearchPlanAbstract:
Related species of flowering plants are often hybridized to generate new horticultural varieties.  Such hybridization is also common in natural populations.  Where two species come into contact and produce successful hybrids, that area is called a hybrid zone.  Natural hybridization in these areas can have important consequences for evolution.  It may contribute to the breakdown of reproductive isolation between existing species, help to reinforce species differences, lead to the production of new species, or result in a stable hybrid zone.  At RMBL, we are investigating the processes responsible for maintaining hybrid zones in plants.  An understanding of these processes is not only of fundamental importance to basic biology.  Such knowledge can be used to prevent transfer of engineered genes from crop plants into populations of related plants, and also to conserve rare species that come into contact with more common relatives.</p><p>

	A common local wildflower is the scarlet gilia (Ipomopsis aggregata).  This red-flowered plant and its close relative, the pale pink to white-flowered I. tenuituba, provide a good example of natural hybridization.  Hummingbirds and hawkmoths transfer pollen between these species.  In the resulting hybrid zones there are gradual shifts (clines) in flower color, length and width as one moves up in elevation towards the I. tenuituba populations.  Natural selection can maintain clines like these in various ways.  One possibility is that hybrids have relatively poor survival and fertility, but this low fitness is balanced by continued production of hybrids through the dispersal of pollen.  Another possibility is that hybrids survive and reproduce particularly well in certain kinds of habitats.  To distinguish between these and other possibilities, we have planted seed from plants from different elevations and their hybrid offspring at several sites.  We are following their survival and reproductive success (with DNA and other genetic markers) to determine relative fitness.  We are also examining the ability of hummingbirds and hawkmoths to transfer pollen between flowers that differ in particular features of morphology.

ResearchPlanTitle: Interaction between food availability, morphology and predation mortality mediated by adaptive behaviour
ResearchPlanAbstract:
My aim with the proposed project is to link community ecology with a more mechanistic approach in order to increase the understanding of the underlying forces affecting population and community structure in streams.  I will concentrate on two mayflies that uses similar resources and are exposed to similar predators (fish and stoneflies).  Those mayflies use very different methods to avoid predators and find resources.  Baetis is a slender and soft-bodied specie, very mobile, with a pronounced tendency to swim or drift when encountered by predators. Ephmerella is a relatively large and hard-bodied, spiny species, rather immobile, that freezes or posture in response to predator encounters.  I will measure the cost and benefits of those behaviural and morphological differences, and how those trade-offs are affected by the presence of multiple predators.  Specifically, how is resource acquisition by those mayflies affected by prey mobility and predators?  </p><p>
Thus I will also ask: what is the cost for their anti-predator defences?  These experiments will be conducted in streams with different predator regimes and in controlled semi-natural experiments.

ResearchPlanTitle:
Impacts of two introduced species on the pollination ecology of the native
fireweed Epilobium angustifolium.
ResearchPlanAbstract:
Introduced plant and animal species can have a variety of impacts
upon the native flora and fauna.  One underinvestigated impact is the
influence an introduced plant species may have upon the reproductive
ecology of a native plant.  The presence of an introduced plant could draw
pollinators, such as bumblebees, away from native species.  This
competition for pollinators could result in the native plant being unable
to make seed and to persist.  Conversely, the presense of an introduced
plant could provide pollinators with additional resources, resulting in
increased pollination of the native plants as a greater number or diversity
of pollinators is supported.  I am exploring these possibilites using two
introduced species (butter-and-eggs Linaria vulgaris and scentless
chamomile Matricaria perforata) that share bumblebee pollinators with the
native fireweed Epilobium angustifolium.  In preliminary studies where the
introduced plants were removed, I found that fireweed growing with
butter-and-eggs  was visited by bees more often than when fireweed grew
alone, but that fireweed growing with scentless chamomile was visited less
often.  In 1999 I will be continuing removal experiments as well as
"invading' patches of fireweed with potted butter-and-eggs or scentless
chamomile.
ResearchPlanOrganisms: Epilobium angustifolium, Linaria vulgaris, Matricaria perforata, Bombus sp.

ResearchPlanTitle:
Ecological Functional Assessment of Colorado Riverine Wetlands: 
A Case Study of the McCabe Ranch Mitigation Wetlands (Gunnison, Colorado)
ResearchPlanAbstract:
Wetlands cover only about 1.5 percent of Colorado (1 million acres) and are of high ecological and economic value (USGS, 1996).  Wetlands provide an array of ecological goods and services which include: 1) habitat for rare hydric plants and wildlife such as aquatic invertebrates, amphibians, fish and migratory waterfowl, 2) water quality improvements through retention of sediments and nutrients, 3) flood attenuation by buffering hydrologic pulses, 4) bank stabilization from rooted hydrophytes and flow rate reduction, 5) biochemical cycling (nitrogen, phosphorus, carbon, etc.) and 6) a source of recreation, timber, and other natural products for commercial use (Mitsch and Gosselink, 1993).  Although valuable, 50% of all Colorado wetlands have been converted and/or drained over the last two centuries (Dahl, 1990).  
Development activities in Colorado wetlands are now regulated by Federal statutory prohibitions and State oversight.  Federal law has established "no net loss policy" for wetlands authorized by the Clean Water Act (Findley and Farber, 1992; NRC, 1995).  The goal of the Clean Water Act to restore and maintain the chemical, physical and biological integrity of the nation's surface waters includes wetlands (Fennessy and Roehrs, 1997).  In an effort to curb degradation of wetlands, Section 401 requires water quality certification by the United States Environmental Protection Agency (USEPA) for any project affecting wetlands and Section 404 requires a developer to obtain a permit from the U.S. Army Corps of Engineers (USACE) in order to develop in wetlands.  The Corps will generally grant a permit if three sequential conditions are met by an applicant: 1) takes all practical steps to avoid adverse impacts to wetlands 2) minimizes unavoidable damage to wetlands and 3) compensates for permanent destruction of wetlands by creating a new wetland or by restoring a degraded one (usually in the same watershed).  Measures taken to meet USEPA and USACE standards for wetlands are referred to as “mitigation” (Marsh et al., 1996; Salvesen, 1990).  According to the USACE and USEPA, compensatory mitigation attempts to provide, at a minimum, full replacement value: “no net loss” of wetlands (USACE and USEPA, 1990).  Thus, if development occurs in Colorado wetlands requiring draining and/or degradation of natural wetlands than the developer will be required to "fully" mitigate (i.e. substitute) for the damage occurring to the natural wetlands.
In 1990, five wetland basins were constructed at the McCabe Ranch Mitigation Wetlands in Gunnison County (two miles west of the City of Gunnison) to substitute for ecological functions lost when natural palustrine wetlands were drained at the Gunnison Airport.   No functional assessment has yet been conducted on these basins, left unmonitored since initial construction.  In order to assess the "success" of the effort to maintain a "no net loss" of Colorado wetland functions,  I propose to conduct a quantitative ecological functional assessment of these palustrine Colorado wetlands to assess whether the constructed wetlands provide similar levels of ecological goods/services as natural reference wetlands.  I wish to continue research initiated last summer to obtain quantitative and qualitative assessments on the status of the following communities: 1) hydrophytes  (emergents, submersed and floating aquatic plants) 2) aquatic invertebrates 3) amphibians 4) fish and 5) birds.  Further, physical parameters (i.e. hydrology, geomorphology, water quality, etc.) will be incorporated into the analysis this year to enhance the assessment.   Such research is novel due to the fact that functions and values of Colorado's wetlands remain largely unstudied (Cooper and Severn, 1992; USGS, 1996) and functional assessment of constructed wetlands beyond 3-5 years after initial construction is relatively rare (Fennessy and Roehrs, 1997).

ResearchPlanTitle: Climate and plant community controls on forest soil carbon stocks and fluxes: potential feedbacks to climate change
ResearchPlanAbstract: My research focuses on how climate affects the rate of carbon movement between plants, the soil, and the atmosphere in the forests of the Fossil Ridge Wilderness. Carbon moves between these major ecosystem compartments primarily through photosynthesis and decomposition. The rate at which these processes occur is often controlled by climate. Carbon dioxide in the atmosphere is thought to be responsible for both historic and predicted climate changes, meaning feedback loops exist between local ecosystems and the global atmosphere. Whether a change in climate results in positive (destabilizing) or negative (self-correcting) feedbacks depends on how ecosystems respond to that change.  For example, if a change in climate slows the rate that carbon is returned to the atmosphere from the soil through decomposition, then that change would result in a negative feedback, moderating global climate change.  On the other hand, a change that speeds the return of carbon to the atmosphere creates a positive feedback, accelerating global climate change.  Forest ecosystems in particular can store large quantities of carbon for long periods of time, keeping carbon out of the atmosphere. Understanding how the carbon cycle in widespread forest types, such as lodgepole pine and Engelmann spruce, responds to climate change will help us decide how to best manage our forests in the coming century.
ResearchPlanOrganisms: Subalpine forest ecosystems (Lodgepole pine (Pinus contorta) and Engelmann spruce (Picea engelmanni)

ResearchPlanTitle: The effects of grazing on the pollinators of generalist pollinated plants
ResearchPlanAbstract:
Different timings of grazing differentially impact the plant community of an area.  Because pollinator species exhibit preferences in which plants they visit, a change in the plant community could affect which pollinators are present.  Pollinators are a key link in plant reproduction and if the pollinators are impacted, then that will affect future plant populations and floral diversity.  I will study plants that are pollinated by many different types of insects which, in turn, pollinate many different species of plants (generalist pollinated plants).  I will first determine the floral diversity and abundance in three areas with differing grazing timings.  I am going to observe areas pre and post-grazing and see the changes in plant floral diversity and density.  I will then observe how the group of pollinators changes for a generalist pollinated plant if the plant community surrounding these species differs. Any change in the pollinator species will affect the efficiency and distance that the pollen, and therefore plant genes, is dispersed.   
Objective
	I propose to study the impacts of different levels of grazing on insect pollinators in Gunnison County, Colorado, USA.  How does the group of pollinators visiting generalist pollinated plants change under different grazing regimes?   If the change in the plant community impacts pollinator abundance, this could affect pollination efficiency and pollen dispersal distance, and therefore plant gene dispersal.  This occurs because grazing can directly impact the abundance of certain pollinators. Grazing can also indirectly change the future plant floral diversity and abundance through variations in the effects on pollinator visitation.

ResearchPlanTitle: Population biology and quantitative genetics of life-history and floral traits of Aquilegia caerulea.
ResearchPlanAbstract: We are examining the quantitative genetics of life-history and floral traits of the blue columbine, Aquilegia caerulea to examine the potential for: 1) pollinator-mediated selection on floral traits and the mating system; and 2) evolution of life-history traits in this long-lived perennial herb.  There is some evidence that observed variation in floral traits such as flower color, spur length, and protandry in this species affect pollinator visitation and the mating system.   However, there is no information about the heritability or genetic correlations of such traits or how specific differences in floral traits independently affect mating success and the mating system.  We are monitoring life-history and floral traits of progeny from controlled, quantitative genetic crosses in a common garden experiment at RMBL.  Data will be analyzed for reciprocal effects as well as maternal, paternal, interaction, and environmental effects to help determine the evolutionary potential of measured traits.  Long-term goals will include manipulative studies of those traits found to be heritable.

ResearchPlanTitle:
FUNCTIONAL DIVERSITY OF MICROBES IN MONTANE SOILS:  
BACTERIA AND THEIR NEMATODE CONSUMERS
ResearchPlanAbstract: Soil bacteria are important members of ecosystems because they recycle dead organic matter into nutrients available for plants and act as food for organisms that consume bacteria.  It is well known that many different bacteria live in soils.  It is less clear what sort of bacterial diversity may be found in RMBL soils and whether they differ in their ecological functions or, in other words, in what they do in nature.  This project will determine what kinds of bacteria live in meadow soils around RMBL and how they function as food resources to one of their major consumers:  tiny roundworms called nematodes.  Different bacteria may be preferred as food by nematodes, which would indicate that the bacteria are functionally diverse.  If the different bacteria are equally preferred as food, then they are functionally similar.  Bacteria are also known to be sensitive to temperature, moisture, and inputs of plant and other organic matter on which they feed.  RMBL research on climate change has demonstrated that these factors are likely to drastically change in mountain soils as a result of global warming.  After examining soil bacteria and their consumption by nematodes, this project will determine how interactions between bacteria and nematodes are affected by climate change experiments being conducted at RMBL.  The techniques for this study primarily involve collecting dozens of small soil cores from RMBL meadows.  The cores will then be sent to several collaborators at institutions such as the Oak Ridge Microbial Biogeochemistry Group and the University of California at Davis to be analyzed for bacterial DNA in the soil and in the gut contents of the nematodes.

ResearchPlanTitle: Do plants send mixed signals? An investigation of the repellent properties of the floral volatiles produced by Polemonium foliosissimum.
ResearchPlanAbstract: Rooted to the ground, plants are compelled to signal insects through visual display and chemical cues.  An extreme example of such is signaling is the uncanny mimicry of the scent and appearance of female wasps by some species of orchids which allows them to entice male wasps seeking mates.  While plants that emit scents that mimic insect pheromones are unusual, allurement of pollinators by scent emission is common.  In the fiercely competitive environment of the coevolutionary arms race, floral herbivores are just as likely as pollinators to be intercepting the fragrant odors of receptive flowers.  This conflict between attracting pollinators and avoiding attraction of herbivores has rarely been studied.  Even less well studied is the potential repulsion of pollinators by scents that are emitted by plants in order to deter floral herbivores.  An ideal system to understand these potential conflicts of plant signaling is found at Rocky Mountain Biological Lab.  There Hylemya sp., a fly larvae, and a seed predator on Polemonium foliosissimum (Jacob’s Ladder) is believed to be repelled by one of two scent morphs produced by this plant.  I intend to document this repellence by comparing rates of herbivore visitation to the two morphs.  I will also ascertain how important scent is in attracting insects and compare pollinator visitation in order to determine whether the repellent plant morph has a deterrent affect on pollination.
ResearchPlanOrganisms: Polemonium foliosissimum and its herbivore Hylemya sp.

ResearchPlanTitle: Spatial Variability of an Ant Mutualist May Constrain: Host Plant Specialization by Membracids
ResearchPlanAbstract: Spatial and temporal variation in mutualisms has been documented in numerous studies (Herrera, 1988; Horvitz and Schemske, 1990).  Variability in the abundance or species composition of one mutualist partner may translate into variable selection on the other partner.  One example of this has been found in a pollination system.  Campbell et al. (1997) found that hummingbirds and hawkmoths impose differential selection on floral traits in Ipomopsis sp.  In this scenario, variable selection by pollinators may result in variation in floral traits.  In essence, specialization by plants on one pollinator may be constrained by spatial or temporal variation in the species composition of the pollinators (Schemske, 1983; Herrera, 1988; Waser et al., 1996).

ResearchPlanTitle:
Movement patterns of butterflies in complex landscapes:
How does the matrix influence the effective isolation of patches?
ResearchPlanAbstract:
My research at RMBL addresses the movement patterns of animals in complex landscapes.  One of the most pressing challenges for conservation biology is to understand the effects on biodiversity when landscapes are fragmented by human land use.  A useful approach to understanding such landscapes is to study naturally patchy habitats, in order to generate predictions and generalities relevant to anthropogenically fragmented areas.  I have begun such a study at RMBL, on a butterfly community inhabiting a system of meadow patches.
The study focuses on the role of the matrix (i.e. the non-habitat surrounding the native habitat patches of interest) in mediating the rates of butterfly movement among the patches.  Traditional island biogeography and metapopulation theories assume that the matrix is uniform and measure isolation among patches simply as the distances separating them.  The various types of matrix surrounding terrestrial habitat patches (both natural and remnant), however, may be differentially permeable to movement of individuals.  Patches therefore may be more or less effectively isolated than simple distance would indicate (and classic models would predict), depending on the type of intervening matrix.

ResearchPlanAbstract: If natural selection always acts in the same direction, it should decrease variation. But much of the variation we see in nature appears to be stable. Is that because new variation is always being created (mutation), or because natural selection favors different variants under different circumstances? I am studying a particular protein in Scarlet Gilia that has many forms. These seem to be maintained in the population because different forms work better at different levels of soil moisture.

ResearchPlanTitle: Factors affecting the evolutionary maintenance of gynodioecy in Geranium
ResearchPlanAbstract:
Geranium richardsonii (wild geranium) produces two types of plants,
bisexual with large hermaphroditic flowers, and female with small male
sterile flowers.  This condition, termed gynodioecy, is relatively rare
but widespread in flowering plants.  Darwin first recognized that this
loss of male reproductive function posed an evolutionary riddle; namely
"how can females achieve fitness equal to hermaphrodites so as not to be
eliminated by selection?".  My ongoing research at RMBL is directed at
quantifying the fitness costs and benefits of gynodioecy in Geranium.  In
particular I am interested in how floral dimorphism affects pollinator
behvavior and the mating system, whether self pollination and inbreeding
depression lower the fitness of hermaphrodites, if females can produce
more and larger seeds, and if the relative fitness of the two morphs vary
according to their frequency in populations.  I use a combination of field
and greenhouse experiments as well as laboratory studies of molecular
variation to address these questions.

ResearchPlanTitle:
Population cycles, habitat utilization and prey choice of the high
altitude bat fauna of the East River Valley.
ResearchPlanAbstract:
Little information exists regarding the diversity and foraging behavior of
bat species at high altitude sites in Colorado.  This project will
document seasonal variation in abundances of bat species near the Rocky
Mountain Biological Laboratory, Gothic, Gunnison Co., CO (9500'), assess
habitat preferences of the bat species encountered, and correlate habitat
preference with the abundance of potential insect prey and diet choice.
Several netting sites in different habitats have been established and
monitored since 1993.  Live bats will be measured for species
identification, non-invasively examined for reproductive condition, feces
collected for diet analysis, and released.  Acoustic monitoring using an
ultrasonic "bat detector" will also be used to assess bat abundance and
activity in different habitats.  In addition, nocturnal insects diversity
and abundance will be assessed using a variety of trapping methods and compared with bat habitat and diet choice. This is a continuation of a long-term monitoring project begun in 1993.

ResearchPlanTitle: The role of soil organic matter and texture in evapotranspiration
ResearchPlanAbstract:
Soil structure plays an important role in both thecarbon cycle and the hydrological cycle.  Across the landscape thedistribution of soil texture and chemistry, and therefore the distributionof plant species, is influenced by parent material.  And yet, over the long term, plants engineer theirenvironment by incorporating carbon from the atmosphere into soil,modifying soil structure and improving its ability to hold water through dry periods.  Global climate modelssuggest that one effect of increased atmospheric carbon dioxide levels(from fossil fuel burning) is a decline in summer precipitation in themid-continental US, soit is worth investigating how different soils will buffer such a shortage.
	The goal of this project is to understand how important the role of organicsoil carbon is relative to the role of soil grain size distribution indetermining soil's moisture holding capacity and how the vegetation and/ororganic matter on different soiltypes affects the rate at which water moves from the soil to theatmosphere.  Results from this study should help explain how differentsoils will react to the same climate perturbation and improve ecosystemscientists' ability to predict the effect of a given change in precipitation on local vegetation patterns.

ResearchPlanTitle: The contribution of inter-site variation in gene flow to geographic variation 	among 	hybrid zones of Ipomopsis aggregata and I. tenuituba (Polemoniaceae).”
ResearchPlanAbstract: Hybrid zones – where genetically distinct populations mate and produce offspring – are important laboratories for the study of evolution. Hybrid zone theory predicts many evolutionary outcomes ranging from reinforcement of isolation between species, to fusion of different species into one depending on assumptions regarding gene flow and hybrid fitness. Because individual plants are unable to move in search of favorable habitat, and because most plants depend on animal pollinators to reproduce, environmental factors may exert an especially large influence on the formation and fitness of hybrids in plant hybrid zones. Two common species of Scarlet Gilia (Ipomopsis aggregata and I. tenuituba) co-occur in isolated contact sites throughout the western United States. These species frequently form hybrid zones; however, those hybrid zones often differ in the abundance of hybrids and the distribution of parent species. This study examines differences in pollinators, flower morphology, and habitat distribution between two Ipomopsis contact sites in western Colorado. One site comprises an extensive hybrid zone and elevational separation of parent species (Poverty Gulch), while the other features a patchy distribution of parents and few or no hybrids (Grizzly Ridge). I predict that differences in the number and behavior of principal pollinators of each species, unique floral morphological incompatibilities, and availability of suitable habitat contribute to the variation in rates of hybridization between Poverty Gulch and Grizzly Ridge. Furthermore, these environmental differences may produce evolutionary dynamics that result in widely different outcomes of contact between this pair of species in different places.

ResearchPlanTitle: Fluctuating Asymmetry as an Indicator of Habitat Quality and Foraging Ability in the Tiger Salamander, Ambystoma tigrinum
ResearchPlanAbstract: I am interested in whether morphological asymmetry is associated with habitat quality and prey-capture ability in the tiger salamander.  In several other species, it has been found that animals and plants experiencing stress tend to be more asymmetric than those living in relatively stress-free environments.  These studies have suggested that the level of symmetry in an organism may be an indicator of habitat quality and ability to survive and reproduce.  I am measuring four traits (distance from eye to jaw, eye to nares, eye to front leg and front leg to hind leg) on each side of salamander larvae from ponds that vary in terms of water quality.  I am conducting behavioral experiments on these larvae to determine whether more asymmetric animals have difficulty catching prey compared to those that are less asymmetric.  If high levels of asymmetry are associated with poor water quality and poor prey-capture ability, researchers may be able to estimate the degree of stress in an amphibian population by measuring the level of asymmetry in some of the individuals of that population.

ResearchPlanTitle: The relationship between the distribution of worker sizes and colony efficiency in the ant species Formica neorufibarbis
ResearchPlanAbstract: Colonies of many different species of ants have workers of different sizes.  Workers of different sizes may specialize on different tasks, such as taking care of brood, foraging for food, or defending the nest.  We observe the behaviors of workers to determine whether we can detect any such specialization.  Additionally, we build colonies that have different size workers to determine whether there is any particular range of worker sizes that is optimal.

ResearchPlanTitle: (1) Population recovery of a semi-sink population of the Broad-tailed Hummingbird  and (2) Migration biology of the rufous hummingbird.
ResearchPlanAbstract:
High –altitude and high- latitude hummingbirds have very low reproduction potentials, their breeding seasons being too short for more than one clutch, bellies too small/eggs too large for more than 2 eggs/clutch,
Nesting success ~ 45%, mean life expectancy of female only 2 years. Consequently, recovery following a population drop by 2/3, as occurred in 1995, is very slow. We are quantifying this and analysing  the genetic variability to see how much of the recovery of the Gothic population of Selasphorus platycercus is due to immigration from source populations, and how much is contributed by local reproduction.  
The close relative, S. rufous, invades Gothic from late June through early August. Some data indicate that some rufous populations are declining, so it has become one of 4 focus species in the Migratory Pollinator Conservation program at the Arizona Sonora Desert Museum, in which I am a co-PI, heading up the rufous study. It is important to continue our work on wintering birds in the state of Jalisco, Mexico, north-bound migrants in the states of Sonora, breeders in Washington and Alaska, and southbound migrants at RMBL and in New Mexico.

ResearchPlanTitle: Local adaptation in Colias butterflies along an elevational gradient: consequences for reproductive isolation
ResearchPlanAbstract: Elevational gradients create a large range in environmental conditions such as temperature, host plant availability, or season length, over a relatively short distance.  Species occurring over such wide ranging conditions often vary for example in thermoregulatory or in reproductive characters between elevations, i.e. they show local adaptation.  The aim of my research is to study local adaptation along an elevational gradient in Clouded Sulphur butterflies (Colias p. eriphyle). These butterflies occur up to 9300 ft and experience a wide range of environmental conditions. However, migration of individuals between elevations may counteract local adaptation if migrating individuals are able to spread their genes through mating or egg laying on different elevations. Therefore, I also study the mating success of migrants. Since migrating individuals have characters deviating from the resident population, they may be less preferable as mates for the resident population. As a consequence, local adaptation in a species may lead to populations that do meet, but don't mate, and this can be a first step in the process of speciation.
Subject: None

ResearchPlanTitle:
Host-parasite interactions in the mountain white-crowned sparrows 
(Zonotrichia leucophrys oriantha
ResearchPlanAbstract: Parasitic organisms are ubiquitous in wildlife.  Nonetheless very little is known about the ways they affect the survival, reproduction and overall well-being of their hosts.  There is however, increasing evidence suggesting that the outcome of these host-parasite interactions in wildlife hinges on additional, external factors such as environmental stress or food availability for the hosts.  Although this is a crucial problem for conservation biologists (which have to manage wildlife populations facing multiple and often interacting threats) very little research on this problem exists to date.  We tackle this question by experimentally manipulating both food availability (through food supplementations) and parasite load (by administering antimalarial drugs) in mountain white crowned sparrows. We then examine how these manipulations effect bird body condition (fat deposits), reproductive success (e.g. mating success, number of fledglings produced) or host survival. We chose to work with these birds because they are common, easy to catch and observe, they are frequently parasitized by several species of blood parasites and are (especially at the beginning of the season) severely food-limited.  This study addresses therefore a little-known issue that is both of theoretical interest in understanding the interactions of species in nature, and of practical importance for wildlife management.

ResearchPlanTitle: Biodiversity and Ecosystem Function: An Investigation of Resilience and Change  under Manipulated and Naturally-Varying Climate
ResearchPlanAbstract:
Anthropogenic climate warming and loss of biodiversity are two major concerns of our time. At their interface lie three critical questions:  
How will climate warming alter the diversity of life on earth?  
What is the relationship between ambient species diversity and ambient 
	ecosystem processes?  
What is the relationship between ambient species diversity and the magnitude and direction of 	ecosystem responses to climate warming? 
These questions are important  because of our intrinsic and economic concern for the preservation of diverse forms of life on earth,  because biological effects of climate warming have the potential to generate feedbacks to the climate system,  and because of inherent interest in understanding the role of ecological diversity and the relation between diversity and stability.   Our research will provide insight into each of these questions for subalpine meadow ecosystems.    By combining investigations of ecosystem responses to a long-term climate manipulation experiment and to interannual climate variability  with observations of patterns of ecosystem characteristics along natural climate gradients,  responses of ecosystems to climate change are studied at a variety of time scales and under a variety of environmental contingencies.    Biodiversity, as measured by the species richness of plants and arthropods, is studied as both a factor that may contribute to the resilience of ecosystem functions under climate change and as an ecosystem characteristic that may be altered by climate change. Our work will be carried out in subalpine meadow habitat at four sites that have been instrumented for automated microclimate measurement and at which we have a rich data base characterizing vegetation phenology, community structure and above ground biomass, the species abundance and distribution of arthropods, and a variety of biogeochemical measures including soil carbon and nitrogen and nitrogen turnover.

ResearchPlanTitle: Lurking at the roadside: limits on the invasive potential of the exotic scentless chamomile (Matricaria perforata)
ResearchPlanAbstract:
I propose to investigate factors that might determine whether a plant species recently introduced to a locale will proliferate to become invasive. The species in question is scentless chamomile (Matricaria perforata), a native of northern Europe that is making its way southward in North America, from its presumed site of introduction in Canada. In the vicinity of the Rocky Mountain Biological Laboratory (RMBL; Gothic, CO), M. perforata is a recent arrival; at present, it seems closely affiliated with anthropogenic disturbance. Yet, its sudden appearance and proliferation along roadsides may signal an impending threat to native biological diversity of the area’s sub-alpine meadows.
	Research conducted during the past two summers, while in residence at RMBL, demonstrated that M. perforata exhibits features favoring its invasive potential, yet the species has not successfully established itself much beyond its roadside strongholds. While neither poor seed dispersal nor preferential germination seem to be preventing M. perforata from establishing itself in the meadows, seedling mortality due to herbivory may be much more dire in the meadow than at the roadside, where the species is abundant.  The  proposed work attempts to reveal factors that might be limiting M. perforata from invading the sub-alpine meadows adjacent to its current roadside stands.
	To pursue this investigation, the demographic fates of hundreds, to thousands, of individual plants will be monitored. Study sites will be established along an extended elevational gradient that brackets the current local distribution of M. perforata. At each site, young plants, as well as seeds will be introduced into experimental plots, along roadsides and in adjacent meadows. A series of exclosure treatments superimposed on these plots, will allow for the impact of herbivory on plant performance and survival to be discerned.
	This project will not only provide fundamental information regarding ecological factors that influence the nature of biological invasions; it will also generate knowledge about the biology of M. perforata that will inform management decisions by agencies charged with coping with exotics.

ResearchPlanTitle: Population dynamics and genetics of Trollius albiflorus, sister species to the rare T. laxus (Ranunculaceae).
ResearchPlanAbstract: Trollius laxus (Globeflower) is a rare and declining plant of eastern North America.  Habitat destruction is the major cause of its decline, but even within protected areas its populations are frequently unstable.  In an effort to understand the factors that influence population size and stability in this species, I am studying the closely related T. albiflorus near the RMBL.  These are the only two species of Trollius in the New World, and were long thought to be disjunct representatives of the same species.  Since it is neither feasible nor desirable to do experiments with a rare species, using its closest relative as a model is a common and powerful approach.  The initial work involves mapping three populations of each species in different types of habitats and long-term monitoring of the survival, growth and reproduction of a subset of individuals in each population.  Genetic fingerprinting will determine the relatedness and genetic diversity of plants within and between populations, and compare the two species.  Subsequent manipulations with T. albiflorus will investigate the potential for light, water or nutrient limitation of survival and reproduction, impacts of grazing and a dipteran seed predator, and other potential limiting factors suggested by the population monitoring.  Results will guide conservation efforts that I am coordinating for T. laxus in New England.

ResearchPlanTitle: Population dynamics of tephritid seed predators feeding on montane Asteraceae, and their parasitoids.
ResearchPlanAbstract: In the spring, the adult females of several species of tephritid flies lay their eggs on the flower buds of composite plants in the vicinity of RMBL.  Upon hatching, the fly larvae spend their entire larval stage feeding upon the ovaries and developing seeds in that flowerhead, pupate, and then emerge as adults in the summer or fall.  Parasitoid wasps also lay their eggs in the flowers, only their larvae seek out and feed upon the fly larvae.  All of these insect species appear to use more than one plant host species, and the plant species used can vary from site to site; frequently, more than one insect species can be found in the same flowerhead.   In addition, two of these host plants (Erigeron elatior and E. speciosus) have been found to produce mostly female adults in two of the fly species (Neotephritis finalis and Tephritis signatipennis), which seems to have resulted in the near local extinction of one of the fly species.  Two of the questions addressed by this study are:  In what ways do the interactions between these insect species change from site to site, given the observed changes in host plant usage?  What is the cause of the observed female-biased sex ratios, and what are their effects upon fly population dynamics?  By answering these questions, this study seeks to reveal patterns in host plant choices, interactions between insect species, and the resultant population dynamics of the flies—all of which are poorly understood.
ResearchPlanOrganisms: Helianthella quinquenervis; Erigeron elatior, E. speciosus, Aster foliaceus, Heliomeris multiflora,

ResearchPlanTitle: Distribution patterns and interactions among sexes, developmental stages, and species of calanoid copepods at Mexican Cut.
ResearchPlanAbstract: A two-year study is proposed to learn details of distribution patterns, mate choice, and cannibalism using two small aquatic crustacean copepod species.  The studies will elucidate principles of basic population ecology and the evolution of life history traits.  Recent laboratory work has shown that larger females of a copepod are at an advantage, both in terms of number of eggs produced and being the preferred mate by males.  Other laboratory work indicates that cannibalism may be a strong factor promoting synchrony of generations and regulating population density.  However, until we learn about copepod distribution in natural conditions, we cannot generalize from laboratory work to nature.  Our studies will determine the applicability of our recent laboratory studies to natural conditions.
Subject: None

ResearchPlanTitle: The interaction between top-down and bottom-up effects in an ant-plant mutualism
ResearchPlanAbstract: Helianthella quinquenervis (the aspen sunflower) secretes nectar from specialized glands called extrafloral nectaries (EFN’s). Ants collect this nectar, and in return protect the plant from herbivores and seed predators (Inouye and Taylor 1979). This interaction is a specific example of a more general category of mutualism involving ant-protection. In ant-protection mutualisms, ants provide protection in return for one or more resources, including sugary excretions (ant-homopteran mutualism), sugary secretions (ant-lycaenid and EFN mutualisms) and shelter (myrmecophytic mutualisms) (Beattie 1985). Ant-protection mutualisms themselves are an example of a more general category of mutualism involving hosts and visitors. In host-visitor mutualisms, hosts provide visitors with some resource, such as nectar, in return for some service, such as pollination, or in the case of ant-protection mutualisms, protection (Bronstein 1994a).

ResearchPlanTitle: GONE BY THE ROADSIDE:  EFFECTS OF ROADSIDE CHEMCALS ON MATRICARIA PERFORATA
ResearchPlanAbstract: Scentless chamomile (Matricaria perforata) has become well established within the Gunnison Basin since its introduction approximately 20 years ago (Kelrick, pers. comm.).  M. perforata is native to Europe, but seems to be capable of existing in a variety of abiotic conditions including those typical of sub-alpine meadows near Gothic. Observations indicate that M. perforata resides primarily along roadsides, although it has been recorded within established meadows (Regan, 1999).  In a study of competition between M. perforata and a native herb, M. perforata outperformed the native species (Fig. 1; Sheikh, 1998). M. perforata is capable of acting as a summer annual, winter annual, or short-lived perennial (Kay, 1994; Bowes et al., 1995).  M. perforata is a moisture-loving plant that can withstand poorly drained soils (Blackshaw, 1997).  The presence of M. perforata on the North American continent makes it an exotic and potentially invasive species.

ResearchPlanTitle: Nutrient preferences of temperate butterflies among the three families Lycenidae, Pieridae and Nymphalidae
ResearchPlanAbstract:
-This abstract is for the lay public and for potential donors.
Adult butterflies have a nutrient poor diet, and they need to enhance it to increase fecundity and collect nutrients they lack from adult and larval stages of foraging.  Males who forage at mud-puddles and dung predominantly accomplish this compensation.  It has been shown that during these foraging episodes, butterflies seek sodium.  However, it has been postulated by Beck et. al (1998) that they also may be looking for other nutrients, or using them as cues that sodium is present.  It is known that nutrients gained from "mud-puddling" are used to increase fitness of individuals.  Males donate nutrients they collect both during larval and adult stages to females during mating in a package called the spermatophore.   Researchers showed that sodium obtained by
mud-puddling is included in the spermatophore, is subsequently used by females in egg production and is important in reproductive success.  This study investigates whether protein is a preferred resource for temperate butterflies of the three families Lycenidae, Pieridae and Nymphalidae, and whether these families differ in their preferences for nutrient resources.  This study is important environmentally because it will be able to help predict the effects on butterfly populations if there is a demise of large predators reducing the mud-puddling resources.
Subject: None

ResearchPlanTitle: Predicting the Demographic Effects of Global Warming on Thermally Sensitive Organisms from PGI Genotype Frequency Changes of Female Colias meadii at Mesa Seco, CO through a Thermal Cycle
ResearchPlanAbstract: Thermally sensitive organisms, such as Colias meadii, will have specific demographic changes in their populations if global warming continues. The range and size of their populations will shift in response to the new level of thermal stress. The new thermal stress will favor individuals with higher levels of thermal stability. Colias meadii on the Mesa Seco can be used to model the demographic changes that may occur to thermally sensitive organisms because it exists across an extreme gradient that maintains different frequencies of individuals with more or less thermally stable genotypes in the core and in the periphery. The study of the flight activity of each genotype in different thermal conditions will reveal which genotypes will be able to nectar and lay eggs in particular conditions. If the most thermally stable genotype has high relative flight activity time in thermally stressful conditions, the population may decrease because this genotype is also the least fecund. However, the thermally stable trait may be critical to the potential adaptation of the entire population. The study of Colias meadii flight activity time through the daily and summer thermal cycle will allow a model to be created to predict the demographic changes of thermally sensitive organisms. It will also provide support for the maintenance of specific adaptive traits within a population that are critical for the conservation of the species.
Subject: None

ResearchPlanTitle:
Scaling in the spatial and abundance distribution of species

Project Duration: 3-4 years
ResearchPlanAbstract:
Empirical work indicates that the dependence of the average number of species in an area on the size
of that area is often a “power-law” dependence, meaning that the number of species goes as the size of the
area raised to a power, where that power is about 1=4. This power-law indicates a type of scale-invariance
in the dependence of species richness on area, in the sense that no matter what sized area one starts with,
the average number of species in an area twice as big will be 21=4 times the average number in the initial
area. Statistical “scaling” relationships in the spatial and abundance distribution of species such as this
one provide clues to principles general to scale and biological composition. We will examine the role of
plant dispersal distances and the distribution of abiotic characteristics such as soil moisture and nutrient
availability in controlling these types of scaling patterns in plant communities. In particular, we will attempt
to connect scaling properties of abiotic distributions with scaling properties of species distributions.
Subject: None

ResearchPlanTitle: Plan 1: Field studies of marmot behavior
ResearchPlanAbstract: The marmots at Rocky Mt. Biological Lab provide an outstanding opportunity for behavioral studies.  Drawing on almost 40 years of background demographic data, familial relationships are known for many individuals.  My research focuses on a variety of questions about the evolution of social and communicative behavior that capitalize on these data. My previous work at RMBL has demonstrated that yellow-bellied marmots communicate the degree of risk they experience when they alarm call by varying the number of calls produced and the rate at which they call.  Interestingly, previous work also found that marmots produce individually-specific alarm calls.  Current work seeks to understand why marmots produce individually-distinctive calls by addressing two questions.  First, are individually-distinctive calls produced to help better inform relatives about threats?  Second, does the ability to perceive individual differences result from marmots trying to gain additional contextual information about the precise degree of risk?  Work involves tape recording marmots and also playing back alarm calls to them.  Back in the lab, videotapes of the experiments are scored to determine whether and how marmots respond to call variants.  Ultimately, such results will give us a better understanding of how communication evolves in an error-prone environment.  While conducting this work, I will continue to collect demographic data on the marmots of RMBL and thus will contribute to a priceless long-term database on marmot population dynamics.
Subject: None

ResearchPlanTitle: Plan2: Avian antipredator behavior
ResearchPlanAbstract:
Wildlife tourism is a huge and growing industry worldwide.  While there have been a number of single-species studies seeking to understand the effects of human visitation on wildlife, recent theoretical advances in the evolution of behavior have not been applied to develop a predictive theory of human impacts.  By studying a large number of different birds with different life history characteristics (e.g., clutch size, age at first reproduction, etc.) and natural history traits (e.g., diet, habitat, etc.), I aim to develop a theory that will enable us to predict which species will be particularly sensitive to human visitation.

Studies of the effects of people on wildlife are often ill-conceived, poorly controlled, and atheoretical.  Researchers (often consultants working on a short-term contract) typically go to a “disturbed” population, make some observations, and then conclude that human visitation is either benign or not.  Rarely are studies designed to compare species in multiple locations (e.g., along a gradient of impact).  And, rarely are the results designed to be integrated to ask broader evolutionary questions which ultimately will reduce the need for single-species studies.  

My research program aims to use recent advances and knowledge about the evolutionary ecology of how species respond to predation risk to develop a more predictive model of human impacts. I will focus on birds both because there is a considerable amount of data on life history and natural history traits, and because they are often negatively impacted by people.  The project will involve detailed and focused studies of likely factors that influence a few focal species’ responses to predation risk; comparisons of species’ responses along a gradient of human disturbance; and the development of a large data base of disturbance distances that will be used to ultimately predict which types of species are most vulnerable to human disturbance.  When this series of studies is completed, wildlife managers will have less need to hire consultants to conduct single species studies.  Ultimately, the outcome of this project will benefit wildlife as they may lead to scientifically-informed set-back distance guidelines. Simultaneously, it will advance our knowledge on the evolutionary-ecology of antipredator behavior.
Subject: None

ResearchPlanTitle: Multi-scale modeling to support climate-related decision-making
ResearchPlanAbstract:
Policy responses to the threat of climate change will include economic incentives to manage the release and sequestration of carbon dioxide (CO2), methane (CH4), and other greenhouse gases. CO2 and CH4 are both associated with land use practices including agriculture, forestry and ranching; thus the economic impacts of climate policy may significantly affect those sectors. In addition, climate change itself will have impacts both on the economic activities in those sectors and on the effectiveness of measures to control emissions or actively sequester carbon. 

Many of the decisions made in response to these changing opportunities and threats will be made by individual land-owners and managers. However, these decisions will have impacts that cross many levels of scale, affecting neighbors, the surrounding watershed, the nation and the globe. My research combines ecological-economic models at the parcel, watershed and global scales in order to provide a practical framework for integrating individual land-use decisions with regional and global impact assessment. The local and regional level models will be based on Gunnison County data, building on research done at RMBL assessing the potential ecosystem impacts of climate change and on local interest in carbon management as an economic option for preserving the viability of ranching.
ResearchPlanOrganisms: Soil carbon; ranchland vegetation; meadow vegetation; forest vegetation

ResearchPlanTitle: Inter- and Intraspecific Competition For Food Sources in Broad-tailed and Rufous Hummingbirds and Sex Differences in Foraging Behavior
ResearchPlanAbstract: The goal of this study is to answer two questions: 1) Does the quality of a food source change the type and extent of inter- and intraspecific competitive interactions in Broad-tailed and Rufous Hummingbirds?  2) Is there a difference in male and female feeding behavior (time spent per feeding bout) in response to an increase or decrease in the quality of a food source?

ResearchPlanTitle:
- Investigation into life history and population dynamics of Swertia perennis. 
- Investigation into life history and population dynamics of Frasera speciosa. 
- Investigation into life history and population dynamics of Corydalis caseana.
ResearchPlanAbstract:
Swertia perennis (Gentianaceae) is a long-lived sub-alpine perennial found in marshes, wet meadows, fen, and adjacent to mountain streams. S. perennis is potentially identified in Europe as an endangered species an in Washington State is listed as critically endangered. I propose to continue studies of population demographics, pollination biology, and life-history of S. perennis, and will consider study of conservation genetics, and effects of population isolation. 

I also propose to continue research and analysis of demography and fitness of Frasera speciosa (Gentianacea). Potential areas of research include study of speciation between high (4000 meters) and low (2000-3000 meters) altitude populations, mechanisms of synchrony in flowering, and sources of environmental drive to synchronous flowering.
ResearchPlanOrganisms: Swertia perennis, Frasera speciosa, Corydalis caseana.

ResearchPlanTitle:
Recruitment Mechanisms and Dispersal of the Mayfly Baetis bicaudatus
Implications on Population Dynamics
ResearchPlanAbstract: Oviposition is a critical recruitment process in insect population dynamics because it determines the initial density of the populations.  In some populations recruitment may be driven largely by biotic interactions like predation or competition, but in others it could be constrained by natural environmental fluctuations.

ResearchPlanTitle: Parental Care in Nicrophorus investigator
ResearchPlanAbstract: Parental care is pervasive throughout the animal kingdom.  However, in most species, female care alone is most common and biparental and uniparental male care is uncommon.  A rare example of biparental care in insects occurs in Sexton carrion beetles (Silphidae:  Nicrophorus).  Pairs find a mouse carcass, dig a brood chamber that houses the carcass, and then the female lays eggs near the carcass.   After hatching, larvae migrate to the carcass where parents regurgitate food and defend the young from intruders.  Single Nicrophorus females or males can raise a brood in controlled experiments without the assistance of the other.  However, in the field males usually remain with the brood and leave only a few days earlier than the female.  What influences the length of time that a male remains with the brood? This 2-year project will test hypotheses explaining length of paternal care.  Year 1 will comprise pilot studies to address basic assumptions believed to be true (but not tested for N. investigator) and year 2 will test hypotheses supported by the work from year 1 with manipulation experiments

ResearchPlanTitle: Shifting Topoclimatic Positions in Montane, Subalpine, and Alpine Meadows: Influences on Carbon Flux, Vegetation, and Water Balance
ResearchPlanAbstract:
Mountainous regions have dramatic changes in topography characterized by soaring peaks, sharp drops, steep glaciated valleys, and high elevations.  This grand backdrop provides an ideal way to examine how varying landscape positions over a short distance can influence the climatic conditions an area can experience given a specific elevation and orientation.  For example, in the Gunnison Basin as elevation increases, temperature decreases and precipitation can increase as well up to a certain point.  Moving from North to South facing slopes will correspond to an increase in solar radiation.  These general factors strongly influence vegetation patterns over small landscape scales and often can determine what can live where.  

My project seeks to understand how changes in landscape position over an elevational and aspect gradient will affect vegetation distribution and carbon dioxide exchange between the atmosphere, the biosphere (in this case, plants), and the soil.  The Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change (IPCC) has predicted that global mean surface temperatures will increase 3.5? Celsius relative to 1990 levels by 2100 due to anthropogenic causes.  It is likely that high elevation regions will respond to climate change quickly due to the tight set of climatic conditions in which organisms can survive.  Additionally, this study will examine whether these systems are a net source or sink of carbon dioxide, a set of data important for developing policy to curtail global greenhouse gas emissions.
Subject: None

ResearchPlanTitle: Plan 1: Effects of resource availability and community composition on multiple-species interactions with Ipomopsis aggregata
ResearchPlanAbstract: Biological communities are formed from a complex web of interactions among multiple species, embedded within a broader physical context. Although the complexity of direct and indirect interactions within a community has long been recognized, our understanding of how a multitude of organisms ultimately shape the ecology of plant communities and the evolution of floral traits is still in its infancy.  For example, pollination biologists have traditionally viewed plant reproduction and plant traits solely as a function of a plant’s attractiveness to its pollinators.  Yet, plants interact with many organisms besides pollinators, and plant success is likely governed by simultaneous interactions with multiple biotic agents, such as herbivores, nectar robbers, or seed predators, as well as environmental factors.  It is relatively unknown how multiple antagonists and mutualists interact to ultimately shape the ecology of plants and the evolution of floral traits in natural communities.  The aim of this work is to understand the simultaneous importance of direct and indirect interactions among several antagonists with their host plant, and how resource availability and community composition affect the outcome of such interactions.  Experiments will examine the combined effects of a nectar-robbing bumblebee, a pre-dispersal seed predator, an ungulate herbivore, hummingbird pollinators, and plant community composition on the reproductive success of a subalpine host plant, scarlet gilia.  This work is novel in integrating the effects of multiple antagonists on the outcome of plant-pollinator mutualisms under different environmental conditions.  Understanding the complexity of plant-pollinator-antagonist interactions will provide a deeper knowledge of how species are ecologically and evolutionarily linked in biological communities.
ResearchPlanOrganisms: Ipomopsis aggregata, Linaria vulgaris, Bombus occidentalis, Selasphorus platycercus, Selasphorus ruf
Subject: None

ResearchPlanTitle: Plan 2: Plant invasions – population dynamics and the role of mutualisms
ResearchPlanAbstract: Biological invasions are a leading environmental threat in the present century and are a primary cause of loss of biodiversity world-wide. Recent estimates suggest that North America alone harbors over 50,000 non-native species. No ecosystem is immune to the threat of invasive plants and animals. Two central goals in the study of invasive exotic plants is to understand what controls their spread and how their spread effects other members of the community. Although there is a growing body of literature documenting the spread of exotic plants and their interactions with native plants, herbivores, and pathogens, relatively little work has examined how mutualists affect the course of invasion. For invasive plants in particular, pollination is one form of mutualism that has the potential to strongly affect plant population growth and spread. The aim of this work is to understand the importance of pollination to the population dynamics of an invasive weed in Colorado, and how invasive weeds interact directly and indirectly with native plant species through competition for shared pollinators. Using the invasive, exotic plant Butter-and-Eggs, Linaria vulgaris (Scrophulariaceae), I will address three overarching hypotheses:  (1) L. vulgaris population growth varies spatially and temporally in different habitats corresponding to different pollinator fauna; (2) Pollinator limitation influences L. vulgaris population dynamics, and native plant species suffer from reduced pollination in the presence of L. vulgaris; and (3) Specific life-cycle stages and reduced pollination will lower the viability of L. vulgaris populations. This work is novel in integrating population dynamics with pollination biology to understand the growth and spread of an invasive, noxious weed. Understanding the complexity of species invasions across habitat types and in conjunction with obligate mutualists will provide a deeper knowledge of the factors controlling the spread of invasive species in biological communities.
Subject: None

ResearchPlanTitle:
Resource allocation across life stages in limnephilid caddisflies
(Trichoptera: Limnephilidae
ResearchPlanAbstract: Organisms are constantly faced with decisions.  One decision that organisms must make is how to divide up energetic resources during growth.  For example, organisms are often faced with the question: how should nutrients and energy be divided among different growing parts within an individual?  By examining trade-offs among growing parts within individuals, we can begin to understand how evolution shaped particular life history strategies.  I exploit this trade-off to ask the question: Do the different stages in a complex life cycle evolve independently or are they linked?  Many organisms, such as insects, marine invertebrates, and amphibians have complex life cycles where development occurs over time through a series of stages (e.g. egg => larva => pupa => adult).  Current theory suggests that these stages evolve independently and selective pressures acting on one stage have very little impact on other stages.  For example, in many insects that undergo complete metamorphosis, the larvae are specialized for feeding and growth whereas the adults are specialized for reproduction and do not feed or grow such that the functions of the two stages are separate.  However, the energy needed for reproduction in the adult stage must first be gained by the larval feeding stage.  Therefore, the stages may not be truly independent of each other.  I use caddisflies (aquatic insects with complex life cycles) to ask questions like: Is adult morphology and behavior impacted by nutritional limitation in the larval stage? Do different adult characters vary in predictable ways in response to such limitation?  Do the sexes differ in how different characters respond to nutritional limitation?  Does nutritional limitation in the larva  influence adult mating behavior, in particular female mate choice?  My general approach to these questions is to combine observation, field experiments, and comparisons among several closely related species.

ResearchPlanTitle: Comparative population dynamics and genetics of Trollius albiflorus and the endangered T. laxus (Ranunculaceae).
ResearchPlanAbstract: Trollius laxus (Globeflower) is a rare and declining plant of eastern North America.  Habitat destruction is the major cause of its decline, but even within protected areas its populations are frequently unstable.  In an effort to understand the factors that influence population size and stability in this species, I am studying the closely related T. albiflorus near the RMBL.  These are the only two species of Trollius in the New World, and were long thought to be disjunct representatives of the same species.  Since it is neither feasible nor desirable to do experiments with a rare species, using its closest relative as a model is a common and powerful approach.  The initial work involves long-term monitoring of the survival, growth and reproduction of a subset of individuals in three populations of each species in different types of habitats.  We have mapped plants in five monitoring plots in three disjunct populations around the RMBL.  Genetic fingerprinting will determine the relatedness and genetic diversity of plants within and between populations, and compare the two species.  Results will guide conservation efforts that I am coordinating for T. laxus in New England.

ResearchPlanTitle: Impacts of Global Warming and Snow Depth on Stress Tolerance, Photosynthesis, and Flowering
ResearchPlanAbstract: Global climate change will result in warmer atmospheric temperatures and changes in precipitation patterns.  This will alter the rate and timing of key processes -- such as photosynthesis and flowering -- that help to determine the characteristics of an ecosystem.  Temperature and precipitation also determine the geographic boundaries for species.  As temperature and precipitation change in the future due to human activities, species may be compelled to shift their distributions.  The responses of plants to freezing temperatures is a fundamental determinant of such boundaries; as climate changes a reduction in freezing limitations may lead to expanded range boundaries.  The goal of my research is to determine how global warming and changes in snow depth will impact photosynthesis and flowering for plants at the Great Basin Desert to subalpine transition zone represented by the meadows at RMBL.  I will measure survival of episodic freezing events, and the subsequent levels of photosynthesis and flower and fruit production.  I will impose episodic freezing (rather than waiting for natural freezing events) using an In Situ Cold Experiment (ICE) apparatus.  This method allows for measurements of plant responses to controlled freezing events in natural field settings.  The responses of photosynthesis and flowering to freezing will be measured for plants under the meadow warming experiment started by Dr. John Harte in 1991.  I will also conduct these measurements for plants on plots on which snow has been removed or added to simulate changes in winter precipitation regimes.

ResearchPlanTitle: Consequences of gene flow between sexual and asexual Arabis species for resistance and tolerance to parasites
ResearchPlanAbstract:
Natural hybrids between sexual and asexual-by-seed (apomictic) plants in the genus Arabis give us an opportunity to examine two basic evolutionary problems and one applied problem: 

 (1) The commonness of sexual reproduction is not easily understood given that asexually reproducing organisms can reproduce faster and thus ought to take over.  Evolutionary biologists have reasoned that there must be an advantage to sexual reproduction or it would not still exist.  However, the small amount of evidence we have from plants in which there are both sexual and apomictic lineages suggests that the apomicts have an even greater advantage than predicted. One hypothesis that may give sexuals an advantage is that sex generates both genetic variation and rare genotypes, which might be advantageous when pests are present.  This hypothesis has been very incompletely tested in plants.

 (2) Seed companies would like to develop crops that reproduce through apomixis because crops produced this way would fix desirable traits (because recombination no longer occurs) and be uniform because the seeds are genetically identical.  One concern, however is that the genetically modified apomicts could escape through hybridization with wild relatives and thereby cause a drastic reduction in biodiversity.  The expectation of seed companies is that hybrids between the engineered apomictic crops and sexual weedy relatives would not last long because most hybrids do not persist, and further that there must be an advantage to sex thus the asexuals will not spread.  As noted above however, this may not be true.  The Arabis system gives us an opportunity to see what happens in nature when sexuals and apomicts meet and cross.

(3) There is evidence that hybridization has been important in the evolution of plants in general  as well as in the genus Arabis.  Our experiments will allow us to determine how hybridization alters resistance expression and how important pest pressure is in limiting the distribution  of the parental taxa and their hybrids.
ResearchPlanOrganisms: 1. Hosts: Arabis holboellii, A. drummondii, A. x divaricarpa
