ResearchPlanTitle: Understanding ecosystem responses to changing plant diversity and global climate warming
ResearchPlanAbstract:
Human impacts on ecosystems across the globe have resulted in dramatic losses of global biodiversity via activities such as habitat destruction, nitrogen deposition, and intentional or accidental exotic invasions. Future changes due to anthropogenic climate warming are expected to exacerbate the rate of declining diversity. Current and projected losses in biodiversity are of concern because of our intrinsic and economic valuation of diverse forms of life, and because of the belief that ecosystem function and stability are inherently tied to diversity. This belief is controversial and has fostered a long-standing debate among ecologists because we do not have a definitive understanding of relationships between diversity and ecosystem processes, nor of the role that various ecosystem parameters have in determining levels of diversity. With my research, I hope to make targeted contributions to three critical questions that lie along the interface of concerns about ecosystem-level effects of climate change and the loss of biodiversity:  

?	How will climate warming alter biodiversity?
?	What is the relationship between species diversity and ecosystem processes?
?	What is the relationship between species diversity and the magnitude and direction of ecosystem responses to climate warming?

Scientists have extensively examined how diversity changes over large-scale climate gradients (i.e., from the equator to the north and south poles). However, less is known about the ecosystem-level consequences of changes in climate, diversity, and ecosystem function and stability.  My research will contribute an understanding of how these issues affect one particular ecosystem type – montane meadow habitat.  My findings could be of value to both ecologists and land managers who are interested in or concerned about the ecological role of diversity and its conservation both now and in the future.
Subject: None

ResearchPlanTitle: LINKING SPECIES BEHAVIOR AND ECOSYSTEM PROCESSES: CASCADING EFFECTS OF NON-NATIVE TROUT ON INVERTEBRATES AND ORGANIC MATTER DYNAMICS IN HEADWATER STREAMS
ResearchPlanAbstract:
My research focuses how organisms affect the transport of materials (e.g. organic matter or sediments, nutrients, or contaminants) in ecosystems.  Using streams as a model system, I am examining how the behavior of organisms is linked to important ecosystem processes, with the working hypothesis that predatory brook trout change the activity levels and consumption of detritus of stream insects, which then affects the quality and quantity of organic matter exported from headwater streams.  Studying the factors that affect the transport of fine organic particles (e.g., sediments) is important because they contain carbon, the element of organic compounds and a major source of energy. In addition, a fundamental feature of stream ecosystems is the transport of materials downstream to rivers, lakes or oceans.  Movement of fine sediments in streams may be influenced greatly by stream organisms that disturb them directly or indirectly through their behavioral activities.  
In RMBL streams I am focusing on how invertebrate activity (i.e., biological processing and disturbance of sediments) affects the transport of energy and how predators modify the behavior of insects, which may indirectly affect organic matter and nutrient transport.  Specifically, I will ask the following questions:  1) does the physical behavior of insects affect nutrient and organic matter transport (i.e., do stream insects act as tiny biological bulldozers, similar to earthworms)?  2) do behavioral effects have measurable effects at the ecosystem-level? (i.e., net effects on export or retention of energy).  3) what is the relative strength of consumptive (e.g., eating organic matter) and non-consumptive (e.g., bioturbation) effects on ecosystem processes in stream food webs?  4) Lastly, do predator chemical cues from trout induced changes in behavior of insects cascade to affect the flux of organic matter  This research is unique because it involves non trophic mechanisms (e.g., bioturbation and anti-predator behavior) and it focuses on changes in ecosystem processes (e.g. fluxes of sediments rather than standing stock).
	This research will determine whether we need to incorporate non-trophic linkages (e.g. behavior and bioturbation) into food webs, and how import they are compared to trophic links.  Moreover, this research blends disparate fields, population and ecosystem ecology, which will lead to a better understanding of complex natural systems.  From an applied perspective, this work will contribute to our knowledge of fisheries management, especially in terms of the ecosystem-level impacts of stocking non-native or even native fish into fishless areas.  With regards to biodiversity and ecosystem function, species that function, as bioturbators may be less common so that when lost or removed their role is not easily replaced—drastically altering ecosystem processes.
ResearchPlanOrganisms: STREAM INVERTEBRATES, MAYFLIES, STONEFLIES, CADDISFLIES, AND TRUE FLIES (DIPTERA)

ResearchPlanTitle: EFFECTS OF TROUT STOCKING ON SUBALPINE LAKES IN CENTRAL COLORADO
ResearchPlanAbstract: Native and/or non-native trout species have been introduced into over 800 previously fishless high-elevation lakes in the state of Colorado.  Surprisingly, there have been no studies to document the impacts of these fish on the native fauna in these lakes. We will compare the invertebrate faunas of fish and fishless lakes in the vicinity of the RMBL.  The patterns of distribution and abundance of these invertebrates with respect to the presence of fish will be used for future grant writing and for the design of experiments to determine cause and effect relationships that underlie the observed patterns.

ResearchPlanTitle: Genetic and physiological studies of differential fitness in an Ipomopsis hybrid zone
ResearchPlanAbstract: Natural hybridization occurs when genetically distinct populations mate successfully to produce at least some viable and fertile offspring.  Biologist have proposed numerous models to predict the evolutionary outcome of natural hybridization, which differ in their assumptions of relative hybrid fitness.  The traditional view holds that hybrids are universally unfit relative to parental taxa, and thus hybridization leads to an evolutionary dead end.  An alternate view states that certain hybrid genotypes may be very fit, perhaps even more fit than one or both of the parents. To distinguish between these two main types of models, it is necessary to test the underlying assumptions of hybrid fitness.  This study will test these assumptions of hybrid fitness in a natural hybrid zone between two related herbaceous plants, Ipomopsis aggregata and I. tenuituba.  Previous studies at this site suggest that first generation hybrids can have different fitness values, depending on the direction of the cross.  These results suggest that interactions between the cytoplasmic and nuclear genomes of the parental species may affect hybrid fitness; additional interactions between genomes following recombination and segregation in later generation hybrids may also cause hybrids with different genotypes to exhibit different fitnesses.  I will further examine this variation in hybrid fitness, using experimentally-produced advanced generation hybrids and natural hybrids.  Specifically, this work addresses three main questions:  (1)  Are differences in survival observed among advanced-generation hybrids?  What are the patterns relative to the genetic constitution of the hybrids?  (2)  Can differences in physiological response explain observed fitness differences?  (3)  Are differences in survival of different hybrid genotypes found in the experimental arrays reflected in the natural hybrid zone?  My work will contribute to the scant number of studies that directly examine the possibility of differential hybrid fitness and its influence on the role of natural hybridization in adaptive evolution.

ResearchPlanTitle: Adaptive significance of facultative paedomorphosis in salamanders
ResearchPlanAbstract:
The aim of the study is to determine the adaptive character of facultative paedomorphosis
(retention of larval traits in the adult) in ambystomatid salamanders. To respond to this
question, I will analyze both sexual dimorphism and resource use in alternative morphs
(paedomorph retain gills at the adult stage and metamorphs are fully metamorphosed) in
varied environments around Rocky Mountain Biological Laboratory. These results will be
integrated into the framework of current ecological and evolutionary theories which predict
polymorphisms in heterogeneous and favorable environments.

ResearchPlanTitle: Comparative population dynamics and genetics of Trollius albiflorus and the endangered T. laxus (Ranunculaceae).
ResearchPlanAbstract: Trollius laxus (Globeflower) is a rare and declining plant of eastern North America.  Habitat destruction is the major cause of its decline, but even within protected areas its populations are frequently unstable.  In an effort to understand the factors that influence population size and stability in this species, I am studying the closely related T. albiflorus near the RMBL.  These are the only two species of Trollius in the New World, and were long thought to be disjunct representatives of the same species.  Since it is neither feasible nor desirable to do experiments with a rare species, using its closest relative as a model is a common and powerful approach.  The initial work involves long-term monitoring of the survival, growth and reproduction of a subset of individuals in three populations of each species in different types of habitats.  We have mapped plants in five monitoring plots in three disjunct populations around the RMBL for long-term monitoring of population size, age structure and reproductive effort.  Experiments examine the influence of herbivores, pollinators, light levels, and timing of emergence and bloom on survival, growth and reproductive success.  Results will guide conservation efforts that I am coordinating for T. laxus in New England.

ResearchPlanTitle: Investigations of a mutualism involving ants and the treehopper Publilia modesta.
ResearchPlanAbstract: Individuals of the treehopper species Publilia modesta feed on the juices of a number of different host plants.  These insects provide food to ants in the form of sugary execretions.  The presence of ants increases the survivorship of the insects.  This study will attempt to determine whether ants benefit the insects by protecting them from predators, or whether the ants increase survivorship by cleaning the membracids.  Additionally, this study will look at why some ant species provide more benefit to the treehoppers, and will also quantify how the positive effects of the ants vary through time and space.
ResearchPlanOrganisms: Publilia modesta, Formica obscuripes, Formica fusca

ResearchPlanTitle: Pollen transfer and the evolution of hummingbird pollination in Penstemon
ResearchPlanAbstract: The preferences and behavior of different animal pollinators can explain a good part of the great diversity of flowers we see in nature. We know that pollinators can impose selective pressures on flowers, enhancing pollinator attractiveness and the efficiency with which they transfer pollen from one plant to another. Within some plant groups, some lineages have shifted form one type of pollinator (e.g. insects) to another (e.g. hummingbirds) during their evolutionary history. This has happened repeatedly in the pant genus Penstemon, which then provides a good system for studying the role that pollinators play in the evolution of floral characteristics. My dissertation project investigates the differences in pollinator efficiency between hummingbirds and bees, and the implication of those differences in the way that bee-adapted and hummingbird-adapted Penstemon flowers present and receive pollen. I combine field and greenhouse experiments, as well as the use of natural variation in flowers with manipulations of floral characters. Studying the details of these interactions can give us insight on how different flowers evolve.

ResearchPlanTitle: Nontarget impacts of biocontrol releases of Larinus planus on Colorado thistle species
ResearchPlanAbstract: A primary risk associated with introduction of non-native species as biocontrol agents is herbivory of nontarget species. The implications for demographics of small populations and even risk of local extinction may be especially pronounce by introduction of exotic herbivorous insects. Studies of the effects of introduced species on native populations will help ecologists and environmental managers understand the risk probabilities of biocontrol applications as well as theory of small population dynamics and regulation, species invasions, and trophic level interactions. Larinus planus is a Eurasian seed head weevil that has been released extensively throughout the Rocky Mountain region as a biological control measure against Canada thistle (Cirsium arvense) (Asteraceae), an invasive, exotic perennial weed species. Previous research has shown that L. planus colonized and reduced seed production of Tracy’s thistle (Cirsium undulatum var tracyi) (Asteraceae), a large-flowered perennial, monocarpic thistle native to Western Colorado and Eastern Utah. The release of L. planus in Colorado is also cause for concern because of potential for adverse impacts on other native Cirsium thistles, including two listed as threatened in Colorado. The purpose of the current study is to assess population dynamics of Tracy’s thistle and to determine any effect L. planus may have on Tracy’s thistle abundance and distribution.
ResearchPlanOrganisms: Larinus planus, Tracy’s thistle, Elk thistle, and Rocky Mountain thistle, Canada thistle

ResearchPlanTitle: Impacts of an introduced florivore, Brachypterolus pulicarius (Coleoptera: Nitidulidae), on native and introduced plants
ResearchPlanAbstract: A conspicuous aspect of the landscape around the East River Valley is the occurrence of non-native plants.  Maybe less conspicuous, but just as important, are the non-native insects consuming these plants.  Brachypterolus pulicarius (Coleoptera: Nitidulidae) was accidentally introduced into North America in the early 1900s, likely as a contaminant of ornamental toadflax (Linaria spp.).  B. pulicarius feeds on the growing apex of toadflax shoots and in toadflax flowers on pollen, anthers, and ovaries.  The host-range of B. pulicarius in North America is unknown.  Moreover, the effects of B. pulicarius on the growth and reproduction of toadflax are disputed.  The goal of this project is to understand the host-range of B. pulicarius in the East River Valley and to determine the impact of B. pulicarius on the growth of L. vulgaris.
ResearchPlanOrganisms: Brachypterolus pulicarius, Linaria vulgaris, native plants in the Scrophulariaceae

ResearchPlanTitle:
Population Dynamics of the Bushy-tailed Woodrat

The Effect of Cattle Grazing on Plant Communities and Carbon Sequestration
ResearchPlanAbstract:
Woodrats.  For animals that are small and nocturnal, like bushy-tailed woodrats, data on the mating system and dispersal patterns are impossible to collect with direct observation.  At several sites in Gunnison County I have monitored resident and immigrant populations of woodrats since 1985.  Thus, I have a wealth of data on longevity, reproduction, mortality and relatedness within populations.  Modern DNA fingerprinting techniques in conjunction with the field data, allow determination of paternity, relatedness, and patterns of immigration and emigration by looking directly at DNA sequences of individuals.  


Cattle Grazing.  In several habitats I have measured plant productivity, diversity and invasive species on grazed and ungrazed land.  These data have been collected several times each summer since 1992.  Two noteworthy results from this continuing long-term monitoring are that in one habitat, there were no significant differences between grazed and ungrazed plant communities, and in a different habitat, elimination of grazing reduced plant productivity.  One way to begin to explain these results is to look at carbon and nitrogen cycling in habitats  that experience different grazing treatments.

On another level, data on C_N cycling bear on the question of how much C is sequestered in high altitude grazed habitats, and whether different grazing mamagement practices significantly affect C storage.  If rangeland systems can contribute to both the environmental and economic well-being of ranchers while also sequestering carbon, appropriate management can be encourage or rewarded for the additional good of mitigating the greenhouse effect.

ResearchPlanTitle: Population biology of Euphydryas gillettii
ResearchPlanAbstract: The butterfly Euphydryas gillettii was introduced from Wyoming to a site on the west side of the East River in Gothic in 1977 with the knowledge of the RMBL Director and Board of Trustees, as part of a study to determine whether the butterfly did not inhabit the southern Rockies because it cannot survive here, or because it is too sedentary to have crossed the Red Desert and invaded the southern Rockies.  Since that time, the population has remained extremely small, with fewer than 100 adults in any given year.  However, in 2002, the population numbers have expanded to 500-1000 individuals within the original release area alone, and the geographic range has also increased substantially.  Given this occurrence, we will document the delayed expansion of the butterfly population, and explore the mechanisms that contributed to that phenomenon, including making and testing predictions concerning future changes.  Our work has implications for management of transplantations and re-introductions of populations, predicting population response to global change, and basic understanding of population dynamic processes.

ResearchPlanTitle: Resource allocation decisions: does larval silk production influence adult morphology and behavior in caddisflies (Trichoptera)?
ResearchPlanAbstract: Organisms are constantly faced with decisions.  One decision that organisms must make is how to divide up energetic resources during growth.  For example, organisms are often faced with the question: how should nutrients and energy be divided among different growing morphological traits within an individual? Trade-offs between traits within an individual are a central component of life-history theory.  Trade-offs are links between traits that constrain the direction and degree of evolution of the traits.  For example, resources available to an individual are finite and use of resources for one trait will be at the expense of another competing trait.  By examining trade-offs among growing parts within individuals, we can begin to understand how evolution shaped particular morphologies and behaviors. For example, in many insects that undergo complete metamorphosis, the larvae are specialized for feeding and growth whereas the adults are specialized for reproduction and do not feed or grow.  Therefore, the energy needed for reproduction in the adult stage must first be gained by the larval feeding stage. I use caddisflies as a model organism to ask questions such as: Is adult morphology and behavior influenced by nutritional limitation or enhancement in the larval stage? Do different adult characters vary in predictable ways in response to such limitation or enhancement?  Do the sexes differ in how different characters respond to nutritional limitation or enhancement?  Does nutritional limitation or enhancement in the larval stages influence adult mating behavior, (female mate choice or male-male competition)?  My general approach to these questions is to combine observational data with manipulative field experiments to gain insight into morphology and behavior of caddisflies.

ResearchPlanTitle: Manuel A. Morales and David W. Inouye
ResearchPlanAbstract:
The aspen sunflower (Helianthella quinquenervis) secretes nectar from special glands called extrafloral nectaries. Although extrafloral nectar is not attractive to pollinators, it is attractive to ants. Ants collect this resource and in return protect the plant from herbivores and seed predators. Because both species benefit, this interaction is called a mutualism.

	Generally speaking, this type of mutualism is extremely common, and up to 1/3 of all plant species in tropical forests possess extrafloral nectaries. Interestingly, ants have been shown to respond to the quality of artificial nectars, but fewer studies have examined the response of ants to variation in host-plant quality. To address this, we propose to study the effects of fertilization on nectar composition, patterns of ant defense and seed production in aspen sunflowers. Results from this study will provide insight into the effects of host-plant quality on the dynamics of mutualism in general (e.g. pollination, seed dispersal). Because mutualism enables the persistence of species in marginal habitats, understanding its dynamics is of great importance to conservation efforts.
ResearchPlanOrganisms: Helianthella quinquinervis plants and Formica sp. ants

ResearchPlanTitle: Effectiveness of methods to control the spread of the invasive weeds, Cirsium arvense (Canada thistle) and Bromus inermis (Smooth Brome)
ResearchPlanAbstract: Nonnative invasive species are a growing problem in Colorado.  Invasive plants disrupt native communities by forming monocultures, in which native plant diversity is decreased.  Changes in plant composition may affect other members of the community, including soil microbes and mycorrhizae, herbivores, pollinators, and even higher trophic levels.  The goal of this research is to determine the best methods of controlling the spread of two nonnative plants, Cirsium arvense (Canada thistle) and Bromus inermis (Smooth Brome), in the East River Valley.  Specifically, I test whether repeated manual removal of Canada thistle is effective at eradicating small populations.  I also test whether sheets of black plastic can be used to kill smooth brome populations.  In order to help restore native plant communities, I plan to reseed sites with native plant seed.  If these efforts prove successful at eradicating invasive plants and reestablishing native plant communities, I will work with other members of the community to apply these methods to other sites throughout the Gunnison Basin.
ResearchPlanOrganisms: Cirsium arvense (Canada thistle) and Bromus inermis (Smooth Brome)

ResearchPlanTitle: Effects of recruitment and post-recruitment processes on abundance of stream insects
ResearchPlanAbstract: This study will help us understand how multiple factors affect the abundance of plants and animals in nature.  The goal of this proposal is to explain patterns of abundance of stream insect populations by conducting observations and experiments under realistic field conditions.  Experiments in natural streams will test whether the abundance of larvae of the most common mayfly species is determined by the number of eggs laid by adults or the amount of food or predators in the larval habitat. This mayfly has a unique egg-laying behavior, is highly vulnerable to trout predation and responds behaviorally to the risk predation and low levels of food (algae) by drifting away from unfavorable habitats mostly during darkness when trout can’t see them.  First, we will predict how recruitment (egg-laying), presence of predators, and amount of food should affect the relative abundance of each mayfly species.  Second, we will measure egg-laying, larval dispersal behavior (drift) and mayfly abundance in natural fish and fishless streams with different levels of food (algae).   Third, in large-scale field experiments we will add or remove rocks and logs used by one of the mayfly species for egg-laying to test directly whether abundance of larvae is a function of recruitment.  Fourth, we will drip water from containers with trout into fishless streams to determine whether drift of mayflies in response to trout chemical cues can explain patterns of abundance in fish and fishless streams.  Finally, we will manipulate multiple factors (recruitment, food and predators)  in stream-side, flow-through chambers to determine which of these factors is most important in explaining natural patterns of larval abundance.  This research can be useful for developing management strategies to preserve natural populations of organisms in these relatively pristine high-elevation streams.

ResearchPlanInstitution: The Open University, Milton Keynes, U.K.
ResearchPlanTitle:
1. The role of nectar chemistry in pollinator foraging and maintenance of a plant hybrid zone.
2. The effects of soil fertility on plant fitness in an ant-tended species.
3. The effects of nectar robbing on nectar chemistry.
ResearchPlanAbstract: It is essential for many plants that their pollen is delivered to another of the same species if fertile offspring are to be produced. Nectar is an important biological resource that is utilized as a food by a wide variety of animals, especially insects and hummingbirds, which carry out the vital role of pollination. Although sugars form the largest component of nectar, amino acids form a substantial fraction. Amino acids are the building blocks of proteins that may be used in growth or as enzymes that regulate many of the biochemical reactions in the body. Although evidence suggests that this resource could have an important role in the nutrition of flower-visiting animals little research has focused on nectar amino acids. Many plants show adaptations that limit the floral visitors and so make the pollination process more efficient, leading to a greater probability of successful mating. Hybrid zones occur when two species cross-pollinate. Usually these hybrids are sterile but occasionally fertile offspring arise. Hybrid zones offer an opportunity to study speciation in plants and pollinators as hybrids (sterile or otherwize) often show characteristics that are intermediate between those of their parents. In this study I will collect nectar samples from two species of gilia, the scarlet Ipomopsis aggregata that is hummingbird visited and the white Ipomopsis tenuituba, which is hawkmoth pollinated. Samples will also be taken from their hybrids. The samples will be analyzed for sugar and amino acid composition. The data collected will be used to plan further experiments in the further where the nectar of plants is swapped for one of an alternative composition. The reaction of the visiting pollinators will help in our understanding of the role of nectar chemistry in speciation and pollination.
ResearchPlanOrganisms: Ipomopsis aggregata, I. tenuituba and hybrids. Helianthella quinquenervis.

ResearchPlanTitle: Rocky Mountain wildflowers – demography, phenology, pollination, seed predation, and ant-plant mutualisms, in the context of climate change.
ResearchPlanAbstract:
The primary goal of my research is to document and explain long-term patterns in the population and pollination biology of Rocky Mountain wildflowers and the animals that use them for food.  I am following plants that I tagged as far back as 1973, and plots that were also established that year.  I am documenting the great amount of variation in timing and abundance of flowering, trying to determine the proximate and ultimate factors that generate this variation, and to elucidate the consequences of this variation for the plants, their pollinators, and herbivores. A major focus for the past few years and the next few will be the consequences of late spring frosts on wildflowers, and the subsequent effects on populations of seed predators and parasitoids that lay eggs in the flowers that are sensitive to frosts.  I am particularly interested in the effects that global climate change is having on the systems I am studying. 

	I am studying the demography of Frasera speciosa and Hymenoxys grandiflorum, phenology of about 65 species, and flowering and biology of Veratrum californicum.  Also the pre-dispersal seed predators of several species of Asteraceae.
ResearchPlanOrganisms: Frasera speciosa, Helianthella quinquenervis, Hymenoxys grandiflorum, Veratrum tenuipetalum, Erythro

ResearchPlanTitle: The impacts of experimental warming and moisture availability on plant moisture stress, photosynthesis, and reproduction
ResearchPlanAbstract: As rising global surface temperatures alter the timing of snowmelt and the length of the growing season in montane and alpine environments, plant distributions are expected to shift.  Therefore, there have been several studies examining the responses of leaf-level and whole-plant physiology and ecosystem processes to warmer temperatures.  An additional area that has strong consequences for both species persistence and dispersal to new ranges under warmer temperatures is that of plant reproduction.  The objectives of my research are to examine how an experimental warming treatment affects reproduction in several subalpine plant species and to identify the mechanisms that underlie these observed responses.  In particular, I will focus on the relative importance of freezing temperatures and water stress on flower and fruit production for plant species that flower soon after snowmelt, when freezing temperatures may be an important factor affecting flower production, and for those species that flower in the summer, when soil moisture availability becomes critical.
ResearchPlanOrganisms: Selected study species are common within the plots and the surrounding area at RMBL.  They may be grouped into development cohorts based on when they initiate flowering.  Species representing the early spring cohort include Claytonia lanceolata (spring beauty, Portulacaceae), Erythronium grandiflorum (avalanche lily, Liliaceae), and Mertensia brevistyla (bluebell, Boraginaceae).  Species representing a mid-season cohort include Delphinium nuttallianum (Nelson’s larkspur, Ranunculaceae), Lathyrus leucanthus (peavine, Fabaceae), and Potentilla pulcherrima (cinquefoil, Rosaceae).  The late season cohort includes Helianthella quinquenervis (sunflower, Asteraceae), Erigeron speciosus (daisy, Asteraceae) and Artemesia tridentata (sagebrush, Asteraceae).  These species have exhibited a variety of responses of flowering to the warming treatment, including increased, decreased, and no change in flower production.

ResearchPlanTitle: Behavioral and Community Ecology of Ant Assemblages Along Climatic Gradients
ResearchPlanAbstract: There is little doubt that multiple processes interact to determine which species are present, their relative abundances, and the interactions among them in different communities.  Some factors operate at a local scale (e.g., behavioral interactions with other species), and others operate at regional scales (e.g., habitat heterogeneity).  Ant assemblages are model systems with which to test the relative importance of local- and regional-scale influences on community structure.  At regional scales, habitat heterogeneity and climatic variation determine the pool of potential species in a community.  But at the local scale, individual behavior and interspecific resource competition act as a filters to determine which species occur at one location.  Few studies, in any group, have explored the links among local- and regional-scale influences while considering the behavioral mechanisms of interactions among species.  The aim of this study is to examine the relationships among individual behavior, community structure and diversity, and habitat heterogeneity along several climatic gradients.
Subject: None

ResearchPlanTitle: Ecology and Behavior of the Burying Beetle (Nicrophorus).
ResearchPlanAbstract: How do reproductive behaviors link to ecological patterns of distribution and abundance?  A beetle with a unique reproductive strategy may provide answers.  Burying beetles locate and bury small, dead rodents, which they use as a food resource for raising their young.  A male/female pair bury and prepare the carcass and remain with their young until the carcass is consumed.  A carcass represents a fixed resource, thus parents are faced with making decisions on whether to maximize offspring size or number.  How do they solve this dilemma?  Do ecological factors, such as competition or overwintering conditions influence their choices?  Can parental decisions have larger-scale impacts on beetle population dynamics and selection on adult body size?  What strategies besides locating and defending resources might each sex employ to increase their reproductive success?  How do the cooler temperatures and shorter seasons at high elevations influence reproductive behaviors, body size, and insect locomotion?  What are the links among small mammal population fluctuations and beetle population dynamics?  In a series of field and laboratory experiments I am collecting evidence to answer these and other questions.
ResearchPlanOrganisms:
Nicrophorus investigator and N. defodiens (burying beetles, Coleoptera: Silphidae)
Small mammals:  Microtus montanus, Peromyscus maniculatus, Zapus princeps, Tamias minimus, Thomomys talpoides

ResearchPlanTitle: While it is apparent that the environment varies and can affect populations of organisms (plants are killed in frosts, animals die of overheating), the relationship between variation in the environment and patterns of evolution is not understood.
ResearchPlanAbstract:
While it is apparent that the environment varies and can affect populations of organisms (plants are killed in frosts, animals die of overheating), the relationship between variation in the environment and patterns of evolution is not understood. 
	The environment varies in space and time and at different scales. For example, if you are in Nevada in the summer it is warmer than Washington State in the summer; if you are in Colorado in a winter snowstorm it is colder than a sunny day in summer. The environment also varies in different amounts over scales of space and time. Looking specifically at time: over long time scales, recent data suggests that global temperature changes over the past 400,000yrs were commonly up to 10degrees Celcius; over much shorter time scales, daily temperature fluctuations in the Mojave desert are around 24degrees Celcius. 
	The relationship between changing environmental temperature and adaptations is dynamic. In response to environmental variation, rapid evolution over short time periods has been observed. However, macroevolutionary patterns in the fossil record indicate some species have been in morphological stasis for millions of years, even though we have evidence that global temperatures changed drastically in the last 400,000 years. How do these apparently conflicting patterns of rapid change on short time periods and little change over long time periods mesh together to form the species we can see around us now?
	I attempt to answer a part of this question by teasing out the different temporal and spatial scales over which the environment fluctuations and the temporal scales of adaptation to determine the variables responsible for different aspects of macro- and microevolutionary patterns.  
	I focus specifically on environmental temperature, because temperature changes can affect the fitness (a measure of how well the population or species is doing evolutionarily) of organisms through changing the speed of biochemical reactions in metabolism. It follows that organisms have different ways to deal with controlling variation in their body temperature. For example, organisms can produce metabolic heat, behaviorally thermoregulate (e.g. moving from sun to shade), or modify their environment by, for example, building structures (niche construction). I can the time scales of evolution of the ways organisms deal with temperature change to give clues about how environmental change affected the population’s evolution.
	I use a model species, the Colias butterfly, because it lives in a highly variable thermal environment, has a fitness highly dependent on body temperature, and for whom protocol for measuring fitness in the wild has been determined.  I measure traits that change on different time scales (seconds to thousands of years) and collect precise measures of environmental variables that affect body temperature on small scales – temporally: 15seconds to 2months; spatially: feet to hundreds of feet, or size of home range. We also measure fitness that indicates how well the population does, in that time and space. Combining this information I will infer the relationships between the environment and organism on the evolution of organisms.
	This preliminary work of examining the environment on small temporal and spatial scales and collecting information on traits that change over small and large scales, will give us further insight into the relationship between micro and macroevolutionary patterns.
	In summary, we currently don’t understand what environmental fluctuations mean for the evolution of organisms.  There is a conservation need for this information, as well, because with global warming increasing the variability of the environment, the affect of the change on biodiversity, the survival of populations, etc. is uknown. This project will be provide data to help start understanding these relationships.

ResearchPlanTitle: Spatial organization and demography of golden-mantled ground squirrels
ResearchPlanAbstract: The demography of ground-dwelling squirrels, particularly reproduction and survival, may be influenced by both intrinsic and extrinsic factors.  Intrinsic influences result from their spatial organization.  Most ground-dwelling squirrels live in social groups comprised of related females; females cooperate in predator defense, thereby enhancing survival, but competition for resources among crowded females may depress reproduction.  Extrinsic factors include the availability of food in the form of herbaceous vegetation.  I am studying spatial organization and demography of the golden-mantled ground squirrel, considered a nonsocial species.  The species has not been studied, but females are believed to live alone in home ranges that do not overlap, presumably denying them the benefits of sociality.  However, these solitary females may obtain some of these benefits; I suspect that some females live adjacent to close relatives, sharing some space and exhibiting some degree of cooperation, with resultant demographic benefits.  Further, my expectation is that survival and reproduction will be affected by the time of snowmelt each spring, which determines growth of herbaceous vegetation, and perhaps by amount of summer rainfall

ResearchPlanTitle: Linking pollination to plant fitness and population dynamics
ResearchPlanAbstract: Ecologists have learned a great deal over the last century about how flowers are pollinated by animals.  Surprisingly, however, virtually nobody has explored the importance of pollination for the plant population.  Obviously if there is no pollination at all and the plant species in question can't reproduce asexually or vegetatively, the population eventually will go extinct.  But beyond that, we simply don't know much.  We don't know how pollination services fluctuate from year to year and site to site, how this "signal" shows up in production of seeds, and especially how the signal persists as those seeds subsequently germinate and grow into the next generation of adult plants.  Our project combines observations, experiments, and computer modelling to fill this gap in knowledge.  Using the common wildflower, scarlet gilia, we are measuring variation through time and space in pollination by hummingbirds and insects, and its effect on seed production.  In 1997-1999 we added seeds to natural populations to mimic "high pollination" and "low pollination" situations, and are now following the resulting seedlings and plants through to maturity.  We are recording how thousands of individual plants grow, which ones die, and which ones flower, and correlating these fates to local conditions around each plant.  All this information is being incorporated into a computer model of population dynamics, which we will use to extrapolate to longer time spans and to other species and ecological conditions.

ResearchPlanTitle: Ecological and geographic scaling of bioenergetic adaptation
ResearchPlanAbstract:
Spatial patterns of genetic variation in the wild can give important clues to the action of natural selection. But patterns alone are subject to multiple interpretations. To understand whether genuine adaptation, random drift proceeses, or other evolutionary forces are responsible for patterns of variation in the wild, we must understand how the genetic variants affect their carriers, how they interact with ecological variables, and how these effects and interactions give rise to fitness differences (if any) among those variants. 
  
We address these issues by study of natural genetic variation in an insect genus, Colias, and in the context of “bioenergetics”, the flow of energy through living systems. This context can unify many seemingly diverse cases of variation.We consider genetic variation in physiological systems which process energy and allocate it to fitness-related activities of the insects in the wild, using techniques of molecular biology, physiological ecology, and population genetics to study bioenergetic adaptation on diverse environmental scales. 

Specifically, we will first study the mechanisms underlying microhabitat specialization of genetic variation in montane and alpine populations of one species. We will then generalize, to study potential divergence in identity and physiological function of variants in  regional populations which may be progressively more different from our initial study system

These studies will illuminate the relationships between ecological and geographic scales of habitat specialization. They will also begin to examine the interaction of adaptive specialization with different levels of species' differentiation, and lead eventually to greater understanding of the general patterns of bioenergetic adaptation among regional populations, incipient species or "semispecies", and more distantly related species alike.
	
At a broader level, these studies will address general questions concerning topics such as: the evolution of physiological organization in living systems; the evolution of protein structure; and, the predictability or repeatability of evolution at large. They may also contribute to understanding of important applied issues in the genetics of conservation, the genetics of agriculture, and the biotic impacts of potential global change.

ResearchPlanTitle: Evolutionary Ecology and Conservation Biology of Tiger Salamanders
ResearchPlanAbstract: Using tiger salamanders as a model system, my research has two main thrusts:  understanding the evolutionary ecology of trait variation, and answering fundamental questions in conservation biology.  My evolutionary ecology research is aimed at understanding how variation in important traits is maintained in natural populations, and how environmental conditions influence the expression and evolution of trait variation.  I study tiger salamanders, which exhibit two distinct polymorphisms in which the “morphs” or forms are induced by different environmental cues.  By following several populations of salamanders in the field, I am gaining unique insight into the ecology and evolution of these life history polymorphisms.  Furthermore, rearing experiments of salamander larvae have allowed me to begin separating cause and effect regarding the production and maintenance of each polymorphism.  One component of my conservation biology research is exploring the use of morphological variation (asymmetry) as an indicator of environmental stress in these amphibians.  Thus far we have found that increased environmental stress leads to increased asymmetry, which may provide an early-warning signal for stressed amphibian populations.  The last component of my research is to understand the mechanisms controlling population fluctuations in salamander populations.  By determining the factors affecting such fluctuations in tiger salamanders, we should gain insight into the general conditions regulating other animal populations, and perhaps learn ways to distinguish natural population fluctuations from declines.  My research thus has direct implications for ecological and evolutionary theory as well as the conservation and management of this and other species.

Ambystoma tigrinum nebulosum

ResearchPlanTitle: Patterns, mechanisms and consequences of oviposition behavior for recruitment of the mayfly, Baetis bicaudatus
ResearchPlanAbstract: We studied populations of the mayfly Baetis bicaudatus from streams located in the East River drainage basin at the Rocky Mountain Biological Laboratory.  The larvae of this species are very abundant and are the primary food source for trout, as well as an important grazer of algae in these high altitude stream ecosystems. Our research seeks to understand the factors that control recruitment of new individuals (oviposition) to these mayfly populations and to investigate how small and large scale variation in recruitment influences abundance of the larvae.   Methods include observations of patterns of oviposition and field experiments to determine the mechanisms and consequences of oviposition behavior to population growth.  Also, large-scale surveys relate patterns of recruitment to variation in mayfly larval abundance at the scale of the entire drainage basin. Finally, a large-scale field experiment manipulating the availability of oviposition sites in 12 natural streams will test whether populations of Baetis larvae are recruitment limited. From the proposed research we will be able to predict fluctuations in populations at local and regional scales.  Furthermore, this research will provide the foundation for understating population dynamics of aquatic insects important to designing realistic conservation programs.

ResearchPlanTitle: Spatial Distribution of Invasive Plants at the Rocky Mountain Biological Laboratory
ResearchPlanAbstract:
Gothic’s remote location is no safeguard against invasive plant species.  Researchers have recorded thirty invasive plant species at RMBL and have formed a weed control program to investigate and research control strategies for the lab.   These invasive plant populations vary in size, density, and persistence on the lab’s acreage.  We propose to map weed populations within RMBL using data collected by lab and community volunteers over the last two years and to investigate the spatial dynamics of invasive plant species and native plant communities.

One component of my research is to map the spatial distribution of invasive plants within the Gothic townsite.  We propose to create a GIS database to map weed patches at RMBL so that researchers will be able to track the spread of weed populations from year to year.  This database could serve as a model for tracking weed populations at other research sites.  We also propose a multi-scale study of plant communities at RMBL to look for relationships between invasive species, plant community composition, diversity, and disturbance
ResearchPlanOrganisms: Linaria vulgaris, Cisium arvense, Bromus inermis, Chrysanthmum leucanthemum

ResearchPlanTitle: Comparing the quality of various animals as pollinators of bee- and bird-pollinated Penstemon species
ResearchPlanAbstract: Penstemon strictus (Scrophulariaceae) is pollinated by various hymenopterans (bees and wasps).  Some of these pollinators are suspected to be better than others at transferring pollen to conspecific flowers.  Bumblebees, for example, are covered with fine hairs that trap pollen deposited on their bodies as they visit flowers.  However, some bumblebee species visit flowers specifically to collect pollen, storing it in their corbiculae (pollen baskets), making that pollen unavailable to other flowers in female phase (ready to receive pollen and fertilze ovules).  Wasps, on the other hand, lack these hairs.  Pollen may simply fall off their bodies.  Which of the common visitors of P. strictus is most efficient at transferring pollen to other flowers?  To answer this question, I will (1) measure visitation rates to the flowers of roadside populations south of Crested Butte, (2) allow hymenopterans to visit flowers and measure proportion of pollen removed (work completed last summer), and (3) allow insects to visit virgin flowers and determine how much pollen is deposited on stigmas.
ResearchPlanOrganisms: F.	Organisms studied: Penstemon strictus, Bombus spp., Pseudomasaris vespoides, Osmia spp., sundry Hymenoptera and Diptera.

ResearchPlanTitle: Matthew Dietz – Impacts of Rural Roads on Avian Behavior, Distribution, and Reproductive Success in a High-elevation Exurban Zone of Colorado
ResearchPlanAbstract: The effects of roads on the survival and reproductive success of forest passerines is of great concern to conservation biologists.  The wildland-exurban interface zone is being developed rapidly in the Rocky Mountain region.  Limited studies have been conducted on the effects of roads on birds, and the majority of those studies simply measure presence or absence of certain species.  Other experimental studies use artificial nests to determine reproductive success in relation to roads.  I intend to combine these two methods with a study of bird foraging behavior as a function of distance to road and level of traffic disturbance.  I will quantify the impacts by using a framework that treats road disturbance and foraging rates at experimental feeders in the same way that previous scientists have examined the trade-off in choice of foraging location between food density and the risk of predation.  This integrated project should provide evidence for the mechanisms involved in bird behavior and reproductive success along a gradient of road disturbance.
ResearchPlanOrganisms: summer breeding resident birds (principally passerines); may particularly concentrate on one or several focal species, depending on abundance

ResearchPlanTitle: Scaling the functional attributes of plants, communities, and ecosystems across elevational gradients
ResearchPlanAbstract: An important question in ecology is to understand how attributes of species influence the functioning of ecosystems.  This study is designed to forge links between variation in the physical environment (e.g., changes in temperature and precipitation with elevation), changes in the functional attributes of plant species (plant size, leaf morphology and physiology etc.) and the functioning of whole ecosystems (the fluxes of carbon and water). Synthesizing this knowledge is critical for predicting responses of the biosphere to climate change. The mountainous landscape in and around RMBL provides enormous range of physical conditions, from warm wet meadows to cold dry ridge tops. The resulting plant communities are likewise both functionally and phylogenetically diverse. We propose to assess how plant functional diversity and whole ecosystem fluxes vary across a range of elevations and environments. Our work at RMBL will be part of a larger global project.  We are in the process of starting similar elevational studies of plant functional diversity and ecosystem fluxes across elevational gradients in SE Arizona and Costa Rica. Data from these field studies will form the basis for the development and testing of mechanistic, predictive models linking the functional attributes of organisms to large scale processes in plant communities and ecosystems.

ResearchPlanTitle: Host-parasite interactions in the mountain white-crowned sparrows (Zonotrichia leucophrys oriantha)
ResearchPlanAbstract: Parasites and pathogens have a ubiquitous but hidden presence in wildlife populations; because of their obscured nature, their true impact on the health and the population dynanics of wildlife has been difficult to discern. Although disease impact in wild animals appears to be exacerbated  by secondary stressors like food shortages or a changing climate, we have only a very poor understanding of the nature and magnitude of these interactions. This study aims to improve our understanding of the relationship between parasitism and stress due to food shortages by studying a model system of white-crowned sparrows and their blood parasites at the Rocky Mountain Biological Laboratory in Gothic, CO. In this study we experimentally manipulate both parasite numbers and food availability by selectively supplementing food and administering antimalarial drugs to this finch population. This allows us to understand 1. the relative importance of these factors on wildlife survival and reproduction, 2. the mechanisms through which these impacts are expressed - e.g. do they involve changes in behavior, hormones or parts of the immune system? Ultimately, insights gained from this study can help us understand and prevent outbreaks of disease in wildlife as well as help manage wildlife populations to ensure their survival.

ResearchPlanTitle: The impacts of freezing and moisture availability on plant moisture status, photosynthesis, and reproduction
ResearchPlanAbstract: As rising global surface temperatures alter the timing of snowmelt and the length of the growing season in montane and alpine environments, plant distributions are expected to shift.  Therefore, there have been several studies examining the responses of leaf-level and whole-plant physiology and ecosystem processes to warmer temperatures.  An additional area that has strong consequences for both species persistence and dispersal to new ranges under warmer temperatures is that of plant reproduction.  The objectives of my research are to examine how an experimental warming treatment affects reproduction in several subalpine plant species and to identify the mechanisms that underlie these observed responses.  In particular, I will focus on the relative importance of freezing temperatures and water stress on flower and fruit production for plant species that flower soon after snowmelt, when freezing temperatures may be an important factor affecting flower production, and for those species that flower in the summer, when soil moisture availability becomes critical.
ResearchPlanOrganisms: Artemesia tridentata, Erythronium grandiflorum, Helianthella quinquenervis, and Erigeron speciosus

ResearchPlanTitle: Sex, Herbivores, and Patch Dynamics in Fireweed (Chamerion angustifolium: Onagraceae).
ResearchPlanAbstract: Fireweed colonizes disturbed soil, and can expand rapidly to dominate a patch of vegetation, spreading clonally via underground stems.  Large “boom and bust” cycles of fireweed populations have been documented in British grassy meadows, and recently fireweed populations have expanded noticeably around the RMBL.  Nonetheless, fireweed is commonly attacked by a large range of herbivores.  A quick survey in July 2002 revealed various kinds of leaf and stem damage on most of the plants, aphids and treehoppers on several plants, and a high percentage of grazed stems.  The central question of our research project is: what role do herbivores play in the dynamics of fireweed patches?  In particular, how do herbivores respond to genetically diverse seedlings, compared to clonal stems?  Can seedlings establish in existing clonal patches, and if so, does their presence in a patch prolong the dominance of the patch, or is sexual reproduction in this species useful mainly for establishing new patches?  How does herbivory influence seedling recruitment, growth and reproduction in sexually vs. clonally produced stems, and patch persistence, expansion, or decline?  And finally, if a patch is heavily attacked, do the plants change their relative investment in sexual vs. clonal propagation?  This study will contribute to our understanding of population expansion in invasive clonal plants, with insights into how herbivores might be used to counter such expansion.

ResearchPlanTitle: How does exurban development affect avian community distributions and abundances?
ResearchPlanAbstract: For decades, scientists have been concerned with the effects of habitat loss on wildlife populations; in the western U.S., the growing trend of sub-dividing ranches into smaller ‘ranchettes’ is a trend of potential concern.  Ranchette development, however, has been studied significantly less than agricultural, urban development, or logging fragments.  I predict that the human disturbances caused by ranchettes are negatively affecting avian communities. I propose to study the characteristics of ranchettes that impact local bird populations. Through understanding the impact on native bird diversity, proper measures can be taken to reduce negative disturbances.
Subject: None

ResearchPlanTitle: Trade-offs in Helianthella quinquenervis between resistance to late spring frosts and susceptibility to predispersal dipteran seed predators.
ResearchPlanAbstract: Helianthella quinquenervis (aspen sunflower) is a sunflower native to the RMBL area.  Late-spring frosts in the RMBL area often kill developing flowerbuds on Helianthella plants, but generally don't kill the plants themselves—and some Helianthella plants still are able to flower and produc seeds even after the most severe late-spring frosts.  Because Helianthella is a long-lived perennial—and so able to flower again in subsequent years even if they lose their flowers to a late-spring frost—the presence of a few seemingly "frost-hardy" Helianthella plants raises the question of why all Helianthella plants are not frost hardy.  This study attempts to address that question by examining whether—over the long term—non-frost-hardy Helianthella plants produce more viable seeds than do -frost-hardy plants.
ResearchPlanOrganisms: Helianthella quinquenervis (Asteraceae); Neotephritis finalis and Trupanea nigricornis (Tephritidae); and Melanagromyza sp. (Agromyzidae)

ResearchPlanTitle: Patterns of diapausing egg production in the calanoid copepod Diaptomus coloradensis.
ResearchPlanAbstract: Calanoid copepods are small aquatic crustaceans that inhabit fresh- and saltwater environments around the world.  They produce two types of eggs: those that hatch immediately (subitaneous eggs) and those which are dormant and usually do not hatch until the following year (diapausing eggs).  Two previous studies carried out by former graduate students indicate that the signal prompting a switch from subitaneous eggs to diapausing eggs is not affected by photoperiod, temperature, or nutrients found in lakes (at least in one species of copepod found in Quebec).  Furthermore, studies carried out at Mexican Cut in 2001 yielded a surprise: we expected to find more diapausing egg production in temporary pond populations since these can dry up—a distinct disadvantage unless the resistant, diapausing eggs are produced.  We found the opposite, and my current research plan is to attempt to learn more about factors which influence production of these two egg types.

ResearchPlanTitle: Phylogeography and genetic structure of Hesperodiaptomus  shoshone and Leptodiaptomus 	coloradensis: a study of current and historical dispersal patterns
ResearchPlanAbstract:
Species are composed of genetically divergent units usually interconnected by some level of gene flow. Because of this restriction in gene flow, natural selection can genetically tailor populations to their environments through the process of local adaptation. My research aims to clarify the ecological and evolutionary consequences associated with gene flow of two freshwater calanoids, Hesperodiaptomus shoshone and Leptodiaptomus coloradensis.  With the aid of molecular markers, I will reconstruct their postglacial dispersal routes and investigate the refugial origins of modern populations of these copepods. Additionally, I will examine dispersal and the extent of microevolution in a watershed and among neighbouring watersheds in the Gunnison area of Colorado. 
A recently growing problem in the western Rockies is the introduction of fish into high alpine lakes for recreational fishing. Many of these lakes and ponds were historically fishless and such introductions could lead to changes in invertebrate community composition. Introduced trout can reduce or eliminate larger, more visible diaptomids from lakes.  I will examine the consequences of such introductions on the genetic diversity of H. shoshone and L. coloradensis.
ResearchPlanOrganisms: Two calanoid copepods: Hesperodiaptomus shoshone and Leptodiaptomus. coloradensis.

ResearchPlanTitle: The interactions of food supplementation, stress, and parasite load on a wild population of White-crowned sparrows (Zonotrichia leucophyrs oriantha) in Western Colorado.
ResearchPlanAbstract: Evidence from laboratory and field studies has shown that habitat degradation and decrease in suitable habitat can increase stress levels, parasite loads and malnutrition of individuals within wildlife populations.  However, the mechanisms through which food availability, stress, and parasite loads interact to affect host fitness are not well known.  This study intends to examine the mechanism of how these factors interact and impact individuals within a wild population of White-crown sparrows (Zonotrichia leucophrys oriantha) during the breeding season.  I hypothesize that chronic stress due to food shortage decreases reproductive success and survival of White-crowned Sparrows (Zonotrichia leucophrys oriantha) through increased susceptibility to parasites.  I will experimentally reduce parasite loads as well as manipulate food availability to study how these factors influence stress level and sparrow fitness.  Stress is reflected in circulating levels of the hormone corticosterone.  Because sparrows are stressed during the early breeding season due to extensive snow cover and at this time food will be supplemented on selected plots.  In addition, sparrows will be selectively administered antimalarial drugs to reduce blood parasite load.  I will determine stress measurements during the early and late breeding season using a standard stress series protocol.  The impacts of these factors will be quantified by looking at host condition, number of eggs laid, number of offspring fledged, and host survival.  This study draws on the fields of avian endocrinology, parasitology, and ecology, and will yield insights into the conservation of wildlife populations.

ResearchPlanAbstract: Compared to the Toronto populations of Linaria, RMBL plants face a very different set of ecological conditions.  Robbing is rare in Toronto but very common at RMBL; flowering seasons are different and, conveniently, non-overlapping, which allows me to make comparisons as well as extend my time in the field; inflorescence design appears to be different between Toronto and RMBL plants in ways that support my “defensive trait” hypotheses (see [d] below); and RMBL has large, presumably clonal patches while Toronto plants are generally more or less “solitary”, indicating differences in reproductive strategies.

ResearchPlanTitle: Effects of spatial arrangements of flowers within inflorescences on foraging behaviour of bumblebees
ResearchPlanAbstract: Plants will produce more self-pollinated seeds with lower success when pollinators probe more flowers before they leave a plant and transfer pollen grains to stigmas on the same plant. Because the number of flowers a pollinator visits on a plant often varies among systems, the consequences of pollinator visitation for plant mating patterns are also variable. One possible cause of this variation is spatial arrangement of flowers within inflorescences.
ResearchPlanOrganisms: Penstemon strictus (Scrophulariaceae) is an ideal species for observation of foraging behaviour of bumblebees on plants. This species produces sufficient amount of pollen and nectar to attract numerous bumblebees throughout their flowering season. Bumblebees visiting P. strictus is mainly Bombus flavifrons, which will minimize possible confusions due to variation in body sizes, proboscis lengths, and activity of substrate enzyme etc. among bumblebee species.

ResearchPlanTitle: Spatial Population Dynamics of Yellow-bellied Marmots
ResearchPlanAbstract: Spatial heterogeneity is one of the most common features of natural populations, and it can also be an important factor influencing population dynamics. Although there has been a considerable amount of theoretical investigation in spatial population dynamics, very few of them were empirically tested. The yellow-bellied marmot population at Rocky Mt. Biological Lab provides an invaluable opportunity for investigating the spatially mediated population processes. The natural marmot population is distributed into distinct colonies that partially interact via dispersal, hence it provides an adequate patchy distribution for studying spatiotemporal patterns. Also, there is a priceless 41 years of detailed demographic data and 10 years of radio-telemetry study, which enable vigorous demographic and dispersal analysis, respectively. My research focuses on a variety of questions regarding the spatial aspect of yellow-bellied marmot population dynamics that capitalize on the analysis of these data. What types of spatiotemporal patterns in population density emerge as a result of interaction between dispersal and local dynamics? What is the population level significance of changes in dispersal rates due to changes in local dynamics? My work involves analyzing the long-term data set, and testing predictions of different spatial models regarding the effects of dispersal and local dynamics on population dynamics. Meanwhile, I will participate in the collection of long-term demographic data, and thus contribute to the long-term database of marmot population dynamics. Ultimately, these results will provide us a better understanding of the predictive powers of spatially explicit demographic models.

ResearchPlanTitle: Sediment movement by yellow-bellied marmots
ResearchPlanAbstract:
The purpose of this research is to quantify the amount of sediment removed by yellow-bellied marmots (Marmota flaviventris) in a single summer season.  Research will be conducted at the Rocky Mountain Biological Laboratory in Gothic, Colorado.  The research will also examine if this sediment removal contributes to landslides, rock falls, or other geomorphologic processes.   The proposed research will be based within the field of Environmental Geography.  The research will contain biogeographic and zoogeomorphic components as well.   Hazards will also be examined in this research to determine if humans are affected by marmots’ excavation of steep hillsides.

Understanding marmots’ interactions with their environment should provide some valuable information on alpine geomorphology and should contribute to the field of zoogeomorphology.
Subject: None

ResearchPlanTitle: A survey of bird-feeding Diptera in the Gunnison Valley: implications for parasite transmission intensity
ResearchPlanAbstract: Climate change is expected to have impacts on parasite transmission via insect vectors.  Predictions have generally referred to human pathogens, although the proposed mechanisms would apply to any vector borne parasite.  The blood parasites of the Mountain White Crowned Sparrow (Zonotrichia leucophrys oriantha, - MWCS) are all carried by Dipteran vectors, and may be a good system to study the effects of climate variability on pathogen transmission.  I am planning to examine the potential for a gradient in transmission as a function of altitude.  I hypothesize that vector abundance drives transmission intensity, and is negatively correlated with altitude.  To test this hypothesis, I propose a two-week intensive sampling of adult and larval dipterans, at two sites in each of four altitudes at Rocky Mountain Biological Laboratory (RMBL).  One sampling period will be early in the nesting season (mid-June), and the second one late (late August).  I hope to provide insight into the variation in vector communities over an elevational gradient, and suggest how this may affect disease transmission under global climate change scenarios.
ResearchPlanOrganisms: Larval and adult Diptera, including families Culicidae, Simulidae, Hippobscidae, and Ceratopogonidae.  There will be no vertebrates used in the research.  Larvae may be collected and reared for identification.

ResearchPlanTitle: Pollinator behavior, pollen transfer, and floral evolution in Penstemon spp.
ResearchPlanAbstract: Most species in the large plant genus Penstemon have flowers adapted for pollination by bees, but hummingbird-adapted species have evolved independently in 10-15 different lineages, producing true convergent evolution.  I study these evolutionary transitions, seeking to understand how floral characteristics, animal behavior, and ecological circumstances interact to cause shifts in pollination mode.  Principal experiments concern the effectiveness of pollen transfer by bumble bees and hummingbirds, and how this is influenced by floral characters.  I use natural and artificial variation in plants to conduct experiments on pollen transfer and pollinatorpreferences
ResearchPlanOrganisms: Penstemon strictus, P. barbatus, Selasphorus rufus, S. platycercus, Bombus spp.

ResearchPlanTitle: While it is apparent that the environment varies and can affect populations of organisms (plants are killed in frosts, animals die of overheating), the relationship between variation in the environment and patterns of evolution is not understood.
ResearchPlanAbstract:
While it is apparent that the environment varies and can affect populations of organisms (plants are killed in frosts, animals die of overheating), the relationship between variation in the environment and patterns of evolution is not understood. 
	The environment varies in space and time and at different scales. For example, temperature is different depending where you are in space: In the summer it is hotter in Nevada than the state of Washington. But temperature also is different depending on time: Colorado during a winter snowstorm is much colder than the same mountain during a sunny day, when it can get downright balmy. There are patterns of temperature change that depend on scale, where we can see some counter intuitive patterns, such as longer amounts of time do not mean greater amounts of temperature change. For example, recent data suggests that global temperature changes over the past 400,000yrs were commonly up to 10degrees Celcius; over much shorter time scales, daily temperature fluctuations in the Mojave desert are around 24degrees Celcius. Can we fit these patterns of temperature change that depends on the time and space examined to understand how these patterns may affect evolution?
	One reason this is an interesting question is counter intuitive patterns in evolution. Over decades we can see morphological changes that almost look like new species emerging, while the fossil record instead shows that there aren’t that many species and the same ones stay around and look the same for millions of years. How do these apparently conflicting patterns of rapid change on short time periods and little change over long time periods mesh together to form the species we can see around us now?
	I attempt to answer a part of this question by teasing out the different temporal and spatial scales that the environment changes over and the scales over which adaptation to temperature occurs. This helps inform the temporal scales of temperature change that may drive different aspects of macro- and microevolutionary patterns.  I will start out by trying to answer what temporal and spatial scales affect microevolutionary dynamics.
	I focus specifically on environmental temperature and ectotherms, because temperature affects fitness (a measure of how well the population or species is doing evolutionarily) of organisms, by basically changing the speed of biochemical reactions in metabolism.. Because temperature is so important, it follows that organisms have many different ways to control their temperature at an optimum even while the environmental temperature varies. For example, organisms can behaviorally thermoregulate (e.g. moving from sun to shade), have metabolic enzymes that work best at certain temperature, or modify the part of the environment they see, by, for example, building structures (niche construction). I can examine the time scales of evolution of the traits organisms use to deal with temperature change to give clues about how environmental change affected the population’s evolution.
	I use a model species, the Colias butterfly, because it lives in a highly variable thermal environment, has a fitness highly dependent on body temperature, and for whom protocol for measuring fitness in the wild has been determined.  I measure traits that change on different time scales (seconds to thousands of years) and collect precise measures of environmental variables that affect body temperature on small scales – temporally: 15seconds to 2months; spatially: feet to hundreds of feet, or size of home range. We also measure fitness that indicates how well the population does, in that time and space. Combining this information I will infer the relationships between the environment and organism on the evolution of organisms.
	We currently don’t understand what environmental fluctuations mean for the evolution of organisms. This preliminary work of examining the environment on small temporal and spatial scales and collecting information on traits that change over small and large scales, will give us further insight into the relationship between micro and macroevolutionary patterns. Understanding these relationships can aid conservation work of preserving biodiversity in the face of global warming, which is predicted to increase the frequency of severe weather events. We need to understand how frequency of temperature change affects the evolution of populations and species over short and long time scales in order to determine management practices to sustain biodiversity. This project will provide data to help start understanding these relationships.

ResearchPlanTitle: Comparing prezygotic isolating mechanisms in uni- and bi-modal plant hybrid zones.
ResearchPlanAbstract: My broad interest is in the evolution of reproductive isolation, and how local environmental circumstances might affect it. Specifically, I study spatial variation in the strength of reproductive isolating mechanisms between two hybridizing species in the Genus Ipomopsis (Polemoniaceae). These plants exhibit characteristics of classic pollination syndromes – hummingbird, and hawkmoth – that might act to reduce gene flow between sympatric populations of the two species. My research compares the strength of reproductive isolating mechanisms between sympatric populations of these species in two locations, one in which hybrids are common and one in which they are rare, and tests the hypothesis that reproductive isolation will be stronger in the low-hybridization site. Changes in flower morphology potentially produce instantaneous assortative mating and thus provide a possible avenue to sympatric speciation that does not require tight linkage between fitness loci and assortative mating loci. In addition to the study described above, I am examining the response of pollinators in the RMBL locale to plants of a hummingbird pollinated species that exhibit an albino flower color mutation, and comparing the pollination services received by the parental species, albinos, and F1 hybrids of both wild type and albino parents in experimental arrays.

ResearchPlanTitle:
Evolutionary ecology of facultative paedomorphosis and cannibalism in
salamanders
ResearchPlanAbstract:
The aim of my research is to explore the eco-ethological traits of amphibian species in an
evolutional perspective. My approach is multi-disciplinary in order to model the extent of
costs and benefits of individual tactics, and includes – among others – the survey of natural
populations, the determination of the environmental factors at the basis of the observed
phenotypic patterns and the characterization of behavioral tactics, reproductive success and
resource use. Specifically, my work at the Rocky Mountain Biological Laboratory focuses on
the proximate and ultimate mechanisms of alternative developmental pathways: facultative
paedomorphosis (retention of larval traits in the adult) and cannibalism in tiger salamander
Ambystoma tigrinum. Such environmentally-induced polymorphisms are of particular interest
because large morphological and physiological changes can be reached without deep genetic
modifications. Determining the factors contributing to the success of new heterochronic
variants, such as the paedomorphs or cannibals, in populations, is thus necessary to validate
this evolutionary perspective. In my study, I analyze optimal foraging in the alternative
morphs across different habitats within their home range (including capture – mark –
recapture), feeding habits of cannibal larvae across time (cf. pond drying), and the effect of
parasites, predator and prey size on diet, specifically cannibalistic habits in mesocosms
experiments and field observations. Because amphibian suffer decline worldwide, this kind of
field surveys is conservation-integrated to characterize habitats determinants favoring
intraspecific biodiversity.
