ResearchPlanTitle:
Plan 2: Isotopic Investigations in the East River Valley: Vegetation Usage of Summer
versus Winter Precipitationï¿½
ResearchPlanAbstract:
Ecosystems in the upper Gunnison basin rely on two distinct water sources throughout
the year: winter and summer precipitation. While winter precipitation is the dominant contributor
to the basinï¿½s water budget, summer precipitation accounts for about 20% of the total water
input. This summer input is undoubtedly critical for some vegetation, especially the forbs and
grasses that germinate, flower, and set seed in a narrow window between late June and late
August. Superimposed on this broad hydrological context, there is evidence of changes in the
timing and amount of precipitation at RMBL. Such climatic changes will undoubtedly affect
vegetation throughout the East River Valley, but it is difficult to predict the direction and
magnitude of these impacts. Stable isotopes of oxygen, hydrogen, and carbon offer a promising
approach to understanding the extent to which different vegetation functional groups (trees,
shrubs, grasses, and forbs) rely on winter versus summer precipitation. This project aims to use
such isotopic tracers (in water and leaf biomass) to delineate the usage of seasonal precipitation
inputs by these different vegetation functional groups. I plan to continue (and expand) this
project for at least five years, thus providing an assessment of such water usage on interannual
time scales. Weather data and water samples collected by the EPA NADP weather station at
RMBL will be a crucial component of this work, and should permit me to extend aspects of my
analysis back for the last 15 years.
ResearchPlanOrganisms:
I will focus initial sampling on the following species for each functional group: trees: Picea
engelmanii, Populus tremuloides; woody plants: Pentaphylloides floribunda (middle flowering
time), Artemisia tridentata (late flowering time); herbs: Mertensia fusiformes (early flowering
time), Potentilla hippiana (middle flowering time), Erigeron speciosus (late flowering time);
grasses: Poa pattersonii (early flowering time), Stipa lettermanii (middle flowering time),
Festuca thurberi (late flowering time).

ResearchPlanTitle: Plan 1: Precipitation in the East River valley is strongly bimodal in nature.
ResearchPlanAbstract:
Precipitation in the East River valley is strongly bimodal in nature. Although the vast
majority falls as snow in winter, ecologically important contributions come from summer
rainfall. These types of precipitation occur in different forms (i.e., snow crystals versus rain
drops), and they are also imprinted with distinct hydrogen and oxygen isotopic signatures. Water
isotope data collected at the University of Colorado field station (Niwot Ridge) document a large
seasonal cycle in the oxygen-18 and hydrogen-2 content of summer rainfall and winter snowfall,
with strong depletions in these heavier isotopes in winter compared to summer precipitation.
This seasonal cycle is driven by the differing source regions of summer and winter storms and
the different condensation histories and temperatures of winter versus summer storms.

ResearchPlanTitle:
Topsoil development and Nutrient regeneration in a Landslide Scar 
(80-yrs after an Earth Flow)
ResearchPlanAbstract: In early 1920s heavy rainstorm triggered off the Gothic Earthflow, in the East River Valley. The landslide event left a conspicuous scar when an irrigation ditch undercut the hillside. The main flow area was completely stripped of plants and topsoil. At present, more than 80 years after the earth flow, the disturbed plant communities have remained distinct from the adjacent relatively undisturbed area in diversity, density and species composition. But there have been no adjacent soil studies to understand how soil in the landslide scar has developed in relation to the relatively undisturbed references adjacent to the scar. This study aims to understand the extent of topsoil development in the landslide scar and identify evidences of biological influence on the soil’s structural development. This study aims to determine how closely nutrient regeneration in the scar follows pattern of plant recolonization across multiple successional stages by following a gradient of plant regeneration and soil development from unaffected, 5m away from the edge (early colonization at the edge of the slide scar) to the most affected parts at the center of the scar (recent/late colonization).

ResearchPlanTitle:
Project 1)  Multiple-species interactions and the evolution of floral traits in Ipomopsis aggregata.  

Project 2)  The effects of an introduced bio-control agent, Larinus planus, on the pollination success of native thistles.
ResearchPlanAbstract:
Project 1)  Plants that require animals for pollination face a critical problem.  On the one hand, they must attract pollinators, while on the other hand they must avoid being preyed upon by enemies that utilize floral cues in locating hosts, such as pre-dispersal seed predators, nectar robbing bumblebees and herbivores.  My previous work has focused on the outcome of these multiple selective pressures on the ecology and evolution of floral traits in scarlet gilia, or Ipomopsis aggregata.  Current controversy surrounds the ability of this plant to compensate for herbivore damage.  Yet, no study to date has accounted for the effects of herbivory over the plant’s lifetime from seedling to flowering adult.  My work will focus on how herbivory in the vegetative, or rosette, stage affects future reproductive success.  


Project 2)  For years, the use of biocontrol agents in controlling the spread of invasive plants has been seen as a silver bullet.  However, mounting evidence suggests that there are often unforeseen complications in the use of biocontrol agents.  Such complications include the propensity for biocontrol agents to switch hosts from the targets they were introduced to control to native, non-invasive species.  My work will focus on the effects of a seed-eating weevil, Larinus planus, which was introduced in Colorado to control the invasive Canada thistle (Cirsium arvense), on the pollination biology of a native, non-invasive host, Cirsium undulatum.
ResearchPlanOrganisms: Ipomopsis aggregata; Bombus occidentalis, Hylemya sp., Cirsium undulatum, Larinus planus.

ResearchPlanTitle: IMPACTS OF ENVIRONMENTAL CHANGE ON PLANT-POLLINATOR MUTUALISMS
ResearchPlanAbstract: Global change will likely alter the patterns of availability and variation in resources, such as precipitation and nutrients, necessary for the growth and reproduction of plants and their pollinator mutualists. Increased awareness and interest in global change have sparked research on the responses of species to projected environmental conditions. However, the effects of global environmental change on ecological interactions, such as plant-pollinator interactions, are rarely considered. This lack of attention is disturbing, given that mutualisms are a shaping force of ecological communities, and pollinator diversity is likely most endangered by global climate change of anthropogenic origin. I am seeking to understand relationships between environmental conditions and plant-pollinator interactions, plant-plant interactions, and pollinator fitness. Together these experiments will provide an understanding of how the diversity of plants, pollinators, and their interactions may shift under global environmental change.
ResearchPlanOrganisms: Focal subalpine meadow wildflowers include Erigeron speciosus (Asteraceae), Ipomopsis aggregata (Polemoniaceae), Potentilla quinquifolia (Rosaceae), Polemonium foliosissimum (Polemoniaceae), and Linum lewisii (Linaceae).  Bee species likely to be observed are Osmia and Bombus spp.

ResearchPlanTitle: Evolution of alternative mating tactics and the costs associated with parental behavior in three secondary cavity nesting species:  mountain bluebirds, Sialia currucoides, tree swallows, Tachycineta bicolor, and house wrens, Troglodytes aedon
ResearchPlanAbstract: Associations between males and females during courtship, mating, and the time used to raise the offspring can be highly variable, even within populations.  In addition, the costs associated with these behaviors can be extensive, especially in high altitude environments where temperature and food resources vary dramatically in a relatively short amount of time.  As part of my research I am interested in determining whether three species of cavity nesting birds (mountain bluebird, tree swallow, and house wren) that are considered socially monogamous (meaning that the male and female exclusively court and mate with each other and subsequently usually stay together to feed and raise offspring) actually turn out to be genetically monogamous.  In other words, in many monogamous birds, the males and females of the “monogamous” pair often mate with other individuals, with the result that the male at a particular nest might not be the genetic father of all of the offspring in his nest.  Both males and females potentially seek to mate with other individuals; a mating tactic referred to as extra-pair copulations (EPC).  These EPC could be of great cost to individuals of species where both the male and female provide extensive parental care to the offspring, especially since males might be expending energy to feed unrelated young and females may lose the help of males that suspect the young are not his offspring.  High altitude environments further exacerbate this cost because energetic costs can be extensive in these environments for organisms that have to maintain a constant body temperature.  In addition, examining the parental behavior and the cost of raising young in these high altitude populations is particularly fascinating, as the cost of raising small offspring that rapidly lose heat to the environment should increase when temperatures are low as the average nightly temperatures at high altitudes.  The young of mountain bluebirds, tree swallows, and house wrens are vulnerable to considerable costs associated with maintaining constant body temperatures due to their small body size.  Therefore, in addition to examining the mating behavior in these birds, I plan to determine how parents offset the metabolic cost of maintaining constant body temperatures of small-bodied offspring during the time of rapid growth associated with the nestling phase of mountain bluebirds, tree swallows, and house wrens.
ResearchPlanOrganisms:
Principal organisms to be studied:
mountain bluebirds, Sialia currucoides
tree swallows, Tachycineta bicolor
house wrens, Troglodytes aedon

ResearchPlanTitle: Impacts of Rural Roads and Human Intrusion on Avian Behavior, Distribution, Physiology and Reproductive Success in a High-elevation Exurban Zone of Colorado
ResearchPlanAbstract: The effects of roads and pedestrian disturbance on the behavior, distribution, physiology, survival and reproductive success of passerines is of great concern to conservation biologists.  The wildland-exurban interface zone is being developed rapidly in the Rocky Mountain region, leading to increases in these two disturbance factors.  Limited studies have been conducted on the effects of roads on birds, and the majority of those studies simply measure presence or density of certain species or use artificial nests as a proxy to determine predation rates and reproductive success in relation to roads.  Studies of pedestrian intrusion have concentrated mostly on effects of disturbance on bird distribution, foraging, and flushing distances.  In addition to conducting point counts of all bird species in relation to the road (as I did in 2003), I intend to investigate the correlation between road disturbance (both distance and traffic) and White-crowned Sparrow (Zonotrichia leucophrys oriantha) 1) breeding-season distribution, 2) nest site selection, 3) nest success, and 4) stress levels.  I will also experimentally test the effects of human intrusion on White-crowned Sparrows with regard to 1) nest success, and 2) stress levels.  The integration of these studies should provide valuable information in determining the effects and specific mechanisms of these common types of disturbance.
ResearchPlanOrganisms: summer breeding resident birds (principally passerines); Mountain White-crowned Sparrows

ResearchPlanTitle: Positive feedback in multi-species plant-pollinator associations
ResearchPlanAbstract: I am studying how plants and pollinators impact each other’s fitness.  While this may seem obvious, the degree to which plants and pollinators depend on each other may be quite variable.  Plants may be more strongly limited by other biotic interactions (e.g., seed predation) or by surviving the harsh alpine environment.  Pollinators may be limited by available nesting and over-wintering habitat or by parasitism.  In particular, I am interested in measuring the magnitude of positive feedback between plant and bee species.  Do the plants that bees depend on for pollen and nectar get anything in return (i.e., are they pollinator limited)?  And do the plants that are pollinator limited provide significant resources to bee populations?  By measuring individual and population-level fitness in a suite of alpine plants and bees, I will test for the degree of symmetrical feedback in plant-pollinator interactions
ResearchPlanOrganisms: I will focus my observations on Bombus and Osmia species present in the meadows, but will also record other bee species present.  Potential plant species for the pollen limitation experiments include Potentilla sp., Linum sp., Castilleja sp., Linaria vulgaris, Penstemon sp., Lupinus sp., Delphinium sp., and Pneumonanthe sp.  Any future demography on particular species will be proposed in renewal applications

ResearchPlanTitle: Scaling the functional attributes of plants, communities, and ecosystems across elevational gradients
ResearchPlanAbstract:
Abstract (Non technical, for visitors and donors)
An important question in ecology is to understand how attributes of species influence the functioning of ecosystems.  This study is designed to forge links between variation in the physical environment (e.g., changes in temperature and precipitation with elevation), changes in the functional attributes of plant species (plant size, leaf morphology and physiology etc.) and the functioning of whole ecosystems (the fluxes of carbon and water). Synthesizing this knowledge is critical for predicting responses of the biosphere to climate change. The mountainous landscape in and around RMBL provides enormous range of physical conditions, from warm wet meadows to cold dry ridge tops. The resulting plant communities are likewise both functionally and phylogenetically diverse. We assess how plant functional diversity and whole ecosystem fluxes vary across a range of elevations and environments. Our work at RMBL is part of a larger global project.  We conduct similar elevational studies of plant functional diversity and ecosystem fluxes across elevational gradients in SE Arizona, NE Mexico, and Costa Rica. Data from these field studies is the basis for the development and testing of theory linking the functional attributes of organisms to large scale processes in plant communities and ecosystems.

ResearchPlanTitle: Phoretic Mite Selection of Burying Beetle Hosts (Nicrophorus investigator)
ResearchPlanAbstract: Certain species of mites infest beetles and exploit them as a means of transportation, a type of interaction called “phoresy.”  The burying beetle, Nicrophorus investigator, found in the vicinity of RMBL, acts as a host to such phoretic mites.  These phoretic mites are dependent upon their beetle hosts for transportation as well as access to suitable reproductive habitat (the beetle’s burial chamber and brood carcass).  Therefore, a phoretic mite’s reproductive success is determined, at least in part, by the mite’s ability to select a beetle host that is most capable of reaching a carcass.  However, not all burying beetles are equally capable of locating and reaching a carcass.  This experiment will use a combination of laboratory trials and field experiments to examine whether phoretic mites differentiate between beetles hosts based on their energetic state, one important aspect of a beetle’s condition that is related to its ability to reach a carcass.
ResearchPlanOrganisms: The burying beetle, Nicrophorus investigator, and associated phoretic mites (no distinction to be made among species of phoretic mites).

ResearchPlanTitle: Modeling Population Dynamics of the Tiger Salamander, Ambystoma tigrinum nebulosum, at the Mexican Cut Nature Preserve, Colorado
ResearchPlanAbstract:
Scientists at Murray State University and Allegheny College are currently involved in a NSF Collaborative-RUI project titled “Collaborative Research on Mechanisms Underlying Salamander Population Fluctuations."  A main goal of this project is to address exogenous and endogenous variables likely to be important to amphibian population fluctuations, including winter mortality, zooplankton abundance, cannibalism by aquatic adults, and demographic convergence among adults (Whiteman and Wissinger, 2001). The project focuses on a demographic analysis and life history study of a montane population of tiger salamanders, Ambystoma tigrinum nebulosum, involving undergraduates with various aspects of observational and experimental research.  
	Amphibian populations have been well documented to fluctuate dramatically, in part because of the high fecundity of females and the dynamic nature of their breeding habitats (e.g., drought, competition, predation).  Yet, no research has examined the ecological causes of such fluctuation in great detail.  In 1990, Dr. Scott Wissinger (Allegheny College) and Dr. Howard Whiteman (Murray State University) began a long-term study of a high-elevation metapopulation of tiger salamanders, Ambystoma tigrinum nebulosum, at the Mexican Cut Nature Preserve near Crested Butte, Colorado.  Their research has elucidated much about the life-history strategies of the salamanders (Whiteman et al., 1995, 1996, Whiteman, 1997) and the effects of the salamander predators on invertebrate prey (Bohonak and Whiteman, 1999, Wissinger et al., 1999a, 1999b).  It has also allowed hypotheses concerning the mechanisms that produce fluctuations evident in this population.  
The population experienced a decline phase in the 1980s, which originally was attributed to acidic deposition (Harte and Hoffman, 1989, 1994a, 1994b).  After the population rebounded dramatically in 1988, Wissinger and Whiteman (1992) found that larval mortality due to pond drying was a more likely explanation for the 1980s decline.  Over the past decade, they have identified a number of other extrinsic and intrinsic variables likely to be important to these population fluctuations, including winter mortality, zooplankton abundance, cannibalism, and demographic convergence among adults (Whiteman and Wissinger, 2001).  A major goal of the Murray State/Allegheny project is to create and parameterize mathematical models of salamander population dynamics.

ResearchPlanTitle: The effects of ski slope fragmentation on avian community structure and behavior
ResearchPlanAbstract: Habitat fragmentation is of serious concern to conservationists and managers alike.  It reduces the suitable habitat available to species, while disrupting their life histories.  Minimizing the effects of fragmentation is of particular importance to maintain a diverse community.  I propose to study how ski slope fragmentation has affected the local avian diversity through comparing species to an adjacent, unfragmented mountain.  In addition, I will record how bird behavior changes in response to crossing differing ski meadow sizes.

ResearchPlanTitle: Spatial ecology and nest site selection in a Colorado cavity-nesting bird community.
ResearchPlanAbstract: In western Colorado, several bird species nest in cavities in aspen trees. Around Gothic, the Red-naped Sapsucker excavates many such cavities, and at least 8 other species make use of abandoned sapsucker cavities for their nests. The sapsuckers seem to prefer nest trees that have been infected by a heartwood fungus; the fungus softens the wood and makes cavity excavation easier. Our studies focus on the relationships between the aspens, fungus, and sapsuckers. Specifically, we are interested in how the natural histories of the sapsucker and heartwood fungus may each affect the distribution of the other, and how aspen natural history influences the dynamics of the whole community. We use a non-invasive monitoring approach to gather a large amount of data with a minimum impact on our subjects.
ResearchPlanOrganisms: Quaking aspen (Populus tremuloides), aspen heartwood fungus (Phellinus tremulae), Red-naped Sapsucker (Syphrapicus nuchalis)

ResearchPlanTitle:
Phylogeography and genetic structure of Hesperodiaptomus  shoshone and Leptodiaptomus 
	coloradensis: a study of current and historical dispersal patterns.
ResearchPlanAbstract:
Species are composed of genetically divergent units usually interconnected by some level of gene flow. Because of this restriction in gene flow, natural selection can genetically tailor populations to their environments through the process of local adaptation. My research aims to clarify the ecological and evolutionary consequences associated with gene flow of two freshwater calanoids, Hesperodiaptomus shoshone and Leptodiaptomus coloradensis.  With the aid of molecular markers, I will reconstruct their postglacial dispersal routes and investigate the refugial origins of modern populations of these copepods. Additionally, I will examine dispersal and the extent of microevolution in a watershed and among neighbouring watersheds in the Gunnison area of Colorado. 
A recently growing problem in the western Rockies is the introduction of fish into high alpine lakes for recreational fishing. Many of these lakes and ponds were historically fishless and such introductions could lead to changes in invertebrate community composition. Introduced trout can reduce or eliminate larger, more visible diaptomids from lakes.  I will examine the consequences of such introductions on the genetic diversity of H. shoshone and L. coloradensis.
ResearchPlanOrganisms: Two calanoid copepods: Hesperodiaptomus shoshone and Leptodiaptomus. coloradensis.

ResearchPlanTitle: The Dispersal of fungi and Bacteria by Ants at Rocky Mountain Biological Station
ResearchPlanAbstract: Ants are known to function as important dispersers of plant seeds, thus contributing to the structure of plant communities.  Ants have also been suspected for a long time to function as important dispersers (vectors) of microorganisms, particularly fungi, but the role of ants in microbial dispersal has never been studied to date.  This study will investigate for the first time the role of ants in the dispersal of fungi and bacteria. Because of their numerical abundance and continual presence in virtually all habitats, ants are a group of animals that are most likely to function as major vectors of microorganisms.  It is not implausible that (a)  there exist specialized fungi that rely on ants for dispersal (analogous to ant-dispersed plants); (b) such fungi and their vectoring ants are linked in a coevolutionary process; and (c) ants therefore are not only important determinants of plant community structure, but microbial community structure as well. Because of a location in a temperate habitat, the Rocky Mountain Research Station presents an ideal setting for this first investigation into ant-dispersed microorganisms.
ResearchPlanOrganisms:
a.	Formica and Camponotus ants at RMBL.
b.	Saprotropic fungi in organic debris on the ground, possibly fungi in the Lepiotaceae (Basidiomycotina).

ResearchPlanTitle: Resource levels, parasite load, and reproduction in a wild population of Mountain White-crowned Sparrows (Zonotrichia leucophrys oriantha) in western Colorado.
ResearchPlanAbstract: Laboratory and field studies have shown that habitat degradation increases the malnutrition, stress levels, and parasite loads of animals.  I propose to examine the mechanisms through which food availability, stress, and parasite load interact to impact a wild population of Mountain White-crowned Sparrows (Zonotrichia leucophrys oriantha) during the breeding season.  I will experimentally reduce host parasite loads and manipulate food availability and study the effects on circulating corticosterone, immune function, and reproductive success.  A standard stress series protocol will be used throughout the breeding season to measure circulating levels of corticosterone, and the cellular and humoral components of the immune system will be measured to assess immune function.  Finally, I will quantify the impacts of parasite load and food availability by measuring the number of eggs laid, number of offspring fledged, and number of surviving hosts.  Experimental field studies investigating the interaction of resource levels and parasite load are vital in developing conservation strategies for avian species.

ResearchPlanTitle: Mating strategies in Female bury beetles, Nicrophorus investigator: A case of brood parasitism.
ResearchPlanAbstract: Reproduction is an essential element of fitness and the ability of an individual to reproduce successfully is often linked to their ability to acquire a particular resource. In the Burying beetles (Nicrophorus), there can be intense competition for access to a small vertebrate carcass which is used as food for larvae during development. The ability of an individual to win a competition has been shown to be correlated with the size of that individual.  But, What happens to smaller individuals who are unable to win a carcass of their own?  I propose that for these individuals brood parasitism is a relatively good option.  In a case o brood parasitism a female may be able to sneak into the nest of another female and leave eggs behind for her to raise.  In order to test whether this is happening in the burying beetle Nicrophorus investigator I will set up breeding experiments with two size females (small and large) to see if there is multiple maternity within one brood.

ResearchPlanTitle: Recovery of species diversity in space and time: Gothic, CO and Mount St Helens, WA
ResearchPlanAbstract:
Ecosystems are continuously perturbed by natural and human-caused disturbances.  Because disturbance resumes the processes of community assembly and ecological succession, my research analyzes how plant species diversity develops in time and space on bare landscapes after severe disturbance in two subalpine systems (1980 eruption of Mount St Helens, WA and 1923 earthflow south of Gothic, CO).

Species diversity in space can be measured by species-area relationships, which are used in reserve design analyses and to predict species loss from habitat fragmentation.  Species-area relationships are typically calculated without a temporal dimension, despite the potential dependence of species richness on seasonal variation in reproduction and recruitment, or annual variation in environmental factors.  My research focuses on this temporal dimension by analyzing how species-area relationships change over time and the characteristics of species-time relationships.  To understand the connections between pattern and process, my research also tests how random models differ from mechanistic models in their predictions of species pattern formation in space and time.  Taken together, this research addresses if and how time should be included in species diversity assessments.
Subject: None

ResearchPlanTitle: Population structure of an ant-tended membracid
ResearchPlanAbstract: The concept of a population is central to ecology and evolution.  Many evolutionary and ecological processes are studied at the scale of populations.  In spite of this, ecologists arbitrarily define a population as a group of individuals in a given area.  Through my research, I develop a new conceptual framework for describing populations in quantitative terms comparable across systems.  Using a membracid-ant mutualism as a case study, I measure membracids' dispersal, spatial and temporal distribution, and genetic structure to quantitatively describe their population structure.  In addition, I investigate possible mechanisms explaining membracids' structure, including the distribution of an ant mutualist, presence of host plants, abundance of predators, and microsite variation in abiotic factors.  Knowing membracids' population structure and the mechanisms behind that structure will clarify the relevant scales at which ecological and evolutionary processes occur.
ResearchPlanOrganisms:
Dominant vegetation includes Artemisia tridentata (sagebrush), Chrysothamnus spp. (rabbitbrush), grasses, and herbaceous perennials.
Publilia modesta (Membracidae) is a phytophagous ant-tended homopteran.  At Almont Triangle P. modesta is most commonly tended by the ant, Formica obscuripes.  Membracids excrete honeydew, which ants collect and consume.  Ants benefit membracids by protecting them from predators (Cushman and Whitham 1989, Morales 2000) and removing honeydew, which is thought to decrease sooty mold growth (McEvoy 1979).  Publilia modesta produces one generation per year at this site.  In May and June, females lay eggs in stems of herbaceous and woody plants.  Nymphs emerge, feed on the host plant on which they were laid, and develop into adults in August and September.  Adult membracids most actively disperse in August and September.  Membracids overwinter at the roots of plants.  At Almont Triangle, primary hostplants include Wyethia spp., Chrysothamnus viscidiflorus,and Balsamorhiza sagittata.

ResearchPlanTitle: Effects of environmental variation on individual life histories and population dynamics
ResearchPlanAbstract: Variation in the environment can take several forms.  Organisms may be exposed to different weather or climate conditions over space and/or time.  The predators, competitors or food items in a community may also change over space and/or time.  I am exploring how such changes affect individual reproduction and survival, and through that, changes in population numbers over time.  My goal is to generate a conceptual understanding that is broadly applicable to diverse organisms. My present research utilizes butterflies as study systems, and has two foci.  First, I am studying the effects of an introduced plant species on the population dynamics and evolution of host plant usage by a native butterfly species.  Second, I am exploring the effects of variation in adult and larval food availability on reproduction and survival, thence population numbers
ResearchPlanOrganisms:
Lepidoptera: Speyeria mormonia, Pieris napi. 
Plants: Viola spp., Erigeron spp., Haplopappus spp., Helenium spp., Viguera spp, Thlaspi arvense, Cardamine cordifolia, Arabis spp., Draba aurea, Descurania richardsoni

ResearchPlanTitle: Are Historical Colorado Silver Miners Optimal Foragers?: Modeling Behavior in a Capitalist Setting
ResearchPlanAbstract: My proposed research will test the ability of mathematical models of  behavior to predict human behaviors in a capitalist setting by examining silver ore foraging strategies in a historic human population in the East River Valley of Colorado.  Marx (1909) suggested that capitalism is fundamentally unique because production (labor) and consumption (reward) are disconnected.  Examining how real human behaviors compare to theoretical predictions will examine if the behavior of capitalists, such as miners, can be more generally understood using models that also apply to animals, hunter-gatherers, and pastoralists.  This research will not only make significant contributions to the body of knowledge in the social sciences, but studying resource extraction in general is of practical application as human population continues to grow and resources become more scarce.
ResearchPlanOrganisms: behavioral remains of dead Homo sapiens

ResearchPlanTitle: Stress and Immune Defense in Yellow-bellied Marmots
ResearchPlanAbstract: I will study the relationship between stress, immune function, and fitness in yellow-bellied marmots at RMBL.  I will document ecto- and endo-parasite infections and study both causes and consequences of variation in infections.  Causally, I will focus on stress.  Stress has a well-documented effect on immunocompetence.  I will quantify stress physiologically by documenting fecal and blood cortisol levels.  Ectoparasites, fecal, and blood samples will be collected during routine trapping.  The relationship between variation in parasite infection and fitness will be studied by the on-going monitoring of marmots at RMBL.

ResearchPlanTitle: Molecular Studies of Rocky Mountain Plant Reproduction.
ResearchPlanAbstract: Newly developed, highly variable molecular markers permit high resolution analyses of plant growth, mating and dispersal.  Amplified fragment length polymorphisms (AFLP) are sufficiently variable to produce a unique genetic fingerprint of individual plants.  This information can then be used to map the spatial extent of clonal plants and to determine the paternity of seeds in sexually reproducing species.  Cytoplasmically inherited genetic markers, such as mitochondrial and chloroplast DNA, are only inherited from the mother and dispersed only via seeds.  Using such markers seed dispersal can be estimated separately from dispersal through pollen.  My studies of mating and dispersal in three Rocky Mountain wildflowers, Delphinium (larkspur), Geranium, and Chamerion (fireweed) will utilize these genetic markers to address such questions as: 1) how does the size of floral display influence pollinator behavior and the amount of self pollination?, 2) how do male sterility genes spread among populations?, and 3) how does herbivory affect the genetic diversity and extent of clonal growth in colonizing plants?
ResearchPlanOrganisms: Geranium richardsonii, Delphinium barbeyi, Chamerion (Epilobium) angustifolium

ResearchPlanTitle: Plant-pollinator community survey of Virginia Basin
ResearchPlanAbstract: The idea that plant-pollinator interactions are highly specialized is central to the evolution of floral morphology.  To test this idea I am conducting a community level survey of plant-pollinator interactions in a montane meadow system.  I plan to compare the degree of plant-pollinator specialization/generalization with flower and insect morphology.  I expect that those plant species that interact with fewer pollinator species will have concealed nectar that only “long-tongued” insects can reach.  During the summer of 2000 I established three study sites in Virginia Basin, along an elevational gradient.  This summer, two students will re-survey one of these sites to determine if and to what extent plants and pollinators vary in their level of specialization/generalization.

ResearchPlanTitle: A Survey of Herbivory in the Gothic area with focus on browsing resistance and tolerance of Aquilegia coerulea, the Colorado Columbine.

I am curious about the impacts of deer browsing upon Aquilegia coerulea, the Colorado columbine (the state flower). Residents of Gothic, the site of the Rocky Mountain Biological Laboratory have observed a decrease in the appearance of columbine and an increase in the appearance of deer browsing inside the fence. I plan to study the fitness of browsed/unbrowsed columbine plants inside and outside the RMBL fence. I hope to get an idea of the future of the columbine and the overall biodiversity of herbaceous plants in the Gothic area compared to the forest surrounding it where there is less human interaction but also less protection for mule deer.

Our work focuses on identifying the adaptive utility of social behavior, communication, and anti-predator behavior.  In addition, we are trying to identify behavioral mechanisms responsible for demographic parameters and focusing on how disease influences survival and fitness. Finally, we are trying to identify the ways that marmots respond to the systematically warmer temperatures that are documented at the RMBL

ResearchPlanTitle: Oviposition in Euphydryas gillettii: Responses to Microclimatic Heterogeneity
ResearchPlanAbstract: How do organisms respond to variation in their environment?  How are choices made which increase or decrease the fitness of that organism?  I am looking to answer these questions using oviposition in the butterfly Euphydryas gillettii at RMBL.  Using tools of behavioral ecology, ecophysiology, and population biology I have the opportunity to discover the environmental basis of oviposition and how E. gillettii is constrained or cued by its environment to lay eggs.  With this information it will be possible to predict how changes in the environment will affect oviposition.  This research will provide insight into how organisms and populations will respond to changes in the environment from processes such as climate change and habitat destruction.  Additionally, as E. gillettii is an introduced species, further knowledge of its biology will aid in the understanding and prediction of invasion

ResearchPlanTitle: -Biodiversity of midges (Diptera:Chironomidae) and spiders (Araneae) at the Mexican Cut Nature Preserve
ResearchPlanAbstract:
The knowledge of spider diversity in Colorado is expanding rapidly with Dr. Paula Cushing’s “Colorado Spider Survey” at the Denver Museum of Nature and Science.  
 As a part of this survey, I am collecting spiders in the Mexican Cut Nature Preserve along with my collections in the surrounding National Forest Lands.  This work builds on Dr. Levi’s RMBL spider list and will deposit specimens in the Denver Museum’s well regarded spider collection.

The tiny flies commonly referred to as midges are diverse and notoriously difficult to identify.  They are an interesting group because of their sensitivity to various pollutants and are often used for biomonitoring.  The Mexican Cut Chironomids have been identified to genus, but further identification has awaited rearing the larvae to adults.  Regular collections throughout the spring, summer, and fall can help us determine which species are present, the number of generations per year and whether each taxa is sensitive to weather events such as drought or the differences in water chemistry and predation between the various ponds at the Mexican Cut.

ResearchPlanTitle: Predator-induced selection on insect flight and dispersal
ResearchPlanAbstract: Insects are fantastically diverse and ecologically and economically important features of life on earth. The development of aerial flight is a hallmark of insects, and the phenomenon is readily apparent from insect pests to pollinators.  Predation has been suggested as a possible selective agent in the evolution of insect flight but has not been systematically explored.  Interestingly, natural selection by predators may select for traits that enhance aerial flight capability thereby increasing the likelihood of dispersal to areas with lower predation risk.  Stream ecosystems are particularly appropriate systems to explore the role of predators on insect flight because most evidence suggests the first insects and earliest flying insects were aquatic.  This research investigates how natural selection by predatory fish, such as trout, affects traits related to adult insect flight and dispersal.  By using a combination of observational surveys in Rocky Mountain streams, whole-stream additions of fish chemical cues, mark-recapture experiments to measure differences in insect dispersal between fish and fishless streams, manipulations of wing length and susceptibility to fish predation, and models to test multiple hypotheses related to natural selection on insect flight.
ResearchPlanOrganisms:
Stream insects (Plecoptera and Ephemeroptera).  
Stream fishes: Brook trout (Salvelinus fontinalis) and Cutthroat trout (Oncorhynchus clarki)

ResearchPlanTitle: Influence of nest cavity location on parental care in a keystone species, the red-naped sapsucker
ResearchPlanAbstract: Keystone species are those species that exert a disproportionately large influence (relative to their abundance) on the surrounding community. One striking example of a keystone species is the red-naped sapsucker, a woodpecker that nests in aspen woodlands in western North America. Sapsuckers excavate cavities in aspen trees, providing essential nesting habitat for many birds, mammals and invertebrates; they also drill sap wells in willows, providing nourishment for themselves and many other species. Previous studies found that the density of sapsuckers declined with increasing distance from willows and that sapsuckers were absent from aspen groves located > 1 km from willows, suggesting that distance to willows affects sapsucker fitness. My objective is to study the influence of cavity-to-willow distance on parental care in sapsuckers. I hypothesize that feeding of nestlings is limited by time spent flying back and forth between nest and willows and thus predict that nestlings will be fed less frequently when willows are farther away. To measure feeding bouts, behavioral observations will be conducted at approximately 20 sapsucker nest sites located in the upper East River Valley, Washington Gulch, and Anthracite Creek drainages. Results from this study will help guide planning of development and management of aspen and willow habitat.

ResearchPlanTitle: Pollination ecology of Viola: effects of spatial and temporal variation in pollinator communities
ResearchPlanAbstract: The goal of this research is to catalogue the pollinating-insect assemblage visiting violet (Viola spp.) populations at several sites varying in elevation, and to determine how variation in the insect community affects violet reproduction. I hope to discover whether pollen-transfer by insects is limiting violet population growth and if the extent of pollen-limitation varies in any systematic way with pollinator community composition and/or the altitude or seasonal flowering pattern of the plant population. To follow up on this descriptive work, and to better disentangle the roles of geography, flowering phenology, and the biotic community in affecting violet reproduction, I plan to conduct transplant experiments in the field and manipulations of pollinator abundance and diversity on enclosed floral arrays. Ultimately, this information should help determine if interactions between violets and their pollinators are likely to be disrupted by global climate change.
ResearchPlanOrganisms: Viola adunca and V. nuttallii are the main proposed study organisms, along with their pollinators, which are expected to be mainly species of solitary bees.

ResearchPlanTitle: Interaction strength estimates derived from population energetics
ResearchPlanAbstract: Predators can impact prey populations by consuming prey, but prey are also known to alter their movements, feeding patterns, and other behaviors in the presence of predators.  In Rocky Mountain streams, experiments have shown that such non-feeding effects of predatory trout can have large impacts on populations of their mayfly prey.  This study will attempt to use observational data in a natural stream setting to estimate prey consumption and non-feeding effects, and compare these results with those obtained through manipulative experiments.  It is hoped that such a comparison will inform the value of observational data in systems not amenable to experimentation.

ResearchPlanTitle: Growing season length and timing as determinants of sub-alpine plant community structure and function
ResearchPlanAbstract: Global temperatures are expected to increase by several degrees Celsius over the next century and the impact of this increase is expected to be especially significant in high altitude ecosystems.  High altitude ecosystems are characterized by short growing seasons and are therefore particularly sensitive to warming trends that affect the length of the growing season.  Simulated warming experiments in these ecosystems have significantly accelerated the date of snowmelt, thereby extending the growing season.  Several studies at RMBL and elsewhere around the world have shown that snowpack depth and snowmelt timing are key determinants of plant productivity and reproductive success.  Few studies, however, have directly examined the effect of growing season length on plant community structure.  As we develop and improve global change models, it becomes particularly important to identify the specific mechanisms that underlie the changes resulting from present and future warming trends.  This study will provide a direct test of the effects of growing season length and timing on sub-alpine plant community structure and function by independently extending the growing season in the spring and fall.  Furthermore, plant communities that are grazed by large herbivores such as cattle, sheep, and elk are likely to show a greater response to longer growing seasons because their effective recovery following damage may no longer be constrained by the end of the growing season.  It is likely that only certain species will be able to capitalize on an extended recovery period and their disproportionate success may have a significant impact on community structure and function.  This experiment will test that hypothesis.  Building upon this experimental work, mathematical models will be developed to facilitate generalized conclusions about the effects of season length and grazing on montane plant communities.  These models can also be integrated into existing large-scale climate change models to improve their accuracy.
ResearchPlanOrganisms: All plant species within the research plots will be included in the study.

ResearchPlanTitle: Ecosystem Responses and Feedbacks to Climate Change
ResearchPlanAbstract: Since 1990, and with continuous NSF support, I have been studying the effects of climate warming on a subalpine meadow (the “warming meadow”) at the Rocky Mountain Biological Laboratory (RMBL) in Colorado. My approach has been to artificially warm meadow plots and directly study responses, but to extend the generality of our findings in the warming meadow we also observe patterns in climate-ecosystem linkages across natural ecological and climate gradients, and carry out  mathematical modeling. Whereas the experimental manipulations provide a means of discovering the actual mechanisms governing ecosystem responses to warming, the gradient studies and the mathematical models provide a means of scaling up the implications of these mechanisms from plot to landscape scale. The single most important conclusion from all our climate-ecosystem investigations is that ecosystem responses to climate change are likely to trigger large feedback effects and that many of these are more likely to enhance, not reduce, the climate warming episode that is now underway as a consequence of fossil fuel burning.   In addition to the meadow studies,  I am also studying how conifer seedlings along their natural elevational range respond to naturally wetter or dryer clusters of years, thereby gaining insight into how the species composition of montane conifer forests change in response to climate alteration.  The study is designed to also determine the extent to which, within conifer species, there is local adaptation to climate conditions along their elevational range

ResearchPlanTitle: Investigating the potential of an ‘invasional meltdown’: is reproductive success of one alien plant invader species facilitated when co-occurring with another?
ResearchPlanAbstract:
Biological invasions are second only to habitat destruction with respect to their impact on biodiversity, with severe consequences on native ecosystems and the economy well documented (e.g. Drake et. al., 1989). However, invasion ecology, whether taken from the point of view of the ecologist or the weed scientist, has in the past typically focused research on the negative impacts that an alien species has on a native species/community (e.g. competition, herbivory), or vice versa (e.g. herbivory, parasitism). Indeed research investigating positive interactions is comparatively depauperate (Kareiva & Bertness, 1997), despite the acknowledgement that facilitative interactions between native and alien species is widespread and can accelerate the alien species’ invasion and establishment into native communities.

     Even more understudied however, are the potential facilitative interactions among alien invaders themselves (Parker et. al., 1999; Grosholz, 2005). With alien species historically established, and an increasing number of new invaders spreading globally, positive interactions - whether direct or indirect – are inevitable. Such facilitation has been shown to turn an otherwise benign invader into an aggressively expanding one as a result of positive feedback between the invaders (Grosholz 2005). Frequent species introductions could therefore have a synergistic effect at a range of scales, and has been termed ‘invasional meltdown’ by Simberloff & Von Holle (1999). Evidence for this has been documented in coastal (Grosholz, 2005), fresh water (Ricciardi, 2001) and terrestrial systems (O’Dowd, 2003), but research on facilitative interactions between alien species remains scarce. 

     The aim of this study is to investigate the impact of two alien species on each other’s reproduction, this effect being mediated via shared pollinators. Linaria vulgaris and Circium arvense are two established alien plant invader species found in the Rocky Mountains. Measures of reproductive success (fruit and seed set) and rates of insect visitation to these plant species will be compared between populations that have been manipulated to represent a range of relative frequencies where these invader species co-occur.
ResearchPlanOrganisms: Two alien invading plant species, Linaria vulgaris (butter and eggs) and Circium arvense (Canadian thistle), and insect visitors to these plants.

ResearchPlanTitle: Treeline response to global change: feedbacks to regional and global climate
ResearchPlanAbstract:
Abstract1: The location of treeline is related to climate conditions, such as the temperature of soil during the summer and whether there is enough water for trees to grow. With global warming, both temperatures and precipitation are likely to change in the Rocky Mountain region. These changes could reasonably lead to shifts in the location of treeline. This project studies the sensitivity of trees growing near treeline to climate, and the potential environmental consequences of a shift in treeline location

Abstract 2: Globally, both high elevation and low elevation treeline are related to climate, with high elevation treeline controlled by root zone temperature and low elevation treeline determined by water availability. Recent climate trends, and predictions for climate change in the Rocky Mountain region, show temperature and precipitation changes, which could reasonably result in shifts in treeline position. Forest differs from both steppe and alpine meadow vegetation in terms of climate-ecosystem interactions, including energy, water and carbon exchanges. As a result, shifts in treeline have the potential to alter regional (and even global) climate if they are widespread. I am proposing some preliminary monitoring and sampling to look for evidence that upper and lower treeline near RMBL are sensitive to climate change, and to estimate the differences among forest, alpine meadow, and sagebrush-steppe ecosystems in terms of energy, water and carbon cycling. This work will build on past research by John Harte, John’s REU students, and myself, and will involve new collaboration with Chris Still. I also hope to integrate students from my 2006 course into the monitoring/sampling effort.

ResearchPlanTitle: Life history strategies in high altitude copepods: diapause and mate choice.
ResearchPlanAbstract: In the summers of 2001 and 2003, I initiated a study in an attempt to unravel factors that affect the type of egg produced by a small aquatic crustacean copepod, Leptodiaptomus coloradensis.  Two types of eggs are produced: diapausing eggs remain quiescent while subitaneous eggs hatch immediately.  Populations differed in their pattern of egg production in ponds at Mexican Cut, not related to pond permanence, density, temperature, or presence of particular predators, all of which have been implicated in studies of other copepod species  What I found especially intriguing was the fact that a population from one permanent pond produced diapausing eggs only while a population from one autumnal pond (one which evaporates in most summers) continued to produce subitaneous eggs, almost assuredly resulting in massive juvenile mortality.  My major objective in this study is to examine the Mexican Cut ponds already studied and to track the fate of individuals in August (which I have been unable to to as yet).  A second aspect of this project is to determine if in mating, males prefer certain females of a certain size range.This work has evolutionary implications relating to factors influencing the degree of sexual size dimorphism in animals.

ResearchPlanTitle:
NEO MARTINEZ –
1.  SPATIAL VARIATION OF FOOD WEB STRUCTURE IN A MONTANE ECOSYSTEM.
2.  WEBS ON THE WEB (WOW):  
INTERNET DATABASE, ANALYSIS, AND VISUALIZATION OF ECOLOGICAL NETWORKS.
3.  SEMANTIC PROTOTYPES IN RESEARCH ECOINFORMATICS (SPIRE)
4.  INTEGRATED UNDERSTANDING OF ECOLOGICAL COMPLEXITY AT MULTIPLE SCALES
ResearchPlanAbstract: This project aims to document the manner in which food webs or “who eats whom” among species vary over the spatial scale of meters to kilometers.  The trophic interactions that comprise food webs occur between two species when members of one species eat members of the other species.  Just as species present in a given area change over distances of this scale (e.g., from Crested Butte to RMBL), the trophic interactions between species that comprise local food webs also change.  This variation will affect the ability of organisms to survive displacement and extinctions caused by climate change and habitat degradation.  Much productive work at RMBL continues on how community composition varies with area.  This work forms a scientific base upon which to construct food webs of montane meadows at various locations around RMBL.  This research involves field and lab observation of trophic interactions between predators and prey, herbivores (including many pollinators) and plants, and parasitoids and insects.  The overall goal is to establish an empirical base from which to test and generate theory about food webs in space in a manner closely related to species-area research.  Ultimately, the connections between the terrestrial food web and a very diverse food web of the East River will address the effects of habitat boundaries on food web structure.

ResearchPlanTitle: A study on the disease dynamics of avian haemosporidian parasites (Protozoa: Haemosproina) and their vectors (Diptera: Culicidae, Simuliidae, Hippoboscidae, Ceratopogonidae) in a breeding community of birds in western Colorado.
ResearchPlanAbstract: I will study the disease dynamics of avian malaria in a breeding Mountain White-crowned Sparrow (MWCS) population outside of the Rocky Mountain Biological Lab in Gothic, Colorado.  This dense population can provide important insights into the transmission of malaria in its natural environment.  Protozoan blood parasites are ubiquitous in populations of vertebrate wildlife, and have been shown to have important impacts on the life history of their hosts.  Understanding the complex, indirect life cycle of malaria in the wild can serve as a prime model for other vector-borne parasites impacting wildlife and human health such as Eastern equine encephalitis, Western equine encephalitis, St. Louis encephalitis, and West Nile Virus.  To understand how hematozoan blood parasites interact with their environment, basic information on these arthropod hosts and hematozoans will be collected.  I will determine in which habitats arthropod hosts breed and where these habitats are located in relation to sparrow breeding territories using CDC carbon dioxide-baited miniature light traps.  This sampling will allow me to answer the following questions: when do arthropod hosts emerge, when do they die for the season, which species do they belong to, and where they are found.  I will use polymerase chain reaction assays for identification of the parasites that the arthropod vectors carry and I will dissect their salivary glands dissected for infective stages of the parasite to measure vector competency.  Common bird species will be trapped and blood drawn from each bird.  This sampling will allow me to answer the following question: do other bird species host the parasites of interest.  I will run PCR analyses and make blood smears to identify molecularly and visually blood parasites in these birds.

ResearchPlanTitle: Patterns and Mechanisms of Biodiversity in Sub-Alpine Wetlands
ResearchPlanAbstract: I will be trying to determine whether or not ponds can be viewed as islands with respect to patterns of diversity.  Furthermore, I will attempt to determine the reason why larger islands have more diversity than smaller islands.  We currently do not know if it is because 1) colonizers choose areas with more diverse habitats, 2) colonizers choose larger areas for their size alone, or  3) colonizers simply have a higher probability of running into larger areas.  This study has important implications with respect to conservation.  The more we understand about the habitat choices made by colonists, the better we will be at designing preserves that attract displaced individuals.  Furthermore, this study will help us learn more about  colonization dynamics of endangered wetland communities.

ResearchPlanTitle: Variation in the strength of cascading trophic interactions across a riverscape
ResearchPlanAbstract: Natural flow regimes of rivers are undergoing considerable modification due to global change and human use of water.  This research will contribute to understanding how natural variation in flow influences the function of river ecosystems. The grazing of algae by insect larvae is a fundamentally important interaction in rivers that is affected by the flow regime. In some streams large amounts of algae result from ‘trophic cascades’ whereby predators like trout suppress grazing leading to increases in algae. In other streams insect grazers are able to keep algae in check. Extreme events like floods and droughts can influence grazer-algal interactions by affecting the abundance and type of grazers, numbers of trout, algal growth rates, and availability of nutrients.  The effects of variation in flow regimes on grazer-algal interactions will be measured across a river-landscape to unravel the controls on the strength of trophic cascades. This work focuses on species interactions fundamental to many ecosystems; thus it will contribute to producing broadly applicable ecological generalities. Furthermore, the project builds on 30 years of research on streams in the East River valley near the Rocky Mountain Biological Laboratory in Western Colorado.  The fate of water resources is hotly debated in Western Colorado, like many other areas around the world.  By advancing understanding of the effects of natural variation in flow regimes on river inhabitants, the research will provide knowledge valuable for the management of rivers with human-induced changes to river flow.
ResearchPlanOrganisms: Brook trout, stream invertebrates and algae.

ResearchPlanTitle: Visual system and behavior in Lycaena spp. (Lepidoptera).
ResearchPlanAbstract: Many insects and hummingbirds visit flowers to drink their nectar and moving among flowers they also carry the plant’s pollen. To detect and choose flowers they use their olfactory and visual senses. The flower visitation behavior of honeybees and other bees has been extensively studied, and the behavior of other insect pollinators has often been extrapolated from what is known about the visual system of bees. But exploring the eyes of butterflies, which are important pollinators in some plant communities, has showed us that their visual systems are far more diverse than among bees, and thus their behavior, including the choice of preferred nectar plants, is an open question. The butterflies from the genus Lycaena have very peculiar eyes, in which the dorsal and ventral halves differ in terms of the colors they can perceive. From this observation we can ask if the butterflies prefer different flowers depending on the half of the eye they use to detect them, the upper half if they are flying above the flowers, or the lower half if they fly close to the ground. I plan to study the relationship between the visual system and nectar feeding behavior in four Lycaena species abundant in the area where RMBL is located, asking the following questions: Which colors can different Lycaena species perceive? Does their sensitivity to different colors match the colors of the flowers they visit? Do different Lycaena species visit different flowers?

ResearchPlanTitle: Effectiveness of methods to control the spread of the invasive weeds, Cirsium arvense (Canada thistle) and Bromus inermis (Smooth Brome)
ResearchPlanAbstract: Nonnative invasive species are a growing problem in Colorado.  Invasive plants disrupt native communities by forming monocultures, in which native plant diversity is decreased.  Changes in plant composition may affect other members of the community, including soil microbes and mycorrhizae, herbivores, pollinators, and even higher trophic levels.  The goal of this research is to determine the best methods of controlling the spread of two nonnative plants, Cirsium arvense (Canada thistle) and Bromus inermis (Smooth Brome), in the East River Valley.  Specifically, I test whether application of the herbicide, Roundup, to Canada thistle is effective at eradicating small populations.  I also test whether sheets of black plastic can be used to kill smooth brome populations.  In order to help restore native plant communities, I reseed sites with native plant seed.  If these efforts prove successful at eradicating invasive plants and reestablishing native plant communities, I will work with other members of the community to apply these methods to other sites throughout the Gunnison Basin.

ResearchPlanTitle: Evolution in plant hybrid zones
ResearchPlanAbstract:
Related species of flowering plants are often hybridized to generate new horticultural varieties.  Hybrids are also common in natural plant populations.  Where two species come into contact and produce successful hybrids, that area is called a hybrid zone.  Hybridization in these areas can have important consequences for evolution.  It may contribute to the breakdown of reproductive isolation between existing species, result in a stable hybrid zone, reinforce species differences, or even lead to new species.  The evolution of species has attracted the attention of biologists ever since the time of Darwin.  At the RMBL, my colleagues and I are investigating evolutionary processes in plant hybrid zones, with an ultimate goal of understanding speciation.   An understanding of these processes is not only of fundamental importance to basic biology.  Such knowledge can be used to prevent transfer of recombinant genes from crop plants into wild populations of related plants, and also to conserve the many rare species that have come into contact with related non-native species.  
	Our work focuses on hybrid zones between the red-flowered scarlet gilia (Ipomopsis aggregata) and its close relative, the pale pink to white-flowered I. tenuituba.  Flowers of these species are visited frequently by hummingbirds and less often by hawkmoths.  These animals can transfer pollen between the species, producing hybrids in some, but not all, areas where the species grow in close proximity.  The fitness of these hybrids relative to the parental species plays an important role in models of speciation.  Speciation requires development of reproductive isolation between the species.  In one model, reproductive isolation evolves as a consequence of reduced fitness of hybrid individuals.  This reduction in fitness can result from poor pollination, if two different pollinators like birds and moths specialize on the extreme forms.  It can also result from adaptation to two different habitats (e.g. wet vs. dry soil), which may cause hybrids high mortality in the parental environments.  We are testing the roles of pollination and physiological adaptation in the development of reproductive isolation.  This work builds on 12 years of experience with these hybrid zones.  We have already characterized pollination of hybrids, finding that flowers with some intermediate traits receive fewer pollinator visits, but in general most hybrids do not suffer low pollination.  Hybrids of certain genetic make-ups can have high survival in particular habitats.  I have two goals for the next few years.  The first is to build on our studies of physiological adaptation to different habitats, by measuring photosynthetic rates of hybrids under different conditions.  The second is to use DNA markers to map traits on to the Ipomopsis genome, thereby determining the genetic basis of traits involved in speciation.

ResearchPlanAbstract: We designed an experiment to determine if there were consistent individual differences in foraging patterns among Yellow-bellied marmots, Marmota flaviventris, when exposed to three novel stimuli in their natural environment. By exposing the marmots to three different novel stimuli we will be able to vary the context of each situation. The three stimuli we utilized were a mirror in the presence of food, a plastic decoy in the presence of food, and food alone. Upon the first onset of foraging in the presence of the stimuli we collected data that allowed us to analyze the time dedicated to vigilance and time spent foraging across a two minute time period. We were also able to calculate how many times the marmot transitioned from foraging to vigilance behavior during the two minute period. From this information we will be able to determine if there are consistent foraging behaviors in marmots. For example, if a subject in a population forages the most in the presence of the goose when compared to other conspecifics, does this same animal forage the greatest amount of time in the presence of the mirror also? If so, rank order through out the subjects is maintained across two contexts and a behavioral syndrome, a suite of correlated behaviors, can be established. If patterns in the foraging behavior cannot be established then the behavior in the presence of the stimuli will be determined to be context specific.

ResearchPlanTitle: The role of hormones in the regulation of feeding behavior and fat accumulation in the yellow-bellied marmot
ResearchPlanAbstract:
Most organisms adjust their behaviors and physiological processes to the changing environmental conditions that occur between day and night.  In nature, animals exhibit patterns of activities that approximate a 24-hour period or circadian rhythm.
Animals must also respond to seasonal cycles as well as circadian cycles.  In recent studies, there is a great body of evidence to support the idea that these the rhythms of activity, both external and internal are controlled by hormones.  The yellow-bellied marmot (Marmota flaviventris) is a ground-dwelling squirrel that must gain significant mass over the summer to ensure over-winter survival.  Yellow-bellied marmots hibernate and do not feed during hibernation, but must rely on stored body fat during winter.  In this study, I propose to study the role of hormones known to control hunger and satiety in controlling the daily and seasonal fluctuations in feeding as a means of storing body fat for hibernatio

ResearchPlanAbstract: How do organisms respond to variation in their environment?  How are choices made which increase or decrease the fitness of that organism? Using tools of behavioral ecology, ecophysiology, and population biology I have the opportunity to discover the environmental basis of oviposition and how E. gillettii is constrained or cued by its environment to lay eggs.  With this information it will be possible to predict how changes in the environment will affect oviposition.  This research will provide insight into how organisms and populations will respond to changes in the environment from processes such as climate change and habitat destruction.  Additionally, as E. gillettii is an introduced species, further knowledge of its biology will aid in the understanding and prediction of invasion biology.

ResearchPlanTitle: Effectiveness of methods to control the spread of the invasive weeds, Cirsium arvense (Canada thistle) and Bromus inermis (Smooth Brome)

Changes in plant composition may affect other members of the community, including soil microbes and mycorrhizae, herbivores, pollinators, and even higher trophic levels.  The goal of this research is to determine the best methods of controlling the spread of two nonnative plants, Cirsium arvense (Canada thistle) and Bromus inermis (Smooth Brome), in the East River Valley.  Specifically, I test whether application of the herbicide, Roundup, to Canada thistle is effective at eradicating small populations.  I also test whether sheets of black plastic can be used to kill smooth brome populations.  In order to help restore native plant communities, I reseed sites with native plant seed.  If these efforts prove successful at eradicating invasive plants and reestablishing native plant communities, I will work with other members of the community to apply these methods to other sites throughout the Gunnison Basin.

ResearchPlanTitle: Reciprocal benefits in a plant-pollinator mutualism
ResearchPlanAbstract:
<p>Every organism is likely involved in one or many mutualistic partnerships (vital cooperative interactions between species).  For example, most flowering plants require animal pollination for successful reproduction and bee pollinators rely on pollen and nectar from flowers for their sole food source.  

</p>Thus, each species has the potential to influence the health of its partner’s population, which could subsequently influence their own population.  </p><p>However, coupled benefits may depend on the quality or quantity of partners and with additional species in the community.  The goal of this research is to test how plant and pollinator traits, population densities, and other interacting species (such as seed predators) mediate the benefits for both partners.  By experimentally manipulating and measuring responses in both species, this study will provide novel insights into the role of mutualisms in coupled ecological and evolutionary processes.   </p>

To follow up on this descriptive work, and to better disentangle the roles of geography, flowering phenology, and the biotic community in affecting violet reproduction, I plan to conduct transplant experiments in the field and manipulations of pollinator abundance and diversity on enclosed floral arrays. Ultimately, this information should help determine if interactions between violets and their pollinators are likely to be disrupted by global climate change.

ResearchPlanTitle: Ecosystem Responses and Feedbacks to Climate Change
ResearchPlanAbstract: Since 1990, and with continuous NSF support, I have been studying the effects of climate warming on a subalpine meadow (the “warming meadow”) at the Rocky Mountain Biological Laboratory (RMBL) in Colorado. My approach has been to artificially warm meadow plots and directly study responses, but to extend the generality of our findings in the warming meadow we also observe patterns in climate-ecosystem linkages across natural ecological and climate gradients, and carry out  mathematical modeling. Whereas the experimental manipulations provide a means of discovering the actual mechanisms governing ecosystem responses to warming, the gradient studies and the mathematical models provide a means of scaling up the implications of these mechanisms from plot to landscape scale. The single most important conclusion from all our climate-ecosystem investigations is that ecosystem responses to climate change are likely to trigger large feedback effects and that many of these are more likely to enhance, not reduce, the climate warming episode that is now underway as a consequence of fossil fuel burning.   In addition to the meadow studies,  I am also studying how conifer seedlings along their natural elevational range respond to naturally wetter or dryer clusters of years, thereby gaining insight into how the species composition of montane conifer forests change in response to climate alteration.  The study is designed to also determine the extent to which, within conifer species, there is local adaptation to climate conditions along their elevational range

Forest differs from both steppe and alpine meadow vegetation in terms of climate-ecosystem interactions, including energy, water and carbon exchanges. As a result, shifts in treeline have the potential to alter regional climate if they are widespread. I am proposing some preliminary monitoring and sampling to look for evidence that upper and lower treeline near RMBL are sensitive to climate change, and to estimate the differences among forest, alpine meadow, and sagebrush-steppe ecosystems in terms of energy, water and carbon cycling. ResearchPlanTitle: A study on the disease ecology of avian haemosporidian parasites (Protozoa: Haemosproina) and their vectors (Diptera: Culicidae, Simuliidae, Hippoboscidae, Ceratopogonidae) in a breeding community of birds in western Colorado.
ResearchPlanAbstract: Understanding the ecology of wildlife pathogens that utilize multiple vertebrate hosts requires identification of the animal species that play the more significant roles in transmission and long-term maintenance of the pathogen.  Currently most mathematical models describing vector-borne disease assume that encounters between vector and host occur randomly.  However, most biting fly species do show preferences for certain vertebrate host species which may facilitate or dilute transmission of vector-borne pathogens and may have serious implications for estimating the reproductive number of the pathogen.  To address these issues, this study focuses on the transmission ecology of avian malaria parasites in a breeding community of birds located outside of the Rocky Mountain Biological Laboratory.  I will investigate the bird host community composition through point counts, and I will assess the feeding patterns of vectors by collecting blood fed mosquitoes throughout the summer of 2007.  I will amplify vertebrate DNA from blood meals with order-specific primers, and I will sequence and identify to species-level any amplified bird DNA.  Additionally, parasite stages from the collected mosquitoes will be amplified using parasite genus-specific primers and sequences.  Vector preference, capacity, and competence will then be calculated.

ResearchPlanTitle: Beaver impoundments as discontinuities of stream networks
ResearchPlanAbstract: Previous studies observing beaver influences on streams have focused primarily on effects downstream of the dams, and have used upstream reaches flowing into beaver ponds as reference sites.  However, the presence of the impoundment causes the water table to rise around the pond and could also affect reaches upstream of the pond through increased upwelling zones within the stream.  Thus, reaches upstream from beaver ponds should be considered separately as potentially-altered systems and both upstream and downstream reaches should be compared to independent reference sites to better understand the spatial extent of effects of beaver activity upstream and downstream of impoundments. In this study, I plan to investigate the effects of beavers on stream invertebrate food webs and life histories both upstream and downstream from beaver ponds along stream continua near the Rocky Mountain Biological Lab in western Colorado. An experimental design comparing beaver modified stream reaches to unmodified reference stream reaches will provide a robust test of the influence of beaver ponds on stream invertebrates both downstream and upstream of beaver impoundments. ResearchPlanAbstract:
(Iï¿½m only providing a non-technical abstract for the invasive species and pollination work. Please ask if you would like non-technical abstracts for the other research in this renewal application.)

Human activities have dramatically altered Earthï¿½s natural systems. Chief among these alterations is the accidental and intentional movement of plants and animals around the world. Biological invasions, the establishment and spread of non-native species into new environments, have substantial economic and environmental costs and are now considered a leading component of human-induced environmental change. Many invasive plants require pollinators for successful reproduction and spread. If invasive plants are very successful in attracting pollinators in their new environment, what impact might this have on the pollination of native flowering species? The aim of this research is to test how an invasive plant affects native plant communities by measuring pollinator visitation, pollination, and native plant seed production. The work will address this aim using the invasive plant, Linaria vulgaris, in the western United States. Linaria vulgaris is considered a noxious invasive species in the Rocky Mountains. The abundant, showy flowers of Linaria vulgaris are very attractive to native pollinators; however, the effects of this invader on native plant-pollinator interactions and native plant seed production are unknown. On a world-wide basis, almost 90% of flowering plants rely on insects or other animals for pollination service, and the conservation of native plant-pollinator interactions has both ecological and economic importance. Results from this project will contribute broadly to our understanding of the effects of invasive species on native species, in this case through a relatively unexplored mechanism, changes in pollination service. Moreover, studies combining pollination biology and species invasions offer an excellent opportunity to train students in experimental methods and natural history, and this research will provide for human resource development at multiple academic levels.
