<p style=\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\"text-indent: 0.5in;\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\" class=\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\"MsoNormal\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\">Global temperatures are expected to
increase by several degrees Celsius over the next century and the impact of
this increase is expected to be especially significant in high altitude
ecosystems.<span>  </span>Climate change is further
expected to alter patterns of precipitation and nutrient availability and human
activities are increasing the amount of nitrogen that enters the terrestrial
environment.<span>  </span>In alpine ecosystems, a
large proportion of this nitrogen collects in the winter snowpack and it is released
in a large pulse at snowmelt.<span>  </span><span>       </span></p> <span style=\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\"font-size: 10pt; font-family: Arial;\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\">My research investigates the effects of enhanced
nitrogen deposition on subalpine plant communities under climate change
scenarios.<span>  </span>I am particularly interested
in the effects of nitrogen pulse timing because climate change may alter
snowmelt timing, potentially desynchronizing the snowmelt nitrogen pulse from
the species that are adapted to take advantage of it.<span>  </span>I am also investigating interactions between
enhanced nitrogen and climate warming and between enhanced nitrogen and
late-season grazing.<span>   </span>Finally, I test
the hypothesis that rapid (pulse) disturbances can lead to abrupt community
changes when superimposed on sustained (press) disturbances.</span>

ResearchPlanTitle: Coalition formation in a semi-social species, the yellow-bellied marmot.
ResearchPlanAbstract: Complex cooperative coalitions are typically described and studied in species with highly developed social and cognitive characteristics.  This definition may be unnecessarily restrictive, however, because coalitions have previously been described in less social species.  A coalition can be defined as the sum of several component traits:  group formation, individual discrimination, and cooperation. With the adoption of a broader ‘trait-based’ definition of coalitionary behavior, it will be possible to study the evolution of these traits, and therefore generate novel insights into the evolution and maintenance of coalitions.  The proposed work applies this approach to study facultatively social male yellow-bellied marmots (Marmota flaviventris).  With the use of DNA microsatellite techniques, I first study the fitness consequences of grouping for male marmots.  Then, through two field experiments, I determine the individual recognition abilities of male marmots and document the presence or absence of male cooperation.  By doing so, this research illustrates the utility of applying a trait-based approach to the study of coalitions and should serve as a model for future studies.
Subject: None

ResearchPlanTitle: Herbivory and the dynamics of a weedy plant (Chamerion angustifolium, Fireweed).
ResearchPlanAbstract: Natural enemies are imported in efforts to control the spread of exotic invasive species, on the theory that these “biological control” organisms have a strong impact on the pest species in its native habitat.  This project examines the influence of herbivores (from a specialist beetle to deer) on the population dynamics and dispersal potential of Fireweed, a native plant that has all the characteristics of an invasive species.  Fireweed disperses to disturbed sites, then spreads by clonal growth, and can dominate patches of meadow.  I am tracking 40+ patches of Fireweed at various stages of development around the RMBL, examining rates and types of herbivory, patch expansion, and seed production,   Results to date indicate that herbivores can have a strong and sometimes surprising impact on Fireweed’s ability to spread, and that the effects of an herbivore species may depend on the presence of another kind of herbivore.
ResearchPlanOrganisms: Fireweed (Chamerion angustifolium – probably – species cluster, taxonomy in dispute) and herbivores, primarily Adoxis obscurus, a chrysomelid beetle.
Subject: None

ResearchPlanTitle: Colony and population structure of Tapinoma sessile
ResearchPlanAbstract: Certain ant species become invasive upon being introduced into a new environment. It is thought that the introduction event and/or habitat disturbance is responsible for the change in ant colony structure, yet it is very difficult to determine the relative roles of these factors.  Being native to North America and found in both natural and urban landscapes, the odorous house ant, Tapinoma sessile, could be an excellent model species to understand how habitat disturbance may impact colony and population structure.  Colonies of T. sessile are abundant and relatively small in natural areas such as at RMBL compared with urban environments in the southeastern U.S where single colonies may contain thousands of workers and hundreds of queens within nests across areas as large as one hectare.  We will measure colony and population parameters such as worker and queen number, foraging ranges, and geographic and genetic distance between colonies in the two ranges.

ResearchPlanTitle: Behavior and Ecology of Burying Beetles (Coleoptera: Nicrophorus)
ResearchPlanAbstract: I have a long-term research project on the population dynamics of the burying beetle Nicrophorus investigator and have conducted a variety of field experiments on their reproduction, including mating and parental care behaviors, and ecology.  There are five areas of research that I am particularly interested in pursuing:  1) predicting the duration and extent of parental care; 2) understanding the role of multiple mating in females; 3) understanding the fitness benefits of alternative mating strategies in males and females, 4) determining the role of dispersal on the local population structure and the potential for local adaptation, and 5) correlating the abundance of rodents with beetle population dynamics. I use a variety of behavioral observation and census and molecular genetic techniques
ResearchPlanOrganisms: Nicrophorus spp, small rodents (Peromyscus, Microtus, Zapus)
Subject: None

ResearchPlanTitle: Spatial organization and demography of golden-mantled ground squirrels
ResearchPlanAbstract: The demography of ground-dwelling squirrels, particularly reproduction and survival, may be influenced by both intrinsic and extrinsic factors.  Intrinsic influences result from their spatial organization.  Most ground-dwelling squirrels live in social groups comprised of related females; females cooperate in predator defense, thereby enhancing survival, but competition for resources among crowded females may depress reproduction.  Extrinsic factors include the availability of food in the form of herbaceous vegetation.  I am studying spatial organization and demography of the golden-mantled ground squirrel, considered a nonsocial species.  The species has not been studied, but females are believed to live alone in home ranges that do not overlap, presumably denying them the benefits of sociality.  However, these solitary females may obtain some of these benefits; I suspect that some females live adjacent to close relatives, sharing some space and exhibiting some degree of cooperation, with resultant demographic benefits.  Further, my expectation is that survival and reproduction will be affected by the time of snowmelt each spring, which determines growth of herbaceous vegetation, and perhaps by amount of summer rainfall.

ResearchPlanTitle: Does the pollen environment affect pollen receipt?
ResearchPlanAbstract: Most plants rely on insects and other animals - the pollinators of their flowers - to reproduce, and this service from the animals often limits the number of seeds a plant makes.  The ultimate goal of our research is to understand why plants often receive less pollen than needed for full reproduction.  We hypothesize that the plant\\\'s pollen environment - how much pollen is available from nearby flowers to be brought to its flowers by pollinators is crucial.  The number of available pollinators itself might be limiting, and this has been studied at the RMBL, but the underlying availability of pollen has not been studied.  We plan two approaches.  First, using several common plant species at the RMBL whose pollination has been well studied, we will explore at what times of day flowers release their pollen.  They should do so when their major pollinators are most active, and (if possible) when insects that steal pollen for food are least active, thereby maximizing the pollen environment.  This prediction will be tested by characterizing the daily activity of pollinators (bumble bees and hummingbirds) and pollen thieves (flies).  Second, by experimentally stripping pollen from flowers, we will measure whether a reduction in the pollen environment detectably reduces pollen receipt, and on what spatial scale.  These studies are first steps toward a deeper understanding of factors that limit plant reproduction, an issue of importance for applied ecology, including crop yield and the persistence of rare plants?
ResearchPlanOrganisms: Ipomopsis aggregata, Castilleja linariaefolia, Lonicera involucrata,Delphinium barbeyi, Aquilegia elegantula, A. coerulea - and the insects and hummingbirds that visit their flowers

ResearchPlanTitle: Social structure and its effects in yellow-bellied marmots
ResearchPlanAbstract: Social structure and interactions can have important effects on animals, for example, through spread of pathogens. My research will examine the social structure and parasites of yellow-bellied marmots (Marmota flaviventris) at RMBL. My work will add to the long-term research of this population of marmots by focusing on novel aspects of social interactions and parasitism. Specifically, I will be using social network analysis and looking at the relationship between social interactions and parasite prevalence and transmission.

ResearchPlanTitle: Evolutionary Ecology and Conservation Biology of Amphibians
ResearchPlanAbstract: Using tiger salamanders as a model system, my research has two main thrusts:  understanding the evolutionary ecology of trait variation, and answering fundamental questions in conservation biology.  My evolutionary ecology research is aimed at understanding how variation in important traits is maintained in natural populations, and how environmental conditions influence the expression and evolution of trait variation.  I study tiger salamanders, which exhibit two distinct polymorphisms in which the “morphs” or forms are induced by different environmental cues.  By following several populations of salamanders in the field, I am gaining unique insight into the ecology and evolution of these life history polymorphisms.  Furthermore, rearing experiments of salamander larvae have allowed me to begin separating cause and effect regarding the production and maintenance of each polymorphism.  One component of my conservation biology research is understanding the mechanisms controlling population fluctuations in salamander populations.  By determining the factors affecting such dynamics in tiger salamanders, we should gain insight into the general conditions regulating other animal populations, and perhaps learn ways to distinguish natural population fluctuations from declines.  My research thus has direct implications for ecological and evolutionary theory as well as conservation and management.

ResearchPlanTitle: Scaling the functional attributes of plants, communities, and ecosystems across elevational gradients: Responses to climate change
ResearchPlanAbstract: An important question in ecology is to understand how attributes of species influence the functioning of ecosystems.  This study is designed to forge links between variation in the physical environment (e.g., changes in temperature and precipitation with elevation), changes in the functional attributes of plant species (plant size, leaf morphology and physiology etc.) and the functioning of whole ecosystems (the fluxes of carbon and water). Synthesizing this knowledge is critical for predicting responses of the biosphere to climate change. The mountainous landscape in and around RMBL provides enormous range of physical conditions, from warm wet meadows to cold dry ridge tops. The resulting plant communities are likewise both functionally and phylogenetically diverse. We propose to assess how plant functional diversity and whole ecosystem fluxes vary across a range of elevations and environments. Our work at RMBL will be part of a larger global project.  We are in the process of starting similar elevational studies of plant functional diversity and ecosystem fluxes across elevational gradients in SE Arizona and Costa Rica. Data from these field studies will form the basis for the development and testing of mechanistic, predictive models linking the functional attributes of organisms to large scale processes in plant communities and ecosystems.

ResearchPlanTitle: CAREER:Linking heterogeneity to the contributions made by species to ecosystem processes
ResearchPlanAbstract: Stream flows are being altered worldwide to meet human needs and there exists a pressing need for ecologists to provide society with an understanding of what flows are necessary to prevent species loss and allow streams to provide essential ecosystem services.  By exploring the relationship between stream flow, heterogeneity, and herbivory, this project provides a basis for understanding the relationship between stream discharge and function; by examining how stream flow and heterogeneity influence species contributions to stream function, it provides a basis for understanding the causes and consequences of species loss.  Ultimately, the project has the potential to provide resource managers with a process-based measure for establishing minimum stream flows.

ResearchPlanTitle: Effects of vegetative damage on life-history traits in Scarlet gilia, Ipomopsis aggregata
ResearchPlanAbstract: Plants may experience damage from herbivores, pathogens, or physical disturbance at any stage of their lives, and the consequences can be variable, ranging from outright mortality to altered life history and changes in vegetative or floral architecture.  It is my goal to examine the long-term consequences of damage that occurs to plants as vegetative rosettes.  Knowledge of such consequences is important to our overall understanding of the ecological and evolutionary responses of plants to herbivores.

ResearchPlanTitle: Immunocompetence and life history trade-offs in passerine birds
ResearchPlanAbstract: Parasites and pathogens have a ubiquitous but hidden presence in natural ecosystems; because of their constant presence, vertebrates have evolved a sophisticated system of immune responses to control infection. Until a few years ago, wildlife physiologists assumed that immune defenses were energetically cheap and always activated. Indeed it was not until very recently that scientists documented that wildlife immune responses are not only costly to an animal but are also under constant modulation. A wild bird for example, must constantly choose how much energy and nutrients need to be allocated towards activation and maintenance of its immune system, somatic growth (e.g. molt) and reproduction. The optimal response depends not only on the time of the year (reproductive vs. non-reproductive season) but also on the amount of food available as well as the overall presence of pathogens. Although we know today that breeding birds down-regulate their immune system during the energetically challenging period of reproduction, there is no clear understanding how the presence of disease or overall food availability impacts reproductive effort. The goal of this study is to disentangle the relationships between up-regulation of the immune system, reproduction and growth in wild birds under different conditions of food availability.

ResearchPlanTitle:
1) Long-term monitoring of the impacts of fluctuating densities of salamanders and inter-annual variation in hydroperiod on pond invertebrate prey communities  (5 yr)

2) Effects of caddisflies on detritus processing, nutrient release, and benthic algae. (1 yr)
ResearchPlanAbstract:
1) Over the past 20 years, we have observed that the two most important variables that affect the community composition of small ponds and wetlands near the RMBL are 1) the presence and abundance of salamander predators, and 2) the hydroperiod (if, when, and for how long the dry in summer or autumn) of the ponds. Thus, on an annual basis, my research team intensively samples the planktonic and benthic invertebrates at the Mexican Cut ponds.   These data, combined with salamander census data collected by Dr. Howard Whiteman allow us to test the hypothesis that overall biomass, and that of particularly vulnerable taxa exhibits long-term oscillations coupled with the salamander population.  Over the past  5 years, we have been slowly changing from a manual, catch-as-catch can method of determining pond hydroperiod to one that relies on continuous monitoring using data loggers.  Each year, we add a few data loggers to ponds at Mexican Cut and to the Kettle Ponds, and each we download data from existing loggers.  Monitoring long-term trends in when ponds dry is of obvious application for understanding how global climate change affects the  ecology of high elevation wetlands and ponds. 

2) Fluctutaions in the abundance of salamanders in the Mexican Cut ponds results in major changes in the density of detritus (dead plant material)-feeding caddisflies.   During summer 2007, we conducted an experiment in which we manipulated caddisfly densities and observed dramatic changes in the rate at which detritus is processed. During summer 2008 we plan conduct additional experiments to determine if increased detritus processing results in the release of nutrients, and hence stimulates the growth of benthic algae.   Our hypothesis is that long-term changes in the abundance of the top predator (salamanders) in the Mexican Cut ponds has cascading effects on invertebrates which in turn affect basic ecosystem processes such as the mobilization of energy and nutrients in detritus into the aquatic food web.
Subject: Long-Term

ResearchPlanTitle: Plant energy investment in changing environments
ResearchPlanAbstract: I am interested in the fitness consequences of patterns of energy allocation in plants in variable environments.  The biotic environments I consider are imposed by interactions with insect herbivores and pollinators.  These plant-insect interactions are of interest for several reasons: they are among the most frequent species interactions; they can lead to unexpected outcomes when pollinators and herbivores interact indirectly through their host plants; and they can place conflicting selection pressures on host plant populations when pollinators and herbivores respond to similar plant characteristics (size, height, visibility).  Conflicting pressures from mutualists and antagonists make ï¿½correctï¿½ energy investment patterns important for plant fitness.  My research will explore energy allocation patterns and fitness consequences in the fireweed host plant-bumblebee pollinator-beetle herbivore system at the Rocky Mountain Biological Lab.

ResearchPlanTitle: A study on the disease ecology of avian haemosporidian parasites (Protozoa: Haemosporoina) and their vectors (Diptera: Culicidae, Simuliidae, and Ceratopogonidae) in a breeding community of birds in Colorado.
ResearchPlanAbstract: I will study the disease dynamics of avian malaria in a breeding Mountain White-crowned Sparrow (MWCS) population outside of the Rocky Mountain Biological Lab in Gothic, Colorado.  This dense population can provide important insights into the transmission of malaria in its natural environment.  Protozoan blood parasites are ubiquitous in populations of vertebrate wildlife, and have been shown to have important impacts on the life history of their hosts.  To understand how hematozoan blood parasites interact with their environment, basic information on these arthropod hosts and hematozoans will be collected.  I will determine in which habitats arthropod hosts breed and where these habitats are located in relation to sparrow breeding territories using CDC carbon dioxide-baited miniature light traps.  This sampling will allow me to answer the following questions: when do arthropod hosts emerge, when do they die for the season, which species do they belong to, and where they are found.  Additionally, understanding the ecology of wildlife pathogens that utilize multiple vertebrate hosts requires identification of the animal species that play the more significant roles in transmission and long-term maintenance of the pathogen.  Most biting fly species do show preferences for certain vertebrate host species which may facilitate or dilute transmission of vector-borne pathogens and may have serious implications for estimating the reproductive number of the pathogen.  I will attempt to sample resting blood fed individuals with resting boxes and from natural resting areas in addition to host-seeking individuals captured in the light traps.  I then will use polymerase chain reaction assays for identification of the parasites that the arthropod vectors carry as well as the vertebrate hosts vectors feed on.  Finally, point counts will be conducted and common bird species will be mist netted and blood drawn from each bird.  This sampling will allow me to determine the abundances of local bird species as well as what blood parasites they carry.  I will then run PCR analyses and make blood smears to identify molecularly and visually blood parasites in these birds.

ResearchPlanTitle: Does stone texture really matter to algae and aquatic food webs?
ResearchPlanAbstract:
Plants form the base in terrestrial food webs, whereas algae form the base of aquatic food webs. In rocky streams, algae are usually dominated by diatoms, which form brownish slippery coats on stones. Diatoms are small, one-celled algae that have beautiful glass-like outer walls and store energy as oil making them highly nutritious for grazing insects and snails.

My research is on the interaction of diatoms and their stone substrates. Previous experiments have shown that stone chemistry has little effect on diatoms. In contrast, the small-scale surface texture of stones influences diatoms by providing crevices that protect diatoms from grazers and floods.

This summer (2008) I will extend this research by investigating whether the diatoms protected by stone texture affect stream food webs via the growth of grazing insects. Diatoms multiply quickly, such that diatoms protected in crevices during intense grazing multiply may spill out, providing additional food for grazers (and allow more grazer growth). 

These investigations will use streamside experiments to see whether the growth rate of grazers, especially baetid mayflies, differs among rocks of different textures. Rocks in the streams near RMBL range from very smooth slate to rougher sandstones and quartzites, allowing this research to be done under near-natural conditions.

If results show that rock roughness affects grazer production, this knowledge will affect our understanding of factors affecting the distribution of grazers in streams and even why some streams are more productive than others.

ResearchPlanTitle: The effect of sampling effort on species diversity estimates of pollinators of uncommon plants
ResearchPlanAbstract: In order to assess the impact of an invasive species on the pollination of native species in a community of flowering plants, a community-wide pollination web is in the process of being constructed.  My project will demonstrate how differences in sampling effort (time spent observing each plant species and recording visitors that interact with the plant) influence the characterization of eight focal plant species and record the visitor species that interact with the plants.  I will quantify the amount of sampling effort that is necessary to fully measure the number of pollinator visitors to each plant.  This will expose inadequacies in the larger pollination web, if present, and frame investigation into the creation of pollination webs in the future.

ResearchPlanTitle: Olfactory abilities of yellow-bellied marmots (Marmota flaviventris) in distinguishing predators
ResearchPlanAbstract: Many prey species have shown a response to the olfactory cues of their predators.  The ability of yellow-bellied marmots to detect and distinguish between predator odors will be studied.  This research can provide more information about antipredator behavior in general, and has applied value to conservation efforts.  The behavior of yellow-bellied marmots will be observed when they are presented with a familiar herbivore odor, and both familiar and novel predator odors.  This will determine whether they can distinguish between predators and non-predators, the riskiness of a predator, and if they are able to detect novel predators.

ResearchPlanTitle: Changing distributions, Changing Climate:  Using Bombus as an Indicator of Global Warming near Crested Butte, Colorado
ResearchPlanAbstract: The goal of this study is to compare the distributions of the bumble bee species of RMBL with their former distributions as described in Graham Pyke’s work in 1974.  Pyke described a pattern of replacement of bees with similar tongue lengths as one moves up an elevational gradient.  Now, thirty-three years later we want to replicate this study to see if the ranges of the bumble bees have changed.  Especially of interest is the question of whether the lower elevation bees are moving up in elevation in response to global warming.
Subject: Climate Change

ResearchPlanTitle: The Effects of Terraced and Non-terraced Beaver Ponds on Benthic Invertebrate Communities
ResearchPlanAbstract: The effects of beavers as ecological engineers are far reaching. Beaver ponds have the potential to greatly affect many hydrological factors such as stream velocity, temperature and nutrient content. However, pondsâ€™ effects on factors such as these vary. The reason for these sometimes conflicting results might be tied to pond morphology, a factor often overlooked. Beaver ponds come in many different shapes and sizes. It is likely that these differences in shape and size play a role in determining each pondâ€™s effects on stream hydrology and downstream biogeochemistry. With this considerable potential for influence of downstream conditions, it is also likely that pond morphology will affect algal growth and food availability for algal grazers and other functional feeding groups of benthic invertebrates. The principle objectives of this research project are to determine: 1) whether benthic invertebrate functional feeding group composition differs between the areas upstream and downstream of beaver ponds; and 2) whether the relative abundances of benthic invertebrate functional feeding groups associated with beaver ponds differ according to pond morphology. In addition to benthic invertebrate sampling, measurements of biogeochemical factors will also be taken into account as possible mechanisms for differences in functional feeding groups between sample sites.
Subject: Phenology

ResearchPlanTitle: Pollination subsidies between wetland and dry meadow habitats
ResearchPlanAbstract: I am investigating how wetland areas might subsidize nearby dry meadows by providing more floral rewards to pollinators and increasing pollinator visitation rates.

ResearchPlanTitle: The effects of ants on membracid size and instar
ResearchPlanAbstract: This project aims to determine the mechanism by which treehopper nymphs grow in the presence of ants.  It is known that nymphs are larger with their mutualist partner (ant) present.  There are two ways in which the nymphs can grow:  (1) growing faster and therefore older with ants present, (2) growing slower but being larger for a given stage of development.  This study will investigate which of the two ways the nymphs are growing by manipulating the presence or absence of ants to the nymphs during development.  Four samples of the nymphs will be taken in four weeks. Stage of nymph development and size of nymph will be determined and analyzed over time with respect to treatment group (ants or no ants)

ResearchPlanTitle: Water Availability and Root Nodulation in Lupine (Lupinus argenteus)
ResearchPlanAbstract: Lupine is one of the few plant species that can trap nitrogen from the atmosphere by means of a bacterium found in its root nodules. My research will focus on whether lupine’s growth rate and maturity is limited by soil nitrogen or by soil moisture along an elevational gradient near Gothic, CO. I will do so by monitoring the growth and production of root nodules at both wet and dry environments of three different altitudes: higher than Gothic—Schofield Pass and Emerald Lake; Gothic—Maxfield Meadow and RMBL town site; and lower than Gothic—Kettle Ponds. I expect that plants in a moist environment will be nutrient limited, rather than drought limited, and should therefore produce more root nodules in response to using up most of the available soil nitrogen. I expect plants in dry sites to be drought limited rather than nutrient limited, and they should therefore require more water than their environment can provide, instead of investing a great deal of energy to produce costly, yet unnecessary, root nodules.
Subject: Climate Change

ResearchPlanTitle:
1)  Implementing management to control the spread of the invasive weed, Bromus inermis (Smooth Brome)
2)  Testing the effectiveness of the herbicide, Round Up, for eliminating satellite Linaria vulgaris (Butter and Eggs) populations.
3)  Restoration of native vegetation at the Bench mine tailings site.
ResearchPlanAbstract: Nonnative invasive species are a growing problem in Colorado.  Invasive plants disrupt native communities by forming monocultures, in which native plant diversity is decreased.  Changes in plant composition may affect other members of the community, including soil microbes and mycorrhizae, herbivores, pollinators, and even higher trophic levels.  The goal of the proposed research is to first determine the best methods of controlling the spread of nonnative invasive plants.  Second, we use the results of the research to guide management of the invasives and restoration of disturbed sites.  Specifically, I propose to do 3 things as part of RMBLï¿½s invasive plant management program. 1)  I plan to test whether application of the herbicide, Round Up, to Linaria vulgaris is effective at eradicating small satellite populations.  2)  I also propose to implement management of smooth brome populations by applying black plastic to a number of populations within the townsite of Gothic.  In order to help restore native plant communities, I would like to add sawdust or small woodchips to sites and subsequently reseed sites with native plant seed. 3)  I propose a plan of action for restoring native vegetation to the Bench mine tailings site.  If these efforts prove successful at eradicating invasive plants and reestablishing native plant communities, I will work with other members of the community to apply these methods to other sites throughout the Gunnison Basin.
ResearchPlanOrganisms: Bromus inermis, Linaria vulgaris, many native plants near the Bench restoration site.
Subject: Other

ResearchPlanTitle: A search for flower constancy and preference among butterflies
ResearchPlanAbstract: My research will ask; are representatives of younger, more advanced butterfly families less flower constant, as might be expected if they have better learning capacities, enabling them to pollinate wider variety of species?  Is constancy a widespread phenomenon, or only a behavior present in primitive families of Lepidoptera?  Also, do butterflies have the ability to discriminate against color in order to chose based on morphology?  A series of experiments for each of three species will be carried out to answer these questions.  A grid of 6x8 cut flowers composed of two species of flower will be arranged randomly and observed for butterfly visitation.  Acrylic paint will be used to manipulate color of the flowers to determine how these species of butterfly choose what they feed from.
ResearchPlanOrganisms: Speyeria mormonia, Lycaena heteronea, Cercyonis oetus, Phyciodes campestris, Wyethia amplexicus, Dugaldia hoopesii
Subject: Other

ResearchPlanTitle: The effects of atmospheric nitrogen deposition on denitrification and nitrous oxide flux in lakes
ResearchPlanAbstract: Elevated nitrogen (N) inputs to lakes can degrade water quality and result in eutrophication, because primary production in freshwater ecosystems is as frequently limited by N as by phosphorus. Microbially-mediated denitrification in lake sediments reduces the effects of N loading by converting N that may otherwise be available for uptake, transformation, or transport, into atmospheric di-nitrogen. Denitrification also produces nitrous oxide (N2O), a powerful green house gas, as an intermediate product. Whereas the effects of anthropogenic N inputs on denitrification and related N2O emissions have been well studied in terrestrial and marine ecosystems, similar research in lakes is lacking. Furthermore, the spatial variability of denitrification in lakes is not well understood. This study will address gaps in our current knowledge through two research elements. First, I will investigate rates of denitrification and N2O emissions in lake sediments across a gradient of atmospheric N deposition in the central Rocky Mountains in Colorado, with comparisons between lakes, within lakes across a water depth gradient, and within the sediment profile.  Second, this study will be among the first to measure N2O emissions from the surface of lakes and to investigate potential sources in the sediments and in the water column. This study will provide insight into the spatial heterogeneity of (1) sediment denitrification and of (2) sediment and water column N2O flux.
Subject: Climate Change

ResearchPlanTitle: Effects of atmospheric nitrogen deposition on phosphorus limitation of freshwater zooplankton
ResearchPlanAbstract: Colorado has a gradient of anthropogenic atmospheric nitrogen deposition from low to high, leaving it vulnerable to phosphorus (P) limitation.  The first year of this study, including work done at RMBL, tested the hypothesis that P-limitation was more frequent for zooplankton in lakes receiving elevated atmospheric deposition of nitrogen (N) due to anthropogenic impacts, and examined possible impacts at the individual, population, community, and ecosystem levels.  Lakes were compared across a gradient of N deposition in the Rocky Mountains of Colorado with RMBL being an area relatively pristine with low N additions.  In 2008 we propose to determine lake variation of denitrification using the same lakes at RMBL as in our 2006 study.  Also, sediment from approximately 4 lakes will be assessed for more intense study focusing on within-lake variations.  Net nitrous oxide flux will also be monitored.
Subject: Other

ResearchPlanTitle: Global Observation Research Initiative in Alpine Environments (GLORIA) at the Rocky Mountain Biological Laboratory (RMBL)
ResearchPlanAbstract: Many alpine species face habitat fragmentation and loss, and even extinction because their narrow elevation, precipitation, and temperature tolerances limit their geographic distribution.  Upward movement of alpine plants with recent warming has already been observed in the European Alps and modeling shows plant species to be most vulnerable in mountain regions.  We are establishing a set of long-term summit sites based at the Rocky Mountain Biological Laboratory (RMBL) as part of a world-wide network called GLORIA (Global Observation Research Initiative in Alpine Environments) to assess the impacts of climate change on alpine communities.  The GLORIA sites at RMBL will strengthen the existing network of GLORIA sites that form latitudinal and elevational gradients within the US.  These include the GLORIA master site based at White Mountain Research Station in the White Mountains of California and sites in the Sierra Nevada and northern and southern Rocky Mountains, from Glacier National Park to Silverton, Colorado.  Long-term, permanent research sites on four summits spanning an elevation gradient in the Ruby Range will be used to detect climate-induced changes in vegetation cover, composition, and migration of alpine and subalpine plant species. The sites include a local summit between Treasury and Cinnamon on the shoulder of Treasury (11,800 ft), Cinnamon Mountain (12,300 ft), Ruby Peak (12,600 ft), and a plateau just below the summit of Treasury (13,300 ft).  The sampling design is focused on the fundamental climatic gradients (altitude, aspect, and large-scale horizontal gradients across the major life zones) and thus will be effective in assessing the current and future large-scale patterns of plant diversity of the world\\\'s mountains.  This research will contribute to a predictive understanding of shifts in the distributions of alpine species with climate warming in the Rocky Mountains and Western U.S.  Results from this work will also expand existing long-term data sets on the effects of climate change in alpine environments and help to identify alpine species at risk of extinction from changing climate.  Community involvement from Crested Butte and surrounding areas would be welcome.
Subject: Climate Change

ResearchPlanInstitution: Odum School of Ecology, University of Georgia
ResearchPlanTitle: Selection dynamics and MHC variability in cyclic montane voles
ResearchPlanAbstract: Determining the dynamics of selection maintaining genetic diversity in natural populations is a major focus of evolutionary biology.  The major histocompatibility complex (MHC) is an ideal tool to investigate key questions concerning temporally varying selective forces.  It has clear consequences for both parasite defense and mate choice, two processes affected by population density.  By investigating how MHC allelic diversity changes non-randomly over time in hosts that undergo dramatic population cycles, and how MHC allelic patterns are influenced by the selection pressures arising from mate choice and pathogen resistance, a greater comprehension of the evolutionary process can be gained.   I will accomplish this with a combination of observational field studies and experiments, using cyclic populations of montane voles and their parasites as a model system.  This will be the first long-term study to explicitly examine the effect of sexual selection combined with parasite-driven selection on MHC allelic variation.  In doing so, my doctoral research will advance knowledge of evolutionary forces that shape host immunogenetic variation, with great relevance to conservation genetics in light of pathogen threats to wildlife populations.
Subject: Other

ResearchPlanInstitution: University of Leiden, IBL, Section Plant Ecology
ResearchPlanTitle: Species traits and the structure of pollination networks
ResearchPlanAbstract: Pollination of flowers by insects is a vital natural process, important for humanity.  In studying pollination we wish to understand what factors determine which insects will visit which flowers.  My previous study of a community of plants and pollinators in southern Spain revealed that who visits whom could be explained surprisingly well by the combination of two simple mechanisms.  First, the nectar that the pollinators search for in flowers is often deeply hidden, and only pollinators with tongues longer than the threshold set by nectar depth will bother to visit a given flower with deep nectar.  Second, the visitors to a given flower type will be a representative sample of all insect species with long enough tongues, and will reflect the relative abundances of these different species, some of which are rare and others common.  I now wish to extend this finding to the very different ecological communities in the Rocky Mountains, to test whether I can again predict who visits whom using simple rules.  Repeating the Spanish study at the RMBL will also allow me to explore additional factors that may constrain insects searching for pollen as a food reward, rather than nectar, and to see if rates of visitation to flowers can be explained by flower and insect characteristics.  More broadly, this research will help biologists to understand fundamental patterns in pollination, an important practical goal.
Subject: Pollination

ResearchPlanTitle: Ecological interactions influence rates of adaptation in response to climate change.
ResearchPlanAbstract: My research at RMBL investigates the factors that influence plant adaption in response to climate change.  More specifically, I study a small wildflower, Androsace septentrionales, which grows from warm, wet elevations to cool, dry elevations.  Androsace septentrionales also grows in meadows that have been experimentally warmed for the past seventeen years.  Through a combination of experiments in natural and controlled environments, I test how genetic variation, plant-plant interactions, and plant-soil interactions influence A. septentrionales\\\' ability to adapt to warmer temperatures.  By increasing our understanding of adaptation in natural systems, this study will improve our ability to predict population and community responses to climate change.
Subject: Climate Change

ResearchPlanTitle: Consequences of genotype and genetic variation for Aphis varians  and Formica cinerea mutualism on Epilobium angustifolium
ResearchPlanAbstract:
The ant Formica cinerea protects the aphid Aphis varians from its predators as it feeds on Fireweed (Epilobium angustifolium) in exchange for so-called honeydew, the carbohydrate rich excrement of the sap-feeding aphids.  These tripartite interactions between plant, aphid and ant in turn have consequences for other arthropods associated with Fireweed, including other herbivores and predators.  This system  encompasses a diversity of interaction types (predation, mutualism, herbivory, parasitism, competition)and can thus serve as model system for the study of evolutionary and ecological dynamics of a whole community.

I am investigating the role of genetic variation in the aphid and the plant for  the interactions between ants and aphids, and how such effects cascade out to affect the entire arthropod community.  Studying the interplay between genetic diversity and the community ecology of Fireweed and its arthropods will provide an important link between evolutionary and community ecology
ResearchPlanOrganisms:
Aphis varians
Formica cinerea
Epilobium angustifolium
Subject: Other

ResearchPlanTitle: Seasonal effects of brood size in Nicrophorus.
ResearchPlanAbstract: As a new collaborating researcher with Rosemary Smith, I intend to expand upon her work with burying beetles in a montane ecosystem.  I will begin preliminary life history and ecology studies of Nicrophorus investigator, using the study areas and experimental techniques employed by Rosemary Smith.  I am particularly interested in pursuing seasonal and parental experience influences on parental care behaviors of the beetles as well as learning molecular genetic techniques to investigate genetic versus behavioral parenting patterns.
ResearchPlanOrganisms: Nicrophorus spp, small rodents (Peromyscus, Microtus, Zapus), possibly frozen laboratory mice (if container-only study).
Subject: Other

ResearchPlanTitle: Long-term population dynamics of Gillette's checkerspot butterfly
ResearchPlanAbstract: Euphydryas gillettii at Gothic is an introduced (but not invasive) species with a known history.  The population was initially relatively stable, but in recent years has exhibited huge fluctuations in density, of 2 (nearly 3) orders of magnitude.  Our work focuses on two questions:  What causes such large-scale fluctuations in population size, particularly of introduced populations?  What are the effects on both spatial and genetic structure of those fluctuations? Our work has implications for management of transplantations and re-introductions of populations, predicting population response to global change, and basic understanding of population dynamic processes.
Subject: Long-Term

ResearchPlanTitle: Restoration of disturbed land in the Gothic Townsite and the Bench Meadow in 2008
ResearchPlanAbstract: Land within the Townsite of Gothic is sometimes disturbed during construction projects, building renovations, electrical work, sewer work, and other types of facilities and building projects.  Disturbed land can be a foothold to invasive plants, can result in erosion, and is visually unaesthetic.  In addition, disturbed land can compromise research sites within Gothic (Research Master Plan 2007).  For these reasons and the fact that Gunnison County requires revegetation after construction, the restoration of disturbed land in and around Gothic is a priority.  In 2008, we expect large disturbances of land within Gothic as the RMBL sewer system is upgraded.  We plan to revegetate this land by transplanting plants and sowing seed.  In addition, we will continue revegetation efforts at the Bench mine tailings restoration site, located south of the RMBL.
ResearchPlanOrganisms: Potentilla gracillis, Heliomeris multiflora, Native brome
Subject: Other

ResearchPlanTitle: The effect of secondary endosymbionts on ant-hemipteran mutualisms.
ResearchPlanAbstract: The conditionality of ant-hemipteran mutualisms is usually explained by optimal foraging in ants determined by honeydew quality produced by the hemipterans. However, secondary endosymbionts in hemipterans may also play an intrinsic role in intimacy in ant-hemipteran mutualism by affecting the quality of resources provided, hemipteran health, or preventing ant predation. This preliminary study seeks to draw potential correlations between different ant-hemipteran associations and their associated endosymbiont populations.
ResearchPlanOrganisms: Ant and Hemipteran interactions on their various Host-plants. Including but not limited to the treehopper Publilia modesta, the aphids Pleotrichophorus utensis Pack & Knowlton and Uroleucon escalantii Knowlton, the ant Formica obscuripes, the sagebrush Artemisia tridentata, the rabbitbrush Chrysothamnus viscidiflorus, the muleï¿½s ear Wyethia spp., the fireweed Chamerion angustifolium (formerly Epilobium angustifolium).
Subject: Other

ResearchPlanTitle: Increased frost damage as a consequence of climate change: A demographic mechanism for changes in montane plant communities
ResearchPlanAbstract: Climate change is affecting plant communities worldwide. Of particular concern is how plant abundances and ranges will respond to future climate changes. We will examine the potential for increased incidence of frost to decrease reproduction and population sizes, and possibly shift the ranges for several frost-sensitive plant species. The incidence of frost has increased in recent years due to earlier snowmelt at the Rocky Mountain Biological Laboratory and other locations around the world. Specifically, we will identify species that are sensitive to frost, test if frost damage can alter the ability of plant populations to maintain themselves, and investigate the impact of the loss of a frost-sensitive species from a plant community. These experiments, combined with existing long-term monitoring, will improve our understanding of the ecology of montane plants and will allow us to better predict how plant populations will respond to future climate change.
ResearchPlanOrganisms: Helianthella quinquenervis, Erythronium grandiflorum, and several other wildflower species
Subject: Climate Change

ResearchPlanTitle: Environmental effects on siring success in Ipomopsis
ResearchPlanAbstract: An important aspect of the evolution of one species into another is reproductive separation between two closely related taxa.  A relatively unexplored aspect of this is how environment can play a role in the functioning of reproductive structures and ultimately influence diverging groups. We are conducting a greenhouse study on an alpine plant, Scarlet gilia, to better understand the influence of soil environments which range from hight to low nutritional quality, on pollen performance.  Previous studies have shown that a closely related species generally grows on different soil types. Our goal is to measure the success of individuals at reproducing when grown on these different soils.
Subject: Pollination

ResearchPlanTitle: The effects of an ant/membracid mutualism on the hostplant and insect community.
ResearchPlanAbstract: Pairwise species interactions that result in the exchange of benefits to both species are termed mutualisms.  The interactions between ants and honeydew-producing hemipterans have proven popular study systems, but the community-level impacts of these relationships remain poorly understood (Styrsky & Eubanks 2007).  To explore the direct and indirect community relations of this type of mutualism, I conducted an experiment in 2007 with a species of ant, a honeydew-producing membracid, an herbivorous beetle and the perennial hostplant that the insects interact upon.  The data indicate that ants reduced herbivory of the beetle on the hostplant, but do not affect plant reproduction.  In the summer of 2008, I wish to return to the same fieldsite in Almont, Colorado to perform an expanded version of the 2007 experiment, utilizing the experimental plants from 2007.  The new experiment will more completely illustrate the nature of the interactions among the four experimental organisms.
ResearchPlanOrganisms:
Formica obscuripes
Publilia modesta
Chrysothamnus viscidiflorus
Ophraella sp.
Subject: Other

ResearchPlanTitle: Lichen Survey for the Global Observation Research Initiative in Alpine Environments (GLORIA) at the Rocky Mountain Biological Laboratory (RMBL)
ResearchPlanAbstract: Remarkable direct effects of climate warming on biological and physical systems are and will be evident across many ecosystems, particularly in alpine environments where structure and function are driven by low-temperatures (IPCC, 2007; Pauli, 2007). In response to climate change, the Global Observation Research Initiative in Alpine Environments (GLORIA) has established a long-term observation network to monitor impacts of climate change on mountain biodiversity at a global scale. Information acquired through GLORIA will contribute predictive understanding of alpine species shifts and abiotic changes, e.g. soil temperature. Monitoring permanent plots in the high mountains for shifts in species composition is one measure of how climate change may affect the ecosystem structure.  Plants at high elevation, in particular, are good indicators of such change because their limits are dictated more by environmental constraints e.g. lower air temperatures at higher elevations, than interactions between species e.g. competition for nutrients with other plant species. Under the umbrella of species to monitor over time, I propose to conduct a lichen survey for the first baseline GLORIA monitoring study at the Rocky Mountain Biological Laboratory (RMBL) in Gothic, Colorado. Monitoring of lichen populations over time has potential to reveal changes unparalleled by other species.
Subject: Climate Change

ResearchPlanTitle: Heritability and monitoring protocols for study of thermoregulatory evolution
ResearchPlanAbstract: We will carry out initial work in preparation for full-scale study of the impact of natural climatic variation and superimposed global climate change on a \"model\" insect study system in high montane and alpine habitats.
Subject: Climate Change

ResearchPlanTitle: Preliminary research identifying study species for exploring how pollinator-mediated interactions between plants change with plant densities and spatial scale
ResearchPlanAbstract: Plant species can influence each other’s pollination success, and previous studies suggest that these interactions are important for plant community structure and evolution.  Both the densities and spatial distributions of the interacting species likely influence the strength and quality (positive or negative) of their interactions.   For my dissertation, I intend to explore changes in these interactions with density and spatial scale.  As a first step, this summer I will identify appropriate study species by measuring the interactions between several pairs of species that flower together at the RMBL and share bumblebee pollinators.
ResearchPlanOrganisms:
Polemonium foliosissimum and a co-occuring mint species
Cirsium arvense and co-occuring bumblebee-pollinated species, including Viguiera multiflora, Delphinium barbeyi, and Heterotheca villosa
Subject: Pollination

ResearchPlanTitle: Symbiont evolution and host social structure: bees and nematodes
ResearchPlanAbstract:
An insect society can serve as a hub of transmission for pathogens, commensals and mutualists (symbionts), but within colony transmission is between close relatives.  If this consanguineous transmission is much more prevalent than between colony transmission, selection may favor more benevolent symbiont strains in social hosts when compared to solitary hosts.  High consanguineous transmission may couple the fitness of the symbiont to that of the host colony.  To test this hypothesis, genetic covariances between social and solitary sweat bee hosts and their nematode symbionts are being measured to represent ï¿½effective transmission.ï¿½  Effective transmission is a measure of within versus between colony transmission, and therefore provides a means to measure the coupling of host and symbiont fitnesses.  Laboratory colonies of social and solitary hosts either with or without symbionts will be used to measure the impacts of infection on host fitness.  
	The consequences of infection will be used to determine if host social structure can align the fitnesses of host and symbiont, leading to selection for more benevolent symbionts in social versus solitary hosts.  This research will also determine if genetic covariances can predict the impact of a symbiont on its host.  Both aspects will provide insights for studies of symbionts of hosts with varying social structure, such as humans.
Subject: Other

ResearchPlanTitle: The Reproductive Strategies of the perennial dicot D. hoopesii
ResearchPlanAbstract: The reproductive strategy of Dugaldia hoopesii will be analyzed for self compatibility through a series of controlled pollination experiments.  Hand pollination of individual flowers with either self pollen or outcrossed pollen will be bagged to prevent further uncontrolled pollination by insects.  Comparison of the subsequent seed setof these two treatments will reveal if this species is capable of self pollination.  Flowering phenology will be determined by observation throughout the flowering season.
Subject: Pollination

ResearchPlanTitle: Studying the success of management strategies to control Linaria vulgaris
ResearchPlanAbstract: Human activities have dramatically altered the earth’s natural systems. Chief among these alterations is the accidental and intentional movement of plants and animals around the world. Biological invasions, the establishment and spread of non-native species, have radically affected both the structure and function of ecosystems. A central goal in the study of invasive plants is to understand how to control their spread. Unfortunately, one management strategy will likely not work against invasive plants that grow in a variety of conditions, from residential to more wild and from small satellite populations to monocultures of the invader. Management strategies are required that control the invader while also taking into account human public health and safety and ecosystem restoration. The goal of this study is to assess the success of various management strategies to control the spread of Linaria vulgaris.
Subject: Other

ResearchPlanTitle: Survey of fungal endophytes in cool season grasses
ResearchPlanAbstract: The proposed research will survey the frequency of fungal endophytes (Neotyphodium, Epichloë, Clavicipitaceae) in native Pooideae grasses of Colorado.  Fungal endophytes in cool season grasses grow in the intercellular spaces of aboveground plant tissues.  In economically important forage and turf grasses, these fungi are known to increase host resistance to herbivory and drought through the production of fungal alkaloids.  Many native grass species have never been examined for the presence of these endophytes.  Very few studies have examined ecological factors that correlate with the frequency of fungal endophytes in nature.
Subject: Other

ResearchPlanTitle: The effects of road dust on reproduction of Delphinium nelsonii and Ipomopsis aggregata
ResearchPlanAbstract: The world, especially Gothic, is a dusty place! For the most part, however, we do not know the effect it may have on plant populations. In my study, I will test whether unpaved road dust falling on a plant affects the amount of pollinators (bees, hummingbirds) that visit it and its ability to grow fruits and seeds. My hypothesis is that plants closer to the road will have lower visitation and fruit and seed production. To do this, I will collect dust at different distances from the road to see if the amount decreases the further away you go. Then, I will monitor the pollinators that visit at these distances and check how much pollen the stigmas (female part of the flower) retain. The last step is counting the amount of fruits and seeds that are produced. I will also manually dust plants that are far away from roads to see if any amount of dust will cause lower reproduction. Further study of dust effects may influence if and where roads are constructed, especially near ecologically sensitive areas.
Subject: Pollination

ResearchPlanTitle: Effect of a reduction in mountain stream flown on the diversity and abundance of benthic algal communities and macroinvertebrates.
ResearchPlanAbstract: This study was undertaken to explore the effect of low water flow (because of global warming or diversion for drinking water) effect the plants and animals that live in benthic streams. Streams South-West of Gothic will be diverted to reduce stream flow by 25% or 50% percent. Algae and invertebrate diversity and abundance will then be compared between the modified streams and the control stream that has not been modified.
Subject: Other

ResearchPlanTitle: Effect of Soil Metals on Pollination of Subalpine Wildflowers
ResearchPlanAbstract: There are over 23,000 abandoned mines in Colorado alone. Mines are a source of metal contamination and can affect plants through their absorption of soil water. Metals influence plant growth and survival, and those plants that survive often incorporate metals into their tissues. Metal accumulation in plant tissue has been studied primarily for use in remediating contaminated sites, not for its ecological impacts. Pollination is an essential ecosystem service, and domestic honeybee populations are in decline, so the health of the native pollination web is especially important. Given that metal accumulation has been studied in foliar tissue, I hypothesize that metals are also accumulated in floral tissue, nectar, and pollen and are then consumed by pollinators.  I will examine the effect of metal contamination on pollination systems through changes in plant diversity, floral abundance and traits, pollination rates, reproductive success, and metal concentration in reproductive tissues.
ResearchPlanOrganisms: Wildflowers: Salix species, Draba aurea, Thlaspi arvense, Lupinus argenteus, Linaria vulgaris, potentially others; their pollinators, in less detail.
Subject: Pollination

ResearchPlanTitle: Pollinator mediated selection in Delphinium nelsonii and Ipomopsis aggregata: does correlational selection explain floral phenotypes?
ResearchPlanAbstract: The concept of pollination syndromes suggests that animal pollinators specialize in flowers with combinations of certain floral traits, such as flower color, shape and the size of the nectar reward.  It has been documented that pollinators prefer specific floral traits, but there has been few data on pollinator preference for combinations of traits.  This study will examine the responses of pollinators to combinations of manipulations of 3 floral traits in two species of flowers in the area: Delphinium nelsonii and Ipomopsis aggregata.  The manipulations will include flower color, spur length, corolla width and the size of the nectar reward.  Manipulated flowers will be placed in an artificial array and pollination visitations to the flowers will be observed.  If one combination of flower traits is preferred over all others, I will conclude that perhaps the concept of pollination syndromes is valid and that it is likely that pollinators prefer certain combinations of traits
Subject: Pollination

ResearchPlanTitle: Aspen heart rot fungus (Phellinus tremulae) distribution in aspen forests in relation to open meadows: implications for red-naped sapsucker (Sphyrapicus nuchalis) nesting habitat
ResearchPlanAbstract: Red-naped sapsuckers are an integral part of the aspen ecosystem in the montane western U.S. They are a double keystone species providing both shelter and nutrients to a variety of organisms within the system. Trees chosen by sapsuckers as nest sites are consistently infected with aspen heart rot fungus. This fungus rots the heartwood of the aspen while leaving the sapwood intact providing a healthy and well-protected yet easily excavated tree. In addition to its importance in being a key variable in nest site selection, the fungus also has important forest management and timber production implications. However, very little is known about the distribution or dispersal of the fungus despite its common occurrence. This study will ask the question of whether fungal density is greater at forest edges than in the interior in order to gain a better understanding of how fungus affects red-naped sapsucker nest choice.
ResearchPlanOrganisms: Aspen (Populus tremuloides), Aspen heart rot fungus (Phellinus tremulae)
Subject: Other

ResearchPlanTitle: Rocky Mountain Bombus pathogen survey:  Are invasive plants affecting  pathogen prevalence and intensity?
ResearchPlanAbstract: Bumble bees (Order Hymenoptera, Family Apidae, Genera Bombus) are commonly infected, to varying intensities, with a number of pathogens or parasites. These pathogens can negatively effect the health and fitness of individual bees and their colonies and adversely effect a colony's ability to withstand stressful situations such as food shortages.  Despite the significant effects of pathogens on populations of bumble bees, nothing is known about the health of bumble bees in the area surrounding the Rocky Mountain Biological Laboratory. This study serves to be a comprehensive survey of pathogens and parasites in various Bombus species over an altitudinal gradient. This work will set a baseline for future studies into Bombus pathogens at RMBL and will inform current and future investigation on Bombus in the region. The second goal of the study is to determine the effect of the invasive plant, Linaria vulgaris, on rates of transmission of Bombus pathogens. Since many pathogens are transferred from bee to bee at flowers, shifts in flower usage can change rates of infection of Bombus. Linaria is a significant study organism in that it has higher floral rewards than any other native plant in the area. Therefore, I expect to see higher rates of infection of Bombus at area that have been invaded by Linaria in comparison of areas that contain only native plant species.Dr. Rebecca Irwin
Subject: Climate Change

ResearchPlanTitle: Do Pond Caddisflies Reap Double Benefit from Detritus Processing?
ResearchPlanAbstract: Recent research has shown that caddisflies in lentic ecosystems may benefit twice from processing detritus: first, from consuming the detritus itself, and then by consuming algal growth stimulated by excreted detritus nutrients.  As caddisfly density increases, use of algae as a food source is also expected to increase.
Subject: Other

ResearchPlanTitle: Effects of water addition on above- and below-ground carbon processes across a montane elevational gradient
ResearchPlanAbstract: High latitudes and elevations are expected to experience disproportionate temperature increases and more frequent extreme rainfall events in the coming decades do to climate change (IPCC 2007).  While water and temperature are limiting factors for plant growth and productivity (Illeris et al. 2004; Niu et al. 2007) most studies focus on the role of temperature on nutrient cycles and plant traits rather than the effects of water on these processes.  A quantitative understanding of the influences of both water and temperature on carbon cycling is needed to anticipate the effects of climate change on montane plant communities.  Here, I propose to test the hypothesis that water is a limiting factor for both decomposition of organic matter and for net assimilation in montane plant communities.  I predict increased photosynthetic and respiration rates from plants and increased respiration from microbes in water treatment plots.  I also expect that microbes will respond faster to water addition than above-ground vegetation because of their short generation times. Specifically, I plan to add water to plant communities along an elevational gradient and measure photosynthesis, soil respiration and decomposition to understand the influence of increased water supply on below-ground and above-ground on carbon balance in plant communities.
Subject: Climate Change

ResearchPlanTitle: Do Traits of Herbaceous Plants in Aspen and Conifer Forest Understories Influence Distribution and Abundance Patterns?
ResearchPlanAbstract: While it is obvious that abiotic conditions constrain the species list located in an environment, do they influence the patterns characterizing the local distribution and abundance of those species within that environment.  By looking at multiple environments from multiple perspectives I will be contributing to our understanding of the degree to which “universal” rather than particular and contingent factors dominate macroecology.
ResearchPlanOrganisms: Herbaceous Plants in Aspen and Conifer Forests Understory
Subject: Climate Change

ResearchPlanTitle: Time budget of yellow-bellied marmots at high and low elevations
ResearchPlanAbstract:
The yellow-bellied marmot (Marmota flaviventris) lives in an environment with harsh weather conditions in mountainous areas, such as the Rocky Mountains in Colorado.  It typically hibernates up to eight months out of the year and emerges from its burrow in early May. The marmots at higher elevations experience shorter active periods and growth periods due to greater length of snow cover compared to lower elevations. During the summer, it is necessary for the marmot to accumulate enough fat to sustain itself during hibernation as food is not stored.  
Marmots do not spend much time active, so how they spend their time is important.  Yellow-bellied marmots have been studied since 1962, there has only been one population time budget created that documented 17 different behaviors, though all of the studied populations resided in low elevation sites.  We will observe yellow-bellied marmots at high and low elevations in order to create a time budget that describes their time spent foraging, sitting/lying, locomotion (moving from place to place), fighting, grooming, and being alert/vigilant. We will see if there are differences in behavior due to the altitudinal and environmental differences.
Subject: Other

ResearchPlanInstitution: University of Puerto Rico, Rio Piedras Campus
ResearchPlanTitle: Butterfly foraging behavior: Can butterflies detect nectar in flowering plants?
ResearchPlanAbstract: Optimal foraging theory states that there are benefits and costs from foraging. As a benefit from feeding, animals gain food. Nevertheless, by foraging, they also spend time and energy looking for food and expose themselves to predators. If the animal shows optimal foraging behavior, the benefits minus the costs from foraging should be maximized. One assumption of optimal foraging theory is that animals can recognize food, which for butterflies means detecting nectar in flowering plants. In the laboratory, several butterflies have been shown to feed more from artificial flowers with scented honey than from pure honey solutions. This may indicate that butterflies have some nectar detection abilities, probably mediated by nectar scent. We plan to test whether butterflies detect nectar in the field when they’re foraging, or if they forage randomly until they find rewarding florets. We will expose different species of butterflies to florets with and without nectar, and record their behavior.
ResearchPlanOrganisms:
Butterflies (three species among the following): Pieris macdunnoughii, Speyeria mormonia, Euphydryas gillettii,Papilio gothica, Papilio rutulus, Cercyonis oetus and Erebia epipsodea

Plants: Pyrrocoma crocea
Subject: Pollination

ResearchPlanTitle:
Current Status and Potential Causes of Population Decline
in Wild Bumble Bee Pollinators
ResearchPlanAbstract: Native bumble bees perform crucial roles as pollinators in all terrestrial ecosystems and have a direct impact on agriculture, particularly on the success of flowering plants requiring buzz pollination, such as blueberries and tomatoes.  Bumble bees have great economic value as managed pollinators for greenhouse tomatoes and sweet peppers, and promise to play increasingly important roles in open field crop pollination as populations of the European honey bee continue to decline.  Nonetheless, an increasing number of scientific (and lay) reports, including a 2006 National Academy of Sciences study, warn of recent population declines in once-widespread species.  There are few quantitative baseline data, however, on current status or potential causes of decline of any U.S. bumble bee species.  This time-sensitive proposal by a multidisciplinary team of bee systematists, geneticists, and pathologists plans to address these major gaps in fundamental knowledge of these native pollinators.  The goals are to quantify apparent ongoing decline of targeted US bumble bee species and investigate two potential causes of putative decline: low levels of genetic variation in fragmented populations and susceptibility to disease.  Research activities will: 1) determine the current and historical distribution and abundance of several speciesï¿½ two undergoing putative population declines (B. occidentalis and B. pensylvanicus), two or three thought to be stable in population numbers (B. huntii, B. bifarius, and B. bimaculatus) and two undergoing putative range expansion (B. vosnesenskii and B. impatiens); 2) use microsatellite tools to determine whether declining populations exhibit reduced genetic variation relative to species with expanding or stable populations; 3) identify and quantify the prevalence of parasites and pathogens found in declining, expanding and stable populations; and 4) investigate the susceptibility of each species to the microsporidium Nosema bombi, as a test of the hypothesis that this pathogen is an agent of decline.  This is the first research to address bumble bee decline on a large scale with interdisciplinary expertise.
ResearchPlanOrganisms:
Bombus (bumblebee) species of the western U.S.
Target species: B. occidentalis, B. huntii, B. bifarius, B. vosnesenskii
Subject: Pollination

ResearchPlanTitle: Grasshopper teaching collection
ResearchPlanAbstract: The goal of my research is to assemble a teaching collection of the grasshopper species that are resident in and around Crested Butte and Gothic. This will be accomplished based on grasshopper specimens collected during three trips to the Crested Butte/Gothic area during August and early September, 2008. Collection procedures will primarily consist of visual searching for individuals and light sweep-netting to capture  individuals that are not as active. Collected specimens will be brought back to the University of Colorado Museum of Natural History where they will be identified, pinned as per museum best practices, databased, and labeled with collection information. The collection, which is estimated to include approximately 100 individuals, will then be donated to the Rocky Mountain Biological Laboratory to be used as an educational tool in facilitating further understanding of the ecology of this region.
Subject: Climate Change

ResearchPlanTitle: Examining the grasshoppers at the Rocky Mountain Biological Lab
ResearchPlanAbstract: Our visit to the Rocky Mountain Biological Lab and its surrounding area is to 1) produce a synoptic collection of grasshoppers for the RMBL, 2) collect Melanoplus dodgei of the area to explore how many species in all of Colordao make up the "dodgei Complex", 3. collect Aeropedellus clavatus, a prairie to high elevation species, that has expanded tibia at sites above tree-line. We are interested in determining whether this enlarged tibia is common in this species above treeline throughout the state, and finally 4) to document the distribution of grasshoppers across Colorado to, in the future, create models that explore where species are currently distributed and make predictions of where they may be found as global warming increase.
ResearchPlanOrganisms: Grasshoppers, particularly Melanoplus dodgei and Aeropedelus clavatus
Subject: Other

ResearchPlanTitle: Reproductive Biology and Demography of Glacier Lilies
ResearchPlanAbstract: I am continuing long-term studies of the environmental factors that affect flowering, pollination, fruiting, and longevity of the glacier lily.  I have been following the growth and the fates of many plants since 1993.
Subject: Long-Term

ResearchPlanTitle: Does the pollen environment affect pollen receipt?
ResearchPlanAbstract: Most plants rely on insects and other animals - the pollinators of their flowers - to reproduce, and this service from the animals often limits the number of seeds a plant makes. The ultimate goal of our research is to understand why plants often receive less pollen than needed for full reproduction. We hypothesize that the plant's pollen environment - how much pollen is available from nearby flowers to be brought to its flowers by pollinators - is crucial. The number of available pollinators itself might be limiting, and this has been studied at the RMBL, but the underlying availability of pollen has not been studied. We are focusing on one plant, scarlet gilia, which is mostly pollinated by hummingbirds and which has been studied for many years at the RMBL.  By experimentally stripping pollen from flowers, we are exploring whether a reduction in the pollen environment detectably reduces pollen receipt, and on what spatial scale. Preliminary results suggest a major drop in pollen receipt for plants within a for meters of stripped plants. We also will explore factors, such as drought, that might reduce pollen production of flowers in nature.  These studies are first steps toward a deeper understanding of factors that limit plant reproduction, an issue of importance for applied ecology, including crop yield and the persistence of rare plants.
ResearchPlanOrganisms: Ipomopsis aggregata and its hummingbird and insect pollinators
Subject: Pollination

ResearchPlanTitle: Life-history trait mediated indirect interactions among insect foragers
ResearchPlanAbstract:
My proposed dissertation research asks if plant reproductive strategies mediate indirect interactions between herbivores and pollinators and explores how pollinator-herbivore-host plant interactions might maintain variation in plant reproductive strategy.  A perennial plant capable of both sexual and asexual reproduction (referred to here as reproductive strategy) is likely to affect and be affected by both herbivore and pollinator foragers; reproductive strategy might therefore be a mechanism for mediation among insect foragers.  
I will use the perennial plant Chamerion angustifolium (fireweed) and its insect foragers to ask three specific questions.  First, does reproductive strategy influence pathways of community interactions among herbivores, pollinators, and plants?  This question will be addressed with field experiments measuring herbivore damage, pollinator visitation, and plant reproductive strategies, and analyzed with structural equation modeling.  The resulting path model will identify relationships among plant traits and forager effects, to be further investigated with manipulative experiments.  Second, do insect foragers affect reproductive strategy?  This question will be addressed with field and greenhouse experiments manipulating leaf damage and pollinator availability, measuring responses in plant reproductive strategy, and analyzing response to treatment with maximum likelihood.  Results of these experiments will indicate if pollinators and herbivores can influence the type of reproductive strategy a host plant expresses.  Finally, does reproductive strategy affect insect foragers, i.e., are there ecological costs associated with reproductive strategy?  This question will be addressed with field experiments   manipulating reproductive strategy, changing either clonal or sexual production.  Herbivore abundance, percent leaf damage, pollinator visitation, and fruit set responses will be analyzed with maximum likelihood to estimate treatment effects.  Results of these experiments will indicate if reproductive strategy carries an ecological cost of herbivory or pollination; the existence of these costs may facilitate the maintenance of both sexual and asexual strategies for plants with variable herbivore and pollination pressures.

I conduct field research at the Rocky Mountain Biological Laboratory, a high-altitude research station located in the former mining town of Gothic, Colorado.  RMBL is renowned for its scientific community of resident and visiting researchers and pristine surroundings composed of private holdings, land trust holdings, lab property, National Forest and National Wilderness.  The Lab is particularly well known for pollination biology research.  Chamerion angustifolium (fireweed) is abundant around RMBL; the plant is a disturbance specialist capable of sexual and asexual propagation, producing many (hundreds per fruit) small wind-dispersed seeds and clonal shoots from rhizomes.  Local pollinators are Bombus spp. and herbivores include caterpillars, beetles, and occasionally deer.
