C. angustifoliumï¿½s long-lived and weedy nature makes it well suited for studying effects that may manifest the year after their cause (such as effects of pollination on herbivory), for measuring and manipulating growth and reproductive strategy (such as promotion or inhibition of clonal growth), and for transplanting clones in the greenhouse and field.  C. angustifoliumï¿½s pollinator suite is readily identifiable in the field and much herbivore activity can be identified by damage patterns, making quantification of insect interactions in the field possible.

Preliminary data indicate a potential pathway of indirect interactions by which herbivore damage might negatively affect fruit set, while proposed experiments will determine the effects of herbivore damage and pollination on asexual reproduction.
Subject: Other

ResearchPlanTitle: Global Observation Research in Alpine Environments (GLORIA) at the Rocky Mountain Biological Laboratory (RMBL)
ResearchPlanAbstract:
Projected changes in climate due to human activities may to lead to large-scale and irreversible effects at continental and global scales [1].  Many alpine species face habitat fragmentation and loss, and even extinction because their narrow elevation, precipitation, and temperature tolerances limit their geographic distribution [2, 3], and due to the expectation of more rapid and larger climate change at high elevations. This is particularly critical on isolated mountains with a high percentage of endemic species at the uppermost elevation levels.  Upward movement of alpine flora with recent warming has already been observed in the European Alps [2, 4] and modeling shows plant species to be most vulnerable in mountain regions [5].  Treeline species have further restricted alpine species’ ranges through increasing growth rates and invasion of alpine habitat as a response to climate warming [6-8].  The collection of standardized, high-quality baseline and monitoring data at multiple sites worldwide can provide reliable prognoses of temporal and spatial changes in biodiversity and habitat distribution of alpine communities.

The Colorado Rocky Mountains provide an excellent setting to assess the impacts of climate change-induced biodiversity and habitat losses in sensitive native alpine communities. GLORIA (Global Observation Research Initiative in Alpine Environments) is a worldwide network of long-term research sites established to monitor climate change in the alpine. We are establishing a set of long-term summit sites based at the Rocky Mountain Biological Laboratory (RMBL) as part of this world-wide effort. The GLORIA sites at RMBL will strengthen the existing network of sites that form latitudinal and elevational gradients within the US and throughout the world.  These include the GLORIA master site based at White Mountain Research Station in the White Mountains of California and sites in the Sierra Nevada and northern and southern Rocky Mountains.  The sites at RMBL lie along a latitudinal gradient within the Rockies that range from Glacier National Park in Montana south to Silverton in southern Colorado and fill an important ecological and latitudinal gap in our current understanding the effects of climate change in alpine environments.
Subject: Climate Change

ResearchPlanInstitution: University of Leiden, Institute of Biology Leiden, Section Plant Ecology
ResearchPlanTitle: Species traits and the structure of pollination networks
ResearchPlanAbstract: Pollination of flowers by insects is a vital natural process, important for humanity.  In studying pollination we wish to understand what factors determine which insects will visit which flowers.  My previous study of a community of plants and pollinators in southern Spain revealed that who visits whom could be explained surprisingly well by the combination of two simple mechanisms.  First, the nectar that the pollinators search for in flowers is often deeply hidden, and only pollinators with tongues longer than the threshold set by nectar depth will bother to visit a given flower with deep nectar.  Second, the visitors to a given flower type will be a representative sample of all insect species with long enough tongues, and will reflect the relative abundances of these different species, some of which are rare and others common.  I now wish to extend this finding to the very different ecological communities in the Rocky Mountains, to test whether I can again predict who visits whom using simple rules.  Repeating the Spanish study at the RMBL will also allow me to explore additional factors that may constrain insects searching for pollen as a food reward, rather than nectar, and to see if rates of visitation to flowers can be explained by flower and insect characteristics.  More broadly, this research will help biologists to understand fundamental patterns in pollination, an important practical goal.
Subject: Pollination

ResearchPlanTitle: Follow-up on: The effects of nitrogen on plant-pollinator mutualisms
ResearchPlanAbstract: Nutrients play fundamental roles in biological systems, affecting plant growth and quality, community structure, and species interactions. Although the effects of nutrients on primary and secondary productivity have been well documented, their effects on mutualistic consumers have rarely been addressed. Nutrient addition could alter pollinator behavior via changes in floral reward quality and quantity. If nutrients strongly affect characters important for pollination, nutrient enrichment may influence not only plant fitness and species composition but also the performance of consumers that rely on nectar and pollen to provision their offspring. Using flowering plants in subalpine meadows and their pollinators, I tested the degree to which nutrient addition affected producers, consumers, their interactions, and the mechanisms by which those responses occurred.
ResearchPlanOrganisms: meadow plants.  all of them.  forbs, grasses, nitrogen fixers.
Subject: Pollination

ResearchPlanTitle: Biodiversity and Ecosystem Function: Pollinator Diversity, Specialization, and Plant Reproductive Success
ResearchPlanAbstract: Pollinator species losses are ongoing and are likely to accelerate in the future.  What will be the functional consequences of these species losses for plant reproduction?  We hypothesize that competition between species--which is lowered when species are lost--is important in shaping pollinator specialization.  Without this specialization, pollinators transfer the wrong kinds of pollen to plants, reducing their efficiency as pollinators while lowering plant reproduction.  We will be examining different meadow sites with different numbers of pollinator species to test this hypothesis.
ResearchPlanOrganisms:
Bumble bees (Bombus spp.)
various plants (flowering plants in meadows)
Subject: Pollination

ResearchPlanTitle: Ecological determinants of nest-site selection by a keystone species: the red-naped sapsucker
ResearchPlanAbstract: Woodpeckers are considered ecosystem engineers, a special type of keystone species, because they excavate nest cavities that provide shelter for other species. In aspen (Populus tremuloides) woodlands of the Rocky Mountains in Colorado, red-naped sapsuckers (Sphyrapicus nuchalis) are the predominant woodpecker, providing nest cavities for multiple bird species. Sapsuckers also create sap wells in willows (Salix sp.), supplying a food resource for many birds, mammals, and invertebrates. Previous work indicated that sapsuckers avoid nesting far (> 300 m) from willows. However, this work did not measure potentially confounding variables, such as the prevalence of the heart-rot fungus, Phellinus tremulae. The sapsuckers nest almost exclusively in aspens infected with Phellinus, which softens the heartwood, making it easier for the sapsuckers to excavate their nests. In summers of 2007 and 2008 we studied the relationship between willow proximity, Phellinus prevalence, and other variables (e.g., elevation). Our results suggested that sapsuckers chose nest sites primarily on the basis of tree suitability (i.e., Phellinus prevalence), not willow proximity. In the summers of 2009 and 2010 we will use more sophisticated methodologies to further tease apart the complex relationships between willow proximity, Phellinus prevalence, and other habitat characteristics.
ResearchPlanOrganisms:
Red-naped sapsucker (Sphyrapicus nuchalis)
Quaking aspen (Populus tremuloides) 
heart-rot fungus (Phellinus tremulae)
Subject: Other

ResearchPlanTitle: Local adaptation in key ecological traits: flowering phenology, drought tolerance and resistance to insect herbivory
ResearchPlanAbstract: We seek to understand the evolutionary, ecological, and historical forces influencing adaptation to local environments in a genetically tractable plant species. We will perform reciprocal transplants across an elevation gradient, using quantitative trait locus (QTL) mapping to identify the chromosomal regions (and ultimately the individual genes) responsible for ecologically important trait variation.  These field experiments focus on three fitness-related traits: resistance to herbivory, age at first reproduction (flowering time), and drought tolerance, which are well-characterized at the molecular level, in order to quantify the fitness consequences of molecular variation within and among populations.
Subject: Phenology

ResearchPlanTitle: RMBLnet: 'remote sensing' grant project
ResearchPlanAbstract:
The RMBL recently received a $480,000 grant from the National Science Foundation to install a weather station network in the Gunnison  Basin.  The award covers the purchase and installation of five permanent weather stations including webcams and audio recorders as well as some sophisticated environmental sensing devices.  All data  will be freely available  to the public via a web site that is currently in development.  (We are tentatively calling this major new source of local environmental information "RMBLnet".)

The stations will be installed this summer in a series of different altitudes (from 8,000 ft to 12,000 ft) to capture  data year round  despite inclement weather.  This grant will also allow the Lab to acquire six or seven additional portable weather stations for RMBL's  research teams to deploy on research sites. Lastly, this grant will also provide some additional specialized equipment  - such as 'dissolved oxygen sensors' for alpine ponds, 'sapflow sensors' to monitor trees and plants as well as 'soil carbon dioxide sensors' for certain research areas .  

These devices will further the understanding of  RMBL scientists about  the effects of climate change.  In addition, government agencies will be using data from this project to augment their ability to correctly forecast such crucial things as how much water to release from reservoirs. 

For anyone with an interest in this project, an initial (somewhat technical) website describing  this project  is available at: 
http://rmbl.info/rmblnet/PI_info/
Subject: Climate Change

ResearchPlanTitle: The Role of Biogenic Aerosols and Pollen in Cloud Formation Processes
ResearchPlanAbstract: The focus of this study is to better understand the role of biogenic atmospheric aerosols in cloud formation processes. Sources of biogenic aerosols include reactions involving volatile organic compounds (VOCs) emitted from vegetation and direct emissions of pollen from trees, grasses, and weeds.  The concentration of water vapor required for vapor to spontaneously condense into pure water droplets is rarely reached in the atmosphere. Fortunately, the water vapor required for droplets to form on tiny particles present in the atmosphere is much lower. Consequently, under most conditions clouds do not form as droplets of pure water, but instead form on these tiny particles, referred to as CCN.   To better understand the role of naturally emitted gases and particles in the cloud formation process, we will make in-situ measurements of aerosol concentration and collect size-select aerosol samples for off-line composition analysis using the Raman microscope, in our laboratory at Texas A&M University.  Coincident with the aerosol sampling, we will measure the concentrations of CCN.  The number of CCN is a critical link between aerosols, clouds and precipitation. Developing a more quantitative understanding of this linkage is necessary for improving our understanding of the Earthï¿½s hydrological cycle.  Biogenic CCN activation as well as cloud formation processes in general are large sources of uncertainty is estimates of how changes in temperature and climate will impact the hydrological cycle in the future. The feedbacks between the terrestrial biosphere and the atmosphere through the biogenic aerosol pathways explored here are likely to be important factors in radiative forcing and future temperature of the Earth.  A better understanding of the biogenic aerosol-CCN linkages is needed to understand the Earth system, including climate change, air quality, haze and visibility, as well as changes in land coverage, biodiversity and ecological changes.
Subject: Climate Change

ResearchPlanTitle: The causes and consequences of ant community structure
ResearchPlanAbstract: Ants are ecologyï¿½s movers and shakers. They are ubiquitous in terrestrial ecosystems where they alter nutrient dynamics, engage in mutualisms, prey on other species, and shape plant community structure. However, the factors that determine community structure of ants in montane ecosystems remains poorly explored. The causes and consequences of ant community structure
Subject: Climate Change

ResearchPlanTitle: Parental investment and reproductive output in burying beetles (Nicrophorus investigator):  influence of seasonal timing and prior breeding experience.
ResearchPlanAbstract: Reproduction is a paramount component of virtually all plants and animals.  Variable environments and diverse animal physiology lead to a wide range of reproductive strategies.  Organisms are predicted to exhibit reproductive strategies that represent the most efficient use of their finite resources while producing healthy and viable offspring.  The genus Nicrophorus (Coleoptera: Silphidae) is well-known for exhibiting repeated reproduction attempts and extensive bi-parental care, two strategies considered to be incompatible.  My study investigates components of the reproductive strategies of Nicrophorus investigator (burying beetles) in a montane ecosystem at Rocky Mountain Biological Laboratory (RMBL) in Gothic, Colorado.  Breeding success for N. investigator can be influenced by carcass availability as well as competition for carcasses from beetles, scavengers, or other insects.  Therefore it is possible for some beetles to breed multiple times in a season, while others may face only one opportunity to breed later in the season.  To test the hypothesis that reproductive behaviors, specifically parental investment behaviors, are influenced by 1) the previous reproductive experience of the adult beetles and 2) the timing of reproduction during the course of the season, I will manipulate breeding opportunities for beetles.  Under natural conditions, adult burying beetles at RMBL emerge from overwinter pupation 3 weeks after snow melts.  I intend to shade and cool groups of beetles in order to delay their emergence from pupation until mid-way through the breeding season.  Parental investment behaviors will be compared between beetles that emerge early and begin reproduction immediately, beetles that emerge early and are forced to wait to reproduce, and beetles that emerge late.
Subject: Long-Term

ResearchPlanTitle: Co-evolutionary and ecological interactions between bittercress, leafminers and plant pathogens
ResearchPlanAbstract: The plant-natural enemy interface is hypothesized to have played a major role in generating a large fraction of terrestrial organic diversity.  However, the mechanisms underlying this unfolding process of co-evolution, including reciprocal natural selection between hosts and parasites, is still not well understood in most natural host-parasite systems.  This project aims to understand the mechanistic and evolutionary basis of interactions between mustard host plants, specialist insect herbivores and associated plant microbes that live in the Rocky Mountains.  Because of the clonal nature of host plant patches in the Rocky Mountain, the opportunity exists to determine the extent to which specialist herbivores, plant pathogenic bacteria and their host-pants are locally adapted to one another at the population-level.  Each of these species is closely related to genetic model organisms (Arabidopsis, Drosophila and Pseudmonas) and I will be able to use genetic tools from these close relatives to understand how the hosts, parasites and pathogens are interacting at the molecular level, within a single leaf of the host plant.  I am also interested in understanding how global climate change influences disease dynamics, because although the specialist herbivore I propose to study only completes a single generation on their host plants at RMBL currently, global climate trends suggests that this species may be able to complete two life cycles per growing season in the future, which would likely affect the host plant's ability to produce seeds for the next year.  I hope to establish this project as a long-term study on plant-insect-pathogen interactions to add to the other long-term studies on plant-insect interactions already underway at RMBL.
ResearchPlanOrganisms: Cardamine cordifolia, Scaptomyza nigrita, Pseudomonas spp.
Subject: Other

ResearchPlanTitle: Ecological Interactions of a Metal Hyperaccumulator and their Implications for Phytoremediation
ResearchPlanAbstract: Plants that can uptake extraordinary amounts of heavy metals are not only of evolutionary and biological interest, but also have economic value in their potential use for contaminant removal.  Because studies began only recently, information on the ecology of metal hyperaccumulators is still limited, and field studies are especially lacking.  I propose to examine several aspects of the ecology of Thlaspi caerulescens, a cadmium (Cd) and zinc (Zn) hyperaccumulating plant.  Specifically, I will study their population dynamics, herbivore interactions, and interspecific competition, using field and laboratory experiments.  The results from this study are intended to provide insights into the ecological impacts of introducing an often non-native hyperaccumulator for remediation of metal contaminated sites.
Subject: Climate Change

ResearchPlanTitle: Predicting climate change-induced shifts of burying beetle distributions
ResearchPlanAbstract: Range shifts due to climate change have been observed across many species.  Novel interactions between species can be expected as species encounter new conditions, resulting in changes to realized niches.  Temperature, physiology and competition may be particularly important to the distribution of burying beetles (Nicrophorus).  I intend to map the distribution of three species of burying beetles in the East River Valley over an elevation gradient.  The relative number of beetles caught at baited traps will be used to determine distributions.  I will include thermal performance (flight temperature) and interspecies competition data in order to create a GIS-based model of species distributions.  With this model I will be able to interpolate for climate change to see how burying beetle distributions will respond to increased temperatures.
ResearchPlanOrganisms: Nicrophorus investigator, Nicrophorus defodiens, Nicrophorus guttula
Subject: Climate Change

ResearchPlanTitle: Selection dynamics and MHC variability in cyclic montane voles
ResearchPlanAbstract:
Determining the dynamics of selection maintaining genetic diversity in natural populations is a major focus of evolutionary biology.  The major histocompatibility complex (MHC) is an ideal tool to investigate key questions concerning temporally varying selective forces.  It has clear consequences for both parasite defense and mate choice, two processes affected by population density.  By investigating how MHC allelic diversity changes non-randomly over time in hosts that undergo dramatic population cycles, and how MHC allelic patterns are influenced by the selection pressures arising from mate choice and pathogen resistance, a greater comprehension of the evolutionary process can be gained.   I will accomplish this with a combination of observational field studies and experiments, using cyclic populations of montane voles and their parasites as a model system.  
This will be the first long-term study to explicitly examine the effect of sexual selection combined with parasite-driven selection on MHC allelic variation.  In doing so, my doctoral research will advance knowledge of evolutionary forces that shape host immunogenetic variation, with great relevance to conservation genetics in light of pathogen threats to wildlife populations.
Subject: Long-Term

ResearchPlanTitle: Lichen Surveys for Global Observation Research Initiative in Alpine Environments (GLORIA) at the Rocky Mountain Biological Laboratory (RMBL)
ResearchPlanAbstract: Efforts have been established on a global scale to monitor the impact of climate change on biodiversity in alpine environments.  The project responsible for this orchestration is the Global Observation Research Initiative in Alpine Environments (GLORIA). The Rocky Mountain Biological Laboratory (RMBL) has been designated as one of the few GLORIA sites in the United States.  Detection of change necessitates systematic, annual observation and monitoring of multiple taxa as well as the physical environment over a long period of time.  I propose to monitor lichen species at sites designated in the RMBL vicinity.  Because lichen species are much more slow growing than higher plants, the monitoring of lichen species is unparalleled by other species. Potential shifts in lichen species composition over time may demonstrate the impact of climate change on an individual organism at a timescale unmatched by vascular plants, for example.  It is imperative to include and support baseline and continuous monitoring of lichen species to meet the demands of this timely issue: climate change.
Subject: Climate Change

ResearchPlanTitle: Understanding How Climate Variations and Climate Change Affect Vegetation Processes in the East River Valley: Growth Patterns, Water Source Usage, and Transpiration
ResearchPlanAbstract: Ecosystems in the upper Gunnison basin rely on two distinct water sources throughout the year: winter and summer precipitation. While winter precipitation is the dominant contributor to the basinï¿½s water budget, summer precipitation accounts for about 20% of the total water input. This summer input is undoubtedly critical for some vegetation, especially the forbs and grasses that germinate, flower, and set seed in a narrow window between late June and late August. Superimposed on this broad hydrological context, there is evidence of changes in the timing and amount of precipitation at RMBL. Such climatic changes will undoubtedly affect vegetation throughout the East River Valley, but it is difficult to predict the direction and magnitude of these impacts. Stable isotopes offer a promising approach to understanding the extent to which different vegetation functional groups (trees, shrubs, grasses, and forbs) rely on winter versus summer precipitation. This project aims to use such isotopic tracers to delineate the usage of precipitation inputs by different plant functional groups across seasons and years. A second goal is to better understand how climate controls tree growth and to assess potential climate change impacts on ecosystems in the East River valley
ResearchPlanOrganisms:
Picea engelmanii, Populus tremuloides, and Abies lasiocarpa 

I may collect occasional leaf and stem samples from the following plant species: Pentaphylloides floribunda, Artemisia tridentata, Mertensia fusiformes, Potentilla hippiana, Erigeron speciosus, Poa pattersonii, Stipa lettermanii, Festuca thurberi
Subject: Climate Change

ResearchPlanTitle: Ecological and evolutionary responses of Androsace septentrionalis, Rock Jasmine, to experimental warming.
ResearchPlanAbstract: My research at RMBL investigates the factors that influence plant adaption in response to climate change. More specifically, I study a small wildflower, Androsace septentrionalis, which grows from warm, wet elevations to cool, dry elevations. Androsace septentrionalis also grows in meadows that have been experimentally warmed for the past twenty years. Through a combination of experiments in natural and controlled environments, I test how genetic variation, plant-plant interactions, and plant-soil interactions influence A. septentrionalis' ability to adapt to warmer temperatures. By increasing our understanding of adaptation in natural systems, this study will improve our ability to predict population and community responses to climate change.
Subject: Climate Change

ResearchPlanTitle: The role of floral scent in pollinator-mediated reproductive isolation between two species of Ipomopsis
ResearchPlanAbstract:
Flowers are generally considered beautiful and often noted because of their strikingly colourful displays and intriguing shapes. Another feature that may add to the overall pleasant impression is floral scent. From an insectï¿½s point of view, all the features of a flower act as sensory signals to attract or deter insect visitation. While the attractants colour and shape have received considerable attention by researchers over a long period of time, the methods to investigate floral scents have only become available over the past decade. Floral scents may convey information to potential pollinators that humans cannot perceive. Therefore the investigation of floral scents may solve many current puzzles in plant-pollinator interactions including the maintenance of reproductive barriers between closely related species. 
In horticulture, plants are often artificially crossed to form new varieties. Where these hybrids appear and persist in natural plant populations, the isolation between two species breaks down. There are many mechanisms that prevent the breakdown of barriers between species. One of them is pollinator-mediated reproductive isolation, where pollen is dispersed only within a species because pollinators visit only flowers with a certain set of species-specific characters. Floral scent is one of the features of a flower that a pollinator may be attracted to. The present study focuses on hybrid zones between the red-flowered scarlet gilia (Ipomopsis aggregata) and its close relative, the pale pink to white-flowered I. tenuituba. The main visitors of these species are hummingbirds and less frequently hawkmoths. These animals can transfer pollen between the species, producing hybrids in some, but not all, areas where the species grow in the same area. We are investigating the effects of floral scent on pollinatorsï¿½ choices to determine whether odours play a role in distinguishing the flowers of the two species of Ipomopsis. Differences in the floral scent profiles of plants at different locations may be partly responsible for the occurrence of hybrids in some areas while they are absent in others.
ResearchPlanOrganisms: Ipomopsis aggregata and Ipomopsis tenuituba and hybrids
Subject: Pollination

ResearchPlanTitle: Genetic variation in reproductive strategies of flies from an altitudinal cline in Colorado (USA) and a latitudinal cline in Finland
ResearchPlanAbstract: Wide-spread Drosophila species with a short generation time and a large population size may hold the greatest promise for demonstrating genetic shifts in photoperiodic responses and thermal optimum during a climate change. We aim to trace variation in the importance of light and temperature cues in evolking diapause in a fly species, Drosophila montana, on an altitudinal cline in in Colorado, and also to analyse the genetic basis of these changes.
Subject: Climate Change

ResearchPlanTitle: Modes of Selfing, Floral Display Size and the Evolution of Plant Mating Systems
ResearchPlanAbstract:
Floral display size, the number of flowers and inflorescences produced by a plant, presents an evolutionary dilemma.  Large displays should be more attractive to pollinators, increasing pollination success and seed production. However, pollinators may visit more flowers on larger displays, increasing the transfer of inbred pollen among flowers on the same plant. This form of self-fertilization incurs costs if inbred offspring are less fit, or self pollination reduces pollen available to fertilize other plants. On the other hand, self-fertilization within a flower may be beneficial if it assures fertilization when pollinators are scarce or unpredictable (Darwin 1876). Floral display size thus represents a tradeoff between the benefits of pollinator attraction and the costs of self-fertilization.
This project investigates the fitness tradeoffs driving the evolution of floral display size in larkspur (Delphinium barbeyi), and the maintenance of gynodioecy (separate female and hermaphroditic plants) in geranium (Geranium richardsonii). A more detailed understanding is needed of how the mechanisms (within flower or between flower crossing) and costs of self-fertilization vary with display size and mate availability. Using floral manipulations (anther removal or pollen addition), combined with a genetic marker approach to assess paternity, I will estimate how the different forms of self-fertilization and reproductive assurance affect different sized plants. I will also investigate the costs of self-fertilization by measuring inbreeding depression at different stages of the plant life cycle. If selfing is costly in terms of offspring fitness, then this may influence the evolution of display size and sex expression.
ResearchPlanOrganisms: Delphinium barbeyi, Geranium richardsonii and their pollinators
Subject: Pollination

ResearchPlanTitle: The role of plant-plant interactions in subalpine ecosystem response to climate change
ResearchPlanAbstract: Through studies conducted at the RMBL it has been shown that sagebrush, a shrub characteristic of the great basin desert, has higher growth rates and increases its cover when heated in subalpine meadows.  Changes in sagebrush cover can have drastic effects on the functioning of subalpine ecosystem, and can alter the biodiversity of those meadows.  In order to understand whether range expansion is likely for sagebrush, at the expensive of native subalpine herbs, I will conduct an in situ heating experiment on sagebrush seedlings transplanted into meadows.  Further, to look at what role the community has in facilitating or retarding sagebrush growth, I will do a factorial experiment combining heating and neighbor removal around sagebrush seedlings in RMBL meadows.  Results of this study will shed light on the community dynamics of subalpine meadows with heating and the role of plant interactions in sagebrush advance with warming.
ResearchPlanOrganisms: Sagebrush (Artemisia tridentata ssp. vaseyana) and the meadow plant communities
Subject: Climate Change

ResearchPlanTitle: Evolutionary ecology of flowers and fleshy fruits
ResearchPlanAbstract: Flowers and fleshy fruits are often showy and brightly colored, and biologists have long gathered evidence consistent with the idea that these traits have evolved as attractants to animal mutualists (e.g., pollinators and seed dispersers).  However, there are many remaining questions about how these structures have evolved, and how ecological interactions continue to drive their evolution.  We propose to investigate two questions: 1) Have fruits and flowers evolved differently, given that they have different biological functions and interact with different types of animals?  We are testing the hypothesis that flower morphology has diverged more than fruit morphology over evolutionary time.  2) What are the roles of fruit waxes?  Many species in the RMBL area have fruits that are coated with a waxy layer that reflects ultraviolet light.  Some animal seed dispersers can see in the UV (e.g., birds), so UV reflectance could improve fruit visibility and attractiveness to dispersers.  However, there are many alternative hypotheses that need to be tested, e.g., the waxes protect against desiccation and UV-reflectance is a byproduct.
Subject: Other

ResearchPlanTitle: Testing climate-related models of range contraction for the American pika (Ochotona princeps)
ResearchPlanAbstract: Alpine species are among those most severely threatened by rapid climate change. Recent resurveys have documented dramatic changes in alpine communities within the last 100 years. One of the primary subjects of these studies is the American pika (Ochotona princeps), a small herbivorous mammal inhabiting high elevation talus slopes of western North America. While pikas are adapted to survive alpine winters, their resting body temperature is only a few degrees below lethal temperature, making them sensitive to changing climates.  Climate change has been linked to disappearing populations of O. princeps in the Great Basin of western North America, but the fate of this species will be determined by trends in the Rocky Mountains, where the bulk of this speciesâ€™ habitat lies. An analysis of data from the Rocky Mountains will expand our understanding of the factors driving changes in the distribution of O. princeps throughout its range. Our primary hypothesis is that population extirpation is directly related to magnitude of warming. Additional hypotheses center on habitat quality and population connectivity. To evaluate these hypotheses, our research team and researchers with the Colorado Division of Wildlife have resurveyed 70 sites occupied by pikas before 1980. A subset of these sites, including three sites in the Gunnison National Forest near RMBL, will be monitored during summers 2009-2011 for further study. We will monitor climate in talus slopes using HOBO temperature data loggers and will monitor pika abundance noninvasively using distance sampling.  We will also assess pika haypile contents, available vegetation, and connectivity to adjacent pika populations.  O. princeps is a conspicuous and charismatic denizen of alpine communities and has become a bellwether species for alpine taxa in peril. The results of this study could expand public awareness and policy surrounding the potentially calamitous consequences of accelerating climate changes.
ResearchPlanOrganisms: O. princeps and numerous alpine plant species consumed and collected by O. princeps.
Subject: Climate Change

ResearchPlanTitle: Life in a Shrinking World: Changes in Altitudinal Distributions of Alpine Mammals due to Climate Change
ResearchPlanAbstract: As global temperatures increase, species are exposed to a range of stressful temperatures, especially in species currently living at their thermal limits (alpine species).  Warming temperatures may force alpine species to move to higher elevations.  We hypothesize that alpine mammals will move to higher elevations to stay within their optimal physiologic temperature range.  We will measure the metabolic thermoneutral zone of mammals at four sites in the western U.S.  We will use the physiologic data obtained in this study to predict range shifts in alpine mammals based on current climate predictions, and will verify predictive models using historic data.
ResearchPlanOrganisms: Spermophilus lateralis, S. tridecemlineatus, Neotamias amoenus, N. umbrinus, N. umbrinus, N. quadrivittatus, Ochotona princeps
Subject: Climate Change

ResearchPlanTitle: Revisiting the Gothic Earthflow
ResearchPlanAbstract: The gothic earthflow has been sampled at 20 year intervals since 1947. This summer will be the 20th year since my sampling was originally done in 1989. I am interested in seeing what changes in plant communities have occurred in the last 2 decades and to contrast disturbed and undisturbed sites. This work is valuable in understanding how systems change and the relative resilience of disturbed and disturbed sites through time and in the face of climatic change.
Subject: Long-Term

ResearchPlanTitle: Bee pollinator phenology and monitoring
ResearchPlanAbstract: Pollination is critical to the reproduction of most flowering plants.  Worldwide, up to 90% of some 250,000 angiosperm species, including wild and crop plants, rely on insects or other animals for pollination, making it an important ecosystem service.  Pollination by native bees alone is directly responsible for $3.1 billion annually in agricultural and forestry products.  Moreover, pollination provides some of the best-known examples of mutualisms and exploitation  and evolutionary and coevolutionary relationships.  Bee pollinators at the RMBL have also been used as model organisms in the study of optimal foraging theory, competitive displacement, and thermoregulation.  A diversity of animals can confer pollination services, including birds, marsupials, and even lizards, but the most common types of pollinators in most regions are insects, especially bees (Hymenoptera, superfamily Apoidea).  Globally, there are estimated to be 20,000-30,000 bee species, with at least 4,000 species in North America, and capturing their diversity, phenology, and relationships with flowering plants has important implications for population, community, and evolutionary ecology, systematics, and conservation biology.  Given growing concerns about bee declines in the UK and potentially worldwide, bees have been identified as an important pollinator group in need of long-term monitoring (Committee on the Status of Pollinators in North America 2007).  The goal of this study is to monitor the phenology and abundance of bees around the RMBL.  This work will be conducted in conjunction with David Inouye and his long-term flowering phenology plots.
Subject: Long-Term

ResearchPlanInstitution: Department of Ecology and Evolutionary Biology, University of Toronto
ResearchPlanTitle: Pollination facilitation in subalpine gentians
ResearchPlanAbstract: Plants that flower together and share pollinators can influence each otherï¿½s pollination and reproductive success in positive, negative, or neutral ways. Pollination facilitation occurs when the pollination of a plant species is enhanced by the presence of another species, and this may be important for the persistence of rare plants, though evidence for facilitation in plant communities is scarce. It is possible that pollination facilitation may occur at larger temporal and spatial scales than researchers have been looking, as these interactions often involve highly mobile pollinators able to forage over large areas and select among different patches, and pollinator populations that are likely to respond with a time-lag to changes in floral resources. A potentially important and ubiquitous mechanism of facilitation may be through pollinator support, which occurs when sequentially flowering plants jointly maintain pollinator populations that are resident in an area by providing floral resources over an extended time, positively influencing the pollination of a later flowering species. In this study, I intend to investigate the pollinator-mediated interactions among plants at large spatial and temporal scales by studying a group of late flowering gentians and an earlier flowering species, Delphinium barbeyi, with which they are likely to share pollinators. In particular, I plan to test the hypothesis that the earlier flowering D. barbeyi supports pollinators and enhances pollination for the late flowering gentians.
ResearchPlanOrganisms: Gentiana parryi, Gentianopsis detonsa (syn. Gentianopsis thermalis), Gentianella amarella, Delphinium barbeyi, Bombus spp.
Subject: Pollination

ResearchPlanTitle:
The Effects of Elk on Aspen Stands and Sagebrush Steppe Communities

Demongraphy and Non-invasive Measurements of Stress Hormones in Bushy-tailed Woodrats and Golden-mantled Ground Squirrels
ResearchPlanAbstract:
Increasing elk populations and decreasing habitat, especially in winter ranges, may lead to an untenable situation.  To assess the ecological impact of elk use of aspen stand and sagebrush habitats, the effects of elk on vegetation will be measured.  Mortality, recruitment, growth and species diversity will be monitored in several sites in the Gunnison Basin across elevational gradients.

Stress is a normal part in the life of a wild animal, and the degree can vary among species as well as within species.  One quantitative measure of stress is the level of glucocorticoids (stress hormones) in an individual.  Capture and handling alone can be a source of stress, and therefore a non-invasive way to obtain hormones is needed.  Feces are a such a source, but current techniques rely on radiolabeling of samples.  We will use a non-radioactive new technique to quantify total stress hormone secretion in marked populations of bushy-tailed woodrats and golden-mantled ground squirrels to assess the applicability of our novel protocol and to measure stress in two species across populations, sex, age and reporductive status.
ResearchPlanOrganisms:
Neotoma cinerea, bushy-tailed woodrat
Spermophilus lateralis, golden-mantled ground squirrel
Subject: Other

ResearchPlanTitle: Microbial ecology of plant-pollinator interactions
ResearchPlanAbstract: Biological communities are formed through webs of interactions among species, and these interactions are often mediated by traits of component species. Within the past decade, attention has turned to characterizing and identifying the factors that shape microbial community structure. Advances in molecular and genetic techniques have now made it possible for researchers to sample microbial diversity more deeply than before (Venter et al. 2004). New research has shown that floral nectar can support populations of yeast species (Brysch-Herzberg 2004, Herrera et al. 2008, Herrera et al. 2009); however the sampling and analytical methods used limit their ability to determine whether floral nectar may support a community of microorganisms. The goal of this study is to examine the community ecology of microorganisms in floral nectar.
ResearchPlanOrganisms: Aconitum columbianum, Aquilegia coerulea, Corydalis caseana, Delphinium nuttalianum, D. barbeyi, Ipomopsis aggregata, I. tenuituba, I. aggregata x I. tenuituba hybrids, Linaria vulgaris, Mimulus guttatus, Penstemon strictus, and Polemonium foliosissimum
Subject: Pollination

ResearchPlanTitle: Endophyte symbiosis and plant population dynamics
ResearchPlanAbstract: Plant species fundamentally vary in their abundance, spanning a range from federally endangered species to severely weedy invaders.  Several hypotheses have been proposed to explain this pattern, but none sufficiently account for observed variation.  In part, this failure might reflect the fact that microbial symbioses (widespread, mutually beneficial associations between microbes and plants) have been largely ignored. Taking advantage of the experimentally tractable symbioses between grasses and microbial endophytes (fungi that live within plant leaves), proposed experiments and demographic models forge a new direction by testing whether and how symbionts affect host population dynamics.  In grasses, endophytes may improve host resistance to herbivory through the production of alkaloids toxic to insects and mammals and also may enhance host tolerance of drought. A clearer understanding of endophyte ecology can offer novel strategies for plant conservation and restoration (e.g., via endophyte additions or eliminations).  Proposed work will integrate teaching and research, by training undergraduate students and bringing contemporary research into the classroom.
ResearchPlanOrganisms:
Poa leptocoma (and its unidentified endophyte, Neotyphodium sp.)

Bromopsis richardsonii (and its unidentified endophyte, Epichloe sp.)
Subject: Other

ResearchPlanTitle: Climate-induced changes in growth and species interactions between stoneflies in alpine mountain streams
ResearchPlanAbstract: Increased temperatures resulting from climate change have impacted the distribution, abundance, and phenology of many species.  These impacts are often due to direct effects on an organismï¿½s physiology, but altered species interactions under climate change may also be important, especially for species already stressed by higher temperatures.  The goal of my research is to predict how stream insects will respond to climate change (e.g., higher temperatures) by investigating species distributions and temperature-dependent interactions of stoneflies in mountain streams.  Alpine streams, like those located at RMBL, contain many unique species and are anticipated to be some of the most vulnerable to climate change.  Combining observational and experimental studies can better predict species range shifts that may be especially critical for species living near the top of an elevational gradient.  Any upslope range shift could lead to mountaintop extinctions, and could have negative consequences for the ecosystem services that mountain streams provide (e.g. aquatic insects as an important food source for fish and other species).
ResearchPlanOrganisms: Megarcys signata (Plecoptera: Perlodidae) and Hesperoperla pacifica (Plecoptera: Perlidae)
Subject: Climate Change

ResearchPlanTitle: Linking heterogeneity to the contributions made by species to ecosystem processes
ResearchPlanAbstract: Stream flows are being altered worldwide to meet human needs and there exists a pressing need for ecologists to provide society with an understanding of what flows are necessary to prevent species loss and allow streams to provide essential ecosystem services. By exploring the relationship between stream flow, heterogeneity, and herbivory, this project provides a basis for understanding the relationship between stream discharge and function; by examining how stream flow and heterogeneity influence species contributions to stream function, it provides a basis for understanding the causes and consequences of species loss. Ultimately, the project has the potential to provide resource managers with a process-based measure for establishing minimum stream flows.
Subject: Other

ResearchPlanTitle: Life History Traits of Marmots at High Elevations
ResearchPlanAbstract:
Yellow-bellied marmots, Marmota flaviventris, are hibernators that must gain sufficient mass to insure overwinter survival.  Marmots may be limited by food availability because of their short growing season.  However when a group of marmots were supplemented with food, there was no significant increase in survival.
Yellow-bellied marmots, Marmota flaviventris, are hibernators that must gain sufficient mass to insure overwinter survival.  Marmots may be limited by food availability because of their short growing season.  However when a group of marmots were supplemented with food, there was no significant increase in survival.
Food availability may be a more important factor at higher elevations.  The variation of habitat, length of active season and food resource availability in the distribution of this species makes it an ideal study subject for examining the role of variation of environmental conditions on life-history traits.  However, relatively few studies have been done on yellow-bellied marmots at higher elevations.  Marmots at higher elevations are hypothesized to have lower frequency of reproduction, changes in social structure and larger home range size.  The changes in life history characteristics may be in response to an even shorter growing season and limited food availability at higher elevations.  The aims of this study are to examine the effects of elevation on life history characteristics of populations of yellow-bellied marmots.
Subject: Long-Term

ResearchPlanTitle: Effects of environmental variation on individual life histories and population dynamics
ResearchPlanAbstract: Variation in the environment can take several forms. Organisms may be exposed to different weather or climate conditions over space and/or time. The predators, competitors or food items in a community may also change over space and/or time. I am exploring how such changes affect individual reproduction and survival, and through that, changes in population numbers over time. My goal is to generate a conceptual understanding that is broadly applicable to diverse organisms. My present research utilizes butterflies as study systems, and has two foci. First, I am studying the effects of an introduced plant species on the population dynamics and evolution of host plant usage by a native butterfly species. Second, I am exploring the effects of variation in adult and larval food availability on reproduction and survival, thence population numbers
ResearchPlanOrganisms:
Speyeria mormonia (Lepidoptera: Nymphalidae)
Viola spp (Violaceae)
Erigeron spp (Asteraceae)
Viguera multiflora (Asteraceae)
Chrysothamnus spp (Asteraceae)

Pieris macdunnoughii (Lepidoptera:Pieridae); used to be P. napi
Thlaspi arvense (Brassicaceae)
various other mustards, including Cardamine cordifolia, Draba aurea, Descurania, Arabis
Subject: Other

ResearchPlanTitle: Ecological factors affecting the fitness of the gynodioecious Polemonium foliosissimum across populations of varying sex ratio
ResearchPlanAbstract: My goal for this first field season is to begin to evaluate ecological factors which may differentially affect the two sex morphs -female and perfect plants- of Polemonium foliosissimum. I will evaluate whether seed predation and pollinator visitation (and ultimately seed set and germination) are influenced by factors intrinsic to the plants themselves such as sex morph and flowering phenology as well as those extrinsic to individuals such as the abundance and proportion of perfect plants (which are sole pollen source) in the population. In addition, because P. foliosissimum is pollinated by several generalist Bombus pollinators, I will evaluate whether the flowering status of the local community (co-flowering species that share pollinators with P. foliosissimum) is important to the fitness of P. foliosissimum plants.
ResearchPlanOrganisms: Polemonium foliosissimum, Bombus spp. (observational only), Hylemya sp.
Subject: Pollination

ResearchPlanTitle: Using elevational gradients to better understand the drivers of wood and litter decomposition.
ResearchPlanAbstract:
We are proposing two decomposition experiments -the first will involve wood decomposition, the second litter.

Coarse woody debris (CWD) indicate an important carbon (C) pool in forests, and little is understood about the controls on fluxes out of this pool (decomposition). This poor understanding results from variation in methodology, and little understanding of the fungal community controlling this process. Slow decay rates of CWD contribute to the importance of the pool as buildup occurs over time and to the difficulty in quantifying decay rates. Decomposition rates and the size of the CWD pool vary along an elevation gradient.1
The most dominant control over decomposition in forests are fungi, contributing up to 90% of total soil respiration.2 Fungi respond to changes in temperature and climate3; but we donï¿½t know how fungal communitiesï¿½ structure and activity may change in future predicted climate. Enzymes excreted by fungi allow metabolism of organic substrates such as lignin and cellulose to which few other organisms have access4, and therefore fungi control much of the C and nutrient cycling in forests. 
Diversity of microbial communities has been shown to vary over an elevation gradient and community structure of wood decomposing fungi varies among tree species. We propose to use an elevation gradient in the Fossil Ridge Wilderness area on the western slope of the Rocky Mountains (or the gradient at RMBL) to examine the effects of elevation on fungal community composition and activity. This site represents a unique opportunity to examine the effects of both substrate species and elevation on wood decomposing fungal communities in a ï¿½cross transplantï¿½ design.

We would also like to use an elevational gradient (near the weather stations) as a proxy for climatic change. Using a multi-factor experiment in and old field, my group has found that the indirect effect of climate change on species distributions has a larger impact on decomposition and nutrient cycling than the direct effects of climatic change on ecosystem processes. We would be interested in setting up a litter decomposition experiment that reflects the current species pool and the projected 'future' species pool at a number of sites along an elevational gradient. So use current and future litter mixtures at current and future distributions. We would also be interested in moving soil monoliths and (perhaps) do that in combination with different litter additions.
Subject: Climate Change

ResearchPlanTitle: Causes and Consequences of Long-term Fluctuations in Salamander Populations in Subalpine Ponds
ResearchPlanAbstract: Over the past 20 years, the salamander population at Mexican Cut has fluctuated dramatically.  Our research is designed to understand the causes of those fluctuations (Whiteman focus) and the effects on the pond food webs and ecosystem function (Wissinger focus).  One group of invertebrates that are sensitive to salamander abundance are cased caddisflies that are the primary decomposers of vascular plant detritus in the ponds.  We are studying 1) how the density of caddisflies affects detritus processing rates, and 2) how that detritus processing affects algal primary production through the liberation of limiting plant nutrients.  The results of our study will provide evidence  for  how fluctuations in the abundance of top predators can have  cascading effects on ecosystem processes like energy flow and nutrient cycling.
Subject: Long-Term

ResearchPlanTitle: Life history traits of the odorous house ant (Tapinoma sessile): A model system for invasive species
ResearchPlanAbstract: It remains unclear whether native pest species such as Tapinoma sessile, like their invasive counterparts, represent single origins of ï¿½urbanï¿½ lineages with existing traits that facilitate success in urban habitats, or whether they represent multiple origins of such traits. On the one hand, the fact that very few native species become pests in disturbed habitats suggests that the traits necessary for such a lifestyle are uncommon and neither very easy to evolve nor very plastic. On the other hand, the phylogenetic diversity represented by species found in urban habitats would tend to suggest that the traits are widespread and potentially easy to evolve or plastic. Our research at RMBL is focused on addressing these issues of the presence of "invasive" life history traits and their plasticity in a natural environment.
Subject: Other

ResearchPlanTitle: Do Facultative Defensive Endosymbionts in Aphids have a Significant Effect in a Quantitative Species Interaction Web?
ResearchPlanAbstract: I am studying a complicated web of interactions in the Almont Triangle region between plant-feeding aphids, aggressive ants, and a host of other insects. The most important feature of this web of interactions is a bacteria that protects the aphid from parasitoid wasps that lay their eggs in the aphids. By combining microbiology and field ecology I hope to be able to measure the direct effect of this defensive bacteria on its infected aphid hosts and the ants, parasitoid wasps, and predators important to aphid ecology.
ResearchPlanOrganisms: The dominant ant Formica obscuripes, the aphid Obtusicauda frigidae, the bacteria Hamiltonella defensa, the big sagebrush Artemisia tridentata.
Subject: Other

ResearchPlanTitle: Manipulating the soil environment to encourage restoration of disturbed land at the RMBL
ResearchPlanAbstract: Linaria vulgaris is a persistent invasive plant that is of particular concern because it has the ability to invade native wildflower fields, outcompete natives, and form a monoculture.  The RMBL has a growing population of Linaria vulgaris that is spreading.  In addition, in 2008, there was major soil disturbance in the heart of the largest population; this occurred when a new leachfield and sewer pipes were installed.  While Linaria vulgaris had a strong foothold in this area before the disturbance, I will attempt to change the soil environment to increase the competitive ability of grasses by increasing soil nitrogen and increase the competitive ability of forbs by increasing water in the soil.  The hope is that changing the soil environment will prevent Linaria vulgaris from forming a monoculture at these sites.  The major objective of this study is to test whether increasing water and/or nitrogen above ambient levels on disturbed soil will affect the relative establishment of natives versus nonnatives, Linaria vulgaris in particular.
Subject: Other

ResearchPlanTitle: Life history characteristics of the high altitude calanoid copepod, Leptodiaptomus coloradensis.
ResearchPlanAbstract: My research interests focus on basic, natural processes that affect distribution and abundance of zooplankton species.  It is my firm belief that we cannot effectively assess the impact of human interference (e.g., fish stocking, addition of chemicals, artificial warming of lakes) until we have a thorough knowledge of natural processes.  I have opted to study factors which influence the production of resting eggs (those that do not hatch immediately) in high altitude ponds, and have found considerable variability in a species of a copepod that lives in ponds virtually untouched by any human intervention.  Different ponds show different patterns in different years.  I have opted to continue a long term data set on this species to understand how natural processes influence not only resting egg production but also other population characteristics: developmental rates, adult sizes attained, and clutch sizes produced.
ResearchPlanOrganisms: the copepod Leprodiaptomus coloradensiss.  (S. I. Dodson thinks that this species is a varient of L. tyrelli, but the name chanhe is not yet officual.)
Subject: Long-Term

ResearchPlanTitle: What limits the distribution of rare Boechera species?
ResearchPlanAbstract: Theory predicts that endemic species lack evolutionary potential due to reduced genetic diversity and/or population numbers; yet such geographically restricted species have evolved in most taxonomic groups. To elucidate the processes which spatially and temporally maintain endemic species I will compare physiology, population genetic structure and hybridization success, within and among closely related pairs of endemic and widespread species. These integrated data will provide insight into the mechanisms which maintain endemic species (a major percentage of total biodiversity in any ecosystem) over long and short term climate change especially as the availability of water decreases2.
ResearchPlanOrganisms: B. gunnisoniana, B. oxylobula, B. crandallii, , B. stricta, B. retrofracta, B. grahamii and B. fendleri
Subject: Other

ResearchPlanTitle: Application to Install Cloned Lilacs at the Proposed Five Permanent RMBLnet Monitoring Sites
ResearchPlanAbstract:
Proposal Overview

The RMBLnet is scheduled for summer 2009 installation over an elevational gradient in the RMBL vicinity.  The RMBLnet components include meteorological and remote sensing instrumentation co-located with biological phenology observations of plants and animals.   The melding of instrumental and phenological data enables discoveries of the climatic controls and drivers of phenology, providing quantitative measures of the nature and pace of ecosystem conditions.  Phenology observations will be acquired mainly by human observations, but also with instruments such as the acoustic sensor, for animal phenology, and remote sensing instrumentation.  Eventually, plant phenology could include native and non-invasive cloned species, such as Syringa x chinensis (lilacs), and observation intervals will be as opportunity permits.  Cloned species provides baseline reference to assess the purely climatic signal by eliminating genetic variability found in any non-cloned organism.  Lilacs were selected because of their well-defined phenological events, cold hardiness, and resistance to heat and drought.  The phenophases to observe are emerging leaves, all leaves emerged, open flowers, full flowering, and end of flowering.  These and full phenology observation protocols are explicitly described at http://usanpn.org/?q=Syringa_chinensis.
Subject: Climate Change

ResearchPlanTitle: Determining Long-Term Success of Revegetation Efforts in Disturbed Sites
ResearchPlanAbstract: The goal of my research is to study the long-term success of Helen Beeson’s transplanting efforts around Mammal Lab and to improve upon her techniques by experimenting with different treatment methods on revegetated plants. I will compare Helen’s initial results to the current state of vegetation around Mammal Lab, quantifying the amount of surviving transplants, native plants that have established naturally, and invasive species. Based on my findings I will also attempt to improve upon Helen’s revegetation techniques by experimenting with different treatments such as fertilizer, nutrient-rich soil, and peat.
ResearchPlanOrganisms: Potentilla gracilis, Linum lewisii, Fragaria virginiana, Erigeron speciosus, and Achilea millefolium
Subject: Other

ResearchPlanTitle: Does water-use efficiency shape the distribution of Ipomopsis parents and hybrids along an environmental gradient?
ResearchPlanAbstract: I will study two species of Ipomopsis wildflowers, which hybridize along a gradient in soil moisture.  I will investigate how plants accustomed to different levels of soil moisture (moist, medium, dry) respond physiologically to changes in soil moisture.  This will help us test the hypothesis that Ipomopsis hybrids are specifically adapted to the soil moisture level where they are found.
ResearchPlanOrganisms: Ipomopsis aggregata, Ipomopsis tenuituba, and their natural hybrids
Subject: Other

ResearchPlanTitle: Species Area Relationship on the Gothic Earthflow
ResearchPlanAbstract: I want to test the theory that predicts that the slope of the species-area relationship at any scale, for any taxonomic group, in any habitat, is uniquely determined as a certain universal function of the ratio of species abundance to species richness at that scale.  This theory has been tested in a variety of undisturbed sites.  My goal is to test its application to a disturbed site, specifically the Gothic earthflow.
Subject: Other

ResearchPlanTitle: Protection at a price: ant interactions with pollinators on aspen sunflower (Helianthella quinquenervis)
ResearchPlanAbstract: The aspen sunflower, Helianthella quinquenervis, recruits ants for protection against seed-parasitism through the secretion of extrafloral nectar. While this ant-plant mutualism is well documented, the interactions between ants and pollinators on the aspen sunflower has not been rigorously investigated. I plan to manipulate both extrafloral resource abundance and ant species composition and occurrence on the aspen sunflower. I believe that exploring ant-pollinator interactions mediated by extrafloral nectaries will expose a reproductive tradeoff between protection from herbivores and successful plant pollination.
Subject: Other

ResearchPlanTitle: Foraging behavior of parasitized and non-parasitized voles under new moon and full moon conditions
ResearchPlanAbstract: Using montane voles and their parasites as a model system, we will examine how parasites indirectly impact the behavior of their hosts to gain a better understanding of how parasites can influence predator-prey relationships and how environmental changes that effect parasite populations can have wider ranging effects in communities.  I will accomplish this by trapping voles and collecting data on age, weight, length, sex, reproductive status, etc. as well as checking for endo-parasites and surveying the animals to check for ecto-parasites (e.g. ticks, mites).
Subject: Other

ResearchPlanTitle: Does Elevation Influence the Distribution and Frequency of Endophyte Symbionts of Festuca thurberi and Poa alpina?  Do Naturally Endophyte Infected Plants and Naturally Endophyte Free Plants Differ in Performance at High vs. Low Elevation?
ResearchPlanAbstract: I propose observations and experiments to address the question:  Does endophyte distribution vary with elevation in microbial symbionts in Poa alpina and Festuca thurberi?  The specific microbial symbionts of interest are the Epichloë endophytes (genera Epichloë and Neotyphodium).  In order to answer this question, I am conducting a two part study which first addresses the question: how does endophyte frequency change with elevation?  The second part of my study will address the question:  do naturally endophyte infected plants and naturally endophyte free plants differ in performance at high vs. low elevation?   I will use a reciprocal transplant experiment to assess plant performance.
Subject: Climate Change

ResearchPlanTitle: Optimal foraging and co-evolution: the foraging of bumble bees on vertical inflorescences.
ResearchPlanAbstract: Bumble bees will be observed foraging on three species of wildflower growing flowers in vertical inflorescences. It will be determined if their foraging behavior is resulting in the maximum net energy gain possible and if their behavior can be predicted using optimal foraging theory.
ResearchPlanOrganisms: Bombus spp., Delphinium nuttallianum, D. barbeyi, Aconitum columbianum
Subject: Pollination

ResearchPlanTitle: Effects of nectar robbing on hummingbird behavior and pollen deposition in Ipomopsis aggregata
ResearchPlanAbstract: This study will focus on determining the effects of nectar robbing  from both the plant and pollinator perspective. From the plant perspective, I will be determining how single-visit pollen deposition by hummingbirds differs from robbed and unrobed flowers of the Ipomopsis aggregata. From the hummingbird perspective, I will determine what are the proximate cues that nectar provides the pollinators to determine its presence or absence.
ResearchPlanOrganisms: Ipomopsis aggregate, Selasphorus platycercus, Selasphorus rufus
Subject: Pollination

ResearchPlanTitle: Solitary bee distribution across meadow types
ResearchPlanAbstract: Collect, identify, and measure tongue lengths of solitary bees; collect, identify, and measure nectar holder tube length of flowering plants
ResearchPlanOrganisms:
Solitary bee species,
Bumble bees species,
Local wildflowers
Subject: Pollination

ResearchPlanTitle: Macroinvertebrate Community Change and Nutrient Cycling in Rocky Mountain Streams
ResearchPlanAbstract: Nutrient recycling is important to ecosystem function in all ecosystems. In streams, the supply of nitrogen and phosphorus to plants, algae, and bacteria can limit their growth. Stream insects have been shown in other studies to supply a significant amount of nutrients to the stream water through excretion. Among other factors, body size contributes to excretion rate. I propose to examine how stream insect body size is related to excretion rate of nitrogen and phosphorus  and how this relationship varies across taxa. Additionally, for a long time people have been using stream insects as a way to monitor water quality in streams. However, no one has determined how changes in the stream invertebrate community impact nutrient recycling in the stream. I plan on investigating how changes in the stream insect community composition influences nutrient cycling in streams using computer models.
Subject: Other

ResearchPlanTitle: Determining whether elevation and willow proximity affect species richness and abundance of cavity and non-cavity nesting birds in aspen (Populus tremuloides) woodlands.
ResearchPlanAbstract: Many environmental factors affect the abundance and richness of bird species.  Riparian areas have been found to be vital in maintaining high species diversity in dry, arid regions, but their importance is less known in areas with abundant precipitation, such as western North America.  In mountainous regions, elevation and topography can have a large influence on avian populations as well.  I will attempt to distinguish between the effects of elevation and distance from willows (which are mostly found in riparian areas) on the species diversity and abundance of birds nesting in aspen groves.  Results could be significant for conservation and management purposes, as riparian areas are often threatened by grazing and other human-induced activities.
ResearchPlanOrganisms: All cavity and non-cavity nesting birds that reside in aspen groves.
Subject: Other

ResearchPlanTitle: Does Chamerion angustifolium, Fireweed, develop induced resistance to previous herbivory damage?
Subject: Other

ResearchPlanTitle: Ant-Aphid Interactions:  Mechanisms that generate density dependence in the benefit of ants to aphids
ResearchPlanAbstract: Our main objective is to investigate and identify mechanisms that cause density-dependence in ant-aphid mutualisms.  With this study, the questions I plan to address are:  (1) Are there physical limitations to the number of ants that can tend a particular colony based with increasing aphid abundance?  (2) Does aphid competition within a colony for plant resources limit the per-aphid resources they are able to produce for ants as the colony increases? (3) Does positive density-dependent predation upon aphids exist?  I will use four different treatments to make experimental comparisons, which will allow me to observe and document mechanisms of density dependence in ant-aphid systems.
Subject: Other

ResearchPlanTitle: The response of Lathyrus, Lupine, Erigeron, and Heliomeris to supplemental nitrogen within a natural soil moisture gradient in a subalpine meadow near the RMBL.
ResearchPlanAbstract: I will add supplemental nitrogen to individual plants occurring is soils with different natural moisture contents.  I will record the response of fertilized plants compared to control plants within either a dry or wet environment.  Since nitrogen and soil moisture are two resources expected to become altered due to human activity and climate change, these data will provide insights into possible future responses of plants experiencing altered resource availability.
Subject: Climate Change

ResearchPlanTitle: Sperm retention in female Nicrophorus investigator
ResearchPlanAbstract: The species of burying beetle, Nicrophorus investigator, partake in biparental care of the young. It has been observed, however, that a female can raise a brood on her own, therefore indicating females have the capability to retain sperm. This study will investigate the length of sperm retention in which the females can still produce viable offspring. This will help explain both male and female behaviors associated with sperm retention and raising the young.
Subject: Other

ResearchPlanTitle: The relationships among butterfly size, visitation rate, handling time, and floral display size
ResearchPlanAbstract: I will investigate if there is a relationship between butterfly morphology, handling time, visitation rate, and floral display size.  I will alter some plant species to make the flowers smaller and others to make flowers larger to see how these alterations impact butterfly visitation rate and handling time.
ResearchPlanOrganisms: Butterflies, Eriogonun subalpinum, Erigonum umbellatum, and Arenaria congesta
Subject: Pollination

ResearchPlanTitle: Cavity Nest Preferences of Mountain Bluebirds
ResearchPlanAbstract: Red-naped sapsuckers are woodpeckers that make a new cavity every year.  In subsequent years other birds inhabit those cavities.  I will be studying several characteristics of the holes in which mountain bluebirds nest, including distance to nearest water, diameter at breast height of tree, height of nest, distance to nearest willows, orientation of nest, distance to edge of forest and density of tree. These measurements will help to understand the preferences of the mountain bluebird.
Subject: Other

ResearchPlanTitle: Cavity Nest Preferences of Mountain Bluebirds
ResearchPlanAbstract: The red-naped sapsucker of western Colorado excavates cavity nests each year in aspen trees infected with heartwood rot fungus. In following years, the nests are inhabited by at least seven species of secondary cavity-nesters. Among these, little is known about the mountain bluebird and what characteristics they choose when selecting a nest site. Our study aims to determine what niche of available cavity nests the mountain bluebird fills. We will measure nest height in the aspen tree, diameter at breast height, distance to edge of forest, distance to water, distance to willows, tree density and nest opening orientation and compare bluebird nests to all nests to determine preferences.
Subject: Other

ResearchPlanTitle: Variation of Vigilance in Yellow-bellied marmots Due to Predator Pressure
ResearchPlanAbstract: Vigilance is a necessary survival behavior in prey species. Little variation (20-30%) can be explained statistically with Yellow-bellied marmots. By observing marmots in their natural environment at RMBL we hope to measure vigilance by performing focals (watching an individual for 2 minutes) which are narrated into a recorder. Software allows us to score these narrations and turn them into time allocations for vigilance behaviors. Predator pressure will be measured by looking for scats at fixed locations surrounding marmot burrows.
Subject: Long-Term

ResearchPlanTitle: Does stigma-anther separation contribute to sexual interference avoidance in dwarf bluebells (Mertensia fusiformis)?
ResearchPlanAbstract: Flowers are the centers of reproduction in plants, producing pollen to give to other plants, receiving pollen from other plants, and producing fruits and seeds that will become the next generation of individuals. Many of the features of flowers, including shape, color, and arrangement of parts, are thought to help the plants produce as many offspring as possible. Two very important flower parts are the anthers, which produce and release pollen, and the stigma, which receives pollen from other plants. The arrangement of these two flower parts can have very important consequences for how many offspring plants can produce. In dwarf bluebells, there is a lot of variation in the arrangement of the stigma and anthers. Why does this variation exist? Does the arrangement of these parts affect how many offspring the dwarf bluebells can produce? My project aims to investigate these questions, and to understand more broadly how the arrangement of flower parts affects a plant's ability to produce offspring.
Subject: Pollination

ResearchPlanTitle: Community carbon dynamics on a fine temporal scale following a precipitation pulse
ResearchPlanAbstract:
Water availability drives photosynthesis by allowing plants to open their stomata for the purpose of taking in carbon. Water also regulates decomposition processes by triggering growth and reproduction of microbes and physically aiding in the process of decomposition of organic matter (Huxman et al. 2004, Ignace et al. 2007).  

Therefore, the water balance is closely linked to the movement of carbon in a system.  Studying carbon exchanges at the community level will help elucidate the mechanisms of positive feedback to global climate change.  I measured rates of CO2 absorption by four plant species and rates of CO2 release by both target species and the soil beneath them.  Additionally I took soil, plant, and air temperatures, soil organic matter and moisture levels of the soil.   These data were used to characterize the activity of community components over time (growing season of summer 2009) following addition of water to plots.
ResearchPlanOrganisms:
Lupinus argenteus 
Artemisia tridentate
Erigeron speciosis
Lathyrus leucanthu
Subject: Climate Change

ResearchPlanTitle: The indirect effects of detritus processing on invertebrate algivore fitness in subalpine wetlands
ResearchPlanAbstract: I will be studying the impact of caddisflies, a wetland insect that eats dead plant material, on liberating nutrients. These nutrients stimulate algal growth, and I will investigate whether or not caddisflies and other wetland invertebrates benefit by eating this algae.  Under competitive conditions (high densities of caddisflies), nutrients are released at a greater rate, due to increased processing.  I hypothesize that algae will become an important food source for caddisflies under high densities, and that snails (an algae eater) will also benefit from increased algal production.  To test my hypothesis, I will create a gradient caddisfly density in microcosms, in order to manipulate nutrient (N and P) release.
ResearchPlanOrganisms: Caddisfly Limnephilus externus and a local species of pond snail (TBD)
Subject: Other

ResearchPlanTitle: Influence of patch area on bird species diversity in coniferous forests
ResearchPlanAbstract: Conifer forest patches are becoming fragmented as a result of human activity.  Bird species diversity can vary in these patches because of reduced area or due to an edge effect.  The goal of this project is to discover a relationship between patch area and bird species richness as well as total abundance.
Subject: Other

ResearchPlanTitle: A balanced diet:  Effects of ant (Hymenoptera: Formicidae) nutritional state on the balance between mutualism and predation upon aphids (Hemiptera: Aphididae)
ResearchPlanAbstract: Several species of ants tend aphids like cattle, collecting their honeydew for food while providing protection to the aphids.  This study looks at how ant diet may cause them to abandon this mutualistic interaction and begin preying upon the aphids.
ResearchPlanOrganisms: Formica podzolica, Tapinoma sessile, Myrmica sp., and several unknown aphid species to be identified (specialists on aspen, fireweed, and valerian)
Subject: Other

ResearchPlanTitle: Observing Environmental Forces that Drive Morphological Variation in an Alpine Annual Plant
ResearchPlanAbstract: I will be looking at environmental factors that correlate with morphological variation in an alpine, annual, flowering plant (Androsace septentrionalis). This research will contribute to the broader understanding of how plants may adapt to climate change. Also the study will look at how individual plants within a population are spatially distributed across an environmental gradient; which will provide insight into how the distribution and abundance of plants are correlated with measures of average plant fitness and how plant population spatial structure may change given anticipated climate change scenarios.
Subject: Climate Change

ResearchPlanTitle: Soil nutrient effects of Formica obscuripes on Chrysothamnus viscidiflorus and Artemisia tridentada
ResearchPlanAbstract: This experiment will be testing the soil nutrient levels at different distances away from ant mounds. I will be growing plants in these different soils with one sample having nutrients and one that does not.
ResearchPlanOrganisms: Chrysothamnus vicsidiflorus, Artemisia tridentada, Formica obscuripes
Subject: Other
