ResearchPlanTitle: Is there a positive correlation between bee size and size parameters of the flowers the bees visit for pollen to provision their nests?
ResearchPlanAbstract: In many different plant communities, bees are very important to pollination.  For example, 80% of plant species of Brazilian Savannah are bee pollinated. Stang et al. (2009) used the nectar to predict network structure, to explain who visits whom in a community.  It would be important to take a pollen perspective as pollen represents the most expensive resource from the plant’s viewpoint. Also some species of bees visit different plants for pollen than for nectar while others are generally nectar collectors. In this work I want to se if there is a positive correlation between bee size and size parameters of the flowers that bees visit for pollen.  Stang et al. (2009) found a pattern where small bees visit just small flowers, and larger bees visit all size of flowers to use nectar.  But I predict that small bees will visit all flower sizes in search of pollen, as the pollen is more accessible than the nectar.  Furthermore small bees can collect pollen from different flower sizes, as they are small and can land in all kinds of surfaces.  I therefore predict that I will find pollen grains from small and large flowers in their nests.  As animals with high requirements of energy may not forage in flowers that do not offer enough caloric reward, and large bees might visit larger flowers because of morphological constraints, I predict that I will find big bees visiting just medium and big flowers.  Furthermore I expect to confirm it finding pollen of flowers that have more or less the same size in their nests. I Will collect flowers of different species and conduct measures on different flower’s traits.  Furthermore I will monitor nine trap nests that have straws with different diameters. I will be removing the straws colonized to sample the pollen and I will identify the origin of them. I will select ten different plant species with different flower sizes to make observations. I will collect all bee species recorded collecting pollen and measure their body size and. Also I will collect the pollen found in their body for identification. I will analyse the data with correlations between bee’s body size and size parameters of the flowers visited.  In the end I will show the data of plant-flower and pollen consumers in a network graph to see if the pattern found in that work differs from those found on webs for nectar consumers.
Subject: Pollination

ResearchPlanTitle: Effects of Diatom, Didymosphenia geminata, on Invertebrate Abundance and Composition in Rocky Mountain Streams.
ResearchPlanAbstract: Didymosphenia geminata is a diatom that secretes a mucopolysaccharide stalk. The stalk can create thick algal mats that can extend for several km and be up to 20 cm thick.  These invasions are known as nuisance blooms.  The blooms have the ability to effect the physical and chemical chemistry of the ecosystem.  I will be studying the algae’s effect on the abundance and composition of invertebrates in the East River. In addition, previous studies have determined that chironomids are significantly abundant in streams that have D. geminata present.  This is a rare finding in the Rocky Mountain streams.  Due to these findings I will also conduct and experiment to determine whether there is evidence that D. geminata acts as a refuge for the small-bodied chironomids against predators.
Subject: Other

ResearchPlanTitle: Tradeoffs Between Territorial Behavior and Song in Mountain White-crowned Sparrows (Zonotrichia leucophrys oriantha)
ResearchPlanAbstract: Bird song is an important aspect of life history because of its importance in mate selection and territory defense. As with many sexually selected traits, bird song has been shown to be a relatively plastic behavior and associated with multiple tradeoffs. While many studies have investigated the impact of parasite-host interactions and the effects on life-history attributes, the impacts of pathogen infection remain to be fully explored. Given the apparent plasticity in song investment, a tradeoff between mounting an immune response and song behavior may be expected. This study intends to contribute to understanding of the basis of behavioral adaptation to disease by further exploring tradeoffs between mounting an immune response and territorial song and behavior.
Subject: Other

ResearchPlanTitle: American Robin repertoires and their individuality
ResearchPlanAbstract:
Avian communication is widely diverse amid the 4000 songbird species (Brenowitz 1997). Birdsong characteristics vary in acoustics, composition, repertoire size, and educational aspects (Williams 2004). Components of avian repertoires include notes, syllables, phrases, and types (Brenowitz et al. 1997).
    Thrushes, recognizable for their elaborate and various songs, may have a repertoire exceeding 100 different song types, while other songbird repertoires have as few as ten types (Ince and Slater 1985; Brumm et al. 2009).   The most common thrush in North America is the American Robin (Turdus migratorius) (Sallabanks and James 1999). 
    Despite its cosmopolitan distribution, communication in the American Robin is remarkably under-studied. Prior studies involving robin songs, most being masters theses that remain unpublished, focused on comparisons of certain syllables rather than the repertoires. One study however, discovered that robin repertoires consist of extensive syllables (Sallabanks and James 1999).  
    Robin repertoires are the basis to understanding the species’ social behaviors and interactions. Therefore this research focuses on estimating the size of robin repertoires within RMBL and its surrounding area to provide further understanding of the complexity of robin communication. Repertoire analysis performed in this study will enhance the prior knowledge on robin individuality, concerning their syllables, and discover how variable syllables are due to their note formation.
Subject: Other

ResearchPlanTitle: How does streambed heterogeneity influences  algal accrual and macroinvertebrate diversity, abundance, and trait distribution?
ResearchPlanAbstract: Humans are altering stream flow worldwide. It is of great importance to understand the ecosystem needs of streams. Velocity of streams is continuously altered due to diversion. Many animals depend upon algal accumulation.   Heterogeneity of cobble creates a more diverse nich for macroinvertebrate species.
Subject: Other

ResearchPlanInstitution: SUNY- College of Environmental Science and Forestry
ResearchPlanTitle: Effects of pollination amounts and relative viability among hermaphroditic and female morphotypes within the gynodioecious species Geranium richardsonii
ResearchPlanAbstract: The wild geranium (Geranium richardsonii) is a gynodiecious plant found around the Rocky Mountain Biological Laboratory in Gothic, CO. We will look at whether or not there is an anatomical relationship between specific stigma lobes and the ovules within the ovary. This will be done by emasculating hermaphroditic plants and then removing 0-5 stigma lobes on various flowers for multiple plants (both hermaphroditic and female)among two populations. Full stigma sets will also be removed. Pollen will be counted on all stigma lobes and will be compared to the seed set.
Subject: Pollination

ResearchPlanTitle: Factors influencing floral traits in montane meadows: competition, environmental filtering, and phylogeny
ResearchPlanAbstract: When you walk through a montane meadow in summer you are bound to see a number of flowers in bloom, and if you look more closely you will notice that these flowers have a large diversity of forms and colors.  Scientists, however, still do not know why so many forms and colors exist. So far, we believe that three major processes are responsible for the set of flower colors and forms in communities: (1) competition between flowers for the pollinators they need to reproduce, (2) environmental factors like temperature, soil moisture and elevation, and (3) the relatedness of the plants in the community. In my study I will collect measurements of flower structure size and color for all species in flower at five different communities in Rocky Mountains of western Colorado for the course of the summer 2009. I will then put the measurements for each species into statistical models to determine if the traits of color and size are more different from each other or less different from each other than what we would expect from random chance.  I will also use test to see if the relatedness of these species is affecting the color and size of flowers.  Finally, I will search online databases for the flowers in my community,  to see if specific flower colors and sizes tend to be found at specific elevations.
Subject: Other

ResearchPlanTitle: Coyotes and Columbines: Do Predators Deter Deer from Eating Colorado Native Wildflowers?
ResearchPlanAbstract: Even though predators do not eat plants, they can affect plants indirectly by killing herbivores or by frightening them and altering their behavior. These indirect effects of carnivores on plants via plant consumers are called “trophic cascades”. We humans have had major impacts on trophic cascades around the planet, not only because we kill large predators (think of wolves), but also because we modify their use of space. Many predators avoid areas of high human activity, and prey often congregate in these “safe havens.” Mule deer have increased dramatically at RMBL over the past two decades, and browsing of preferred wildflowers – like blue columbine, the Colorado State flower – has also increased. We hypothesize that this has happened because coyotes avoid the RMBL townsite in the summer, and deer have learned that RMBL is a safe place for their fawns. To test this hypothesis, we will determine 1) whether coyotes are more active, and deer less active, away from the RMBL; 2) whether deer avoid experimental depots of coyote scent; and 3) whether herbivory on palatable plant species is correlated with natural or experimentally-induced spatial variation in deer activity. Results of this study will have important implications for Colorado’s game and predator management policies
Subject: Climate Change

ResearchPlanTitle: Snowshoe Hare Population Density in a Subalpine Forest Ecosystem in the Southern Rocky Mountains, Colorado
ResearchPlanAbstract: The Snowshoe Hare represents a signature mammal of the sub-alpine forest, and it is a common species at the Rocky Mountain Biological Laboratory.  It survies the winter by molting into a pure white coat and nibbling on woody stems during cold winter nights.  The population density of hares is unknown in the area, however, snowshoe hare population density is apparently synchronized regionally.  This study is an attempt to extend research from Taylor Park, Colorado by the Colorado Division of Wildlife and Colorado State University on snowshoe hare density, with primary focus on long-term population fluctuation.  Hares in their northern range have classic 10-year cycles with a 5-25 fold change in numbers from peak to low densities.  In the sourthern portion of their range, less is known about whether hare populations cycle.  This infomration is important to the management of newly re-introduced lynx in the Southern Rocky Mountains.  The long-tern success of the lynx re-introduction is largely dependent on the abundance of their primary food base, the snowshoe hare.  Further, this research will help to answer a long standing question about the character of population flcutuation in southern snowshoe hares and seeks to address the hypothesis of a new southern range paradigm that snowshoe hares have 10-year cycles with reduced peaks and lows.  We will trap snowshoe hares in baited live-traps in mid-January and attach an ear tag to each hare.  trapping will occur over a four night period and data include numbers of captured and tagged hares, and numbers of recaptured hares.  These data are used to calculate the population density using software called Program DENSITY.  The results of this study will hekp to understand the basic population ecology of snowshow hares in their southern range and will caontribute to the research and management of the lynx in Colorado.
Subject: Long-Term

ResearchPlanTitle: Life in a Shrinking World: Changes in Altitudinal Distributions of Alpine Mammals due to Climate Change
ResearchPlanAbstract: As global temperatures increase, species are exposed to a range of stressful temperatures, especially in species currently living at their thermal limits (alpine species). Warming temperatures may force alpine species to move to higher elevations. We hypothesize that alpine mammals will move to higher elevations to stay within their optimal physiologic temperature range. We will measure the metabolic thermoneutral zone and activity of mammals at four sites in the western U.S. We will use the physiologic data obtained in this study to predict range shifts in alpine mammals based on current climate predictions, and will verify predictive models using historic data.
ResearchPlanOrganisms: Neotamias minimus, N. umbrinus,  N. quadrivittatus, Ochotona princeps
Subject: Climate Change

ResearchPlanTitle: Evolution of plants in natural populations: Ecological speciation, elevational gradients, and flower-pollinator associations
ResearchPlanAbstract: An understanding of evolution in natural populations often requires long-term studies that integrate a variety of methods. I propose a combination of ecological, physiological, and genetic studies of three questions related to plant evolution. These studies should help elucidate some mechanisms responsible for current plant diversity and may also help in predicting responses to global warming. First, I will continue my ongoing work on species formation, using hybrid zones between the wildflowers Ipomopsis aggregata (scarlet gilia) and Ipomopsis tenuituba (slendertube skyrocket). The centerpiece of this project is a reciprocal transplant experiment designed to test models for ecological speciation by comparing natural selection on floral traits with selection on vegetative and physiological traits in both parental and hybrid habitats. Second, I propose to investigate local adaptation over an elevational range of about 1,000 m in Ipomopsis and to test potential factors that set the upper range limit. Third, I will use manipulations of flower traits to test hypotheses about the roles of specific insect and bird pollinator types in floral evolution. This project will assess natural selection for combinations of multiple traits, using a variety of local wildflowers in the phlox family.
ResearchPlanOrganisms: Ipomopsis aggregata, Ipomopsis tenuituba, Polemonium foliosissimum, Polemonium pulcherrimum
Subject: Long-Term

ResearchPlanTitle: The Genetics of Inbreeding in Mimulus guttatus
ResearchPlanAbstract: Advances in genetics have brought new tools to bear on unanswered questions, such as the genetic basis and evolution of inbreeding. We propose to advance knowledge in this area using the emerging model system Mimulus guttatus. Previous work on the genetics and evolution of inbreeding has suffered from poor experimental design, insufficient statistical power, and a lack of control for whole-genome duplication. We will use genotype data from field collections of M. guttatus populations to estimate the selfing rate and inbreeding load. Using improved statistical methodology, we will determine if there is a negative relationship between selfing rate and inbreeding load, while simultaneously estimating the effect of whole-genome duplication on this relationship. If inbreeding load is due to recessive or partially recessive mutations, purging will occur as inbreeding increases homozygosity and exposes these mutations to selection. In this scenario, purging will increase population fitness. This is contrary to the predominant view that inbreeding reduces fitness. These data will further our understanding of the evolution and genetics of inbreeding in natural populations.
Subject: Other

ResearchPlanInstitution: USDA ARS Poisonous Plant Research Laboratory
ResearchPlanTitle: The chemical ecology of Delphinium, Lupinus, and Veratrum.
ResearchPlanAbstract: The genera Delphinium, Lupinus, and Veratrum are potentially toxic and/or teratogenic to herbivores on rangelands. The bio-active compounds responsible for the toxic and/or teratogenic potential of these genera represent different types of alkaloids and are well characterized chemically. Our general research interests relate to the chemical ecology of these bioactive compounds. The proposed research will survey the nectar and pollen of select species within these genera for the presence of these alkaloids. If the pollen and/or nectar are found to contain these compounds, follow-up studies will be pursued in the future to determine if there is any adaptive advantage to having these alkaloids in the pollen and/or nectar. In addition, we plan to determine if experimental manipulations of temperature results in changes to the qualitative and/or quantitative composition of the toxic alkaloids in Delphinium nuttallianum.
ResearchPlanOrganisms:
Delphinium nuttallianum
Delphinium barbeyi
Veratrum californicum
Lupinus argenteus
Subject: Pollination

ResearchPlanInstitution: University of North Carolina at Wilmington
ResearchPlanTitle: Mammalian Response to Climate Change During the Last Glacial Maximum in North America
ResearchPlanAbstract: Cave faunas are unparalleled in their documentation of ecosystem dynamics through time. In particular, vertebrate remains from fossiliferous caves can provide a direct record of faunal diversity, turnover, and the paleoecology of these animals across geologic time. Cement Creek Cave is a multi-chambered limestone cave located outside Crested Butte, Colorado, at an elevation of 2950m. Excavations completed here in 2007 have yielded rich deposits of vertebrate fossils dating from over 40,000 years ago to present. This record spans a period of well-documented climate and ecological change, both in North America and globally. It includes the culmination of the Last Glacial Maximum at 19,000 B.P. and subsequent recession of continental ice sheets. The extent to which these changes affected the ecology of Colorado and the Southern Rocky Mountains will be brought into finer resolution with analysis of the Cement Creek Cave fauna. Here, we propose to analyze carbon and oxygen stable isotope signatures from fossil tooth enamel to elucidate paleoecological changes in the region of Cement Creek Cave. These isotopes are proxies for the dominant types of vegetation in a region and the source of ingested waters, respectively. Results of both isotopic analyses are also indicators of climate and temperature in a given region. To obtain isotope samples, enamel will be extracted from fossil teeth of marmots (Marmota spp.) and other herbivores including rabbits and hares (Leporinae spp.). Apart from the Cement Creek Cave fossils, we will also gather a set of modern marmot and leporid enamel samples to facilitate comparison of late-Pleistocene conditions to those at present. Accordingly, we request small enamel samples from specimens housed in the biological collections of the Rocky Mountain Biological Laboratory. For each individual, one tooth will be selected for enamel extraction using a fine drill. This procedure causes minimal impact to the specimen while still allowing for adequate enamel for use in analyses. Specimens in the RMBL collections are ideal for this work as many have been collected in the same region and elevation as our study site. In addition to stable isotope inferences of mammalian paleoecology, the vertebrate paleontology of Cement Creek Cave is being described (Emslie 2002, Emslie pers. comm.). This work will describe the diversity of montane mammals in the late-Pleistocene, as well as potential faunal turnover engendered by paleoclimatic changes. An important part of this research is to obtain detailed data on the small mammal community structure operating in the vicinity of Cement Creek Cave today. We will use small mammal live-trapping and mark-recapture methods to survey the dominant habitat types found in the region as delineated in the literature (i.e., subalpine forest, mesic/dry meadows, and sagebrush park) and to classify small mammal diversity. This will be an extension of fieldwork that began elsewhere in the Upper Gunnison Basin in summer 2009. This work will provide valuable data for comparison to the Cement Creek Cave fauna and for other future studies of small mammals in Colorado and the Southern Rocky Mountains.
ResearchPlanOrganisms:
Our stable isotope analyses focus on:
Marmota flaviventris, Sylvilagus nuttallii, Lepus americanus, Lepus townsendii

In addition, any of the following small mammals may be encountered during live-trapping:  
Sorex cinereus, Sorex monticolus, Sorex nanus, Sorex palustris, Ochotona princeps, Thomomys talpoides, Microtus longicaudus, Microtus montanus, Microtus pennsylvanicus, Myodes gapperi, Phenacomys intermedius, Peromyscus maniculatus, Zapus hudsonius, Neotoma cinerea, Tamias minimus, Spermophilus lateralis, Spermophilus elegans, Tamiasciurus hudsonicus.
Subject: Climate Change

ResearchPlanTitle: The effect of high altitude and climate change on the phenology, parental behavior and population dynamics of three secondary-cavity nesting bird species.
ResearchPlanAbstract: Global climate change affects a multitude of environments in various ways. However, global climate change may have its largest impacts in environments that are greatly affected by even minor changes in average temperatures, precipitation and snow cover. For example, the population dynamics of the majority of plants and animals that live in high altitude environments are greatly affected by the number of snow-free days during their reproductive and growing stages as well as the amount of snow during the winter and when the snow cover melts in the spring. Even changes as little as a few additional days added on to the growing season by an earlier snow melt can have a big impact on the size and emergence of the insect populations. Since those insects are fed to the offspring of many nesting birds, that, in turn, can affect the beginning and length of the reproductive season in these bird populations. Since 1994, I have been examining the length of the reproductive period, the parental behavior, and the population dynamics of Mountain Bluebird (Sialia currucoides), House Wren (Troglodytes aedon) and Tree Swallow (Tachycineta bicolor) populations found at high altitude in the environment at and near the Rocky Mountain Biological Laboratory. These three species live in cavities that are either provided to them by humans (i.e. bird nest boxes) or are naturally formed by cavity excavating species (i.e. woodpeckers). While not yet significantly different from those early years, the date that the young leave the nest in Mountain Bluebirds and House Wrens has gradually become earlier and earlier in the summer, possibly reflecting the earlier snow melt and earlier emergence of their insect prey. In contrast, Tree Swallows have been relatively constant in the date the young leave the nest but, based on casual observation, have possibly decreased in population size. I plan to continue to study the nesting, behavior and population dynamics of these three species and relate those dynamics to temperature and precipitation trends in the high altitude environment at the Rocky Mountain Biological Laboratory.
ResearchPlanOrganisms: Mountain Bluebird (Sialia currucoides), House Wren (Troglodytes aedon), Tree Swallow (Tachycineta bicolor)
Subject: Phenology

ResearchPlanTitle: Ecology and evolution of floral trait variation
ResearchPlanAbstract: Communities of flowering plants are characterized by a large range of variation in floral morphologies, including differences in size, shape, color, orientation, scent, and nectar volume/composition. This variation may have been shaped by habitat filtering (in which some species are excluded because their traits do not allow high fitness in the local abiotic or bitoic environment), competitive or mutualistic interactions between species, and by the evolutionary relatedness of a given species to others in the community. I propose to investigate patterns of floral trait variation in montane meadow communities using newly developed phylogenetic and trait analysis methods to determine the relative importance of these processes.
Subject: Pollination

ResearchPlanTitle: Testing adaptive explanations for floral variation in Mertensia fusiformis
ResearchPlanAbstract: In alpine habitats, patchiness in snow accumulation and timing of spring snowmelt produces marked variation in the timing at which plants begin to flower, even over small spatial scales. Thus, plants in early- and late-melting patches can experience very different conditions during their flowering periods, despite growing in close proximity. If the difference in flowering time between early and late patches is sufficiently great, there may be little cross-pollination and genetic exchange between plants growing in the two patch types. This can result in the plants adapting to the conditions specific to the local flowering time. This study will evaluate the evidence for this type of adaptation in alpine bluebells. This species shows pronounced variation in floral characteristics that may be related to the local timing of snowmelt and flowering. Specifically, I will test whether early- and late-flowering plants are visited by different pollinators, and whether natural selection imposed by pollinators can explain the differences in floral morphology among populations. I will also test an alternative hypothesis: that the different flower types differ in sensitivity to cold weather conditions, and that this variation in susceptibility is responsible for the observed patterns. This project fits into a larger plan of research investigating how the timing of flowering and timing of pollinator activity are responding¡ªecologically and evolutionarily¡ªto climate change.
ResearchPlanOrganisms: Mertensia fusiformis and its pollinators (Bombus bifarius queens and Osmia spp.)
Subject: Pollination

ResearchPlanTitle: Chemical signaling in Brook trout and antipredator responses of an aquatic insect (Baetis bicaudatus)
ResearchPlanAbstract: Olfactory perception is particularly important when visual cues are limited, as is the case in aquatic ecosystems. Furthermore, aquatic environments are conducive to dissolving and dispersing chemical information. Thus, in those ecosystems, chemicals cues often mediate the communication among organisms, which use chemical information from the environment for behavioral decision making related to foraging, reproduction and the assessment of predator risk. In particular, recent experimental and field studies have demonstrated that many aquatic organisms, including invertebrates and vertebrates, show specific anti-predator responses to chemical alarm cues emitted by predators. Recent studies have also demonstrated the importance of non-consumptive effects whereby chemical cues emitted by predators influence prey to use different habitats, forage at different times, change their activity levels or otherwise alter their foraging behavior. Therefore, chemical predator recognition may elicit avoidance responses that significantly affect prey fitness. However, to date, few chemicals released by fish have been fully characterized in terms of origin, release, olfactory detection, and prey responses. The principal goals of this project are: 1) to explore anti-predator mechanisms of detection and responses of an aquatic insect (the mayfly Baetis bicaudatus), to a predatory Trout (Brook Trout, Salvelinus fontinalis); 2) to test whether this prey species exhibit innate or learned predator recognition; and 3) to determine the origin of the chemical cues released by the trout that are responsible of the anti-predator behavior observed in their prey.
Subject: Other

ResearchPlanTitle: 1. THE EFFECTS OF CASTILLEJA MINIATA ON COMMUNITY AND ECOSYSTEM DYNAMICS 2. Will the imprint of ant activity on soil microbial and plant communities persist once those communities are inactive?
ResearchPlanAbstract: Parasitic plants are common in nature, but their effects on the rest of the ecosystem are poorly understood. Here, we propose to a series of observations and experiments to understand whether, and how, Castilleja miniata affects montane plant communities and ecosystem processes.
Subject: Long-Term

ResearchPlanTitle: Microbial ecology of plant-pollinator interactions
ResearchPlanAbstract: Floral nectar serves to attract pollinators to facilitate reproduction. Comprised of sugars and amino acids, this reward is prone to infestation by microorganisms. Research has shown that microorganisms can alter nectar chemistry, potentially reducing its suitability for pollinators. This reduction in suitability may alter pollinator preference This research will explore the direct and indirect effects of microorganisms on pollinator behavior and plant fitness mediated through nectar traits.
Subject: Pollination

ResearchPlanTitle: Pollinator diversity and foraging specialization
ResearchPlanAbstract: Pollinator species losses are ongoing and are likely to accelerate in the future. What will be the functional consequences of these species losses for plant reproduction? We hypothesize that competition between pollinator species--which is lowered when species are lost--is important in shaping pollinator specialization. Without this specialization, pollinators transfer the wrong kinds of pollen to plants, reducing their efficiency as pollinators while lowering plant reproduction. To test this hypothesis, we will temporarily and non-destructively reduce bee and plant diversity and abundance in several meadow sites, and compare manipulated to non-manipulated sites. We will measure short-term specialization of pollinators through 1) monitoring foraging behavior; 2) analyzing pollen loads carried by bees; and 3) analyzing pollen loads on flowers.
ResearchPlanOrganisms:
bees: focus on Bombus spp and also Osmia bucephala; will also be doing community inventory across all bee species.
plants: community inventory, flower bagging, targeted stigmatic removals
Subject: Pollination

ResearchPlanTitle: The effect of ecological factors on sex ratios and demographic trends in Polemonium foliosissimum
ResearchPlanAbstract: I am studying the roles that ecological factors, such as pollinators, seed predators, and herbivores, play in the ecology and evolution of the gynodioecy, a breeding system characterized by the presence of female and hermaphroditic sex morphs. Any ecological factor that influences the fitness of the sex morphs can have profound effects on this system. For example, because females only acquire fitness through seeds while hermaphrodites do so through pollen and seed, females are expected to have higher seed fitness. Thus, if seed predators preferentially attack hermaphrodites, this could provide the needed fitness advantage for females to be maintained. One reason gynodioecy is of interest is that it is thought to be the most likely intermediate in the evolutionary path from hermaphroditism to dioecy (characterized by male and female plants), which has occurred in more than half of all flowering plant families. My research, which uses demographic modeling, will allow me to look at how these ecological factors influence sex ratios but also population growth rates, thus having both evolutionary and management implications. I am particularly interested in exploring how herbivores, by changing the timing of flowering of plants, influence the subsequent interaction between those plants and mutualist pollinators and antagonist seed predators.

ResearchPlanTitle: Linking butterfly traits to fitness to forecast butterfly responses to climate change
ResearchPlanAbstract: Increasing global temperatures have begun to profoundly affect terrestrial communities. The Alpine areas in Colorado have seen greater increases in temperature over the past fifty years than other parts of the country on the order of 0.4 C per decade (culter.colorado.edu). This makes Mead/’s Sulphur and Clouded Sulphur- both Rocky Mountain butterflies that have been studied extensively for their close functional relationship between wing coloration patterns and temperature as well as larval thermal ecology- of great research interest. We will collect data addressing how environmental conditions interact with larval and adult physiology to constrain distributions. Comparing modern measurements to previous data collected at RMBL and elsewhere will address whether butterflies physiology has already responded to climate change. This research will serve to parameterize an ecophysiological distribution model, which will be tested by hindcasting past distribution changes and used to predict future distribution shifts.
ResearchPlanOrganisms:

ResearchPlanTitle: Life history, phenology, and reproductive success of glacier lilies
ResearchPlanAbstract: I will continue long-term observations (begun in 1990) on environmental factors influencing flowering, fruiting, and survival of glacier lily plants. I will conduct supplemental-pollination experiments to determine whether fruiting is limited by pollination deficits. Past experiments have detected a trend of deteriorating pollination service.
Subject: Long-Term

ResearchPlanTitle: 1) Sex under siege: multiple species effects on a gynodioecious plant, Polemonium foliosissimum. and 2) Effects of vegetative damage on life-history traits in Scarlet gilia, Ipomopsis aggregata.
ResearchPlanAbstract: NON-TECHNICAL ABSTRACT: Plants employ diverse mating strategies to succeed. Although most flowering plants produce “perfect” flowers – i.e., flowers that function both as females in producing seeds and males in producing pollen – in some species the sexes are expressed in different plants, a term called “dioecy”. The path from perfect flowers to separate sexes has evolved in over half of all plant families. Gynodioecy, whereby some plants produce perfect flowers while others produce flowers with vestigial anthers, is common and thought to be an evolutionary intermediate between full hermaphrodites and complete separation of the sexes. The evolutionary trajectories, or selection pressures, that promotes the separation of the sexes remains a mystery. I am interested in asking how the interactions of plants with animals that include pollinators, seed predators and herbivores, affect the sexes differently and thus may help explain sex-ratios in a gynodioecious plant, Polemonium foliosissimum. By understanding the gender-specific effects of multispecies interactions my work will provide insight to the conditions under which dioecy might evolve. Polemonium foliosissimum is a perennial plant that occurs throughout the Elk and West Elk Mountains. It is pollinated primarily by bumblebees. It is grazed by deer, cattle and sheep. In the course of our work, in addition to the questions outlined above, we hope to determine how public lands could be managed to preserve native pollinators by discovering how herbivores impact their host plants. We will provide data to the Forest Service that could be useful in developing grazing and deer control strategies that support local and regional biodiversity.

bumblebees

ResearchPlanTitle: Characterization of the species-area relationship on the Gothic earthflow as a test of the maximum entropy SAR in a high-disturbance area
ResearchPlanAbstract: Disturbance ecology is a broad field that has far-reaching consequences for issues of land conservation and preservation of biodiversity. Ecosystems that undergo large-scale disturbances such as clear-cutting of forests, forest fires, avalanches, hurricanes, and land- and mudslides can often lose biodiversity in those areas in the short-term as a result of the disturbance. Using the Gothic earthflow as an example of a high-disturbance, primary succession area, we measure the abundance and distribution of plants at the species level. By considering the presence and number of each species in larger and larger nested plots, we can create a “species-area relationship” or SAR. SAR’s represent the scaling of biodiversity with increasing area, and so are important for understanding the robustness of ecosystems, patterns in macroecology, and risks of extinction having to do with both natural and human-induced disturbances to landscapes. We then use this data to test the predictions of the Maximum Entropy information theory species-area relationship, which is a theory that may replace the standard power-law SAR most commonly found in ecological literature.
ResearchPlanOrganisms: Plants (to be counted and identified, but not collected or harmed)
Subject: Other

ResearchPlanTitle: Effects of climate-induced vegetation changes on alpine food web dynamics
ResearchPlanAbstract: Alpine ecosystems are currently some of the fastest changing places on Earth. Both observational studies and warming experiments have shown significant shifts in plant community composition as a product of global climate change, including changes to the balance of grasses and forbs and an increase in shrubbiness. Given the broad range of plant functional groups in alpine habitats, such changes in species composition and dominance could have a large impact on the structure and functioning of these ecosystems. For example, plants play a crucial role in mediating trophic interactions, so vegetation shifts could have cascading effects on the entire food web. A better understanding of the feedbacks between the plant community and the rest of the biological community on ecosystem functioning is of utmost importance for our overall understanding of the consequences of global climate change. I am interested in studying how alpine invertebrate systems are responding to these climate-induced changes in vegetation. In particular, I am curious about the mechanisms behind the response of the food web (changes in top-down or bottom-up processes) and about feedback to the plant community that may be occurring. The preliminary data collected during this exploratory study will lay the groundwork for my entire PhD dissertation research through the characterization of an appropriate set of focal species and the identification of potential long-term study plots over a comprehensive range of habitat conditions.
ResearchPlanOrganisms: I have not yet determined the principal organisms of my research, but I will be trying to choose an invertebrate predator (probably a generalist spider species) and an invertebrate consumer (possibly a generalist grasshopper species) in order to reconstruct simple tri-trophic food webs in areas with varying plant communities.
Subject: Climate Change

ResearchPlanTitle: The effects of spot application of the herbicide, Milestone, on the invasive plant, Cirsium arvense (Canada Thistle), and native vegetation.
ResearchPlanAbstract: Invasive species are a growing problem around the world, in the U.S., and in Colorado. Invasive plants disrupt native communities by forming monocultures, which decrease native plant diversity. The goal of this research is to test whether 1) adding nutrients to alpine meadows decreases stem density of C. arvense and 2) spraying Milestone on C. arvense in combination with adding nutrients can eliminate C. arvense over time.
Subject: Other

ResearchPlanTitle: Climate & climate change around RMBL
ResearchPlanAbstract: The present study aims to characterise the climate in the area around RMBL, consider temporal links in these climatic patterns, and determine how the climate has changed over about the last 100 years.  We shall focus on temperature and precipitation, as these are standard climatic parameters that are recorded at weather stations throughout the world, they are known to affect organisms in many ways, and they are known to be changing through human-induced influences on the climatic system. We distinguish between precipitation that falls as snow from rainfall, and include other climatic variables where available, and consider time scales that range from an hour to a century. The present study will also use changes in climate at RMBL as a case study to show the utility of placing local changes in climate in the context of longer time periods and larger regions. We shall test the links of local changes in temperature and precipitation with larger scale climate patterns, such as the El Niño Southern Oscillation (ENSO), Pacific Decadal Oscillation (PDO), and Atlantic Multidecadal Oscillation (AMO). In addition, an opportunity to examine the effects of climate change on bumble bees and the flowers they visit has been provided by surveys that were carried out near Crested Butte, Colorado in 1974. Given the general trend toward warmer temperatures, we hypothesized that there would be alterations of the historic distributions, with bees and their food plants moving up in altitude in order to remain within their preferred climate zones and in 2007 we sought to test this hypothesis by repeating the 1974 surveys. We aim to test this hypothesis by comparing the results of the 1974 surveys with results of surveys in 2007 and subsequent years.
Subject: Climate Change

ResearchPlanTitle: Optimal foraging by flower-visiting animals, co-evolution between them and the plants they visit, and structure of plant-pollinator communities
ResearchPlanAbstract: Optimal foraging theory (OFT) has been relatively successful in explaining the foraging behaviour of nectar-feeding animals, but has, however, been little extended to include the behaviour of animals that are collecting pollen as well as or instead of nectar, the behaviour of animals that are simultaneously searching for mates or avoiding becoming someone else’s meal, patterns of community structure such as the number of co-existing species and differences between such spp, patterns of interactions amongst co-existing spp at various trophic levels and coevolution between flower-visiting animals and the plants they visit. My aim is to develop and test such extensions of OFT by developing and testing models that aim to understand the foraging behaviours exhibited by flower-visiting animals and co-evolution between them and the plants they visit, and incorporating these models into attempts to understand patterns of community structure, webs of inter-species interactions, and co-evolution between plants and their pollinators.
ResearchPlanOrganisms: Flower-visiting animals and the plants they visit.
Subject: Pollination

ResearchPlanTitle: Functional and evolutionary genomics of host-parasite interactions in bittercress and its parasites
ResearchPlanAbstract: The plant-natural enemy interface is hypothesized to have played a major role in generating a large fraction of terrestrial organic diversity.  However, the mechanisms underlying this unfolding process of co-evolution, including reciprocal natural selection between hosts and parasites, is still not well understood in most natural host-parasite systems.  This project aims to understand the mechanistic and evolutionary basis of interactions between Cardamine cordifolia (Bittercress) mustard host plants, specialist insect herbivores and associated plant microbes that live in the Rocky Mountains.  This system was studied in an ecological context in the 1980s and 1990s and I seek to add a genetic component to this body of work.  Because of the clonal nature of host plant patches in the Rocky Mountain, the opportunity exists to determine the extent to which specialist herbivores, plant pathogenic bacteria and their host-pants are locally adapted to one another at the population-level.  Each of these species is closely related to genetic model organisms (Arabidopsis, Drosophila and Pseudmonas) and I will be able to use genetic tools from these close relatives to understand how the hosts, parasites and pathogens are interacting at the molecular level, within a single leaf of the host plant.
ResearchPlanOrganisms: Cardamine cordifolia, Scaptomyza flies, Pseudomonas bacteria, fungi

This application is for installation of total precipitation gauges for the permanent stations.

ResearchPlanTitle: Relating body mass, population biomass and the strength of positive and negative interspecific interactions in a plant/arthropod web
ResearchPlanAbstract: Interspecific interaction strength has become an important concept, yet most ecologists have focused on quantifying negative interactions in food webs without considering positive interactions, such as mutualisms. Several food web studies have found that interaction strength correlates positively with the body size ratio and the population biomasses of the interacting species. Many mutualisms include consumer-resource effects, and the strength of mutualisms may scale with body size and biomass as well. I propose to investigate whether the strength of mutualisms between ants and honeydew-producing hemipterans show the same correlations by quantifying a web of interactions occurring among plants and their associated arthropods in Almont, Colorado. Using a nested factorial experiment, I will quantify interaction strengths with several ecological currencies and metrics to relate positive and negative interactions in the same web and for comparison to other studies. Also, I wish to investigate the stoichiometric patterns in this interaction web and how mutualisms between ants and honeydew-producing membracids leverage top-down and bottom-up trophic cascades. Through these studies, I hope to reveal the similarities between a common mutualism and negative types of interactions and to better understand the importance of positive interactions in ecological systems.

ResearchPlanTitle: Biodiversity of aquatic macroinvertebrates, midges (Diptera: Chironomidae) and spiders (Araneae) at the Mexican Cut Nature Preserve and Upper Gunnison Basin.
ResearchPlanAbstract: The biodiversity, life history and distribution of aquatic macroinvertebrates is key to understanding biomonitoring data and interpreting the health of our local streams and ponds. My research will continue to help us understand the invertebrates of the upper Gunnison basin. I am also working with the “Colorado Spider Survey” at the Denver Museum of Nature and Science. As a part of this survey, I am collecting spiders in the Mexican Cut Nature Preserve along with my collections in the surrounding National Forest Lands. In addition the tiny flies called midges are common, diverse and notoriously difficult to identify. They are an interesting group because of their sensitivity to various pollutants and are often used for biomonitoring. The Mexican Cut Chironomids have been identified to genus, but further identification has awaited rearing the larvae to adults. Regular collections throughout the spring, summer, and fall can help us determine which species are present, the number of generations per year and whether each taxa is sensitive to weather events such as drought or the differences in water chemistry and predation between the various ponds at the Mexican Cut.

ResearchPlanTitle: Pollination facilitation in subalpine gentians
ResearchPlanAbstract: Plant species that flower together and share pollinators can influence each other’s pollination and reproductive success in positive, negative, or neutral ways. Pollination facilitation occurs when the pollination of a plant species is enhanced by the presence of another species, and this may be important for the persistence of rare plants, though evidence for facilitation relative to competition in plant communities is limited. Pollination facilitation may occur at larger temporal and spatial scales than researchers have been looking, as these interactions often involve highly mobile pollinators able to forage over large areas and select among different patches, and pollinator populations that are likely to respond with a time-lag to changes in floral resources. A potentially important and ubiquitous mechanism of facilitation may be through pollinator support, which occurs when sequentially flowering plants jointly maintain pollinator populations that are resident in an area by providing floral resources over an extended time, positively influencing the pollination of a later flowering species. In this study, I intend to investigate the pollinator-mediated interactions among plants at large spatial and temporal scales by studying a group of late flowering gentians and an earlier flowering species, Delphinium barbeyi, with which they share pollinators. In particular, I plan to test the hypothesis that the earlier flowering D. barbeyi supports pollinators and enhances pollination for the late flowering gentians.
ResearchPlanOrganisms: Gentiana parryi, Gentianella amarella var. acuta, Gentianopsis detonsa var. elegans (syn. G. thermalis), Delphinium barbeyi, and medium and long-tongued Bombus spp.

This study will collect information related to the ecology and population biology of osha. Such information may help to manage this species in the wild.

ResearchPlanTitle: Change in ant community composition across and elevation gradient after 15 years
ResearchPlanAbstract: Dr. John Harte has the longest running climate manipulation experiment currently in existence. Over a decade ago when the experiment was first begun, ant community composition was recorded in the experimental plots and three other control sites along an elevation gradient. Preliminary data collected last year in the warming meadow suggests that ant community composition may have shifted up in elevation in a predictable manner. We propose to return this year and thoroughly sample the historical plots along the elevation gradient to determine 1) if there have been changes in community structure over time, and 2) if those changes are species specific or if the entire community responds in the same manner. Ants are one of the most ecologically important and abundant group of organisms at these sites, and changes in their abundance and community composition may have profound implications for plant and animal communities.

The Landscape of Fear and Trophic Cascades: Does Human

ResearchPlanTitle: Willow Selection by the Red-Naped Sapsucker (Sphyrapicus nuchalis ): The effects of tree and branch characteristics on foraging behavior
ResearchPlanAbstract:
How and where animals choose to forage has been a long-standing and extensively researched topic in ecology. As with other behaviors, such as courtship and mating, foraging comes with an associated trade-off: the energy content of the food acquired, balanced against the cost of the energy needed to obtain that food. In all cases, optimal foraging theory predicts that an individual should favor the foraging strategy that delivers the greatest net energy intake, thus delivering the highest fitness payoff. (Kamil, 1985)
	The Red-Naped sapsucker (Sphyrapicus nuchalis) is a small species of woodpecker found in montane woodlands of the Rocky Mountains. Daily et al. (1993) highlighted the ecological importance of the Red-Naped sapsucker in the subalpine ecosystem in Colorado, labeling this bird a “double keystone species”. Not only do their old nest cavities in aspen trees provide nest sites for a half dozen other bird species: including the tree swallow and   the mountain bluebird but they also drill sap wells in willow trees, which provide a food source for hummingbirds, insects, and even small rodents.   
	While all four species of sapsuckers have a varied diet which includes invertebrates, and aspen sap and bast, their diet consists heavily of willow sap. As Tate (1973),  Savignac et al. (2006) and Daily et al. (1993) concluded, sapsuckers' reliance on willows is an important component of their life history.  
The importance of these abundant birds to the   Colorado sub alpine ecosystem is evident. (Walters, 1990) Yet, while a substantial amount of research has been done on the habitat and nest site selection of this species, there is little published literature relating to foraging behavior. 
 	The goal of this project is to link the foraging behavior of Red-Naped Sapsuckers in Gothic, CO, to the characteristics of individual willow shrubs and branches. The project will draw on both historical data obtained from old well scarring and observations of feeding sapsuckers. By linking foraging trends to such variables as branch diameter and branch orientation, this study will determine if the birds are preferentially choosing willows and or willow branches based on certain physical attributes. Preliminary data collection on old well scarring already shows several strong trends; for example, sapsuckers are drilling more holes on east facing branches than west, and more holes on interior branches than exterior ones.
	While this study is not a direct test of optimal foraging theory, it will provide data about the foraging behavior of a Colorado keystone species. In addition,the behavioral trends reported in this project will be useful for further inquiries on the foraging strategies of the Red-Naped Sapsucker.

ResearchPlanTitle: Nutrient stimulation of stalk production in Didymosphenia geminata.
ResearchPlanAbstract: More information is needed on the utilization of phosphorus by D. geminata and other environmental variables influencing stalk production to understand the environmental conditions that facilitate blooms. In a microcosm study I will manipulate nutrient conditions to identify whether inorganic phosphorus, organic phosphorus, and/or iron stimulate bloom behavior. In another experiment I will measure inorganic and organic phosphorus uptake by D. geminata mat material with and without added iron. I will quantify phosphorus stored in the pore water of the mat, in the stalk material, and in the cells, in relation to the stream water. Together, these experiments will explore phosphorus utilization by D. geminata and test whether phosphorus and iron concentrations in the water column determine stalk production.

ResearchPlanTitle: Testing the Oviposition Cues That Drive Preference of Hylemya for Different Sexes of    Polemonium foliosissimum
ResearchPlanAbstract: This study analyzes individuals of the plant Polemonium foliosissimum that are hermaphrodite and females and their relationship to a pre-dispersal fly seed predator.  I am interested in understanding which cues (floral traits) the fly uses in selecting a plant to lay eggs on.  I also want to know if the cues the fly chooses are parallel to that of pollinators.  This study is important because it can reveal which plants are at risk by the pre-dispersal seed predator and may bring into light why female plants exist in the population.  Is one sex more fit than the other?  It would also be interesting to know if the fly uses the same cues as pollinators in plant selection because the pollinator may ensure that a plant gets pollinated.  If the fly does not select the same plant as the pollinator, the larvae of the fly might not be able to feed if seeds do not develope on the plant and die.
ResearchPlanOrganisms:
Polemonium foliosissimum (plant)
Hylemya sp. (insect)
pollinators-possibly bumble bees.
Subject: Other

ResearchPlanTitle: How does the condition and multiple captures of Microtus montanus relate to infection?
ResearchPlanAbstract: This study proposes two major questions.  The first of these questions is if body condition varies in its relation to infection.  The second question compounds the first one, and asks if body condition influences the severity of parasite infections. The Montane vole, Microtus montanus, serves as an excellent model organism because of regular population fluctuations, which provide a backdrop to observe effects of host abundance on infection measures.  To attain answers to these questions we will be measuring both the condition and infection status of voles.  Voles will be trapped in Longfellow traps, placed on three grids at different areas.  Condition will be measured by weight, length, and reproductive status on the site.  Infection will be measured by fecal flotation tests performed at the lab with fecal samples from the traps.  The fecal samples will be tested for parasite intensity, abundance, and richness.  After this is done, the data will be added to two years worth of other data. These tests will ascertain what kind of relationship, if there is one, be it positive or negative.   The complex cycle between condition and infection is an important aspect to study because of its influence on growth, preservation, population dynamics and evolution of populations.
Subject: Long-Term

ResearchPlanTitle: Scaptomyza nigrita Damage and Inducible Glucosinolates in Cardamine cordifolia
ResearchPlanAbstract: Cardamine cordifolia A. Gray (Bittercress, Cruciferae) is a native, rhizomatous mustard plant that grows throughout the southern Rocky Mountains, Sierra Nevada Mountains, and Cascade Mountains.  Cardamine cordifolia produces characteristic glucosinolates, or mustard oils, which are secondary metabolites used primarily as defense compounds to deter pathogens and insect herbivores.  Scaptomyza nigrita Wheeler (Diptera: Drosophilidae), a leaf-mining fly, utilizes bittercress for oviposition sites, adult food and larval food.  When the larvae hatch in early to mid-June, they form characteristic foliar mines.  In this study, I will determine whether S. nigrita attack induces glucosinolate production.  Using genotypes from two sites, I will introduce larvae to rhizomatous and undamaged plants and then quantify the area mined per leaf, leaf weight and glucosinolate production using HPLC.  The results will be used to determine if the plant defense response is systemic or local, if there is variation between geographic locations, and how the glucosinolate composition and concentration changes.
Subject: Other

ResearchPlanTitle: Assessing the costs and benefits of induced plant defenses in Cardamine cordifolia (Brassicaceae)
ResearchPlanAbstract:
Far from passive victims of herbivory as presented in popular imagination, plants have evolved both constitutive and induced defenses in the face of attack by natural enemies such as herbivores and microbial pathogens. Constitutive defenses are those that are constantly present: Spines on a cactus, for example, prevent grazing by large vertebrates. In contrast, induced defenses are heightened levels of response to plant attack and are induced in reaction to damage or elicitors from natural enemies. Theoretically, induced defenses evolved in the context of tradeoffs and resource constraints; there may be some cost to deploying these weapons, so plants use these tools only when benefits outweigh costs.

This proposal seeks to evaluate the costs and benefits of such induced defenses in the heartleaf bittercress (Cardamine cordifolia), a mustard endemic to the Rocky Mountains. The costs will be assessed through an evaluation of the impact of plant defenses on plant growth (do defenses require the plant to divert resources from growth), and the benefits through an evaluation of the impact of plant defenses on leaf-miner performance. Leaf miners are common herbivores of the bittercress.
Subject: Other

ResearchPlanTitle: Nectar and Pollen Rewards of Invasive Plants and their Native Counterparts
ResearchPlanAbstract: Many invaders are equipped with a wide suite of mechanisms that help them out-compete native plants. Recently, there is growing recognition that invasive plants may affect native plants by luring away shared pollinators. The goal of this research is to explore the properties that make invasive plants strong competitors for pollination services from insects and birds. I will address the question: How common is it for invasive species to offer more attractive nectar and pollen rewards than their native counterparts? I will examine floral rewards from a broad selection of native-invader pairs by measuring nectar volume, nectar production rate, nectar concentration, pollen volume, and pollen protein content.
ResearchPlanOrganisms: Linaria vulgaris, Penstemon strictus, Cirsium arvense, Cirisum parryi, Cirsium eatonii, Concolculus arvensis, Matricaria perforata, Erigeron speciosus, Chyrsanthemum leucanthemum, Cynoglossum officinale, Lithosperum ruderale, Hackelia floribundia, Tragopogon dubuius, Agrtoseris glauca, Descurania sophia, Descurania pinnata, Erodium cicutarium, Geranium richardsonii, Barbarea vulgaris, Draba sp.

ResearchPlanTitle: A comparison of flowering phenology and pollinator interactions with Frasera speciosa populations in montane, sub-alpine, and alpine communities
ResearchPlanAbstract: This summer’s masting of the monocarp Frasera speciosa, or Monument Plant, has provided the infrequent opportunity to study the interaction of this plant species with potential pollinators.  Specifically, it is an opportunity to study pollinator interactions across a range of elevations.   I propose several questions related to this point.  How does the pattern of flowering on a F. speciosa inflorescence affect pollinator movement?  Is this pattern of flowering an adaptation to reduce geitonogamus pollination?  What affect does altitude have on the intra-plant flowering pattern of this species?  Does this potential difference flowering pattern affect the behavior of potential pollinators? These questions will be tested using observations of the flowering pattern of this species as well as the interactions of potential pollinators with this species. Information gained from this research project will not only broaden the body of knowledge regarding Frasera speciosa it will also contribute to the study of pollinator interactions in alpine environments.
Subject: Pollination

ResearchPlanTitle: Resolving the effects of microclimate and competition from sage on forb performance in a rocky montane meadow
ResearchPlanAbstract: Mountain big sagebrush (Artemisia tridentata var. vaseyana) has replaced forbs as the dominant form of vegetation in the warmest, driest section of a 20-year-long meadow warming experiment. It is not known whether this is due to enhanced competitive status of A. tridentata or due to simultaneous, independent effects of warming negatively impacting forb performance and positively impacting A. tridentata recruitment and growth. This study examines the effect of A. tridentata  on the special distribution and performance of four shallow-rooted forb species (Delphinium nelsonii (syn. D. nuttallium), Erigeron speciousus, and Potentilla gracilis and Potentilla hippiana). It also examines the effect of microhabitat on the performance of the same forb species. If a strong effect of microhabitat and no effect of proximity to sage are observed, then competition alone does not underlie shifting dominance in the meadow warming experiment.
ResearchPlanOrganisms:
Artemisia tridentata var. vaseyana
Delphinium nelsonii

ResearchPlanTitle: Do Ants Have a Positive or Negative Effect on Aphid Populations: Mutualism or Not?
ResearchPlanAbstract: I will be testing whether the species interactions between aphids and ants is beneficial for aphids or antagonistic. Aphids excrete a sweet nectar from there sugar rich diet from plant sap. Ants will use this excretion as a food source and will protect the aphids from potential predator and other competitors. It has been shown in other studies that the range of potential benefit or detriment can differ depending on, but not limited to: plant sex, aphid population density, and absence/presence of ants. We will compare the populations of the different treatment groups to see if ants and plant sex has an impact on aphid population growth. As well, to test the mechanism behind the effects of plant sex, aphid density, an ants on aphid populations, we will observe the fitness, emigration rates, and predation of individual aphids.
ResearchPlanOrganisms: Valeriana edulis, Aphis valerianea, Formica podzolica, Tapinoma sessile

ResearchPlanTitle: EFFECT OF COVER AND OBSTRUCTION OF VIEW IN HUMAN IMPACTED HABITAT ON VIGILANCE OF THE GOLDEN-MANTLED GROUND SQUIRREL (Spermophilus lateralis).
ResearchPlanAbstract: Looking at how man-made structures such as cars, dumpsters, cabin and outhouses effect the ground squirrels anti-predatory behavior. Will be observing the ground squirrels and marking them to be able to identify individuals from a non-invasive distance. This study will give insight to how ground squirrels adjust their behavior, using structures as cover or they cause an obstruction of view.

ResearchPlanTitle: Effects of altitude on co-flowering phenology in a montane wildflower community
ResearchPlanAbstract: Phenology, the timing of various events in a species’ life cycle, is an important life history trait. It is especially important in the montane wildflower communities of the Colorado Rockies. But, the timing of when different plants flower often changes with changes in altitude. As altitude increases, more flowers should flower at the same time meaning that the way wildflower communities operate changes according to altitude. I plan to study how altitude changes the flower timing in those communities. In addition, studying these wildflower interactions can serve as the beginning of a long-term climate change study, helping us to better understand how and when climate change affects montane ecosystems
ResearchPlanOrganisms: Montane Wildflowers of the Rocky Mountains (e.g.

ResearchPlanTitle: Dispersal and Social Behavior of two Subalpine Whirligig Beetles (Coleoptera: Gyrinidae: Gyrinus)
ResearchPlanAbstract: Two species of aquatic surface dwelling whirligig beetles (Coleoptera: Gyrinidae: Gyrinus)will be marked and observed for dispersal. Whirligig beetles often live in large aggregations. Their interesting social behavior will also be observed and recorded. Our study sites (kettle ponds) are disturbed yearly by cattle grazing starting in mid- July. We hypothesis that populations will disperse away from heavily disturbed ponds once grazing begins.
ResearchPlanOrganisms: Two species of whirligig beetles (Coleoptera: Gyrinidae: Gyrinus)

ResearchPlanTitle: Effects of muti-species interactions in gynodioecious populations of Polimonium foliosissimum.
ResearchPlanAbstract:
Gynodioecy is a dimorphic breeding system in which male sterile individuals coexist with hermaphroditic individuals of the same population. In order for female plants to be maintained within these populations they must have beneficial effects that will be selected for evolutionarily. (Asikainen et al. 2005) found that female plants produce abundantly more seed then their hermaphroditic counterparts; furthermore, they discovered that these females were also suffering less seed predation. This suggests that having female plants within a population could be highly beneficial to overall fecundity. Also, for plants that are reliant on animal driven pollination it is important to be able to attract potential pollinators. Given this, it would be expected that female plants would put more energy into floral display; however, this is not the case. (Asikainen et al. 2005) has shown that floral display is actually more important to male function which leads to larger more showy flowers in hermaphroditic plants as well as showing that  pollinators often prefer larger flowers that might have more to offer in terms of pollen and nectar loads. However, it is also possible that herbivores may also be choosing plants with showier flowers and higher rewards (Knight et al. 2008). In addition hermaphroditic plants, by virtue of producing pollen, incur risk that male function is reduced by pollen thieves. 
Although pollen theft is highly understudied, it is thought that its influence could lead to pollen limitation, and as a result force changes in the morphology of the affected plants. Furthermore, pollen theft has been shown to reduce overall fitness at not only the plant level but at the population level as well. As thieves continue to consume the pollen straight from the anther pollen limitation begins to occur. In pollen limited population’s fecundity is severely reduced. Plants have many ways of responding to pollen theft. They might overproduce pollen to compensate, or they may become gynodioecious (Hargreaves et al. 2009). In this study I will be looking at pollinators and pollen thieves in two separate sex ratios of P foliosissimum to determine whether or not thievery is leading to pollen limitation in overwhelmingly hermaphroditic populations.
Subject: Pollination

ResearchPlanTitle: The Effects of Bee Sampling on Solitary Bee Abundance and Diversity in Montane Meadows
ResearchPlanAbstract: Although solitary bees compromise over 85% of bee species (Michener 2000) little research has been conducted on them compared to the number of studies on honey bees and bumble bees. Unlike eusocial bees, solitary bees do not have a queen or workers; instead there is only one female laying the eggs and providing the pollen for the larvae. The most common method to sample solitary bees is using pan traps. Pan traps are the most efficient bee catching method in both agricultural and semi-natural habitats (Westphal et al. 2008). However the problem with the pan trap method is that it kills the very insect researchers are trying to study. The objective of this project is to determine if repeated and long term sampling using standard pan trapping techniques has any adverse effect on a bee abundance or diversity. To test whether pan trapping has any effect on bee abundance and diversity, I will compare abundance and diversity between sites that have been sampled only once vs. sites that was sampled throughout the 2009 and 2010 flowering seasons.If pan trapping has a negative effect on bee abundance or diversity, then I would expect that sites that have been sampled multiple times would have lower abundance and/or diversity than sites that have been sampled only once. I predict that there will be a lower abundance and/or diversity at the sites sampled repeatedly than the sites that have only been sampled once.
ResearchPlanOrganisms: Andrenidae, Apidae, Colletidae, Halictidae, and Megachilidae
Subject: Other

ResearchPlanTitle: Oviposition Preference and Larval Performance of the Leaf Miner, Scaptomyza nigrita (Drosophilidae) on its Native host plant, Cardamine cordifolia (Brassicaceae)
ResearchPlanAbstract: The link between preference of ovipositing female insect and the larval performance and survival on the host is a key component in understanding the evolution of plant/insect interactions, and host specialization in particular. Oviposition preference of females and the relationship between larval performance and survival varies among and within species, ranging from strong to weak, and can correlate with local ecology. I will study the link between the leaf mining fly, Scpatomyza nigrita, and its host plant, Cardamine cordifolia. Persistent herbivory by S nigrita is suggested to influence the distribution of C cordifolia. In addition, a greater concentration of herbivory and mines are observed on lower and mid stem leaves. This study will use an experimental approach to test the following hypotheses (1) Adult S. nigrita prefer to feed and oviposit on plants in open sunlight and if this is linked to larval performance and (2) Adult S. nigrita prefer to feed and oviposit on older leaves relative to younger leaves.
Subject: Other

ResearchPlanTitle: The Effect of Flower Abundance and Morphology on Plant-Pollinator interactions in Alpine Meadows
ResearchPlanAbstract:
Plants pollinated by animals differ greatly in their number of interactions with visitor species (Waser et al., 1996, Bascompte et al.2003). Additionally, their interactions in a community are often organized as nonrandom networks, showing distinct and repeated complex patterns (Olesen et al. 2007). In order to understand the differences in the number of interactions experienced by different plants, this network is best studied at a community level; and should elucidate the specific traits that engender pollinator selection. In the past however, it has seldom been done this way- most studies of plant-animal mutualisms involve a small number of species; or if a large number of species is included, these studies seldom include species traits (Waser et al. 1996).  

            Traits that potentially influence which insect visits which plant species are: shape, size, color and scent of flowers. These traits however are not successful in predicting which flower visitors will pollinate which plants; nor, the diversity and number of visitors plants receive (Ollerton et al. 2009). Recent studies have revealed that pollinators with shorter proboscises have a more specialized pattern of flower visitation due to the stronger size-constraints they face when considering their corolla depth-proboscis length threshold. The threshold refers to the inability of flower visitors to have access to nectar in flowers when their proboscis is shorter than the corolla depth of the flower (Stang et al. 2006, 2007, 2009). Another important determinant of the number of flower visitor species is the abundance of the flowers. The more abundant a plant is, the more flower visitors are expected (Stang et al. 2006).

            The traits which will be studied in this research project are floral abundance and floral tube depth threshold; and their influence on the number of flower visitor species visiting plant species. The expectations are: the more abundant a plant is, the more flower visitors are expected; and the shorter and thinner the tubes are, the more restricted the number of pollinators that can reach nectar due to morphological constraints of their mouth parts will be. The number of visitor species will likely decrease with increasing size constraints (Stang et al. 2006).  Although one study has been completed before, this study was implemented at a low elevation in a Mediterranean plant-pollinator community. As of now, there is no data available for other communities. Testing to see if the proposed traits are also important in other communities by determining the number of visitor species is noteworthy. This experiment will test the importance of abundance and morphology in an alpine community located at Virginia basin in Colorado. In 2000, three sites in Virginia Basin were analyzed, followed a year later by a return to the middle site to resurvey (Alarcón 2004). In this study however, no morphological data was gathered. In my proposed research, I will repeat the plant pollinator visitation network study. The data collected in the proposed observational study will allow for a comparison to be made with a simultaneously conducted study by Martina Stang, at about 3000 meters, in a dry meadow near the town site of Gothic. The two communities differ in their percentage of visitors, with the lower site being dominated by bees and the higher site being dominated by flies. This difference could influence the importance of the nectar depth size threshold in determining generalization degree and community pattern.
Subject: Pollination

ResearchPlanTitle: BOTTOM-UP EFFECTS OF THE BLOOM-FORMING DIATOM, DIDYMOPHENIA GEMINATA, ON BROOK TROUT, SALVELINUS FONTINALIS, IN ROCKY MOUNTAIN STREAMS
ResearchPlanAbstract: The invasive stalked diatom Didymosphenia geminata creates filamentous mats that can cover up to 100% of stream bottoms. This alga drastically alters the structure of stream bottoms, and in so doing causes changes in the invertebrate community structure. Trout in streams with didymo blooms have been shown to exhibit a 32% lower growth rate. I propose a number of hypotheses to explain this phenomenon, based on shifts in invertebrate assemblages toward small-bodied taxa with low per-mass caloric content, and trout bioenergetic responses to these shifts.
ResearchPlanOrganisms: Salvelinus fontinalis, Didymosphenia geminata, aquatic macroinvertebrates.
