Subject: Other

ResearchPlanTitle: A study of correlational selection through floral manipulations of Polemonium foliosissimum (Polemoniaceae)
ResearchPlanAbstract: I intend to study pollinator choice through floral manipulations of Polemonium foliosissimum (Towering Jacob’s Ladder). Pollinators often decide which flowers to visit based on combinations of floral traits, and so traits of interest to pollinators are often genetically linked. Thus, selection for floral traits is often additive such that the response to one trait depends on response to another trait(s). This linking of traits is known as correlational selection. I intend to study correlational selection by pollinator communities on floral shape and color. I will first individually manipulate color and shape by painting flowers and then by flattening blossoms from a tubular into an open morphology. I will then combine the two sets of manipulations to examine changes in the visiting pollinator community.
ResearchPlanOrganisms: Polemonium foliosissimum and all visiting pollinators (butterflies, bumblebees, solitary bees, flies)
Subject: Pollination

ResearchPlanTitle: Identifying the underlying genetic basis of social behavior in a facultatively eusocial bee (Halictus rubicundus)
ResearchPlanAbstract: The origins of social behavior have fascinated generations of biologists, Darwin included. Our proposal aims to identify genetic differences between solitary and eusocial forms of a socially polymorphic sweat bee with a view to honing in on the genes that underlie social behavior.
ResearchPlanOrganisms: A common sweat bee: Halictus rubicundus
Subject: Other

ResearchPlanTitle: Aspen community dynamics in the Gunnison Basin, Colorado
ResearchPlanAbstract: Aspen (Populus tremuloides) forms keystone forests in the southern Rocky Mountains that promote extremely rich and productive understory plant communities. Recent aspen dieback is likely to drive changes in understory plant communities through changes in light environment. The purpose of the proposed research is to assess recent changes in aspen stand structure and understory plant community composition in the Gunnison Basin, Colorado, by resampling a series of 19 stands originally surveyed in 1964 and 1994. Comparisons of current and historic conditions will be used to quantify the extent and direction of recent changes in this region. We also propose to examine relationships between understory composition and light levels, to test whether recent canopy dieback is driving shifts away from shade-tolerant understory species. Lastly, the project provides unique hands-on experience with forest research to two undergraduate biology students at Western State College.
Subject: Long-Term

ResearchPlanTitle: Investigating larval trematode communities in the aquatic snails surrounding Gothic and Crested Butte: A look at changes in community composition after more than 50 years.
ResearchPlanAbstract: Trematode parasites are a diverse and prolific group of organisms found world-wide. These multi-host parasites commonly use aquatic snails as their first intermediate hosts. They are responsible for such disease as Schistosomiasis, cattle liver fluke, and cercarial dermatitis (better known as swimmer's itch). In 1957 Hunter et al. investigated the first reported case of cercarial dermatitis in Colorado (found at Lake Grant in Crested Butte). Hunter et al. conducted detailed studies of the trematode communities surrounding Crested Butte and the RMBL from 1957 to 1960. This record is the only record of its kind in the whole state of Colorado (and much of the West) detailing such early trematode prevalences. I would like to re-survey these water bodies (the kettle ponds and Lake Grant) to see if trematode communities have changed substantially since the late 50s, and if so, what may have caused this (climate change, land use change, nutrient enrichment, etc.).
ResearchPlanOrganisms: aquatic snails (Lymnaeids and Physids) and their larval trematode parasites
Subject: Long-Term

ResearchPlanTitle: Parasite population genetics at a pocket gopher contact zone
ResearchPlanAbstract: Pocket gophers and the lice that parasitize them have a long history of tandem evolution.  We have studied the large scale, macroevolutionary patterns of this system extensively.  In this work, we will study the fine scale, microevolutionary patterns that precede speciation by studying louse and gopher population genetics where different chromosomal forms of the gopher, Thomomys talpoides, come together in a region with very high population density at Gothic, Colorado.  We plan to examine the genetics of each louse from each gopher to determine, for example, whether the degree of genetic differentiation in lice will depend on host relationships.  Will louse populations residing on a single host individual be more genetically similar to one another than they will be to lice on neighboring host individuals?  Will louse populations on genetically similar hosts be more genetically similar to one another than to louse populations on opposite sides of the contact zone?
Subject: Other

ResearchPlanTitle: Continuing Studies of Ecosystem-Climate Interactions at the RMBL Warming Meadow
ResearchPlanAbstract: A 20 year climate manipulation experiment will be continued.  It is providing science and decision makers with critical information about how ecosystems respond to climate change and how those responses generate feedbacks to the climate that tend to exacerbate the warming.
ResearchPlanOrganisms: All plant species in the plots, and to a lesser extent arthropods and microorganisms
Subject: Climate Change

ResearchPlanTitle: Assessing the individual and interactive effects of ecological players on sex morphs and population growth of the gynodioecious Polemonium foliosissimum
ResearchPlanAbstract: My research investigates the extent to which herbivores, seed predators, and pollinators influence gynodioecy- a breeding system characterized by separate female and hermaphroditic sex morphs- and population growth generally, in Polemonium foliosissimum.  Sex morphs may face different selective pressures from ecological players and may have different life-history strategies as a result. My research uses experimental manipulations and demographic modeling to explicitly account for these life-history differences. Demographic vital rate data (e.g. probability of survival, seedling-juvenille transition, and reproductive output) is obtained by tracking marked plants for multiple years. By also collecting demographic data on experimental plants (e.g. those inside herbivore exclosures, with seed predators removed, and/or with supplemental pollen added), I can build alternative vital rate transition matrices to model population dynamics expected under different ecological conditions (e.g. with vertebrate herbivores removed, increased pollinator service etc.). Demographic modeling will allow me to assess which vital rates are most important to population growth rates, how ecological players differently affect the vital rates of sex morphs, and ultimately how these effects translate into ultimate long-term fitness differences among sex morphs in a sexually dimorphic species. Because this modeling will permit me to assess the importance of herbivores, pollinators, and seed predators to 1) relative fitness differences in sex morphs and 2) population growth rates more generally, my research has both ecological and evolutionary implications.
Subject: Pollination

ResearchPlanTitle: A Long-Term Study of Molluscan-Trematode Communities in Gunnison County, CO:  differentiating the effects of global versus local anthropogenic disturbance
ResearchPlanAbstract: Trematode parasites are responsible for numerous diseases of medical and veterinary importance (Schistosomiasis, Fasciolosis, etc.).  Trematode parasite communities have also increasingly been used to assess the degree to which certain aquatic ecosystems have been impacted by anthropogenic activities.  The abundance and virility of these parasites are known to change with human-impacted ecological factors such as climate, nutrient state, and physical disturbance.  There have been few studies documenting the changes in trematode parasite abundance and diversity in aquatic snails (their first host) over long time periods (50+ years) and no studies of this kind in the Western United States.  More detailed long-term studies are needed to determine how trematode communities will respond to further anthropogenic change (both local and global).  My project will allow comparison of present-day snail infection levels to extremely detailed data collected over 50 years ago at RMBL to evaluate the effects of local disturbances (housing developments, dam-building, etc.) and global disturbances (climate change) on trematode communities.
ResearchPlanOrganisms:
aquatic snails:  (Helisoma trivolis, Lymnaea palustris, Physa propinqua)
parasitic trematodes:  various
Subject: Long-Term

ResearchPlanTitle: Climate & climate change around RMBL
ResearchPlanAbstract:
Despite the large and growing literature in relation to climate change biology, approaches to this topic have been patchy and lacking in integration.An excellent location to further our understanding of climate change and how it is affecting biodiversity is the area around the Rocky Mountain Biological Laboratory (RMBL) in Colorado, USA.   
The aims of this project are to:
&#61567;	Characterise the climate in the “local” area around RMBL, especially with regard to diurnal, seasonal and elevational patterns, consider links among these climatic patterns, and determine how the climate has changed over about the last 100 years
&#61567;	Use changes in climate at RMBL as a case study to show the utility of placing local changes in climate in the context of longer time periods and larger regions (e.g., testing the links of local changes in temperature and precipitation with larger scale climate patterns, such as the El Niño Southern Oscillation, Pacific Decadal Oscillation, and Atlantic Multidecadal Oscillation)
&#61567;	Further explore relationships between flower plot and climatic data
ResearchPlanOrganisms: None at present; bumblebees in the future
Subject: Climate Change

ResearchPlanTitle: Predicting interspecific interaction strength in a mutualistic/antagonistic food web: are body mass, population biomass or stoichiometry simple proxies?
ResearchPlanAbstract: Food webs describe feeding relationships among species and measure the magnitudes of speciesï¿½ effects on one another as ï¿½interaction strengths.ï¿½ Most of these interactions are weak, but the few interactions that are strong are most important for determining community stability. Though there is great need to understand when strong interactions will occur, interaction strengths in food webs are often criticized as phenomenological and thus unpredictable. Yet, some believe the metabolic theory of ecology has the potential to link an organismï¿½s bodily needs to their effects in food webs. Of central importance to this theory, body mass, population biomass, and stoichiometry (elemental composition) are species characteristics that have promise for indicating the strengths of species interactions. In the proposed study, I will evaluate the usefulness of these traits for predicting interaction strengths in a mountain meadow food web. This web is special in that it includes positive types of interactions (mutualisms) in addition to the negative effects (predation, herbivory) usually studied in food webs. By focusing on positive interactions between ants and honeydew-producing insects and negative interactions between the honeydew-producers and the plants they consume, I will also evaluate whether different kinds of ecological relationships are predicted by body mass, population biomass, and stoichiometry.
ResearchPlanOrganisms: Formica obscuripes, Publilia modesta, Chrysothamnus viscidiflorus, Uroleucon escalantii
Subject: Other

ResearchPlanTitle: Pollinator losses and plant function: An assessment of pollination network resilience in the face of climate change.
ResearchPlanAbstract:
Global climate change (GCC) is projected to cause dramatic shifts in many ecological processes, disrupting ecosystem services and directly threatening pollination interactions. GCC is likely to disrupt the overlap in seasonal timing (i.e., phenology) of flowering production and of pollinator emergence/foraging activity, leading to potentially mismatched interactions between both plants and animals. 

Recent work based on pollination networks suggests that pollination interactions will be highly resilient to ongoing environmental change because pollination networks are dominated by generalist interactions. I hypothesize that networks are much less resilient to perturbations.  These predictions are based on assumptions that all interactions in the network are positive; meaning every visit from a pollinator to a plant is beneficial, an assumption known to be false. 

My dissertation research, based in both empirical and modeling techniques, will help evaluate whether existing pollinator network analyses that are based just on visitation rates, provide robust models for evaluating impacts of global climate change on pollinator services, or whether incorporating additional information on the importance of pollinator fidelity and plant reproductive success provide different predictions.
Subject: Pollination

ResearchPlanTitle: Elevational shifts in plant traits: consequences for multitrophic community interactions and feedback on plant trait selection
ResearchPlanAbstract: Plants defend themselves against a variety of herbivores, often producing chemical compounds that are distasteful or interfere with herbivore growth and reproduction.  Like in humans and other animals, this immune response is energetically costly.  Given the other challenges of living in a region with a short growing season, we expect a) plants to defend themselves only when herbivores pose a threat to their survival and reproduction, and b) plants will tailor the defense response to the specific type of herbivore (leaf-chewing vs. sap-feeding) eating them.  Simultaneously, plants produce substances like nectar to attract pollinators, which may affect the amount of herbivory the plant experiences if other species that protect or prey on the herbivores are also attracted.  As elevation increases, the increased environmental stress on plants is likely to reduce the amount of energy available to resist herbivory.  At the same time, producing pollen (males) or seeds (females) may trade-off with defense differently because male reproduction is less costly (needing only to survive to transfer pollen to females) than female reproduction (requiring resistance to herbivores during the process of seed maturation).  I will measure plant defensive chemicals across the flowering cycle and elevational range of the native wildflower valerian (Valeriana edulis) to understand how time, changes associated with elevation, and plant sex have shaped plant defensive characteristics.  To test a possible cause for such patterns, I will perform experiments to determine the impact of herbivores on plant fitness by studying their interactions with other insects in the community and their distribution over the elevational range of valerian.
ResearchPlanOrganisms:
Valeriana edulis
Formica podzolica
Aphis valerianae
Macrosiphum valerianae
Two unknown heteroneuran lepidopterans (larval host is Valeriana edulis)
Grasshopper (Orthoptera: Acrididae)
Subject: Other

ResearchPlanTitle: Variation in herbivory between habitats in Ligusticum porteri (Apiaceae)
ResearchPlanAbstract: Plants are often 'on the menu' for more than one herbivorous insect.  In the case of the parsley-like plant Ligusticum porteri which insect is dining on its flowers depends on the 'restaurant'. In the shade of an aspen stand, L. porteri flowers are eaten by caterpillars. While in open meadows, you are more likely to find aphids sipping away at the phloem sap of inflorescences.  Many environmental factors could be responsible for this pattern. For example, plants in sunny meadows may be a good meal for aphids but not for caterpillars.  Alternatively, these difference may be due to the community found in each habitat rather than the plants themselves.  For instance, interactions with predators could determine where herbivores choose to dine.  In this study, we are using a series of experiments to disentangle these various environmental factors.
ResearchPlanOrganisms:
Ligusticum porteri (Apiaceae)
Aphids 
Lepidopteran larvae (Family Crambidae)
Subject: Other

ResearchPlanTitle: Consequences of human-accelerated environmental change on a ï¿½keystoneï¿½ species.
ResearchPlanAbstract: Baetis bicaudatus is a remarkable mayfly species whose larvae are common in high elevation streams such as those draining the watershed of the Rocky Mountain Biological Laboratory. Although this species is an important prey item to both trout and predatory stoneflies, it can achieve high densities in streams containing one or both predators. Baetis larvae eat attached algae and are the most efficient among all species of grazers in these streams, disproportionately consuming more food, even when it is at very low levels. Unlike other mayflies, Baetis populations have not shown declines with recent increases in the nuisance diatom, Didymosphenia geminata, which has recently proliferated with changes in streams potentially exacerbated by environmental change. My research will address four potential direct and indirect consequences of human accelerated environmental change on populations of this mayfly, which is an important player (ï¿½keystone speciesï¿½) in high elevation stream ecosystems. First, recent drought conditions and increasing activity of beavers in the region are associated with increasing prevalence of a parasitic mermithid nematode, which has the potential to negatively affect Baetis populations. Second, recent upstream habitat shifts of brown trout and predatory stoneflies typical of lower elevations could replace brook trout and the predatory stoneflies coexisting with Baetis, potentially changing the predation regime under which populations are currently sustained. Third, extreme hydrologic events, such as droughts and floods, affect availability of rocks protruding out of streams that are used by these mayflies for oviposition (egg laying), which could critically alter the ability of Baetis populations to recruit new individuals. Fourth, warming temperatures can accelerate the development of Baetis through their larval stage and have the potential to narrow the window of time after metamorphosis from the aquatic larvae for short-lived winged adults to find the best rocks for oviposition. Fifth, proliferation of Didymospenia could indirectly affect Baetis populations by favoring their parasites or new predators. Field surveys and field experiments conducted at different scales and levels of complexity will be implemented to test the effects of those four potential threats to Baetis populations.
ResearchPlanOrganisms: Stream organisms, including trout, invertebrates and algae.
Subject: Climate Change

ResearchPlanTitle: Education Experiences Program
ResearchPlanAbstract: This plan describes potential impacts of activities conducted through RMBL's informal education program.
Subject: Climate Change

ResearchPlanTitle: Identifying the underlying genetic basis of social behavior in a facultatively eusocial bee (Halictus rubicundus)
ResearchPlanAbstract: The overall aim of our project is to generate population genomic data from two divergent social phenotypes of a facultatively eusocial sweat bee, Halictus rubicundus, to allow immediate screening of genetic (SNP) variation and identification of candidate genes underpinning the social transition in this species. These analyses will provide the background data for a full application to identify the genes and transcriptional networks underpinning altruism in the socially diverse sweat bees.
ResearchPlanOrganisms: A common and native sweat bee, Halictus rubicundus
Subject: Other

ResearchPlanTitle: Pollinator Diversity and Foraging Specialization
ResearchPlanAbstract: Pollinator species losses are ongoing and are likely to accelerate in the future. What will be the functional consequences of these species losses for plant reproduction? We hypothesize that competition between pollinator species--which is lowered when species are lost--is important in shaping pollinator specialization. Without this specialization, pollinators transfer the wrong kinds of pollen to plants, reducing their efficiency as pollinators while lowering plant reproduction. To test this hypothesis, we will temporarily and non-destructively reduce bee and plant diversity and abundance in several meadow sites, and compare manipulated to non-manipulated sites. We will measure short-term specialization of pollinators through 1) monitoring foraging behavior; 2) analyzing pollen loads carried by bees; and 3) analyzing pollen loads on flowers.
ResearchPlanOrganisms: bees (Hymenoptera: Apoidea), especially bumble bees (genus Bombus); various flowering plant species
Subject: Pollination

ResearchPlanTitle: CLINAL VARIATION & LOCAL ADAPTATION ALONG AN ELEVATIONAL TRANSECT OF IPOMOPSIS AGGREGATA
ResearchPlanAbstract: Many recent studies of plant populations have demonstrated species range shifts in response to climate change. These range shifts for montane species moving up in elevation are of particular interest because small changes in elevation can correspond to large changes in environmental factors.  The extent to which a species can shift its range will depend upon its ability to tolerate the environmental changes that occur with elevational shifts as well as what factors currently limit the upper range boundary of a species.  This study seeks to understand the amount of variation in populations of Ipomopsis aggregata, Scarlet Gilia, across a 1000 m elevational gradient, and the consequences of this variation for population adaptation to environmental change. In addition, we hope to elucidate the factors limiting the upper elevational range of the species and thus the potential for range expansion.
Subject: Climate Change

ResearchPlanTitle: The Role of Floral Yeasts in Plant-Pollinator Mutualisms
ResearchPlanAbstract: Plants are subject to a myriad of interactions with organisms both seen and unseen. These interactions are often mediated by traits of the plant species, with one key example being floral nectar which mediates interactions between plants and their mutualist pollinators. Comprised of sugars and amino acids, floral nectar is prone to infestation by microorganisms such as yeasts. This work seeks to determine the role of floral yeasts in plant-pollinator interactions, their effects on host fitness, and whether changes in nectar traits driven by yeast metabolic activity are involved.
ResearchPlanOrganisms: Delphinium nuttallianum, Bombus appositus, Bombus nevadensis, Bombus californicus, Bombus flavifrons, Bombus frigidus, Bombus kirbyellus, Selasphorous platycercus, Metschnikowia reukaufii
Subject: Pollination

ResearchPlanTitle: Do the clonal characteristics of aspen (Populus tremuloides) increase or reduce its resilience to drought?
ResearchPlanAbstract: In my work I will research how drought affect male and female Aspen clones.
Subject: Climate Change

ResearchPlanTitle: Causes and consequences of variation in the strength of ant-hemipteran interactions
ResearchPlanAbstract: Many species of ants and aphids engage in mutualistic interactions, where aphids feed ants and ants in turn protect aphids from their predators.  These ant-aphid mutualisms constitute classic defining examples of mutualism, and have contributed in important ways to the understanding of mutualisms generally.  Yet these interactions are not always beneficial to both parties, and in particular it is clear that ants can have neutral or negative effects on aphids based upon the biotic and abiotic conditions under which the interaction occurs.  This research seeks to investigate the causes and consequences of variability in ant-aphid interactions in two separate but complementary ways.  First, it will document the causes behind observed variation in ant-aphid interactions between high and low elevation sites.  And second, it will test whether competition among ants for access to aphids benefits aphids or ï¿½ alternatively ï¿½ whether potentially superior mutualist ants are excluded by competitively superior ants that are poor quality mutualists.
ResearchPlanOrganisms: Formica podzolica, Aphis varians, Chamerion angustifolium and other aphid-tending ants and ant-tended aphids.
Subject: Other

ResearchPlanTitle: Adaptive management of Linaria vulgaris
ResearchPlanAbstract: Invasive species are a leading component of global environmental change and are the second leading cause of biodiversity loss worldwide. The goal of this research is to identify management strategies that can be used to control the invasive plant Linaria vulgaris (yellow toadflax, or butter-and-eggs). Linaria vulgaris is a noxious weed listed by the State of Colorado; it is an escaped ornamental from Mediterranean regions and is common in disturbed as well as undisturbed areas and rangelands. The project uses an adaptive management approach to understand what strategies will best control L. vulgaris given its density, the interspersion of native species, the size of the L. vulgaris population, and how close it is to areas that humans live in or recreate on (see attached decision tree). I will continue to monitor a number of experiments that have already been set up that involved a variety of treatments, including pulling, conventional herbicide application, organic herbicide application, resource manipulations, and top-soil removal. In addition, I propose to set up two new experiments, one in which I manipulate carbon, and one in which I follow the consequences of L. vulgaris removal on native pollination interactions in the remaining native species. Taken together, this work will provide important insight into strategies that may help control L. vulgaris under different conditions as well as some of the ecological consequences of that control.
Subject: Other

ResearchPlanTitle: Paleoecological Studies of Sediment Pollen and Tree Rings from the Rocky Mountain Biological Laboratory, Gunnison County, CO.
ResearchPlanAbstract: Analysis of sediment pollen provides a method for resonstructing climate change, vegetation change, and land use change for the time represented by the lake sediment accumulation.  Dendrochronology, tree-ring science, also provides an effective way to reconstruct changes in tree growth which can be attributed to clime and weather events, insect oubreaks, and other types of environmental change.  I propose to use both methods to reconstruct a history of land use, vegetation change, climate change, and drought in the area of Gothic.
Subject: Climate Change

ResearchPlanInstitution: University of North Carolina Chapel Hill
ResearchPlanTitle: Linking butterfly traits to fitness to forecast butterfly responses to climate change
ResearchPlanAbstract:
Increasing global temperatures have begun to profoundly affect terrestrial communities (Parmesan 2006; Huey, Deutsch et al. 2009). The alpine areas in Colorado have seen greater increases in temperature over the past fifty years than other parts of the country on the order of 0.4 C per decade (culter.colorado.edu).  This makes Colias meadii, Colias alexandra, and Colias eriphyle of great research interest because they are Rocky Mountain butterflies that have been studied extensively for their close functional relationship between wing coloration patterns and temperature (Watt 1968; Kingsolver 1983; Kingsolver 1983; Watt 1992) as well as larval thermal ecology, (Sherman 1973). 

We will collect data addressing how environmental conditions interact with larval and adult physiology to constrain distributions.  Comparing modern measurements to previous data collected at RMBL and elsewhere will address whether butterflies physiology has already responded to climate change. This research will serve to parameterize an ecophysiological distribution model, which will be tested by hindcasting past distribution changes and used to predict future distribution shifts.
ResearchPlanOrganisms: Colias meadii, Colias p. eriphyle, Colias alexandra
Subject: Climate Change

ResearchPlanTitle: Soil geomorphology and landscape evolution of the Upper East River Valley
ResearchPlanAbstract: Soils are an important interface between geology and biology; however, very little is known about the soils around RMBL. Soil development is a function of climatic conditions, biological activity, local relief, aspect, parent material, and the amount of time sediments are exposed at or near the surface.  Combined with an understanding of surficial processes, soil stratigraphy aids in the subdivision of the local succession of deposits and correlation of unconsolidated sediments.  The distribution and properties of soil stratigraphic units can be used to evaluate landform evolution and age, landform stability, surface processes and even past climates. Potential research questions include:  What are the dominant relationships between soil and sediment properties with elevation, slope, aspect, rock type, or the relative age of surficial deposits? Is there a correlation between soil properties and dominant vegetation patterns? What is the late Quaternary history of landscape change in this environment?
Subject: Climate Change

ResearchPlanTitle: Microbial Characterization of the Mt. Emmons Fen
ResearchPlanAbstract:
The Mt. Emmons fen, located near Crested Butte, CO, is a stable geological structure supported by a continuous inflow of metal-laden groundwater. Sitting on top of a climax-type porphyry molybdenum deposit, its pH 3 water contains elevated levels of a variety of metals, including Cd, Al, Fe, Mo, and Zn. With concentrations exceeding water quality standards set by the State of Colorado, no one has studied its microbiology.  This research will be (i) the first to characterize the functional processes used by microorganisms following thousands of years of adaptation to metal toxicity; and (ii) determine how a climax microbial community responds to metals and how these responses are linked to the fenï¿½s biogeochemistry.
While microbial resistance to metals is well established, how microorganisms evolve in the presence of metals, how microbial activity can transform metals for remediation, and how microorganisms may work together to address metal toxicity is largely unknown.  Most work looking into microbial metal-resistance focuses on mining- or industrial-impacted sites.  These types of systems force populations to adapt rapidly or face elimination.  Due to the long-term exposure to metals, we expect the fen microbial community to show diverse microorganisms with unique metabolic abilities, especially adapted to metal toxicity.  The overall objectives of this work are to use advanced molecular DNA sequencing methods to characterize the microbial community associated with the fen and to identify novel responses to the presence of toxic metals.  This information will contribute to our understanding of how microorganisms transform metals in the environment, which has direct implications for metal containment and remediation, as well as contributing to our understanding of basic fen microbiology.
Subject: Other

ResearchPlanTitle: Evaluating the ultraviolet cues in Orchidaceae
ResearchPlanAbstract: The goal of this project is to photograph ultraviolet cues in flowers that are invisible to humans, but visible to plant pollinators such as bees and butterflies. With knowledge about these cues in many plant species within the Orchid family we can evaluate whether closely related species have similar cues. This may be important if for example certain bee species like a particular type of cue (big round circle near the center of the flower)and these bees drop in numbers such as we have seen with honey bees and bumble bees. If orchids are rare they may not get pollinated by the low numbers of bees. By understanding whether pollinators of the same kind like the same ultraviolet flower cues, we may be able to predict which rare flowers would be in jeopardy when certain bee (or other) species decline in number.
Subject: Climate Change

ResearchPlanTitle: Long-term studies of phenology and plant demography in the context of climate change
ResearchPlanAbstract: This research focuses on understanding variation in timing and abundance of flowering (i.e. flowering phenology) in sub-alpine wildflower communities in the vicinity of RMBL. One aim of this work is to elucidate environmental variables that generate this phenological variation. Another goal is to determine the consequences of this variation for plant demography (population growth) and for animals that interact with the wildflowers. There seem to be effects of climate change on flowering phenology and floral abundance for individual species the wildflower community as a whole. It also appears that bumble bees, important pollinators of many wildflower species, are shifting their altitudinal distributions, presumably in response to climate change. Some of the earlier flowering species have experienced loss of seed to frost damage, which may have demographic consequences.
ResearchPlanOrganisms:
All flowering species in long-term phenology plots

Wildflower populations:Helainthella quinquenervis,Hymenoxys grandiflorum,Frasera speciosa, Veratrum tenuipetalum, and Delphinium barbeyi

Insects in the Research Meadow, continuing a long-term sampling effort using a malaise trap for 48 hours/week.
Subject: Phenology

ResearchPlanTitle: Can nectar secondary metabolites mitigate nectar robbing and at what cost to pollination?
ResearchPlanAbstract: Floral nectar is produced as a reward for pollinators, but can also contain compounds that may be distasteful or even toxic to nectar-collecting animals.  One hypothesized function of these noxious compounds is that they made help plants deter animals that collect nectar without transferring pollen.  In fact, animals that damage flowers while stealing nectar may lead a plant to produce distasteful compounds in nectar in order to prevent further nectar theft.  How effective these compounds are at discouraging these nectar robbers and how frequently they also deter legitimate pollinators is currently unknown.  Linaria vulgaris is an invasive weed that is visited by a number of bumble bee species, including the nectar robber Bombus occidentalis.  In this study, I will examine whether damage due to nectar robbing leads to increases in noxious nectar compounds.  I will also look at how both nectar robbers and pollinators respond to nectar containing artificially high and low concentrations of these compounds.  This research will provide novel insight into the functional significance of putatively toxic nectar compounds and the effect of these compounds on plant-pollinator interactions.
ResearchPlanOrganisms: Linaria vulgaris, Bombus occidentalis, Bombus appositus, Bombus bifarius, other Bombus species
Subject: Pollination

ResearchPlanTitle:
REVISITING EDWARD WARREN 100 YEARS LATER:
DOCUMENTING LOCATION AND EXTENT OF BEAVER HABITAT NEAR CRESTED BUTTE, COLORADO
ResearchPlanAbstract:
This study proposes to document the extent and changes in beaver(Castor canadensis) locality and habitat in the areas surrounding the Rocky Mountain Biological Laboratory over the past 100-plus years. This study would not be possible without the very clear locational descriptions of beaver habitat in the area as described in Edward Warrenï¿½s journals, supplied to me by RMBL, which was begun in 1899.  Mapping of the habitat and locations described by Warrenï¿½s work and a summer field season will include and utilize satellite imagery, aerial photography and maps currently available. During the coming summer field season I propose to ï¿½ground truthï¿½ the extent and location of beaver habitat, lodges, dams and caches.  I will then be able to confidently document changes in location and extent of beaver habitat in the area. If possible, given the precise site information, using past and present data, I hope to link beaver populations with specific habitat and the number of lodges and dams. 
A thorough documentation of the extent and changes over the last one hundred years in beaver habitat in the Crested Butte region will be completed.  Further, I hope to advance understanding of the criteria for which beaver choose their lodge locations and link this to population size.  I hope to be able to provide information that can be used in wildlife management and habitat conservation.  
This research will serve as my Masterï¿½s thesis.   I hope to publish the results as well.
Subject: Climate Change

ResearchPlanTitle: Potential impacts of local adaptation and elevation migration on a subalpine plant population in decline due to long-term experimental warming.
ResearchPlanAbstract:
When climatic change surpasses tolerance limits, plant and animal populations have four possible general responses-- they can adapt to their local changing environment, migrate to more suitable habitats, shrink into suitable refugia, or go extinct.  Our research program investigates the potential roles of natural selection, phenotypic plasticity, migration, and hybridization in preventing the extinction of a short-lived subalpine forb, Androsace septentrionalis, forb in a warming mountain meadow. 

Thus far we have shown that long-term experimental warming in a mountain meadow (the ï¿½Warming Meadowï¿½) has caused the dramatic decline of Androsace septentrionalis. We have also documented substantial life-history and morphological variation both within the Warming Meadow and between populations of A. septentrionalis at high and low elevation, suggesting that enough raw genetic material may exist for adaptation to treatments and natural climate gradients. 

Our research uses a use a novel combination of common gardens, reciprocal transplants (with both field and greenhouse-collected seed), and molecular analyses to determine if experimental populations are beginning to adapt in situ to warmed conditions, and whether gene flow from other microsites or elevations can enhance the ability of warmed populations to persist. This combination of field experiments and analysis of spatial genetic structure will enable us to characterize A. septentrionalisï¿½ potential responses to natural and experimental climate variation.
Subject: Climate Change

ResearchPlanTitle:
GENE FLOW PATTERNS AND POLYPATERNITY IN THE BURYING BEETLE, 
NICROPHORUS INVESTIGATOR, OF GUNNISON NATIONAL FOREST, COLORADO, USA.
ResearchPlanAbstract: Insect biodiversity is a critical aspect of ecosystem functioning.  Insects function as nutrient cyclers, sources of food for many animals, and are considered valuable model organisms for a number of different research disciplines.  Observing the patterns and processes governing different aspects of insect ecology in existing, natural populations is of considerable valuable to evolutionary ecologists and conservation biologists alike, given that many modern landscapes are threatened by habitat fragmentation, altered ecosystem functioning, and native species declines. Nicrophorus investigator is a species of burying beetle found widespread throughout the East and Slate River watersheds of Gunnison National Forest in Colorado, USA, and has been the subject of various ecological studies conducted by Idaho State University researchers for the past decade.  The most recent of these investigations, concerning patterns of gene flow within this group of burying beetles, has been made possible by technological advances in DNA genotyping and statistical techniques.  Gene flow is an indirect measurement of dispersal ability, and is a valuable tool for identifying habitat characteristics that either promote or limit animal movements.  The DNA markers used for this type of research, microsatellite DNA loci, have been developed for N. investigator, providing a means for determining the amount and directionality of gene flow from one group of beetles to another, to cluster individuals into inter-breeding groups, and to determine the parentage of individuals.
Subject: Other

ResearchPlanTitle: Mating system of golden-mantled ground squirrels
ResearchPlanAbstract: The golden-mantled ground squirrels at the Rocky Mountain Biological Laboratory spend most of the year hibernating to save energy during the long, cold winter.  Once squirrels emerge in spring, they only have a few months in which to consume enough calories for hibernation, avoid predation, and reproduce.  This time constraint suggests that females should mate with the first male they come across so that their pups ï¿½ born mid-summer ï¿½ have time to grow before winter. On the other hand, females may prefer to delay mating to choose a better male, or even mate with multiple males to ensure pregnancy. I am collecting data on the emergence times and interactions between marked male and female golden-mantled ground squirrels during this early-season breeding period to determine female mating strategies. While mating itself is hard to observe, I plan to calculate when mating occurred by counting backwards from when litters are born. Also, I will use locations of potential mates and paternity tests of pups to determine whether individuals of this species mate monogamously or with more than one partner. My research on this population of golden-mantled ground squirrels will test whether female mating strategies may give this species flexibility to adapt to changing conditions.
Subject: Other

ResearchPlanTitle: The effect of flowering phenology on pollen limitation and plant fitness.
ResearchPlanAbstract: Phenology is an important life history trait that can dramatically affect fitness, survival and species interactions. In high altitude meadows, snowmelt is the principle environmental cue triggering spring flowering. Climate change, among other factors, is thought to be responsible for recent trends in early snowmelt dates, which in turn is altering flowering phenology. Loss in flowering plant fitness due to altered phenology is suspected but requires further investigation, and the factors affecting changes in plant fitness have not been thoroughly investigated. The goal of this study is to investigate how flowering plant fitness is affected by phenology, and the role that biotic and abiotic factors play in affecting flowering plant fitness, given altered phenology. Additionally, I will investigate whether the phenologies of ground nesting bees are affected by the same environmental cues as flowering plants in order to assess the likelihood of phenological matches vs. mismatches.
ResearchPlanOrganisms: I am still in the process of determining the ideal focal species, and to a certain extent, this choice will depend on which species appear in my study plots (described below), but the top candidates are: Potentilla pulcherrima (Rosaceae), Erigeron speciosus (Asteraceae), Delphinium nuttallianum (Ranunculaceae), Mertensia fusiformis (Boraginaceae), Campanula rotundifolia (Campanulaceae), Erythronium grandiflorum (Liliaceae), Senecio triangularis (Asteraceae) and Claytonia lanceoliata (Portulacaceae).  I would eventually like to incorporate studies of ground nesting bees into the project.  The bee portion of the study is likely to include many species of ground nesting bees, but most likely from the genera Andrena (Andrenidae), Halictus (Halictidae) and Lasioglossum (Halictidae).
Subject: Phenology

ResearchPlanTitle: Invasive Plant Management and Revegetation in Gothic
ResearchPlanAbstract: Invasive species are a growing problem around the world, in the U.S., and in Colorado (Enserink, 1999).  Invasive plants disrupt native communities in a variety of ways.  Invasive weeds can form monocultures, which decrease native plant diversity.  Changes in plant communities likely have reverberating effects throughout the ecosystem.  For example, changes in plant composition may affect the abundance and composition of herbivores, pollinators, and even higher trophic levels. In addition, soil abiotic factors and soil communities may be affected by changes in plant communities.  This proposal outlines on-going and future projects in invasive plant management and revegetation in the Gothic townsite.
ResearchPlanOrganisms: Linaria vulgaris, Bromis inermis, Cirsium arvense
Subject: Other

ResearchPlanTitle: Facilities Projects 2011
ResearchPlanAbstract: This plan describes RMBL Facilities projects planned for 2011.
Subject: Other

ResearchPlanInstitution: City of Boulder Open Space and Mountain Parks
ResearchPlanTitle: A Gunnison County Bat Assemblage
ResearchPlanAbstract: Bats are known to be important components of ecosystems, devouring tons of insects nightly here in North America.  Despite their importance, there continues to be a lack of baseline data available concerning roost sites and population dynamics.  In light of the increasing concern about the status of bat populations, the USGS has begun efforts to compile and evaluate the fragmented information available on the topic (O’Shea and Bogan, 2003).  While there have been excellent research efforts on the front range of Colorado over the last 15 years (Adams, 2010), there remains a lack of information in Gunnison County.  I propose to survey 12-15 sites ranging from 11,000 feet in the upper East River Basin to 7000 feet on the Gunnison river system.  Species richness, diversity, and evenness will be determined using mist nets and Anabat acoustic monitoring equipment.  I may conduct water quality assessments to determine mineral content to test the hypothesis that lactating females will choose calcium rich sites (Adams, R.A et all, 2003).
Subject: Long-Term

ResearchPlanTitle: VECTORING OF PHYTOPATHOGENIC PSEUDOMONAS SYRINGAE BY LEAF-MINING DROSOPHILA: ECOLOGICAL AND EVOLUTIONARY IMPLICATIONS
ResearchPlanAbstract: The vast majority of animals on earth are insects that feed on plants (herbivores), and most of these insect herbivores prefer to feed on a small subset of all plant species (specialists). Just about every plant on earth harbors some kind of bacteria on/in their leaves. Among these, one type in particular is perhaps the most prevalent leaf-associated bacteria in the world: Pseudomonas syringae. These bacteria disperse worldwide through clouds in the atmosphere, raining down on earth by nucleating snow and rain droplets. They often cause severe disease in leaves of plants (both wild and domesticated). It logically follows from these observations that insect herbivores (read: most animals) regularly interact with bacteria (read: Pseudomonas syringae) every day while going about their business. Thus, plant-insect interactions will nearly always have the potential to be influenced by leaf-associated bacteriaï¿½a fact commonly ignored in plant-insect research. The converse is also true: leaf-associated bacteria will very often interact with insects that may modify the ways these bacteria are able to make a living. For example, wounds in leaves created by herbivores may make the plant more easily infected by P. syringae, allowing more leaves to become infected than would otherwise. Many P. syringae strains cause severe damage to the plants they infect: but if a bacterium is stuck in a leaf and is making that leaf die, how does it get out before it destroys its own habitat? In environments where it is hard to find a healthy host plant to infect, bacteria like P. syringae might benefit from hitching a ride from plant to plant on insects that are specialized to feed on certain plants. In the environment surrounding the Rocky Mountain Biological Laboratory in Gothic, CO, P. syringae causes disease on the water-loving herb, heartleaf bittercress (Cardamine cordifolia) that is frequently infested with specialized herbivorous flies (Scaptomyza nigrita) that poke holes in its leaves to feed. In this study we ask, how does feeding on plants by these flies influence the ability of disease-causing bacteria to move from plant to plant? Do leaf-associated P. syringae bacteria harm the flies that feed on these leaves, or do flies have behaviors that keep them out of contact with these bacteria? Understanding the interactions between insects and bacteria on their shared host plant will help us discover new biological patterns and mechanisms that implicate microbes in one of the most common phenomena in the terrestrial biosphere: plant-insect interactions. Our research will also shed light on how insect herbivores contribute to the spread of plant diseases within and between natural populations of native plants in the Rocky Mountains.
ResearchPlanOrganisms:
Cardamine cordifolia (Brassicaceae)
Scaptomyza nigrita (Drosophilidae)
Pseudomonas syringae (gamma-Proteobacteria)
Subject: Other

ResearchPlanTitle: Investigating population genetic structure, local adaptation, and the importance of plant defenses in the interactions between a specialist leafmining fly (Scaptomyza nigrita) and its host plant, heart leaf bittercress (Cardamine cordifolia)
ResearchPlanAbstract:
Plants and the insects that feed on them make up a tremendous portion of the diversity found in nature, and the outcomes of interactions between plant hosts and their insect herbivores play an important part in shaping ecological communities.  Evolutionary biologists often speak of these interactions in terms of an â€œarms race,â€ in which plants benefit from developing more effective weapons â€“ ranging from toxic chemicals to spikes and thorns â€“ to combat the insects feeding on them, and insects benefit from increasing their ability to evade plant defenses.  The intensity of the battle between plants and insects can vary, however, from one place to another.
A perfect example of a plant exposed to different numbers of insect pests depending on where it grows is heart leaf bittercress, a perennial mustard with beautiful white flowers that is widely distributed along streams around the RMBL.  The insects that feed on it tend to be found in the sun, and one insect â€“ a fly called Scaptomyza nigrita, which eats tunnels through the leaves during its larval stage and tears open holes to drink leaf juices as an adult fly â€“ can damage almost every leaf of every plant in some very sunny sites.  On the other hand, plants growing in deeply shaded areas often have no obvious visible damage at all.  Because every plant has its own genotype â€“ a unique combination of DNA â€“ some plants will resist insects better than others.  If this allows these plants to stay healthier and produce more seeds, we would expect these more resistant plants to have more offspring and increase in frequency at sites where high numbers of insect attackers pose a bigger cost to less resistant plants.  As a result, bittercress populations that have long been engaged in battles with insects might be better at resisting them, while populations that have spent generation after generation in the safety of the shade may have weaker defenses (because insect feeding pressure hasnâ€™t built them up yet).  The same story could happen with variation in elevation instead of sun and shade, but this time, think of climate differences between a valley and a mountaintop as the pressure that differs between plants living in different areas, instead of insect abundance.
	In fact, a few studies have shown that plants from different locations, despite being the same species, differ in their ability to defend themselves from insect attack.  However, weâ€™re still not sure if the forces insects exert on plants are strong enough to cause plant populations under consistent insect attack to differ from other groups of plants that are very close by â€“ say, in the same valley or hillside.  To test this, I will collect plants from sun and shade, valleys and mountaintops from around the RMBL, and plant them all together in a set of â€œcommon gardens,â€ where they all experience the same conditions.  If plants perform best in the habitat they came from â€“ for example, if plants from populations that are always attacked by lots of insects actually do resist insects better than plants from the shade â€“ thereâ€™s evidence for â€œlocal adaptation.â€  We know there can be quantifiable differences between plants growing far away from each other, even when theyâ€™re both the same species; this experiment will help us determine whether a plantâ€™s environment might lead one population of plants to differ even from its neighbors.
	In addition to moving looking for performance differences between bittercress plants, Iâ€™ll also be collecting leaf tissue from bittercress and the fly that specializes on it.  By extracting DNA, sequencing it using powerful new technology, and comparing sequence data from the entire genome across individuals from different locations â€“ such as the next valley or the next state over â€“ we can infer relationships between populations, and get a good idea of how theyâ€™ve moved across the landscape and colonized new areas in their distant past.  Itâ€™s one way scientists have traced the path of early humans as they expanded across the globe, with more resolution than ancient bones or tools can give us.  Iâ€™ll use a similar method to see how glaciers and climate changes have influenced how bittercress has moved across the Rockies â€“ and whether that pesky fly has been following it around the whole way.
Subject: Other

ResearchPlanTitle: Selection of sap-well sites by an ecosystem engineer and keystone species: the red-naped sapsucker (Sphyrapicus nuchalis)
ResearchPlanAbstract: A keystone species is an organism whose effect on the environment is disproportionately strong relative to its mass or abundance, so much so that the speciesï¿½ removal would cause dramatic changes in the surrounding community. Conserving a keystone species requires an adequate understanding of its habitat requirements. One of the most important keystone species is the Red-naped Sapsucker, a woodpecker that nests in aspen woodlands of western North America. Sapsuckers excavate a new nest cavity every year, providing future nest chambers for several species of birds, mammals, and insects. Sapsuckers also create sap wells in trees and shrubs, thereby incidentally supplying food for other sap feeders. Therefore, local extinction of sapsuckers could trigger a decline in local species diversity; this is a conservation concern because sapsucker habitat has undergone widespread degradation. The primary objective of my research is to determine the criteria used by sapsuckers in their choice of sap well sites in trees and willow. The study area will be sapsucker habitat (aspen-dominated forests and willow) throughout the upper East River Valley near RMBL, Washington Gulch, and West Brush Creek.
ResearchPlanOrganisms: Red-naped sapsucker (Sphyrapicus nuchalis), quaking aspen (Populus tremuloides), and willows (Salix subcoerulea, S. pseudocordata, and S. brachycarpa)
Subject: Other

ResearchPlanTitle: Quantifying environmental and biological controls on soil CO2 fluxes in East River valley forests
ResearchPlanAbstract: My proposed research seeks to mechanistically understand soil respiration in the dominant forest communities around the RMBL by individually quantifying the contributions from its two sources, plants and microbes.  To do this, I will combine automated measurements of soil CO2 concentrations and soil respiration with isotope (radiocarbon, 14C) source partitioning methods in two vegetation communities (spruce/fir and aspen forests) located in the RMBL research meadow.  This novel approach will provide information on how environmental and biological factors control plant and microbial respiration sources of CO2 to the atmosphere, and assess potential climate change impacts on ecosystems in the East River valley.
ResearchPlanOrganisms:
Picea engelmanii and Abies lasiocarpa and soil microbes
Populus tremuloides and soil microbes
Subject: Climate Change

ResearchPlanInstitution: USDA ARS Poisonous Plant Research Laboratory
ResearchPlanTitle: The chemical ecolgoy of Delphinium
ResearchPlanAbstract: The genus Delphinium is toxic to herbivores on rangelands.  The bio-active norditerpene alkaloids responsible for the toxic potential of Delphinium are well characterized chemically.  Our general research interests relate to the chemical ecology of these bioactive compounds.  The proposed research will survey the nectar and pollen of select species within this genus for the presence of these alkaloids.  If the pollen and/or nectar are found to contain these compounds, follow-up studies will be pursued in the future to determine if there is any adaptive advantage to having these alkaloids in the pollen and/or nectar.  In addition, we plan to determine if plant phenology or experimental manipulations of temperature result in changes to the qualitative and/or quantitative composition of the toxic alkaloids in Delphinium nuttallianum.
Subject: Pollination

ResearchPlanTitle: Monitoring plant phenology near six RMBL weather stations
ResearchPlanAbstract: Climate change affects phenology of organisms.  Long term datasets are essential in order to make this statement.  This proposal outlines a long term plant phenology protocol that makes use of climate data collected at RMBLï¿½s 6 weather stations, which are placed along an elevational gradient.
Subject: Phenology

ResearchPlanTitle: 1. Linking spatial and temporal patterns of pollinator foraging to plant reproduction in plant communities. 2. Testing adaptive explanations for floral variation in Mertensia fusiformis (Boraginaceae).
ResearchPlanAbstract:
1. As most flowering plants rely on animals to disperse pollen among flowers, reproduction for plants will reflect pollinator foraging patterns, which will vary with many pollinator and plant attributes. As an example, all flowering plants are patchily distributed in space and in flowering time and occur in communities in which they share pollinators with other plants. Pollinators are likely to display foraging patterns both spatially and temporally in plant communities that reflect economical foraging decisions bound by memory and learning constraints. So pollinators’ foraging decisions in these patchy resource environments with many species will affect the pollination service they provide to plants. These peculiarities in foraging have been given little attention and mean that the ecological context of a plant will influence its reproductive success in ways not considered before. In particular, pollination facilitation, when the pollination of a plant species is enhanced by the presence of another species, may be more common than is currently acknowledged. I aim to highlight the importance of spatial and temporal scale in plant-pollinator interactions, including pollinator foraging responses at different spatial and temporal scales in plant communities, and how these can affect plant reproduction in a community context, often in positive ways. Specifically, I propose to investigate, (1) the range of sizes of individual Bombus foraging areas and how they change over time and as floral resources change, in an attempt find the spatial and temporal scales that they respond to differences in floral resources, (2) if pollinator site constancy can lead to positive interactions between sequentially flowering plant species, and (3) if highly preferred plant species benefit less preferred species (i.e. the magnet species effect) due to the dynamics of pollinator foraging.

2. In alpine habitats, patchiness in snow accumulation and timing of spring snowmelt produces marked variation in the timing at which plants begin to flower, even over small spatial scales. Thus, plants in early- and late-melting patches can experience very different conditions during their flowering periods, despite growing in close proximity. If the difference in flowering time between early and late patches is sufficiently great, there may be little cross-pollination and genetic exchange between plants growing in the two patch types. This can result in the plants adapting to the conditions specific to the local flowering time. This study will evaluate the evidence for this type of adaptation in alpine bluebells. This species shows pronounced variation in floral characteristics that may be related to the local timing of snowmelt and flowering. In a previous study, we tested whether early- and late-flowering plants are visited by different pollinators, and whether natural selection imposed by pollinators can explain the differences in floral morphology among populations. As expected, late-flowering populations experienced a different suite of pollinators than early-flowering populations: Nectar-foraging bumble bee queens and male solitary bees predominated early in the season, but the number of pollen-collecting female solitary bees increased dramatically later in the season. Furthermore, we found significant differences among pollinators in their abilities to transfer pollen to stigmas at different heights. Because pollen-collecting bees were relatively ineffective at transferring pollen to short-styled plants, they should select for longer styles if plant fitness is limited by pollen receipt. However, although plants in late-flowering patches tended to have longer styles than those in early patches, this difference was not consistent. This may be a result of small sample size, and I propose to do more extensive population sampling of style length in early- and late-flowering populations to show general patterns. This will lead to a project measuring pollinator-mediated selection on style length in early and late populations.
ResearchPlanOrganisms: 1. Gentiana parryi and Delphinium barbeyi and medium- and long-tongued Bombus spp. 2. Mertensia fusiformis and short-tonged Bombus spp. and Osmia spp.
Subject: Pollination

ResearchPlanTitle: Leaf venation networks: proxies for climate variation, past and present?
ResearchPlanAbstract: Climatic variation is key to understanding the global carbon cycle and the evolution of species. However, our knowledge of past climates decreases rapidly with increasing geologic time. Fortunately detailed climate records may be preserved in fossilized leaves. I am developing a model that simultaneously predicts atmospheric CO2, humidity, and temperature based on measurements of leaf vein networks and stomata. Using the unique environments near RMBL, I will test this model on aspen leaves spanning a wide range of environmental conditions and elevations. Confirmation of model predictions on modern leaves will enable fossil leaf vein networks to become useful climate records.
Subject: Climate Change

ResearchPlanTitle: Dwarfs on purpose:  Comparative ecological genetics of adaptation in the high elevation endemic Mimulus tilingii
ResearchPlanAbstract: A major goal in evolutionary biology is to understand how organisms adapt to novel or changing environments. A particularly dramatic example of ecological specialization in plants involves alpine endemics, which have evolved characteristic suites of adaptations, such as compact growth forms and tolerance to freezing temperatures, in response to similar selective regimes.  We are investigating the ecological and genomic basis of this common ecological transition to alpine environments using the mountain monkeyflower, Mimulus tilingii. In contrast to the widely-distributed, lowland progenitor species Mimulus guttatus, Mimulus tilingii populations are confined to alpine regions throughout western North America, in discrete “habitat islands.” These populations provide a unique set of replicate evolutionary experiments for how Mimulus tilingii has adapted to common ecological influences imposed by alpine environments. Preliminary analyses indicate that there have been at least three evolutionary origins of Mimulus tilingii in the Cascades, Sierra Nevadas, and Olympic Mountain ranges.  On one hand, Mimulus tilingii is both physically and genetically distinct from its progenitor species, Mimulus guttatus.  For both species, geographically distant populations (>750km) are more similar to each other than to populations of the other species growing nearby.  However, the disjunct distribution of Mimulus tilingii suggests a complex of closely related species in multiple stages of adaptation to similar montane environments.  Indeed, genetic studies suggest that there is a distinction among populations in the Cascades of Washington, Oregon, and southern British Columbia, in the Sierra Nevada of California, and the Olympic Mountains of Washington.  Further, morphological differentiation suggest selection on vegetative traits characteristic of montane plants, and is consistent with habitat-mediated selection driving morphological evolution.  I am now proposing to expand my sampling to include populations in the Rocky Mountains, which will provide a geographically distinct evolutionary lineage for future comparative studies for how Mimulus populations have diverged in response to similar ecological conditions.
Subject: Long-Term

ResearchPlanTitle: Linking spatial genetic differentiation to animal-mediated pollen dispersal in Ipomopsis aggregata
ResearchPlanAbstract: Animal transfer of pollen has important evolutionary consequences for plant populations. Characterizing the geographic scale over which animals transfer pollen provides insight into the evolutionary potential of a population and its potential to respond to environmental changes.  However, it is difficult to directly assess geographic patterns of animal-mediated pollen movement, and even harder to determine how this translates into genetic exchange at different spatial scales, due to the near impossibility of following long flights of pollinators (much less of observing pollen transfer and subsequent fertilization).  However, reliable indirect estimates of where pollen and pollinators have come from may be obtained from the genotypes of pollen on flowers and on pollinatorsï¿½ bodies.  I propose to characterize the extent to which populations of Ipomopsis aggregata are genetically differentiated at a hierarchy of spatial scales, and then to determine the mechanisms that explain the observed levels of differentiation.  Specifically, I will attempt to link genetic differentiation in I. aggregata to the relative contributions of different pollinators to pollen movement and subsequent fertilization at different spatial scales.
Subject: Pollination

ResearchPlanTitle: Investigation of mule deer (Odocoileus hemionus) foraging behavior when exposed to the scent of the predatory coyote (Canis latrans)
ResearchPlanAbstract:
A trophic cascade is an ecological process where predators affect the plant biomass of an ecosystem by limiting the population of herbivores.  Predators limit herbivore populations both by predation and changing the behavior of the prey. One herbivore behavior in particular that affects plant biomass is foraging.  Multiple studies have produced evidence that herbivores change their foraging behaviors when they sense, either by sight or by smell, that a predator is nearby or has recently passed through the area. What this study aims to accomplish is to investigate whether this pattern of adjusted foraging behavior when a predator is detected is true for mule deer (Odocoileus hemionus).  Like all members of the deer family, mule deer rely on their sense of smell of detect danger.  The predator species that will be used in this investigation, in the form of a urine sample, is the coyote (Canis latrans) an animal that is known to prey on mule deer.
      The two locations used are Western Bench meadow and a meadow across the road and north of Ore House.  Feeding stations will then be set up in both areas consisting of a feed block specifically designed for deer.  Both feed blocks will be set 30 meters from the nearest cover.  I will not be able to begin the manipulations until the deer are habituated to the food.  All behavior observations both during the habituation and manipulation periods will be recorded only when the deer is within 10 meters of the feed block.  The observations made during the manipulation period will also be scored and analyzed using the JWatcher program after each observation period.  The two hour observation periods will take place either in the early morning around sunrise (5:00 AM to 7:00 AM), close to sunset (7:00 PM to 9:00 PM), or if possible on a given day, both times.  I will alternate sites every observation period.  While I am observing the I will be as far away from the feed block as possible so long as I am still able to see it.
      For the manipulation, a petri dish with either water or coyote urine treated gelatin crystals will be placed on a plate whose face has been spray painted black.  The petri dish and plate will be placed next to the feed block only during the times I am observing and recording the deer behavior.  When I arrive at the site, I will place the petri dish and plate at the appropriate place and will remove it when I have finished observing.  The coyote urine treatment will be used every other time I visit the particular site.
Subject: Other

ResearchPlanTitle: The Effects of Hemiparasitism by Castilleja miniata on Community Structure and Ecosystem Function in Alpine Systems
ResearchPlanAbstract: Parasitic plants are represented in most plant assemblages, but their effects on the community and ecosystem are largely unstudied and poorly understood. The purpose of this study is to determine if the hemiparasitic plant Castilleja miniata influences the structure of plant communities and ecosystem processes by measuring total plant biomass, community composition, and diversity.
Subject: Other

ResearchPlanTitle: Vegetation Pattern Dependency upon Slope and Soil Type Along Southwest-Facing Hillslopes of the Upper East River and West Brush Creek Watersheds
ResearchPlanAbstract: Vegetation distribution patterns on a macro-scale across watersheds surrounding the Gothic townsite have yet to be analyzed in depth.  Through observational analysis, we have assessed a reoccurring trend of aspen (Populus tremuloides), wet meadow species characterized by willow (Salix) and skunk cabbage(Symplocarpus foetidus), sage brush (Artemisia tridentata), as well as dry meadows that are predominately mixed forbes and grasses (Poaceae) along the southwest-facing hill slopes of the Upper East River and West Brush Creek watersheds.  Prior to formal soil tests, our observations allowed us to detect the Mancos Shale as the soil type for lower elevations of the Upper East River’s southwest-facing slope while the dominant soil type of West Brush Creek from the Maroon Formation. Aspen stands were predominantly distributed across slopes of a particular gradient in both watersheds whereas wet and dry meadow and sage brush species were limited in their abundance on the West Brush Creek southwest-facing hill slope.  To explain this observation, we hypothesize that aspen species occurrence is more dependent upon slope gradient rather than soil type whereas the primary species of wet and dry meadows as well as sage brush (Artemisia tridentata) has higher dependency upon soil type than slope gradient. Using ArcMap10 on a portable field laptop, we will create a vegetation distribution map of both watersheds and then overlay the image with soil survey maps of the area to assess whether our hypothesis of species dependency upon soil type or slope gradient is indeed verifiable.
ResearchPlanOrganisms: Populus tremuloides, mixed forbes, Artemisia tridentata, Poaceae, Salix, Symplocarpus foeidus
Subject: Other

ResearchPlanTitle: Ecological causes and consequences of flower color polymorphism in Boechera stricta.
ResearchPlanAbstract:
Biologists have long been interested in understanding the maintenance of phenotypic variation within populations because heritable phenotypic variation is the basis of evolution by natural selection. Polymorphisms can be maintained by selection if all the morphs are beneficial (either frequency- dependent selection or balancing selection). Alternatively, polymorphisms can be neutral and retained, for example, as a phylogenetic artifact. In general, we lack a fundamental understanding of the evolutionary processes that influence and maintain phenotypic variation.
	Flower color is an excellent example of a trait that can vary within populations, and it can influence adaptive evolution in plant, pollinator and herbivore communities. Furthermore, Boechera stricta is a great species for studying adaptive flower color polymorphism. Boechera stricta (Brassicaceae) is a primarily self-pollinating, genetically well-defined perennial species that is closely related to the model organism Arabidposis thaliana. Most B. stricta flowers have white petals, however some populations maintain a low frequency of a purple flower morph. Very little is known about the nature of the purple morph or its genetic underpinnings, and the vibrancy of the purple petals can range from deep purple to pale purple-pink. Because B. stricta is predominantly self-pollinating and does not rely on pollinators for pollen dispersal, the reasons for maintaining a rare flower color morph remain unclear. It may be in response to the local abiotic and biotic environmental conditions, and thus the purple morph could be a plastic response to the environment. The objectives of this observational study are two faceted: first, we will determine the frequency of the purple morph in the Boechera stricta population near the Rocky Mountain Biological Laboratory (RMBL); second, we will collect environmental and phenotypic data that will allow us to determine if there are environmental factors that correlate with flower color. A secondary aspect of this study will be to investigate and quantify the pollinator community of B. stricta, determine whether pollinator species visit both color morphs, or show preference for the common white flower morph, and assess the extent of pollen movement between flower color morphs.
Subject: Other

ResearchPlanTitle: Ditching the Doozies: Does the duration of parental care vary with mate condition in the burying beetle Nicrophorus investigator?
ResearchPlanAbstract: Burying beetles (genus Nicrophorus) exhibit a unique suite of parental behaviors usually restricted to endothermic vertebrates (birds and mammals) and advanced, eusocial insects (e.g. termites, ants, and bees) (Scott 1998). Understanding the dynamics of this exceptional parental system will assist in illuminating the determinants of some highly contentious fields of evolutionary biology, such as cooperation, conflict, sociality, and selection. Typically, females provide full care to the offspring from the time of egg-laying to maturity while males desert the brood and their mates earlier (Trumbo 1991). In this experiment, we plan to investigate the causes for this phenomenon by manipulating female condition (size and nourishment) and recording the effect on male parental duration. Assuming that males provide care predominantly to protect against competitors (both intra- and interspecific), we predict that there will be no considerable change in male parental care.
Subject: Other

ResearchPlanTitle: Can breeding bird density influence vocal individuality in bird song
ResearchPlanAbstract: We plan to study how breeding bird density will influence individuality in bird song. We will record Wilson Warblers, Yellow Warblers, Green Tailed Towhees, Red Winged Blackbirds and House Wrens. We will then analyze their songs to determine if individuals of the same species differ in their songs. We hypothesis that birds in greater densities will have more individuality in their songs.
ResearchPlanOrganisms: Red winged blackbirds, house wrens, yellow warblers, wilson warblers and green tailed towhees
Subject: Other

ResearchPlanTitle: Foraging Patterns of a primary food resource (Salix spp.) by a keystone species: the Red-naped Sapsucker (Sphyrapicus nuchalis)
ResearchPlanAbstract: Re-naped Sapsuckers are a keystone species in the subalpine/montane forests of the Colorado Rocky Mountain region. One of this specie's primary food sources is comprised of three species of willow (Salix spp.). This study will investigate the relationship between the Red-naped Sapsucker and Salix. It will attempt to find patterns in the feeding habits of the Red-naped Sapsucker as well as preferences of certain willows over others. This will be done by measuring the stress level of willow stems that have been fed on by sapsuckers as well as the proportion of stems affected per plant. Investigating these patterns can lead to a better understanding of the coevolutionary relationship between the Red-naped Sapsuckers and Salix.
Subject: Other

ResearchPlanTitle: The Effect of Vegetation on Mule Deer (Odocoileus hemionus) Habitat Preference
ResearchPlanAbstract: I wish to continue previous RMBL research by asking the question, "Are deer more common inside or outside Gothic?"  Past summers, students have found deer to be more prevalent inside Gothic because of the avoidance of coyotes.  If I indeed find that deer remain more common inside Gothic, I wish to consider two reasons to explain why this may be occurring: (1) the abundance of highly palatable plants is greater inside than outside Gothic; and (2) the ratio of area of open landscapes to closed landscapes is greater inside than outside Gothic.
Subject: Other

ResearchPlanTitle: Mule deer (Odocoileus hemionus) Response to Yellow-Bellied Marmot (Marmota flaviventris) Alarm Calls.
ResearchPlanAbstract: Animals can sometimes make sounds, such as alarm calls, that allow others of its own kind to recognize an incoming threat, be it a predator, intruder, etc. Other animals can sometimes eavesdrop on the conversation and use this information for their own kind. This is important for scientists, behavioral ecologists especially, to study because it can change the way that the other animal or group searches for food, the amount of time it spends looking for predators, its group characteristics, habitat choice, and also gives information about its cognitive abilities. Previous researchers have noted that mule deer, which frequent the Gothic townsite and the valley in general, do respond to marmot alarm calls, cat sized rodents related to squirrels. These are usually elicited due to the deer’s presence, however marmots do share a predator that deer and fawn must be wary about: the coyote. This study seeks gather data on the response of mule deer to the marmots alarm calls versus the white crowned sparrow song, in order to quantify a true behavioral response across this population.
Subject: Other

ResearchPlanTitle: The effects of climate change on plant traits and fruiting phenology in Delphinium Nuttallianum.
ResearchPlanAbstract: Scientists predict an increase in earth temperature by several degrees over the coming century due to climate change caused by greenhouse gases.  It is my goal to mimic climate change on plots of subalpine meadow containing Delphinium with plexiglass warming frames.
