Then, I will observe the effects increased temperatures have on flowering time, fruiting time, number of flowers produced,plant height, and nectar volume.  Additionally, I will monitor the effects supplementary watering has on the same variables in Delphinium.
Subject: Climate Change

ResearchPlanTitle: The changes of soil properties and nutrient cycling in response to ant colony age and establishment.
ResearchPlanAbstract: This study will test how ant colony age influences nutrient availability and soil properties over time. It will give insight into long-term ecosystem response to ant colonization.
Subject: Other

ResearchPlanTitle: Sweet rewards: Do floral resources mediate the ant-aphid interaction on Valeriana edulis?
ResearchPlanAbstract: Relationships that develop over time between different groups of organisms, especially related to direct energy exchange through foraging behavior, are an important facet of ecological dynamics. Understanding the tradeoffs, causes, and consequences of interactions between food resources and foragers lends insight into the evolutionary history of an ecosystem. In this study, the plant Valeriana edulis, ants, aphids, and other insects which utilize resources of V. edulis, are used at a  model system of food-forager interactions at the community level. The goal of this study is to add to existing knowledge of the interactions observed in this specific system in order to generate a more comprehensive understanding of the community dynamics. I will be denying or allowing ants access to floral nectar to address the question: How does the availability of floral nectar affect ant-aphid interactions, and does this effect differ between male and female plants?
ResearchPlanOrganisms: Valeriana edulis, ants (various species of Tapinoma, Formica, and Myrmica), aphids (Aphis valerianae)
Subject: Climate Change

ResearchPlanTitle: A Montane Warming Meadow Experiment: Testing Models Predicting Species Abundance Distributions and Species Area Relationships
ResearchPlanAbstract: I will be conducting an experiment in the Warming Meadow, which was set up in 1989 by John Harte and co-workers. This facility will be used specifically to test the Maximum Entropy Theory of Ecology (METE) and its validity under disturbed conditions (the warm plots) and undisturbed conditions (the control plots). METE predicts the distribution, abundance, and energetics of species across multiple scales and taxonomic groups, and is advantageous over traditional theories of species abundance distribution (SAD) and species area relationships (SAR) because of its least-biased probability distribution inference requiring only four state variables: area of the ecosystem (A), number of species (S), numbers of individuals (N), and metabolic rate of individuals. Census data will be collected in six of the ten plots (three heated and three control plots) and will be analyzed to determine if the hypothesis that the theory will fail under disturbed conditions can be accepted. Overall, METE can provide knowledge to estimate biodiversity and predict analysis of evolution of an ecosystem, such as those responding to habitat degradation and climate change.
ResearchPlanOrganisms: All plants in the research meadow.
Subject: Climate Change

ResearchPlanTitle: Diptera Behavioral Response to Targeted Bombus Removal
ResearchPlanAbstract: The current trend of declining bumblebee species leads to changes in the foraging behavior of the other pollinators. These behavior changes result in decreased plant reproductive success and biodiversity. This study examines the behavioral changes in the diptera pollinators in order to provide insight to understanding the consequences of losses of pollinator species and further knowledge of pollination model systems.
ResearchPlanOrganisms: Bumblebee (Bombus) pollinators and diptera pollinator species
Subject: Pollination

ResearchPlanTitle: The effects of Formica obscuripes ant nests on the aboveground and belowground biodiversity and nutrient cycling in the Almont Triangle Wilderness area of colorado.
ResearchPlanAbstract: The effects on biodiversity from Formica obscuripes on the soil and surrounding vegetation can have a large impact. Studies have been conducted on aboveground vegetation as well as belowground nutrients, however most of the studies conducted are in isolation of either above or below ground. This study will ask four major questions. 1) How do ants alter ecosystems? 2)What are their effects on aboveground vegetation surrounding their nests. 3) What are the effects on belowground nutrients. And 4) what are the effects on belowground biodiversity? It is hypothesized thas these ants will alter their local ecosystem in such a way as to shift the vegetation types surrounding the nests as well as have consequences on the nutrients within the soil. Ultimately this could reduce the biodiversity of the soil by either competition  or predation, or indirectly from altered nutrients in the soil.
Subject: Other

ResearchPlanTitle: Does Species Diversity of Caddisflies Enhance Detritus Breakdown and Nutrient Release in Temporary Ponds?
ResearchPlanAbstract: Detritivores like caddisflies are pivotal in releasing energy to the rest of the aquatic trophic cascade. Caddisflies are large aquatic invertebrate larvae that perform this ecosystem function, allowing energy and nutrients to re-enter food webs. According to previous studies, habitats with only one species of caddisfly present had an absence of functional redundancy—no other organism plays their role—and so they are especially important in their ecosystem. Our study seeks to determine to what degree species-level diversity of caddisflies is important to detritus processing where more than one species of caddisfly coexists. Would it have a negative impact if a species were lost? To answer this, we manipulated the diversity of caddisflies in microcosms to study to what degree their role is functionally redundant. We predict that more detritus is processed in the presence of multiple caddisfly species than in the presence of a single species at the same total population density. We also predict that higher detritus processing will lead to more nitrogen and phosphorus in the water and thus higher algal growth.
ResearchPlanOrganisms: Caddisflies (Limnephilus externus, Limnephilus sublunatus, Limnephilus tarsalis)
Subject: Other

ResearchPlanTitle: Presence of Spermophilus lateralis and Tamias minimus in montane meadows with various distances from cover surrounding the Rocky Mountain Biological Laboratory
ResearchPlanAbstract: The golden-mantled ground squirrel (Spermophilus lateralis) and the least chipmunk (Tamias minimus) in the Rocky Mountains have very similar habitats and diets.  Yet, they do not exclude each other but can coexist.  Rosemary Smith found that in meadows with area less than or equal to 18 m from cover, T. minimus was predominant.  It meadows exceeding 20 m, both species were observed.  These species slightly differ in habits likely because of differences in sensitivities to predation risk (Smith 1991).  I will be observing similar meadows with various distances from cover to determine whether this trend is still true twenty years later.
Subject: Other

ResearchPlanTitle: Factors that affect the repeatability of personality in Marmota flaviventris
ResearchPlanAbstract: Animal personality is becoming increasingly more relevant to the science community because of its impact on reproductive success.  Measuring personality however can be difficult because many things can affect how an animal responds to a given test.  Some factors include human disturbance and multiple test runs.  I will examine how these two things affect the repeatability of personality tests for boldness and exploration in yellow-bellied marmots.
Subject: Other

ResearchPlanTitle: A comparative study of plant-pollinator interactions on three mine sites in the East River Valley, Colorado
ResearchPlanAbstract: This study will examine the species of plants and pollinating insects along a 50m line from the entrance to three old silver mines around Gothic, attempt to identify a plant species that shows up at all distances from the mine entrance on each site, and study what species of insect pollinate that plant, and how often, as a function of distance from the mine.
ResearchPlanOrganisms: Angiosperm and insect species occurring near the sites of silver mines
Subject: Pollination

ResearchPlanTitle: Butterflies and Climate along an Elevation Gradient
Subject: Climate Change

ResearchPlanTitle: The effect of floral scent manipulations of Ipomopsis aggregata and Polemonium foliosissimum on the behavior of insect visitors and seed predators
ResearchPlanAbstract:
Pollination dynamics represent an essential component of species interaction webs. In order to understand the development and potential future directions of these interactions, It is important to study the ecological and evolutionary impacts of signal traits. However, studies on the relationships between floral characteristics and pollinators have a decided bias towards measurements of visual characteristics like flower color and shape. As a result, the genetics and ecology of these parameters are relatively well studied. The advent of better, more cost-effective technology has allowed an expansion in this field of research to include the effects of floral fragrance.
	The assemblage of floral volatiles (chemical scents) of two related species from the Polemoniaceae (Phlox) family, Ipomopsis aggregata and Polemonium foliosissimum, have recently been analyzed. However, no information is available on the effects of the dominant chemical – pinene – on the behavior of insect visitors to the flowers of these plants. In addition to potential pollinators, Hylemya flies frequent both I. aggregata and P. foliosissimum as host plants for their eggs. This project attempts to measure the effect of augmented pinene treatments on the behavior of both of these insect groups. The results will aid in understanding the role of pinene as a floral fragrance volatile.
ResearchPlanOrganisms:
Ipomopsis aggregata
Polemonium foliosissimum
Hylemia sp.
Bombus sp., solitary bees, flies
Subject: Pollination

ResearchPlanTitle: Hybridization between the invasives Tragopogon pratensis and  T. dubius in the Gunnison Valley
ResearchPlanAbstract: Hybridization can be dangerous in invasive plants because it can create offspring with new genotypes that are more fit than their parent species, and can thus become more aggressively invasive.  Hybridization has recently been occurring between the two invasive plants Tragopogon pratensis and Tragopogon dubius in Gunnison Valley.  Not much is known about the two plants or their hybrid in this area, so I will be conducting a survey of Tragopogon populations around Gunnison Valley to find out where each of the different species are occurring and how frequently.  I will also be planting Tragopogon seeds from each of the parent species and the hybrids at two different elevations of around 8500 and 9800 feet, to see how the different taxa perform at two different altitudes.  Lastly, I will conduct a pollinator experiment:  Whether a pollinator visits only one species or more than one species in its movement can determine how frequently a hybrid is formed.  I will plant five individuals from each parent species in pots and observe the movement of pollinators that visit the flowers in the pots.  If pollinator movement species does not occur often, then that can explain why we do not see many hybrids.  If pollinator movement between species does occur often, then perhaps we are not seeing hybrids very often because the hybrids are not fit and have low survival.
Subject: Other

ResearchPlanTitle: Intraspecific variation of herbaceous angiosperms along an elevation gradient
ResearchPlanAbstract: Intra-specific variation is important because it represents a species capacity to adjust to environmental variability throughout the habitat in which it grows. Recently, there has been a renewed interest in intraspecific variation; however, little is known about how conspecific variation of functional traits may relate to plant community structure. Further, it is still unclear how plant species that express greater variation in functional trait measures perform within and across separate communities. In this study, we will quantify the amount of intraspecific trait variation across several species of herbaceous angiosperms by measuring SLA values, plant height, leaf thickness, and leaf water content. This project will address two prominent hypotheses in functional trait ecology: The first hypothesis states that species that express a higher degree of functional trait variation will compete more effectively within as well as across plant communities. The second hypothesis is that intra-specific trait variation should match variation in interspecific trait variation.
Subject: Climate Change

ResearchPlanTitle: The Effect of Ant Tending on the Fitness of Aphid During and After Colony Establishment
ResearchPlanOrganisms:
Valeriana edulis
Aphis valerianae
Tapinoma sessile
Formica sp.
Subject: Other

ResearchPlanTitle: Fungal endophytes and the evolutionary and ecological divergence of host grasses
ResearchPlanAbstract: Symbiosis has long been considered an important factor in why populations diverge. Lately, positive interaction, in which at least one of the interacting species benefits, has been gaining attention as a mechanism allowing multiple species to coexist and as a process that can lead to genetic divergence. In this study, we will use grasses with fungal endophytes living in them to explore how positive interactions can affect the ecology and evolution of organisms. We will perform crosses of grasses of the same species with and without endophytes to observe these symbionts’ effects on mating preference. In addition, we will compare the niches of grasses with and without endophytes through observations and through experiments in which we manipulate the environment of the plants.
ResearchPlanOrganisms:
Poa leptocoma, Poa reflexa, Festuca thurberi (all are grasses)

Neotyphodium sp., other fungal endophytes of aforementioned grasses
Subject: Other

ResearchPlanTitle: Behavioral Syndromes in yellow-bellied marmots: Is there a correlation between boldness and exploration?
ResearchPlanAbstract: Animal personality typically refers to a behavioral manifestations stable across time and contexts (Sih et al. 2004, Réale et al. 2007). Personality has been shown to shape fitness and population dynamics though such traits as dominance, response to stress, and reproductive performance. Within the personality framework, behavioral syndromes refer to personality traits expressed population-wide  that are  consistent over a variety of contexts (e.g., an individual might be aggressive in mating, feeding, parental care), or correlations between different traits (e.g aggression and boldness) (Réale et al. 2007). Behavioral syndromes can shape the coevolution of traits in a population, and of particular interest are the fitness trade-offs and potentially non-adaptive behavior that may emerge when traits are correlated across contexts. Yellow-bellied marmots (Marmota flaviventris) offer an ideal opportunity to study behavioral syndromes.  Armitage and Van Vuren (2003) demonstrated that yellow-bellied marmots vary along a shy-bold continuum and that these behavioral phenotypes correlate with dispersal, play behaviors, and recruitment success. It remains uninvestigated, however, whether there exists in yellow-bellied marmots a correlation between boldness and novelty-seeking; it is this I intend to investigate.
Subject: Other

ResearchPlanTitle: Effects of species composition change under experimental warming on soil microclimate in a montane meadow.
ResearchPlanAbstract: Documented changes in the plant community under experimental warming in montane meadows could have significant effects under future climate change. The transition from small, green meadow plants like "Fleabane," "Cinquefoil," and "Helianthella" toward more shrubby "Sagebrush" could have effects on the soil microclimate. The purpose of this study is to quantify those vegetation effects on soil temperature and soil moisture.
ResearchPlanOrganisms: Artemisia tridentata, Erigeron speciosus, Potentilla gracilis, Helianthella quinquenervis, and Festuca thurberi.
Subject: Climate Change

ResearchPlanTitle: Trade-offs Associated with Food Availability and Predator Avoidance Behavior
ResearchPlanAbstract: Organisms within Ecosystems must deal with trade-off costs daily. Trade-off costs are universally found in predator prey systems. Prey must graze to obtain food which exposes them to predators. Prey must decide how long to graze, where to graze, and when to graze. Prey must also decide what body size will maximize both their fitness and chance of survival. Baetis bicaudatus is a mayfly species found in both fish and fishless streams which must deal with trade-off costs. Baetis drift from rock to rock in order to find food. This presents a risky situation as brook trout are visual feeders which eat drifting Baetis. Baetis react to this threat by changing life history strategies. In streams containing fish, Baetis forage for food at night and mature at a smaller size. However, it is not known whether food availability or predator presence plays a larger role on Baetis behavior. The overall objective of the study is to manipulate the environment of these mayflies using treatments with or without chemical cues from brook trout and different levels of periphyton in order to determine whether an interaction exists between food availability and predator avoidance behavior.
Subject: Phenology

ResearchPlanTitle: Local adaptation to habitat-specific herbivory levels in Cardamine cordifolia
ResearchPlanAbstract: I will be testing to see if the plant Cardamine cordifolia has been driven to locations of shade from sun because of the insects that feed on them.  Plants in the sun have a higher defense mechanism than plants in the shade because of higher the abundance of insects that feed on them. This change in location might be due to the fact that there is a trade off between higher defenses and better reproduction.  I will test this by using multiple sun and shade common gardens.  I'll put fly larvae into both to see in which (sun or shade) plant it does better.  If it does better in the shade then I will know that plant defenses in the shade from flies who attack them have been lowered.  This may be a type of survival method for the plant.  This is important to study because it will provide data as to why plants change habitat for survival needs.
Subject: Climate Change

ResearchPlanTitle: Causes of predation intensity in an ant/aphid mutualist system
ResearchPlanAbstract:
I will be doing research in understanding how food quality and quantity affects predation and trophic cascades, due to human pollutants altering the Nutrient:Carbon ratio. Predation is an important factor determining the strength of lower trophic levels. I will also test how the strength of the two common generalist predators differ, Crab spider and Seven spotted lady bug
Questions: 1. How does food quality and quantity affect the strength of predation on ant-tended aphids? 2. How does the identity of two common generalist predators affect the strenght of predators on aphids? Hypothesis: 1. Greater quality and quantity of food causes stronger predation. 2. Spiders will reduce aphid abundance.
ResearchPlanOrganisms: Western Thatching ant(Formica obscuripes),Seven-spotted ladybug (Coccinella septempunctata), Crab spider (Thomisidae)
Subject: Other

ResearchPlanTitle: The effects of phenology on the reproductive success of Delphinium nuttallianum.
ResearchPlanAbstract: The goal of this study is to investigate the impact of manipulated phenology on the reproductive success of Delphinium nuttallianum via its interactions with pollinators, nectar robbers and herbivores. I will be changing the phenology of D. nuttallianum by manipulating snowpack.I have 20 plots which are divided into four groups: snow addition, snow removal, disturbance control and true control. I have selected 6 plants within each plot, although my unit of replication will be the plot itself and thus the mean of the surviving plants in each plot. I will be monitoring the effects of this changed snow melt time on the interactions between D. nuttallianum and its pollinators, nectar-robbers, and herbivores. I will also collect fruit from the plant in order to count the number of seeds it produces and thereby measure the reproductive success of each plant.
ResearchPlanOrganisms: Delphinium nuttallianum; Bombus (nevadensis, californicus, appositus, and flavifrons); Selasphorus platycercusseveral.
Subject: Phenology

ResearchPlanTitle: Evaluating the mycorrhizal associations of Polemonium foliosissimum, and observing for differing responses to herbivory
ResearchPlanAbstract: In this observation and experiment, I will be evaluating the relationship between a plant species, Polemonium foliosissimum, and it's mycorrhizal symbionts.  Mycorrhizae are soil fungi that inhabit the roots of plants and extract nutrients from the soil to exchange with the plants for photosynthetic products.
Subject: Other

ResearchPlanTitle: Range Responses to Climate Disruption by Avian Species at Altitudinal Gradients
ResearchPlanAbstract: Climate disruption can cause dramatic changes in species’ ranges, potentially escalating into local and complete extinction. Range shifts related to climate disruption have been observed in numerous taxa, both towards the poles and higher altitudes. Studies examining changes in avian species' altitudinal ranges are few and far between. Montane studies are advantageous for the studying future changes at latitudinal gradients with considerable efficiency. I will ask whether changes in the avian community of the southern Rocky Mountains are consistent with the predictions of climate disruption. To answer this question, I will perform a retroanalysis of Gothic Breeding Bird Survey data collected over the past thirteen years. In addition, I will design and implement a protocol for point-count surveys at multiple points along an elevational gradient. If monitoring continues, the insights achieved from the Gothic Breeding Bird Survey will be given greater power.
ResearchPlanOrganisms: Avian species of the southern Rocky Mountains
Subject: Climate Change

ResearchPlanTitle: Biotic Factors Influencing Feeding Preferences of Scaptomyza nigrita (Drosophilidae) on Host Plant Cardamine cordifolia (Brassicaceae)
ResearchPlanAbstract: Biotic stress factors may influence adult female Scaptomyza nigrita, a vinegar fly to have feeding preferences towards its host plant Cardamine cordifolia when certain defense mechanisms are activated by biotic stress from organisms feeding on them. The influence of biotic stress on C. cordifolia causes either one of two plant hormonal pathways to be activated. The induction of either pathway my resulting in less or more feeding conducted by S. nigrita.
ResearchPlanOrganisms: Scaptomyza nigrita, bacteria, and Cardamine cordifolia
Subject: Other

ResearchPlanTitle: Investigating Patterns and Proximate Causes of Juvenile Dispersal In Golden-Mantled Ground Squirrels
ResearchPlanAbstract: Dispersal is a common behavioral phenomenon among animals and typically male-biased in mammals. It is when an individual leaves its birthplace in search of another location; exploratory excursions usually precede dispersal. This behavior has not yet been explored with the golden-mantled ground squirrel (Spermophilus lateralis), so it would be beneficial to have this information to use as a model in other studies or in conservation. I will track the female and male pups and see how far they explore each day before they disperse. In this population of ground squirrels, some females disperse and some remain near their natal area. It is possible that the females who stay have stronger affiliative relationships with their mothers. I will be observing maternal-pup interactions to determine if and how these relationships are formed: I expect that female pups with a higher proportion of affliliative interactions with their mothers will be less likely to disperse away from their natal area. So I will test whether or not males travel farther than females and if more males disperse more than females. I will also test whether or not female pups with more positive interactions are less likely to disperse.
Subject: Other

ResearchPlanTitle: Indirect Effects of The Co-Pathogens of Cardmine coridoflia, Pseudomonas syringae and Scaptomyza nigrita
ResearchPlanAbstract: Cardamine Cordifolia is affected by many pathogens. Two of these pathogens include the herbivorous fly Scaptomyza nigrita, and the bacteria Pseudomonas syringae. This experiment will analyze the effects that these to pathogens have on each others fitness.
ResearchPlanOrganisms: Cardamine cordifolia, Scaptomyza nigrita, and Pseudomonas syringae
Subject: Other

ResearchPlanTitle: Paleoclimate reconstruction from leaf venation networks
ResearchPlanAbstract: Climate is a key determinant of plant form and function, but a strong mechanistic linkage between these factors remains lacking. Leaf venation networks may provide a solution, because they constrain carbon and water fluxes that determine plant performance and fitness in different climates. Fossil leaves often preserve details of leaf veins - thus a model based on leaf venation network physiology could provide accurate fine-scale estimates of climate. I test two hypotheses: first, that leaf-controlled water supply is matched to climate-controlled water demand, and second, that leaf vein density can be optimally matched to climate independent of evolutionary history or constraint. These hypotheses then yield quantitative predictions via a model that links community-mean leaf vein density to temperature, aridity and carbon dioxide. I test this model in two modern floras and then reconstruct 4.6Myr of paleotemperature at 21 points spanning the Cretaceous-Tertiary boundary.
ResearchPlanOrganisms: Populus tremuloides and other angiosperm plants
Subject: Climate Change

ResearchPlanTitle: The effect of decreased snowpack on net ecosystem exchange in a subalpine meadow
ResearchPlanAbstract: Climate scientists predict that the intermountain west will see less precipitation as snow and faster melting snow in the spring. This means a longer growing season for subalpine meadows, but it also means changing water dynamics. Will less snow and earlier snowmelt dates lead to an increase or decrease of this important but susceptible carbon sink? I aim to answer this question using a snow manipulation which will allow me to change growing season length and available water, while keeping temperature constant.
Subject: Climate Change

ResearchPlanTitle: Behavioral and evolutionary ecology studies of mammals and birds at the RMBL
ResearchPlanAbstract: I study the evolutionary ecology of marmots, deer and birds. Marmot studies are now in their 50th year, making the RMBL marmots a priceless window into the effects of climate change as well as a priceless demographic record. In addition to these topics, we study a variety of behavioral and ecological traits that have survival consequences. With deer and birds, I study the evolutionary ecology of fear. I focus on antipredator behavior because much can be learned from simple behavioral experiments that shed light not only on fundamental issues, but also those with some practical relevance (e.g., how do humans influence risk assessment in animals and what's the spatial distribution of those impacts).
Subject: Long-Term

ResearchPlanTitle: Integrating behavior and ecology of the burying beetle.
ResearchPlanAbstract: I have a long-term research project on the behaviors and population dynamics of the burying beetle Nicrophorus investigator and have conducted a variety of field experiments on their reproduction, including mating and parental care behaviors, and ecology. There are five areas of research that I am particularly interested in pursuing: 1) predicting the duration and extent of parental care; 2) understanding the evolution of sperm storage and multiple broods; 3) understanding the fitness benefits of alternative mating strategies in males and females, 4) understanding the interactions between beetles and their phoretic mites, and 5) using environmental variables to predict rodent abundance, beetle abundance, and community dynamics in the burying beetle assemblage. I use a variety of research techniques including: behavioral observations, population censuses, molecular genetic techniques and GIS to detect patterns of gene flow and parentage, isotopic analyses to detect species interactions.
ResearchPlanOrganisms:
Nicrophorus investigator, N. defodiens, N. guttula and their mites.
Microtus montanus, Peromyscus maniculatus, Zapus princeps, Tamias minimus,  Thomomys talpoides, Spermophilus lateralis.
Subject: Long-Term

ResearchPlanTitle: Abiotic factors affecting plant and pollinator phenology, and the role of phenology in plant-pollinator interactions.
ResearchPlanAbstract: Phenology is an important life history trait that can dramatically affect fitness, survival and species interactions. In high altitude meadows, snowmelt is the principle environmental cue triggering spring flowering. The factors affecting pollinator emergence, however, are much less understood, making it difficult to assess how climate change could affect the temporal overlap of plants with their pollinators. In addition, changes in flowering plant reproduction due to altered phenology have been observed, but the factors driving these changes have not been thoroughly investigated. The goal of this study is to investigate the mechanisms by which altered phenology affects plant fitness, and to assess the likelihood of phenological mismatches between plants and their pollinators.
ResearchPlanOrganisms: Flowering plants: Potentilla pulcherrima (Rosaceae), Erigeron speciosus (Asteraceae), Delphinium nuttallianum (Ranunculaceae), and Claytonia lanceoliata (Portulacaceae). Ground nesting bees: I have marked out a field site that I suspect contains nests from the following genera: Andrena (Andrenidae), Halictus (Halictidae) and Lasioglossum (Halictidae). The exact taxa within this site will not be known, however, until after emergence.
Subject: Phenology

ResearchPlanTitle: How Bees see it: selection on floral ultraviolet patterns in silverweed cinquefoil (Argentina anserina)
ResearchPlanAbstract: Pollinators see flowers in a different light than humans. In particular they see in the UV spectrum and can ascertain ‘hidden’ patterns on flowers that go undetected by our eyes. While the maintenance of intraspecific flower color variation has been, and still is, a major field of study, patterns in the UV spectrum are little understood. Flower patterns in the UV spectrum differ between individuals that show no apparent variation in the visible spectrum such that floral diversity can be much greater than we think. These patterns have long been thought to have evolved in response to pollinators. For example, a widespread ‘bull’s eye’ pattern of UV-absorption at the center of a flower is though to function as a landing pad for pollinators and increase a plant’s reproductive fitness. Alternatively, the chemicals that absorb UV and give rise to these visual patterns may protect the plant’s reproductive parts from harmful UV radiation that is damaging to pollen and photosynthetic machinery. My research aims to describe floral variation in the UV spectrum using UV photography, and understand how UV patterns can influence plant fitness through protection from UV radiation and though pollinator attraction. At RMBL I will utilize the altitudinal and associated UV gradient to not only describe patterns in variation, but experimentally test selective mechanisms on floral UV traits in the circumboreal perennial herb, silverweed cinquefoil (Argentina anserina). UV floral traits are a relatively unexplored source of floral variation and understanding potential selective processes that have given rise to this variation will give evolutionary biologists a more holistic view of floral evolution. Furthermore, understanding whether the UV environment selects for floral UV traits will be important to predict phenotypic shifts in response to globally increasing UV irradiance.
Subject: Pollination

ResearchPlanTitle: Evaluating the invisible: defining bees preferences for UV patterning in flower petals.
ResearchPlanAbstract: Many flowering plant species have cues on their petals that are important for pollinators busy selecting which flower to visit and where to find a nectar or pollen reward. In Virginia, my lab group has experimentally altered the ultraviolet cues that are found naturally on black eyed susan petals. We have determined that bees prefer big ultraviolet cues over little ones, and solid ultraviolet patterns over disrupted ones. Bees are important pollinators globally and they are declining in numbers for a multitude of reasons. Simultaneously, climate variation is affecting plant blooming patterns and survival in alpine communities like the one at RMBL. The showy goldeneye is a very common flowering plant in alpine communities like RMBL. We want to broaden our research and determine whether what we have seen in black eyed susans is actually a more general phenomenon by asking questions with showy goldeneys such as, "Do bees prefer flowers with larger ultraviolet cues over smaller ones?"
Subject: Pollination

ResearchPlanTitle: Variation in herbivory between habitats in Ligusticum porteri (Apiaceae)
ResearchPlanAbstract: Why do we have a green world? Plants cannot run away from the things that like to eat them, and there are any number of herbivores for any given plant species, including humans. My work seeks to unravel why herbivory varies with habitat for Ligusticum porteri; this species is commonly known as 'bear root' and is also collected as a medicinal herb. In addition to human harvesters, aphids and caterpillars target L.porteri in the aspen understories and open meadows where this species is found. Aphid colonies are much more common in open meadows, while the opposite is true for caterpillars. My research examines the role of habitat, genotype and species-interactions in explaining this pattern.
ResearchPlanOrganisms:
Plant: Ligusticum porteri
Aphid: Cavariella aegopodii
Subject: Other

ResearchPlanTitle: Native and non-native red fox populations in Colorado.
ResearchPlanAbstract: The native Rocky Mountain red fox (Vulpes vulpes macroura)is considered to be restricted to high elevations by specialized adaptations or interspecific competition. However, there is no published research concerning the ecology or conservation status of the native Rocky Mountain red fox which was only recently confirmed in Colorado(2009). This population of native red foxes faces the same challenges that other extinct species faced that were restricted by specialized adaptations to high elevations, such as elevational shifts in vegetation, decrease in range, and asynchronous availability of food and habitat resources; all of which are factors attributed to climate change. Additionally, it is believed that the non-native red fox (Vulpes vulpes), generally of Eurasian origins, could negatively impact the native red fox in a number of ways, including displacement or hybridization, that may lead to the loss of special adaptive genes correlated to the harsh high elevation environment. Colorado law does not distinguish between native and exotic red fox, and trapping remains legal. With stressors like the possible encroachment of exotic red foxes from the lower elevations, and landscape changes in higher elevations caused by climate change, research is needed to understand the Colorado red fox population’s native, non-native, and/or hybrid composition, size, and distribution. To analyze such information, I propose to collect genetic material from the red fox populations along a transect that extends approximately 190km from Crested Butte to Denver. In addition to using standard genetic methods to determine genetic diversity, population connectivity, and effective population size, I will use GIS mapping to analyze the relationship between genetic results and landscape features. Ascertaining such information is critical to establish effective conservation and management practices, appropriate to the red fox lineage.
ResearchPlanOrganisms: Native Rocky Mountain red fox (Vulpes vulpes macroura) and non-native red fox (Vulpes vulpes)
Subject: Other

ResearchPlanTitle: Linking spatial genetic differentiation to animal-mediated pollen dispersal in Ipomopsis aggregata
ResearchPlanAbstract: Animal-mediated gene flow has important evolutionary consequences for plant populations. Gene flow via pollen or seed dispersal can maintain genetic diversity within populations, slow local adaptation, or decrease divergence. However, it is difficult to directly assess geographic patterns of animal-mediated pollen movement, and even harder to determine how this translates into gene flow at different spatial scales, due to the near impossibility of following long flights of pollinators. I will use genetic techniques to determine the mechanisms that explain the observed levels of genetic differentiation in populations of Ipomopsis aggregata. Last summer I extensively sampled populations of I. aggregata in the geographic area around RMBL, obtaining leaf tissue from over 800 individuals. I am currently determining levels of differentiation among geographic areas separated by as little as 0.2 km and as much as 50 km. The research I will conduct this summer will allow me to link patterns of genetic differentiation in I. aggregata to the relative contributions of different pollinators to gene flow at different spatial scales.
ResearchPlanOrganisms: Ipomopsis aggregata, bumble bees (genus Bombus), and hummingbirds (Selasphorus platycercus and S. rufus)
Subject: Pollination

ResearchPlanTitle: RMBL Environmental Education Program 2012
ResearchPlanAbstract: This research plan outlines the EE program at RMBL in 2012.
Subject: Other

ResearchPlanTitle: A Long-Term Study of Molluscan-Trematode Communities in Gunnison County, CO
ResearchPlanAbstract: There have been few studies documenting the changes in trematode parasite abundance and diversity in aquatic snails (their first host) over long time periods (50+ years) and no studies of this kind in the Western United States. This project allows comparison of present-day snail infection levels to extremely detailed data collected over 50 years ago at RMBL. The first year data were collected (August 2010) it was found that Grant Lake had higher trematode prevalence (74%) than it had had any year previous. However, in 2011 Grant Lake only had a trematode prevalence of 12%, possibly due to the late snow-melt date. If, as suggested, spring warming at lower elevations and latitudes happened ahead of snow melt at higher elevations, north-bound spring migrants would have had no choice but to bypass higher elevation staging areas (such as RMBL) due to a lack of available habitat and forage. Snail species have also shifted in these ponds with disturbance-adapted species (Physa) increasing while less-adapted species (Lymnaea and Helisoma) have been reduced. It has also been discovered that in some habitats larval leaches infest the majority of the snails, possibly leading to snail population crashes. Taking these new data into account, it is necessary to collect one more year's worth of data to (1) test if differential climate change between low and high elevations is responsible for year to year differences in trematode prevalence in a way that was not present in the past data and (2) conform this study as closely as possible to the past study by collecting three years worth of data comparing 1957, 1958, and 1959 to 2010, 2011, and 2012.
ResearchPlanOrganisms: various trematode parasites within aquatic snails of the genus Physa, Lymnaea, and Gyraulus
Subject: Long-Term

ResearchPlanTitle: How do functional differences associated with clone size, gender, and landscape position influence aspen’s water relations and resilience to drought?
ResearchPlanAbstract: While links between Sudden Aspen Decline and drought are becoming clear, our understanding of the biological mechanisms underlying Sudden Aspen Decline are not well understood. At RMBL, I will investigate how functional differences associated with clone size, gender, and landscape position influence aspen’s water relations and resilience to drought.
Subject: Climate Change

ResearchPlanTitle: Co-dominant plant species effects on community dynamics and ecosystem function
ResearchPlanAbstract: Dominant plant species have been shown to influence community structure and ecosystem function such as net primary productivity and carbon cycling. Dominant parasitic plants can exert even stronger impacts on plant communities and ecosystem function resulting from greater resource utilization from their neighbors. I propose to examine the impacts of co-dominant parasitic plants in the genus Castilleja on the structure and function of alpine meadow ecosystems along an elevational gradient. I predict that the effects of Castilleja species on community dynamics and ecosystem function will vary across elevation given strong variation in both biotic (plant composition) and abiotic (temperature and precipitation) factors.
Subject: Climate Change

ResearchPlanTitle: Collaborative studies of plant population dynamics
Subject: Other

ResearchPlanTitle: Insect community ecology
ResearchPlanAbstract: I plan to collect data on three insect communities and their associated plants, looking at the networks of interacting species and how they change over elevational gradients or other ecological gradients. For the first, I will record the occurrence of galls on the stems and leaves of Gambel oak trees. I am also interested in how these insect communities respond after major disturbances to the oaks, such as fires and spring freezes. Second, I will record the presence of tephritid flies in the seed heads of different species of daisies and sunflowers, looking at how the communities of seed predators is affected by the local plant community. Third, I will be working regionally, although not locally, on insects that feed on the invasive nodding thistle, particularly two beetle species that have been introduced for biological control of this pest. Because nodding thistle does not occur in the RMBL area, I am not including details for that project.
ResearchPlanOrganisms:
Gambel oak (Quercus gambelii) and the various species of Cynipid wasps that induce galls on these oaks. 
Tephritid flies that are seed predators of daisies (Erigeron spp).
Subject: Other

ResearchPlanTitle: Context-dependence of interspecific interactions and ecosystem function in a warmed world
ResearchPlanAbstract: How do the environment and the community of plant species influence one another? Are plants competing for resources like light and minerals, or are they helping each other by sheltering each other from the weather? How does carbon move through an ecosystem? I am examining how the answers to those questions change as you move through different ecosystems in space, or change the environmental conditions at any individual location. The mountains around RMBL set the stage for this experiment by providing many distinct environments that vary widely as elevation changes. At multiple sites along a mountain slope, I will be constructing miniature open-top greenhouses to simulate increased temperature, and removing the dominant plant species to gain insight into how plant species interact under different climate conditions. Over several years, I will measure plant growth and how carbon moves through the soil. I predict that the changes in plant communities induced by warming will have an effect on ecosystem carbon storage beyond the direct effect of warming itself, and that the different types of plant interactions that prevail at different elevations will determine how plants respond to warming and the presence of dominant species.
ResearchPlanOrganisms: Common plant species of open meadows at various elevations
Subject: Climate Change

ResearchPlanTitle: Testing for mechanistic and evolutionary links between changing climates and biological responses: the effects of warming winters on insect overwintering physiology.
ResearchPlanAbstract: Our global climates are rapidly changing, and both policy and scientific consensus call for concentrated efforts to document and predict biological responses. Both average summer and winter temperatures have increased over the last 30 – 50 years, and temperature has profound effects on organismal biology and population dynamics. Though current models have substantially improved our ability to predict changes in species ranges and distributions, mechanistic and evolutionary links between organisms and changing climates represent a major gap in our knowledge that limits precise and long-term forecasting. We propose to initiate a study of the relationship between warming temperatures and physiology in high altitude butterfly populations in Colorado, including an analysis of evolutionary potential. Our proposed work will test 1) whether winter warming negatively affects overwinter survival mediated through metabolic physiology and life cycle timing (establishing a mechanistic link between organism and environment), and 2) whether populations harbor variation in overwintering physiology that may evolve in response to warming winters (establishing evolutionary potential). This study will address one additional, unresolved problem in climate change biology. Changes in temperature affect organisms differently in summer versus the winter, and we currently lack studies that examine biological effects in both seasons. Our proposed study will parallel a study by collaborators examining the effects of warming summers on growth and reproductive physiology in the same field populations. Combined, our studies will provide the first glimpse at biological responses to climate change across an entire year.
Subject: Climate Change

ResearchPlanTitle: Timing of reproduction in golden-mantled ground squirrels: causes, consequences, and implications for climate change
ResearchPlanAbstract: Mammals living in high-altitude environments must time their reproduction carefully so that offspring are born when food is available. For hibernating squirrels, food does not become available in the spring until melting snow stimulates growth of green vegetation, hence these squirrels often must emerge from hibernation and mate before the snow melts. However, we don’t know what cues females use to anticipate the time of snow melt, in order to determine the correct time to mate, and we don’t know what the consequences are for females that mate too late or too early. This study proposes to address both questions. The results will not only increase our understanding of how mammals adapt to the strong seasonality of high-altitude environments, but it also may enhance our understanding of the effects of climate change. Scientists fear that one consequence of warming temperatures is that the cues that animals use to anticipate seasonal events may no longer accurately predict those events.
Subject: Long-Term

ResearchPlanTitle: Dwarfs on purpose: Comparative ecological genetics of adaptation in the high elevation endemic Mimulus tilingii
ResearchPlanAbstract: A major goal in evolutionary biology is to understand how organisms adapt to novel or changing environments. A particularly dramatic example of ecological specialization in plants involves alpine endemics, which have evolved characteristic suites of adaptations in response to similar selective regimes. We are investigating the ecological and genomic basis of this common ecological transition to alpine environments using the mountain monkeyflower, Mimulus tilingii. In contrast to the widely-distributed, lowland progenitor species Mimulus guttatus, Mimulus tilingii populations are confined to alpine regions throughout western North America, in discrete “habitat islands.” These populations provide a unique set of replicate evolutionary experiments for how Mimulus tilingii has adapted to common ecological influences imposed by alpine environments. Preliminary analyses indicate that there have been at least three evolutionary origins of Mimulus tilingii in the Cascades, Sierra Nevadas, and Olympic Mountain ranges. I am now proposing to expand my sampling to include populations in the Rocky Mountains, which will provide a geographically distinct evolutionary lineage for future comparative studies for how Mimulus populations have diverged in response to similar ecological conditions.
ResearchPlanOrganisms: Mimulus tilingii and potentially Mimulus guttatus
Subject: Other

ResearchPlanTitle: Implications of pollen harvesting by bees for plant-pollinator community interactions.
ResearchPlanAbstract: A critical, yet often overlooked component of plant-pollinator interactions is pollen harvesting by bees. For bees, pollen comprises the exclusive food resource used to successfully raise larval offspring. For plants, pollination is necessary for sexual reproduction. Without pollen resources for bees, and without pollination services for plants, many bee and plant populations would suffer from decreased reproduction. Recent studies have revealed that the pollen requirements of bees can be substantial. Because of this, pollen harvesting can result in the removal of huge amounts of pollen from plant populations that would otherwise be available for pollination. To date, relatively little attention has been paid to the importance of pollen harvesting by bees and its implications for plant-pollinator interactions at the community scale. With this research, I will use artificial trap-nests to attract common solitary bees in order to ask three primary questions: (1) what species of pollen are bees harvesting at RMBL, (2) how much pollen is being harvested by bees, and (3) what is the availability of pollen resources? This information will provide me with the baseline data necessary to carry out future detailed study of the importance of pollen harvesting in order to fill in key gaps and greatly improve our current understanding of plant-pollinator community interactions.
Subject: Pollination

ResearchPlanTitle: Bacterial Influences on Plant-Insect Interactions in the Wild
ResearchPlanAbstract: Most plants on earth harbor bacteria in or on their leaves, though scientists are only beginning to understand the many ways they affect their plant hosts. Many bacteria are known to cause disease in plants, while others can help plants by bolstering the plant immune system against other pathogens. But it is difficult to predict how any given bacterial species will behave when put into a leaf because plant-associated bacteria can be so diverse. In addition to various bacteria living in their leaves, plants must also face a plethora of insect herbivores capable of consuming large amounts of leaf tissue. One native plant in particular, heart-leaf bittercress (Cardamine cordifolia), is fed on by an herbivorous fly, Scaptomyza nigrita, as well as several species of bacteria within the genus Pseudomonas. These flies feed only on this single plant species, and their larval offspring develop within the leaves. Thus, the flies can be strongly affected by other factors—including bacterial infection--that influence the health of their host plant. My previous research at RMBL showed in the laboratory that Pseudomonas bacteria are capable of affecting the choices that adult Scaptomyza flies make when seeking a host plant, as well as stunting the growth of developing fly larvae within Pseudomonas infected plants. This summer, I propose to ask several questions to help understand how leaf bacteria affect the interactions between plants and their insect herbivores under field conditions. What types of Pseudomonas bacteria are found on Cardamine plants, and do these bacteria occur on other plant species in the area? Does Pseudomonas infection in Cardamine plants in the field affect the attractiveness of the plants to the flies, and are the plants more or less negatively impacted by the combination of bacteria and flies, versus flies or bacteria alone? Through seeking answers to these questions, I hope to reach a deeper understanding the ways unseen bacteria are distributed across plant species and how they might play a role in shaping the outcome of plant-insect interactions.
ResearchPlanOrganisms:
Scaptomyza nigrita (Diptera; Drosophilidae)
Heart-leaf bittercress, Cardamine cordifolia (Brassicaceae)
Various species of Pseudomonas leaf-associated bacteria, cultured from C. cordifolia and other flowering plant species sympatric with this plant (to be determned).
Subject: Other

ResearchPlanTitle: Soil Geomorphology and Landscape Evolution of the Upper East River Watershed
ResearchPlanAbstract: Soils are an important interface between geology and biology; however, very little is known about the soils around RMBL. Soil development is a function of climatic conditions, biological activity, local relief, aspect, parent material, and the amount of time sediments are exposed at or near the surface. Combined with an understanding of surficial processes, soil stratigraphy aids in the subdivision of the local succession of deposits and correlation of unconsolidated sediments. The distribution and properties of soil stratigraphic units can be used to evaluate landform evolution and age, landform stability, surface processes and even past climates. Potential research questions: What are the dominant relationships between soil and sediment properties with elevation, slope, aspect, rock type, or the relative age of surficial deposits? Is there a correlation between soil properties and dominant vegetation patterns? What is the late Quaternary history of landscape change in this environment?
ResearchPlanOrganisms: None. Soils and hillslope or fluvial sedimentary deposits.
Subject: Climate Change

ResearchPlanTitle: Pollinator losses and plant function: An assessment of pollination network resilience in the face of climate change.
ResearchPlanAbstract: Global climate change (GCC) is projected to cause dramatic shifts in many ecological processes, disrupting ecosystem services and directly threatening pollination interactions. GCC is likely to disrupt the overlap in seasonal timing (i.e., phenology) of flowering production and of pollinator emergence/foraging activity, leading to potentially mismatched interactions between both plants and animals. Recent work based on pollination networks suggests that pollination interactions will be highly resilient to ongoing environmental change because pollination networks are dominated by generalist interactions. I hypothesize that networks are much less resilient to perturbations. These predictions are based on assumptions that all interactions in the network are positive; meaning every visit from a pollinator to a plant is beneficial, an assumption known to be false. My dissertation research, based in both empirical and modeling techniques, will help evaluate whether existing pollinator network analyses that are based just on visitation rates, provide robust models for evaluating impacts of global climate change on pollinator services, or whether incorporating additional information on the importance of pollinator fidelity and plant reproductive success provide different predictions.
Subject: Climate Change

ResearchPlanTitle: Do differences in density and duration of cattle grazing alter plant, arthropod and soil communities and effect carbon cycling?
ResearchPlanAbstract: Rangelands make up to 70% of land around the world and provide valuable economic, societal, and ecological benefits. Therefore, how we manage these rangelands can have significant impacts on ecosystem services including biodiversity and soil carbon storage. Balancing yield (grazer biomass) with goals like maintaining biodiversity and increasing carbon storage belowground are increasingly becoming management goals in the western US. My work will examine how different grazing intensities (number of cattle per area per day) impacts biodiversity of plant, insect, and soil communities as well as plant cover and soil carbon content.
Subject: Other

ResearchPlanTitle: Evolutionary Ecology and Conservation Biology of Amphibians
ResearchPlanAbstract: Using tiger salamanders as a model system, my research has two main thrusts: understanding the evolutionary ecology of trait variation, and answering fundamental questions in conservation biology. My evolutionary ecology research is aimed at understanding how variation in important traits is maintained in natural populations, how environmental conditions influence the expression and evolution of trait variation, and the ecological consequence of this variation. I study tiger salamanders, which exhibit two distinct polymorphisms in which the “morphs” or forms are induced by different environmental cues. By following several populations of salamanders in the field, I am gaining unique insight into the ecology and evolution of these life history polymorphisms. One component of my conservation biology research is understanding the mechanisms controlling population fluctuations in salamander populations. By determining the factors affecting such dynamics in tiger salamanders, we should gain insight into the general conditions regulating other animal populations, and perhaps learn ways to distinguish natural population fluctuations from declines. Another conservation focus is understanding the distribution of chytrid fungus in tiger salamanders, because they act as sentinel species for the management of other amphibians. By determining the distribution of chytrid in salamander populations, we can better understand how to conserve and restore threatened amphibians, such as boreal toads and leopard frogs, which are more susceptible to this fungus that salamanders. My research thus has direct implications for ecological and evolutionary theory as well as conservation and management.
ResearchPlanOrganisms: Ambystoma tigrinum nebulosum (no matter what the state legislature says).
Subject: Long-Term

ResearchPlanTitle: Ecology and evolution of plant-insect-microbial interactions using bittercress, leafmining flies and endophytic bacteria as a model.
ResearchPlanAbstract: A classic study at the RMBL by Svata Louda and colleagues showed that natural enemies of plants, herbivorous insects in particular, can drive the distributions of their hosts plants into the shade of spruce and willow trees. Here, we revisit this classic system and will test whether plants are locally adapted to sun and shade habitats, if the tradeoff defenses and growth in the context of light environment. We will use classic field ecological tools, greenhouse studies, quantitative genetics studies and population genomics. In addition a second study aims to determine how a third player, leaf-dwelling bacteria that are important pests of crop plants, may influence a plant's susceptibility to attack by the leafmining flies, and how the flies influence the plant's susceptibility to attack by the bacteria. Studies such as these are rare in relatively pristine environments and this is one of the first of its kind on a system that has had the time to co-evolve over long periods of time.
ResearchPlanOrganisms:
Cardamine cordifolia (Brassicaceae)
Scaptomyza nigrita (Drosophilidae)
Pseudomonas spp. bacteria (Pseudomonaceae)
Subject: Other

ResearchPlanTitle: Direct versus indirect affects of global climate change on plant-pollinator mutualisms
ResearchPlanAbstract: Rising temperatures and earlier snowpack melting due to climate change have been linked to alterations in the distribution, phenology, growth, and reproduction of many plants and animals. As individual species respond in different ways to climate change, ecological relationships, such as those between plants and pollinators, will change as well, thereby altering community composition, ecosystem functioning, and increasing the risk of species extinctions. Changes in snowpack melting in response to climatic shifts are likely to alter the phenology of plants and also influence water availability in the soil at any given point during the growing season. This may have important consequences for plant populations. I intend to investigate what impact water availability has on the pollination and subsequent reproductive success of the tall fringed bluebell, Mertensia ciliata (Boraginaceae). I will conduct a water manipulation experiment on M. ciliata populations using a randomized block design with water addition, water removal, and control treatments. I will collect data on plant and floral traits, pollinator visitation, and seed set. Using these data, I will assess the extent to which variation in water availability impacts M. ciliata plant performance and floral rewards and whether this has any indirect effect on pollination and seed set. Moreover, these data will form the foundation of my dissertation research investigating how plant-pollinator mutualisms are responding to changing environmental resources due to climate change.
Subject: Climate Change

ResearchPlanTitle: Baetis parasitism in a changing environment
ResearchPlanAbstract: The ecology of parasitism in streams has received slight attention, even for very common species. For example, Baetis mayflies, which are abundant, strong interactors in high-elevation streams of the western USA, are parasitized by mermithid nematodes that have potential to cause high mortality rates and mediate interactions of Baetis with food resources, competitors and predators. Although abundant, Baetis may be vulnerable to direct and indirect effects of climate change on the high-elevation environment, including higher prevalence of parasites associated with warming water and periodic drought conditions. Because Baetis is both a highly efficient herbivore and important prey for stream predators, its response to environmental change could affect other components of the stream community. A key to understanding the fate of Baetis in altered ecosystems will be elucidating effects of the â€œhand in the puppetâ€â€”a parasite with the potential to infect > 25% of individuals and to mediate nearly every ecological interaction in which its host participates. This study proposes to test for effects of mermithid parasitism on populations and community interactions of Baetis mayfly hosts, emphasizing trophic processes in the context of environmental change. Through complementary experiments and field observations, we will document causes and consequences of parasitism for important biological interactions of its hosts, including: 1) Baetis population growth; 2) interactions of Baetis with its predators; 3) the potential for closely related Baetis species to compete for food; 4) effects of encroaching distributions of the nuisance diatom Didymo (which may increase parasitism) and brown trout (which may consume more Baetis than typical predators); and 5) the accumulation of pollutants in parasites and their Baetis hosts.
Subject: Climate Change

ResearchPlanTitle: Scaling long-term functional attributes of plants, communities, and ecosystems: Responses to climate change across elevational gradients:
ResearchPlanAbstract: An important question in ecology is to understand how specific traits of species influence the functioning of ecosystems. This study is designed to forge links between variation in the physical environment (e.g., changes in temperature and precipitation with elevation), changes in how plants and ecosystems work. Specifically, variation in functional measures of plants (plant size, leaf morphology and physiology etc.) and the functioning of whole ecosystems (the fluxes of carbon and water) characterize how changes in climate influence biology. Connecting how plants work in different environments with variation in ecosystem processes is critical for predicting responses of the biosphere to climate change. The mountainous landscape in and around RMBL provides enormous range of physical conditions, from warm wet meadows to cold, dry ridge tops. The resulting plant communities are likewise both functionally and phylogenetically diverse. I propose to continue monitoring how plant functional diversity and the functioning of whole-ecosystem fluxes vary across a range of elevations and environments and across years ï¿½ spanning from cool wet years to increasingly dryer and hotter years. Our work at RMBL is part of a larger global project. We are continuing to build a global baseline of data by which to compare RMBL data using elevational studies from Arizona, California, Oregon, Mexico, Costa Rica, and Peru. Data from these field studies, combined with data from RMBL, now forms the basis for the development and testing of mechanistic, predictive models linking the functional attributes of organisms to large scale processes in plant communities and ecosystems.
Subject: Climate Change

ResearchPlanTitle: Linking spatial patterns of pollinator foraging to pollination in communities
ResearchPlanAbstract: As most flowering plants rely on animals to disperse pollen among flowers, reproduction for plants will reflect pollinator foraging patterns, which will vary with many pollinator and plant attributes. As an example, all flowering plants are patchily distributed in space and occur in communities in which they share pollinators with other plants. Pollinators will forage in ways that reflect economical foraging decisions bound by memory and learning constraints. So pollinators’ foraging decisions in these patchy resource environments with many species will affect the pollination service they provide to plants. Local patterns of pollinator foraging and some reproductive consequences for plants are fairly well known, however, we know little about foraging patterns at broader scales, such as pollinator responses to the spatial distribution of multiple species, particularly at an individual-pollinator level. These peculiarities in pollinator foraging have been given little attention and mean that the ecological context of a plant will influence its reproductive success in ways not considered before. I aim to highlight the importance of considering broader spatial scales when examining pollinator foraging responses in plant communities and the effects on plant reproduction. Specifically, I propose to investigate, (1) if interactions between pollinator sharing plants are scale-dependent and can extend over broad distances, and (2) the importance of plant spatial distribution in governing the direction of interactions between pollinator sharing plant species.
ResearchPlanOrganisms: Delphinium barbeyi, Gentianopsis detonsa, Gentiana parryi, and medium- and long-tongued Bombus spp.
Subject: Pollination
