ResearchPlanTitle: Metabolic costs of warm winters in Colias butterflies
ResearchPlanAbstract: Our global climates are rapidly changing, and both policy and scientific consensus call for concentrated efforts to document and predict biological responses. Both average summer and winter temperatures have increased over the last 30 â€“ 50 years, and temperature has profound effects on organismal biology and population dynamics. Though current models have substantially improved our ability to predict changes in species ranges and distributions, mechanistic and evolutionary links between organisms and changing climates represent a major gap in our knowledge that limits precise and long-term forecasting. We propose to initiate a study of the relationship between warming temperatures and physiology in high altitude butterfly populations in Colorado, including an analysis of evolutionary potential. Our proposed work will test 1) whether winter warming negatively affects overwinter survival mediated through metabolic physiology and life cycle timing (establishing a mechanistic link between organism and environment), and 2) whether populations harbor variation in overwintering physiology that may evolve in response to warming winters (establishing evolutionary potential). This study will address one additional, unresolved problem in climate change biology. Changes in temperature affect organisms differently in summer versus the winter, and we currently lack studies that examine biological effects in both seasons. Our proposed study will parallel a study by collaborators examining the effects of warming summers on growth and reproductive physiology in the same field populations. Combined, our studies will provide the first glimpse at biological responses to climate change across an entire year.
Subject: Climate Change

ResearchPlanTitle: Dendroecological reconstruction of alpine treeline dynamics
ResearchPlanAbstract: The alpine treeline ecotone â€”the interface between closed-canopy subalpine forest and alpine tundraâ€”is a dynamic vegetation zone responsive to environmental change across multiple spatial and temporal scales. Recent upslope advance of trees into the alpine zone has been documented in many mountain ranges around the world, and these shifts in ecotones are likely to have severe ecological consequences including reduced and fragmented habitat for alpine species, altered hydrologic regimes of soils, and disrupted carbon and nutrient cycling in mountain ecosystems. Upslope advance of trees is predicted to continue or accelerate in response to human-caused climate change. In this study, we investigate temporal (decadal to centennial) variability in the movement and structure of treeline ecotones at RMBL. We will reconstruct the rate of treeline movement and the spatial pattern of stand conditions within the treeline environment as well as within the subalpine forest. Reconstructions of tree establishment and growth over time will be accomplished by collecting tree-ring data in transects spanning the subalpine and alpine zones. This study addresses the need for spatially-explicit information on the temporal stability of treeline dynamics.
ResearchPlanOrganisms: Englemann Spruce (Picea engelmannii) and Subalpine Fir (Abies bifolia)
Subject: Climate Change

ResearchPlanTitle: Cheating in pollination mutualisms: The effect of secondary nectar robbing on plant reproduction
ResearchPlanAbstract: In ecology, mutualisms exist when two species interact in such a way that both gain a benefit from the interaction. However, each mutualist partner must also pay a â€œparticipation costâ€. When this cost is high, we often see one mutualist taking advantage of the benefit provided by its partner without providing a benefit in return, or â€œcheatingâ€. Plant-pollinator mutualisms are often disrupted by cheating when pollinators exhibit a behavior called nectar robbing, which is characterized by perforating and extracting nectar through a hole in the side of the flower rather than â€œlegitimatelyâ€ extracting nectar from the floral opening. In this example, the pollinator gets its benefit from the mutualism (a food source), but the plant misses out on its benefit (pollen transfer). Pollinators can take cheating a step further by taking advantage of holes already created by a nectar-robber, or secondary robbing. The effects of secondary robbing on plant reproductive success has not been well investigated, but are potentially very important as many more pollinator species can secondary rob as can primary rob. Whatâ€™s more, the frequency and constancy of these behavioral switches (the â€œrulesâ€ governing switching) have not been clearly identified. My work addresses these gaps in the research, asking: What is the effect of secondary nectar robbing on plant reproductive success? The answer to this question is largely dependent on a number of variables relating to the community, including the diversity of plants and pollinators and the timing of the interactions. I will measure the effects of secondary nectar robbing by bumble bees by creating experimental robbing treatments in Ipomopsis aggregata (Polemoniaceae) and Linaria vulgaris (Plantaginaceae), recording subsequent pollinator and robber visitation, and measuring pollen receipt and seed set. My project will be one of the first to address the effects of secondary robbing on plant success, and the observations will also provide insight into the â€œrulesâ€ of cheating in these mutualisms.
Subject: Pollination

ResearchPlanTitle: Climate change impacts on montane meadow carbon balance
ResearchPlanAbstract: Ecosystems carbon budgets are governed by the complex interaction of abiotic factors (temperature and precipitation), and biotic responses (photosynthesis and respiration). Global warming is expected to alter large-scale patterns in temperature and precipitation, with specific predictions of earlier snowmelt and decreased summer precipitation in the Inter-mountain West. It is currently unclear how these changes will influence the balance of carbon budgets in montane ecosystems. Montane meadows typically store more carbon than they release, thus acting as carbon sinks. However, it is possible that warming will cause meadows to become carbon sources, which would create a positive feedback by further increasing atmospheric carbon. A warming experiment has been implemented at the Rocky Mountain Biological Laboratory for the past 20+ years, and has helped to address the question of carbon dynamics in future climates. With this study I will investigate how montane meadows respond to warming at various time scales. In addition, I will utilize plant functional traits as a link between environmental drivers and ecosystem responses.
Subject: Climate Change

ResearchPlanTitle: POTENTIAL ROLE OF FISH MUCUS DWELLING BACTERIAL COMMUNITIES AS AN ANTI-PREDATOR ALARM CUE FOR BAETIS MAYFLY LARVE
ResearchPlanAbstract: Olfactory perception is particularly important when visual cues are limited, as is the case in aquatic ecosystems. Furthermore, aquatic environments are conducive to dissolving and dispersing chemical information. Thus, in those ecosystems, chemicals cues often mediate the communication among organisms, which use chemical information from the environment for behavioral decision making related to foraging, reproduction and the assessment of predator risk. Previous studies on the mayfly Baetis bicaudatus have demonstrated the importance of non-consumptive effects whereby chemical cues emitted by fish predators influence prey to use different habitats, forage at different times, change their activity levels and alter their foraging behavior. Therefore, chemical predator recognition may elicit avoidance responses that significantly affect prey fitness. However, up to date nothing is known on the origin and nature of the chemical cues released by the fish that are responsible of the anti-predator behavior observed in the mayfly species. Previous studies conducted in RMBL showed that the responses of Baetis to trout (nocturnicity and reduced drift) do no depend on fish feeding status, thus we discarded alarm cues from conspecific as the origin of the cue that makes Baetis to respond. As a consequence, we pointed out fish cutaneous mucus as the origin of the signal. This mucus is mainly composed by gllucids and proteins that are provided in the fish diet and are partially metabolized by the microbioal community that live associated with the skin mucus. In this sense, mucus microbiota may have a role as an alarm cue for Baetis larvae. The principal goals of this project are: 1) to test the anti-predator responses of Baetis to different fish species; 2) to evaluate the potential role that fish mucus-dweeling microbiota may have as an alarm cue for Baetis.
Subject: Other

ResearchPlanTitle: Life-history tradeoffs in Mountain White-crowned Sparrows
ResearchPlanAbstract: Bird productivity and parasite loads are impacted by numerous environmental variables, including nest-site characteristics, immune defense, and food availability. Understanding how these factors interact to influence specific reproductive parameters (e.g., nest survival, number of young fledged) and fitness can provide crucial information to bird conservation efforts. Wild birds are constantly moderating how they allocate energy to daily activities that optimize their survival and reproduction. However, the extent to which these factors may decrease bird productivity by altering life history tradeoffs remains poorly understood. For example, this optimal response during breeding season depends not only on the amount of food available, but the presence of pathogens, and how well a nest is concealed from predators by surrounding vegetation. This research applies experimental and observational approaches to elucidate the patterns associated with these tradeoffs.
Subject: Long-Term

ResearchPlanTitle: Mycorrhizal fungal community structure along an elevational gradient
ResearchPlanAbstract: Global changes will alter interactions among organisms. Symbiotic relationships might be particularly vulnerable because partners may respond in unique ways to the pressure, but partners are reliant on each other for persistence. For example, flower and bumblebee phenologies are becoming disjunct, leading to a decline in plant seed set and potentially leading to a decline in plant populations. Although disjuncts in aboveground plant-pollinator and plant-herbivore symbioses under global change have been described, belowground plant-mycorrhizal relationships have yet to be explored. Mycorrhizal fungi associate with 80% of plant species and play a crucial role in nutrient acquisition, survival, and production of supporting plant community [28]. Because fungal communities are structured by some combination of biotic and abiotic factors, it is widely regarded that fungi will susceptible to global change, particularly drought and warming. Although gradient analysis is frequently used in studies of plant and animal assemblages, very few studies have used elevational gradients to understand fungal assemblages. Understanding how mycorrhizal fungal species and communities are distributed along an elevational gradient may help us better understand how fungal and plant communities will structure under novel environmental conditions.
Subject: Climate Change

ResearchPlanTitle: Effects of nitrogen deposition on top predator control of community production and diversity
ResearchPlanAbstract: As a driver of global change, increasing atmospheric nitrogen (N) deposition is having widespread fertilization effects on ecosystems and is altering plant production and diversity. This N-addition can change interactions between plants and consumers and potentially modify the cascading effects that top predators generate across ecological webs. I propose to study how N deposition alters the cascading effects of black bears, which as top predators of ants create indirect benefits for plants. Continuing an N-addition experiment mimicking deposition in a sagebrush meadow where bears forage for ants, I will investigate how N and bears affect the production and diversity of a plant-arthropod community. I expect that the community will be controlled more by fertilization than by cascading bear effects as N-additions persist. Illuminating connections between the indirect ecological effects of global change and top predators, this study will have management implications for both N deposition and bears.
ResearchPlanOrganisms: I study a community dominated by the plants Artemisia tridentata and Chrysothamnus viscidiflorus.  Arthropods include Publilia modesta treehoppers and other insect herbivores, and Formica obscuripes ants and others arthropod predators.
Subject: Other

ResearchPlanTitle: Comparative study of wing development in Caddis Flies (Order: Trichoptera)
ResearchPlanAbstract: I propose to do field work at the Rocky Mountain Biological Laboratory, Crested Butte, Colorado, USA in order to examine the development of wing tissues in larval caddis flies (Order Trichoptera). Caddis flies are the closest living relatives to butterflies and moths (order Lepidoptera), but unlike the Lepidoptera, the developmental biology of caddis flies is poorly studied because they are nearly impossible to rear in captivity. Studying caddis fly wing development will provide important insights into what wing development might have been like in the earliest and most primitive moths, and allow us to better understand the directions that the evolution of wings has taken in both groups. Key objectives are to conduct a pilot study to determine if using field-caught caddis fly larvae is a viable means of documenting the stages of development of the wing primordia in this group of insects. I plan to document the stages in the morphological development of the wing primordia of two or more species of caddis flies so that they can be compared to each other, and also compared to the development of similar structures in other groups of insects. Finally, I will harvest wing primordia and DNA from caddis flies and transport them back to the laboratory at the University of Manitoba so that they can be used in immunohistochemistry experiments to detect patterns of protein expression in these tissues. These patterns can also be used as a basis for comparisons between caddis flies and other groups of insects. Taken together, these efforts will transform the study of developmental biology of caddis flies and yield important new insights into the evolution and development of insects in general, and the evolution and development of butterfly and moth wings in particular.
Subject: Other

ResearchPlanInstitution: University of North Carolina Chapel Hill
ResearchPlanTitle: Linking butterfly traits to fitness to forecast butterfly responses to climate change
ResearchPlanAbstract: Increasing global temperatures have begun to profoundly affect terrestrial communities (Parmesan 2006; Huey, Deutsch et al. 2009). The alpine areas in Colorado have seen greater increases in temperature over the past fifty years than other parts of the country on the order of 0.4 C per decade (culter.colorado.edu). This makes Colias meadii and Colias eriphyle of great research interest because they are Rocky Mountain butterflies that have been studied extensively for their close functional relationship between wing coloration patterns and temperature (Watt 1968; Kingsolver 1983; Kingsolver 1983; Watt 1992) as well as larval thermal ecology, (Sherman 1973). We will collect data addressing how temperature affects larval and adult physiology to constrain distributions. Comparing current measurements to those previously reported will enable us to test if butterflies physiology has already responded to climate change. This research will serve to parameterize an ecophysiological demographic model, which will be tested by hindcasting past distribution changes and used to predict future distribution shifts.
Subject: Climate Change

ResearchPlanTitle: Hybridization and Invasiveness in Tragopogon
ResearchPlanAbstract: The proposed research tackles two problems in contemporary evolutionary ecology. First, does hybridization (mating between species) increase the invasiveness of plants? Many damaging invasive plants species have a history of hybridization, but experimental tests are needed to determine if gene exchange causes the invasion or is simply a byproduct of plant species expanding their ranges and encountering other species as mating partners. Second, can phylogeny (patterns of relatedness in a group of species) be used to understand how often pollinators visit flowers? Here, a prediction is that plant species without close relatives in a community may have access to fewer pollinator visits, because appropriate pollinators may be at low abundance. Such a finding would have implications for our understanding of which species might be better at colonizing new habitats.
ResearchPlanOrganisms: Tragopogon spp., flowering plants, flower-visiting insects
Subject: Other

ResearchPlanTitle: Soil geomorphology and landscape evolution of the Upper Gunnison Basin
ResearchPlanAbstract: Soils are an important interface between geology and biology; however, very little is known about the soils around RMBL. Soil development is a function of climatic conditions, biological activity, local relief, aspect, parent material, and the amount of time sediments are exposed at or near the surface. Combined with an understanding of surficial processes, soil stratigraphy aids in the subdivision of the local succession of deposits and correlation of unconsolidated sediments. The distribution and properties of soil stratigraphic units can be used to evaluate landform evolution and age, landform stability, surface processes and even past climates. Potential research questions include: What are the dominant relationships between soil and sediment properties with elevation, slope, aspect, rock type, or the relative age of surficial deposits? Is there a correlation between soil properties and dominant vegetation patterns? What is the late Quaternary history of landscape change in this environment?
Subject: Climate Change

ResearchPlanTitle: Relating Soil CO2 flux to Microbial and Organic Matter Properties in a Subalpine Meadow
ResearchPlanAbstract: The amount of carbon dioxide (CO2) in the atmosphere is increasing. We understand that the consequences of this increase are a warmer, drier world; however the influence of a changing climate on elemental cycling of carbon (C) are not well understood. There are many factors that play a role in C cycling with plants, animals, microorganisms, soil and water all playing central roles. Concerted efforts to predict how these factors influence the storage and export of soil C are represented by modeling efforts, however empirical data are needed to validate results and refine predictions. I aim to collect empirical data on the relationship between the transfer of C from the atmosphere to the soil via spruce and aspen trees in a sub-alpine meadow, and how the molecular structure of soil C influences if it stays in the soil, or is returned to the atmosphere.
Subject: Climate Change

ResearchPlanTitle: Timing of functional group loss and carbon dynamics across apline meadows
ResearchPlanAbstract: The implications of permanent loss of species and or species groups (e.g., functional groups) from plant communities have been shown to alter community dynamics and ecosystem properties, yet the effects of timing of species or species groups' loss from plant communities is not well understood. As a result, I would like to manipulate the timing of functional group (graminoids, forbs, nitrogen fixers) loss in alpine meadow communities both at high and low elevation sites to determine how such losses will influence the ability of these systems to sequester carbon (C) from the atmosphere.
Subject: Climate Change

ResearchPlanTitle: Castilleja voucher specimens and Adaptive advantages of genome duplication in Fireweeds in response to predicted global climate changes
ResearchPlanAbstract: Global climate changes are occurring at unprecedented rates, appear to be more pronounced in Northern temperate latitudes, and have resulted in the contraction and expansion of species ranges. For species with limited dispersal abilities, such as some plants, one of the only options may be to adapt to new climate conditions. Plants may face even more pressures as increasing temperatures tends to have positive effects on pathogen and insect populations, which could subsequently have negative effects on plant populations because natural enemies most oftendecrease plant fitness. In plants, whole genome duplication (polyploidy) is common and has significantly contributed to species biodiversity. Surprisingly, there is little information about whether closely related individuals that differ in their number of chromosomes (cytotypes) evolve at different rates in response to selection pressures. My initial objective is to examine and test whether genome duplication influences genetic variability and selective responses to changes in climate and pest pressures. I propose to address these objectives with a series of collections, experiments, and analyses of cytotype and genetic data. Studies will focus on a visually dominant plant, Chamerion angustifolia (Fireweed) and will span Alaska, Colorado, and Michigan. In the short-term, I will visit sites in Alaska, Colorado and Michigan to identify field sites to census pest populations, measure abiotic variables and collect leaf and seed material for subsequent ploidy determination, genetic analysis, and greenhouse selection studies. A long term goal is that this research will contribute to growing fields aimed at understanding how species will respond to the direct and indirect affects of climate changes and at how genome duplication influences evolutionary dynamics at the level of the phenotype and genotype.
Subject: Climate Change

ResearchPlanTitle: Studies on Drosophila montana
ResearchPlanAbstract: N/A
Subject: Climate Change

ResearchPlanTitle: I. Continuing Studies of Ecosystem-Climate Interactions at the RMBL Warming Meadow II. Continuing Studies of the Disturbance Macroecology.
ResearchPlanAbstract: Part I. Our research is providing a better understand of how ecosystems respond to climate change and how climate change is affected by ecosystems. In particular, we are learning that woody plants like sagebrush can increasingly dominate non-woody flowering plants under warming and thereby greatly alter subalpine meadow plant communities. This shift in vegetation is also leading to a significant reduction of soil organic matter, with the lost carbon emitted to the atmosphere as carbon dioxide. Because carbon dioxide is a greenhouse gas, this process can accelerate global warming if it occurs on a large scale. Modeling work we have carried strongly suggests that it will, indeed, occur on a large scale. Part II. Understanding patterns in the abundance, distribution, and energetics of species in ecosystems is critical to our ability to predict extinction rates under global warming or under land use changes. We have developed theory that does provide that understanding of pattern and tested it in over 50 ecosystems around the world. The one category of ecosystem in which the theory seems to fail is systems undergoing rapid change because of human disturbance. We are gathering macroecological census data from disturbed ecosystems at RMBL to better understand the patterns of failure of the theory.
Subject: Other

ResearchPlanTitle: Long-term research on phenology, pollination, and plant demography.
ResearchPlanAbstract:
My research projects focus on long-term studies of the timing and abundance of flowering, and how they are changing in response to the changing climate. I am also studying the demography of some wildflower species, altitudinal distributions of bumble bee species, hummingbird demography and the phenology of their migrations and nesting.

[Note from Science Director] This research plan outlines a supplementary resaerch project involving hummingbird demography and phenology.
Subject: Phenology

ResearchPlanInstitution: University of California Riverside, University of Arizona
ResearchPlanTitle: Pollination, reproduction, and herbivory of wildflowers
ResearchPlanAbstract: Pollination, reproduction, and survival of wildflowers are critical to the health of natural ecological systems in meadow habitats of the Rocky Mountains. We are continuing our long-term (40+ years) studies of the pollination of the low larkspur and of scarlet gilia by bumble bees and hummingbirds, and of the consumption of these plants by mule deer. In particular we will continue to explore how road dust and climate variation influence reproduction, and how consumption by deer affects the mixture of plant species found in meadows.
Subject: Pollination

ResearchPlanTitle: Microbial Characterization of the Mt. Emmons Fen and Other Nearby Metal-Impacted Systems
ResearchPlanAbstract: The Mt. Emmons fen, located near Crested Butte, CO, is a stable geological structure supported by a continuous inflow of metal-laden groundwater. Sitting on top of a climax-type porphyry molybdenum deposit, its pH 3 water contains elevated levels of a variety of metals, including Cd, Al, Fe, Mo, and Zn. With concentrations exceeding water quality standards set by the State of Colorado, no one has studied its microbiology. This research will be (i) the first to characterize the functional processes used by microorganisms following thousands of years of adaptation to metal toxicity; and (ii) determine how a climax microbial community responds to metals and how these responses are linked to the fenâ€™s biogeochemistry. While microbial resistance to metals is well established, how microorganisms evolve in the presence of metals, how microbial activity can transform metals for remediation, and how microorganisms may work together to address metal toxicity is largely unknown. Most work looking into microbial metal-resistance focuses on mining- or industrial-impacted sites. These types of systems force populations to adapt rapidly or face elimination. Due to the long-term exposure to metals, we expect the fen microbial community to show diverse microorganisms with unique metabolic abilities, especially adapted to metal toxicity. The overall objectives of this work are to use advanced molecular DNA sequencing methods to characterize the microbial community associated with the fen and to identify novel responses to the presence of toxic metals. This information will contribute to our understanding of how microorganisms transform metals in the environment, which has direct implications for metal containment and remediation.
Subject: Long-Term

ResearchPlanTitle: 1) Consequences of Climate-Induced Range Shifts on Multiple Ecosystem Functions 2) Paleolimnological Evidence for Changes in Climate in the Elk Mountains of central Colorado
ResearchPlanAbstract: Closely related species that make similar contributions to ecosystem function often replace each other along environmental gradients, resulting in wholesale shifts in community composition. Replacements along gradients can occur locally within habitats (intertidal, soil moisture, aquatic permanence) and at broader regional scales (elevation, latitude). Many ecologists have reported shifts in distributions at both scales as a result of a changing climate, yet the functional consequences of these community rearrangements are poorly understood. We have identified range shifts in species replacements along a pond-permanence gradient (temporary to permanent) within elevations, and along an elevational gradient from montane to subalpine ponds in the central Rocky Mountains that are both associated with changes in climatic variables. This research explores how climate-driven species range shifts in a dominant group of detritivores (caddisfly larvae) along both gradients will affect multiple ecosystem functions, including the transfer of detrital energy to detritivore secondary production, release of detritus-bound nutrients for algal uptake, bottom-up effects on herbivores, and overall system productivity. The research will investigate the degree to which 1) species replacements along permanence and elevational gradients are functional replacements in terms of detritus processing rates and their cascading effects on brown (detrital) and green (algal) trophic paths, 2) the interactive effects of species shifts across the permanence gradient within an elevation and those associated with upslope range shifts across elevations, and 3) changes in ecosystem processes with community rearrangements scale up to affect ecosystem function at the whole pond level.
Subject: Climate Change

ResearchPlanTitle: Predator-induced effects on insect flight and dispersal across landscapes
ResearchPlanAbstract: Unraveling the mechanisms that govern the movement of individuals is key to understanding a major determinant of the fates of individuals, the structure and dynamics of populations, communities, ecosystems, and the evolution and diversity of life. Insects exhibit remarkable variation in flight and dispersal that are important to investigate because many insects are ecologically and economically important. In addition, studying the genetic to ecological factors that explain variation in flight and dispersal is fundamental because the evolution of flight presaged the most extensive animal radiation in evolutionary history. Selection by predators on their prey for enhanced flight performance to escape being eaten was presumably intense during the evolution of winged animals, such as insects. Yet, a mechanistic understanding by which even contemporary predator-induced selection affects insect flight traits and subsequent dispersal ability, propensity, and the fate of dispersers is lacking. This research project will address this important knowledge gap by investigating how predatory fish affect flight traits and dispersal of insects, such as stoneflies, that live in rivers during one life stage and on land as winged insects during their final life stage. Using four linked objectives, this research will use observations, experiments, and a model to provide one of the first integrative studies of predator effects on flight traits at the biochemical, physiological, and morphological levels, how these traits are ecologically linked to dispersal distance and directionality, and their interaction with landscape-scale habitat conï¬guration in river networks. In so doing, this study will transform understanding of contemporary selective agents on insect flight and dispersal. This research will benefit society by providing information on factors affecting landscape-scale movements of adult aquatic insects, some of which are human pests or disease vectors, and will have implications for understanding the impacts of introduced predators on traits of prey species. Integrating research and education are key components of this project that will be achieved by training and mentoring at least 10 undergraduates, plus a graduate student, and exposing them to a vibrant research and teaching community at an internationally recognized field station, the Rocky Mountain Biological Laboratory. Public outreach activities informing non-scientists about the biology of freshwater organisms will be coordinated through the Rocky Mountain Biological Laboratoryâ€™s Kidâ€™s Nature Camp, Adult Science Tours, and Citizen Science Geek Week.
Subject: Other

ResearchPlanTitle: Hydro-biogeochemical Cycling Within the East River Floodplain
ResearchPlanAbstract: This proposal seeks to explore the possibility of utilizing RMBL and its environs within the East River Catchment as a new field study site for the Lawrence Berkeley National Laboratory's (LBNL) 'Sustainable Systems' Science Focus Area (SFA) research project (http://esd.lbl.gov/research/projects/sssfa2/). The LBNL SFA project seeks to address the following overarching science questions: How will climate-induced changes in hydrology and vegetation affect subsurface nutrient inputs, flowpaths, biogeochemical cycling and microbial metabolic potential at the scale of the local catchment or watershed? How will these processes evolve with time, and what effect will interactions and feedbacks have on watershed biogeochemical functioning? The primary focus is on quantifying the role than coupled surface water-groundwater processes play in constraining biogeochemical cycles of critical elements, such as C, N, S, Fe, Mn, etc., within soils and alluvial sediments within floodplain deposits, such as those along the East River. Unprecedented insight into the vast range of nutrient cycling pathways catalyzed by subsurface microflora will be informed through detailed meta-omic (genomic, transcriptomic, proteomic) analysis of soil, sediment, and pore/river/groundwater samples ultimately leading to the development of a first-ever genome-enabled watershed simulation capability. This proposal therefore seeks to explore the relevance of RMBL and locations within the upper East River Catchment to this effort through targeted sampling of porewater, groundwater (as available), and stream water along an elevation gradient within the catchment.
Subject: Climate Change

ResearchPlanTitle: . How do functional differences associated with clone size, gender, ploidy, and landscape position influence aspenâ€™s water relations and resilience to drought?
ResearchPlanAbstract: This study is investigating whether and how polyploidy and gender of aspen clones influence growth and water-use efficiency in the Gunnison River Basin in Colorado. Supporting evidence will be provided by an observational study centered at RMBL that identifies the frequency of polyploids and gender relative to environmental characteristics that relate to water availability. If aspen polyploids and gender vary consistently with environment â€“ for example, and if polyploids or males are found in drier environments than diploids or females, then this suggests that polyploids and gender influence adaptation to environmental conditions. Also, comparisons of water use efficiency measures between populations (and their ploidy and gender frequency) will show physiological and adaptive differences. The outcomes from this research seeks to provide a basis for evaluating genetic and environmental contributors to drought response in aspen.
Subject: Climate Change

ResearchPlanTitle: The role of dispersal in the golden-mantled ground squirrel
ResearchPlanAbstract: Changes in density and genetic diversity are thought to have important consequences for population-level attributes which affect a speciesâ€™ long-term sustainability. At RMBL, drastic fluctuations in the density of the golden-mantled ground squirrel have been observed since 1990 with some years reaching as low as 7 adults (Kneip et al. 2011). Incoming individuals from adjacent sites have been recognized to greatly contribute to the changes in the population size and are speculated to have increased the genetic diversity in the existing population in Gothic (McEachern et al. 2011). However, no studies have yet been conducted to reveal the movement patterns of the species and its role in driving the metapopulation dynamics. In order to understand the causes and consequences of variations in density and the effect of movement on the long-term persistence of the golden-mantled ground squirrels at RMBL, I plan to study the density, movement behavior, population dynamics, and genetic structure of the species for the populations that exist near RMBL. To be more specific, patterns of individual movement will be analyzed with radio-telemetry and information on movement distance, movement frequency, and mortality rate during movement will be gathered. In addition, I will collect DNA samples from adjacent sites to RMBL to analyze the genetic pattern of the metapopulation structure in the East River Valley. This will help identify the role of movement on the genetic composition of the populations in the site, along with radio-telemetry. The effects of movement on the population dynamics and genetic composition of populations are poorly understood for the golden-mantled ground squirrel, and therefore, examining the role of the speciesâ€™ movement will allow a better understanding of the conservation status of the species and develop better management options in the future. Reference) Kneip Ã‰, Van Vuren DH, Hostetler JA, Oli MK (2011) Influence of population density and climate on the demography of subalpine golden-mantled ground squirrels. Journal of Mammalogy 92: 367-377. McEachern MB, Van Vuren DH, Floyd CH, May B, Eadie JM (2011) Bottlenecks and rescue effects in a fluctuating population of golden-mantled ground squirrels (Spermophilus lateralis). Conservation Genetics 12: 285-296.
Subject: Other

ResearchPlanTitle: Context-dependent effects of butterfly gut symbionts on host fitness
ResearchPlanAbstract: The gut flora are believed to provide critical services to most animals. Research on their effects has focused on the physiological benefits they impart, but to understand this symbiosis it is essential to measure its impact on host reproductive fitness. In nature, the fitness outcomes of gut symbioses likely depend on host food availability. I will investigate how food availability mediates the effects of gut symbionts on host reproductive output, using a butterfly study system. I will experimentally measure the effects of butterfly feeding regime (ad libitum versus restricted) and the presence (versus absence) of the gut flora on butterfly egg output and egg chemistry. I will also characterize gut community composition as an important covariate. I predict that under food restriction, the cost of maintaining the gut flora will outweigh its benefit and host fitness will be reduced, but under unrestricted feeding, the gut flora will increase host fitness. This project will quantify the fitness effects of the gut floraâ€”which are poorly understood and have rarely been measuredâ€”while accounting for variation in gut community composition. Furthermore, it will be the first to place symbiont effects in the context of a major environmental variable (food availability), providing a more realistic understanding of gut symbioses in natural systems.
ResearchPlanOrganisms: the butterfly Speyeria mormonia, and its gut microbes
Subject: Other

ResearchPlanTitle: The ecological and evolutionary consequences of multispecies interactions and invasive species
ResearchPlanAbstract: In my research, I combine concepts and techniques from studies of plant-pollinator and plant-herbivore interactions to understand the ecological and evolutionary consequences of pollination mutualisms and invasive species. More broadly, my work explores how species interactions affect ecological and microevolutionary processes and services and how microevolution can in turn shape and constrain biodiversity and species interactions. My research focuses primarily on interacting suites of plants and insects because plants and insects can be easily manipulated, they make up a significant portion of world biodiversity, and both perform critical ecosystem services. My five-year research plan is broken down into five projects: 1) Ecology and management of the invasive plant Linaria vulgaris, 2) Temporal and spatial variation in species interactions with Ipomopsis aggregata, 3) Context dependency in the exploitation of pollination mutualisms (with Judie Bronstein) 3) Secondary chemistry of floral rewards: impacts on plants, pollinators, and their interactions (with Daniel Cook), 4) Bee pollinator phenology and monitoring (with David Inouye), 5) Yeasts in floral nectar (with Robert Schaeffer).
ResearchPlanOrganisms: Linaria vulgaris, Ipomopsis aggregata, Anticlea (=Zigadenus) elegans, Mertensia ciliata, Delphinium nuttallianum and barbeyi, Lupinus spp., Senecio spp., Bombus occidentalis, Bombus flavifrons, other solitary and social bees
Subject: Pollination

ResearchPlanTitle: Project 1. Effects of stress on life history and fitness in variable environments; Project 2. Non-native species, native species and evolutionary traps.
ResearchPlanAbstract: Variation in the environment can take several forms. Organisms may be exposed to different weather or climate conditions over space and/or time. The predators, competitors or food items in a community may also change over space and/or time. I am exploring how such changes affect individual reproduction and survival, and through that, changes in population numbers over time. My goal is to generate a conceptual understanding that is broadly applicable to diverse organisms. My present research utilizes butterflies as study systems, and has two foci. First, I am studying the effects of an introduced plant species on the population dynamics and evolution of host plant usage by a native butterfly species. Second, I am exploring the effects of variation in adult and larval food availability on reproduction and survival, thence population numbers.
ResearchPlanOrganisms: Speyeria mormonia, Viola spp, Pieris macdunnoughii, Thlaspi arvense, Cardamine cordifolia, Boechera stricta, Draba aurea, Descurainia incana
Subject: Long-Term

ResearchPlanTitle: Direct and indirect effects of frost events on plant-pollinator interactions in sub-alpine regions of Colorado
ResearchPlanAbstract: Global climate change is predicted to disrupt trophic interactions, which can lead to a loss of biodiversity and important mutualistic relationships. The mutualistic partnership between flowering plants and bees, which is essential to the reproductive success of both partners, is predicted to change due to increasing temperatures from climate change. One way that climate change could alter mutualistic interactions is through temporal mismatching, in which bee emergence and plant bloom no longer overlap. This mismatch could cause both members of the mutualism to decline. While previous studies have examined the effects of increasing temperature on temporal mismatches, they fail to examine a key component of climate change, which is an increase in the frequency of stochastic weather events. One weather event that is predicted to increase is frost, which may have a strong impact on plant-pollinator interactions and plant fitness through both direct and indirect effects. For example, it is unknown whether flowers that experience frost events lose their attractiveness to pollinators, and the relative importance of the direct effects of frost damage on plant fitness versus the indirect effects mediated through changes in pollination are unexplored to my knowledge. The objective of this research is to study how frost events, which are predicted to increase with increasing temperatures, affect plants directly and indirectly via changes in plant-pollinator interactions by asking the following questions: 1) How do pollinators respond to plants that have been exposed to frost events? 2) Are plants exposed to frost pollen limited for plant reproduction?
Subject: Climate Change

ResearchPlanTitle: New approaches for macroecology under disturbance and non-steady states
ResearchPlanAbstract: Disturbance and disequilibrium are common features of all ecosystems, and are becoming more important under global change. However current macroecological theory has limited ability to predict the dynamics of these non-steady-state systems. I will develop and test more robust theory for three major ecological axes: community composition, abundance, and functional distribution. At RMBL, these tests will be carried out via experiments on alpine plant communities subject to perturbation / disturbance from nitrogen and phosphorus fertilization. Each year I will measure dynamics along all three major ecological axes. This experiment will become a long-term alpine observatory with a unique ability to assess the impacts of anthropogenic disturbance in a sensitive North American ecosystem.
Subject: Long-Term

ResearchPlanTitle: Evolution and Biogeography of Polemonium (Polemoniaceae)
ResearchPlanAbstract: Polemonium is a widespread genus with a center of diversity in the western U. S. A. Previous phylogenetic studies have lacked adequate sampling of Rocky Mountain taxa. Two of the species occurring in Colorado, Polemonium foliosissimum and Polemonium viscosum are morphologically complex and both are under-studied. Members of the P. viscosum complex are ecologically well-studied but knowledge of this species is lacking in a phylogenetic context. RMBL represents a station that makes a large portion of the genusâ€™ range in the Rocky Mountains accessible.
Subject: Other

ResearchPlanTitle: THE EFFECTS OF POLLINATOR SPECIES LOSSES ON POLLINATION NETWORKS
ResearchPlanAbstract: Pollination networksâ€”the linkages between plant and pollinator speciesâ€”are an increasingly important way of understanding system-level trends affecting plant and pollinator communities and their interactions. Simulation models based on pollination networks suggest that plant communities will be highly robust to pollinator species losses, but such results remain untested in nature. Previous work of ours from RMBL suggests that pollinator species losses drive changes in the behavior of remaining species, especially in terms of floral fidelity, with negative implications for plants. We hypothesize that pollinator species losses will drive changes to the structure and dynamics of pollination networks, with negative consequences for plant pollination functioning. To test this hypothesis, we will temporarily and non-destructively reduce bee and plant diversity and abundance in several meadow sites, and compare manipulated to non-manipulated sites in terms of several attributes of network structure and dynamics, as well as measures of pollination function.
Subject: Pollination

ResearchPlanTitle: A) The potential for climate-induced disruption of plant-microbe symbioses along altitudinal gradients,B) King of the hill: Why are alpine plants restricted to high elevations?
ResearchPlanAbstract: Species are moving up mountainsides in response to climate warming. As shifts in species distributions occur, ecologically important interactions between species may be disrupted, with as yet unknown consequences. The coupled dynamics arising from species interactions can produce complex, nonlinear, and unanticipated ecological responses to climate change. Novel species responses may feedback on the rate of climate change itself by altering processes that influence pools and fluxes of carbon. Fungal symbionts, such as endophytes and mycorrhizal fungi, are now well documented to improve plant resilience to climate variability. Fungi also play critical roles in carbon storage and cycling. Therefore, the potential for climate change to decouple plant and fungal symbiont interactions deserves careful attention. This project will gauge the potential for plant-fungal symbioses to become destabilized under future climates and test the consequences of disruptions for individual plant species and carbon allocation processes. First, the distributions of fungal symbionts colonizing plant leaves and roots will be described along replicated elevation gradients in the Rocky Mountains, using microscopy and DNA sequencing. This work constitutes the largest altitudinal survey of fungal symbionts anywhere in the world. Second, an NSF-funded, 22-year warming experiment will be leveraged to test, for the first time, whether fungal responses to climate warming match distributional patterns along natural, altitudinal gradients. Third, reciprocal transplants of plants and fungi will mimic range shifts under a 3Â°C warmer climate and directly test the consequences of symbiosis decoupling. Fourth, functional assays will evaluate how disrupted symbioses affect local carbon allocation. Broader Impacts: A majority of the budget is allocated to training the next generation of scientists, including students from underrepresented groups at the University of New Mexico, a majority-minority institution. K-12 outreach includes high school teacher training and curriculum development, visits to underserved schools, and a kids nature camp and adult citizen science program supported through the Rocky Mountain Biological Laboratory.
Subject: Climate Change

ResearchPlanTitle: Determinants of ant-hemipteran interactions
ResearchPlanAbstract: Many species of ants and aphids engage in mutualistic interactions, where aphids feed ants and ants in turn protect aphids from their predators. These ant-aphid mutualisms constitute classic defining examples of mutualism, and have contributed in important ways to the understanding of mutualisms generally. Yet these interactions are not always beneficial to both parties, and in particular it is clear that ants can have neutral or negative effects on aphids based upon the biotic and abiotic conditions under which the interaction occurs. This research seeks to investigate the causes and consequences of variability in ant-aphid interactions in three separate but complementary ways. First, it will test for the consequences of thermal environment for ant interactions with aphids. Second, it will test whether competition among ants for access to aphids benefits aphids or â€“ alternatively â€“ whether potentially superior mutualist ants are excluded by competitively superior ants that are poor quality mutualists. And third, it will test for the consequences of feeding by insectivorous birds, and the extended consequences for the arthropod communities associated with ants and aphids.
ResearchPlanOrganisms: Ants, aphids, , insect-gleaning birds, the host plants Populus tremuloides, Chamerion angustifolium, Ligusticum porteri, and associated arthropods
Subject: Other

ResearchPlanTitle: Exploring the effects of phenology and ecological community context on plant-pollinator interactions.
ResearchPlanAbstract: The timing of life history events â€“ phenology â€“ is intimately tied to the growth, survival, and reproduction of organisms. Following this, the best time to grow and reproduce should coincide with the peak of food availability within a season. This idea forms the basis of the phenological match-mismatch hypothesis, which has now received considerable attention from biologists in light of phenological changes attributed to climate change, especially with regard to plant-pollinator interactions. For example, as temperatures warm, plants are flowering earlier and bees are emerging earlier, but not necessarily at the same rate. This creates the potential for mistimed interactions, when bees may be active when their preferred pollen and nectar resources are unavailable. Although the phenological responses of plants to climate change are relatively well understood, we know very little about how pollinator phenology responds to climate change. Therefore, my dissertation research at the RMBL focuses on bee phenology and how it aligns with the availability of flowering food resources. I study bee-plant interactions across multiple sites and years ultimately to understand how variation in climate contributes to bee reproduction.
Subject: Phenology

ResearchPlanTitle: Climate change induced shifts in abiotic resources may alter pollination success: A test with Mertensia ciliata (Boraginaceae)
ResearchPlanAbstract: Rising temperatures and earlier snowpack melting due to climate change have been linked to alterations in the distribution, phenology, growth, and reproduction of many plants and animals. As individual species respond differently to climate change, ecological relationships, such as those between plants and pollinators, may be disrupted, potentially altering community composition and ecosystem functioning. Warmer springs and earlier snowpack melting are likely to alter the timing of plant reproduction (i.e. phenology) and also influence water availability in the soil during the growing season. I am investigating the potential effects of climate change on plant-pollinator mutualisms, as mediated by plant responses to water availability and phenological (i.e. flowering timing and pollinator emergence) responses to temperature. For this research, I am examining the extent which floral rewards, pollination, and seed set of the tall-fringed bluebell, Mertensia ciliata (Boraginaceae), respond to experimental manipulations of water and flowering phenology. Also, to put these experimental results into a landscape scale context, I am monitoring soil moisture, flowering, and seed set in fifteen M. ciliata populations along an elevational gradient. Initial results indicate that reducing soil water availability negatively impacts M. ciliata flower size (corolla width and length) and seed set. Changes in both temperature and water availability may be responsible for observed shifts in M. ciliataâ€™s distribution and phenology. These projects will help determine how climate change induced shifts in abiotic resources may be altering pollination success.
Subject: Climate Change

ResearchPlanTitle: â€œUnderstanding How Climate Variations and Climate Change Affect Vegetation Processes in the East River Valley: Growth Patterns, Water Source Usage, and Transpirationâ€
ResearchPlanAbstract: Ecosystems in central Colorado rely on two distinct water sources throughout the year: winter and summer precipitation. While winter precipitation (snow) is the dominant contributor to the basinâ€™s water budget, summer precipitation accounts for about 20% of the total water input. This summer input is undoubtedly critical for most vegetation, especially after snowmelt water has been used or evaporated. As snowmelt advances earlier in the year, the duration of the early summer dry season before monsoon rains arrive lengthens and further stresses vegetation. This project aims to synthesize multiple years of data from dendrometer bands (that record tree growth increments), sapflow sensors (that measure water moving through trees), and stable isotopes in xylem water (to constrain rooting depths and relative use of winter versus summer precipitation). The goal of this synthesis is to improve our understanding of water and carbon cycling by the dominant tree species around RMBL (Engelmann spruce, subalpine fir, and trembling aspen), to determine how inter-species functional differences influence these patterns, and to provide baseline climate change information as hydrological patterns and temperatures change with warming.
ResearchPlanOrganisms: Engelmann spruce, subalpine fir, and trembling aspen
Subject: Climate Change

ResearchPlanTitle: Life-history Tradeoffs in Mountain White-crowned Sparrows
ResearchPlanAbstract: This study is a long-term investigation into the life histories of Mountain White-crowned Sparrows (Zonotrichia leucophrys oriantha). This study aims to elucidate the extent and the nature of these tradeoffs associated with endoparasite and ectoparasite loads, elevation-based weather and climate patterns, habitat quality, landscape context, and food availability. Additional variables of interest include nest survival, productivity (number of young fledged) and behavioral response in a free ranging population of Mountain White-crowned Sparrows. This will be tested experimentally by manipulating food availability and observationally using field sites at different elevations and of varying habitat structure. Additionally, we will examine these tradeoffs for individual birds to test for effects of variables such as age, sex, or infection status on avian life history choices.
Subject: Long-Term

ResearchPlanTitle: An Assessment of Parasitism Rates in Mason Bees
ResearchPlanAbstract: Nest parasitism rates in mason bees are poorly understood and mostly unstudied, and can vary drastically between areas. Evidence exists from studies of other bee and wasp species for the effects of 1) the density of individuals nesting in the same location and 2) the availability of floral resources for females to provision their nests on parasitism rates in mason bees. I expect that increased density of individual nests in a single location and reduced amounts of floral resources in the vicinity of mason be nests will have a significant positive effect on the rates of parasitism in nesting mason bees. Through the use of trap nests for ease of observation of mason bee nesting activities, I will manipulate, through a number of field experiments at the Rocky Mountain Biological Laboratory, the density of mason bee nests between a number of nesting locations, as well as the amount of floral resources available to nesting bees by covering flowers in areas surrounding mason bee nesting boxes with floating row covers. I will record the number of mason bee nesting cells parasitized and observe the behaviour of bees and parasites at nesting boxes in both of these experiments.
ResearchPlanOrganisms: Mason Bees (Osmia spp.) and wasps of the family Sapygidae
Subject: Other

ResearchPlanTitle: Occurrence of secondary nectar robbing through facilitation by primary nectar robbers
ResearchPlanAbstract: Pollinators have a way of modifying their behavior in such a way that they negatively affect plant reproduction. This behavior, called nectar robbing, comes in two forms: primary, where a pollinator perforates the flower at its base and removes nectar through the hole; and secondary, where a pollinator removes nectar through a hole created by a primary nectar robber. While it's been established that this behavioral modification can reduce the amount of fruits and seeds produced by plants, the ecological contexts in which it occurs is largely unknown. My research aims to identify these ecological contexts.
Subject: Pollination

ResearchPlanTitle: The maintenance of females in gynodioecious populations of Polemonium
ResearchPlanAbstract: Most angiosperms are hermaphroditesâ€”they produce pollen (male gametes) and ovules (female gametes). Some, however, reproduce through an alternative breeding system in which some plants are typical hermaphrodites and others have lost male function and reproduce only through seeds. The maintenance of what is called â€œgynodioecyâ€â€”wherein some plants function only as females while others are hermaphroditesâ€”is an evolutionary conundrum. Theory tells us that for gynodioecy to be evolutionarily stable, females must reap a significant advantage over their hermaphrodite counterparts. But how that advantage is garnered remains unknown for most gynodioecious species. Particularly lacking is a thorough knowledge of how interactions among plants and their mutualist pollinators, as well as antagonists such as seed predators, herbivores and pollen thieves, differ between the sexes and contribute to the maintenance of females. In the course of my work at study sites around the RMBL, I am asking questions fundamental to furthering out understanding of plant breeding systems. The overarching goal of my work is to address: â€œWhat are the selective and demographic consequences of species interactions for females and hermaphrodites of a gynodioecious plant?â€ By understanding the gender-specific effects of multispecies interactions, we will gain insight into how females are maintained.
ResearchPlanOrganisms: Polemonium foliosissimum, bees and flies -- observed only
Subject: Other

ResearchPlanAbstract: This proposal describes outreach and education activities.

ResearchPlanTitle: Formal Education Course Activities 2014
ResearchPlanAbstract: This proposal describes activities by the RMBL courses: Methods in Field Ecology and Research Training in Wildlife Biology, as well as activities undertaken by Jessica Forrest's course.
Subject: Climate Change

ResearchPlanTitle: Invasive Plant Management and Revegetation in the Gothic Townsite
ResearchPlanAbstract: This proposal describes invasive plant management and revegetation efforts.
