ResearchPlanTitle: Tracking Vegetation Change in the East River Basin â€“ The Role of Herbaria; and Mating System Dynamics of Rocky Mountain Wildflowers
ResearchPlanAbstract: I have two ongoing research projects at RMBL. I have a long history of research on plant genetic structure and mating systems with Delphinium nuttallianum, Delphinium barbeyi, and Geranium richardsonii. More recently, my career and research focus have shifted to include a major emphasis on museum collections, particularly herbaria, the use of historical specimen information to track vegetation change, and the digitization and dissemination of collection information for research and education. My activities at RMBL over the past 5 years have also shifted to reflect this emphasis on herbaria and vegetation change. Over the next 5 year period, 2014-2018, I propose to spend the major portion of my efforts on herbarium-related activities, including the creation of an online, interactive virtual herbarium for the East River Drainage, and use archival specimen records, surveys, and photos to track changes in vegetation in the region. While concentrating on these herbarium-related projects, I also plan to analyze and synthesize several long-term data sets on plant mating systems for publication, resurvey old research sites to detect possible changes in population density and sex ratio, and initiate new collaborations with researchers at RMBL utilizing new genetic techniques.
Subject: Long-Term

ResearchPlanTitle: Evolutionary functional genomics of Colias (Lepidoptera, Pieridae)
ResearchPlanAbstract: Research on evolution by me and my research group has always included work at RMBL as an essential field component. For some time, we focused on mechanisms of maintenance of natural genetic variation at a small number of genes coding for three catalytic proteins, enzymes, embedded in energy-processing pathways central to all cellular life. We are now extending our approach to study natural variation in all the genes, hence their enzyme-catalyst protein products, making up an entire "module" of living organization: the intact pathway of energy processing known as glycolysis, together with its links to related processes. Initial data in hand argue for a wide range of evolutionary dynamics affecting genes of this "module" in wild insect populations. Our new work will probe the interactions between these insects and their environments which produce these diverse dynamics at different genes of this pathway. The results will extend basic understanding of how animals' adaptation to their environments works, and may also illuminate important problems of application to agriculture, medicine, and the genetics of conservation.
Subject: Other

ResearchPlanTitle: Effects of pollinator-mediated selection on reproductive isolation of two sympatric Mertensia (Boraginaceae) species
ResearchPlanAbstract: Ecological studies on differences in flower morphology and floral visitors between closely related species allow us to examine formation of flowering species, especially for species that rely on insect pollinators for reproduction. The presence of closely related species in the same habitat provides an excellent opportunity to study this issue. I predict lengths of male and female reproductive structures within flowers, as well as floral orientation, to influence pollination success of two Mertensia species (M. fusiformis and M. brevistyla) at Rocky Mountains Biological Laboratory. Through pollinator observation, flower manipulation, and hand pollination, I will examine how floral characteristics influence reproductive isolation between two closely related species occurring within the same area. I will observe the type of floral visitors that enter M. fusiformis and M. brevistyla populations and determine which species they visit. If the visitors prefer one flowering species over the other, then I predict visitor fauna to be different between the species. To understand how floral morphology influences pollinator preference, I will manipulate floral orientation and record pollinator choices. If pollinator preference does differ between species, then I predict experienced pollinators of each Mertensia species to choose floral orientations similar to their preferred species (i.e., pendant flowers in M. fusiformis and upright flowers in M. brevistyla). Lastly, I will perform hand pollination to compare pollination success within and between species. If reproductive isolation between flowering species occurs after pollination, then I predict pollination success to be greater within species than between species.
ResearchPlanOrganisms: Mertensia fusiformis, Mertensia brevistyla, and associated insect pollinators
Subject: Pollination

ResearchPlanTitle: Linking floral and population dynamics
ResearchPlanAbstract: Long term records of flowering at the RMBL have been invaluable for studies of climate change in the Rocky Mountains, and basic ecological research. As part of this on-going project to record any seasonal shifts in flowering periods and abundance, we will collect data that help us relate the historical records of flower abundance to the population sizes of wildflowers. Because most high elevation wildflowers are long-lived perennials, it is important to be able to link year-to-year variation in flower abundance to any underlying trends in the abundances of these plants.
Subject: Phenology

ResearchPlanTitle: Arbuscular mycorrhizal fungal community response to ongoing global change: an observational and experimental approach
ResearchPlanAbstract: Communities of plants and soil organisms are changing in response to climatic change and these shifts will likely alter the ecosystem functions that humans rely on. My work aims to understand how shifts in community interactions above- and belowground alter ecosystem function. Using an observational and experimental approach my work will explore how climatic change and species interactions alter community structure and ecosystem function. I have established a series of observational plots as well as a manipulative warming Ã— dominant plant species removal experiment along an elevational gradient to ask: (1) What biotic and abiotic factors structure arbuscular mycorrhizal communities along elevational gradients, (2) How will these communities respond to warming and changes in dominant plant communities and (3) How will changes in community interactions alter the carbon cycle? To date, my works shows biotic and abiotic factors that structure mycorrhizal communities vary across an elevational gradient. Fungal colonization of plant roots displays a unimodal pattern across the gradient, with colonization being highest at middle sites. Additionally, I have found RMBL plant communities are composed of species that vary greatly in their reliance on mycorrhizal fungi with root colonization varying between 12-80% among common plant species. This summer, I will build on this work by continuing my observational and experimental work. I will also add an ecosystem component to my work, by measuring carbon pools and stocks.
ResearchPlanOrganisms: Arbuscular mycorrhizal fungi and plant hosts
Subject: Climate Change

ResearchPlanTitle: Altitudinal distributions of bumble bees
ResearchPlanAbstract: Animal distributions are predicted to move upward on mountains as climate changes. Data on bumble bee distributions are available around RMBL from 1974, 1998, 2006, 2007. By updating those surveys , we can determine whether these movements are taking place.
Subject: Climate Change

ResearchPlanTitle: Mating System Dynamics of the Alpine Butterfly Parnassius Smintheus
ResearchPlanAbstract: I will describe various aspects of the Parnassius smintheus mating system through observational and experimental methods. In summer 2014 I will investigate how local topography may serve as a source of environmental variation that elicits variation in mating behaviors of both sexes Parnassius smintheus, and the consequences for mating system dynamics.
Subject: Other

ResearchPlanTitle: Quantifying environmental and biological controls on soil CO2 fluxes in East River valley forests
ResearchPlanAbstract: My proposed research seeks to mechanistically understand soil respiration in the dominant forest communities around the RMBL by individually quantifying the contributions from its two sources, plants and microbes.  To do this, I will combine automated measurements of soil CO2 concentrations and soil respiration with isotope (radiocarbon, 14C) source partitioning methods in two vegetation communities (spruce/fir and aspen forests) located in the RMBL research meadow.  This novel approach will provide information on how environmental and biological factors control plant and microbial respiration sources of CO2 to the atmosphere, and assess potential climate change impacts on ecosystems in the East River valley.
Subject: Climate Change

ResearchPlanTitle: Collection of Colias sp. for whole genome sequencing
ResearchPlanAbstract: My graduate research has been focused on dormancy (hibernation) of insects, which is an important adaptation to survive winter and also to synchronize life-cycles with important events (eg. host-plant and mate emergence). Many aspects of dormancy are poorly understood and especially the genetic variants that alter the dormancy response. In the Rocky Mountains there are three species of butterflies: Colias philodice lives at the lowest elevations (8,000 ft), C. alexandra lives at the middle elevations (8-11,000 ft), and C. meadii lives at the highest elevations (11,500 ft). The curiosity of these butterflies is that C. philodice and C. meadii have an optional dormancy, whereas C. alexandra have an obligate dormancy. This provides an interesting system to study dormancy and how it can be altered in different species. I ultimately will use whole genome sequencing to look for genes that show strong differentiation between the species which will illuminate candidates for an obligate vs. optional dormancy response. Ideally I would like population samples of 20 individuals of each species.
ResearchPlanOrganisms: Colias philodice, C. alexandra, and C. meadii
Subject: Phenology

ResearchPlanTitle: DIversity of microbiota in bumble bees of the Rocky Mountains
ResearchPlanAbstract: We are investigating the microorganisms, both bacterial and viral, that live in bumble bee guts. Bumble bees are among the most threatened species, and their microbiota plays both beneficial and harmful roles. We are finding out if each species has different bacteria and viruses, or if these are spread across species. In some cases this spillover of organisms could contribute to declining populations. We are going to determine if bees at higher elevations are relatively disease free because they are less exposed to honey bees, an introduced pollinator that has been shown to spread viral disease to native bumble bee populations in other places.
Subject: Pollination

ResearchPlanTitle: Long term studies of plant evolution in an era of global change
ResearchPlanAbstract: An understanding of evolution in natural populations often requires long-term field studies. Over the next five years, I propose studies of two major questions related to evolution and how evolution is influenced by global change. These projects capitalize on prior knowledge gained from my 30 years at RMBL studying Ipomopsis (scarlet gilia and slendertube skyrocket) and other plants. First, I will continue to measure natural selection on vegetative and flower traits to determine the sensitivity of natural selection to snowmelt date and summer precipitation. These data will also be used to predict responses of plant populations to climate change. Second, I will characterize how pollination and herbivory together generate natural selection favoring specific combinations of plant traits that work together in synergy. This second project will incorporate study of how insects respond to plant fragrance compounds, expanding knowledge of this poorly understood sensory mode.
Subject: Long-Term

ResearchPlanTitle: Ecology of glacier lilies
ResearchPlanAbstract: As part of long term studies now in their third decade, I annually measure the rate of pollination and seed set of a population of glacier lilies. I also collect demographic data on about 220 plants maintained in a transplant garden, to determine how long-term growth and survival are related to pollination and sexual reproduction.
Subject: Long-Term

ResearchPlanInstitution: University of Copenhagen/ University of Tennessee
ResearchPlanTitle: Global Change in Mountains
ResearchPlanAbstract: Plant and soil communities interact with each other in a diversity of ways running the gamut from positive to negative. These interactions result in services humans rely on such as water purification and carbon sequestration. Global changes, such as species invasions and warming, are altering the ways plant and soil communities interact. Thus, understanding plant-soil interactions will help us predict how the ecosystem services humans rely on will respond to global change.
ResearchPlanOrganisms: Ha, I love this - Plants and soils - Carbon and water, Fungi and bacteria - possibly ants/
Subject: Climate Change

ResearchPlanTitle: Phenology, flower albedo, & soil moisture: a positive feedback between vegetation and climate change? AND Effects of pollination success on plant demography
ResearchPlanAbstract: Earlier biological events are a hallmark of climate change across the globe. Indeed, many wildflowers are blooming earlier in the Rocky Mountains as the climate changes. Some plant species counter intuitively suffer increased frost damage when spring comes early; this happens because temperatures can still dip below freezing in June, even if the snow melts early. We are studying whether or not this loss of flowers alters the amount of sunlight that is reflected back from the Earth's surface. Green leaves reflect less light than yellow flowers, which could result in even warmer and drier soils in years when snowmelt is early. Understanding these relationships among biological timing, flowers, sunlight, and climate are critical for accurate predictions of how our natural areas will respond to future climatic changes.
Subject: Climate Change

ResearchPlanTitle: Ecological Significance of Pollen Secondary Chemistry
ResearchPlanAbstract: The goal of this study is to understand the ecological significance of secondary compounds in pollen. Secondary compounds are fundamental to plant defense against herbivores. However, these same compounds are expressed in floral rewards, including pollen and nectar. While the ecological significance of nectar secondary compounds is well explored, the importance of pollen secondary compounds for plants, pollinators, and their interactions is almost unknown. Through a series of observational studies and experiments, we will study the ecological significance of secondary compounds of pollen in the subalpine larkspur (Delphinium barbeyi, Ranunculaceae). We will measure D. barbeyi pollen secondary compound identities and concentrations and compare them to other plant tissues and rewards. We will then ask (1) how D. barbeyi pollen affects bumble bee pollinator pollen collection behaviors and colony fitness, (2) whether D. barbeyi pollen secondary chemistry affects pollen-pollen interactions at the stigma surface, and (3) the degree to which D. barbeyi pollen may be adaptive. This work will expand our understanding of the roles secondary compounds play in plant-pollinator interactions and plant and pollinator fitness. More broadly, the synthesis of our findings will build a more integrative understanding of the ecological significance and evolutionary consequences of consumptive interactions between plants and animals.
ResearchPlanOrganisms: Delphinium barbeyi, other co-occurring plant species, Bombus flavifrons, Bombus appositus
Subject: Pollination

ResearchPlanTitle: Dwarfs on purpose: Comparative ecological genetics of adaptation in the high elevation endemic Mimulus tilingii
Subject: Long-Term

ResearchPlanTitle: Uncovering the mechanisms of change in plant reproduction and plant-pollinator interactions due to early snowmelt and frost events
ResearchPlanAbstract: Phenology is an important life history trait that allows an organism to perform synchronously with itâ€™s environment. An organismâ€™s phenology is dependent on abiotic cues, such as precipitation, temperature, and photoperiod. Over the past 50 years, climate change has altered these abiotic conditions, thus altering the phenology of organisms in both terrestrial and aquatic ecosystems. Because plants are dependent on annual weather conditions, their phenology can respond rapidly to climate change. In sub-alpine regions where plant phenology is strongly linked to the timing of snowmelt, we might start to see spring plants bloom earlier each year due to thinner snowpack and earlier melting. Although long-term research on plants has shown that climate change is altering their phenology, we do not know how altered phenology directly and indirectly affects plant growth and reproduction. For example, phenological changes expose plants to altered abiotic conditions, such as temperature, precipitation, soil moisture, and nitrogen availability, which might directly affect plants by impacting growth or reducing reproductive potential. Additionally, early snowmelt might put plants at a greater risk of exposure to spring frost, which can delay flowering time or kill the plants completely. Early snowmelt and frost events can also have indirect effects by altering interactions between plants and their associated organisms, such as herbivores and pollinators. In order to examine these direct and indirect effects, I will use a series of field experiments in which I manipulate snowmelt timing and frost exposure to address the following questions: 1) How do changes in abiotic conditions due to early snowmelt directly affect plant growth, floral traits, and plant reproduction, and 2) What are the indirect effects of altered phenology on plant reproduction through changes in plant-pollinator and plant-herbivore interactions?
Subject: Climate Change

ResearchPlanTitle: Bees sharing plants and plants sharing bees: diurnal bumble bee foraging patterns and allelopathic pollen
ResearchPlanAbstract: Bumble bee species can greatly overlap in the floral resources they use. Iâ€™m interested in whether bumble bee species show predictable patterns in how they share floral resources throughout the day. That is, do individual plant species tend to receive more visits from one species of bumble bee in the morning, and a different species in the afternoon? If patterns exist, there are practical implications for sampling bumble bee distributions across an altitudinal gradient. Sampling tends to occur non-randomly (climbing up the mountain in the morning and down in the afternoon), which could result in missed and biased species sightings due to non-random daily foraging patterns of bees. Of less pragmatic interest, non-random patterns in bumble bee foraging could affect competitive interactions among bumble bee species. Just as multiple bee species can share a common plant species, multiple plant species may share a common pollinator. When pollinators are inconstant foragers (i.e., switching between plant species) there will be improper transfer of one speciesâ€™ pollen to the other speciesâ€™ stigmas. This can cause problems if the pollen from the donor plant contains biochemicals that impact the success of the correctly deposited pollen, known as pollen allelopathy. In June, I will continue investigations started by the Thomson lab on the importance of deposition of allelopathic dandelion pollen on native wildflowers at the RMBL. Later, I will test other species to identify a system for further research. A prime pair of candidate species will be aspen sunflower and sneezeweed.
ResearchPlanOrganisms: Bumble bees, dandelions, various wildflowers (aspen sunflower, sneezeweed)
Subject: Pollination

ResearchPlanTitle: How do joint spatial and temporal shifts affect plant-pollinator interactions along elevational gradients?
ResearchPlanAbstract: Species are shifting in space and time in response to climate change, and these shifts can both expose species to novel abiotic environments and alter their interactions with other species. Much concern about the effects of climate change-induced shifts has been focused on plant-pollinator interactions, which require plants and pollinators to align in sometimes narrow windows of space and time. We propose to study how interactions among bumble bees and forbs have changed in association with documented spatial and temporal shifts that are known to have occurred in the last 40 years at the Rocky Mountain Biological Lab. In particular, we plan to resample established elevational transects to determine if the degree of temporal overlap has changed as a result of upward shifts of bumble bees and/or earlier flowering of forbs. This work will add botanical depth to studies that have heretofore been focused primarily on bees. We also aim to determine if there is evidence for shifts in bumble bee phenology and forb ranges. We will use both observational and manipulative approaches, recording bumble bee visits and performing hand pollinations and reciprocal seed transplants. The data will provide insight into how bumble bee-forb interactions have changed and whether these changes are due to joint spatial and temporal shifts, which have rarely been studied together.
Subject: Pollination

ResearchPlanTitle: Elucidating Hydrogeochemical Processes in the Upper East River Catchment
Subject: Climate Change

ResearchPlanTitle: Constraints on local adaptation: the roles of cue similarity and gene flow in maintaining an evolutionary trap
ResearchPlanAbstract: Locally adapted populations are common, and the processes that promote or constrain divergence among populations over small geographic scales have been widely explored. Yet, it is still unclear how these processes operate in cases of persistent maladaptive behaviors, such as occur in evolutionary traps. Rapid environmental changes can disrupt specialized recognition systems that organisms depend on to successfully interact with their environment, wherein responses to previously reliable cues result in preference for a poorer quality resource. While there is some evidence of local, adaptive â€˜escapeâ€™ from evolutionary traps, many organisms encountering these novel selection pressures show no change in the maladaptive behavior. This is the case with the native herbivore/invasive plants system I propose to study. Pieris macdunnoughii recognizes Thlaspi arvense as a potential host, but the plant is lethal to all larvae. Over many generations of exposure to T. arvense, a population of P. macdunnoughii butterflies at Gothic, CO, have shown no change in preference for the plant. I will explore the evolutionary mechanisms maintaining this evolutionary trap, examining the variation and heritability of egg-laying preference traits in several populations of P. macdunnoughii, genetic connectivity of these populations, and differences in selection pressures across invaded environments. The proposed work will span three years and will build on several decades of research conducted at the Rocky Mountain Biological Laboratory.
ResearchPlanOrganisms: Pieris macdunnoughii (Pieridae, Lepidoptera), Thlaspi arvense (Lepidea, Brassicacea)
Subject: Long-Term

ResearchPlanTitle: Evolutionary Ecology and Conservation Biology of Amphibians
ResearchPlanAbstract: Chytridiomycosis (chytrid) is a fungal infection that is decimating amphibian populations globally. In south-central Colorado, chytrid has been negatively impacting the endangered boreal toad. While research exists about how chytrid infects amphibians, studies explaining how it is spreading or what abiotic and biotic conditions can impact its spread are extremely limited. My research goal is to expand on this information by creating a distribution model of chytrid presence in south-central Colorado while highlighting areas that are most susceptible to infection. I will be incorporating a variety of variables â€“ including, but not limited to, hydrography, animal movements and migration, precipitation, and topography â€“ into my model to determine optimal chytrid habitat. Once completed, this information will be presented to Colorado Parks and Wildlife to aid in boreal toad restoration and conservation efforts. While the boreal toad is the focal species for this research, they are reclusive and rare due to their decreasing populations. Therefore, tiger salamanders and chorus frogs will be the primary focal species used to determine chytrid presence at a site.
ResearchPlanOrganisms: Bufo boreas boreas (boreal toad), Ambystoma tigrinum nebulosum (Arizona tiger salamander), Pseudacris spp. (chorus frogs)
Subject: Climate Change

ResearchPlanTitle: Examining reproductive isolation and trait adaptation in Mertensia brevistyla and M. fusiformis
ResearchPlanAbstract: There are about 352,000 species of flowering plants in this world. This incredible flora diversity is largely generated by biological differences between species and maintained by processes that prevent mating between species. Reproductive isolation may depend on spatial and temporal distribution of flowering species, pollinators' behaviors, pollinators' and flowers' morphologies, and/or survival and fertility of hybrids. To understand how species diversify and evolve, I am investigating barriers that prevent hybridization between two species that share similar geographic distribution and flowering time. Furthermore, I am examining the biotic and abiotic selective agents that act on floral orientation as a potential reproductive barrier between the species. For this research, I am focusing on two closely related bluebell species (Mertensia brevistyla and M. fusiformis) that co-occur at Kebler Pass. I will be conducting observational and experimental studies to record pollinator assemblages and pollen movement between the two species. In an experimental study, I will manipulate floral orientation in both species and test the effects of pollinator visitation and handling time, and water and temperature inside flowers on plant reproductive success. These studies will help determine how pollinators and/or environmental conditions select for certain floral traits, which may ultimately promote reproductive isolation between species.
Subject: Pollination

ResearchPlanTitle: Ecological Genetics of Boechera stricta
ResearchPlanAbstract: Few studies have identified the genes that underlie ecologically important trait variation in nature and the evolutionary processes that influence these polymorphisms. To understand the adaptive consequences of complex trait variation, we must establish a direct relationship between genetic polymorphisms and phenotypic traits, and investigate the fitness consequences of this variation in natural environments. Here we propose to identify genes controlling complex traits in nature, to examine ecological and molecular evidence for natural selection, and to involve undergraduates in data collection and statistical analyses of ecologically important traits in the field.
Subject: Other

ResearchPlanTitle: Herbivory and Harvest in Ligusticum porteri
ResearchPlanAbstract: Plants are targeted by a variety of consumers--from insect herbivores to human harvesters. My research explains patterns of harvest and herbivory and describes how plant populations respond. My present focus is on the ant-aphid-Ligusticum system. Aphids are small herbivores that colonize the flower clusters of Ligusticum. Ants are mutualist partners of aphids: they protect aphids from predators in exchange for sugary honeydew. Experimental field work revealed that ants are attentive mutualist partners in open meadows, but much less so in the aspen understory. Current project seek to determine the mechanism for the breakdown of this mutualism in the shade. I have also conducted a harvest sustainability study for Ligusticum, since this plant is a popular herbal antibiotic.
ResearchPlanOrganisms: Ligusticum porteri, Aphis helianthi, Lygus and ants (4 groups)
Subject: Other

ResearchPlanTitle: Competition dynamics of pollinators and nectar robbers: how differences in foraging strategy can alter competitive ability through changes in foraging efficiency
ResearchPlanAbstract: Species interactions, including mutualism, are thought to happen in a multi-species context. Pollination, a classic example of mutualism, is no exception. Plants interact with multiple pollinator species, and recent research has examined how those pollinator species compete for nectar benefits provided by the plant. Additionally, some species that pollinate in some contexts act as "nectar robbers" in others. Nectar robbers remove nectar from flowers from a hole chewed at the base of the flower, rather than foraging "legitimately" through the floral opening. My research investigates whether species that switch between legitimate foraging and nectar robbing are able to gain a competitive advantage over species that only forage legitimately by increasing their foraging efficiency.
ResearchPlanOrganisms: Bombus appositus, Bombus bifarius, Corydalis caseana
Subject: Pollination

ResearchPlanTitle: Patterns of pollinator species and functional diversity across a climate: Implications for plant reproduction
ResearchPlanAbstract: My research seeks to understand whether the diversity of pollinators visiting native flower species changes across elevation, and if so, are there repercussions for pollination and reproduction of those plants? I am also interested in whether the identity of pollinators, i.e. what species they are, reflects their importance for the local pollination community, or whether their functional traits - specific morphologies or behaviors that are potentially important for pollination - more accurately reflect their relative contributions. As climates continue to warm and species adapt and move, it is crucial to understand the underlying importance of biodiversity for plant community persistence.
Subject: Pollination

ResearchPlanTitle: King of the hill? Climate change effects on biotic interactions in alpine plant communities.
ResearchPlanAbstract: Climate change is causing speciesâ€™ ranges to shift1. While observations of species range movements and local extinctions are common, few studies have tested the mechanisms causing these range shifts. To understand the causes of range movements, itâ€™s important to first understand what causes a speciesâ€™ to have a geographical range. A possible explanation for range boundaries is the Dobzhansky-MacArthur hypothesis (D-MH), which proposes that species ranges are most limited by inhospitable abiotic conditions (e.g., low temperature) at their high altitude/latitude range boundaries, and by biotic interactions (e.g., competition) at their low altitude/latitude boundaries2. In mountain ecosystems, plant distributions show natural boundaries at elevation limits that are replicated across many peaks, providing a tractable system to test the D-MH in the context of climate change. The abiotic limitation of species high range limits is well supported3,4, so I focus on the biotic limitation aspect of the D-MH and propose two transplant experiments to evaluate the intensity of competition at speciesâ€™ low elevation range limits: 1) Do low elevation plant competitors reduce the fitness of alpine plant species to a greater extent than alpine competitors? and assess the intensity of natural enemy attack at low elevation range limits: 2A) Do low elevation insect herbivores and fungal pathogens suppress the fitness of alpine plant species more than high elevation herbivores and pathogens? 2B) Does the negative effect of insects or pathogens on plant fitness intensify with warming along a natural climate gradient? To test these questions, I will transplant alpine plant species at the center of their ranges and below their current low altitude range boundaries in order to simulate current vs. future climate regimes as well as the current and novel biotic community. We will combine transplants with manipulations of competition and insect/pathogen damage to assess the importance of intensified antagonistic interactions as a potential cause of upward range shifts. My work will complement a newly funded NSF project investigating beneficial plant-fungal symbioses along elevation gradients.
Subject: Climate Change

ResearchPlanTitle: Beyond the ecological: can presence of an invader affect floral selection in a native species?
ResearchPlanAbstract: Biological invasions are known to have tangible economical and ecological effects on the invaded ecosystem. A common trend is that native plant species are negatively affected by the presence of an invasive plant species. As the amount of pristine ecosystems decreases and the amount of invaded non-pristine areas increases, we need to start thinking about the effects that invasive species could have on the evolution of native species. In other words, can native species adapt to invasions? Here I propose to study the evolutionary and ecological effects that the invasive plant Linaria vulgaris (butter and eggs) has on the native plant Penstemon strictus (Rocky Mountain Penstemon). I will observe plants of P. strictus in the absence and presence of L. vulgaris. I will document pollinator visitations to P. strictus and pair these observations with floral measurements of these plants. This way I will be able to analyze whether or not the presence of L. vulgaris causes changes in the traits that the pollinators are selecting for in P. strictus (traits like flower size and nectar production). A change in natural selection with the presence of L. vulgaris would suggest that the invader has an evolutionary effect. To study the ecological effects of L. vulgaris on P. strictus, I will look at whether P. strictus fruit production and pollinator visitation is different in the presence and absence of L. vulgaris. Finally I will study whether different types of pollinators move different amounts of L. vulgaris pollen to individuals of P. strictus. This is of particular interest because foreign pollen (pollen from another species) can reduce the reproductive success of a species.
ResearchPlanOrganisms: Penstemon strictus Benth. [Scrophulariaceae] and Linaria vulgaris Mill. [Scrophulariaceae]
Subject: Pollination

ResearchPlanTitle: Baetis parasitism in a changing environment
ResearchPlanOrganisms: Baetis bicaudatus (Ephemeroptera) and Gasteromermis spp. (Nematoda: Mermithidae)
Subject: Other

ResearchPlanTitle: Ecology and evolution of flowering plants in a changing climate
ResearchPlanAbstract: Due to human consumption of natural resources and production of industrial pollutants, global changes are occurring, from rising temperatures to increased variability of weather patterns. Humans, animals, and plants are affected by these changes and will continue to face uncertainty in the future. One noticeable change in our ecosystem is earlier appearance of vegetation and flowers. Although reproduction may only occur a couple of weeks earlier than a few decades ago, these changes may influence how plants and their pollinators interact. In Colorado, wildflower communities are particularly susceptible to these changes because flowering too early may expose them to frost. Therefore, understanding if these changes will eventually reduce overall population size is vital. This summer, I propose to examine how flowering species in Colorado are affected by earlier flowering and if and what the consequences may be for future population growth.
ResearchPlanOrganisms: Castilleja sulphurea, Polemonium viscossum, Mertensia oblongifolia
Subject: Phenology

ResearchPlanTitle: Integrating Ecological Stoichiometry and Disease
ResearchPlanAbstract: Ecologists have made great strides in understanding how species interactions and abiotic conditions can mediate infectious diseases. However, the role of host diet quality, or nutrition, in disease is less well understood, especially in the context of ecological stoichiometry (the balance of multiple chemicals in ecological interactions and processes). The goal of the proposed research is to explore how changes in the form and availability of nutrients propagate through food webs to affect infectious disease, and how infection can alter a species role in the flux of nutrients through an ecosystem. I propose to study how changes in the algal community in streams around RMBL are related to the prevalence and virulence of whirling disease in trout. I am also interested in how infection in trout and other aquatic organisms can affect ecosystem processes such as nutrient cycling. This work is expected to not just increase our understanding of whirling disease, but infectious disease in general, and to have important implications for other wildlife and human diseases.
ResearchPlanOrganisms: Myxobolus cerebralis, Tuifex tubifex, Brook trout (Salvelinus fontinalis), & Rainbow trout (Oncorhynchus mykiss)
Subject: Other

ResearchPlanTitle: Belowground consequences of aboveground symbioses under climate change
ResearchPlanAbstract: Leaf litter decomposition is fundamental to global carbon and nitrogen cycles, recycling nutrients to soil and plant communities and thereby affecting ecosystem function and productivity. Understanding how climate change will affect leaf litter decomposition is important to predicting how ecosystems will respond to global change. While belowground decomposers are well-known drivers of decomposition, little work has examined the role of aboveground microbes, particularly those that reside in living plants. Plant leaves host a diversity of endophytic fungi, which may influence decomposition rates by affecting litter chemistry and the decomposer community; however, no studies have considered how aboveground microbes may influence litter decomposition under differing climate scenarios. To address how aboveground microbes affect litter decomposition under differing climate and temperature regimes, this study will ask: 1) How does fungal endophyte symbiosis affect litter decomposition along altitudinal gradients? and 2) How does endophyte symbiosis affect litter decomposition under experimental warming? To our knowledge, this work will be the first test for interactions between aboveground microbes and decomposers under climate change scenarios in montane and alpine environments. The study will therefore increase understanding of how climate shifts may influence decomposition in globally important systems.
ResearchPlanOrganisms: Festuca thurberi, Poa leptocoma, Trisetum spicatum, EpichloÃ« sp.
Subject: Climate Change

ResearchPlanTitle: Biodiversity of aquatic macroinvertebrates, midges (Diptera: Chironomidae) and spiders (Araneae) at the Mexican Cut Nature Preserve and Upper Gunnison Basin.
ResearchPlanAbstract: The biodiversity, life history and distribution of aquatic macroinvertebrates is key to understanding biomonitoring data and interpreting the health of our local streams and ponds. My research will continue to help us understand the invertebrates of the upper Gunnison basin. I am also working with the “Colorado Spider Survey” at the Denver Museum of Nature and Science. As a part of this survey, I am collecting spiders in the Mexican Cut Nature Preserve along with my collections in the surrounding National Forest Lands. In addition the tiny flies called midges are common, diverse and notoriously difficult to identify. They are an interesting group because of their sensitivity to various pollutants and are often used for biomonitoring. The Mexican Cut Chironomids have been identified to genus, but further identification has awaited rearing the larvae to adults. Regular collections throughout the spring, summer, and fall can help us determine which species are present, the number of generations per year and whether each taxa is sensitive to weather events such as drought or the differences in water chemistry and predation between the various ponds at the Mexican Cut.
ResearchPlanOrganisms: Aquatic macroinvertebrates, with an emphasis on midges as well as spiders
Subject: Long-Term

ResearchPlanTitle: Individual bumble bee foraging behaviour in the context of climate change
ResearchPlanAbstract: This research addresses how bumble bees might respond to changes in the wildflower community that are driven by climate change. The wildflower community is changing around the Rocky Mountain Biological Laboratory: the season is extending and flowers are declining mid-season, while some key plant species have fewer flowers in years with early snowmelt. It is important to understand how bumble bees respond to this trend toward fewer floral resources, because colonies need to forage on a series of flowers throughout the growing season to grow and reproduce. However, we do not know how flexible individual foragers are in their flower choices over time. If individuals are flexible when resources are scarce, this may bode well for their population persistence under continued climate change. I am proposing to uniquely mark individual bumble bees of multiple species in meadows with low and high floral resources, and record what flower types each bee visits within and across foraging bouts. I will also document overall bumble bee abundances in these meadows, to document floral associations at the species level. These details of individual foraging behaviour are fundamental to bumble bee ecology, but are largely unknown.
ResearchPlanOrganisms: Bumble bees and the flowers they visit
Subject: Pollination

ResearchPlanTitle: Estimates of effective population size across a community of herbaceous plants
ResearchPlanAbstract: Climate change poses a very real threat to all natural ecosystems. As conditions change contemporary plant communities will experience environments that are substantially different from historical norms. This transition in conditions will result in concurrent selection for all members of a community, only some of which may effectively mount an adaptive response. Predictions for which species may persist via adaptation, or become extirpated can be made through comparisons of effective population size; a term that generally describes the capacity of a population to respond to selection. By using genomic data and coalescent models, I will estimate historic effective population sizes for each species within a local herbaceous community, to derive general predictions about community change over the course of adaptation. Additionally, I will combine these data with those from other communities to explore whether factors such as endemism, phylogenetic similarity, habitat consistency, and range size contribute to the relationships between census and effective population sizes.
ResearchPlanOrganisms: Herbaceous plants of the sub-alpine community
Subject: Climate Change

ResearchPlanTitle: Larval performance of Parnassius smintheus as a function of host plant and host plant rearing conditions
ResearchPlanAbstract: Parnassius butterfly larvae and eggs will be collected during the first year. Larvae will be used both years for experiments with both host plants. Questions posed will involve the larval butterfly preference for and performance on its host plants.
Subject: Other

ResearchPlanTitle: Evaluating the utility of sediment records near RMBL for paleoenvironmental analysis
ResearchPlanAbstract: Lake sediments can provide valuable records of past ecology, disturbance, and climate. The primary goal of this yearâ€™s research is to evaluate the potential of lake sediments near RMBL as paleoenvironmental records. This will be accomplished by recovering several sediment cores and the imaging of sediment profiles and lake basins using ground penetrating radar.
Subject: Climate Change

ResearchPlanTitle: Evolutionary ecology of schistosomes in North America
ResearchPlanAbstract: Avian schistosomes (~14 genera) belong to a family (Schistosomatidae) of trematodes that live in the mesenteric blood system of birds and mammals. They have a two host life cycle, using marine and freshwater aquatic snails as intermediate hosts. Avian schistosomes are globally distributed, predominately in birds that use water, waterfowl in particular. Schistosomes are most well known for two diseases, human schistosomiasis (some mammalian schistosomes), and their cause of cercarial dermatitis, or swimmerâ€™s itch (mostly avian schistosomes, but some mammalian too) in people. In the case of swimmerâ€™s itch, larvae emerging from the snails look for a bird host, but can accidentally penetrate people, causing an allergic reaction of intense itching at site of contact for about a week. A majority of the swimmerâ€™s itch reports are from recreational water sites around the world and areas where aquaculture (e.g. rice field) requires people to work in water. A large gap in our knowledge has been how many species of schistosomes are there, and in what hosts and where do they occur? These questions are critical to addressing the natural history of the parasite as well as the disease dynamic predictions. These questions are essentially being addressed in a grant proposal to collect schistosomes from key places around the world, with a focus in North America. Several interesting patterns have emerged, however, one in particular requires additional sampling. Based on data collected by Dr. John Mischler and my previous collections, it looks like there might be a couple of species of schistosomes that are found only at high elevation (RMBL) and high latitude (Churchill Manitoba and Edmonton Alberta, thus far). Reasons for this are yet unknown, but are suspected to be related to the particular snail host (Stagnicola) and migratory habitat preferences of the duck host. Right now however we do not yet know the bird (definitive) host. In addition to the schistosome work, very little survey work has been completed on snail-trematode dynamics, and none at high elevation. The affect of land use/environmental changes on snail-trematode communities has rarely been address. This is surprising given that trematodes in particular are tropically transmitted, and thus are indicators of ecosystem diversity and change. Dr. John Mischler for his dissertation thesis address change in trematode communities in snails compared to a study done in the same area in the 1950â€™s due to changes in land use as well as yearly impact of, for example, early or late arrival of spring. For trematodes and snails to become active after winter, they require a certain number of consecutive warm temperatures before the snails are active, then following that is trematode activity. Plus, new infections of next generation of snails canâ€™t take place unless the hosts are visiting the water sites. These data will contribute to our overall understanding of how snail-trematode dynamics reflect ecosystem changes, and thus also our ability to predict the appearance of particular parasites, importantly those that cause disease in people or domestic animals. Thus the goal of these collections are to 1) continue collections of avian schistosomes in high elevation to determine if they are particular to high elevation/latitude as well as to asses overall schistosome diversity at high latitude relative to past collections around North America and 2) to collect snails and trematodes at 2-3 points from June-August to determine snail and trematode diversity across the summer and related that back to past collections from the same ponds as well as climate data. In 2012, there was early snow melt, and the diversity of trematodes, particularly avian schistosomes was high (Mischler unplublished). However, in 2014, no schistosomes were found, snail densities were low and trematode diversity was also low (Mischler and Brant ,unpublished). Thus far in 2015, it appears snow pack is low at RMBL, and thus we will see if we can predict that there should be higher diversity of schistosomes and other trematodes as there was in 2012, or if other factors might play a role in determining the patterns we find at the end of this year.
Subject: Climate Change

ResearchPlanTitle: Sweat bee transcriptome
ResearchPlanAbstract: Sweat bees are plastic in their social behavior; some exhibit complex eusocial behavior, others are solitary, and a few straddle these two extremes of sociality. One such example is Halictus rubicundus, which is eusocial at low altitudes (e.g. Salt Lake City) but solitary at high altitudes (e.g. RMBL). This project explores the genetic underpinning of the differences in social behavior in this species by using next generation sequencing approaches to identify genes that differ consistently between eusocial and solitary forms.
ResearchPlanOrganisms: Halictus rubicundus, a common and widespread sweat bee
Subject: Other

ResearchPlanTitle: Genetic basis of rust fungi-induced pseudoflower formation in Boechera stricta
ResearchPlanAbstract: Our abstract was sent to the science director in an email.

ResearchPlanTitle: Investigating Plant-Herbivore Relationships in Boechera stricta in a Climate Change Context
ResearchPlanAbstract: Our study will quantify changes in insect herbivore diversity and abundance in relation to B. stricta over an elevational gradient, and produce preliminary data to model changing plant-herbivore interactions in relation to climate change. we will be answering the following questions: (1) Herbivore density decreases as elevation increases. (2) Species richness and abundance of insects will decrease as elevation increases. (3) Herbivores will experience a longer growing season at lower elevations because of earlier snow melt, causing more herbivory to occur overall at lower elevations than at higher ones.
Subject: Climate Change

ResearchPlanTitle: Effects of early snowmelt and frost on plant-pollinator interactions
ResearchPlanAbstract: Climate change is causing snow to melt earlier, which is causing some plant species to bloom earlier. These plants that bloom early are often damaged by frost. Early flowering and frost damage can affect how many pollinators visit plant species. In my study, I will use plots that have had snow removed early, plots that have been covered to protect them from frost, plots with both treatments, and plots with neither treatment, and I will compare pollinator visitation rates among these four treatments. I plan to answer the following questions: 1) How does early snowmelt and frost affect plant communities? and 2) Does variation in the phenology of flowering plants affect pollinator visitation rate?
ResearchPlanOrganisms: flowering plants and pollinators (esp. bees and flies)
Subject: Climate Change

ResearchPlanTitle: Utilization of naturalized mustard Thlaspi arvense by insect enemies along an elevational gradient and under different soil moisture conditions
ResearchPlanAbstract: Thlaspi arvense is an exotic Eurasian mustard that was introduced to this area (Gunnison Basin) in the late 1800s. It's been studied at RMBL for 40 years in relation to its relationship with native butterfly Pieris macdunnoughii, from which it elicits egg-laying behavior. Unfortunately none of the P. macdunnoughii larvae that hatch on T. arvense survive. Taking this relationship into consideration, and because we have never found live insects feeding on T. arvense and have found few signs of herbivory on the plant, I want to know if any native insects are able to eat or lay eggs on T. arvense. I'll explore this by conducting herbivory surveys on T. arvense quadrats along an elevational gradient, as T. arvense may be subject to different herbivore communities or environmental stressors at different elevations. I'll also include a water exclusion treatment, since drought conditions may affect defensive chemical production and therefore may also affect amount and type of herbivory experienced by the T. arvense individuals. I also am interested in finding out if insects that use native mustards are able to consume or lay eggs on T. arvense. I'll collect herbivores of native mustards from the field and introduce them to potted T. arvense individuals, noting any amount and type of herbivory, as well as the survival status of the insect on a daily basis. With this research I hope to resolve some of the questions surrounding T. arvense and its possible enemies in this part of its naturalized range.
Subject: Phenology

ResearchPlanTitle: Vegetative Cover and Elevation; Predictors of Singing Male Sparrow Densities?
ResearchPlanAbstract: See undergraduate research proposal submission.

ResearchPlanTitle: Environmental Fitness Correlates and Fitness Consequences of Flower Color Polymorphisms in Boechera Stricta
ResearchPlanAbstract: Boechera stricta exhibit a color polymorphism in which flower petals may vary from white to pink to purple. Because this mustard is primarily self-pollinating, this color change is most likely not a result of pollinator selection. Instead, other factors like soil pH, extreme temperatures, drought, and herbivory may be selecting for the production of darker pigments because chemicals produced in the pigment- creating pathway may help plants deal with stressful conditions. I plan to study these environmental factors that may be correlated with pigment production to understand why this polymorphism exists in Boechera stricta.
Subject: Other

ResearchPlanTitle: How does a Heterogeneous Environment's Moisture Content Affect Plant Traits
ResearchPlanAbstract: An organismâ€™s niche and its functional traits are perpetually intertwined. A plantâ€™s functional traits vary due a multitude of different evolutionary and environmental factors. Because of the multitude of different elements that form a plantâ€™s traits and environmentâ€”a casual model between the two is difficult to establish. An organismâ€™s niche could be thought of the environment in which it functions and effectsâ€”and a its functional traits help it to function properly within its environment. But does the plant have its functional traits so it can be successful within its environment, or does its function traits help to shape its environment? While this question has not been answered, it is know that a plantâ€™s traits reflect its ecological strategies. For example, most cacti live in extremely hot environments, so their strategic response is to have a thick, fleshy body to help store water and nutrients. An environmental filter is the determining factor of what environment a species can properly function in, thus so, it is pivotal in community assembly. As environmental variance expands, so does the range of environmental filtersâ€”as there are more options in which an organism can function. However, only a few studies have been conducted that look at the correlations between functional traits and environmental heterogeneity. This study aims to fink a linkage between trait variance and environmental variance in alpine environments. It plans to do this by looking at the functional traits of different organisms in plots with varying levels of ecological richness.
Subject: Other

ResearchPlanTitle: Exploring the rules influencing aggregation and sociality in a facultatively social species, yellow-bellied marmots (Marmota flaviventris)
ResearchPlanAbstract: Animal aggregation is one of the most basic and widespread social phenomena and plays a significant role in the development of sociality in many species. Many previous studies, however, have tended to focus on obligately social species. Limited progress has been made on observing the factors determining group formation and social interaction development in facultatively social animals. Thus, we aim to explore the rules that influence social interaction and hence social structure in a facultatively social species, yellow-bellied marmots (Marmota flaviventris). In particular, our project will address two main questions: (1) How do yellow-bellied marmots decide whether or not to belong to a social group? and (2) How do yellow-bellied marmots decide whether or not to interact with other group members? We plan to answer these questions by creating models that capture the social mechanisms under which these animals aggregate and form social networks. Ultimately, we hope to provide a more comprehensive picture of how ecological factors act to change behavioral conditions and social tendencies in a facultatively social species.
Subject: Long-Term

ResearchPlanTitle: Latitudinal variation of flowering and fruiting phenology in Boechera stricta: testing for adaptive response to climate across the species range
ResearchPlanAbstract: The timing of plant life cycle events (phenology), such as flowering and fruit maturation, is considered especially responsive to the environmental shifts associated with anthropogenic climate change (Prendeville et al. 2013). Comparing phenological trait variations among genotypes originating from across a range-wide latitudinal gradient, when grown in a common garden, can provide insight into future population performance (Paccard et al. 2013). Local adaptation should cause each population to evolve advantageous phenological traits based on the environmental conditions in its place of origin. If a population cannot adaptively keep pace with the changing climate, traits that previously provided an advantage may become unfavorable, therefore causing a decline in reproductive success and overall fitness (Kawecki & Ebert, 2004). On a system scale, species across trophic levels may differ in their physiological or life-history responses to novel environmental conditions, disrupting previously synchronous relationships, such as those involving pollination, seed dispersal, food sources, or habitat (Parmesan, 2006). Boechera stricta (Brassicaceae) is a short-lived perennial forb native to western North America. A broad geographic and environmental distribution makes B. stricta an excellent species in which to examine trait variation among populations (Rushworth, Song, Lee, & Mitchell-Olds, 2011). Intraspecific populations existing over an elevation gradient often adjust functional traits in accordance with variation in environmental conditions (Anderson, Inouye, Mckinney, Colautti, Mitchell-Olds, 2012). A recent study by Anderson and Gezon (2014) conducted at Rocky Mountain Biological Laboratory (RMBL; Gothic, Gunnison County, Colorado) showed both plasticity and heritable genetic variation in flowering time among discrete local populations of B. stricta, but comparative studies quantifying differences in phenology between geographically distinct populations on a range-wide latitudinal scale have yet to be conducted. Such an investigation can provide evidence of contemporary clinal adaptation, helping elucidate the speciesâ€™ ability to adapt in accordance with current climate projections (Pratt & Mooney, 2013). Historical phenology data for many northern plant taxa indicate accelerated flowering time when grown under controlled conditions, while plants from lower latitudes show slower reproductive development. Since phenological traits are often positively correlated, it is expected that time to fruit maturation will follow a similar pattern (Prendeville et al. 2013; Paccard et al. 2013). I hypothesize that northern genotypes of B. stricta will exhibit more rapid reproductive phenology than southern genotypes when grown in a common garden, implying possible adaptive evolution of these traits to the local environmental conditions of their area of origin. Further monitoring of heritable clinal variation in phenology is necessary to predict plant fitness as climate change proceeds (Carlson, Cunningham, & Westley, 2014). With this study I propose to investigate phenological trait variation in Boechera stricta genotypes originating from populations spanning a latitudinal gradient, specifically addressing the following questions: 1) What is the extent of variation among populations in flowering and fruit maturation phenology? 2) What is the relationship between geographic origin and intraspecific phenological heterogeneity? 3) How does flowering time influence individual fitness? 4) If significant population differentiation exists, is it a result of natural selection or neutral genetic drift?
Subject: Phenology

ResearchPlanTitle: How does dust affect sexual reproduction in different plant species?
ResearchPlanAbstract: Roads not only serve as systems for efficient transportation on land, but they also serve as sources of dust. The U.S. alone has a total of 3,980,817 miles (6,406,504 km) of road, of which 2,605, 331 miles (4,192,874 km) are paved and 1,375,486 miles (2,213,630 km) of which are unpaved road.[1] On hot dry summer days, unpaved roads are more prone to dust suspension by ether cars or strong winds. When dust particles are picked up and suspended into the air, they can be transported over long distances.[2] Suspended dust can be moved on a regional, continental, and even global scale.[2] While there have been studies on the effects of roads on wildlife [3], the effects that dust has on vegetation are poorly understood. Dust can affect vegetation in several ways; a thin layer of dust can accumulate on a plants leaves, interfering with its ability to photosynthesis. In addition, dust that is small enough, has the potential of clogging up the stomataâ€™s of the plants. This can eventually lead to problems in respiration and transpiration [4]. Dust can also accumulate on a plantâ€™s flowers, potentially making them less appealing to herbivores, pollinators, and other species that use the plant for food or habitat. While our team will be collecting information that will help us understand the affects that dust has on vegetation, the main focus for this study is to determine the degree to which road dust affects sexual reproduction. We will be studying three different plant species with the goal of understanding what characteristics make a plant more susceptible to the affects that dust may have on a plants sexual reproduction.
ResearchPlanOrganisms: Three different plant species (they have yet to be decided on)

ResearchPlanTitle: Understanding the Relative Influence of Dominant and Subdominant Alpine Meadow Species on Ecosystem Carbon Dynamics using a Plant Functional Trait Approach
ResearchPlanAbstract: In my study, I will address how dominant and subdominant species alter ecosystem carbon (C ) dynamics (C input via net primary productivity and C output via soil respiration) by altering above- and belowground plant functional traits overtime. I predict that subdominant species, by having plant functional traits that represent resource conservation, will hinder ANPP and soil respiration respectively slowing down C dynamics.Twenty-four quadrants of 2m x 2m will be placed in a completely randomized design within the site, spaced 1m apart. Eight quadrants will have the dominant species removed; eight others will have the subdominant species removed; and lastly eight other quadrants will be controlsâ€”no removal done. Removal will be done by clipping the species targeted down to 1cm from the ground twice a week during the experiment duration. Community diversity of plants affects ecological processes such as carbon input and output. We will measure carbon input by quantifying leaf area index and net primary productivity as influenced by dominant and subdominant species. To determine the influence of dominant and subdominant species on carbon output, I will measure soil respiration in each of the twenty-four quadrants from 11am-2pm to analyze these processes affected by plant composition.
ResearchPlanOrganisms: Veratrum California, Delphinium barbeyi, Thalictrum fendleri,  Potentilla gracilis,Frasera speciosa

ResearchPlanTitle: The influence of genetic variation of Populus tremuloides on ant-tended aphid communities
ResearchPlanAbstract: The intricate and complex nature of ecological systems has historically limited the study of genetics to the level of pairwise interactions between organisms (Antonovics 1992). In recent years however, the growing interest in analyzing evolutionary processes between species has broadened into the field of community genetics, allowing for the examination of genetic effects on a multi-species level (Whitham 2003). These effects have been quantified in several systems, illustrating the utility of community genetics as a method for understanding the evolutionary landscape of multi-species systems (Whitham, 2006). I propose to investigate ant-aphid mutualisms present on quaking aspen (Populus tremuloides) with relation to the ploidy level of the aspen clone. This study hopes to provide further insight into how a common polymorphism in this foundational species of the Intermountain West influences associated arthropod community structure.

ResearchPlanTitle: Does snowmelt affect bumblebee colony buildup?
ResearchPlanAbstract: Bumblebees are important pollinators, especially in mountainous regions. It is important that these pollinators are protected because any change in their phenology, or the phenology of the plants they pollinate could throw our whole biosphere out of sync. My research focuses on how changes in climate (early/late snowmelt, temperature change... etc.) affects colony buildup in bumblebees and the diversity of plants to choose from.
Subject: Climate Change

ResearchPlanTitle: Effects of warming on herbivory and fungal pathogen loads on alpine grass species
ResearchPlanAbstract: As the climate warms, speciesâ€™ ranges may shift in search of conditions that satisfy their niches (Lenoir et al., 2008). Furthermore, herbivory is predicted to increase in intensity as global temperatures increase (Adler et al., 2007). The Dobzhansky-MacArthur hypothesis (D-MH), which reasons that while unfavorable abiotic factors limit the upper altitude of speciesâ€™ ranges, biotic interactions limit their lower altitude ranges; provides a potential explanation for changes in community dynamics as well as why high-elevation species are additionally vulnerable to climate change (Brown, 1995). We will assess the future feasibility of a test of the D-MH by observing insect herbivory and fungal pathogen loads on transplanted alpine grass species, Festuca brachypylla, Poa alpina, and Elymus scribneri, to a novel elevation on Mt. Avery, lower than where the species naturally thrive. Furthermore, we will examine the direct and long-term effects of warming on biotic interactions by collecting data on damage by herbivores and fungal pathogens on three dominating grass species, Festuca thurberi, Poa pratensis, and Acknatherum lettermanii, in a warming meadow at the Rocky Mountain Biological Laboratory (RMBL).
ResearchPlanOrganisms: Festuca brachypylla, Poa alpina, and Elymus scribneri; Festuca thurberi, Poa pratensis, and Acknatherum lettermanii

ResearchPlanTitle: Quantifying within-season trait distributions of flowers and their pollinators in Colorado Rocky Mountain dry meadows
ResearchPlanAbstract: The available evidence strongly suggests that plant and pollinator systems are dynamic and change across the season (AlarcÃ³n et al. 2008, Olesen et al. 2008, P.J. CaraDonna unpublished data). However, most studies do not investigate how interactions may be influenced by changing plant and pollinator trait distributions within a single season. The main goal of this project is to examine within-season patterns of floral traits and pollinator traits. Our primary question is whether floral and pollinator traits vary directionally, remain constant, or are indistinguishable from random across the season. To answer this question, I will explore whether there are quantifiable trends in flower traits and pollinator traits by measuring a broad sample of traits across 35-40 floral species and 60-65 pollinator species throughout the 2015 growing season. The answer to this question can lead to explorations of the mechanisms that create this pattern, and perhaps relate to trait phenology in corresponding pollinator species, ultimately generating a deeper understanding of the community composition and how it fluctuates over the course of a season.
Subject: Phenology

ResearchPlanTitle: Does Bumble bee Diet Breadth Vary With Floral Abundance in a Meadow?
ResearchPlanAbstract: As our climate continues to change it is difficult to predict how different species will react and adapt to the environment. In recent years the Rocky Mountain Biological Laboratory has been affected by early snow melt, which appears to be becoming more frequent. With early snow melt, plants grow earlier and their flower buds are more susceptible to frost. Also, in early snow melt years, plants might be more prone to drought stress. Together this suggests that community floral abundance may be lower in early snow melt years. Indeed, some abundant wildflowers produce fewer flowers in in early snow melt years. Does bumble bee diet breadth vary with floral abundance in a meadow? This question is important for the response of bumble bees to climate change due to fewer flowers during early snow melt years. My hypothesis is that bumble bee diet breadth decreases with an increase in the floral abundance of a meadow. If there is a large floral abundance in a meadow then bumble bees will specialize in which flowers they choose to forage from, while bumble bees in meadows with low flower abundance will be more generalized and will need to visit more flower types to obtain the food resources they need.
Subject: Pollination

ResearchPlanTitle: Pigmentation as stress response in Androsace Septentrionalis
ResearchPlanAbstract: Plant responses to human-caused climate change are an important component of understanding the extent to which climate change affects ecosystems. All species, including plants, respond to stressors in two ways: ecologically and evolutionarily. Examined together, ecological and evolutionary responses provide a complete view of speciesâ€™ responses to climate change, and possible future changes within an ecosystem. Among other functional traits used to examine environmentally-caused responses to climate change, changes in leaf pigmentation is a recurring sign of phenotypic plasticity in plants and is thus useful for examining plastic responses to climate change. My proposed project investigates leaf pigment variation in a small montane plant across a wide climate gradient. Using digital and chemical analyses, I will examine leaf color differences across common gardens to examine 1) the pigments responsible for observed color variation, 2) the relationship between leaf color and a suite of abiotic variables, and 3) genetic differences in plastic responses to stress. This study will provide insight into the evolutionary and ecological responses to new stresses effected by climate change on plants in montane systems.
Subject: Climate Change

ResearchPlanTitle: Caddisfly larval growth and development as functions of temperature fluctuations during pond drying
ResearchPlanAbstract: Previous research has demonstrated that the larval stages of temporary-pond amphibians and aquatic invertebrates, can detect cues that signal pond drying, and one would predict that those cues should lead to accelerated growth and development, as to emerge before desiccation. Although, it has been observed in a variety of cases that development rates have slowed down with pond drying. An alternate hypothesis proposed to answer this question is one in which increased temperature fluctuations during drying, due to higher surface area to volume ratio, might affect caddisfly larvae metabolic rates and the tradeoffs associated with allocating energy to maintenance, growth, and development. The purpose of this study is to determine tolerance of growth and development rates of the caddisfly species Asynarchus nigriculus during high temperature fluctuations in drying ponds at The Mexican Cut Nature Reserve (MCR). This will be done in three ways, first with a laboratory control experiment, rearing the larvae at various constants to determine temperatures that offer optimum growth and development. The second is a field experiment, in which we will rear larvae in small, high temperature fluctuating microcosms and large, low temperature fluctuating microcosms, as to compare time spent at suboptimum temperatures and the performance curve created from the control experiment. Finally, this experiment will be grounded in ecological relevance by monitoring temperature fluctuations in drying ponds at The MCR.
ResearchPlanOrganisms: Caddisfly larvae of the species Asynarchus nigriculus

ResearchPlanTitle: How Relative Angle of a Predator and Prey Animal to a Refuge Determines Flight Initiation Distance in Yellow-Bellied Marmots (Marmota flaviventris)
ResearchPlanAbstract: The dynamics between predator and prey behavior drive ecological communities. In particular, the response of prey to predatory threats and how they assess risk and danger has been the subject of much study in the past two decades. Studies have shown that prey employ an economic approach to assessing risk, where the cost to fitness and survival due to flight is weighed against other factors of survival. These decisions and assessments often manifest as, but are not limited to, how closely a predator can approach a prey organism before the prey flees, known as the â€œflight initiation distanceâ€ or FID, and the relative angle of a predator and prey to a refuge. This study seeks to test FID in yellow-bellied marmots, and how it is affected by a marmot's relative angle to a predator and its refuge.
Subject: Other

ResearchPlanTitle: Plant selection of mycorrhizal symbionts in response to abiotic stress
ResearchPlanAbstract: Mycorrhizae perform many functions that ensure the survival & stress tolerance of plant hosts, which include increased nutrient acquisition, increased water absorption, and increased pathogen tolerance [1]. We know that plant investment in mycorrhizae is a plastic trait that depends on resource availability [2,3] but relatively little is known of the dynamic that occurs between plants and mycorrhizae in response to shifting abiotic conditions brought about by climate change or other anthropogenic factors. Since mycorrhizae are crucial to plant survival, understanding plant response to global change requires understanding responses of plant-fungi relationships to environmental changes. For instance, soil nutrient status and soil moisture levels have been shown by numerous authors to alter the structure and function of mycorrhizal communities, however, drivers of these patterns remain elusive. Preliminary work conducted by my RMBL mentor, Jeremiah Henning, and previous RMBL REU students Krissy Dominguez and RisÃ« Schnieder, has shown that two fungal types (arbuscular mycorrhizal (AM) fungi and dark septate endophyte (DSE) fungi) commonly co-occur in plant roots within this system. Additionally, previous work has demonstrated that mycorrhizal colonization at the plant community level shifts across an elevational gradient. Specifically, as elevation increases, AM colonization rates decrease and DSE colonization rates increase (Figure 1). To explain this pattern, follow-up work by Henning and Schnieder tested whether differences in fungal physiology and seasonality were driving the observed pattern in focal plant species, P. gracilis. However, they found that AMF colonization was consistently higher throughout the growing season at low elevation and DSE colonization was consistently higher than AMF at high elevations, although DSE colonization increased throughout the growing season which corresponds to decreases in water availability (Figure 2). Both fungal groups are able to provide plants with limiting nutrients, increase drought tolerance, and protect against pathogens, but they differ in their efficiencies to perform these functions. Several authors have shown that AM preferentially allocate phosphorus to their plant symbionts [4] and preliminary work by Dominguez and Henning, suggests that DSE preferentially allocate nitrogen to host plants (Figure 3) and have greater abiotic stress (including drought) tolerance than AMF overall [5]. Thus, this previous work has lead me to hypothesize that fungal colonization patterns are driven by host plants selection of symbionts that help to avoid abiotic stress. I propose to conduct two manipulative experiments that test whether plant selection of symbionts to reduce abiotic stress is driving the observed large-scale patterns of fungal distribution. Here I am asking: 1) Do host plants select fungal associates that alleviate nutrient limitation? 2) Do host plants select fungal associates that alleviate water limitation? Two experiments will be used to address these questions. The first experiment is a nutrient addition/limitation experiment. A nitrogen addition will lead to phosphorous limitation, so we expect to see an increase in AM colonization. A phosphorous addition will limit nitrogen availability, so we expect to see an increase in DSE colonization. In a nitrogen and phosphorous treatment we expect to see decreased colonization of both AM and DSE. Additionally, we will use a labile carbon addition, which will limit both nitrogen and phosphorous in the soil, so we expect to see an increase in both AM and DSE colonization. The second experiment is a water manipulation experiment to test if water limitation affects mycorrhizal colonization. We expect that average water availability will maintain an average amount of fungal colonization, with colonization decreasing as water availability decreases (Figure 4).

ResearchPlanTitle: Elevational and temporal variation in Ipomopsis floral traits
ResearchPlanAbstract: This study will begin by addressing the following question. 1. How do present day elevational clines in corolla length, corolla width, and nectar production compare with those observed in 1992 (Campbell et al. 1997) for populations of Ipomopsis located in Poverty Gulch, Gunnison County, Colorado? To explore the potential causes of temporal shifts in clines, we will then use the reciprocal transplants to answer the following: 2. To what extent are elevational differences in corolla length and width due to phenotypic plasticity versus genetic differences? 3. Are the elevational differences adaptive? Based on known patterns of floral traits, we predict that populations of Ipomopsis will exhibit relatively short and wide corollas in the species I. aggregata in lower elevations, while the species I. tenuituba expresses longer narrow corollas at higher elevation (Campbell 2004). If these patterns are adaptive, we predict that long, narrow flowers will increase fitness measured as seed production at high elevation while short, wide flowers will have higher fitness at low elevation. Adaptive patterns of this sort would have favored sharper clines over time, whereas increased hybridization (as proposed by Campbell et al. 2008) could have led to shallower clines.

ResearchPlanAbstract: Nicrophorus investigator is a carrion beetle species commonly found near the Rocky Mountain Biological Laboratory that typically involves the use of a sound known as stridulation. This year, I will observe the roles of stridulation in competition, mating and communication.
