ResearchPlanTitle: Habitat Selection in Nicrophorus Investigator
ResearchPlanAbstract: The source-sink hypothesis explains differences in reproductive success in two habitats, and suggests that organisms in source habitat are better competitors. A test of this hypothesis would lead to the following predictions: Beetles that are large are more likely to â€œwinâ€ intra-specific competitive encounters and will select and successfully defend carcasses in the sun which are a better resource (higher quality habitat) for the beetles. In contrast, adult beetles that are small are less likely to win intra-specific competitive interactions; and thus may reproduce primarily in â€œsinkâ€ habitat- selecting carcases in the shade even though they are of lower resource quality. This study will directly test these predictions by observing Nicrophorus arrival at carcasses, competitive interactions, body size, and reproductive success in two habitat types.
Subject: Other

ResearchPlanTitle: How do distributions of belowground grass-fungal symbioses change over altitudinal gradients in the Colorado Rocky Mountains?
ResearchPlanAbstract: Fungal symbioses distributions over altitudinal gradients are not well understood and may be important in predicting future fungal distributions as well as terrestrial ecosystem distributions in response to climate change. As temperatures increase, plants will likely move up in altitude away from environments that are newly hostile. Symbioses between plant roots and fungi may play an important role in mitigating this shift. There are various species of root-associated fungi that play different ecological roles. Mycorrhizal fungi form an interchange with plants in which they often provide plants with soil nutrients in exchange for carbon. Arbuscular mycorrhizal fungi has been shown to increase nutrient and water uptake by plants while dark septate endophytes can increase drought and heat tolerance. Understanding the distribution of these fungi is likely important for understanding future plant communities as the climate changes. My research will aim to quantify fungal colonization in roots as part of a broader study. The broader study is the largest altitudinal survey of fungal symbionts in the world that we know of. The study has quantified above and below-ground fungi as well as other soil properties and environmental factors across multiple host grass species and multiple altitudinal gradients. I will clear and stain roots, mount them on microscope slides, and quantify % colonization under the microscope. Understanding the distribution of these below-ground symbiotic fungi is an important step in being able to predict and understand changing plant communities.
Subject: Climate Change

ResearchPlanTitle: Ecosystem Carbon Dynamics
ResearchPlanAbstract: Global warming, driven by anthropogenic greenhouse gas emissions has been predicted to increase global temperatures by 2-4 Celsius by 2090 (IPCC 2014). The predicted rate of warming is explicitly linked to the the level of carbon present in earthâ€™s atmosphere at a given time (Bonan et al. 2002). Climate change driven warming has both direct and indirect consequences for ecosystem level carbon dynamics (Oleson 2000, Poulter et al. 2011, Lal 2004). Warming directly influences soil properties including soil moisture and respiration rates (Ehrenfeld 2010); in addition, the metabolic activity of soil biota and plant roots may be sped up by warming, increasing carbon turnover (i.e. increased respiration). Additionally, warming can influence plant communities directly by increasing productivity and indirectly alter plant community composition by favoring species with particular traits, influencing carbon dynamics (Lavorel 2002). Plants that are more responsive to warming often exhibit traits differences that affect carbon dynamics such as faster decomposition rates of their litter (Bardgett et al. 2010). Although most of the worlds carbon resides within soils and plant tissues, very little is known on how the direct and indirect effects of warming combine to influence the overall addition and loss of carbon from terrestrial systems. The effects of climate change will be especially evident in high latitude and montane ecosystems (IPCC 2014). These systems often support diverse plant and belowground communities, and typically harbor substantial carbon reserves, thus providing an ideal system for studying ecosystem carbon dynamics in response to warming (Niu et al. 2013).Montane ecosystems also present a unique opportunity for climate based research, as the gradient allows sharp contrast of various regimes across a relatively tight geographic area. Due to the integral role terrestrial carbon reserves play in regulating the amount of carbon present in the atmosphere, it is imperative that we better understand the influence of climate change on ecosystem carbon dynamics. Net Ecosystem Exchange (NEE) provides a unique tool to analyze the ratio of gross carbon uptake via photosynthesis and respiration, allowing communities to be designated as a net source of sink of carbon. This is the single most important parameter as it reflects whether additional carbon is being added to the atmosphere or taken out of it. In order to pursue this particular question, we have removed dominant species to (a) simulate the effect of foundation species loss on the remaining plant community, which is known to dramatically impact ecosystem function (Ellison 2005, frontiers in ecology) and (b) because dominant speciesâ€™ traits tend to be the optimum value to maximize either competitive ability or stress tolerance, we expect that removing dominant species with higher competitive ability will have a greater net impact on NEE than removing stress-tolerant dominant species. In addition to species removal we have established warming chambers to pursue the direct effects of global warming on ecosystem carbon dynamics.
Subject: Climate Change

ResearchPlanTitle: Effects of increased secondary nectar robbing on pollination visitation
ResearchPlanAbstract: Nectar robbers are organisms that feed on the nectar of a plant obtained through holes that have been chewed into the flower and â€œstealingâ€ the nectar, often bypassing the pollination service. Primary nectar robbers are organisms that create an opening in the petal from which to remove nectar, while secondary nectar robbers are organisms that use the holes created by primary robbers. Nectar robbing removes the nectar reward which ultimately results in lower food intake of legitimate pollinators; this might result in behavioral changes of pollinators. For example, hummingbirds have been observed to not only bypass nectar robbed flowers, but to increase the distance between them and such flowers, likely in order to find alternative unrobbed sources of nectar; this results in decreased pollination of the nectar robbed plants and therefore decreased reproductive success. Data has shown that secondary nectar robbing can result in increased reproduction costs beyond that caused by primary robbing alone. However, the mechanism that drives this response is unknown. One prediction is that hummingbird pollinators are further deterred as plants incur more and more secondary robbing. My experiment will test this prediction.
Subject: Pollination

ResearchPlanTitle: Sedge Workshop and Feidl Trip
ResearchPlanAbstract: Eminent botanist, Tony Reznicek (University of Michigan) will be returning to Colorado to provide a workshop on the sedges of Colorado focused on the west slope. Denver Botanic Gardens, Colorado Native Plant Society, and University of Colorado Denver are collaborating to offer this â€œsedgeventâ€ that will combine a workshop at the picturesque Rocky Mountain Biological Laboratory in Gothic with two days of field trips. The workshop will be held on Friday with an hour of lecture and then focus the rest of the day on identifying fresh specimens. Saturday and Sunday, we will venture out into the field focusing on areas around Crested Butte. The workshop is targeted at advanced beginners to those with intermediate skills.
Subject: Other

ResearchPlanTitle: A Multiscale Approach to Modeling Carbon and Nitrogen Cycling within a High Elevation Watershed
ResearchPlanAbstract: Soils, floodplains and shallow aquifers are the least understood components of the carbon cycle, yet they represent the largest reservoir of terrestrial carbon and are highly sensitive to shifts in climate, vegetation, and the resulting water balance. As a result, processes that occur in these environments represent a key knowledge gap in our predictive understanding of nutrient cycling and terrestrial ecosystem function, which in turn limits our ability to model ecosystems over large scales. To provide an approach for developing improved model descriptions, we propose to develop reactive transport descriptions of subsurface carbon (C) and nitrogen (N) transformations and fluxes at multiple scales (soil profile to watershed), using field data collected from a high-elevation catchment in Colorado to constrain the models. Key elements of the proposed approach are (1) mechanistic treatment of C and N cycling using a multi-component model that includes transport of dissolved and gaseous species (i.e. a reactive transport model), and (2) quantifying spatial variability in processes through time and space.
Subject: Climate Change

ResearchPlanTitle: Warming and species Removal in Mountains (WaRM)
ResearchPlanAbstract: At the Rocky Mountain Biological Laboratory, I use a combination of natural environmental variability, experimental studies in the field, and statistical models to address three key questions about the interactive effects of human-caused global changes on plant community interactions and ecosystem carbon dynamics. Key question 1: What are the effects of warming and the loss of dominant species along environmental gradients, both locally and globally? Warming and local species extinctions may have different effects depending on the suite of species present in the local community. To explore this, I am increasing temperature with miniature greenhouses and removing dominant plant species at multiple elevations, measuring effects on the plant community and the carbon cycle. Key question 2: What are the relative effects of the nonliving environment and species interactions on plant community dynamics and ecosystem function? Humans are causing biodiversity loss and disrupting the cycles of essential elements in ecosystems. To explore these complex interactions, I am fertilizing a site with organic and inorganic nitrogen and removing dominant plant species, measuring effects on the plant community and decomposition rates in the soil. Key question 3: Can we use plant traits to predict how plants are distributed on the landscape? In this era of global change, it is critical not only to understand how species' characteristics relate to their environment, but also to take the next step and predict where species are -- and will be -- found across the landscape. To construct statistical models to make these important predictions, I am collecting plant community data, plant trait data, and ecosystem function data at over a dozen sites ranging widely in climatic conditions. I am inputting these data into a cutting-edge statistical model to determine where we can -- and cannot -- predict which plants live where.
Subject: Climate Change

ResearchPlanTitle: Distribution of caddisfly larvae in streams across gradients in elevation and shear stress
ResearchPlanAbstract: This research investigates species richness and abundance of hydropsychid caddisfly larvae across gradients in elevation. Caddisflies are dominant ecosystem engineers in many streams, often reaching densities of 1,000 to 10,000 individuals per square meter. Hydropsychid caddisflies act as ecosystem engineers in two primary ways. First, they can alter suspended sediment loads by filtering and eating material out of the water column. Second, they can increase streambed stability by binding rocks together with silk they produce and weave into mesh nets. Although the distribution of caddisflies has been correlated with a variety of physical factors (temperature, dissolved oxygen, flow levels), very few field studies have explicitly mapped caddisfly density or species richness and correlated these estimates with geomorphic variables such as elevation, slope, velocity, shear stress, and grain size. This research is a critical next step to determine how these ecosystem engineers might operate across various local- and landscape-scale gradients under changing climate regimes.
Subject: Climate Change

ResearchPlanTitle: Contact metamorphism of the Mancos Shale: controls on East River morphology
ResearchPlanAbstract: This project will investigate and map contact metamorphism of the Mancos Shale that comprises exposed bedrock in the East River valley. During the Tertiary geologic period, numerous igneous rocks were emplaced around the Crested Butte area as part of the Mount Carbon Igneous System. These hot igneous rocks metamorphosed surrounding sedimentary rocks in the subsurface, including the Mancos Shale. Portions of the Mancos Shale near the town of Gothic and the Rocky Mountain Biological Laboratory appear to be metamorphosed to slate, a rock that is much harder and less permeable than shale. Changes in rock properties and mineralogy with metamorphism impact landscape evolution as rocks weather and erode at Earth's surface. Specifically, I hypothesize that contact metamorphism of the Mancos Shale controls form and shape of the East River. Where the East River downcuts into more competent slate, river sinuosity is lower and the river more channelized compared to the wide meandering floodplains where the East River is downcutting into easily weathered and less competent shale. Mapping of the boundaries of contact metamorphism combined with chemical and physical analyses of Mancos Shale samples will highlight the connections between underlying geology defined millions of years ago and modern earth surface processes that generate the topography and morphology of the East River valley we see today.
Subject: Other

ResearchPlanTitle: Causes and consequences of sex-specific responses to climate change
ResearchPlanAbstract: Ecological differences between the sexes are widespread, and sex-specific responses to climate change may occur as a result. Unbalanced sex ratios can have strong negative effects on populations because many individuals that are capable of reproducing are unable to find a mate. The goals of this study are to understand (1) how climate change is affecting the sexes of a long-lived plant species (Valeriana edulis), (2) how these responses will affect the viability of Valeriana populations and the species that depend on Valeriana, and (3) how the distribution of Valeriana may be altered by ongoing climate change. This work will ultimately contribute to our understanding of the fundamental ecological processes that control the distribution and abundance of species on the landscape.
Subject: Climate Change

ResearchPlanTitle: Mechanisms driving the elevational variation in an ant-aphid mutualism on aspen (Populus tremuloides)
ResearchPlanAbstract: While mutualisms are recognized as context-dependent, little is known about the specific abiotic mechanisms that drive this context-dependency, particularly across environmental gradients. In previous summers at RMBL, I and other students in Kailen Mooneyâ€™s lab found that ants tend aphids on aspen (Populus tremuloides) more frequently within low-elevation than within high-elevation valleys in Gunnison County. As a result, survival rates of aphid colonies are greater at low elevations. Moreover, we determined that overall ant abundance does not vary with elevation. However, ant foragers consume more artificial honeydew from baits at lower elevations, which likely drives the elevation-dependency of this ant-aphid mutualism. I propose to continue to investigate why ant-aphid mutualisms on aspen vary with elevation by evaluating the specific abiotic mechanisms driving the elevation-dependency of these mutualisms, whether the attractiveness of aphid honeydew for ants depends on elevation, why ants consume more sugar at lower elevations, whether the competitive abilities of different ant taxa correspond to their qualities as mutualists, and how ant-aphid mutualisms affect the broader community of arthropods on aspen.
ResearchPlanOrganisms: Ants (multiple species), aphids (multiple species associated with host plant), Populus tremuloides (host plant), and other arthropods associated with aspen canopies (e.g. leaf-rolling caterpillars, leaf-mining caterpillars, membracids)
Subject: Other

ResearchPlanTitle: Integrating stream research, teaching and outreach to inform advocacy by conservation organizations and influence policy makers
ResearchPlanAbstract: RMBL shares the Upper East River basin with other special interests, such as recreation, development of open space associated with the Mt. Crested Butte ski area, abstraction of water for snowmaking and irrigation, hard rock mining and cattle grazing. Such multiple uses of the drainage basin potentially threaten the quality of the receiving streams that are critical not only to the integrity of the ecosystem, but also to sustaining research, educational and outreach functions of RMBL. In 1976 the RMBL obtained a non-consumptive water rights decree that protects minimum flows in streams of the drainage. Since that time stream ecologists at RMBL have used invertebrates as biological indicators of stream quality, with the goal of protecting the health and biodiversity of those streams. The primary goal of this project is to continue the invertebrate sampling of streams in the Upper East River basin that can be used as a reference for more disturbed streams in the region such as those in the Coal Creek drainage. In addition we will continue long-term surveys of the trout and stream algae populations (including Didymosphenia geminata) in the Upper East River basin. By coordinating methods for assessing stream quality enabling early detection of environmental problems we are positioned to influence public policy to prevent or mitigate human-mediated changes that fall outside the range of acceptable conditions needed to sustain healthy stream biota. We hope to provide a model system for assessing the threats to high elevation streams resulting from human accelerated environmental change, extraction of mineral resources, proliferation of invasive species, population growth and associated construction of dams and diversions. Our long-term dataset obtained from relatively pristine streams within a backdrop of environmental change can thereby be used as a reference for comparison to streams in other parts of the Colorado River drainage basin that are vulnerable to ongoing and future threats.
Subject: Long-Term

ResearchPlanInstitution: University of California, Berkeley, and Lawrence Berkeley National Laboratory
ResearchPlanTitle: Soil as a carbon reservoir: The role of iron cycling in soil organic matter stabilization and mineralization in an acidic, iron-rich fen
ResearchPlanAbstract: Stabilization of soil organic matter (SOM) is a critical process in the global carbon (C) cycle and in mitigating climate change. Long-term storage of C in soils depends on stabilization of SOM and its protection from decomposition processes that release C-based greenhouse gases (i.e. carbon dioxide and methane) back to the atmosphere. Iron (Fe) minerals may play an important role in long-term C storage in soils by binding to, and protecting, SOM from decomposition. However the underlying mechanisms are not fully understood. To begin bridging varying levels of understanding, we need a comprehensive dataset on Fe and SOM characteristics across a landscape that is rich in both Fe and C. Thus, the key objective of the proposed study is to investigate Fe-SOM interactions in an acidic Fe- and C-rich fen to gain new understanding of the role of Fe cycling in the storage of C in soils.
Subject: Climate Change

ResearchPlanTitle: Using natural tracers to study ecohydrological pathways in the southern Rocky Mountains
ResearchPlanAbstract: The pathways that water take through an ecosystem can be complex. The canonical view is of precipitation either percolating or running off from a soil and then either evaporating, transpiring or adding to groundwater. This perspective neglects a number of ecologically important but lesser studied hydrological pathways. For example, the canopy often intercepts precipitation and this water may be taken up by leaves through foliar absorption or evaporated back to the atmosphere. Other processes such as dew fall may contribute to the water available to plants and may act to recycle water that otherwise would evaporate and be lost from the ecosystem. Furthermore, it has been observed that water entering a soil appears to be partitioned between molecules in small pore spaces that are used by plants and water that rapidly moves through the soil and contributes to streamflow and groundwater. In other words, water in the soil is not a homogenous mixture but made up of pools that are neatly partitioned between biologically and hydrologically available. This proposal will use natural tracers of the water cycle (stable water isotopes) to explore dynamics of the ecohydrological continuum in RMBL. We will measure soil, plant, and surface water sources to characterize the pathways that connect the water pools in the system. The broader goal is to understand how these pathways will be altered in a warming climate and how this will influence the vulnerability of forests in the greater Rocky Mountains. The proposed work at RMBL is being completed in parallel to another project by the PI looking at 120,000 year-old wood samples from Snowmass, CO. This period in Earthâ€™s history was the last time the growing season climate in Colorado was significantly warmer than today. We will combine the field measurements at RMBL with geochemical analyses of these ancient wood samples to study how plant water sources and water stress today compares to a Rocky Mountains that was as much as 5Â° warmer than today.
ResearchPlanOrganisms: Populus tremuloides, Picea engelmanii, Abies lasiocarpa
Subject: Climate Change

ResearchPlanTitle: Paleoenvironmental reconstruction in the greater RMBL area from lake and fen sediments
ResearchPlanAbstract: Lake and fen sediments are rich archives of information about past environments. Near RMBL, these sediments have the potential to reach back 18,000 years to the Last Glacial Maximum. Through the analysis of pollen grains, charcoal fragments, and sediment geochemistry, the goal of this project is to reconstruct past vegetation communities, fire dynamics, and climate in greater RMBL region. Increased understanding of the impacts of past climate changes on ecosystems provides valuable information that will help land managers better prepare for future conditions.
Subject: Climate Change

ResearchPlanTitle: Demography and spatial organization of golden-mantled ground squirrels
ResearchPlanAbstract: Inter-annual variation in population density is thought to affect individual habitat settlement decisions, with potential consequences for fitness. In mammals, spatial organization might be influenced not only by density, but also through consistent within-population differences in behavioral type, which might affect an animalâ€™s use of space through personality-driven foraging movement and dispersal. I will quantify density-dependent habitat selection and its fitness consequences in a high elevational population of golden-mantled ground squirrels, Callospermophilus lateralis. I will also characterize C. lateralis spatial structure and quantify the effects of density and behavioral type on spatial organization in this species. I will achieve this by analyzing behavioral data collected via natural observations and experimental assays in the field. Results will further our understanding of the causes and consequences of changes in habitat use, providing insight to the fields of wildlife management and conservation. This is especially important in the face of anthropogenic disturbance and human-induced rapid environmental change.
Subject: Long-Term

ResearchPlanTitle: How do floral visual cues and pollen cues influence plant selection and individual preferences by the solitary, oligolectic bee, Osmia iridis (Hymenoptera: Megachilidae)?
ResearchPlanAbstract: Both habitat destruction and modern agricultural practices continue to alter both the diversity and abundance of flowering plant species. This negatively impacts the surrounding bee populations that are completely dependent on flowers for food. Not only do bees sustain themselves with floral rewards, they also gather pollen to feed to their developing larvae. Unlike honeybees and bumblebees that are social, the majority of the 20 000 bee species worldwide are solitary. Most of these solitary bee species are pollen specialists and will only collect pollen from a fraction of the available floral resources. Iâ€™m interested in understanding what cues specialist bees use to find their preferred host plant and how these bees respond to shortages of their preferred plants. In flight cages, I will present nesting bees with different nonhost plants, some of which resemble their host in terms of floral shape or floral color and others that are superficially distinct but more closely related to the host. I will observe the willingness of the bees to visit these different nonhost plants for pollen and I will assess whether visual cues or relatedness affect their selections. As the flowering plant community continues to change with human disturbance and climate change, understanding the cues involved in host selection and the host range available to bee species is necessary for the conservation of our native pollinators.
ResearchPlanOrganisms: Osmia iridis, Lathyrus lanszwertii and 8 nonhost plant species. A table I have included in my research proposal provides a summary of the potential nonhost plant species as well as my estimates of the number of plants I would need for each species.
Subject: Pollination

ResearchPlanTitle: Effects of climate and vegetation on the American pika (Ochotona princeps)
ResearchPlanAbstract: Climate change is affecting ecosystems worldwide. Alpine communities are among the most affected by these changes. Species in these communities have evolved key adaptations to thrive in cold, wet environments. As temperatures warm and precipitation patterns become more variable due to global climate change, many alpine species are expected to be impacted. This research focuses on the American pika, a small lagomorph (rabbit relative) inhabiting broken rock slopes in the mountains and high plateaus of western North America. Population declines in the Great Basin region at the end of the 20th Century caused concern for populations elsewhere in the species range. Previous research in the Southern Rocky Mountain region, including some sites near Rocky Mountain Biological Laboratory, indicates variable success of pika populations in the face of equally variable changes in climatic and vegetation regimes. This study will investigate these patterns in greater depth, tracking pika behavior, survival, and population dynamics, as they respond to changes in climate and vegetation. This study will be conducted at two sites in Gunnison County: Virginia Basin and North Pole Basin. At both sites, pikas will be live trapped and marked with ear tags each year. Samples of fur, ear tissue, and fecal material will also be collected during trapping. In addition to this pika-specific information, data on available forage and selectivity will be collected through surveys of surrounding standing vegetation as well as pika haypile contents. In order to assess climate at these sites, temperature data loggers will be deployed below the talus (in pika haypiles) and in nearby trees. Pika survival will be determined through a resurvey of pika populations in subsequent years. Factors such as temperature, forage diversity, and stress levels (determined from hair and fecal samples) will be assessed as potential explanatory factors for these survival patterns.
Subject: Climate Change

ResearchPlanTitle: Effective population size and population structure: describing adaptive capacity in the Upland Herbaceous plant community
ResearchPlanAbstract: The ability to adapt will be a crucial component of plant speciesâ€™ response to climate change. The general capacity to adapt is quantified by effective population size (Ne), which describes the strength of genetic drift in evolution. There are multiple methods which have been developed to measure Ne, including genetic methods which can calculate a historic (deep time) or contemporary (recent time) estimates, the later of which undergoes greater change from year to year. Adaptation is greatest in populations with large Ne, and larger populations have greater Ne. Abundance, as an analogue for total population size, is therefore expected to be the strongest determinant of Ne. Conversely, limited gene flow, evident in the form of population structure can reduce Ne. In the upland herbaceous plant communities of the Gunnison Basin, many species have decreased in abundance which should depress estimates of contemporary Ne without strong effects on historical Ne. Many of these same species also have expanded their ranges by moving into other areas, such as the low elevation sagebrush community. Population expansion should preserve genetic diversity, and thus bolster Ne, but only when there is not significant population structure between or within communities. To test how changes in abundance, expansion, and population structure affect adaptability, I will compare historic and contemporary Ne for at least 10 upland herbaceous species that have increased or decreased in abundance and ranges that have expanded or remained static. Overall, I expect species with high population structure to have lower Ne given their abundance. I expect that species with larger decreases in abundance to also have a greater difference between contemporary and historic estimates of Ne. Knowledge of how adaptability changes over short timescales and what ecological factors are most responsible is crucial for understanding how species will respond to climate change.
Subject: Climate Change

ResearchPlanTitle: Pollen Use by Bees
ResearchPlanOrganisms: Lupinus argenteus, Delphinium barbeyi, Bombus appositus, Bombus bifarius, Bombus sylvicola, other Bombus spp
Subject: Pollination

ResearchPlanTitle: Potential for the alpine species Mimulus tilingii to adapt to changing climate compared to the widespread species Mimulus guttatus
ResearchPlanAbstract: Abstract: The main long-term goal of the proposed research is to determine the potential for adaptation to future climatic conditions in both a geographically restricted species (Mimulus tilingi) and a widespread species (M. guttatus), as well as to make comparisons between the two. Results from this research will help in determining conservation and management plans for plant species that are restricted geographically and cannot easily migrate. In the short-term, collection of germplasm is required to preliminarily assess the differences in environmental tolerance between M. guttatus and M. tilingii to accurately determine the next step in this project. Thus, my goal for this summer is to simply collect seed in order to use it in further experiments. This proposal outlines the long-term goals of the project in order to justify the current seed collection. Additionally, Dr. Carrie Wu, a researcher at RMBL who is also studying M. tilingii, is fully aware of my plans and our research is meant to exist congruently but not to directly overlap or make use of resources needed by the other.
Subject: Climate Change

ResearchPlanTitle: Determining the relative role of dominant vs. subordinate plant species on community dynamics and ecosystem function in an alpine ecosystem
ResearchPlanAbstract: My research addresses the role of plant functional traits influencing dominance patterns across alpine meadow communities and in turn the impacts of dominant vs. subdominant alpine meadow plant species to affect community dynamics and ecosystem processes such as the fluxes of carbon. I use observational studies where I quantify variation in above- and belowground plant functional traits that are critical for resource acquisition ultimately affecting abundance patterns from mesic to dry alpine meadows. Additionally, with the use of field experiments, I manipulate the abundance of dominant and subdominant plant species to assess their impacts on overall biodiversity and associated ecosystem carbon dynamics in the form of carbon input via productivity and output via soil carbon loss. More specifically, with the use of plant removal experiments, I have manipulated the presence of both dominant (e.g., Festuca thurberi and Veratrum californicum) and subdominant (e.g., Potentilla gracilis and Delphinium barbeyi ) alpine meadow species in dry and mesic meadows and have tracked changes in community biodiversity and carbon to determine biosphere and atmosphere feedbacks.
Subject: Climate Change

ResearchPlanTitle: Spatiotemporal shifts in response to climate change for plants and pollinators
ResearchPlanAbstract: Species are responding to climate change by shifting the timing of life history events, migrating to track historical climates, and adapting to novel environments. Past research at the RMBL has looked at community wide changes, from the disruption of plant-pollinator mutualisms via phenological mismatch to an overall increase in the length of the flowering season. I am interested in how species-specific responses play out in plant-pollinator interactions with a focus on understanding what drives these changes at the scale of an individual organism. For example, by studying the longevity of individual flowers, I am hoping to uncover whether a longer flowering season is attributable to increased floral longevity of the earliest flowering cohort of plants or to the responses and turnover of many individuals with an average lifespan. This becomes important when we consider phenological mismatch, as plants that flower before pollinators arrive may not be at a disadvantage if floral longevity increases with earlier flowering time. From a spatial perspective, there can be selection for plants to shift upward in elevation in order to track climate and/ or range shifts in pollinator species. The success of migrating plant populations is up to individual seedling survivorship, which can be affected by local adaptation to historical environments. I am investigating selection to shift upwards and local adaptation in the bumble bee pollinated, herbaceous plant, Erythronium grandiflorum.
ResearchPlanOrganisms: Bumble bees, E. grandiflorum, D.  nutallianum, Hydrophyllum capitatum, Hydrophyllum fendleri, Lathyrus leucanthus, Vicia americana, Linum lewisii
Subject: Pollination

ResearchPlanTitle: Mechanisms of Color Vision in Hummingbirds
ResearchPlanAbstract: My aim is to conduct a series of behavioral experiments in the field to establish baseline visual abilities of the Broad-tailed Hummingbird (Selasphorus platycercus) with respect to color and pattern vision. I will use artificial feeders equipped with a carefully controlled light source to attract free-flying hummingbirds, which will be banded and individually marked by David Inouye. By changing the visual stimulus at the feeders and modifying the sugar reward, I will create conditions under which the birds can discriminate among different color wavelengths. My initial experiments will involve color perception only. In the future, I will use a similar paradigm to test pattern discrimination in hummingbirds. These experiments exploit the natural feeding behavior of hummingbirds and will establish an experimental framework with several key advantages, including that hummingbirds: 1) feed regularly at artificial feeders, 2) learn quickly, 3) can behave naturally (undisturbed) during the experiments, and 4) can be individually marked and easily observed.
Subject: Other

ResearchPlanTitle: Geomorphic controls on freshwater food web energy flow in mountain watersheds: preliminary research
ResearchPlanAbstract: Watershed morphology shapes the structure and function of freshwater ecosystems in predictable ways, yet our understanding of the consequences of these patterns for stream food webs is coarse. Lakes are prominent geomorphic features of many headwater catchments and drive the ecology of the streams that flow from them. However little is known about the extent to which the biophysical features of lakes control patterns of energy flow in the food webs of lake outlet streams. Because of their influence on the timing and magnitude of organic matter cycled within lakes, factors such as lake area, morphometry, and basin orientation that influence the amount of organic matter routed downstream are likely to drive in-stream production. In the Rocky Mountains of the western U.S., high elevation lakes are predicted to experience increasingly earlier snowmelt and longer ice-free periods â€“ changes that will alter the timing of planktonic phenology and subsidies to downstream food webs. The extent to which these changes will affect food webs in mountain headwater streams is unknown. This research will (i) quantify how different biophysical features of lakes alter the timing and patterns of energy flow in the food webs downstream of those lakes, and (ii) explore how those interactions are altered by anticipated changes in climate. The specific research proposed for summer 2016 will generate preliminary data and demonstrate feasibility in support of a full funding proposal that will address these two goals through a combination of multi-lake field surveys and mesocosm experiments. The primary research aim of this preliminary work is to collect phytoplankton, zooplankton, terrestrial organic matter, and stream biofilm samples to determine the extent to which these organic matter end-members can be distinguished isotopically using natural abundance ratios of 2H, 13C, and 15N. A secondary aim, in support of a possible undergraduate independent research project, is to collect samples of parasitized and non-parasitized mayfly larvae of different taxa to determine the extent to which their microbiomes differ.
Subject: Other

ResearchPlanTitle: Baetis parasitism in a changing environment
ResearchPlanOrganisms: Baetis bicaudatus, Salvelinus fontinalis, Gasteromermis spp.
Subject: Climate Change

ResearchPlanTitle: Beyond the ecological: can presence of an invader affect floral selection in a native species?
ResearchPlanAbstract: Biological invasions are known to have tangible economic and ecological effects on the invaded ecosystem. A common trend is that native plant species are negatively affected by the presence of an invasive plant species. As the amount of pristine ecosystems decreases and the amount of invaded non-pristine areas increases, we need to start thinking about the effects that invasive species could have on the evolution of native species. In other words, can native species adapt to invasions? Here I propose to continue the study of the evolutionary and ecological effects that the invasive plant Linaria vulgaris (butter and eggs) has on the native plant Penstemon strictus (Rocky Mountain Penstemon). I will observe plants of P. strictus in the absence and presence of L. vulgaris. I will document pollinator visitations to P. strictus and pair these observations with floral measurements of these plants. This way I will be able to analyze whether or not the presence of L. vulgaris causes changes in the traits that the pollinators are selecting for in P. strictus (traits like flower size and nectar production). A change in natural selection with the presence of L. vulgaris would suggest that the invader has an evolutionary effect. To study the ecological effects of L. vulgaris on P. strictus, I will look at whether P. strictus fruit production and pollinator visitation is different in the presence and absence of L. vulgaris. Last year I was able to collect this information. Although I was unable to find statistical evidence for ecological and evolutionary effects there were trends in this dataset that suggest that such effects could be occurring in this system. For summer 2016 I propose to conduct the same experiments as last year in order to increment my sample size and include yearly variation in my analysis. Finally I will study whether different types of pollinators move different amounts of L. vulgaris pollen to individuals of P. strictus. This is of particular interest because foreign pollen (pollen from another species) can reduce the reproductive success of a species.
Subject: Pollination

ResearchPlanTitle: Ecology and impacts of invasive Brassicaceae in high altitude ecosystems
ResearchPlanAbstract: In addition to the effects of climate change, invasive plants are of growing concern in high altitude ecosystems. Several invasive plants in this region belong to the mustard family (Brassicaceae), and produce a class of chemicals known as glucosinolates. Glucosinolates of invasive plants in the Northeast are known to disrupt longstanding symbiotic relationships between native plants and soil micro-organisms, but whether or not this phenomenon is occurring elsewhere, such as the Rocky Mountains, is unknown. This study investigates the ecology of invasive mustard plants in high altitude ecosystems. We are interested in the effects on native vegetation and soils, and how these effects vary along elevation gradients and in response to climate change.
Subject: Climate Change

ResearchPlanTitle: Integrating trait evolution and community ecology to better understand selection in nature
ResearchPlanAbstract: It is common knowledge that ecological interactions drive evolutionary change. However, the converse of this relationshipâ€”how evolution affects ecologyâ€”remains understudied, largely because these two forces were long believed to operate on disparate time scales. In the past few decades, evidence has mounted for the capacity of microevolutionary change to occur rapidly, over the course of a single or a few generations. Recognizing that ecology and evolution are contemporary counterparts requires us to consider the potential of reciprocal rather than just unidirectional interactions between them. Here, I propose to investigate the impact of microevolutionary change on ecological interactions between a focal plant and its insect herbivores, and to assess how reciprocal interactions between ecological and evolutionary forces influence patterns of diversity at both the genetic and organismal levels.
ResearchPlanOrganisms: Boechera stricta and associated insect herbivores
Subject: Other

ResearchPlanTitle: Assessing mechanisms of coexistence among early flowering plants under a changing climate
ResearchPlanAbstract: Maintaining biodiversity, or the number of species present in a given place, is important to safeguard essential ecosystem functions and for production of goods and services valuable to humans. How species that share a limited number of resources are able to live in the same place at the same time is a fundamental scientific question. Because these species share common resources, their ability to coexist is particularly sensitive to environmental conditions, and any change in their interactions with each other could result in extinction. Specifically, warming temperatures are causing plants to begin blooming earlier in the season for some species, while others are actually blooming later than in the historical past. If all of the species in the community respond differently to the same environmental cue, certain plants might now flower at the same time and thus compete for the same pollinators. My research examines the relationship between timing of life cycle events and the ability of two plant species to coexist. I am interested in examining these questions for two, early co-flowering species in the Rocky Mountains, Claytonia lanceolata and Fragaria virginiana. To understand how these species coexist in the community, I will first determine (1) phenological overlap of C. lanceolata and F. virginiana, (2) the strength of interspecific and intraspecific competition for biotic and abiotic resources, and (3) begin a demographic study on F. virginiana and continue collecting demographic data on C. lanceolata. With this information, I will be able to ask how climate change will affect how these two species interact through altering competition for pollinators and non-living resources such as nutrients and light.
Subject: Phenology

ResearchPlanTitle: A Hidden World: Meiofauna Communities in Moss and Lichens along an Altitudinal Gradiant
ResearchPlanAbstract: Lichens and mosses are microhabitats for tardigrades "water bears", rotifers, nematodes, mites and protozoans. We will collect these small habitats along an altitudinal gradient and examine them under a microscope. We will record the species and abundance of organisms present. We expect to find new species and differences in community structure along the altitudinal gradient. This is the first study of meiofaunal communities in mosses and lichens in western Colorado.
ResearchPlanOrganisms: My principal organisms are lichen, moss and the microscopic organisms that live in them (tardigrades, rotifers, nematodes, mites and protozoans).
Subject: Other

ResearchPlanTitle: Comparative study of wing development and mitochondrial genome adaptation to high elevation in Caddisflies (Order: Trichoptera)
ResearchPlanAbstract: Caddisflies are the closest relatives of butterflies and moths, yet they are little studied. Unlike most butterflies and moths, they have aquatic larvae. I will be comparing how caddisfly wing development with how butterflies and moths build their wings. I will also be studying how the DNA in the mitochondrion (the powerhouse of the cell) of caddisflies has adapted to low oxygen conditions at high elevation. Ability to tolerate to low oxygen conditions may play a role in determining the altitudinal ranges of different caddisfly species.
Subject: Other

ResearchPlanTitle: Effects of experimental shifts in soil moisture and flowering phenology on plant-pollinator interactions
ResearchPlanAbstract: Plant-pollinator mutualisms are vital to maintaining the functional integrity of most terrestrial ecosystems and to global crop production. Recent changes in climate, however, may disrupt these ecologically and economically important relationships. Warmer springs and early snowmelt associated with climate change are altering the timing of plant reproduction and pollinator emergence (i.e. phenology), potentially disrupting historic plant-pollinator mutualisms. Decreased snow cover and early snowmelt are also likely to reduce soil water availability during the growing season, potentially altering the capacity of plants to attract pollinators via changes in floral traits. The aim of my dissertation research is to investigate the mechanisms driving plant-pollinator responses to changes in water availability and phenology associated with warmer springs and early snowmelt. Over that last four years at RMBL, I have tested extent which floral rewards, pollination, and seed set of the tall-fringed bluebell, Mertensia ciliata (Boraginaceae), respond to experimental manipulations of water and flowering phenology. I propose to extend the research I have already completed for my dissertation with two projects. First, in order to gain some understanding of the potential demographic consequences that changes in phenology may have on populations, I propose to plant seeds from my 2015 phenology manipulation experiment in a common garden using a randomized block design and to return in 2017 to assess germination and growth. Second, I propose to examine the potential interactive effects that shifts in water availability and flowering phenology may have on pollination and plant reproduction. To do this, I will directly manipulate soil moisture and flowering phenology and measure effects on plant and floral characters, pollination, and seed set. These experimental results will be integrated with ongoing observations of individual, population, and co-flowering community level responses to natural variation in soil moisture and phenology. As warmer springs and early snowmelt often co-occur, so too will changes in flowering phenology and water availability. Decreased pollination success due to differences in flowering time may be exacerbated by drought-induced changes in floral attractants, resulting in further declines in seed set. Moreover, even if plants receive the same number of pollinator visits, reduced soil moisture could impact resource availability for seed provisioning. Understanding the extent to which these mechanisms interact is an important next step to improving the ecological realism of this work and its utility for predicting how plant-pollinator interactions may respond to future climate change.
ResearchPlanOrganisms: Mertensia ciliata (James ex Torr.) G. Don. (Boraginaceae)
Subject: Pollination

ResearchPlanTitle: Facilities Projects at RMBL 2016
ResearchPlanAbstract: The research committee annually reviews the RMBL Facilities Plans for impacts and conflicts. There are very few projects involving ground disturbance in 2016.
Subject: Climate Change

ResearchPlanTitle: Long-term studies of phenology and plant demography in the context of climate change; also Demography, genomics, and foraging behavior of hummingbirds (collaborators Whiteman and Stoddard)
ResearchPlanAbstract: This research focuses on understanding variation in timing and abundance of flowering in sub-alpine wildflower communities in the vicinity of RMBL. One aim of this work is to elucidate environmental variables that generate this phenological variation. Another goal is to determine the consequences of this variation for plant demography and for animals that interact with the wildflowers. There seem to be effects of climate change on flowering phenology and floral abundance at the species and community level. We will also continue some previous work on hummingbird demography and genomics (collaborator Whiteman), and start a project on hummingbird vision (collaborator Stoddard)
Subject: Long-Term

ResearchPlanTitle: Watershed Function SFA: ecohydrology component tasks
ResearchPlanAbstract: Climate change and human activities - whose numbers and lifestyles drive an ever-increasing demand for clean water, food, and energy - are significantly reshaping interactions between vegetation, soils, subsurface and fluvial compartments of watersheds throughout the world. While watersheds are recognized as the Earthâ€™s key functional unit for assessing and managing water resources, hydrological processes in watershed mediate most if not all biogeochemical processes that support life on Earth. In spite of the importance of watershed function to agriculture, energy, urban and other societally important systems, the scientific community is at an incipient stage of developing predictive understandings of how watersheds function from a hydrological and biogeochemical perspective, and how they will respond to increasingly frequent perturbations, such as floods and droughts. Several challenges inhibit the ability to predict watershed dynamics, including significant bedrock-through-canopy variability and the vast scale range over which microbes, plants, minerals and fluids that interact within the heterogeneous watershed template. Currently, there are huge uncertainties associated with predicting watershed function and dynamics at space and time scales relevant for underpinning actionable management of watershed systems. The Watershed Function Scientific Focus Area (SFA) aims to substantially reduce this uncertainty through developing approaches to quantify and predict the cumulative watershed hydrological and biogeochemical response to perturbations. In particular, the Watershed Function SFA takes a systems-within-systems view to develop and test new â€˜scale-awareâ€™ approaches to predict the cumulative watershed downgradient response to a perturbation based on detailed information available from select subsystems within the watershed. The Watershed Function SFA will develop and test the ability of scale-aware approaches to predict how mountainous watersheds retain and release water, nutrients, carbon and metals downgradient. In particular, the SFA will quantify how droughts, early snowmelt, and other perturbations that are expected to be increasingly common will influence mountainous watershed dynamics that impact downstream water availability and biogeochemical cycling at seasonal to decadal timescales. We choose to work within mountainous watersheds due to the critical role of mountainous watersheds for supplying water for the world as well as to their vulnerability to global warming, which is expected to lead to a cascade of unknown effects on downgradient water availability, nutrient loading, carbon cycling, and water quality. We propose to initiate this project in a headwater catchment of the Upper Colorado River Basin, perhaps the most important Basin in the Western US, which supplies municipal water to more than 1 in 10 Americans, irrigation water and nutrients to more than 5.5 million acres of land, and supports more than 4,200 megawatts of electrical generating capacity, providing power to hundreds of local areas and millions of people, and supports diverse ecosystems that provide other societally relevant services. The theme-based hypothesis for which I am co-lead with Eoin Brodie focuses on ecohydrology and is: Feedbacks between hydrology-driven changes in vegetation and vegetationdriven changes in hydrology will increase evaporative loss, decrease groundwater recharge, and decouple microbial biogeochemical processes that control organic matter turnover and nutrient fluxes in mountainous watersheds.
ResearchPlanOrganisms: plants, soils, and microbes in mountain meadows
Subject: Climate Change

ResearchPlanTitle: Exhumation history of Tertiary plutons in the Elk and West Elk mountains from (U-Th)/He thermochronometry
ResearchPlanAbstract: We will perform a pilot (U-Th)/He thermochronometry (i.e. AHe) study on the Crystal pluton, Gothic pluton, and Copper Creek Sill so as to document the erosion history of the Elk and West Elk mountain ranges during the past 35 million years. AHe analysis determines the age at which a rock cooled below a temperature of about 75ËšC. Combined with a knowledge of the geothermal gradient, which is the rate at which the temperature increases with depth in the Earth, this AHe analysis will reveal when these igneous intrusive rocks, which comprise magma that cooled at depth, passed through a given depth of burial during the erosion episodes that removed the once overlying rock to expose them at Earthâ€™s surface. It is important to know when Coloradoâ€™s mountains experienced pulses of rapid erosion because that erosion history can help constrain the history of mountain uplift that formed the range and the development of the river system that drains it. Geologists donâ€™t actually know when and why the Colorado Rockies reached their current elevation, but many assume that uplift of the mountain range triggered a simultaneous episode of rapid erosion. That is a distinct possibility, but rapid erosion episodes can also be triggered by climate change or drainage reorganization. In the case of Coloradoâ€™s mountains, alternative explanations for rapid erosion include uplift of the mountain range itself, episodes of pronounced global cooling that occurred about 15 million years ago and again at 5 million years ago, and a major reorganization of the river drainage network, which created the modern Colorado River system, at about 6 million years ago. By constructing an erosion history for the Elk and West Elk mountains over the past 35 million years, we will be able to compare the actual erosion record to the dates of these alternative incision triggers. This comparison will offer insight into the growth history of the mountain range and into evolution of the climate system and the Colorado River drainage network that have sculpted its modern topography.
Subject: Other

ResearchPlanTitle: Are secure individuals more vigilant?
ResearchPlanAbstract: Group size is a common measure of sociality and has been used to better understand the concept of â€œsafety in numbers.â€ Using vigilance as a measure of perceived predation risk, many studies have found support for the â€œgroup size effect,â€ an inverse relationship between group size and vigilance. However, the group size does not always explain the variation seen in individual vigilance. Group size is but one of many social attributes, such as dominance and social relationships. Studies have shown that individual safety may be found not only in numbers, but also in how connected an individual is with others in its social group. To test the hypothesis that an individualâ€™s connectedness creates a sense of security, we will focus on yellow-bellied marmots and ask whether the strength of social relationships is associated with time allocation to vigilance and foraging. If connectedness creates a â€œsense of security,â€ then more connected individuals will allocate less time to vigilance during bouts of foraging compared to less connected individuals.
Subject: Long-Term

ResearchPlanTitle: Pollen thieves and pollen limitation on gynodioecious Polemonium foliosissimum (Polemoniaceae) fitness
ResearchPlanAbstract: Leafy Jacob's ladder (leafy Polemonium) is subject to attack from a species of fly related to the common house fly that tend to eat the plant's pollen. Pollen is used as a resource to attract pollinators such as honey bees, bumble bees, flies, and hummingbirds. When the protein-rich pollen is stolen from the plant, this may cause the plant to change its strategy with respect to spending energy in its resources that will either attract more pollinators or will defend itself from herbivores and insects. The leafy Polemonium has flowers with pollen (hermaphrodites) consisting of both male and female reproductive organs and female flowers that do not produce any pollen. By looking at the visitation of the flies eating leafy Polemonium's pollen, it becomes important to see if the flies are affecting the amount of seeds produced by Polemonium, as this is an indicator of fitness, or how successful the plant is. In order to determine if fitness is different between the hermaphroditic and female flowers, some of the male reproductive organs on the hermaphrodites that produce pollen, called anthers are being removed. What this does is to more or less change the hermaphrodites to appear to be normal females, whereas the flies consuming pollen, called pollen thieves may also decrease amount of normal pollen produced on flowers had the anthers not been removed. We are looking to see if pollinators continue to visit flowers when pollen is removed or not removed in order to determine if there are any changes to fitness by counting the numbers of seeds produced by the leafy Polemonium.
Subject: Pollination

ResearchPlanTitle: Is sodium a catalyst in terrestrial communities and ecosystems
ResearchPlanAbstract: The purpose of this project is to look at salt (Na) in ecosystems and to assess the need for salt among species on different levels of the food chain. My research will center on whether or not plants spike their nectar with salt to attract pollinators and on pollinators' needs for salt at different elevations. This project is pertinent to studying climate change as knowing about the role and geography of sodium in ecosystems can help to predict the future consequences of climate change.
ResearchPlanOrganisms: Ipomopsis and Delphinium (wildflowers) and Pollinators (Hummingbirds and or bees and butterflies)

ResearchPlanTitle: Road Dust
ResearchPlanAbstract: I am studying three different things at rmbl to see if they are linked. A dominant wildflower, scarlet gilia, flies (hylemya sp.), and seed count. The objective is find find a cause and effect. To see if road dust influences their host selection and ultimately effects the seed set in the population of the wildflower.

ResearchPlanTitle: Temporal Variations in Mountain White-Crowned Sparrow Nestling Feeding Frequency
ResearchPlanAbstract: Mountain White-Crowned Sparrows (Zonotrichia leucophrys oriantha) are unique in that their nestlings, which require parental care for 9 days before fledging, have a 25% higher metabolic rate than other open-nesting passerines (Weathers et. al. 2003). This unusually high energetic demand requires that parents frequently feed their young; however, female sparrows must balance their time between bouts of foraging and protecting vulnerable nestlings from extreme temperatures. I hypothesize that in the early nesting season, feeding will mostly occur in the mid-morning through the afternoon because females must insulate their nestlings during the cold early mornings. Later in the summer, feeding will occur more often during the early morning hours so that the mother can shade her nestlings from the hot afternoon sun. Particularly, I expect these trends to be most pronounced when the nestlings are 0 to 3 days old, before they have developed thermoregulatory capabilities. I intend to test this by monitoring Mountain White-Crowned Sparrow nests with data loggers that record temperature every two minutes and a nest camera that will reveal the frequency at which nestlings are fed.
Subject: Other

ResearchPlanTitle: Understanding the Influence of Parasitism on Consumer Driven Nutrient Recycling by Aquatic Insects
ResearchPlanAbstract: We will be studying the effects of paratism on consumer-driven nutritrient recycling. Parasites can affect the excretions of their hosts in dramatic ways by feeding on them. Shifting of the excretions can affect microbes and higher consumers as the parasite infection grows. We will be collecting insect larvae, half parasitized and half unparastized. We will be testing the excretions of each inidividual and then comparing how paratism affects their excretions. We expect to see a difference between the excretions of unparastized and parasitized insects. We also expect the difference between the excretions to grow as the parasite infection grows.
ResearchPlanOrganisms: Megarcys signata/ mites, Rhithrogena/ Chironimid, and Baetis Bicaudatus/ Mermithid
Subject: Other

ResearchPlanTitle: Mutualistic Networks Over Time: The Effects of Changing Floral Abundances on Plant-Pollinator Interactions
ResearchPlanAbstract: Plant pollinator interactions are particularly important from a conservation standpoint. We are going to study the effects of changing plant flower abundances on the number of species with which they interact. We predict that increasing floral abundance (as a plant begins to bloom) will lead to an increase in the number of species a plant interacts with due to an increase in within-species competition. We will test this by comparing our data on the number of interactions with other species with a random model that predicts the number of interactions based solely on abundance and not an actual change in niche-size. If our data indicates that there is a greater increase in plant-species interactions that those predicted from a random model, we will infer that there is a significant change in the number of species a plant interacts with as its abundance increases.
ResearchPlanOrganisms: Plants and Pollinators in the Gothic area
Subject: Pollination

ResearchPlanTitle: Local adaptation in Boechera stricta
ResearchPlanAbstract: To deal with changing climatic conditions such as temperatures and water availability, many plants adapt to their local environment to ensure that they can survive even in conditions that might not be ideal. It is important to understand plantsâ€™ ability to adapt to their environment so that we can understand how their survival and reproduction will be impacted by climate change or other disturbances. This study aims to analyze the effect of climate change on local adaptation in montane ecosystems, specifically through seed germination success and fitness in Boechera stricta, a hardy perennial forb of the brassicaceae family with a wide natural geographic and elevational range. Boechera stricta primarily self-fertilizes, resulting in many families with distinct genotypes from varying environments and varying local adaptations. Since the 1970s, B. stricta flowering has advanced approximately 13 days, likely due to changes in temperature, season length, and timing of snowmelt. This change in phenology demonstrates that the effects of climate change can already be seen in natural B. stricta populations. This study will manipulate the timing of snowmelt in B. stricta plots at varying elevations and will analyze the levels of seed germination success and fitness with regards to factors such as family of origin.
Subject: Climate Change

ResearchPlanTitle: Effects of Helianthella quinquenervis Extrafloral Nectaries on Ant Abundance and Community Structure
ResearchPlanAbstract: I will be finding how ant abundance is affected when the mutualism between extrafloral nectaries are taken away, and/or kept, observing the ants nutritional needs, and will be observing the how the ant community structure is affected.
Subject: Other

ResearchPlanTitle: Effects of early snow melt and frost on reproductive success of subalpine forbs
ResearchPlanAbstract: In this study, I seek to expand upon the investigation of Gezon et al. (2016) by exploring the factors impacting reproductive success in two other subalpine wildflowers. By comparing seed set in plots with early snow removal or natural snow melt and exposed to or protected from frost, I will investigate the way in which this complex suite of variables interact to impact reproductive success. Additionally, by comparing the response of species which flower at different times throughout the summer which have different phenological responses to climate change, I will explore the manner in which species with different flowering periods respond to climate change related variables.
Subject: Climate Change

ResearchPlanTitle: Plants and Elevation
ResearchPlanAbstract: I will be attempting to correlate hyperspectral images with leaf and community traits.

ResearchPlanTitle: Energetic Costs of Asteraceae Specialization in Osmia Mason Bees
ResearchPlanAbstract: Osmia mason bees are solitary nesting bees that provision pollen for offspring in holes in trees and other woody material. Some local species are specialists on the pollen of the plant family Asteraceae. This specialization is commen, yet Asteraceae pollen is low in protein and difficult to use for non-specialist bees. Specialization on this pollen protects the bees from brood parasitism by a sapygid wasp, although the mechanism of this protection is not well understood. However, there may be costs to using this low quality pollen, such as the need to provision more pollen relative to bees using other pollens, or the need to make more foraging flights in order to provision enough of a protein mass for offspring.
Subject: Pollination

ResearchPlanTitle: Response diversity to environmental variables in different bee species
ResearchPlanAbstract: With the issue of climate change looming over important ecosystem functions such as plant-pollinator interactions in which bees play a vital role, we will examine response diversity in different bee species. Specifically, we are curious as to whether different bee species respond differently to climate change related environmental variables such as temperature, precipitation, and snow melt timing. Additionally, if they do, we will investigate whether their responses are correlated to certain shared traits, which would allow us to make predictions about responses by other bee species not included in this study.
Subject: Climate Change

ResearchPlanTitle: Effects of Tephritid fly-damaged Aspen Sunflowers on Pollinator Visitation of Floral Neighbors
ResearchPlanAbstract: I hope to determine if flower damage from seed predators influence patterns of pollinator visitation. Tephritid flies (a type of fruit fly) are known to lay eggs inside of flowers in the sunflower family, where their larvae feed on the developing seeds. These flies not only hinder seeds from maturing, but discolor the flowers in the process. If pollinators find these discolored flowers visually unappealing, the flowers may receive fewer pollinator visits, and therefore produce fewer seeds. If these flowers receive fewer pollinator visits, it is possible that the surrounding flower community will receive fewer visits as well. These effects may ultimately change floral composition in a community.
Subject: Pollination

ResearchPlanTitle: Comparing clines in floral and vegetative traits along an elevation gradient in an Ipomopsis hybrid zone
ResearchPlanAbstract: This study aims to test predictions about the mechanisms driving speciation in a naturally occurring Ipomopsis hybrid zone by measuring several clines in floral and vegetative traits along an elevation gradient. If speciation in the Ipomopsis hybrid zone can be attributed to pollinator-driven divergent selection, clines in floral traits will be steeper than clines in vegetative traits. Alternatively, if speciation can be largely attributed to environmentally-driven divergent selection, clines in vegetative traits will be steeper than clines in floral traits.
Subject: Other

ResearchPlanTitle: Effects of phenological change on Ligusticum porteriâ€™s volatiles and trophic interactions
ResearchPlanAbstract: We will study how elevated temperature and phenological stage impacts floral volatiles and herbivory of Ligusticum porteri. Aphids are L. porteri's primary herbivore, which have a mutualistic relationship with Ants. We will be monitoring the phenological stage and insects present on L. porteri in three treatment groups throughout the summer. We will advance the phenology of L. porteri using open top warming chambers (OTC). The OTCs will remain on plants for the entire study in the advanced phenology and increased temperature treatment group, and will be removed after 10 days for the advanced phenology group. Floral volatiles will be captured using silicon tubing (ST) and analyzed by thermal desorption coupled to gas chromatography mass spectrometry (TD-GC-MS) from each treatment group to quantify the volatiles released. Aphids from existing colonies will be placed onto test plants and monitored to determine their growth rate. It is unknown how advancing host-plant phenology will impact aphid and ant interactions and overall abundances. We will be able to determine if differences in volatiles emitted and aphid populations are observed are due to advanced host plant phenology or warming itself.
Subject: Phenology

ResearchPlanTitle: Biochemical effects on the susceptibility of Boechera stricta to the rust pathogen Puccinia monoica
ResearchPlanAbstract: How do fungal infections vary across a population or a multitude of populations? Puccinia is a rust fungus that infects its host plant and completely hijacks the hostâ€™s biochemical mechanisms in order to reproduce. This can be observed in the mustard Boechera stricta. In Boechera, the fungus enters and sterilizes the plant, rendering it unable to reproduce. It then forces Boechera to grow a bright yellow pseudo flower in order to spread the fungal spores further. What evolutionary mechanisms enable these infections to be successful? Conversely, what mechanisms have plants developed to combat the fungi? A hypothesis for this question may be that certain chemical compounds in mustard called glucosinolates, which are responsible for defense against herbivores and pathogens, facilitate resistance to fungal infection. Puccinia is successful; this is obvious simply by observing it in nature, but Puccinia infections are not seen in clusters; therefore, something must be preventing infection in some plants. Glucosinolate are not all the same; they differ in the molecular side chains, presumably causing different effects. By isolating species of Boechera stricta to differ in only the type of glucosinolate they produce, a correlation between the susceptibility of the plant to fungal infection may be seen. A manipulative experiment where several known genotypes of Boechera (IV) are exposed to the fungus and their response (DV) is observed, may yield results concerning the ecological and biochemical significance of plant/fungal interactions
Subject: Phenology

ResearchPlanTitle: Plant Thermoregulation
ResearchPlanAbstract: The purpose of this experiment is to observe which plant traits, such as leaf area, angle, and mass, stomatal conductance and ratio, absorbance, and plant height affect a plant's ability to thermoregulate. By observing how these traits affect a plant's ability to thermoregulate, we can determine which traits affect the rate at which species thermoregulate. This will give us a better understanding of which species will be more adapted to survive in a given community as the climate is changing.

ResearchPlanTitle: Larval feeding behavior and leaf components that affect the survival of Pieris macdunnoughii on the invasive mustard Thlaspi arvense
ResearchPlanAbstract: Pieris macdunoughii is a small white native butterfly to the Rocky Mountain region. The females mistakenly lay their eggs on an invasive mustard plant, Thlaspi arvense. This plant is lethal to the larvae, causing them to die before they become butterflies. There are chemicals, glucosinolates, in the leaves that are used in defense against herbivores. One specific chemical, sinigrin, has be found to release toxins such as hydrogen cyanide. I am exploring how P. macdunnoughii larvae change their feeding behavior when present with T. arvense and when sinigrin is added to leaves from plants they usually consume and develop on, such as Cardamine cordifloria.
