ResearchPlanTitle: The Effects of Nest Site Selection and Microclimate on Nest Success in the Mountain White-Crowned Sparrow
ResearchPlanAbstract: Nest site selection is crucial in determining nest success during the breeding season (Wells and Fuhlendorf 2005). Nest site characteristics can determine susceptibility to nest predators as well as the microclimate of the nest. Each decision regarding nest site selection comes with an inherent trade off. The goal of this study is to identify the most important nest site characteristics to better understand how these factors can affect nest survival throughout the breeding season. Local nest microclimate will be examined, as well as major nest site factors such as nest height, concealment, distance from the nearest road, nesting substrate, wind susceptibility, and nest composition.
Subject: Other

ResearchPlanTitle: Effects of experimental warming on herbivory and fungal pathogen load on subalpine grass species Festuca thurberi, Poa pratensis, and Achnatherum lettermanii
ResearchPlanAbstract: Does climate warming alter theÂ relationship between plants and their insect herbivores and fungal pathogens?Â We will utilize the warming experiments at RMBL and multiple years of data to observe how the amount of damage by plant enemies changes in an altered climate over time. Many experiments that involve manipulatingÂ climate only look at the direct effectsÂ of climate on plant communities. This ignores the indirect effectsÂ of climate change on plant-enemy interactions (insect herbivores andÂ fungal pathogens). With the longest running outdoor warming experiment and 25 years of warming data this allows us a unique opportunity to see how grasses, specifically Festuca thurberi, Poa pratensis, and Achnatherum lettermanii handle an increased growing season and longer exposure to attack. Hypothesis: Warming will increase these species infection and herbivory rates due to an extended growing season from early snow melt which allows for higher metabolic rates in insects and fungi. Prediction: Within our warming plots, the rates of herbivory and fungal pathogen laod will increase over time as compared with our none-warming, control plots.
ResearchPlanOrganisms: Festuca thurberi, Poa pratensis, Achnatherum lettermanii (Poaceae)
Subject: Climate Change

ResearchPlanTitle: EFFECTS OF EXPERIMENTAL SHIFTS IN SOIL MOISTURE AND FLOWERING PHENOLOGY ON PLANT-POLLINATOR INTERACTIONS
ResearchPlanAbstract: This study will investigate the importance of different pollinators to M. ciliata reproduction across flowering phenology using the approach suggested by Neâ€™eman et al. (2010). According to this approach, pollinator importance can be described as the product of visit probability (measured here by pollinator visitation frequency) and pollinator performance (measured here as seed set) for each type of pollinator. Based on pollinator visitation rate, pollinator diversity, and seed set data collected last summer, we hypothesize that bumble bees will have increased pollinator importance for M. ciliata relative to other pollinators later in the flowering season. We predict that the proportion of pollinators that are bumble bees will increase and we will see greater seed set in the flowers they have pollinated relative to other pollinators as the flowering season progresses. This study builds on previous research by investigating how the various pollinators differ in their contribution to seed set and providing insight into whether or how pollinator performance changes with flowering time.
Subject: Pollination

ResearchPlanTitle: Do social interactions increase basal stress levels in breeding female yellow-bellied marmots?
ResearchPlanAbstract: Why do many animals live in social groups? Although many benefits of group living have been found, the formation of social groups also comes at a cost. A good way to assess how the social and ecological environment is affecting an individual is through stress levels. High levels of stress, measured via concentration of fecal glucocorticoid metabolites (FGMs), indicate a suboptimal environment. We will be investigating how group size, individualsâ€™ social network (as determined by their social interactions), and litter size affect stress in female yellow-bellied marmots with confirmed litters.
Subject: Other

ResearchPlanInstitution: University of North Carolina at Chapel Hill
ResearchPlanTitle: Effects of Plant Diversity on Selection for Insect Resistance in Boechera stricta
ResearchPlanAbstract: In this study, I plan to use sites with both manipulative and observational plots to ask about the effects of surrounding plant communities and their diversity on selection of plant defense. By studying endogenous populations of B. stricta across several sites, I plan to ask the following questions: 1A. Do naturally-occurring B. stricta plants experience different selective pressures on insect resistance depending on neighboring plant diversity? 1B. Is species diversity per se or species composition a stronger influence on the selective pressures plants face on insect resistance? I will combine my observational work of naturally occurring B. stricta with experimental arrays that vary in allele frequencies for the BCMA gene. Specifically, I will use data collected from the arrays to ask the following: 2A. Does neighboring plant diversity influence herbivory? 2B. Does the BCMA allele favored by natural selection change depending on the context of the surrounding plant community? Or does the extent to which one allele is favored depend on that context? Finally, I will compare experimental populations, which have nearly one hundred plants per square meter, with natural populations, which usually have under ten individuals of the focal species. I will use this difference to ask about density effects: 3A. Are plant diversity effects of selection density-mediated? In other words, does plant diversity have a stronger effect when there is a greater ratio of heterospecific to conspecific plants with which to interact?
Subject: Climate Change

ResearchPlanTitle: Understanding how leaf endophytes are affected by climate change: Examining composition, diversity and growth rates of fungi in grass species with warming
ResearchPlanAbstract: Climate change (or global change) is occurring at an unprecedented rate with a 2â€“3Â° C increase in mean annual temperatures and shifts in precipitation location and frequency (Stott et al. 2010, Kivlin et al. 2013). Changing climatic patterns have been observed to alter responses of plants and other biota (e.g. through altitudinal shifts in plant community distribution, change in composition of ecological communities, etc.). While existing literature relates primarily to direct responses of plants and animals to climate change, no research currently exists which examines the direct physiological effects of warming on leaf endophytes, thus highlighting the need for this work. Ubiquitously, plants have been shown to associate with soil microbe symbionts including mycorrhizal fungi, nitrogen fixing bacteria and fungal endophytes. These microbes are increasingly being recognized for their potential to influence host populations and mitigate abiotic stressors associated with climate change (Cahill et al. 2008, Rudgers et al. 2009, Ranelli et al. 2015). We will focus on leaf endophytes as they have been found in all plant species surveyed to date and have many documented benefits. These benefits include increased resistance to herbivores, competitive ability, plant vigor, drought-tolerance and nutrient content of plants (Clay & Rudgers 2005, Rudgers et al. 2009, Kivlin et al. 2013). The relationship between climate change and leaf endophytes is being explored as observations suggest that endophyte distribution is influenced by climate (Kivlin et al. 2013) and understanding how these organisms will respond to change is crucial; they have the potential to influence feedback loops, dictate how plants thrive in changing climates and are helpful in predicting the ecological dynamics of changing communities (Rudgers et al. 2009) Three grasses from the warming meadows at the Rocky Mountain Biological Laboratory (RMBL) in Gothic, Colorado will be sampled for their leaf endophytes: Festuca thurberi, Poa pratensis and Achnatherum lettermanii. We chose grasses in the Poaceae family due to their practicable abundance, diversity and distribution. It has been estimated that there are 10,000 species of grasses in existence which cover roughly 20% of all land area (Shantz 1954, Barker et al. 2001). By constraining hosts to this single functional group, we reduced confounding effects of hostsâ€™ ecological roles (Kivlin et al. 2013). Another factor which contributed to the selection of grasses as the host clade is that they dominate montane and alpine meadows and, unlike trees, span the full altitudinal range (Shaw 2008). This ability to account for altitudinal variation in alpine areas allows for the surveying of diverse communities across which many fungi are able to disperse. The inclusion of natural sharp gradients also allows for the investigation of the relative importance of abiotic and biotic drivers of fungal distributions (Ranelli et al. 2015). The warming meadows are comprised of ten 3Ã—10 m plots located on an east to southeast facing glacial moraine, with their long dimension parallel to the hill slope. Control and experimental plots alternate and are separated by a 3 m gap to ensure that control plots are not affected by the warming experiment. Electric heaters are suspended 2.5 m above experimental plots and provide uniform heating (22 watts per square meter) to simulate warming predicted due to doubled atmospheric carbon dioxide levels. Heaters have been turned on continuously since 1990. Ultimately, this research seeks to understand factors associated with climate change, such as warming, that may directly influence the dependent variables of growth rates, diversity and composition of endophytic fungi in grasses. The treatment includes the cultivation of leaf endophytes from these three grasses and observation of change in the three dependent variables. The cultivated endophytes will be exposed to both ambient air conditions and cooled conditions. The results will then be compared to estimate temperature after initial collection and its role in changing the dependent variables. It is hypothesized that warming will decrease endophytic growth rates, decrease diversity and change composition of the endophyte communities.
Subject: Climate Change

ResearchPlanTitle: Behavioral strategies of golden-mantled ground squirrels
ResearchPlanAbstract: The field of behavioral ecology is important for understanding the consequences of differences in behavior between individuals, which may contribute to their fitness (Lind and Cresswell, 2005). Observing and quantifying the behaviors of free-ranging mammals in their natural habitats is especially difficult to observe due to the large scales of time and space that such research often requires. In addition, behavioral studies focusing on small, asocial mammal species typically receive little interest from researchers, possibly because they are assumed to not be as informative to studies on sociality (Ferron 1985, Jesmer 2011). Few behavioral studies focus on asocial sciurids. The golden-mantled ground squirrel (Callospermophilus lateralis; GMGS) is classified as the least social of five levels of sociality in ground-dwelling squirrels because of the predominance of agonistic interactions between adults (Michener 1983, Ferron 1985). Despite their seeming lack of a complex social structure, golden-mantled ground squirrels exhibit a wide range of behaviors and interactions, in which males and females play different roles and have different energetic demands in terms of reproduction. Males do not provide parental care to pups, while females have a gestation and lactation period of approximately two months (Ferron 1985, Bartels and Thompson 1993). Both sexes face the challenge of storing enough fat for hibernation while remaining slim and agile enough to escape predation. The primary objective of this study is to collect behavioral observations of GMGS to compare variation in activity budgets (the average percentage of time spent on different activities) and social interactions between a) males and females and b) adults and juveniles throughout the active season. I will attempt to answer the question of how the differences in energy expenditure and demands for survival associated with age and sex affect behavior in GMGS. I will also follow changes in behavior within individual reproductive females to see if activity budgets change between the early season, when females are tending to pups underground, and later in the season, after pups emerge. I expect to find that reproductive female individuals respond to the demands of caring for their litters by exhibiting more alert behaviors in the early season. In late summer, after the lactation period, my expectation is that females exhibit more foraging/feeding behaviors in order to gain the fat necessary for hibernation. I hypothesize that males spend the majority of their time foraging/feeding because of the weight loss they experience during the breeding season (Bronson 1979) and because they are known to store more fat than females (Blake 1972). I also suspect that juveniles have the highest percentage of time out of any group spent foraging/feeding, because they triple their body weight between emergence and hibernation (Meister 1996). Overall, this study will provide insight into the behavioral dynamics of golden-mantled ground squirrels, a classified asocial species with conflicting demands for survival during the summer.
Subject: Other

ResearchPlanTitle: Does Stress Explain Variation in Marmot Parenting Behavior?
ResearchPlanAbstract: I will be using glucocorticoid, alarm calling, social interaction, focal observation behavior, and pup survival data to study the relationships between stress, maternal care, and pup survival in marmots.
Subject: Climate Change

ResearchPlanTitle: Behavioral responces in Mountian White-Crowned Sparrows
ResearchPlanAbstract: Hello My name is Ryan Baker and my project for the summer is on "Varriation in Behavioral Aggression of Mountain White-Crowned Sparrows at Different Elevation Gradients." I am researching this to test the dispotic distribution hypothesis to find out why and how elevation effects this species and how climate change could affect this and many other species in the future. I will be hikeing to high, mid and low elevation sites each morning to collect data on behavioral responces of Mountain Whitecrowned Sparrows though live traps and observational studies.
Subject: Climate Change

ResearchPlanTitle: Community Floral Color Variation Across an Elevation Gradient
ResearchPlanAbstract: The goal of this study will be to determine if plant communities at higher elevation have a different floral color composition of those at lower elevation and if that difference is pollinator relevant. Similar to plants, pollinator composition changes with increasing altitude as certain species are better able to function in the harsh conditions found at higher elevation. In general, at lower elevations hymenopterans are more abundant at lower elevations whereas at higher elevations dipterans and lepidopterans become more abundant and important as pollinators (Shrestha et al 2014). It is well supported in the literature that flower color in under selection by pollinators (Arnold et al 2009, Shrestha et al 2014, Pellisier et al. 2012). According to the pollination syndrome hypothesis, bees tend to have a preference for UV- blue and blue flowers, whereas flowers that appear white and yellow to humans are generally associated with fly pollination (Arnold et al 2009). Thus, with a shift in pollinator guilds, it may be expected that blue flowers may dominate at lower elevations and a larger proportion of white (bee-blue-green) and yellow flowers may be the dominant species in communities of higher elevations (Arnold et al 2009). Fieldwork for this study will focus on expanding an existing database of floral spectral reflectance data. These spectra will then be combined with existing vegetation community composition data sets (along 6 elevation gradients) to document patterns of community color change with elevation.
Subject: Pollination

ResearchPlanTitle: Testing for Nutrient Limitation in Alpine Ponds across elevational and permanence gradients
ResearchPlanAbstract: We will test for limiting nutrients in a variety of shallow ponds in the Gothic, Colorado area. Nutrient limitation in context dependent, and in the case of this experiment we will look at ponds at both high (3900m) and low (2900m) elevation, as well as along a permanence gradient (temporary to permanent). Nutrient diffusing substrates will be set out in ponds, spiked with either nitrogen, phosphorus, or both, to determine which may limit in the pond. We expect that ponds at higher elevation will have less phosphorus input, and therefore be phosphorus limiting. On the other hand, ponds at lower elevation are expected to have greater phosphorus input from subsurface and above-ground water flow, and therefore be nitrogen limiting. This matters in the context of both understanding basic ecosystem function in these ponds, as well as understanding how the pond dynamics may change over time with climate change.
Subject: Other

ResearchPlanTitle: The Effects of Ants on Ecosystem Dynamics: Investigating the Ecological Influence of Ant Mounds in the Rocky Mountains
ResearchPlanAbstract: Although small in size and stature, ants can act as ecosystem engineers as they transform the land during the construction of large and elaborate nesting mounds. An influx of organic materials into mounds by workers leads to the accumulation of an abundance of organic matter and soil nutrients (Laakso & Setala, 1998). The concentration of nutrients within mounds can significantly surpass the stores contained by both vegetated and bare soils (Jones & Wagner, 2006). Moreover, this surplus of nutrients encourages the proliferation of microorganisms in the soil, which in turn speeds the rate of decomposition, and CO2 production, in mounds as compared with the surrounding soil (Jilkova, Picek, & Frouz, 2015; Jones & Wagner, 2006). In certain mounds, the total microbial biomass has been found to be up to three times higher in mound material than in the surrounding soil (Laakso & Setala, 1997). However, it is unknown how ant-mediated increases in nutrient conditions affect interactions between fungi and how fungal interactions with host plants are affected. Ant activity and the resulting ant mounds may directly and indirectly influence ecosystem function through a number of different pathways. With so many biotic and abiotic factors in play, the net effect of ant mounds on ecosystem functioning is still not well understood. With this project I will explore the direct and indirect effects of ant activity on soil properties, aboveground and belowground organisms, and overall ecosystem functioning. I will measure the direct changes in soil moisture, soil temperature, and soil carbon fluxes within ant mounds, as well as indirect interactions between co-occurring plant symbionts (arbuscular mycorrhizal fungi and dark-septate endophytes) and resulting changes in plant community composition around ant mounds in the Almont Triangle.
Subject: Other

ResearchPlanTitle: Carbon Dioxide Flux Measurements in Alpine and Subalpine Soils of the East River Watershed: Relationships with Landscape Features
ResearchPlanAbstract: Soils are some of the largest terrestrial reservoirs for carbon, and soil respiration - the exchange of carbon dioxide among the soil and the atmosphere - is a major component of the carbon cycle. Soil respiration is highly sensitive to soil moisture and temperature conditions; changes to these conditions may result in a net release of carbon. I propose to monitor soil respiration, moisture, and temperature as these factors vary with landscape features including topography, aspect, and vegetation type. By accounting for small-scale variability (differences in surface CO2 flux at points a few meters from each other), and temporal variability (across the summer season), I hope to improve our ability to understand and model soil respiration on the landscape scale. This understanding could prove invaluable as climates change and sensitive ecosystems, such as these, respond.
Subject: Climate Change

ResearchPlanTitle: SEX RATIO AND REPRODUCTIVE SUCCESS ALONG ELEVATIONAL GRADIENTS OF GYNODIOECIOUS POPULATIONS OF GERANIUM RICHARDSONII
ResearchPlanAbstract: We are investigating sex-ratio, reproductive success, and comparing sex-ratio to previous studies as means of looking at climate change effects on gynodioecious populations of Geranium richardsonii.
Subject: Climate Change

ResearchPlanTitle: Habitat Patch Use by Red Squirrels
ResearchPlanAbstract: N/A
Subject: Other

ResearchPlanTitle: Riparian Zone bog influence on dissolved organic carbon inputs into water catchments: understanding the East River tributaries in the Rocky Mountains.
ResearchPlanAbstract: Dissolved organic Carbon (DOC) acts as a crucial part of our soil and water cycle. DOC is a critical chemical attribute of freshwater systems, affecting the physical, chemical, and biological makeup of water sources (Gergel, 1999; McKnight, et al., 1993). This project aims to quantify the impact of small, wetland riparian zones on the overall Organic Carbon chemistry of the East River Watershed catchment system. This includes 1) measuring DOC contribution to overall stream organic fluxes, 2) characterizing the subsurface flow path gradients as water travels downhill towards streams, and 3) noting how DOC changes throughout the season within our specific Rock Creek catchment area. Together, these three specific goals will create a picture of DOC movement along the entire catchment water flow over time, both underground and in the streams themselves.
Subject: Climate Change

ResearchPlanTitle: Behavioral and evolutionary ecology studies of mammals and birds at the RMBL
ResearchPlanAbstract: I will describe two research programs in sequence. The first is a continuation of long-term studies of yellow-bellied marmot behavioral and evolutionary ecology. The second is a continuation of a set of studies that broadly address the question of the evolutionary ecology of fear in mule deer and birds. I am 'bundling' these studies into one omnibus proposal so as to streamline review and to streamline my ability to continue to support a variety of undergraduate REU and student research projects at the RMBL.
Subject: Long-Term

ResearchPlanTitle: Implications of Early Snowmelt for Plant Communities and Plant-Fungal Interactions
ResearchPlanAbstract: Climate warming is causing a trend toward less snowfall, and earlier spring snowmelt. Snowpack is very important in alpine ecology, as it impacts nutrient cycling, plant diversity and time of flowering, the water cycle and even tropospheric air temperatures. Warming may especially affect mountain ecosystems because of the large changes in the types of species and in growing conditions that happen across small distances. This research seeks to understand how plant species and their fungal partners will be affected by early snowmelt. Here we ask, 1) will plant diversity and the types of species living in a given place change with early snowmelt?, and 2) if earlier snowmelt causes harder growing conditions for plants, will plants recruit more fungal partners to help them deal with those stressors?
Subject: Climate Change

ResearchPlanInstitution: Norwegian University of Science and Technology
ResearchPlanTitle: Evolution in complex terrains: assessing the environmental sensitivity of natural selection across a topographically complex alpine landscape
ResearchPlanAbstract: Alpine plants are expected to be disproportionally affected by ongoing climate change. However, recent research suggests an important â€˜buffering effectâ€™ in complex alpine terrains, mediated by topographically controlled variation in microclimate. While short-term responses can occur through short-distance migration into microrefugia, or phenotypic adjustment to minor climatic perturbations, long-term persistence is likely to require tracking of changing adaptive optima, an evolutionary process. This study aims to quantify variation in phenotypic selection on floral and whole-plant traits of an alpine plant species across a complex alpine landscape, and the environmental dependency of selection at large (hundreds of meters to kilometres) and small scales (metres). This knowledge should contribute towards our ability to predict evolutionary responses to climate change in heterogeneous terrains.
Subject: Climate Change

ResearchPlanTitle: The consequences of phenological overlap on plant reproduction in the face of climate change
ResearchPlanAbstract: Phenology is an important life history trait because the timing of an organism's emergence affects its survival and reproduction. Because an organism's phenology is often dependent on abiotic cues, climate induced changes in the environment can greatly alter its phenology. As a result, organisms that respond to these changes at different rates both within and across trophic levels can become more or less overlapped both temporally and spatially. This can lead to changes in biotic interactions, thus impacting reproductive success for one or both of the interacting species. Under climate change, some plant species that have historically had staggering phenology are becoming more synchronous in their blooming due to increasing temperatures and early snowmelt, which might lead to facilitation and/or competition for pollinators. If an additional plant species helps lure pollinators to an area, then both plant species could benefit due to increased pollinator visitation. Competition might occur if one species lures pollinators away from another or causes increased heterospecific pollen transfer. Either scenario could have strong plant fitness consequences. The goal of this proposal is to understand the effects of flowering phenological overlap for the spring beauty, Claytonia lanceolata, using observations and experiments. Claytonia, which is the first species to bloom in the spring in the Rocky Mountains, shares pollinators with the bluebell, Mertensia fusiformis. Over the last 40 years, Mertensia phenology has been becoming more overlapped with Claytonia. This overlap could result in higher pollinator visitation to Claytonia due to facilitation, or reduced pollinator visitation and/or higher heterospecific pollen deposition on Claytonia stigmas due to competition if the shared pollinators are switching between plant species during foraging bouts. By examining the effects of phenological overlap between two common spring-blooming species, we will gain a greater understanding of the consequences of climate change on pollination mutualisms and fitness.
Subject: Climate Change

ResearchPlanTitle: Evolutionary Ecology and Conservation Biology of Amphibians
Subject: Long-Term

ResearchPlanTitle: Behavior and Ecology of Burying Beetles
ResearchPlanAbstract: I have a long-term research project on the behaviors and population dynamics of the burying beetle Nicrophorus investigator and have conducted a variety of field experiments on their reproduction, including mating and parental care behaviors, and ecology. There are five areas of research that I am particularly interested in pursuing: 1) understanding reproductive behaviors, including parental care and communication; 2) understanding population dynamics and species interactions; 3) using long-term data to develop predictive models of burying beetle population dynamics; 4) developing digital science education resources for K-12 and college-level students; and 5) establishing new research collaborations at RMBL. I use a variety of research techniques including: behavioral observations, population censuses, molecular genetic techniques, GIS models, and isotopic and chemical analyses to study trophic interactions and nutrient cycling.
ResearchPlanOrganisms: Nicrophorus (burying beetles); small rodents (mice and voles)
Subject: Long-Term

ResearchPlanTitle: Timing of reproduction in golden-mantled ground squirrels: causes, consequences, and implications for climate change
ResearchPlanAbstract: Mammals living in high-altitude environments must time their reproduction carefully so that offspring are born when food is available. For hibernating squirrels, food does not become available in the spring until melting snow stimulates growth of green vegetation, hence these squirrels often must emerge from hibernation and mate before the snow melts. However, we don't know what cues females use to anticipate the time of snow melt, in order to determine the correct time to mate, and we don't know what the consequences are for females that mate too late or too early. This study proposes to address both questions. The results will not only increase our understanding of how mammals adapt to the strong seasonality of high-altitude environments, but it also may enhance our understanding of the effects of climate change. Scientists fear that one consequence of warming temperatures is that the cues that animals use to anticipate seasonal events may no longer accurately predict those events.
Subject: Climate Change

ResearchPlanTitle: Scaling long-term functional attributes of plants, communities, and ecosystems: Responses to climate change across elevational gradients
ResearchPlanAbstract: An important question in ecology is to understand how specific traits of species influence the functioning of ecosystems. This study is designed to forge links between variation in the physical environment (e.g., changes in temperature and precipitation with elevation), changes in how plants and ecosystems work. Specifically, variation in functional measures of plants (plant size, leaf morphology and physiology etc.) and the functioning of whole ecosystems (the fluxes of carbon and water) characterize how changes in climate influence biology. Connecting how plants work in different environments with variation in ecosystem processes is critical for predicting responses of the biosphere to climate change. The mountainous landscape in and around RMBL provides enormous range of physical conditions, from warm wet meadows to cold, dry ridge tops. The resulting plant communities are likewise both functionally and phylogenetically diverse. I propose to continue monitoring how plant functional diversity and the functioning of whole-ecosystem fluxes vary across a range of elevations and environments and across years - spanning from cool wet years to increasingly dryer and hotter years. Our work at RMBL is part of a larger global project. We are continuing to build a global baseline of data by which to compare RMBL data using elevational studies from Arizona, California, Oregon, Mexico, Costa Rica, and Peru. Data from these field studies, combined with data from RMBL, now forms the basis for the development and testing of mechanistic, predictive models linking the functional attributes of organisms to large scale processes in plant communities and ecosystems.
Subject: Climate Change

ResearchPlanTitle: Effects of Advancing Peak Flow Hydrology on Stream Nutrient Dynamics and Primary Productivity
ResearchPlanAbstract: Many studies have examined how streams and their biota are adversely affected by climate linked increases in temperature, habitat loss or fragmentation, and changing precipitation, disturbance regimes, and terrestrial linkages. However, we lack an understanding of how climate induced changes in the phenology of seasonal transitions could affect stream ecosystems. Studying these phenological changes is pressing because they could accompany and compound the other ecological impacts of climate warming on stream ecosystems. The goal of my research is to explore how the phelogical advance of the "vernal window", or the transition between winter and the beginning of the spring/summer growing season, can directly and indirectly affect both nutrient dynamics and primary productivity in streams. I will use experiments, comparative observations, and hydrologic modeling to investigate these questions.
Subject: Phenology

ResearchPlanTitle: Ecology and impacts of invasive mustard species in high altitude ecosystems
ResearchPlanAbstract: The broad research aims of this work are to characterize distribution, abundance, and phenotypic variation of introduced (non-native) plants in sub-alpine habitats of the region. We are investigating whether and how these species affect native plants, herbivores, and soil organisms. We are also conducting a survey to map the current locations of the invasive plant Thlaspi arvense and its relatives and to begin help predict the likelihood of its spread in the future.
Subject: Climate Change

ResearchPlanTitle: Characterization of groundwater flow and associated geochemical fluxes in mineralized and unmineralized bedrock in the upper East River and adjacent watersheds, Colorado
ResearchPlanAbstract: Our project investigates the hydrology of mountainous areas that contain mineral deposits. Even if they are not mined, the mineral deposits may contribute metals to groundwater, which in turn may emerge in springs and contribute metal loads to streams and rivers. Through a series of geophysical and hydrological methods, we seek to characterize the groundwater flow system, primarily in the Mt. Emmons area, and to evaluate the role of groundwater transport of metals to shallow water bodies.
Subject: Other

ResearchPlanTitle: Evolutionary genetics of broad-tailed hummingbirds
ResearchPlanAbstract: Hummingbirds are among the most remarkable animals on the planet. They are able to hover, fly backwards and migrate over great distances, including across the Gulf of Mexico, non-stop. Darwin noted that their bills were remarkably well adapted to fit the nectar tubes of the flowers that they visit. This suggests that plants and the hummingbirds might be co-evolving. We are studying one of two species of hummingbird that visits RMBL and the only one that routinely breeds there, which is called the broad-tailed hummingbird. It nests in Mexico and flies up to the Rocky Mountains in summers. We are interested in understanding why we have found so much variation in the length and curvature of the bills of these birds at RMBL. We hypothesize that this variation between hummingbirds is due to their interactions with a diversity of flowers at RMBL. Short billed birds might visit shorter tubed flowers and longer billed birds longer tubed flowers. This variation could impose something called spatially varying natural selection on the birds, and actually cause genetic variation for bill length variation to be maintained in the population. Regardless of why it is maintained, we are interested in identifying the genes that control variation in bill length. Thus, we are sequencing the genomes of many broad-tailed hummingbirds and linking this to measures of bill length. We also collect pollen from the faces and fills of the birds and we are able to identify some of the plant species that have been visited by hummingbird individuals because each plant species has a distinct pollen morphology. In the end, our hope is to understand the genetic basis of a complex trait (bill morphology) that is highly variable in the RMBL populations of broad-tailed hummingbirds. These data will also be useful for tracing the evolutionary history of the birds, and can be used to understand their evolutionary potential, particularly in light of climate change.
Subject: Other

ResearchPlanTitle: The Role of the Environment in the Evolution of Developmental Variation
ResearchPlanAbstract: Variation in traits associated with development can be found in many species on Earth today from height in humans to flowering time in plants. Developmental variation is often attributed to variation at the genetic level. In humans, height is controlled by several genes and alternative types at each gene. However, the environment also plays a role in creating variation. Humans that are well nourished and have diets high in calcium are often taller than those who are malnourished. Thus, genes and environmental factors interact to produce developmental trait variation. My research aims to understand how genetic variation controlling developmental traits spread in a species as a result of organisms experiencing environmental variation. To do this, I am using the ecological model system, Boechera stricta, in its natural environment. Using over 400 collections that have DNA sequence data available, I am testing the effects of herbivory on the genetic variation controlling the development of branches. My research hopes to explain how environmental perturbations lead to genetic variation that produce variation in development.
Subject: Other

ResearchPlanTitle: Distribution of web-spinning caddisfly larvae in streams across gradients in shear stress
ResearchPlanAbstract: This research investigates species richness and abundance of hydropsychid web-spinning caddisfly larvae across gradients in shear stress. Caddisflies are dominant ecosystem engineers in many streams, often reaching densities of 1,000 to 10,000 individuals per square meter. Hydropsychid caddisflies act as ecosystem engineers by increasing streambed stability by binding rocks together with silk they produce and weave into mesh webs. The web structures they build also provide habitat and low-flow refuge for other macroinvertebrates. Although the distribution of caddisflies has been correlated with a variety of physical factors (temperature, dissolved oxygen, flow levels), very few field studies have explicitly mapped caddisfly density or species richness and correlated these estimates with geomorphic variables such as velocity, shear stress, and grain size. The research proposed here is a critical next step to determine how these ecosystem engineers might operate across various local- and landscape-scale gradients under changing hydrological regimes.
Subject: Climate Change

ResearchPlanTitle: Contact metamorphism of the Mancos Shale: Impacts on East River morphology
ResearchPlanAbstract: Intrusion of igneous rocks into the sedimentary rocks of southwestern Colorado ~30 million years ago resulted in contact metamorphism of the Mancos Shale that makes up the bedrock of the East River Valley in the vicinity of the Rocky Mountain Biological Laboratory. Changes in rock properties related to the metamorphism have important implications for how water moves through the rock, the weathering susceptibility of the minerals, the release of carbon from the rock, and the long-term landscape evolution of the East River corridor. This project analyzes the chemical and physical changes caused by metamorphism of the Mancos Shale and relates those changes to modern earth surface processes. Mapping, detailed rock analysis, and laboratory experiments will help us answer the question: "How do geologic processes that occurred millions of years ago impact the landscape of the East River today?"
Subject: Climate Change

ResearchPlanTitle: Connections of terrestrial and freshwater ecosystems along a hydrological gradient
ResearchPlanAbstract: Terrestrial and aquatic ecosystems are connected by materials and organisms that move between them. Terrestrial leaves and insects fall into freshwater ecosystems becoming food for various pond organisms. Freshwater insects emerge into terrestrial ecosystems becoming food for predators such as spiders and birds. However, if a pond dries before the freshwater insects complete their life cycle and emerge, then the stranded insects become food for foragers and detrivores in the terrestrial system. This switch between the two food pathways to terrestrial food webs is dependent on pond hydrology (temporary permanent ponds). As the freshwater ponds experience shifts in hydrology due to changing climate/precipitation, the terrestrial/freshwater connections could shift, resulting in altered food-web interactions in both ecosystems. I will deploy traps capturing the movement of the leaves and insects between terrestrial and pond ecosystems, and make quantitative observation of birds foraging over and around ponds. This data will inform future work studying the intimate connections between ecosystems during a time of change.
ResearchPlanOrganisms: Terrestrial and aquatic invertebrates + bird observations
Subject: Climate Change

ResearchPlanTitle: How will climate-induced phenological shifts influence competition for abiotic resources?
ResearchPlanAbstract: The time of the year when a plant begins to grow, produces flowers, and loses its leaves is important for successful reproduction, survival, and potentially future growth. Plants rely on environmental cues, such as temperature and the amount of sunlight, to time these life cycle events. Therefore, the time when a plant begins to flower can be very sensitive to climate change. For example, snow has been melting earlier in the season in subalpine regions than the recent past as a result of warming temperatures. Since the time of flowering for some plants occurs shorty after snowmelt, they track these warm temperatures and emerge or flower earlier in the season. Interestingly, not all plants respond similarly to the same environmental signals; some flowering species do not flower any earlier. As each plant species responds differently to earlier snowmelt, species that didn't flower together in the past have the potential to overlap now. If plant species grow and flower at the same time, they could compete for resources (water, nutrients, soil). My research examines the link between climate change, the timing of life cycle events in plants, and how they compete for resources. I propose to manipulate flowering phenology of plants in resource competition experiment. I will observe how competition for soil and light resources between two co-flowering species changes under early snowmelt conditions. The results from this research have the potential to help us predict how climate change may affect species interactions in the future.
Subject: Climate Change

ResearchPlanTitle: Addressing the missing link: uniting demographic life history theory and pollination biology to understand the ecological consequences of pollinator declines
ResearchPlanAbstract: Pollinator populations are in decline across the globe, but we have a very poor understanding of the ecological consequences. There is widespread concern that many flowering plant species will decline in tandem with pollinators because approximately 87% of flowering plants rely on animal pollination for their reproduction. Increases in pollination typically increase the number of seeds a plant can make, and because of this, scientists who study pollination often assume that changes in the amount of pollination have direct consequences for the persistence of plant populations. However, the number of seeds a plant makes typically does not limit population growth, especially for perennial plants. This suggests that alterations to pollination may not actually have extensive consequences for population persistence. No studies have connected pollinator-mediated declines in seed output to plant population growth rates. This project makes that connection using mathematical population models informed by data from a pollination field experiment. In doing so, this project will advance basic scientific knowledge by bridging two ecological subfields that are surprisingly disconnected, and it will substantially increase our understanding of the ecological consequences of pollinator declines.
Subject: Pollination

ResearchPlanTitle: Community and Ecosystem Consequences of Species Range Shifts in High-Elevation Ponds
ResearchPlanAbstract: Climate change is altering environmental conditions in habitats around the world. In response to these changes, many species are shifting their geographic ranges to seek refuge in habitats that now have the proper environmental conditions. Novel species interactions resulting from these range shifts may affect the ability for range-shifting species to successfully colonize these newly suitable habitats. Furthermore, these interactions have the potential to significantly alter ecosystem processes such as nutrient cycling or the decomposition of dead plant matter known as detritus. Using a community of caddisflies in high-elevation ponds, our study aims to investigate the role competitive interactions between resident and range-shifting species in setting species range margins and how these interactions might alter the rate of detritus breakdown, an important ecosystem process. With several range shifts already documented in this system, we will perform a manipulative caging experiment using resident species and a naturally introduced range-shifting species.
Subject: Climate Change

ResearchPlanTitle: A Mechanistic Approach to Investigating Climate Change and Invasion in a Vulnerable Ecosystem
ResearchPlanAbstract: Climate change is a dynamic threat facing natural areas with major shifts in plant and animal communities expected to occur over the next hundred years. Ecosystems that are geographically unique and isolated are especially at risk due to the long evolutionary history of adaptations to specific habitats. The alpine meadows of the Rocky Mountains are one such habitat, a unique landscape quintessential of the American west. The plants adapted to this niche are unable to move further north or higher in elevation, as conditions become inhospitable, due to the island like quality of their habitats. Several studies address how alpine and sub-alpine meadow plant communities will shift in response to increases in temperature, reduction of snow pack, altered precipitation patterns, and plant invasions. Researchers have investigated the effects of warming on plant communities in the Rockies but this study is unique in its ecological and spatial scale and incorporation of multiple disturbances (i.e. climate change and invasion). In earlier research one variable that has remained largely unexplored is how belowground microbial communities, which ecologists are only just becoming able to thoroughly and completely observe due to advances in molecular techniques, will respond to these impending environmental changes. By building on past research we can make meaningful predictions about plant microbial interactions and the implications that changes in their population structure and ecology will have on this invaluable ecosystem in the future.
ResearchPlanOrganisms: soil microorganisms, invasive mustard species, Festuca spp.
Subject: Climate Change

ResearchPlanTitle: Environmental and genetic variation in phytochemistry: investigating an invasive mustard plant in the subalpine area
ResearchPlanAbstract: The role of the environment and genetics in determining defensive chemical production in plants is not fully understood and may be tied to the rapid evolution of invasive plant species. The defensive chemicals produced in the mustard family have the potential to disrupt other plants, insects and soil organisms. Thlaspi arvense is an invasive mustard of European origin that was likely introduced to the Gunnison Basin in the 1880s. I will investigate the genetic and environmental interactions behind the production of defensive chemicals produced by this particular invasive mustard plant in subalpine meadows.
Subject: Climate Change

ResearchPlanTitle: Environmental History of RMBL
ResearchPlanAbstract: My aim is to is to research and write an environmental history of the Rocky Mountain Biological Laboratory, a high-altitude biological field station located on the West Slope of the Colorado Rockies. The Lab was built on the site of an old silver mining town, Gothic, which flourished briefly in the early 1880s. This project will document how the landscape has transitioned through eras of mining, scientific research and experimentation, and more recently increasing recreation pressure and management as legally designated wilderness. This work will also chart the history of ecological science itself, through early days in the 1920s of doing mostly natural history and description, to more recent eras of greater experimentation and studying ecology are larger spatial and temporal scales. It should also reveal more about how competing interests in the last few decades -federal management of wilderness, and explosion of outdoor recreation use, and a growing emphasis on working landscapes in the region- have interacted or conflicted with the scientific mission of the Lab.
Subject: Other

ResearchPlanTitle: Mechanisms of Color Vision in Hummingbirds
ResearchPlanAbstract: Our goal is to conduct behavioral experiments in the field to establish baseline visual abilities of the Broad-tailed Hummingbird (Selasphorus platycercus) with respect to color and pattern vision. This is critical because much of what we know about avian â€“ and indeed animal â€“ color perception has been determined in the lab; such studies, while fundamental, remove the relevant ecological context and fail to account for variation in color perception and/or cognition in a population. Our experiments, by contrast, exploit the natural feeding behavior of hummingbirds, allowing us to investigate mechanisms of color vision in the wild.
Subject: Other

ResearchPlanTitle: Predicting plant community response to climate change in the Rocky Mountains: a turf transplant experiment
ResearchPlanAbstract: The goal of this study is to inform predictions of how plant communities will respond to climate change. We will recreate the conditions of a warming, drying climate by moving small sections of plant communities from high to low elevations. We will then measure a variety of plant and community characteristics to assess changes to plant community composition and functioning.
Subject: Climate Change

ResearchPlanTitle: The roles of local adaptation, local extinction, and migration in a mountain wildflower's response to contemporary and experimental climate change
ResearchPlanAbstract: My research investigates three questions related to our understanding of plant responses to climate change: can local warming drive local extinction?; is present-day climate change disrupting adaptation to local conditions?; and can assisted migration mitigate extinction risk of warming populations? Over the course of my PhD, I established two ongoing field studies at RMBL aimed at answering these questions. Both studies focus on Rock Jasmine, a native wildflower in the Primrose family. The first study, in which I document the effects of long-term experimental warming on the viability of Rock Jasmine populations, has thus far revealed how local warming is driving local population declines. Results from this study predict that experimentally warmed populations will go extinct in the next few years, and my current work tests these predictions. Results from the second study, a transplant experiment conducted across a wide elevation gradient and in experimentally warmed plots, suggest that contemporary climate change may be driving a mismatch between naturally occurring A. septentrionalis populations and their local conditions. Results also suggest that the upward movement of lower-elevation individuals may boost Rock Jasmine in warming microclimates. Both of these results are preliminary, however, as they focus on only early stages in Rock Jasmine's lifecycle (emergence from seed and early-seedling survival). My current work focuses on extending assessments of Rock Jasmine transplant performance through later life stages (i.e. adult survival and reproduction) to gain a more complete understanding of i) the effects of climate change on local adaptation and ii) the potential for assisted migration to reduce extinction risk due to climate change.
Subject: Climate Change

ResearchPlanTitle: Virus diversity in Boechera stricta populations across an elevational gradient:
ResearchPlanAbstract: Plant viruses are ubiquitous across ecosystems and have both coevolved with ancestral hosts and adeptly colonize new hosts. To date, however, plant-virus interactions remain understudied in natural systems despite evidence that consequences of pathogen pressure effect ecological and evolutionary outcomes for plant hosts. Furthermore, evidence that environmental conditions impact host resistance to viruses justifies a need for more research on how climate change will shift plant-virus dynamics. Baseline data on natural plant viromes (virus-host systems) are needed to track climate-induced shifts, and may be gathered using novel RNA sequencing techniques and classical field biology surveys. If funded, I will study plant-virus dynamics in high and low elevation populations of the crucifer Boechera stricta across a latitudinal cline, in what will be the first survey of viral diversity and host resistance in alpine plants. By combining ecological field studies with genomic scans for viral RNA, I will record concurrent viral biodiversity and variability of host resistance traits. Outcomes of this work may be generalizable across mountain ranges worldwide and will be useful for the conservation of alpine ecosystems threatened by shifting pathogen ranges.
Subject: Climate Change

ResearchPlanTitle: Determination of the Timing, Rates, and Processes of Erosion and Incision in the Elk and West Elk Mountain Ranges
ResearchPlanAbstract: The Elk and West Elk mountains host ~20 granitic plutons that were intruded within the last 34 Ma, when the landscape surface stood at least 1-2 km above the tops of the present granitic peaks. Because the granites resist erosion better than the Paleozoic-Mesozoic sedimentary rocks into which they intruded, the landscape has evolved into one of isolated granitic mountains that stand above glacially carved river valleys, and that have been significantly glacially sculpted themselves. We will study these granitic mountains in two different ways. The first is to characterize how the rock glaciers hosted by these mountains form and to determine how efficiently they erode the mountain landscape. The second is to use (U-Th)/He thermochronometry (AHe) to determine when the granitic plutons that form these mountains was exposed by erosion. Colorado doesn't have any glaciers, but it does have over 1000 rock glaciers. Geomorphologists have extensively studied how glaciers form and how they erode the landscape, but far less attention has been paid to rock glaciers. The granitic mountains of the Elk-West Elk region are an ideal place to study rock glaciers because there are so many of them that have developed on the same rock type. The ability to eliminate rock type as one variable allows us to concentrate on the other factors that influence the formation and movement of rock glaciers. Each of the 20 Elk-West Elk granitic mountains serves as a 'thermal dipstick' that records the rock's progressive cooling from top to bottom as erosion stripped away the surrounding sedimentary rock during exhumation of the granite. Thanks to the presence of these many thermal dipsticks, the Elk-West Elk region represents a natural laboratory within which to explore the erosional history at the upstream end of the Colorado River drainage network using AHe. We will characterize that erosional history in order to test which (if any) of three proposed models for the onset of erosion is correct. One model suggests that major erosion began about 10 million years ago, a second model favors a 5-million-year-age for its onset, and the third model argues that major erosion didn't begin until the last few million years.
Subject: Other

ResearchPlanTitle: Bumble bee responses to floral resource variation
ResearchPlanAbstract: This research addresses how bumble bee populations respond to variation in the wildflower community, a community that is changing directionally under climate change. Around the Rocky Mountain Biological Laboratory, the wildflower season is extending and flowers are declining mid-season. It is important to understand how bumble bees respond to this redistribution of floral resources, and variation in floral resources more generally, because colonies need to forage on a series of flowers throughout the growing season to grow and reproduce. However, we do not have a good understanding of how the different life stages of bumble bees are affected by the timing and abundance of floral resources, and how the timing and abundance of earlier bees can affect the production of reproductive bees at the end of the season. Furthermore, we do not know how flexible foragers are in their flower choices when resource availability varies. If bees are flexible when resources are scarce, this may bode well for their population persistence under continued climate change. I am proposing to continue my observations of bumble bees and flowers at weekly intervals at six sites during the entire flight period. Understanding the relationships between bee foraging and abundance and floral resource variation is fundamental to bumble bee population ecology and to predicting bee responses to environmental change.
ResearchPlanOrganisms: Bumble bee species and the plant species that they visit.
Subject: Pollination

ResearchPlanTitle: Temporal and spatial shifts in plant-pollinator communities under climate change
ResearchPlanAbstract: Species are shifting in space and time in response to climate change, and these shifts can both expose species to novel abiotic environments and alter their interactions with other species. Much concern about the effects of climate change-induced shifts has been focused on plant-pollinator interactions, which require plants and pollinators to align in sometimes narrow windows of space and time. Given the changing climate and documented upward shifts in bumble bee elevational distributions in the last 40 years at the Rocky Mountain Biological Lab, pollination success of wildflowers may increase with elevation, and plants might have higher fitness at the leading edges of their distributions. I propose to build on prior work conducted in 2015 that showed seed set of several species was positively related to elevation. In particular, I propose to continue to use reciprocal transplants initiated in 2015 and 2016 to test if focal plant populations are locally adapted to elevational zones and/or perform better at high elevation at the seed and seedling stages. Results will be contrasted between species that exhibit no significant shifts in flowering phenology and those that are flowering significantly earlier to better understand the consequences of joint shifts in time and space for interacting species. This field project will be coupled with greenhouse work at the University of California-Riverside, using common gardens to measure how plant traits differ among populations from different elevations in controlled conditions, including warmer and drier conditions expected under climate change and those that reflect historical climate. Addressing these objectives will contribute to the overarching goal of understanding how climate change-driven shifts in phenology and range affect mutualistic interactions.
Subject: Climate Change

ResearchPlanTitle: Youth Science and Adult Education Plan 2017
ResearchPlanAbstract: This is a description of youth science programming led by Ann Colbert and adult education led by Amy Ellwein for 2017. These activities need to be annually reviewed by the research committee.
Subject: Climate Change

ResearchPlanTitle: CAUSES AND CONSEQUENCES OF BLOOMS OF THE STALK-PRODUCING DIATOM DIDYMOSPHENIA GEMINATA
ResearchPlanAbstract: The freshwater algae, Didymosphenia geminata, which has been described as rock snot by the media, has recently formed massive blooms in many pristine, low-nutrient rivers worldwide for reasons that are presently unknown. In general, algae provide food resources for many animals, such as stream invertebrates, that are important food for fish. Recently, the enormous increase in biomass of the stalk-producing diatom, Didymosphenia geminata, in many rivers worldwide has generated concern because of the potential negative impacts on these rivers and the salmonid fishes that they often support. Here I build on my previous research exploring how blooms of Didymosphenia affect invertebrates and fish. This project will address questions related to the causes of Didymosphenia blooms and their consequences to other vertebrates. First, are climate-induced changes in the timing and magnitude of stream discharge drivers of D. geminata blooms? Second, does reducing the concentration of phosphorus in stream water trigger D. geminata blooms and does increasing phosphorus concentration curtail blooms? Third, can blooms of D. geminata be explained by differential gene expression among populations? A combination of field experiments and long-term observations in streams with and without Didymosphenia blooms will be used to understand the causes and consequences of the recent emergence Didymosphenia, a native species that now has invasive-like characteristics. This research has direct application to a recreationally and economically important service provided by streams in Gunnison County and beyond. This study will also contribute to our understanding of how environmental changes, such as those related to climate-induced changes in the timing of streamflow will affect native species and ecosystems.
Subject: Climate Change

ResearchPlanTitle: Determining the relative roles of biogeography, abiotic environment, and biotic neighborhood on mycorrhizal fungal community composition and coexistence
ResearchPlanAbstract: Mycorrhizal fungi, which form a symbiotic association with the roots of plants, play a crucial role in the flux of nutrients through an ecosystem. Two major functional guilds of mycorrhizal fungi, arbuscular (AM) and ectomycorrhizal (ECM), vary in their functional traits and physiological relationships with plant hosts. Although most plants host only one of these two fungal guilds, a few species host both types and can allow us to tease apart the costs and benefits of associating with each of these guilds across different environments. Because it hosts both AM and ECM symbionts across its life history and has a wide geographical and environmental range, Populus tremuloides is an ideal host for understanding how environment drives fungal community composition. By collecting soil cores across an elevational gradient at the Rocky Mountain Biological Lab, I will characterize in situ patterns of fungal guild colonization of Populus tremuloides while quantifying clone age, elevation, temperature, nutrient availability, and water stress using both root colonization rates and metagenomic technologies. This study will elucidate what factors determine the distributions of plant and fungal symbionts across spatial and abiotic scales gradients.
Subject: Other

ResearchPlanTitle: Sex chromosome evolution in the Salicaceae
ResearchPlanAbstract: In the majority of plant species individuals produce flowers that are "perfect" and are capable of producing both pollen and seed. However, there are some species that have separate male and female individuals. The Salicaceae, which is a family of trees and shrubs that includes poplars and willows, contains almost exclusively species that have separate sexes. Further, the mechanisms through which these plants become males or females appear to differ dramatically within the family. As a result, these species present exciting models to understand how separate sexes evolve. We are sequencing the genomes of a large number of willow and poplar species to gain new insight into this process.
Subject: Other

ResearchPlanTitle: Survey of insect-pathogen and insect-plant interactions within the Gunnison District
ResearchPlanAbstract: During the upcoming summer of 2017, I wish to conduct a series of surveys in the US Forest Serviceâ€™s Gunnison District examining plant and insect populations. My research interests focus on insect host-pathogen interactions, plant-herbivore interactions, and plant demography. Given that Iâ€™m not familiar with the species in the Gunnison District and surrounding areas, the scope of any potential project is unknown at this time. Since this is an initial survey and the scope of the project will change, I have marked the duration down for 2 years, at the most.
Subject: Other

ResearchPlanTitle: Variation in bumble bee diet breadth with differences in resource abundance
ResearchPlanAbstract: This research addresses how flexible bumble bees are in respect to the food sources they use, and how that flexibility might allow them to deal with climate change. In the RMBL area, wildflower meadows are changing: the growing season is getting longer, but the number of flowers produced is staying the same, meaning there are fewer flowers available at any one time. We need to understand how bumble bees might be able to deal with these changes, because they rely on flowers for all of their nutritional needs. However, it is unknown how flexible individual bees are in their foraging habits. If they are flexible in their foraging when flowers are scarce, the bees may be able to get enough resources in spite of the shortage. I will capture, mark, and observe individual bumble bees in meadows with abundant and scarce flowers, and record what flower species they visit. I will also pool this information to examine flexibility at the population and species levels.
Subject: Pollination

ResearchPlanTitle: Assessing the Role of Oxbow Deposits in Carbon and Nitrogen Dynamics within Alpine Watersheds
ResearchPlanAbstract: Despite their abundance and constant interaction with the atmosphere and rivers, both sources of gaseous and dissolved inputs, floodplains are poorly understood components of the global carbon cycle that are not well represented in Earth system models. This is partly due to a lack of knowledge about carbon fluxes in soils and groundwater, especially from subsurface sources. The high rate of microbial respiration within floodplains also makes them important players in carbon and nitrogen cycling. What remains elusive, however, is the extent of the controls of floodplain water levels on microbial carbon and nitrogen cycling through space and time, a gap that this study seeks to bridge by investigating their relationship in the East River floodplain. Because understanding upstream processes might help us predict the impacts of changing hydrological regimes on downstream water quality and because floodplain sediments have a major imprint on the global carbon cycle, it is crucial to understand how hydrology and nutrient cycling are coupled within river floodplains.
Subject: Phenology

ResearchPlanTitle: Microbial dormancy over an elevational gradient
ResearchPlanAbstract: Despite the broad impacts microbial dormancy has on ecosystems and ecosystem models, dormancy as a response to climate-change related environmental stressors is poorly understood. Dormancy is an essential bet-hedging strategy used by microbes to both tolerate unfavorable conditions and increase overall community diversity. Accurate estimates of dormancy levels have been shown to greatly improve existing models of microbial systems. However, the ways in which dormancy structures bacterial and fungal communities across a climate gradient remain unclear. I am proposing a genomics-based, integrated field and laboratory study of the use of dormancy by bacterial and fungal communities across a natural climate gradient. My central hypothesis is that bacterial and fungal communities will resort to increased levels of dormancy in response to climate-related shifts in environmental conditions. A better grasp of microbial dormancy will improve our ability to model microbial communities and ecosystems, thus leading to a more thorough understanding of the effects climate change will have on microbial communities and the myriad of environmental processes that they support.
Subject: Climate Change

ResearchPlanTitle: The Impact of Population Density on Didymosphenia geminata Stalk Production
ResearchPlanAbstract: Didymosphenia geminata is a freshwater algae that grows best in low-nutrient, unshaded rivers. It has become problematic in many areas of the world, as it sometimes secretes carbohydrate stalks that form thick mats (blooms) in rivers, inhibiting the success of fish and other invertebrates in the river. It is of importance to understand what triggers this stalk production, so that D. geminata blooms can be managed in places where it has become a problem. The researcher will (1) observe natural D. geminata growth and stalk production, through setting microscope slides in Copper Creek and East River, and (2) will analyze whether a cell signaling mechanism, such as quorum sensing (population density), is a factor in stalk production, through placing specific cell densities in well plates and observing stalk production or lack thereof.
Subject: Other

ResearchPlanTitle: The Effects of Early Snow-Melt on the Pollination and Seed Production of Delphinium nuttallianum
ResearchPlanAbstract: For this summer, we plan on conducting an experiment to test if accelerated snow melt causes a seed reproduction decrease within the flower, Delphinium nuttallinium. We will be using three pollination treatments to test this throughout 4 plots (two experimental and two control.) Treatment one will consist of the plant being excluded for its entire life cycle, Treatment two will consist of double hand pollination and treatment three will consist of open pollination. We expect to find that treatment 1 will have the lowest amount of seed production for the manipulated plot, and treatment 2 will have the highest amount of seed production for the controlled plot.
Subject: Climate Change

ResearchPlanTitle: Water availability and its influence on the composition and effectiveness of Penstemon strictus pollinators
ResearchPlanAbstract: Plant-pollinator interactions are fundamental to the diversity and stability of the food webs that sustain our ecosystems. Without pollination, angiosperms would not be able to set seed and reproduce, and most organisms would lose their primary source of nutrients and resources. Owing to the fact that pollination services are becoming increasingly threatened by anthropogenic impacts, a thorough understanding of the factors that influence the success of pollen transfer is imperative. This project evaluates how water availability influences pollinator effectivenessâ€”the amount of conspecific pollen deposited on the stigma in a single pollinator visit. Many researchers have compared and assessed pollinator effectiveness, but little work has been done to relate environmental factors to effective conspecific pollen deposition. I will be performing a water manipulation experiment on Penstemon strictus plants growing at the Lupine Trail just north of Crested Butte, CO. The pollinator community consists of three species of bumblebees (Bombus flavifrons, Bombus bifarius, and Bombus californicus) as well as solitary bees, wasps, and flies. I will determine if water availability influences nectar production and pollen production, pollinator handling time, and the amount of conspecific pollen deposited in a single pollinator visit to find out how different insects compare in their relative effectiveness and if their relative effectiveness is influenced by water availability.
ResearchPlanOrganisms: Penstemon strictus and pollinators (Bombus flavifrons, Bombus bifarius, and Bombus californicus, solitary bees, wasps, and flies)
Subject: Pollination

ResearchPlanTitle: The Effect of Floral Resource Removal on Plant-Pollinator Interactions
ResearchPlanAbstract: Through observing plant-pollinator interactions within their community context, we can begin to understand the dynamic nature of ecological communities. This study seeks to examine the question of how plant-pollinator interactions respond to change through the removal the important and abundant floral resource, Helianthella quinquenervis (Asteraceae). The objectives of this study are to examine the following questions: 1) How do pollinator visitation rates vary between control plots and removal plots? 2) How does variation in visitation influence fruit production and seed set in plant species? and 3) How do pollinator communities differ between the control plots and removal plots? Understanding how the removal of an important floral resource alters pollinator visitation rates and community composition is a critical first step to comprehending how plant-pollinator networks respond to change.
ResearchPlanOrganisms: Bumblebees, Solitary Bees, Wasps, Montane Wildflowers
Subject: Pollination

ResearchPlanTitle: The maintenance of flower colour polymorphism across elevations in Boechera stricta
ResearchPlanAbstract: My research will focus on the maintenance of flower colour polymorphism across an elevation gradient in the self-pollinating species, Boechera stricta. I will determine whether there are abiotic and biotic correlates of flower colour, the fitness consequences of this polymorphism, and whether flower colour and pigment production are plastic traits. I will do so by sampling B. stricta individuals across an elevation gradients at sites in the Gunnison National Forest and RMBL. I will measure and analyze environmental factors at each site, and plant traits of each individual along a transect. By doing so, I will determine why flower colour variations exist in self-pollinating species, which can have important ecological and evolutionary implications.
Subject: Other

ResearchPlanTitle: A STUDY OF A CLIMATE CHANGE-INDUCED FEEDBACK COMPOSED OF EARLY SNOWMELT, SHIFTING PHENOLOGY, FLORAL ALBEDO, AND SOIL MOISTURE IN HELIANTHELLA QUINQUENERVIS
ResearchPlanAbstract: Climate change has led to higher temperatures in sub-alpine regions, resulting in earlier snowmelt. In years with early snowmelt and increased temperature, Helianthella quinquenervis, the alpine sunflower in the Asteraceae family, flowers early. While flowering early lengthens the growing season for montane wildflowers, it also exposes them to the harsh abiotic factors that accompany early spring time. Specifically, the low temperatures of June nights increases the likelihood that developing H. quinquenervis flower buds experience frost damage, and the flowers do not produce seed in that year (Inouye 2000). If a significant portion of H. quinquenervis experience frost damage, the albedo of the meadow should decrease as the meadow that was once blanketed in yellow flowers turns green. Green absorbs more sunlight than yellow, which could lead to even warmer and drier soils in years that are already warm and dry.
Subject: Climate Change
