ResearchPlanTitle: Effects of Variation in Solitary Bee Phenology
ResearchPlanAbstract: When an organism reproduces can have really important effects on how well its offspring grow and survive. This can be especially important in seasonal environments where climate conditions might be really harsh for extended periods of time. This means that organisms have to reproduce at very specific times to make sure their offspring have enough food and have enough time to grow enough before winter comes. Our project will be investigating what these factors mean for solitary bee reproductive timing.
Subject: Phenology

ResearchPlanTitle: The Role of Castilleja spp. In Plant and Mycorrhizae Communities Within Various Climates
ResearchPlanAbstract: Castilleja is a group of hemiparasitic plants from the family Orobranchaceae. Previous studies in the Gothic area noted that their presence decreases species evenness (when weighted on the dominant species) allowing for other species to fill previously occupied niches. This study wishes to expand on said research by looking at three questions. First how does climate across and elevational gradient mediate Castilleja's effects. Secondly how does the presence of Castilleja affect the interactions between host plant and their mycorrhizae. The final question we are looking at is how climate change alters Castilleja's biomass and density.
ResearchPlanOrganisms: Castilleja miniata, Castilleja rhexiifolia, and Castilleja sulphurea
Subject: Other

ResearchPlanTitle: Succession in the Rocky Mountains: community convergence, diversity, and colonizer traits
ResearchPlanAbstract: Understanding succession (the progression of a plant community from bare ground) has important implications for understanding the structure of communities and for restoration. This study monitors plots in which all vegetation was removed in order to learn what plants grow back, what traits allow them to be successful, and how quickly the community returns to its original composition.
ResearchPlanOrganisms: Alpine and subalpine colonizers in meadows and grasslands
Subject: Long-Term

ResearchPlanInstitution: University of Toronto St. George Campus
ResearchPlanTitle: Species Co-occurrence Patterns and Mechanisms for Rhyacophila in High-Altitude Streams
ResearchPlanAbstract: Species throughout nature are constantly interacting with each other and with their environment. These interactions can determine the ability of a species to be successful within a particular ecosystem. Species that co-exist have the potential to either directly or indirectly affect each otherâ€™s overall well-being. Therefore, it is possible that species can form positive and negative associations based on these interactions. This associations can be tested by running a species co-occurence analysis. Rhyacophila is a genus of caddisflies, which belong to a group of terrestrial insects that complete their aquatic larval stage in freshwater streams. Previous work done has shown that different proportions and abundances of species of Rhyacophila co-exist throughout various streams in the Upper East River Basin in Gunninson National Forest. We will conduct a species co-occurrence analysis to determine if there are any positive and negative associations between different Rhyacophila species. We will measure various environmental factors to obtain descriptive data about potential causes of species co-occurrences. We will then conduct an experiment to test whether or not competitive interactions can have an affect on predation rates on mayfly prey. These protocols in combination will enable us to examine species co-occurance patterns and test potential mechanisms explaining distributions of Rhyacophila in high-altitude streams.
Subject: Other

ResearchPlanTitle: Does it stay or does it go: exploring seasonal influences on nutrients across topography in a Colorado mountain watershed
ResearchPlanAbstract: Nutrients are a key factor in the environment. This study focuses on Nitrogen specifically. As the environment changes this influences nitrogen through changing factors such as, temperature or precipitation. Nitrogen helps plants to grow and can be harmful to areas if there is too much in that area. The purpose of this study is to see how changing seasons influence nitrogen in a mountain environment and if the observations and results can be used to predict changes in other environments.
Subject: Climate Change

ResearchPlanTitle: Bill shape variation as a function of pollen composition between and within sexes of Broad-Tailed Hummingbirds (Selasphorus platycercus)
ResearchPlanAbstract: Broad tailed Hummingbirds (BTH) are a very common bird found in Gothic and the surrounding area. The common assumption has been that both males and females feed on the same flower. However, in 2016 is was discovered that male and female BTH feed on different flowers. It was also observed that there is variation within the bill shape of BTH. This project aims to link the variation in BTH bill shape to flower preference and how flower preference varies with sex.
Subject: Other

ResearchPlanTitle: Effects of Road Dust
ResearchPlanAbstract: Dust is a particulate material that is removed from the land surface by wind erosion and is small enough to be suspended in the atmosphere (Bagnold 1941). One of the primary causes of dust spreading into the atmosphere is unpaved roads. Road dust is easily dispersed by tire friction and is capable of traveling up to 200 meters from the road (Forman and Alexander 1998). The Rocky Mountain Biological Labâ€™s (RMBL) prime source of dust would likely be road dust, bringing forth the question: Does road dust have an ecological repercussion? A study by Waser, et al. (2016) discovered that in 19 of 20 independent tests wildflowers carried less pollen (up to six times less) on their stigmas in dusty conditions than in un-dusty conditions. However, dust did not consistently affect the seed set between dusted and undusted flowers. Most of these tests involved the wildflower Ipomopsis aggregata (scarlet gilia). One mechanism that could contribute to these previous findings is compensatory herbivory. Specifically, the anthomyiid fly Hylemya sp., a pre-dispersal seed predator, oviposits between the sepal and the corolla of scarlet gilia flowers. Once the eggs hatch the larvae crawl into the maturing ovary and eat the developing seeds. After eating the seeds they bore an exit hole and leave to pupate in the ground. Therefore, few or none of the seeds in an attacked ovary enter the seed pool (Zimmerman 1980). In his 2016 project, Danny Ramirez supports the idea that Hylemya females were prone to lay eggs in undusted individuals rather than dusted individuals (Ramirez 2016). What this means is that measured seed sets of undusted flowers could be reduced, thereby resembling seed sets of dusted flowers, even though the undusted flowers have more pollen. This year I will be replicating the Ramirez study, asking the question: Do Hylemya females prefer undusted individuals?
Subject: Climate Change

ResearchPlanTitle: Determing Territories of male Mountain White Crowned Sparrows at high and low elevations during the incubation period
ResearchPlanAbstract: Mountain White Crowned Sparrows are adapted to live in low and high elevations. They tend to nest in the lower Willow branches and tall grasses. Like all songbirds, male Mountain White Crowned Sparrows sing on the edge of their territories to guard their mates. During the female Mountain White Crowned sparrow incubation period, males tend to sing louder and more frequently due to a more intense drive to protect their nest and mate. By the use of GPS tracking, territories of these male Mountain White Crowned Sparrows can be mapped and data can be collected on the size of the territories. In high elevation environments, Mountain White Crowned Sparrow resources including food, water, and nest sites are more spread out so it would be suggested that the territory of the male would be larger than that of low elevation. In low elevation, territory size would be hypothesized as being smaller due to the closer proximity of resources. Through the use of GPS mapping and observation of select males at specific nest sites, data will be collected and this hypothesis will be tested.
Subject: Other

ResearchPlanTitle: Is Compensatory Growth Costly ?
ResearchPlanAbstract: Compensatory growth, as an example of phenotypic plasticity, allows organisms to accelerate their growth rate in order to compensate for stunted or reduced growth. Compensatory growth has been demonstrated across an array of taxa, and has been shown to help buffer populations against periods of intense seasonal stress, but may have costs on the physiological level, including reduced immune function, anatomical efficiency, physical output, and bone growth and density. We will be investigating the effects of compensatory growth on overwinter survival and longevity in the yellow-bellied marmot, Marmota flaviventer, a ground-dwelling, sciurid rodent. The yellow-bellied marmot faces a short active season with which to gain mass, and is thus an excellent compensatory model. We predict reduced overwinter survival and longevity across all age groups.
Subject: Long-Term

ResearchPlanTitle: Phenology and Phenotypic Variation of Thlaspi arvense Along an Elevational Gradient
ResearchPlanAbstract: Thlaspi arvense, a flowering plant in the Brassicacaea family, was introduced to the Gunnison valley in the 1800s, and has persisted since. The invasion of T. arvense has deleterious effects on native species; prior studies done at the Rocky Mountain Biological Laboratory have shown reduced fitness for native Pieris butterflies when eggs were oviposited on T. arvense instead of native glucosinolate-containing mustards. Thlaspi arvense has the potential to disturb native plant communities and disrupt important mutualisms among species. In order to determine which factors influence the growth and spread of T. arvense populations, we will study its phenology and the variation of certain phenotypic traits along an elevational gradient. At six sites along an elevational gradient, we will assess a random subpopulation of plants and measure stem height, branching, fruit number and phenologic category (measured on a 1-5 scale). At each site, 2-3 plots of 2x2 m will be established and visited weekly to document change. To determine relationships among and between sites, ANOVA will be used.
Subject: Phenology

ResearchPlanTitle: Can yellow-bellied marmots learn foraging innovations?
ResearchPlanAbstract: Instances of innovation in the animal kingdom are numerous and taxonomically widespread. Innovation is defined as â€œa process that results in new or modified learned behaviour and that introduces novel behavioural variants into a populationâ€™s repertoireâ€ (Reader & Laland, 2003, p. 14). As innovation has fitness consequences, it is an adaptive behavior and has been shown to facilitate subspecies diversification, range expansion, and tolerance of harsh environments (Lefebvre, Ducatez & Audet, 2016; Â Sol, Stirling, & Lefebvre, 2005; Sol, Lefebvre, & RodrÄ±Ìguez-Teijeiro, 2005; Sol & Lefebvre, 2000). The presentation of a novel problem to wild populations in their natural habitat may be the most robust approach for assessing a species innovativeness. In this study we hope to determine whether marmots possess innovation abilities and whether innovative propensity is correlated with factors such as sex, age, boldness and docility. We will do so by analyzing interactions individuals have with a two action puzzle box, which will be placed outside individuals' burrows opportunistically. We will then analyze videos capturing all interactions and use the information to asses how innovative propensity and innovative learning are affected by a host of factors.
Subject: Other

ResearchPlanTitle: Associative learning in species of ants based on environmental cues emitted by plants.
ResearchPlanAbstract: The project will deal with associative learning in ants based on environmental cues. We hypothesize that, ants use environmental cues to recognize species of plants that have acted as viable hosts for resources in past interactions. The experiment predicts that ants will use associative learning to recognize these plant species as favorable species to forage upon.
ResearchPlanOrganisms: Ants(Formica and rufa and Formica fusca) , Ligusticum porteri, and Helianthella quiquenervis
Subject: Other

ResearchPlanTitle: Impact of pond drying on bird predation of aquatic insects
ResearchPlanAbstract: One of the potential effects of climate change is a change in regional hydrology. With warmer temperatures ponds systems will dry sooner, leaving those aquatic insects who are dependent on ponds for the larval stage of their lives stranded. When these insects are able to successfully emerge from the water as adults they are an important food source for terrestrial predators. Our research hopes to investigate the response of terrestrial birds as predators to drying ponds and how that relationship might shift with changing climate.
Subject: Climate Change

ResearchPlanTitle: affects of climate change on ecologically important bees and flowers
ResearchPlanAbstract: There is evidence that humans in turn, have sped up the process of greenhouse gas emission and warmed Earth. This has led us to climatic changes. These new conditions will have stresses on our animals and their responses will change. Winters could be harsher, and summers could be longer. These changes will cause snow to melt earlier, flowering plants to bloom earlier than previous years and many species will also come out of hibernation earlier. Bees pollinate many plants. Many native bees have adapted themselves to pollinate specific flowers. Bees and flowers have coevolved throughout the years in a mutualistic relationship. Bees will move pollen from flower to flower, attending to the reproductive success of the flower and in return obtain food. To monitor the response of plants and pollinators to climate change, Rebecca Irwin, in addition with David Inouye, have been monitoring the phenology and abundance of bees and flowers since 2009. This long-term study is conducted at the Rocky Mountain Biological Laboratory (RMBL) in Colorado, USA. We hope that the historical data will support a few unanswered questions.

ResearchPlanTitle: Genetic basis of plant-ant interactions: ant recruitment and herbivore protection in Boechera stricta
ResearchPlanAbstract: Mutualisms are defined as interactions among different species that enhance the fitness of the involved partners and tend to be based on the exchange of rewards and services. Ant-plant mutualisms are a common form of symbiosis, that tends to be well studied. However, there has been little attention on whether this type of interaction is truly beneficial to both individuals. There has also been minimal examination on whether the genetic basis of plants contributes to the success of this mutualism. In our study we wish to address these questions through the observation of the ant-plant interaction in our experimental garden.
Subject: Other

ResearchPlanTitle: Measuring Caddisfly Nutrient Cycling
ResearchPlanAbstract: When organisms die in aquatic ecosystems, their nutrients would be locked inside the dead tissues if "detritivores" did not eat those dead tissues and release the nutrients back into the water. Caddisfly larvae are the dominant detritivore species in the Mexican Cut Preserve kettle ponds. Kettle ponds are glacial remnants, and in the Mexican Cut they occur with different levels of permanence; permanent ponds stay all year, temporary ponds fill up one season a year, and semi-permanent ponds fall somewhere between those two . Caddisflies have evolved breeding cycles alongside these ponds, trading fitness between predator vulnerability and tolerance of dry spells. The permanence of these ponds is shifting towards more temporary, which is changing which caddisflies can live in which ponds. We aim to look at the nutrient levels in each of the different permanence levels of ponds within several different types of tissues which can hold the nutrients: Organic Matter on the pond bottoms, Two different aquatic plants, a sedge and Isoetes, zooplankton in the water, and general water nutrient levels through a survey of ponds in the mexican cut, as well as concentrating caddisflies in a cage in a larger pond and observing the levels of nutrients compared to distance from the cage. These will tell us the current nutrient levels and tell us what effect the caddisflies are having on their ecosystem. With this information, we can make predictions about the future of these kettle pond ecosystems as the caddisflies are changing their distribution.
Subject: Climate Change

ResearchPlanTitle: Effects of water availability on the Regeneration of Quaking Aspens Populous tremuloides.
ResearchPlanAbstract: Quaking aspen trees are suffering from sudden death. It's main culprit are droughts. The more dry their environment is the more they get sick, the more they get sick, the faster they die. My experiment will be testing the effects of water availability on the regeneration of quaking aspen.

ResearchPlanTitle: Effect of Blood Parasite Loads on Incubation Efficacy of Mountain White-Crowned Sparrow
ResearchPlanAbstract: Mountain White-crowned sparrows with higher blood parasite loads will have a higher off bout frequency hence the incubation will be longer.

ResearchPlanTitle: Effects of Nectar Robbing on Other Robbers and Legitimate Pollinators
ResearchPlanAbstract: I plan to study the effects of nectar robbing on the abundance of other insects as well as the effects on nectar consistency.

ResearchPlanTitle: Assessing Plant Community Assembly Along Elevational and Environmental Gradients: A Functional Niche Hypervolume Approach
ResearchPlanAbstract: I propose to combine species-level trait data available through the Enquist Labâ€™s long- term RMBL plant trait database with supplementary current-year trait data to assess community- level trait space dynamics at six sites along an elevational gradient. I will address the following questions: (1) How does the volume, overlap, and packing of trait space within communities (i.e. at each site) change along elevational or environmental (e.g. temperature, precipitation) gradients? (2) How do the observed patterns of trait space dynamics compare to predictions of niche-based community assembly theory? Specifically, I will test the long-standing idea that abiotic factors play a larger role in community assembly at higher elevations where abiotic conditions are more stressful, and that biotic factors such as competition are more important at lower elevations where biotic interactions are more intense (Dobzhansky 1950, Pianka 1966, MacArthur 1972).

ResearchPlanAbstract: Looking at the effects of road dust particulates from unpaved roads have on the life history of Ipomopsis aggregata. Specifically continuing to investigate if the particulates effect the floral lifespan of the plant.
