ResearchPlanTitle: Delineation of shallow subsurface flow from groundwater flow using environmental tracers and isotopic composition in East River tributaries of the upper East River Basin
ResearchPlanAbstract: Environmental tracers such as CFCs and SF6, and other stable isotopes are important resources for understanding hydrologic processes and estimating the age of young groundwater. Young groundwater is more susceptible to contamination than older water and recharges more quickly. Therefore, testing the isotopic composition of major drainages provides vital information on water quality and how water moves through the watershed. Since groundwater is a major source for the hydrologic budget, our goal is to determine how waters from the East River Basin recharge. The East River drainage area in central Colorado spans 84.7 km with the East River being a major contributor to the Gunnison River, accounting for 25% of total streamflow (Battaglin et.al 2012). Copper Creek and Rock Creek, tributaries of the East River, account for approximately 28% of total flow (Carroll 2016), and are of primary interest for the study. Groundwater in the study area is predicted to be less than fifty years old, making environmental tracing feasible. By tracking tributaries to their source and sampling for water chemistry, we can delineate which streams emerge as groundwater flow or shallow subsurface flow.
Subject: Climate Change

ResearchPlanTitle: Nicrtophorus- ant interactions over small mammal carcasses
ResearchPlanAbstract: Carcasses are a unreliable nutrient resource utilized by many organisms, particularly arthropods. This study will investigate interactions between burying beetles, which use carcasses as a means to raise their brood, and ants that scavenge all resources including carcasses. Further research in this area could provide insight into carrion ecology.
Subject: Phenology

ResearchPlanTitle: Effects of D. germinata on the American Dippers life history
ResearchPlanAbstract: The American dipper is a semi-aquatic bird that forages primarily on stream invertebrates and small fish in mountain streams like those near the RMBL (Price and Bock 1983). American dipper populations have been undergoing severe declines in parts of its range and hence, it is important to understand their responses to several environmental factors that may negatively affect their breeding biology (Anderson et al. 2008, Sullivan and Vierling 2012). We hypothesize that a suite of factors related to dipper breeding performance are negatively affected by D. geminata induced changes to the invertebrate community. Dippers preferred invertebrate prey are large-bodied mayflies, stoneflies and caddisflies that typically dominate the stream invertebrate communities near RMBL, and dippers presence/absence and territory size can be predicted from variation in stream invertebrate community composition (Feck and Hall 2004). Previous studies have demonstrated that AMDI occupancy and reproduction can be negatively affected by water quality issues (e.g., pollution) that reduce populations of their primary aquatic prey species, though the relative effects caused by D. geminata remain unknown. D. geminata blooms cause a substantial shift in stream invertebrate community composition, in which the preferred prey of dippers, the larger-bodied mayflies, stoneflies, and caddisflies (dippers preferred prey) decrease in abundance and smaller-bodied midges and oligochaete worms increase in abundance. Given the conservation status of AMDI and the continued spread of D. geminata, this research could prove of significance in AMDI conservation (Blanco and Ector 2009). Thus we predict that dipper behavior and other metrics of performance will respond strongly to D. geminata blooms.
Subject: Climate Change

ResearchPlanTitle: Western State Colorado University Mammalogy Field Trip
ResearchPlanAbstract: I will travel to RMBL for one January weekend with 24 students from Western State Colorado University. Will will do some mammal tracking exercises int he Maroon hut on Friday night and prep for a tracking snowshoe hike on Saturday morning. We will walk through the Gothic townsite along an RMBL approved path in single file pattern with a few stops where we will congregate around tracks or interesting winter ecology sites. We will further hike above the RMBL townsite to USDA FS land and break into 6 small groups with each group digging two snow pits. The snow wil be trampled by snowshoes on one pit and left untouched for the control pits. Students will measure the depth of each snow event measure the temperature within each snow layer. Students will build thermal profiles and answer questions about the impact of human activities on the subnivean environment used by a number of wintering mammal species. WE will also hike around the area and discuss winter ecology of mammals and observe wildlife and their adaptations for the winter environment.
Subject: Other

ResearchPlanTitle: Pathogenic and symbiotic microorganisms associated with bumble bees
ResearchPlanAbstract: The central goal of this project is to explore the communities of microorganisms that inhabit bumble bee species, and to include both a spatial and temporal dimension. Bumble bees are hosts to both pathogenic and beneficial microbes, and these organisms may have large effects on bumble bee populations and communities. The extent to which these organisms vary spatially and temporally is unknown, as it is their ability to switch between different host species. For these long term data, bees are collected, their guts removed and preserved for DNA and RNA analyses, and the carcasses are pinned. COI bar codes are determined for each bee, to verify species. This dataset would provide a unique long-term picture of the dynamics of microorganisms associated with a community of related host species. Additionally, it will provide insight into the microorganisms impacting the health of bumble bee populations.
ResearchPlanOrganisms: Bombus species and their associated miroorganisms.
Subject: Long-Term

ResearchPlanTitle: Local adaptation in the context of climate change
ResearchPlanAbstract: Human activities have caused the climate to change rapidly. In mountainous regions, plants and animals have already moved to cooler locations higher in elevation to escape increasing temperatures. However, many plant species simply do not have the seed dispersal capacity to migrate upslope fast enough to track changing conditions. These species risk extinction if they cannot adjust to new climates in their current locations. I seek to understand the ecological and evolutionary consequences of climate change for plant species with limited migratory potential. My focal species, Drummond’s rockcress (Boechera stricta), is a mustard plant native to the Rocky Mountains. It tolerates a broad range of conditions, and can grow in elevations as low as 6,500 feet and as high as 12,000 feet. Low elevation populations have adapted to make use of a long growing season. Similarly, high elevation populations have adapted to complete their life cycles in shorter seasons at lower temperatures. When the fruits of this species mature, the seeds fall directly to the ground, and are not dispersed by animals, wind or water. The broad elevational tolerance and limited seed dispersal of this species make it an exemplary candidate to explore whether evolution can keep pace with rapid climate change. My lab uses a novel experimental approach to test hypotheses about the response of plants to climate change. In five sites ranging in elevation from 8300 feet to 11500 feet, we expose experimental plants to current conditions as well as simulated future conditions (early snowmelt and elevated temperatures). All experimental plants come from sites around the Rocky Mountain Biological Laboratory. These experiments are critical for investigating whether climate change will diminish fitness in native plants and disrupt evolution, and the results will inform emerging conservation decisions. For example, will conservationists need to relocate populations to cooler sites to ensure the survival of some species? Will some species be able to adjust to changing conditions? The answers to these questions will shape conserva-tion priorities, provide insight into the fate of communities, and enhance our understanding of evolutionary processes in contemporary landscapes.
Subject: Climate Change

ResearchPlanTitle: Soil geomorphologic controls on the distribution of plant communities AND Cenozoic landscape evolution of watersheds in the Upper Gunnison Basin
ResearchPlanAbstract: My research is focused broadly on the evolution of landscapes to understand the factors that drive and resist landscape change. My tools include field and GIS mapping, field and laboratory analyses of sediments and soils, and relative and numerical dating (luminescence and cosmogenic dating, etc.) of surficial deposits and landforms. In my research through RMBL, I am currently interested in the following: 1) The impact of the Mancos Shale on the distribution of meadows and forests. Geology can strongly impact the composition and distribution of plant communities, especially in extreme environments or with certain rock types. The Mancos Shale appears to exert strong controls on vegetation patterns in upper Gunnison River watersheds and may be the reason that Crested Butte is the “Wildflower Capital of Colorado”. This new project will use field work and GIS to map major plant community types and compare with slope, aspect, and rock units. Surficial deposits, such as river deposits, alluvial fans, or glacial deposits, will also be identified and mapped using a combination of field work and GIS for comparison with plant communities. 2) Landscape evolution of the Cement Creek watershed. Most valleys in the upper East River watershed have a relatively short record of landscape change. Their geomorphic history is largely confined to the last 15,000 years or so, as older surficial deposits have been scraped away by the most recent glaciers. Cement Creek, however, contains an unusual set of well exposed surficial deposits and landforms that suggest a much longer and complicated history. Unraveling that history will require detailed field mapping and rigorous description of surficial deposits.
Subject: Other

ResearchPlanTitle: Linking herbivore abundance to snowmelt timing
ResearchPlanAbstract: Timing of snow melt is a key determinant of when mountain animals and plants initiate their life cycles in spring. In my research, I have also documented that the timing of snow melt affects the abundance of aphids, a type of sap-sucking herbivore. Years with early snow melt dates have fewer aphid colonies. My work combines these observations with experiments to determine the mechanisms by which snow melt timing determines aphid abundance. Results from my research can give insights into aphid outbreaks in other natural and managed ecosystems.
ResearchPlanOrganisms: Aphids (Aphis helianthi); Osha (Ligusticum porteri); Lygus bugs
Subject: Other

ResearchPlanTitle: Reproductive consequences of climate change-driven alterations in co-flowering between two subalpine plant species
ResearchPlanAbstract: Climate change is shifting the flowering phenologies of temperate, subalpine plant species, resulting in alterations in co-flowering patterns. Shifts in co-flowering may alter the degree to which plant species interact for pollinators and therefore plant reproductive success. Using a short-term field experiment that is based on results from a long-term flowering phenology data set, I will examine how climate-driven shifts in co-flowering between Linum lewisii and Potentilla pulcherrima are affecting the reproductive success of L. lewisii. Long-term data show that L. lewisii is co-flowering less than it used to with P. pulcherrima, as the climate changes. To decrease co-flowering overlap even further between L. lewisii and P. pulcherrima, two treatments will be applied in which P. pulcherrima flowers will be removed (50% and 100% removal), in addition to an unmanipulated control. Pollinator visitation, pollen deposition, and fruit and seed set will be measured on L. lewisii plants to determine how changes in the degree of co-flowering with P. pulcherrima affect its pollination and reproductive success. Each plot will also be subdivided into two pollination treatments, control and pollen addition through hand pollination, to determine whether any changes in reproduction are due to changes in pollination or some other factor. I hypothesize that L. lewisii in plots with less flowering overlap will experience less competition for pollinator services and higher reproductive success. Climate change is projected to create less-overlap of L. lewisii with P. pulcherrima, and therefore, my results could show that climate change is having a positive impact on fitness in some subalpine species. These results, in conjunction with the literature on interactions between plant species for pollinators, could help researchers begin to understand how climate-induced shifts in co-flowering will impact plant-pollinator relationships and the reproductive success of plant species.
Subject: Climate Change

ResearchPlanTitle: Host-plant selection of Aphis helianthi
ResearchPlanAbstract: Host-plant selection is a critical process for the successful establishment of aphid colonies. Migrating aphids need to choose plants of high nutritional quality and avoid natural enemies in order to thrive. In our system near Crested Butte, CO, years with early snowmelt result in diminished aphid populations on our study plant, Osha. During these years, migrating aphids are faced with plants in later stages of development, and plants already colonized by a predator, Lygus bugs. This scenario provides an ideal system to study species interactions between plants, aphids, and their natural enemies. My questions are (1) how does plant phenology affect aphid host-plant choice and (2) is that choice mediated by the presence of natural enemies? We will perform choice tests to determine whether aphids prefer plants of early or late stages, and whether they make the decision to avoid plants with predators. As the trend for earlier spring and early snowmelt continues, aphids will likely be faced with this tradeoff often in the future. The results will allow us to see how host-plants and predators affect aphid abundance in this subalpine system.
ResearchPlanOrganisms: Ligusticum porteri, Aphis helianthi, Lygus hesperus
Subject: Phenology

ResearchPlanTitle: The weathered bedrock vadose zone: A hidden control on water availability in the western United States
ResearchPlanAbstract: In seasonally dry or water-limited environments such as the western United States, the water stored in the fractures and matrix of weathered rock may be an ecologically significant hydrologic reservoir that strongly influences watershed response to change. Few direct observations of hydrologic dynamics in weathered rock underlying mountainous regions exist and there is no theoretical basis for upscaling point measurements of water storage in weathered rock to the landscape scale. As a result, this region is not explicitly parameterized in Watershed and Earth System models. This two-year exploratory project seeks to develop a field-tested, diagnostic model for predicting subsurface hydrologic structure and rock moisture dynamics across mountainous landscapes. The proposed research will investigate the coupling between processes driving erosion and subsurface weathering in mountainous landscapes through a combination of field data collection and numerical modeling. Specifically, we will test the hypothesis that the balance between channel incision and the drainage of fresh bedrock, dictates the depth extent of weathering, and thus a landscape’s capacity for rock moisture storage. To test this hypothesis, we will leverage existing infrastructure at four on-going study sites, three associated with the Eel River Critical Zone Observatory (ERCZO) and one with the Berkeley Lab’s Watershed Function Scientific Focus Area (SFA), to generate a cross-site dataset of subsurface hydrologic structure and rock moisture dynamics that can be used to test our hypotheses. During the two-year period, we will conduct field campaigns focused on 1) quantifying the pace of landscape evolution via cosmogenic radionuclide analyses 2) characterizing subsurface structure via geophysical surveying and analysis of core, and 3) monitoring moisture dynamics via neutron and nuclear magnetic resonance logging. In parallel, we will leverage existing software to develop a coupled landscape-evolution and reactive transport model to numerically explore rock moisture storage resulting from the balance between and evolving ground surface and weathering fronts. Together, the cross-site dataset and modeling effort will be used to evaluate a bedrock drainage control on subsurface structure, and contribute to the project goal of developing a theoretical framework for predicting subsurface structure, and the role of moisture storage in rock, across mountainous landscapes. The proposed exploratory research directly supports the DOE SBR mission of advancing a predictive understanding of how watersheds function as complex hydrobiogeochemial systems and their response to change by advancing a diagnostic model for the distribution of subsurface properties that control the belowground fluxes of water and solutes. The proposed work also offers an opportunity for collaboration between the ERCZO and LBNL Watershed Function SFA towards the common goal of understanding subsurface controls on landscape response to change through data sharing and modeling efforts beyond the scope of the current funded projects.
ResearchPlanOrganisms: N/A (just looking at rocks and water)
Subject: Other

ResearchPlanTitle: Mosquito range shifts and ecophysiology in the Rocky Mountains
ResearchPlanAbstract: Climate change is having major impacts on animal and plant populations, and as an increasing number of studies shows, these effects can lead to range shifts, local adaptation or in some cases extinction. Population responses are often evaluated in isolation from the ecological webs they are part of, yet their fate as local conditions change is intricately tied to the fate of the populations on which they rely, be they a food resource or a predator. This proposal seeks to evaluate the effects of climate change on altitudinal range shifts in mosquitoes with special consideration for Culex tarsalis, the main vector of West Nile virus. This work will build upon studies performed in the late 60’s and again in 2007 that already hint at a change in mosquito species distribution. Work performed along the Gunnison and East river in the Rockies, spanning over 1000m from Gunnison to the high alpine, has found that C. tarsalis were in 2007 found at higher elevations than they had been 40 years before. This research will further examine this range shift and examine whether the populations are adapting to new conditions or simply migrating along with the climate. Additionally, we hope to identify nectar sources of this and other mosquito species to assess whether mosquitoes act as pollinators or nectar thieves and if so, to what extent the associated plants may be affected by these range shifts.
Subject: Climate Change

ResearchPlanTitle: Effects of chronic low-level nitrogen deposition on consumer control of a plant-arthropod community
ResearchPlanAbstract: Human activities have doubled the amount of biologically-available nitrogen on Earth. Much of this nitrogen is emitted to the atmosphere and falls to the ground far from its source, blanketing landscapes with nitrogen fertilizer. Though the ecological effects of ‘atmospheric nitrogen deposition’ have been well-studied near sources of nitrogen, much less is known about the elevated, but low-level deposition that occurs more broadly. In particular, it is unclear how low-level nitrogen fertilization indirectly affects predators and the influence of predators on herbivores and plants, especially across the long timespans over which nitrogen deposition occurs. I propose to study how long-term nitrogen deposition impacts the effects of black bears on a plant-arthropod community. My previous research showed that bears can indirectly benefit plants by eating ants and suppressing positive relationships between ants and herbivorous insects, but that the effects of bears weaken under short-term nitrogen enrichment. In this study, I will extend an ongoing experiment to a total of 13 years to evaluate how long-term exposure to low-level nitrogen enrichment affects the influence of bears within a sagebrush/rabbitbrush ecosystem. This work will help us understand the ecological repercussions of nitrogen pollution and inform efforts to manage both nitrogen deposition and bears.
ResearchPlanOrganisms: sagebrush/rabbitbrush community, including thatch ants, treehoppers, aphids, and black bears (observationally)
Subject: Long-Term

ResearchPlanTitle: Fitness consequences of temperature-mediated bee-plant synchronization in a high-altitude solitary bee population
ResearchPlanAbstract: The effects of climate change on ecological communities are real. In particular, it is well established that increased temperatures can modify the timing of flowering and pollinator emergence. Solitary bees, whose females build nests independently, are no exception. To ensure bee survival and reproduction, solitary bee emergence must be timed with plant flowering. This synchronization between bees and plants is at the heart of the mutualistic (mutually beneficial) interaction. However, bees and plants do not share the same physiology, meaning that they may respond differently to changing environmental conditions. With increased temperatures, we may expect a change in temporal overlap between plants and bees. If temporal overlap increases with temperature, then we may expect increased bee reproductive success. On the other hand, with reduced temporal overlap, food availability is diminished for the bees, possibly coming at a great reproductive cost. The goal of my research is to determine if Osmia iridis, a solitary bee species living in Colorado, will produce fewer offspring because of a lack of synchronization with its preferred plant Lathyrus lanszwertii. So far, little is known about the effects of temperature variation on bee fitness as a result of modified temporal overlap. With a forecasted continuing rise in global temperatures, understanding how temperature will affect plant-pollinator interactions may prove critical in the near future.
ResearchPlanOrganisms: Osmia iridis, Lathyrus lanszwertii, Vicia americana
Subject: Phenology

ResearchPlanTitle: Connecting MIcrobial Composition Responses OBserved in EcosystemS (MICROBES) to long-term soil carbon cycling under global change
ResearchPlanAbstract: Soil microorganisms control the processing of dead plant material into the formation of soil organic matter needed to sustain plant productivity. However, current scientific approaches largely overlook MIcrobial Composition Responses OBserved in EcosystemS (MICROBES) that are responses for this process. For example, it is unknown how microbial taxa differ in the types of plant compounds they degrade. Furthermore, the consistency of microbial communities and the functional roles they play in degrading soil organic matter is unknown over the growing season and along elevation gradients. Our work will characterize the composition and consistency of soil bacteria and fungal populations and communities along six elevational gradients at the RMBL. We will trace their effect on various pools of soil organic matter over three years. To understand how this process may change with climate change, we will compare elevational gradients to patterns of soil microbial communities and soil organic matter storage in a 27-year long warming plot at the RMBL. We expect that microbial communities will be temporally and spatially dynamic in ways that have never been captured because scientists do not repeated study the same ecosystem. Furthermore, we expect that by accounting for these dynamic processes that we can predict the rates of soil organic storage and decomposition better than current modeling efforts.
Subject: Climate Change

ResearchPlanTitle: Oligochaete Abundance and Distribution in the East River
ResearchPlanAbstract: Whirling disease is on the rise since its introduction in the United States in 1958 and is a health problem both in fisheries and in wild populations of salmonids. Prevalence of the disease is dependent on ecological context and interactions among multiple other species, including the oligochaete worm Tubifex tubifex, and the myxozoan parasite Myxobolus cerebralis, the causative agent of whirling disease in salmonid fishes. To form a deeper understanding of the life cycle of whirling disease in a particular drainage, it is important to first understand the abundance and distribution of T. tubifex as there are hot spots in rivers of M. cerebralis which are hosted inside of T. tubifex. This research aims to compile a distribution map of T. tubifex in the East River drainage to determine particular species strains and infection rates in a changing climate over time.
Subject: Long-Term

ResearchPlanTitle: Effects of Linaria vulgaris and water availability to the pollination of Penstemon strictus
ResearchPlanAbstract: Biological invasions are known to have tangible economic and ecological effects on the invaded ecosystem. As the quantity of pristine ecosystems decreases and the amount of invaded non-pristine areas increases, we need to understand the mechanisms by which invasive plants species influence the pollination of native species. Here I propose to continue the study of the evolutionary and ecological effects that the invasive plant Linaria vulgaris (butter and eggs) has on the pollination of the native plant Penstemon strictus (Rocky Mountain Penstemon). I will observe plants of P. strictus in the absence and presence of L. vulgaris. I will document pollinator visitations to P. strictus and pair these observations with floral measurements of these plants. This way I will be able to analyze whether the presence of L. vulgaris causes changes in the traits that the pollinators are selecting for in P. strictus (traits like flower size and nectar production). A change in natural selection with the presence of L. vulgaris would suggest that the invader has an evolutionary effect. To study the ecological effects of L. vulgaris on P. strictus, I will look at whether P. strictus fruit production and pollinator visitation is different in the presence and absence of L. vulgaris. Our results show that during the last three years there has been variation in the flowering overlap of these two species, with 2016 being a year of non-overlap. During this time, there has also been year-to-year variation in pollinator visitation rates, and changes in phenotypic selection. For this summer, I am proposing to conduct the same experiments as the previous three years to increment my sample size and further understand the impact of year-to-year variation on the pollination related processes of P. strictus. In addition, I am proposing to continue work done by Ashley Morse, a RMBL 2017 summer research program student, studying whether water availability influences the effectiveness of different P. strictus pollinators.
Subject: Pollination

ResearchPlanTitle: POPULATION DYNAMICS AND LIFE HISTORIES OF SUBALPINE MASON BEES
ResearchPlanAbstract: My research aims to understand the factors regulating wild bee populations, particularly in the context of environmental change. The research proposed for 2018-2020 has two parts. The first investigates how specialist solitary bees (i.e., bees that depend on only one kind of plant for pollen) are affected by the seasonal timing of flowering of their preferred plants, and whether specialist bees can use the pollen of non-native plant species. Specifically, we will test (using experimental transplants of bee eggs) whether bees that specialize on pollen from the sunflower family are able to develop successfully on the pollen of common dandelion—and whether using dandelion pollen actually confers a benefit to these bees by letting them be active earlier in the season than would otherwise be possible. We will also examine whether bees that specialize on Nevada peavine are well-synchronized (seasonally) with their floral host-plant—and, if there is variation in synchronization, whether that variation affects reproduction in these bees. To do this, we will continue observations begun in 2013 of bee nesting success at multiple sites around RMBL. The second part of my RMBL research investigates how warming temperatures affect generation times in bees and their parasites. Many insects have shortened their generation times as temperatures have risen around the world (e.g., completing a generation in one year instead of two), and our past research shows that this could happen for some bees around RMBL, as well. However, these bees are attacked by parasitic wasps that also seem to benefit from warmer temperatures. I will conduct an experiment to test whether these parasitic wasps benefit more or less than their bee hosts from warmer temperatures during larval growth – in other words, whether further warming is likely to be a net benefit or cost for the bees.
ResearchPlanOrganisms: Solitary bees (Osmia spp., Megachilidae) and their parasites.
Subject: Pollination

ResearchPlanInstitution: University of Colorado at Colorado Springs
ResearchPlanTitle: The Bottom-Up Effects of Snowmelt on Aphid Populations
ResearchPlanAbstract: Climate change will increasingly alter the prevalence of crop pest outbreaks in the future. Predicting these outbreaks is important to ensure food security. In order to understand why these outbreaks happen we will study how snowmelt dates affect the host plants of insect herbivores, particularly aphids and lygus bugs, two particularly destructive species found on agricultural crops. Previous research has shown that both aphid and lygus bug populations significantly correlate with date of snowmelt, but why this correlation occurs is still a mystery. This project will help us understand if those changes in insect herbivore abundance is connected to either an altered plant phenology or the resultant increased water stress of their host plants.
ResearchPlanOrganisms: Aphis helianthi, Lygus hesperus, Ligusticum porteri
Subject: Climate Change

ResearchPlanTitle: Phytochemistry, phenology, and genetics of a non-native mustard plant, Thlaspi arvense
ResearchPlanAbstract: The impacts of climate change alter species distributions and provide new evolutionary opportunities for species to expand and experience different selective pressures. Range shifts can lead to the establishment of non-native plants that negatively impact their new surroundings. Studying invasive plants in high altitude ecosystems can improve our understanding of how climate change affects plant range expansion, with strong environmental gradients across elevation allowing the investigation of potential climate change scenarios. In the subalpine meadows of the Rocky Mountains, invasive plants threaten the balance of native species. Members of the mustard family produce chemicals that impact landscapes across the food chain, disrupting associations between native plants and beneficial soil organisms as well as native insects. Native mustards are a vital component of the subalpine meadows, tied with the lifecycles of native herbivores such as Pieris butterflies. Non-native T. arvense mustard plants attract these butterflies to lay eggs as well, yet the level of chemicals produced in its leaves is toxic to larvae. My research will elucidate the evolutionary mechanisms behind the expansion of non-native mustard plants into novel sub-alpine ecosystems and potential invasion population dynamics in the landscape.
Subject: Climate Change

ResearchPlanTitle: Constructing a nutrient landscape to explore the role of nutrition in driving interaction patterns and diet breadth of bees
ResearchPlanAbstract: Bees are essential pollinators in many ecosystems. However, recent pollinator declines have emphasized the need to understand their basic ecology so that effective conservation strategies may be implemented. Bees acquire their food from floral resources – pollen and nectar. Pollen is the main source of protein and lipids while nectar provides the necessary carbohydrates to sustain foraging activity. The nutritional content of pollen and nectar is highly variable, and we know little about the nutritional requirements and preferences of most wild bee species. I will quantify the macronutrients (e.g., protein, carbs, and lipids) contained in floral resources in the plant community. The nutrition data will be used to construct ecological networks and determine the nutrient acquisition of foraging bees. Understanding how nutritional preferences drive resource use and diet breadth of bees will allow us to predict how changes in the composition of floral resources influence the population dynamics of wild bee species.
Subject: Pollination

ResearchPlanTitle: Linking changes in plant species’ relative abundance, and associated functional traits, to affect ecosystem functioning
ResearchPlanAbstract: Linkages between species’ relative abundance and ecosystem function are important to predict ecosystem resistance and resilience to current and future global change pressures. In fact, both the direct ‘removal’ of species or the ‘reduction’ of species abundance, via changes in climate, can be avenues to tackle community and ecosystem ecology questions on how changes in species’ relative abundance shape ecosystem function. Here I propose to: (1) continuing monitoring ecosystem recovery (plant biodiversity, carbon input and output) from two long-term removal experiments that took place from 2013-2016 and (2) track net ecosystem carbon flux, both the vegetation and soil components, from a long-term climate warming manipulation where plant biodiversity has experienced both species loss and shift in dominance.
Subject: Climate Change

ResearchPlanTitle: Scaling Plant Reproductive Phenology Using Drone Photogaphy
ResearchPlanAbstract: The timing of summer wildflower blooms is one of the most sensitive indicators of climate change, and has strong effects on pollinators like hummingbirds and bumblebees. Pioneering research at RMBL has monitored blooms consistently for decades, but those measurements are taken at small study plots, and it's been difficult to link small-scale measurements of flower timing to landscape-scale abundance of nectar and pollen, which is the key property of plant communities that really matters to pollinators. In this project we will use high-resolution imagery from drones and new computer vision techniques to link plot-scale and landscape-scale measurements of flower abundance and timing.
ResearchPlanOrganisms: Vascular plants of 5 target species: lanceleaf spring beauty (Claytonia lanceolata), glacier lily (Erythronium grandiflorum), fused bluebells (Mertensia fusiformis), yellow montane violet (Viola praemora), and alpine pennycress (Noccaea fendleri).
Subject: Phenology

ResearchPlanTitle: A Mechanistic Approach to Assessing Disturbance from Climate Change and Invasion on Sub-alpine Meadow Ecosystems
ResearchPlanAbstract: Disturbance is a dynamic threat facing natural areas with major shifts in plant and animal communities expected to occur over the next hundred years. Ecosystems that are geographically unique and isolated are even further at risk due to the long evolutionary history required for habitat specialists to adapt. The high-elevation meadows in the Rocky Mountains are one such habitat, a unique landscape quintessential of the American west. The plants that have adapted to fill this niche are unable to move further north or higher in elevation, as most plants do when local conditions become inhospitable, due to the island like quality of their habitats. Several researchers have attempted to quantify how exactly alpine and sub-alpine meadow plants communities will shift in response to the increases in temperature, altered precipitation patterns, and invasion. Microbial community dynamics have remained largely unexplored until recently. The purpose of this research is to examine these interactions in the context of future changes through both novel and established techniques.
ResearchPlanOrganisms: Thlaspi arvense, Noccea fendleri, Festuca thurberi
Subject: Other

ResearchPlanTitle: The effects of global change on montane ecosystems
ResearchPlanAbstract: I am using environmental gradients and experimental field manipulations to address questions about the interactive effects of global change drivers on plant community structure, fungal community structure, and ecosystem carbon (C) dynamics. I am not adding any new additional experiments, only maintaining current projects which include: The following research plan consists of three currently ongoing studies: 1) Manipulation of temperature and presence of dominant species at multiple elevations in the field, measuring effects on the plant community, fungal community, and the carbon cycle (Warming and Removal in Mountains; WaRM). 2) Manipulation of organic and inorganic nitrogen (N) and presence of dominant species at a single site in the field, measuring effects on the plant community and fungal community (Fertilization experiment). 3) Collection of plant community, plant trait, fungal colonization, and ecosystem function data across many sites ranging widely in climate conditions to construct a model of plant community as a function of traits and climate (observational plots).
Subject: Climate Change

ResearchPlanTitle: The net effects of multiple ant mutualists on aphid demography
ResearchPlanAbstract: Mutualisms – reciprocally beneficial interactions between two species – can play important roles in structuring populations and maintaining biodiversity. Most mutualisms (e.g., pollination, seed dispersal, and ant protection) involve networks of interacting species, but we have a limited understanding of the importance of species diversity within mutualisms. If mutualist species provide complementary benefits or respond differently to environmental changes, species diversity may be important for enhancing partner fitness and maintaining mutualisms. On the other hand, species often compete with each other for access to mutualist partners, which may interfere with the services that they provide. Thus, in order to fully understand the consequences of species diversity in mutualisms, it is important to evaluate both the composition of and interactions between partner species. However, few studies have evaluated the population-level effects of associating with multiple mutualist partners. For my doctoral dissertation work at RMBL, I propose to investigate the effects of interacting with multiple ant mutualists on aphid populations. In ant-aphid mutualisms, ants protect aphids from predators, and in exchange, aphids excrete a sugary reward called “honeydew” that the ants consume. By censusing aphid colonies and constructing demographic models, I will compare the effects of multiple ant mutualists on aphid population growth and evaluate the mechanisms underlying differences in ant effects. In so doing, I hope to enhance scientific knowledge about the ecology and role of species diversity in mutualisms.
ResearchPlanOrganisms: Ants (multiple species), the aphid Aphis helianthi, the host plant Ligusticum porteri (osha), and aphid natural enemies (e.g., mirids, ladybird beetles, parasitoid wasps, syrphid fly larvae)
Subject: Other

ResearchPlanTitle: Evolutionary Ecology of Floral Color
ResearchPlanAbstract: Flower color is central to plant-pollinator interactions, but several outstanding questions remain. How do floral colors vary geographically, i.e. across elevations or between habitats? What are the roles of abiotic agents (e.g. climate) and biotic agents (e.g. pollinators) in shaping floral colors within communities and across gradients? Has climate change shifted the timing or composition of floral colors presented to pollinators? The proposed research will attempt to answer these and other questions by expanding a database of floral spectra from flowering species in the RMBL area (currently at 212 species). This database can be used to estimate both 'raw' and pollinator-relevant measures of color for each plant species, which in turn can be connected to other RMBL datasets and ongoing experiments (e.g. phenology datasets, snowmelt manipulation experiments, and vegetation surveys) to answer the specific questions.
Subject: Pollination

ResearchPlanTitle: Community and Ecosystem Consequences of Upslope Species Range Shifts in Alpine Ponds
ResearchPlanAbstract: In response to changing climate, species are shifting their distributions. Even as we observe these changes, the exact mechanisms that limit the distributions of species and the consequences of their shifts remain elusive. Using field experiments and observational studies, I aim to understand the relative role of species interactions and environmental conditions for determining the geographic ranges of caddisflies that inhabit mountain ponds and wetlands. From this work, we will gain understanding of the processes that control species geographic ranges more broadly.
Subject: Climate Change

ResearchPlanTitle: Shifts in Florally Important Soil Microbial Phenology
ResearchPlanAbstract: Species are shifting in time and space in response to global climate change and these shifts can both expose species to novel abiotic and biotic environments and alter their mutualistic interactions with other species. Soil microbial communities regulate many vital ecosystem processes which impact plant survival, phenology, and landscape-scale patterns of floral and faunal abundance and diversity. Microbial ecology as a field is in its infancy so it is unknown how microbial communities will be impacted by global climate change, nor is it known how changes to soil microbial communities will impact their plant symbionts. I propose to assess the change in the ratio of active versus dormant microbial species revenant to plant growth within a growing season and over several years to predict how warmer, drier conditions associated with climate change will alter the species richness and functional diversity of the microbial community important to plant success. Beyond this, I aim to predict how the upward elevational shift of two bumble bee pollinated legume species at RMBL may be facilitated by the soil microbial symbionts of a third legume species. The proposed field projects will be coupled with growth chamber work at the University of California, Riverside, using a common garden to measure how microbial communities alter the growth rate and germination success of legumes found at RMBL. These projects will contribute to the understanding of how climate change-driven shifts in the phenology of the active ratio of the soil microbial community directly and indirectly affect mutualistic interactions.
ResearchPlanOrganisms: Lathyrus lanszwertii var. leucanthus, Vicia americana, Lupinus sp., soil microbial community
Subject: Climate Change

ResearchPlanTitle: Geologic Hazards and Engineering Geology mapping
ResearchPlanAbstract: The purpose of the summer field mapping and reconnaissance is to better understand the engineering geology features in and around RMBL. Field work will specifically assess rock fall potential and hazards, landslide potential and hazards, as well as human activity impacts on the engineering structures and integrity of infrastructure in the east river valley. The projected outcomes of the summer field season are several derivative geologic maps that are a visual representation of the hazards assessment. This work will be supplemented with computer aided modelling of rock fall and landslide potential.
Subject: Other

ResearchPlanTitle: Community and ecosystem consequences of species range shifts
ResearchPlanAbstract: One of the most commonly reported outcomes of climate change is the expansion of low-land species into higher elevation habitats. Despite the common occurrence of these range shifts, scientists still have a poor understanding of why some species move and not others, and what are the consequences of range shifts for the functioning of ecosystems. Researchers at RMBL have observed these distributional changes in a suite of species, including the caddisflies that perform important ecological functions in high elevation ponds. This project focusses on measuring the variation in within and between species of caddisflies across their elevational range to 1) understand what might enable some species to move and not others, and 2) understand how these moments influence the role caddisflies play in cycling nutrients and energy in pond ecosystems. This research serves as a model for understanding how changes in species distribution that result from a changing climate can impact ecosystem functions that translate into provision of ecosystem goods and services (food, fiber, clean water, waste recycling) to societies
Subject: Climate Change

ResearchPlanTitle: Community-wide analysis of floral volatile scent profiles in a subalpine dry meadow
ResearchPlanAbstract: While plant-pollinator interactions are recognized as mediated by floral signals, little is known about the role of floral scent in structuring interaction networks at the community scale. Floral advertisements (color and scent) are shown to influence pollinator behavior, but the role of floral scent alone has less clear influences on the insect pollinator community. In other words, can floral scent profiles be used to predict the composition of pollinator visitation to plant species within a network? I propose to continue my project, started in Summer 2017 with six initial species, to characterize the floral volatiles emitted by each wildflower species within a single subalpine meadow field site, identify and quantify certain volatile compounds that may be associated with specific pollinator visitation, and examine the relationships of plant olfactory traits with network links.
ResearchPlanOrganisms: 45 species of wildflowers identified based on previous research of plant-pollinator networks conducted by CaraDonna et al. (2017) -- List of species included in project description
Subject: Pollination

ResearchPlanTitle: Ecological contexts of balancing selection in nature
ResearchPlanAbstract: Plants have evolved a variety of strategies to survive and thrive in their environments, despite lacking the ability to move themselves around to escape stress and predation. Producing chemical defenses that are distasteful or toxic to herbivores is a common strategy that plants utilize to protect themselves against consumption by many insects, which can cause reductions of reproductive fitness. Defensive chemicals produced by the wild mustard species Boechera stricta are highly diverse both across the species range and at a fine spatial scale of meters and kilometers in natural habitats in and around the Rocky Mountain Biological Lab. How high levels of diversity are maintained for traits that directly impact fitness is a fundamental question in evolutionary ecology, since evolutionary models predict eventual decreases in genetic and trait diversity as “winning strategies” become most common over long periods of time. Fitness tradeoffs are one way in which variation in traits can be maintained over evolutionary time. In a tradeoff scenario, a trait that confers a fitness benefit in one environment is costly in another environment. This study aims to better understand variation in plant chemistry in Boechera stricta, and test for fitness tradeoffs associated with chemical defense traits under different environments. Specifically, using a manipulative field experiment, I will investigate how two selective agents—herbivore pressure and drought stress—interact to influence the fitness effects of chemical defenses in B. stricta.
Subject: Other

ResearchPlanTitle: Allosomes and dioecy in plants as drivers of multi-level biodiversity
ResearchPlanAbstract: The vast majority of plants don't have separate males and females--most plants are capable of producing both pollen and seeds. However, there are rare groups of plants that have separate males and females. Whether one of these plants develops as a male or female is determined, like in most animals, by the inheritance of sex chromosomes like the X or Y chromosome in humans. We don't know much about how plant sex chromosomes have evolved, and so in our project we're hoping to create new genome sequences for plants with separate males and females, and map the sex chromosomes so we can understand more about this process.
Subject: Other

ResearchPlanTitle: Characterization of the microbial communities of the Mt. Emmons Fen
ResearchPlanAbstract: Microorganisms, including the bacteria, are widely distributed in naturally-occurring environmental systems, such as soils and waters. They play important roles in nutrient cycling, plant growth, and overall ecosystem health. The Mount Emmons Fen, located outside of Crested Butte, CO, is a wetland system fed by a natural supply of acidic, metal-containing water. Just as dependent on microorganisms as other environmental systems, the types and diversity of bacteria of fens in general are not well understood. The aim of this study is to identify and monitor the types of bacteria associated with the Mount Emmons Fen. From this information, we can learn more about the health and stability of the Fen as a unique ecosystem. As a protected system, the microbial characterization of the Fen can also provide baseline data as an early indicator to perturbation.
Subject: Other

ResearchPlanTitle: Does a fine-scale mosaic of antagonistic biotic interactions maintain defensive chemical diversity in a native plant population (Cardamine cordifolia)?
ResearchPlanAbstract: Even though some plants may look alike, they are often different at the chemical level. For example, different varieties of a food crops may taste different because they produce different natural chemicals. Many of the chemicals that plants produce serve an important purpose in nature: they are distasteful or toxic to insects, so they help plants defend their stalks and leaves from being eaten. I will profile the variety of defensive chemicals produced by wild mustard plants in the Rocky Mountains, and I will study how these chemicals protect these plants from insects in their natural habitat. Lessons learned from this work have the potential to guide the breeding of more pest-resistant crops, which is important because insects cause many millions of dollars in damage to crop plants each year (including numerous crop plants in the mustard family). Many of these same chemicals also contribute to desired tastes in mustard crops, and they are used in preventative treatments against cancer. But ultimately, this project seeks to understand, from an ecological and evolutionary perspective, how plants persist despite constant attack from voracious insects in nature.
ResearchPlanOrganisms: Focus: Cardamine cordifolia; Incidentally: associated herbivores, Scaptomyza nigrita, leaf beetles (Phaedon spp.), and psyllids (to be identified)
Subject: Other

ResearchPlanTitle: Does Road Dust Affect Hylemya Oviposition in Scarlet Gilia (Ipomopsis aggregata)?
ResearchPlanAbstract: A previous study conducted at RMBL has found that road dust affects wildflower pollination and reproduction, this study included Ipomopsis aggregata. In 19 of 20 independent tests wildflowers carried less pollen on their stigmas in dusty conditions, but their seed sets were not consistently affected. The study lists compensatory herbivory as a mechanism that could contribute to the inconsistent seed set, therefore for this study we will be looking at the pre-dispersal seed predator the Anthomyiid fly Hylemya spp. We studied whether road dust affects Hylemya oviposition. We found more Hylemya eggs in experimentally undusted than in dusted Ipomopsis aggregata plants, both on a per-flower and whole-plant basis. On average there were 4.3 eggs per undusted plant and 2.2 eggs per dusted plant. This study also compared the results of a similar 2016 study. In both years undusted plants had higher egg loads, but egg loads were overall higher in 2016. Overall, between both years, 11.43% of undusted elongated buds had an egg and 5.22% of dusted elongated buds had an egg with a significant difference.
Subject: Pollination

ResearchPlanTitle: Relationship Between Invertebrate Abundance and Mountain White-Crowned Sparrow Nest Success
ResearchPlanAbstract: Mountain white-crowned sparrows’ (Zonotrichia leucophrys oriantha; hereafter referred to as MWCS) diets fluctuate across seasons. They have differing nutrient requirements based upon their lifestages and environmental factors. Invertebrate population dynamics function in such a way that their abundance, as well as the fact that in most insects, the transition from egg to adult occurs in less than one year, prompts the question of whether these changes influence the nesting success of MWCS who depend upon these organisms as food. Invertebrate population fluctuation is often influenced by environmental factors, such as temperature (ËšC) and precipitation (mm), which were also examined for correlation with MWCS nesting success to determine whether a nest could be successful, with sufficient invertebrate prey available, despite temperature and precipitation extremes. Data was collected in the East River Valley, Colorado over a period of five years. These data were used to perform statistical modeling with program MARK with nesting success as the dependent and invertebrate abundance, temperature, and precipitation as the independent variables. This study helps us to understand the resource requirements of MWCS throughout the nesting season so that we may predict future patterns in population fluctuation based on environmental factors.
Subject: Other

ResearchPlanTitle: Comparing rates of detritus breakdown in nine alpine ponds
ResearchPlanAbstract: It is well known and widely accepted that in stream systems, detritivores are the primary processors of detritus. The nutrients that are released by the breakdown of the detritus, as well as the animals themselves, provide nutrients for all other organisms in the system downstream. This idea has been applied to wetland and pond systems; however, there is no published literature investigating whether or not this is true. In this study, we plan to analyze detritus breakdown rates in 9 subalpine ponds (3 permanent, 3 semi-permanent, and 3 temporary) at the Mexican Cut in the Nature Conservancy. The dominate detritivores by biomass in these systems are Limnephilidae caddisflies. There will be 120 total containers containing 5 g of sedge placed into the nine ponds; half will be covered with coarse mesh (20 mm) to allow detritivore access while the other half will be covered in fine mesh (2 mm) to discourage detritivore access. Every 10 days, a set of containers will be removed from each pond and brought back to the lab. The sedge will be dried and weighed, and detritivores in each container will be identified as well. We expect to see the sedge in the coarse mesh containers to decay faster.
Subject: Long-Term

ResearchPlanInstitution: University of North Carolina at Chapel Hill
ResearchPlanTitle: Effects of abiotic and biotic stress on plant fitness and herbivore defense in Boechera stricta
ResearchPlanAbstract: Abiotic and biotic factors influence plant fitness by altering the physical environment and resource availability. According to the stress gradient hypothesis, increasing stress in an environment increases positive, or facilitative, plant-plant interactions and decreases negative, or competitive, interspecies interactions. I will investigate how variance in abiotic stress modifies interactions between the wildflower Boechera stricta and its plant neighbors. I will also analyze how neighbor density may affect insect herbivory by altering apparent access to the plant. I hypothesize that more stressful environmental conditions will lead to increased facilitative plant interactions, whereas less stressful environmental conditions will lead to increased competitive plant interactions. I also predict that a higher density of neighboring plants will confer greater defense and less insect herbivory, whereas a lower density of neighboring plants will confer less defense and greater insect herbivory of B. stricta individuals. I will test these hypotheses by conducting a common garden experiment where rainout shelters will be used to manipulate soil moisture, and the density of neighbor vegetation naturally varies across microsites. I will collect data on B. stricta survival, fecundity, and insect herbivory under these varying combinations of drought and neighbor density. I will also perform neighbor removals in several natural populations of B. stricta to isolate the relationship between neighbor vegetation density, herbivore defense, and plant fitness.
Subject: Other

ResearchPlanTitle: Do White-Crowned Sparrows listen to local species alarm calls?
ResearchPlanAbstract: This playback experiment is to see if White-crowned sparrows listen to local species alarm calls. I have 5 different categories of call: American Robins, Lincoln's sparrows, Gray Jays, Yellow-Bellied marmots, and White-crowned sparrows. Each of these categories have 5 exemplars, except American Robins, which as 4. I play one playback per bird. The stimuli have all been normalized and the amplitude adjusted to 85dB. The playback consists of 30 seconds of silence to gauge baseline behavior, followed by the stimulus and 60 seconds of silence to record response. I record the birds behavior by dictating into an audio recorder using an ethogram with the following behaviors: stand and look, preen, chink, hop, walk, forage, out of site, fly, and vocalize.
Subject: Other

ResearchPlanTitle: Determining the Effects of Climate-Induced Range Shifts on Caddisfly Population Dynamics
ResearchPlanAbstract: Caddisflies are a species of aquatic insects that are fundamental in providing nutrients to plants and animals in alpine habitats. Being detritivores, caddisflies eat decaying plant material and transfer captive nutrients back into the ecosystem. The geographic distribution for many caddisflies is restricted in part by time of snowmelt and the temperature of the water which varies across elevational and local hydrological gradients. Because of this, climate change is having a significant effect on the distribution of caddisfly species around Gothic, Colorado. Scientists have documented that species typically found in lower elevation have begun to expand their range into higher alpine ponds. However, it is unknown how elevation will affect their population dynamics and their rate of nutrient recycling. Thus, understanding how elevation affects caddisfly growth and population size is key to understanding how climate change will affect alpine communities globally. To have a better understanding of this concept, I will study 20 ponds that span a gradient of 7,700 – 11,500 feet in elevation to see how the change in elevation affects mortality rate, population density, adult body size, and adult emergence time of three species of caddisfly: Limnephilus externus, Limnephilus picturatus, and Asynarchus nigriculus. I will take density samples of these species in each pond 2-3 times throughout the summer. In addition, pupae will be placed in emergence chambers to collect and measure the adults. This study is important because understanding how climate change is affecting foundational species may help us better understand the far-reaching effects of climate change.
Subject: Climate Change

ResearchPlanTitle: The effect of climate change on plant communities in the Rocky Mountains: how floral traits along an elevational gradient of reciprocally transplanted transplanted and control turfs
ResearchPlanAbstract: Alpine climates are characterized by a variety of inhospitable conditions that can fluctuate over short vertical distances. Thus, elevational gradients have been used to study how changes in climate can influence plant form, function, and diversity. In my study, I plan to examine how shifts in temperature and elevation influence floral traits using a novel experimental set of transplant communities. After examining flower diameter, flower radius, flower length, height of the highest flower and number of flowers, I expected that flower diameter, flower radius, flower length and height of the highest flower will increase as elevation is increased because there are fewer pollinators in the alpine and there is increased precipitation in the alpine. I expect the number of flowers to decrease because alpine environmental conditions are more severe, stunting growth.
Subject: Climate Change

ResearchPlanTitle: The impact of social network integration and position on the likelihood of summer survival in yellow-bellied marmots (Marmota flaviventer)
ResearchPlanAbstract: For many animals, group living serves as an effective strategy for mitigating predation risk, thereby increasing their longevity. However, in yellow-bellied marmots, sociality is correlated with decreased longevity, in addition to lower reproductive success in females. This phenomenon has a seasonal component: marmots who are more social in the active season have higher rates of over-winter mortality. As facultatively social animals, yellow-bellied marmots have some degree of phenotypic plasticity, and therefore are either choosing to be social or are forced into group living due to ecological constraints. Here, I explore the tradeoffs marmots weigh when they engage in social behavior during the active season by investigating the relationship between summer survival and social network integration and position. I will use social network analysis, and a community detection algorithm, to determine if social statistics are predictive of an individual marmot’s ability to avoid summer predation.
Subject: Other

ResearchPlanTitle: Measuring the level of human disturbance from 2010 to 2018 on Yellow-Bellied Marmot Colonies
ResearchPlanAbstract: The continuing expansion of the human footprint leaves extensive environmental change in its wake, both locally and globally (French et al., 2010). This includes destructive effects by urban development, as well as simple and more subtle influences; such as the introduction of or increase of human presence in a natural area. At the Rocky Mountain Biological Laboratory, humans other than researchers visit the site to participate in ecotourism or for recreational activities such as hiking and mountain biking. Studies have shown that animals exposed to humans more often can experience negative effects, including increased levels of stress, increased time spent of anti-predator vigilance behavior, and even develop a habituation to humans. To better inform studies of animal behavior at RMBL and in other locations, it is important to understand the level of human disturbance that is occurring. Following the protocol of a previous study conducted in 2010 at RMBL, the amount of bikers, hikers, and vehicles that pass within 300 meters of any of six focal marmot colonies will be recorded during the peak tourist season of July. A function will be created to document human disturbance from 2010 to 2018 on these marmot colonies. By documenting how and where the land is used by humans, researchers at RMBL will be able to pair human disturbance data with any current projects as well as understand what the site is being exposed too. Also, any trends in the human disturbance over the past eight years could be used to help inform future conservation efforts.
Subject: Long-Term

ResearchPlanInstitution: University of North Carolina at Charlotte
ResearchPlanTitle: Does Ecotourism influence the physiological traits of stress, rate of mass gain, and annual survival in yellow bellied marmots?
ResearchPlanAbstract: Ecotourism, although commonly supported and encouraged, is not free from creating anthropogenic disturbances and negative consequences on wildlife. This research aims to examine how motorized vehicles, hikers, and bikers differentially impact the physiological traits of short-term stress, chronic stress, rate of mass gain, and annual survival in yellow bellied marmots in the East River Valley. This research expands upon a 2010 project that examined human disturbance on marmot anti-predator behaviors. A positive correlation between the different types and levels of human impact on marmot physiology would indicate the negative impact of ecotourism. These results could imply future questions on the use of our natural spaces.
Subject: Other

ResearchPlanTitle: The impacts of early snowmelt and summer precipitation on the physiology and leaf morphology of Ipomopsis aggregata
ResearchPlanAbstract: Climate change is predicted to induce earlier snowmelt and variation in summer precipitation in an alpine environment. With these changes, populations may go extinct, there might be changes in traits, and in natural selection. This study will explore how earlier snowmelt and variation in summer precipitation will impact the water-use efficiency, specific leaf area, and trichome density of Ipomopsis aggregata.
Subject: Climate Change

ResearchPlanTitle: Nutrient excretion rates of common aquatic taxa in high elevation ponds at the Mexican Cut Nature Preserve
ResearchPlanAbstract: Nutrient cycling is crucial for proper functioning of aquatic ecosystems. Animals play an integral part of this process, especially in nutrient poor ecosystems such as the high elevation ponds at the Mexican Cut Nature Preserve. Nutrients such as nitrogen (N) and phosphorus (P) are both limiting nutrients; animal excretion increases the availability of these nutrients. We plan to determine the mass-specific excretion rate for common taxa in these ponds and estimate the importance of animals, functional groups, and taxa to supplying overall nutrient demand. We ask: How does each taxon differ in its N, P, and N:P excretion rates? What is the total uptake of nutrients in these ecosystems? To answer these questions we will measure both excretion rates of aquatic macroinvertebrates (insects, insect larvae, copepods, etc.) and pond nutrient uptake by microorganisms within the water column and on the pond bottom. We will determine excretion rates by collecting macroinvertebrates and placing individuals in plastic bags filled with filtered water and allowing them to incubate for approximately one hour. Control bags will be made without macroinvertebrates to provide a baseline for comparison. Water samples will be collected from the bags for each N and P and analyzed at the lab. To measure pond nutrient uptake we will place cylinders in pairs at six representative locations in a total of nine ponds. Nutrients will be added at known concentrations to each cylinder, and the rate of decline will be measured by taking samples at set intervals.
Subject: Climate Change

ResearchPlanTitle: Evaluating differences in critical thermal limits of solitary bees
ResearchPlanAbstract: Climate change is predicted to impact pollinators through both direct and indirect mechanisms: directly by a creating stressful environment through warming temperatures and indirectly by changing their interactions with other organisms by altering the timing of the availability of their food sources and competitors. While much work has been done at RMBL to evaluate the indirect mechanism of climate change impact on pollinators, less is known about the direct impact of temperature stress. To fill this gap, I will be measuring the critical thermal limits of solitary bees. Critical thermal limits are defined as the nonlethal upper and lower temperature at which an organism could not escape a threat, such as a predator. I will be evaluating the factors driving differences in limits among species and determining how well these limits predict bee abundance in hotter-than-average years, as a proxy for conditions under long-term warming. I will also be evaluating if there are local adaptations of thermal limits of the same species captured at different elevations. A finding of differences in thermal limits at different elevations may suggest the ability of bees to adapt to warming temperatures.
Subject: Climate Change

ResearchPlanTitle: The effect of surrounding bloom color on pan trap success in Rocky Mountain bees
ResearchPlanAbstract: Plant-pollinator interactions provide critical services in both natural and agricultural systems. On a global scale, bees are particularly influential but face concerns over declining populations. In order to monitor the health of bee populations and communities, accurate sampling methods are needed. Current sampling protocols utilize a combination of pan-trapping (colored plastic bowls filled with soapy water) and sweep netting. While pan-trapping has its benefits, little is known on how surrounding bloom color impacts the success of similarly colored pan traps. An analysis of a long-term data set from the Rocky Mountains (Colorado, USA) may help provide a better understanding of bee cognition, improve interpretations of current sampling methods, and allow for more accurate sampling methods to develop.
Subject: Phenology

ResearchPlanTitle: The Effects of Selfing and Outcrossing on Boechera stricta Fitness
ResearchPlanAbstract: Maintaining high levels of self-fertilization within a population increases homozygosity, exposes deleterious alleles, and may cause inbreeding depression. Yet, many species of flowering plants have evolved to self-fertilize a majority of the time. Often, self-fertilization is favored over outcrossing when small populations experience harsh or stressful environments. Self-compatibility may evolve after a founder event or when natural selection favors high reproductive assurance, such as when there is limited pollinator activity. When this occurs, selfing syndrome, the reduction of petal size and pollen production, may follow. In order to test for inbreeding depression and signs of selfing syndrome in Boechera stricta, I will perform controlled crosses and and measure trait variation among selfed and outcrossed genotypes in a common garden experiment.
Subject: Phenology

ResearchPlanTitle: The Effects of Soil on the Variation in Morphology and Phenology of Thlaspi arvense in Subalpine Meadows
ResearchPlanAbstract: The ability of soil to retain moisture can seriously impact plant growth. Deep, rich soils can retain moisture from snow melt into the dry season more efficiently than shallow, sandy soils that lose water to runoff. This affects the amount of resources plants put into their roots or stems. Plants growing in soil that does not hold water well might need to put more energy into longer roots in the search for water, instead of making more leaves for photosynthesis. Similarly, soil composition can impact the physical qualities of plants--how tall they grow, how many leaves they have, etc. There are many factors impacting the behaviour of plants and how they respond to challenges. Thlaspi arvense, an invasive mustard, has demonstrated success in many habitats in the subalpine meadows of Gunnison County. Rapid evolution and flexibility to changing conditions is a significant component of the ability of invasive species to expand and respond to climate change. To predict where invasions will be particularly dense or harmful to native ecology and inform conservation agencies, it is necessary to study the qualities of soils that favour the growth and reproductive success of T. arvense so appropriate measures can be taken.
Subject: Phenology

ResearchPlanTitle: Across Caste Differences of Floral Resource Use in Bombus spp.
ResearchPlanAbstract: Bumble bees play an important role in plant-pollinator networks, and have been broadly categorized into three groups based on proboscis length (tongue length): short, medium, and long. However, this overlooks the variation within each species of Bombus. The differences between castes (queens, workers, and males) may play an important role in the floral resources each caste, and the species, as a whole, visits. This project aims to quantify the variation across different castes of up to sixteen species of Bombus around the Rocky Mountain Biological Laboratory, and if the differences in proboscis length translates to differences in floral resource use across castes.
Subject: Pollination

ResearchPlanTitle: Mix and Match: Transplanting fungal symbiotic partners across elevational gradients to gauge responses in migrating Elymus hosts
ResearchPlanAbstract: Within the next century, arid and warm conditions are expected to increase for ecosystems across North America, especially in montane systems. Such conditions will alter species distributions, making important foundational graminoid species move up-slope in elevation as high-elevation areas become more habitable to low-elevation species. Species interactions are crucial factors that can determine successful establishment by species into novel environments. Interactions between plants and fungi can help or hamper their establishment, but not much is known of the effects of climate change on such interactions. As graminoids move up-slope, they may either bring their fungal symbionts with them, lose them and encounter a novel fungal consortia, or have the roles of their symbionts change. To investigate what happens with fungal symbionts during upward migration, I propose a field study that will transplant low-elevation Elymus elymoides and broad-range Elymus trachycaulus plants into low- and high-elevation sites. Three soil treatments of sterile soil, soil from low-elevation sites, and soil from high-elevation sites will be applied to give each plant a consortia of fungi that may mismatch their abiotic environment. This experiment will investigate how host plant performance is affected when symbionts are mismatched as a result of climate change. I hypothesize that performance will be reduced when the symbiont is mismatched with its abiotic environment.
Subject: Climate Change

ResearchPlanTitle: Nesting Preferences of Osmia Bees in the Rocky Mountains
ResearchPlanAbstract: Mason bees are a group of solitary bees that nest in holes in wood, and can sometimes be seen nesting in “bee hotels”, also called nest-blocks. These bees are very important pollinators both in nature and in orchards around the world. Interestingly, we still know very little about what attributes of the nest-block, its placement, and the area around it are attractive to mason bees. To test this question, we have set up bee nest-blocks at several sites around RMBL where bees can nest any time throughout the summer. We will measure several characteristics including the health of each tree with a nest-block; the number of potential (natural) nest-holes around each artificial nest-block; and the internal temperature of each nest-block. At the end of the summer, we will also record the number of nests per bee species in each block. We expect that mason bees will prefer warmer nest-blocks placed on dead trees in areas with more natural holes. This study will provide vital information on mason bee nesting preferences to support future efforts to study, conserve, or manage mason bees.
Subject: Pollination

ResearchPlanTitle: Are ants botanists?: Ant associative learning of plant volatiles in the context of foraging behavior

ResearchPlanTitle: The Lesser of Two Evils: Effects of Plant Bug vs Mutualist Aphid Herbivory on the Fitness of Ligusticum porteri
ResearchPlanAbstract: On Ligusticum porteri plants, ants protect populations of aphids from predators in exchange for sugar harvested from the plant. Lygus bugs omnivores which feed on L. porteri but also predate the aphids. This study seeks to compare the fitness of plants dominated by Lygus bugs to that of plants dominated by ant and aphids under varying degrees of stress. Arthropod populations on the study plants will be controlled by introducing aphids and/or Lygus to mesh bags on flowering stalks. Some plants will also be subjected to stressful warming. Change in plant fitness will be assessed throughout the study using physiological measurements. The effect of Lygus herbivory on aphid honeydew quality will also be assessed.
ResearchPlanOrganisms: Ligusticum porteri, Aphis asclepiadis (previously A. helianthi), Lygus hesperus
