ResearchPlanTitle: Mountain White-crowned Sparrow Project
ResearchPlanAbstract: This long-term study on Mountain White-crown Sparrows involves trapping and handling birds in order to take measurements on features like culmen (beak), tarsus (leg), wing, and tail lengths, as well as mass and a blood sample. In addition, we band birds with a serial number and color band combination. These sparrows breed yearly in the East River Valley, and we also find and monitor nests throughout the breeding season. Because these sparrows have been monitored for so many years, we can examine yearly changes and assess influences of things like human disturbance, increased tourism, and climate change on sparrow populations and morphologies.
Subject: Long-Term

ResearchPlanTitle: Variation in nectar content between wet and dry subalpine meadows
ResearchPlanAbstract: Pollinating bees visit flowers in order to forage for nectar and pollen, their major sources of nutrition. The plant communities that a bee interacts with vary across time and space. Water contributes to some of this variation: some sub-alpine meadows have characteristic dry plant communities, and others have characteristic wet plants. Different flowers provide different nutritional rewards for visiting bees. As a result of this variation, foraging wild bees may be presented with a mosaic of meadows, each with higher or lower amounts and concentration of nectar. We aim to directly estimate the community-level variation in floral nectar quantity and quality, that is, the amount of sugar available to a bee in each meadow. These data will be combined with a separate pollinator visitation study, in an effort to understand the effects of nutritional variation on pollinator networks.
Subject: Pollination

ResearchPlanTitle: Effects of Light Transparency on Aspen Understory Species Along an Elevational Gradient (subject to change)
ResearchPlanAbstract: Trembling aspen (Populus tremulodies) is a keystone species found throughout North America. P. tremulodies is a successional species which aids the regeneration of Eco systems after disturbance. However, Climate Change is altering aspen forest dynamics, aspen forest die- off in the American Southwest is predicted to increase in the next few years as temperatures increase. As forests change, so does their understory. Forest die-off will affect the understory plant communities, which play crucial part on regional biodiversity. In this study, the relationship between aspen canopy light transparency will be measured in correlation with richness and abundance of aspen understory shrub, grass and forbs cover along an elevational gradient throughout Crested Butte (Colorado). I predict that aspen understory forbs will decrease richness and abundance, aspen understory shrub and grass species will increase in richness and abundance with increasing canopy light transparency, as the elevational gradient increases. (insert meters here) , if the results of this study are consistent with my hypothesis, aspen forests community dynamics will be better understood and can possibly provide a better pathway for aspen forest management. (Subject to change)
Subject: Climate Change

ResearchPlanTitle: The Effects of Climate-Driven Changes in Co-flowering between Linum lewisii and Potentilla pulcherrima on Pollinator Services
ResearchPlanAbstract: Anthropogenic climate change is affecting many ecosystems. Changes in the melting of snowpack have altered flowering phenology in subalpine meadows. The subalpine meadows at the Rocky Mountain Biological Laboratories in Gothic, Colorado are experiencing shifts in co-flowering patterns. Two flowers, Linum lewisii and Potentilla pulcherrima, which had significant historical co-flowering overlap are now having 25% less overlap. The consequences of this shift are not well known and could be having an effect on plant-pollinator interactions. Although L. lewisii can self-pollinate, this would result in vegetative reproduction and outcrossing is necessary to produce fruits and seeds. This means that pollinator services are important to L. lewisii. This decrease in overlap may mean that there is fewer pollinator services competition. This short-term study look will look at pollinator visitation rates and pollen deposition on L. lewisii by providing different treatments to plots that would decrease their overlap even further. There will be two synchrony treatments in addition to a control. The treatments are 100% removal of P. pulcherrima flowers and 50% removal of P. pulcherrima flowers. I would expect that pollinator visitation rates are lower when there is less overlap and that there is more heterospecific pollen deposition. It may be possible that earlier snowpack melt due to climate change is having a positive effect on subalpine plant species. It is important to understand the effects of these changes because they will provide critical knowledge on mechanisms for the preservation of native plant and animal communities.
ResearchPlanOrganisms: small bee and fly pollinators, Linum lewisii, and Potentilla pulcherrima
Subject: Pollination

ResearchPlanTitle: What abiotic and biotic factors predict the shape of plant diversity-productivity relationships?
ResearchPlanAbstract: Anthropogenic influence over biodiversity has greatly altered ecosystem functions and services. One of the most important ecosystem functions related to diversity is productivity. Despite the importance of the relationships between plant diversity and productivity, their shapes are hotly debated and what determines variation in shapes is not well understood. Understanding what factors predict the shapes of biodiversity-productivity relationships, such as what determines maximum productivity, can aid in prioritizing ecosystems for conservation efforts. Here, we examine plant diversity-plant productivity relationships from local to landscape scales in a mountain ecosystem. Specifically, we compare fits of linear and Michaelis-Menten models to plant species richness predictions of productivity. Additionally, we evaluate whether the humped-back model of productivity and diversity applies in the system. Finally, we construct models of plant richness-productivity relationships for local communities and derive their parameter estimates to ask: what abiotic and biotic factors predict the shapes of the plant richness-productivity relationships within sites? In this study, we collect plant community composition data including species richness and plant cover representing productivity in 67 sites across 6 peak-valley combinations spanning elevation gradients. Also, abiotic and biotic factors will be recorded in all sites within gradients. We hypothesize that the plant richness-productivity relationship across the landscape will show a positive linear model. Also, we predict that larger slopes of the linear models would have higher resources and less climatic stress. This research tries to clarify the shapes of the relationships and identify factors that cause variation and can predict the relations.
Subject: Climate Change

ResearchPlanTitle: Spatial and Temporal Patterns and Mechanisms of Coexistence in Closely Related Rhyacophila Species
ResearchPlanAbstract: Environmental change and shifting resource availability impact the survival, interaction and co-existence of species within an ecosystem. We will study Rhyacophila, a genus of caddisfly that in its larval state lives at the bottom of cold, oxygen rich and fast flowing streams. Previous research has shown that there are seven species, five common ones, that occur in the high alpine streams of the Upper East River Basin in the Gunnison National Forest. We aim to first, document which species of closely-related Rhyacophila coexist and do not coexist in the same streams, and second, understand what environmental and biotic mechanisms may influence those patterns. We will sample the invertebrate populations and key environmental factors along previously sampled sites and then conduct a species co-occurrence analysis to understand the relationships between different species of Rhyacophila. Multivariate analyses will be used to explain the abundance of these species. In addition, we will look at the persistence of patterns over time using an unprecedented long-term data set. Because Rhyacophila are particularly sensitive to environmental change, this study can provide clues to climate change related impacts and serve as a comparative model for more threatened aquatic systems in Colorado.
Subject: Other

ResearchPlanTitle: Local Adaptation in Boechera stricta in the context of climate change
ResearchPlanAbstract: Local adaptation in seed germination and seedling establishment in the context of climate change using Boechera stricta. In 4 of our gardens, we set out large-scale experiments last fall with 4 treatments: (1) snow removal (simulating future climates), (2) control (contemporary climates), (3) snow addition (simulating historical climates) and (4) snow addition & supplemental watering (simulating even more historical climates). We are asking whether patterns of local adaptation are more prominent in treatments 3 and 4 than 1 and 2.
Subject: Climate Change

ResearchPlanTitle: Comparing Plant-Pollinator Network Structure between Drought and Non-Drought Years
ResearchPlanAbstract: Network analyses are an ecological method that can be used to examine multi-species interactions and, in this case, the mutualistic relationship between plants and pollinators. Two indices of interest for this study are specialization, the dependency of each species on a few exclusive partners, and connectance, the number of links realized out of the possible interactions within a network. Natural perturbations, such as drought or climate change, have the potential to alter the structure of these networks. Drought, in particular, will be studied, comparing network structure data between 2017 and 2018, the latter being considered the second driest year on record in East River Valley in western Colorado, USA. Phenological mismatch and the decrease in relative abundances as a result of drought are predicted to cause changes in network structure. Specialization is hypothesized to increase with more competition while connectance is expected to decrease in this more specialized network structure. Quantitative networks will be built at three sites by collecting floral visitation data through capturing of pollinators. The indices calculated from 2017, a non-drought year, and 2018, a drought year, will be compared.
Subject: Pollination

ResearchPlanTitle: First order controls on soil and leaf moisture
ResearchPlanAbstract: This project aims to identify where soil and foliar moisture in the Crested Butte area in late June is being held and how it corelates to first-order controls such as topography, geology, climate, and vegetation. The expectation is that relatively high moisture values will be in areas with high snow accumulation and late persistence into late spring and in topographic lows indicative of flow convergence and streamflow generation. Sampling will be conducted across the area at multiple sites (see figure 2) involving a variety of soil and vegetative properties collected as part of the National Ecological Observatory Network (NEON) ground campaign. NEON ground data will be correlated with LiDAR topographic data, raster maps of vegetation type, density and height and Airborne Snow Observatory (ASO) data collected in March and May 2018 for snowpack location, depth, and water content. In addition, detailed temporal data from RMBL meteorological stations and the SNOw TELemetry (SNOTEL) networks will enhance NEON spatial data with respect to precipitation, air temperature, as well as soil moisture and temperature. Time permitting, stream flow data will be analyzed within the Upper East River and Washington Gulch to link soil and leaf moisture to possible hydrologic partitioning of precipitation to either evapotranspiration, runoff, or groundwater recharge.
ResearchPlanOrganisms: aspen, conifers, veratrum, many more that will be sampled

ResearchPlanTitle: The Effects of Declining Aspen Forest Health on Rocky Mountain Birds
ResearchPlanAbstract: Due to the effects of climate change, aspen forests are declining. With this, there are likely to be impacts on the avian community within the East River Valley. With the use of acoustic recorders and aspen tree health data, the effects of this aspen forest decline on total avian conservation value as a function of species richness and species composition will be measured. The results will depict not only how bird community richness and composition change as a response to declining aspen forest health, but also, how the conservation value of birds differs in varying environmental conditions.
Subject: Climate Change

ResearchPlanTitle: The impact of elevation and warming on types and quantity of VOCs
ResearchPlanAbstract: We will be comparing soil carbon content across multiple different elevation gradients to test for nutrient and moisture levels effect on microbial carbon degradation rates. We will also be comparing rates against warming plots that have been increased by 2.1ï‚°C over the past 28 years. We will analyze the effect of the differencing elevation gradients and warming plots on the diversity and quantity of microbial volatile organic compounds (VOCs) produced in soil.

ResearchPlanTitle: Friend or Foe? Effects of Tapinoma sessile on Nicrophorus investigator Reproductive Success
ResearchPlanAbstract: Vertebrate scavengers, burying beetles, ants, flies, fungi, and microbes compete for ephemeral carrion resources. Burying beetles require a carrion in order to successfully reproduce, and so they have mechanisms to combat competition from fly eggs, fungi, and microbes, but interactions between ants and beetles have not been extensively studied, and are not yet well understood. Interactions between the ant species Tapinoma sessile and the burying beetle Nicrophorus investigator may yield a diffuse mutualistic relationship involving the predation of undesired dipteran eggs from the carrion. This study aims to analyze the effects of T. sessile on N. investigator’s reproductive success.
Subject: Other

ResearchPlanTitle: Drought impacts on pollen limitation in alpine meadows
ResearchPlanAbstract: Pollen limitation is a common phenomenon in terrestrial, animal-pollinated plants, but several theoretical frameworks suggest that pollen limitation should be rare at equilibrium conditions. One proposed theory is that widespread pollen limitation is the result of pervasive anthropogenic disruption of pollinator species. Alternately, widespread pollen limitation may be an equilibrium state resulting from “bet hedging” in allocating resources to attracting pollinators among stochastic abiotic conditions. A direct prediction of this theory is that pollen limitation should be greatest when abiotic conditions are less stressful. Alpine meadows near Gothic, CO, USA, provide an opportunity to test this theory directly over a drought gradient (wetter conditions/less stressful - drier conditions/more stressful). Soil water content will be measured at each of seven meadows using a soil water content meter, and pollen limitation will be measured by comparing seed set of pollen-supplemented plants to naturally pollenated controls. All data analysis will be completed in R. A linear regression will be used to compare soil water content to pollen limitation to test the prediction of higher pollen limitation under wetter, less stressful conditions. Ultimately, the results of this study will help test a prominent theory explaining the widespread occurrence of pollen limitation.
Subject: Climate Change

ResearchPlanTitle: Behavioral Correlates of Innovation Success in Facultatively Social Marmots
ResearchPlanAbstract: Innovation has transformed ecology and evolution, so understanding behaviors that lead to innovation success can have profound implications and applications in animal populations and human society. Past research has implicated persistence, behavioral selectivity, and neophobia as key characteristics that define an individual’s ability to innovate. Exploring this research in socially flexible yellow-bellied marmots can disentangle these factors and reveal which one, if any, is most influential to innovation success. Marmot colonies will have the opportunity to engage with a two-action puzzle box and obtain a food reward, and afterwards, individual behaviors will be scored and compared against social metrics. We predict that high degrees of persistence, behavioral selectivity, and neophilia will correlate with innovation success. With the onset of climate change, the results of this study can guide conservation management, as innovative behaviors can be adaptive in changing landscapes and drive species redistribution. In addition, innovation success is highly valued for developing better goods and services in anthropogenic industries.
Subject: Other

ResearchPlanInstitution: University of Colorado, National Snow and Ice Data Center
ResearchPlanTitle: SnowSCAPE, SnowDOMES, DustProc (full titles in Research Plan)
ResearchPlanAbstract: Variations in snow accumulation and melt across the landscape provide the main source of water and nutrient flows in mountain river basins. To accurately anticipate the impacts of environmental disturbances to the snow/water system (e.g. climate shifts, dust-enhanced snowmelt, forest change from fire or insects) on water availability and nutrient cycling, robust observations and simulations of seasonal snow dynamics are needed. Snow properties and patterns vary significantly across landscapes, and traditional snow measurement locations are too sparse to monitor this variability in snow. Therefore, understanding and simulating interactions of snow with other hydrologic and biochemical components of the basin remains challenging. The scope of activities in the Watershed Function SFA (WFSFA) presents an unparalleled opportunity to improve our understanding of the role of snow dynamics in watershed function and snowpack sensitivities to disturbances in a well-instrumented and integrated study environment. The four projects covered here contribute to DoE WFSFA and RMBL activities by improving seasonal snow observations and modeling, which can then be integrated with other studies. The research aims to address the following five questions: Q1 (SnowSCAPE): What processes dominate snow and snowmelt distributions in the WFSFA and subcatchments over hourly to decadal time scales and from hillslope to basin spatial scales? Q2 (SnowSCAPE): What degree of model complexity (scale, process representation) is required to simulate snow accumulation and melt in the WFSFA, and how does this requirement intersect with mesoscale meteorology and fine-scale subsurface hydrology and transport models in use? Q3 (SnowDOMES): How does the relationship between snowpack depth and density change with respect to landscape-driven physical processes in the WFSFA? Q4 (DustProc): How do deposited aerosols, namely dust, impact watershed biogeochemistry and ecology? Q5 (SnowEx): What is the distribution of snow-water equivalent (SWE), and the snow energy balance, in different canopy types and densities, and terrain across the WFSFA domain? These projects aim to study mountain snow accumulation and melt dynamics through application of high resolution (10 m) snow models over the entire East River domain, supported by field measurements, in-situ monitoring, and Airborne Snow Observatory (ASO) snow depth and albedo mapping. To examine the roles of model resolution and physical process representation when simulating snowpack dynamics in the East River basin, we will also run the models at multiple resolutions (such as 3 m, 10 m, 100 m, 1000 m), and physical components of the model (e.g., wind redistribution, canopy shading) will be progressively altered to assess changes in snowmelt dynamics and patterns. We will explore responses of snow cover (temperature, duration, structure), infiltration, and snowmelt to disturbances in climate, vegetation, and dust deposition over hourly to multi-year time scales leveraging existing projects in the SFA exploring these scenarios. Output from the snow models will be integrated with other SFA models (e.g. groundwater or nutrient flow models) at multiple resolutions to explore subsurface flow and nutrient transport response to variations in the snow cover. This project is strongly complementary to ongoing efforts at RMBL, as it embraces a system-of-systems perspective in quantifying seasonal water balance components and their connection to changes in climate, ecologic, and geochemical systems.
Subject: Other

ResearchPlanTitle: Disturbance Macroecology
ResearchPlanAbstract: Macroecology is the study of patterns in the distribution, energetics, and abundance of individuals and species within ecosystems. Understanding these patterns is critical for estimating species diversity at spatial scales too large to census directly, for estimating extinction rates under habitat loss or degradation, and for optimally designing reserves. Successful macroecological theory exists for undisturbed ecosystems in which macroecological patterns are not changing significantly from year to year. However, many ecosystems are undergoing dramatic changes as a consequence of human disturbance, and in such systems successful macroecological theory is lacking. The broad goal of this research is a dynamic, falsifiable and tested, theory of macroecology applicable to systems undergoing change, whether as a consequence of human disturbance or as a consequence of natural disturbance regimes in which ecological succession is relatively rapid. In short, we seek a general theory of both static and dynamic macroecology. Toward that end, spatially explicit census data from disturbed ecosystems are needed both to guide theory development and to test theory. Research at RMBL that we have carried out over the past decade has contributed such data, and in relatively undisturbed habitats has provided some of the data used to test macroecological theory in static, undisturbed, habitats. But to advance and test dynamic theory, acquisition of more data from disturbed ecosystems is needed. In the Upper East River Valley there are many opportunities to acquire census data from sites undergoing disturbance, including from decadal trends in climate, from invasive species, and from erosion events. This project will obtain such data and will thereby contribute to the advancement of macroecological theory.
Subject: Other

ResearchPlanTitle: Watershed Rules of Life
ResearchPlanAbstract: Rivers are the circulatory systems of the continents, delivering land-derived water, pollutants and elements to the ocean. They are also sites with unique organisms, food webs, and microbial communities that can transform these materials during transport to the ocean. Microbes are the engines for these transformations, with considerable capacity to remove or alter important elements (e.g., carbon, nitrogen, phosphorus, mercury, arsenic), produce greenhouse gasses, and support food webs. However, due to large changes in water flow from day to day, and the big differences in the types of streams and rivers across the landscape, understanding how riverine microbes impact the chemistry of rivers is difficult. This project will research a set of "Watershed Rules of Life" that govern the establishment of riverine water column microbial communities that are critical to understanding rivers as circulatory systems. The researchers have proposed a set of hypotheses that adds microbial ecology into the scaffolding of hydrology and geomorphology in order to research these Watershed Rules of Life. The hypothesis will be tested by field work and modeling in a diverse set of watersheds throughout the United States. The knowledge gained by these studies will allow for a broader understanding of rivers in both the U.S. and other temperate regions of the world. The investigators will interact with the Yale New Haven Promise Internship program, which provides internships for students from New Haven interested in STEM. Professor Raymond will also interact with students at the Crested Butte Community School. This project will train graduate and undergraduate students at UMass, OSU and Yale. Findings will be incorporated into courses taught by the investigators. The researchers will target the emergent property of microbial functional trait distributions across the physical templates of watersheds and in response to hydrologic variability. The project will sample the Connecticut, Deschutes, Gunnison and Willamette watersheds, which are similar in size but differ in climate and geomorphology. Within each watershed, sampling will focus on streams of different sizes, the impact of reservoirs and hydrologic variability. The proposed research will develop mathematical expressions that relate multiple indices for the development and activity of planktonic microbial communities to stream order, stream hydraulics (e.g., velocity and depth), flow variability, and temperature. These indices will be based on metagenomics for genomic diversity, metatranscriptomics for gene expression, and microbial 16S rRNA gene amplicon sequencing for phylogenetic diversity in riverine samples. Microbial indices will be compared to modeled estimates of the time scale for water column microbial community development (i.e., residence time) and microbial transformation rates (e.g., denitrification). It is hypothesized that geomorphology (e.g., depth, velocity), discharge variability, and temperature are the main determinants of when and where distinct planktonic microbial riverine communities emerge in the water column of river networks.
Subject: Climate Change

ResearchPlanTitle: Spatial genetic structure of alpine Mimulus
ResearchPlanAbstract: A major goal in evolutionary biology is to understand how organisms adapt to novel or changing environments. A particularly dramatic example of ecological specialization in plants involves alpine endemics, which have evolved characteristic suites of adaptations in response to similar selective regimes. We are investigating the ecological and genomic basis of this common ecological transition to alpine environments using the mountain monkeyflower, Mimulus tilingii. In contrast to the widely-distributed, lowland progenitor species Mimulus guttatus, Mimulus tilingii populations are confined to alpine regions throughout western North America, in discrete â€œhabitat islands.â€ These populations provide a unique set of replicate evolutionary experiments for how Mimulus tilingii has adapted to common ecological influences imposed by alpine environments. Preliminary analyses indicate that there have been at least three evolutionary origins of Mimulus tilingii in the Cascades, Sierra Nevadas, and Olympic Mountain ranges. I am now proposing to expand my sampling to include populations in the Rocky Mountains, which will provide a geographically distinct evolutionary lineage for future comparative studies for how Mimulus populations have diverged in response to similar ecological conditions.
Subject: Climate Change

ResearchPlanTitle: Continuing Archival Research on RMBL History
ResearchPlanAbstract: Located high (approximately 9,500 feet) on the western slope of Colorado in Gunnison County, the Rocky Mountain Biological Laboratory (RMBL) considers its surrounding landscape to be the laboratory itselfâ€”yet it is located on the site of a former 1880s-era silver mining town, called Gothic, perched just below the continental divide and reflecting a past history of extractive uses in the area. Faced with a recent influx of both winter and summer recreation demands, wilderness designation, and future unknowns associated with climate change, the Lab is navigating an interesting set of challenges with regard to land managementâ€”both land that RMBL owns directly and the surrounding federal and privately-owned landscapesâ€”and scientific certainty. By documenting the history of this field station, my research should reveal some of the broader ways in which the landscape itself, and our ideas about its meaning, can shape the kinds of science done in a given place. This multi-year project explicitly investigates this more place-based scientific inquiry developing over time, in a place where perennially returning scientists themselves are becoming nearly â€œindigenous,â€ spending entire careers conducting summer field work to understand the dynamics of specific ecosystems or species.
Subject: Other

ResearchPlanTitle: Pollination and reproduction of montane wildflowers
ResearchPlanAbstract: Pollination, reproduction, and survival of wildflowers are critical to the health of natural ecological systems in meadow habitats of the Rocky Mountains. We are continuing our long-term (45+ years) studies of the pollination of the low larkspur and of scarlet gilia by bumble bees and hummingbirds. In particular we will continue to explore how road dust and climate variation interact to influence wildflower pollination and reproduction, and the role of insects that consume plant seeds within fruits.
ResearchPlanOrganisms: Ipomopsis aggregata, Delphinium nuttallianum, Linum lewisii, Castilleja spp., Hylemya sp. (Anthomyiidae)
Subject: Pollination

ResearchPlanTitle: General Observational Studies on Plant-Herbivore Interactions
ResearchPlanAbstract: I wish to conduct a series of surveys/observations in the US Forest Service’s Gunnison District examining plant and insect populations along with their interactions. My research interests focus on insect host-pathogen interactions, plant-herbivore interactions, and plant demography. The areas of current interest include: 1) ant-aphid mutualisms and how they may affect plant-pollinator interactions particularly on fireweed; 2) long-term dynamics of grasshopper populations in the area; 3) population dynamics of the aspen tortrix along with its associated diseases and parasites; and, 4) anti-herbivore defenses in heartleaf bittercress and the implications of these defenses for herbivore fitness. However, as one can tell from the above, the current plan is focused on observational studies and no manipulative experiments are being planned at this time.
ResearchPlanOrganisms: General Observation - no specific study organisms.
Subject: Other

ResearchPlanTitle: RMBL Phenology Project; associational effects
ResearchPlanAbstract: We will continue the RMBL phenology project, counting flowers in permanent plots throughout the season. We will also continue work on ways that local plant neighborhoods affect interactions of focal plants with herbivores, seed predators, and pollinators.
Subject: Phenology

ResearchPlanTitle: Montane and alpine plant community response to climate change
ResearchPlanAbstract: Predicting the responses of species to environmental change is a key goal for ecology. My research focuses on developing datasets and testing theory to reach this goal. I work on two complementary systems - communities of alpine plants, and landscapes of aspen forests. In both cases I have observed strong recent mortality likely driven by drought. My work focuses on monitoring these changes and offering approaches to better forecasting the future of these systems.
Subject: Climate Change

ResearchPlanTitle: Effect of climate variability on bee phenology and abundance; Secondary chemistry of floral rewards; Ecology and management of invasive plants; Tick distributions
ResearchPlanAbstract: My five-year research plan is split across five projects. (Projects 1 and 2) Assessing how climate variability affects bee phenology and abundance and the mechanisms involved. We will add to a 10-year dataset that is addressing how climate and flowering patterns directly and indirectly affect the phenology and abundance of bees, and how bee life history traits may buffer them (or make them more susceptible) to changes in climate. This dataset is publicly available online and is well-resolved to the species level, making it an exemplary resource for not only my lab and the RMBL community but also the scientific community at large. (Project 3) Exploring the secondary chemistry of floral rewards and how particular pollen species affect bee disease. There is growing recognition that secondary compounds are not only expressed in foliar tissue, but also floral tissue and nectar and pollen rewards. We are building off a tritrophic effects framework to assess how nectar and pollen diets have indirect effects on bees by mediating host-parasite interactions. (Project 4) Investigating invasive plant biology. We will continue a long-term management project on Linaria vulgaris assessing how various management strategies affect L. vulgaris abundance and spread. (Project 5) Tick distributions in Gunnison County. Ticks are important vectors of disease transmission in humans, domesticated animals, and wildlife. We will continue monitoring tick distributions north of Almont and across an elevation gradient from Almont to Mexican Cut.
Subject: Pollination

ResearchPlanTitle: Biotic interactions and demography in a changing climate
ResearchPlanAbstract: To gain a better understanding of the long-term population consequences of natural herbivory and pathogen damage that may intensify as low elevation communities invade alpine zones, I propose a continuation of demographic data collection of the focal grass species (Poa alpina, Festuca brachyphylla, and Elymus scribneri) in their natural environment. The data will be used parameterize a Matrix Projection Model (MPMs) which take discrete individual body size metrics and predict demographic performance. By using exemplar populations of target species to predict survival, growth, and reproduction of a given range of body sizes paired with detailed measures of natural enemy damage to individuals, I will be able to estimate the demographic consequences of altered biotic interaction with climate change. With this data, I will be able to infer whether or not a given target species will go extinct as a result of increased negative biotic interactions from encroaching low elevation herbivore and pathogen communities.
Subject: Long-Term

ResearchPlanTitle: Quantifying environmental and biological controls on soil CO2 fluxes in East River valley forests
ResearchPlanAbstract: My proposed research seeks to mechanistically understand soil respiration in the dominant forest communities around the RMBL by individually quantifying the contributions from its two sources, plants and microbes. To do this, I will continue long term automated measurements of soil CO2 concentrations in two vegetation communities (spruce/fir and aspen forests) located in the RMBL research meadow. These measurements will be combined with novel radiocarbon (14C) source partitioning methods. New to this research plan are measurements of vegetation and snow phenology via digital cameras (PhenoCams) and adding remote communication abilities to the site. This unique approach will provide information on how environmental and biological factors control plant and microbial respiration sources of CO2 to the atmosphere, and assess potential climate change impacts on ecosystems in the East River valley.
Subject: Climate Change

ResearchPlanTitle: Can herb-chronology be used to monitor population dynamics of herbaceous species? An investigation using long-term data from the U.S. Rocky Mountains and tallgrass prairie
ResearchPlanAbstract: Understanding what factors drive the year-to-year variability of herbaceous populations is important for maintaining ecosystem function of areas with little to no woody component. Abundance, survival, and reproductive effort of herbaceous populations are highly sensitive towards annual climate and ecological conditions. Long-term monitoring currently exists as the only way for piecing together the year-to-year variability in abundance and other vital rates of certain herbaceous populations to these environmental factors. Unfortunately, due to limits on time and budgets, the amount of long-term monitoring of such populations is vastly unfulfilled when considering the amount of species in herbaceous landscapes which are important for ecosystem functioning. In this proposed study we investigate a new method for long-term monitoring which may overcome the time and resources needed to inform us about the annual variability in herbaceous population dynamics. We consider the utility of annual growth rings contained in the perennial woody belowground organs of herbaceous species as potential proxies for annual abundance and vital rates of populations. The field of herb-chronology finds that a majority of perennial forbs studied contain distinct annual rings. In most cases growth rings have annual variation tied with environment in the same way population dynamics co-vary with environment. With available long-term population data on dozens of herbaceous species (spanning across several different functional groups) from three Long-term Ecological Research (LTER) sites and one biological field station scattered across the Great Plains and the Colorado Rockies, we will investigate if the annual variation in ring chronologies can serve as a proxy for annual variation in population abundance and vital rates. In addition, we will monitor plant individuals from the same species for three field seasons at each site in a sequence of plots to observe how ring growth correlates with annual aboveground biomass, fecundity, and survival, while also considering how these relationships vary with size, age, and functional group.
ResearchPlanOrganisms: Helianthella quinquenervis, Hymenoxys grandiflora, Veratrum tenuipetalum, Ipomopsis aggregate, Delphinium nuttallianum, Valeriana edulis, Agoseris glauca, Arenaria congesta, Arnica latifolia, Eriogonum umbellatum..and others that are tentative
Subject: Climate Change

ResearchPlanInstitution: Idaho State University, Idaho Museum of Natural History
ResearchPlanTitle: Building Collections Resources for Research and Education at RMBL; and Using Archival Herbarium Data to Track Vegetation Change in the East River Basin
ResearchPlanAbstract: The primary objective of my previous research plan, 2014-2018, was to develop an interactive, virtual herbarium for the East River Valley. That goal has been realized with the complete digitization of the RMBL Herbarium and the ongoing digitization of other herbaria in the Southern Rocky Mountains as part of the NSF-ADBC grant creating the Consortium of Southern Rocky Mountain Herbaria. Over the past 5 years I have digitized the RMBL herbarium (ca. 8000 specimens) and mammal (ca. 650 specimens) collections and made them publically available online via the SEINet and iDigBio aggregated databases. All herbarium specimens have been digitally imaged, georeferenced and their label information transcribed into online databases, allowing sophisticated searches based on taxon, locality, elevation, collector, and date. Specimen images allow determination of phenological stage and other morphological information. The RMBL Herbarium now contains the most comprehensive collection of specimens from Gunnison County of any herbarium worldwide. When combined with data aggregated from other herbaria, these historical specimens provide an unprecedented resource to examine vegetation change over time and space in the Gunnison Basin. Over the next 5 year period, 2019-2023, I propose to use these herbarium records as a baseline to survey and track vegetation changes at a series of historically well-collected sites spanning the elevational gradient from sagebrush to the high alpine. In particular, I will resurvey sites collected by Harriet G. Barclay between 1929 and 1978, as well as sites surveyed by Jean Langenheim from 1948-1951. I will establish a long-term monitoring program at a number of sites with the most complete historical data. In addition to these surveys, I will continue to curate the herbarium and other natural history collections, mentor students, assist students, researchers and the public with plant identifications and locality mapping, and collaborate in citizen science projects with other members of the RMBL and Crested Butte Community.
Subject: Long-Term

ResearchPlanTitle: Space and time dynamics of transpiration in the East River watershed: biotic and abiotic controls
ResearchPlanAbstract: Evapotranspiration, or ET, is the combined loss of water from surface to the atmosphere by soil evaporation and plant transpiration. The amount of ET influences how much of the rain and snow that fall in a watershed support streamflow and groundwater recharge. While ET is controlled to a first-order by energy, with more energy leading to more ET, the transpiration component of ET can be difficult to predict because plants have diverse strategies to both access and conserve water supplies. Notably, plants can tap into deep water pools and continue to transpire long after surface soils have dried out. Furthermore, plants can generate long lateral root systems that move down a hillslope towards the stream, which also enables them to continue to transpire when the local soil water has dried out. On the other hand, plants can close their stomata or reduce the flow through the xylem to conserve water under certain conditions even when surface soil water might be available. Needless to say, the behavior of transpiration is complex and dependent on the species, the community dynamics, the location in the watershed (such as snowpack and depth to groundwater) and the regional climate. In this project, we will look at the behavior of transpiration for Subalpine fir, Engelmann spruce and Aspen along a hillslope in the East River Watershed. We will use this data to assess how transpiration varies through the year and how it responds to the local conditions such as depth to groundwater, radiation and snowpack. The work will shed light on how trees compete for available water, particularly at the interface between aspen and conifer stands. We will use this data to test competing theories on what triggers plants to switch between use of deep (i.e. groundwater) versus shallow water pools and in doing so provide a critical new dataset to improve models on the hydrology of the East River Watershed. The information gathered on transpiration will also be broadly applicable to understanding the resilience of typical fir, spruce and aspen ecosystems in the western US to climate change.
Subject: Climate Change

ResearchPlanTitle: Searching for the limits to pathogen adaptation with a wildflower model system
ResearchPlanAbstract: What limits pathogen adaptation? Understanding pathogensâ€™ strategies for infecting hosts is important for disease control in systems ranging from public health to agriculture. Additionally, it is critical to understand the role of the environment in modulating the balance of host-pathogen interactions, especially in the context of anthropogenic climate change. Previous research has focused either limits to pathogen aggressiveness, the rate of host manipulation, or infectivity, the range of host species (or genotypes) a pathogen can infect. However, the link between these two factors has never been investigated. Using demographic and epidemiological field surveys of a fungal pathogen (Melampsora lini) infecting wild flax (Linum lewisii) coupled with greenhouse inoculation experiments in this same system, I will investigate the relationship between aggressiveness and infectivity, and the role of environmental factors in modulating this association. My findings will have important implications for both basic evolutionary and ecological research and for the management of agricultural pathogens.
ResearchPlanOrganisms: Lewis flax (Linum lewisii) and Melampsora lini (flax rust)
Subject: Other

ResearchPlanInstitution: Northwestern University & The Chicago Botanic Garden
ResearchPlanTitle: Nest Site Characteristics and Timing of Emergence in Solitary Ground-Nesting Bees
ResearchPlanAbstract: Recent concerns of pollinator declines have prompted habitat conservation efforts. However, population trends for solitary bees are understudied due to knowledge gaps in their natural-history. Approximately 85% of solitary bees nest underground, yet their nesting requirements remain largely unknown. An improved understanding of solitary ground-nesting bee nest habitat would allow for more targeted conservation efforts. This study aims to determine the nest site characteristics of ground-nesting bees in a subalpine ecosystem. My project aims to describe the ecological characteristics that best predict nest presence, and whether nest depth can serve as an indicator for relative emergence times. Information from this study will increase the efficacy of pollinator habitat conservation efforts.
Subject: Pollination

ResearchPlanInstitution: Northwestern University and The Chicago Botanic Garden
ResearchPlanTitle: The effects of climate change on plant phenology: teasing apart the effects of early snowmelt and warmer temperatures
ResearchPlanAbstract: There is still much unknown about precipitation’s role as a cue for phenology, e.g. the timing of life cycle events. Changes phenological events in plants caused by climate change have unknown consequence for reproductive success. I will use a field experiment to study how warmer temperatures and earlier spring snowmelt affect reproductive cycles in five perennial plant species in subalpine meadows. The goals of this project are to: 1) distinguish between the effects of snowmelt and temperature on phenology, 2) quantify the changes to the timing and duration of leaf out, flowering, and fruiting caused by climate change, and 3) asses the consequences of these phenological shifts for fruit and seed production. Understanding the drivers of phenology will help us to predict how continued changes to the climate will impact plant species reproduction and abundance.
ResearchPlanOrganisms: Viola praemorsa, Delphinium nuttallianum, Lathyrus leucanthus, Potentilla pulcherrima, Erigeron speciosus
Subject: Phenology

ResearchPlanTitle: Evolutionary causes and consequences of pollen defense
ResearchPlanAbstract: Pollination plays an essential role in ecosystem functioning and agriculture. Yet, this mutually beneficial interaction between plants and pollinators is frequently exploited by antagonists such as herbivores and microorganisms. Such antagonists could play an important role in the evolution of pollination, with potential costs for pollinators. Indeed, chemical compounds that are found naturally in plants and that are known to defend against herbivores have been observed in the pollen of several plant species. Since pollen constitutes an essential part of the diet of several pollinators, including the most important pollinators of most ecosystemsâ€”bees, defense compounds in pollen could have important impacts on the ecology and evolution of pollination. My doctoral research seeks to understand the evolutionary and ecological causes of defense secondary compounds in pollen and their consequences for the ecology and evolution of pollination. I will first test if defense compounds from Lupinus argenteus pollen affect the interactions between plants and their pollinators, insect antagonists, and pollen-colonising microorganisms using field observations and experiments. I will then test if pollen defense compounds can limit the pollen types used by bees by comparing the capacity of various bee species to tolerate defense compounds from different types of plants. Finally, I will investigate the effect of pollen-colonising microorganisms on plant reproduction by manipulating the concentration of microbes in pollen. I will also verify if pollen defense compounds help plants mitigate the impact of those microorganisms by testing the effect of pollen defense compounds on the pollen microbiome composition, abundance and diversity.
ResearchPlanOrganisms: Perennial plants, bees, thrips, beetles, microorganisms
Subject: Pollination

ResearchPlanTitle: Impacts of drought on the reproductive output of solitary bees in a subalpine habitat
ResearchPlanAbstract: Alterations in global climate have resulted in significant changes in the prevalence and severity of extreme weather events such as drought. Periods of drought in ecosystems that are not historically dry can have substantial repercussions on regional ecologies as organisms sustain abnormal reductions in water availability. Since bees require flowers for survival and reproduction, drought-induced decreases in flower availability and reward production (nectar and pollen) may negatively impact bee survival and reproduction. However, bees also require warm and sunny conditions for foraging, suggesting that the elevated temperatures and lack of storm events characteristic of droughts may also be of potential benefit to bees. The net effect of increasing and worsening drought on bee populations is therefore unclear. The Southwestern United States are predicted to experience particularly severe climatic changes including reduced snowpack, earlier snow melt, heat waves, and reduced summer rainfall. These drought conditions have already become apparent in many areas including the West Elk Mountains of Colorado. In my proposed project, I plan to investigate the impacts of drought in this region on the populations of several solitary bee species. My project would entail collecting data on soil moisture, flower abundance and reward production, as well as bee foraging and nesting activity.
ResearchPlanOrganisms: Solitary bees (Osmia iridis, Osmia montana, Osmia subaustralis, Osmia coloradensis, Osmia montana, Hoplitis fulgida)
Subject: Climate Change

ResearchPlanTitle: Quantifying Stream CO2 Concentrations and Fluxes in the East River Watershed, CO
ResearchPlanAbstract: The release of carbon dioxide from streams to the atmosphere has recently been recognized as an important, though poorly quantified flux within the natural carbon cycle. Our current lack of understanding of the processes that control these fluxes represents a fundamental gap in our ability to monitor and predict how the natural carbon cycle will respond to ongoing changes in climate. This proposed research will use high resolution mapping and monitoring of in-stream CO2 concentrations and fluxes across the East River watershed to develop a process-based model that may be scalable to other systems. In particular, this research will be synergistic with ongoing research efforts led by Lawrence Berkeley National Laboratory to characterize watershed-scale biogeochemical processes.
Subject: Other

ResearchPlanTitle: Scientific talk in the field: Appropriation of specialized forms of talk within the activities of a scientific community at a biological field station
ResearchPlanAbstract: The current vision for K-12 science education (NRC, 2012) and undergraduate biology education recognizes participation in rigorous scientific conversations as a cornerstone for science learning (AAAS, 2011). Historically, classroom talk in biology education settings has been impoverished, focusing on teacher-led whole class talk that prompts students to display what they know by repeating "correct" answers expected by the teacher (Schwarz & Baker, 2017). The current vision of biology education aims to move away from this pattern of classroom talk and towards the specialized forms of talk that appropriate how biologists communicate about their ideas (e.g. scientific argumentation). However, such a shift requires research on the specialized forms of talk that scientists use in practice. This study aims to address this need by examining the specialized forms of talk that scientists use within their community of practice at a biological field station and how more peripheral members of the community appropriate these forms of talk through interaction within scientific activity.
Subject: Other

ResearchPlanTitle: Dissecting the cognitive and neuroanatomical roots of pollinator foraging behavior
ResearchPlanAbstract: Bees often vary in several important attributes of foraging behavior; including the number and identity of plant species they tend to visit, as well as how they visit them. The extent to which bees vary in these traits consistently and strongly differs between closely-related species. We are exploring the cognitive and neuroanatomical basis of variation in pollinator behavior and determine the degree to which individuals, populations, and species vary in these features.
Subject: Other

ResearchPlanTitle: Ecology and evolution of hostâ€“microbe interactions under co-infection
ResearchPlanAbstract: Interactions between species are a potent source of natural selection that can impact where species can live and how their traits evolve. But the complexity of the ecological backdrop against which species actually interact makes it difficult to predict how quickly, or in what direction, populations will evolve as a consequence of such interactions. My research explores how various features of this so-called ecological backdrop impact the distribution of organisms as well as the evolution of their traits by altering the strength, direction, and efficiency of natural selection arising from species interactions. Ultimately, I want to build stronger connections between extant patterns of biological diversity and the various ecological and evolutionary forces responsible for generating it. To do so, I study a plant species which often gets attacked by insect herbivores as well as various groups of pathogenic bacteria. I have spent several years working out how interactions between the plant and either the insect or the microbial colonizers impact the other colonizer. These so-called "indirect effects" have far-reaching ecological consequences for the insects and the microbesâ€”and especially for the plants. The next step in this research direction involves understanding how insectâ€“plant interactions impact the evolution of the microbes that colonize these plants. Which genes or pathways are important at fending off chemicals that become enriched in plant tissues following herbivory? How do insects alter which bacterial genotypes gain a competitive edge within plant tissues? How will insects increase the epidemic spread of certain bacteria, and will this impact the ability of plants to persist in the face of overlapping environmental stressors? Answers to these questions will help us understand the importance of indirect interactions, compared to direct interactions, between species in shaping the numbers, types, and abundances of organisms that we observe within natural settings. We may also discover general principles for how epidemic spread of plant diseases is either stifled or amplified by the presence of insect herbivores.
ResearchPlanOrganisms: Cardamine cordifolia; Scaptomyza nigrita; various Pseudomonas spp. bacteria
Subject: Other

ResearchPlanTitle: Modeling the seasonal abundance and population dynamics of solitary bees
ResearchPlanAbstract: To predict the number of individuals of a species that are active on a landscape, it is important to understand how species’ abundances change throughout a season – we call this the seasonal abundance curve. The shape of solitary bees’ abundance curves are unknown, which often limits the scope of our studies to the community level. This makes it challenging to determine how factors such as climate change are affecting bee emergence phenology. This gap in knowledge is due to limits in how frequently we can sample bee destructively without affecting the very populations that we want to study. To address this gap, I will gather fine-scale time-series data on the abundance of three native, solitary bee species that are found around the RMBL. By marking bees of these species that can be identified in the field with a non-toxic paint, I will be able to overcome the challenge of measuring their populations without affecting them. I will then use these data to develop a mechanistic model to describe how emergence and mortality rates interact to shape bees’ seasonal abundances. Further, I will measure how bees’ foraging decisions and habitat preferences vary across space in order to more accurately estimate bee abundance. This work will allow us to examine the population dynamics and phenological responses to climate change of bee species beyond the three that are the focus of this study.
ResearchPlanOrganisms: Halictus rubicundus, Panurginus cressoniellus, Dufourea harveyi, Potentilla pulcherrima
Subject: Phenology

ResearchPlanTitle: The role of environmental variation in population dynamics and life history: case studies in three butterfly systems
ResearchPlanAbstract: We are interested in the mechanisms by which environmental variation affects the numbers of individuals in a population, their survival and their reproductive success. Such variation may either be abiotic (eg, weather, climate) or biotic (eg, predators, non-native species, microbes). We are using three study systems focused on butterflies in this work. The first, involving the Mormon fritillary, deals with the effects of flower nectar availability on butterfly flower choice, egg composition, and reproductive success. The second, involving Gilletteâ€™s checkerspot, examines an isolated set of populations, testing hypotheses concerning factors controlling population numbers and dispersal proclivity. The third, involving the sharp-veined white butterfly, deals with the interaction of the butterfly and a non-native, invasive mustard, which the butterfly recognizes as a larval host plant, but which is lethal to the larvae. This interaction has persisted for over 100 years. We are interested in the mechanisms maintaining this maladaptive relationship.
ResearchPlanOrganisms: Speyeria mormonia, Erigeron speciosus, Heliomeris multiflora, Pyrrocoma crocea, Hymenoxys hoopesii;Euphydryas gillettii, Lonicera involucrata;Pieris macdunnoughii, Tlhaspi arvense, Cardamine cordifolia
Subject: Long-Term

ResearchPlanTitle: Disentangling direct and indirect effects of climate change on tri-trophic interactions
ResearchPlanAbstract: Global climate change has ecological consequences for herbivore-plant interactions that occur across multiple trophic levels. However, experiments investigating the effects of climate change on herbivore-plant interactions within a multi-trophic framework are rare. In this study, I propose to investigate the combined effects of multiple abiotic stresses on plant-herbivore interactions within the context of plant defences from a bottom-up and top-down perspective. By manipulating environmental conditions in the field, I will investigate the effects of abiotic stress on direct and indirect plant defenses and its consequences for plants, herbivores, and herbivore’s natural enemies. Additionally, I will use herbivore and predator exclusions to (1) disentangle the direct effects of abiotic stress on plants from the indirect effect mediated by herbivores, and (2) discriminate between the indirect effects on herbivores resulting from bottom up (host-plant to herbivore) and top-down forces (predator to herbivore). This study will provide further insight into links between abiotic and biotic drivers that shape herbivore-plant interactions while enhancing our understandings of the ecological impacts of global climate change on multi-trophic systems.
ResearchPlanOrganisms: Cardamine cordifolia (Rocky Mountain bittercrest), Scaptomyza nigrita (Diptera), and Chalcidoidea (Hymenoptera).
Subject: Climate Change

ResearchPlanTitle: Scaling Plant Reproductive Phenology using Drone Imagery
ResearchPlanAbstract: For the past four decades RMBL has housed monitoring programs that track the timing of flowering for Rocky Mountain wildflowers. This data has served as a critical indicator of the shifting climate, and has been important to improving our understanding of how mountain plants and their animal partners are adjusting to reduced snowpack and warmer growing season temperatures. Despite their importance, these long-term monitoring plots represent a tiny sample of a large landscape where climate and plant community composition vary. In this study, we are reconstructing landscape patterns of flowering using very high-resolution aerial imagery collected with unmanned aerial vehicles (drones). Utilizing cutting edge equipment and new advances in machine learning, this data will allow us to make predictions of flowering time and pollinator resource abundance at the landscape scales that matter to animal pollinators.
Subject: Phenology

ResearchPlanTitle: Mechanisms of alpine community assembly
ResearchPlanAbstract: Climate change threatens alpine plant communities at several levels, including species declines. Since facilitative interactions are an important community assembly mechanism in stressful environments, such as the alpine, changes in species abundance from climate change could perpetuate further changes to community structure. Shifts in the frequency of seed-adult interactions may be particularly important because they could feed back to community structure by influencing seed distribution patterns and dispersal into suitable microhabitats. For example, adult plants can alter seed dispersal outcomes by blocking and trapping seeds, and by influencing the abundance of seed dispersers. However, dispersal mediated seed-adult interactions are poorly understood, particularly in the alpine. In alpine plant communities near RMBL, I will provide an improved understanding of dispersal mechanisms and their influence on plant fitness and community structure. I will focus on 1) seed trapping and retention, and 2) ant dispersal by a species that nests primarily in vegetated areas. I will pair these data with demography and vital rate data to test whether high interaction probability (e.g., due to high trapping or ant dispersal) corresponds with improved vital rates when species co-occur. I will also measure and compare microhabitats and their influence on germination success. The improved understanding of seed-adult interactions from this project will provide insight on the mechanisms that structure alpine communities, as well as how climate change may impact these mechanisms.
Subject: Climate Change

ResearchPlanTitle: Understanding bee foraging, diet breadth, and the structure of plant-pollinator networks through the lens of nutritional ecology
ResearchPlanAbstract: My research combines nutritional ecology, foraging ecology, and ecological networks to determine how pollen and nectar nutrients contribute to bee diet breadth, foraging patterns, and network architecture. I will conduct macronutrient analyses of nectar and pollen collected from bee-visited plants; multiple years of bee-flower interaction observations; and quantitative analysis of network structure. To date, no studies have examined how nutrition drives the diet breadth of native bees and ecological network structure. By understanding the nutritional ecology of native bees and the implications for plant-pollinator interactions, my research will provide valuable information for supporting pollinator health and help to mitigate pollinator declines.
Subject: Pollination

ResearchPlanTitle: Investigating shifts in microbial metabolic phenology in the context of drought stress
ResearchPlanAbstract: Species are shifting in time and space in response to global change and these shifts can expose species to novel abiotic and biotic environments and alter their mutualistic interactions with other species. Soil microbial communities regulate many vital ecosystem processes (e.g., nitrogen fixation) which impact plant survival, phenology, and landscape-scale patterns of floral and faunal abundance and diversity. It is unknown how natural microbial communities will be impacted by aspects of global change such as drought, nor is it known how changes to soil microbial communities will impact plant symbionts. Some soil bacteria, such as nitrogen-fixing rhizobia, can undergo metabolic dormancy in extremely dry conditions. As drought conditions increase with global change, I aim to understand how microbial phenology, or the changes in the ratio of metabolically dormant to active soil microbes, is altered by global change. I propose to assess dormancy in rhizobial species relevant to plant growth within a growing season and over several years to predict how the drought conditions associated with global change will alter the functional diversity of the microbial community important to plant success. In combination with common garden studies aimed at understanding how complete or partial mismatches among plants and their rhizobial community affect plant germination success and phenology, this fieldwork will contribute to the understanding of how global change-driven shifts in the phenology of the active ratio of the soil microbial community directly and indirectly affect mutualistic interactions.
ResearchPlanOrganisms: Legumes Lathyrus lanszwertii var. leucanthus and Vicia americana. Additionally, the rhizobial species associated with these legumes will be sequenced
Subject: Phenology

ResearchPlanTitle: Demography and the germination niche: Species distributions and sources of life history variation in hybridizing Potentilla
ResearchPlanAbstract: Understanding determinants of species geographic distributions is a longstanding aim in ecology, evolution, and conservation biology – it may help us better predict species’ invasion and the likelihood and outcomes of species’ interactions, pinpoint causes of rarity, and forecast how species may respond to changing environments. Factors like competition and barriers to dispersal may result in species not being their most abundant in the habitats that would otherwise be most favorable to them. Further, environmental tolerances can vary among populations, making drivers of species distributions more challenging to uncover. By studying the structure and sources of variation that underlays species’ performance across environments, we aim to clarify how environmental tolerances influence species’ geographic distributions. In 2018, we initiated multi-year projects with these aims in mind. Working with cinquefoil species in the Rose family that are common in the Colorado alpine, we tagged plants in different environments to track survival and population growth over time. We measured plant characteristics like height and number of leaves, to link these traits to plant performance in different environments. As we re-survey tagged plants each year, we will be able to determine how traits influence survival and ultimately population growth in different environments. We also took an experimental approach to understanding how species fare in different environments, and how that varies among populations. We installed grids with seeds from multiple populations per species into two common garden locations. Such transplants help disentangle how environment and genetic differences each influence performance (here, successful germination). Before a plant can establish in an environment, it must germinate; studying the sensitivity of this life stage to environmental differences therefore provides useful information for understanding species’ geographic distributions. We propose to continue our demographic and experimental work in 2019 and 2020. We will measure reproductive effort, survival, growth, and addition of new individuals within our demographic plots. We also propose to tag additional individuals and supplement our environmental measures, within the populations we are currently tracking. We will survey our common garden transplant grids for germination.
ResearchPlanOrganisms: Potentilla pulcherrima, Potentilla hippiana, and their natural hybrid
Subject: Other

ResearchPlanTitle: Discovering geologic and ancient methane contributions to contemporary food webs
ResearchPlanAbstract: Despite the likely contribution of fossil and geologic methane to freshwater systems and the potential for methane to be transformed ecologically into less harmful forms, the freshwater biotic processes affecting this greenhouse gas source are poorly known. Here we propose to investigate the role of abiotic, thermogenic, and fossil methanogenic methane subsidies in supporting freshwater floodplain ecosystems by providing a carbon source to the carbon-limited shallow aquifer food web (deep hyporheic zone). Our primary objective is to quantify contributions of carbon from various methane sources to the aquifer food web. We will combine standard approaches and cutting edge techniques to determine methane sources and contributions to aquifer organisms, then develop new approaches for discovering methane source contributions to freshwater ecosystems. Specifically, we will 1) determine methane sources to a focal aquifer site using isotopic, geochemical, and radiocarbon dating techniques, 2) quantify contributions of each of these methane sources to microbial and invertebrate biomass using mixing model approaches with methane data from our focal site, and 3) constrain predictions of methane contributions to biomass and potential geologic and/or fossil subsidies at a broader range of sites using both traditional techniques and biochemical relationships that we build using our focal site.
Subject: Other

ResearchPlanTitle: Wild bumble bee energetics: underlying mechanisms and ecological drivers
ResearchPlanAbstract: The invaluable relationship between bumble bees and flowering plants is largely influenced by energetic exchanges. Bumble bees rely on flowering plants to collect pollen and nectar, which are their primary nutrient sources, and plants rely on bees to efficiently cross-pollinate. Pollination behaviors involve activities, such as flight, that have high energy demands. To perform these tasks, bees consume nectar which contains useful carbohydrates (sucrose, fructose, glucose) that are converted to energy through physiological processes. Therefore floral resources, particularly floral nectar, play an important role in the energetic processes underlying important pollination behaviors. However, there is little evidence showing exactly how floral resource availability at the landscape scale influences energetic processes at the molecular level in individual bees. This project aims to explore whether there is a landscape-level relationship between the amount of nectar-derived sugar available in flowers and the levels of sugars (glucose and trehalose) detected in the hemolymph of bumble bees foraging in those landscapes.
Subject: Pollination

ResearchPlanTitle: Exploring spatial variation in interaction diversity in plant-pollinator communities
ResearchPlanAbstract: The act of pollination is comprised of individual interactions between plants and animal pollinators. These interactions have been found to be highly variable, with the same pollinator often visiting different flowers in different environmental contexts. My work will explore patterns in this interaction variability. Specifically, I will explore how distance between sites and differences in elevation can contribute to changes in the interactions between pollinators and plants.
Subject: Pollination

ResearchPlanTitle: Exploring the Relationship Between Flight Morphology and Metabolic Rates in E. gillettii
ResearchPlanAbstract: Exploring the Relationship Between Flight Morphology and Metabolic Rates in E.â€¯gillettiiâ€¯â€¯ Abstractâ€¯ Dispersal can beâ€¯an adaptive mechanism byâ€¯individualsâ€¯to changes in theirâ€¯environment. With climateâ€¯changeâ€¯and anthropogenic landscapeâ€¯impacts, it isâ€¯even moreâ€¯crucial to understand movement and dispersal of individualsâ€¯andâ€¯their populations.â€¯Weâ€¯can studyâ€¯dispersalâ€¯by assessingâ€¯morphological flight characteristics andâ€¯movementâ€¯abilityâ€¯ofâ€¯individualsâ€¯and populations.â€¯Movement ability can beâ€¯related to flight metabolic rateâ€¯which is a measure ofâ€¯theâ€¯energyâ€¯expenditureâ€¯required during a flight.â€¯We need to further explore whether wing morphology is related to flight metabolic rate and dispersal history of individuals. Our study willâ€¯exploreâ€¯theâ€¯relationship among flight characteristics such as wing morphology and flight metabolic rates for threeâ€¯populations ofâ€¯E.â€¯gillettiiâ€¯in threeâ€¯different sites (401, Main and Avalanche) at Rockyâ€¯Mountainâ€¯Biologicalâ€¯Lab.â€¯â€¯
Subject: Other

ResearchPlanTitle: The importance of pollen theft to reproductive success in Polemonium foliosissimum.
ResearchPlanAbstract: Over 75% of the flowering plants in temperate regions are pollinated by insects, and the evolution of floral traits has most often been attributed to attracting pollinators. Plants reward their mutualist pollinators primarily with nectar and pollen. Yet, not all insects that utilize nectar and pollen for food are pollinators. Here, I wish to examine how pollen thieves – small flies in the family Muscidae – affect reproductive success in the sub-alpine plant, Polemonium foliosissimum (commonly called “sticky polemonium”). When watching these flies, one can see that they often completely strip the anthers of pollen and they don’t pollinate the plant. In addition to robbing the plant of pollen, they may render plants functionally female (i.e., removing much of their male gametes) and alter sex-ratios for a sticky polemonium which has an unusual mating system whereby some plants are typical hermaphrodites and others don’t produce pollen. Thus, these pollen thieves may have important consequences in enhancing pollen limitation for both females and hermaphrodites, altering sex ratios and, ultimately, affecting the ecology and evolution these plants as well as others.
ResearchPlanOrganisms: Polemonium foliosissimum, Muscid flies, Bombus spp.
Subject: Pollination

ResearchPlanTitle: Climate effects on forest structure, dynamics and hydrologic function
ResearchPlanAbstract: Across the West, climate change is expected to increase ecosystem water stress through persistent higher temperatures and greater frequency of drought events. Temperature and water availability are important drivers of forest structure and change in this region, with important effects on disturbances such as insect outbreaks and fire. We seek to use observations collected at RMBL on the physiology of common tree species and the demographics (recruitment, mortality, and growth) of forest plots to understand how the forest will respond to climate change and increasing disturbance. Our work will focus on questions and measurements that will improve projections of forest vulnerability to change. Our proposal complements ongoing work at RMBL focused on climate change in meadow ecosystems and on hydrology of mountain watersheds.
ResearchPlanOrganisms: Trees (Picea Engelmannii, Abies lasiocarpa, Pinus contorta, Pinus flexilis, Pseudotsuga menzeii, Populus tremuloides) and forest ecosystems
Subject: Climate Change

ResearchPlanTitle: SPATIAL VARIATION OF AN EXOTIC PLANT ON A NATIVE HERBIVORE
ResearchPlanAbstract: Local adaptation usually leads to specialization. When introduced species invade locally adapted species communities, they reshape interactions in the ecosystem. The outcomes of these invasions depend on various factors such as the frequency of interactions, the strength of the interactions and the genetic architecture of the interacting species. Identifying and predicting the outcomes of these interactions is crucial to understand how invasive species affect the life history and populations of native species. Pieris macdunnoughii (the Sharp-veined butterfly) has adapted to feed on native mustard plants in USA. Thlaspi arvense (Field Pennycress), an exotic mustard, was introduced to Gothic in 1800s and P. macdunnoughii recognizes it as a potential host plant. However, none of the butterfly progeny survive on the plant. Previous studies have also shown that the abundance of T. arvense has a fitness cost of 3% of the offspring, thus creating an â€œevolutionary trapâ€. I plan to build up on decades of previous ecological work carried out on this system at the Rocky Mountain Biological Laboratory to identify the molecular mechanisms in the persistence of this evolutionary trap.
ResearchPlanOrganisms: Pieris macdunnoughii, Cardamine cordifolia, Thlaspi arvense, Draba aurea, Descurainia incana and Boechera stricta.
Subject: Long-Term

ResearchPlanTitle: Developing Boechera stricta as a model system in plant-microbiome evolution
ResearchPlanAbstract: The microbes that live inside plants perform many important functions for their hosts, such as improving drought resistance, stimulating flowering, and protecting against disease. Despite the importance of this symbiotic relationship, we don't understand how it evolved. This proposal would collect data and samples that would lay the groundwork for research into the evolution of plant microbiomes.
Subject: Other

ResearchPlanTitle: QUANTITATIVE NETWORK STRUCTURE AND FUNCTION; SNOWMELT ACCELERATION AND POLLINATION NETWORK STRUCTURE AND FUNCTION
ResearchPlanAbstract: This renewal research application covers two distinct but related projects, both of them focused on pollination networks, their responses to perturbation, and the relationship between structure and function. The first project was approved by the RMBL research committee in my 2016 application, and the second project was approved as an extension in 2017. Both of these projects are collaborative efforts between PI Brosi and his graduate students Xingwen Loy and Connor Morozumi. The first project, “Quantitative Network Structure and Function” is currently funded by NSF and has two primary objectives: A) accurately measuring of quantitative network structure (i.e. intensity of interactions) with a focus on testing predictions about quantitative structure from theoretical work we are leading; and B) comparing network structure and function (seed production across multiple plant species) in drought (2018) vs. non-drought years (2016, 2017, and 2019 hopefully!). The second project, “Snowmelt Acceleration and Pollination Network Structure and Function”, is focused on temporally shuffling interaction partners in pollination networks via medium-scale (10 x 14 m) snowmelt acceleration experiments that are controlled and spatially replicated. The temporal re-shuffling occurs via changes in plant flowering phenology in manipulated patches, whereas we expect the pollinator community to remain relatively unchanged given that the scale of movement of individual pollinators is typically much larger than the spatial scale of our plots.
Subject: Pollination

ResearchPlanTitle: Bumble bee responses to floral resource variation
ResearchPlanAbstract: This research addresses how bumble bee populations might respond to variation in the wildflower community, a community that is changing directionally under climate change. Flowers are critical to bumble bee population persistenceâ€”colonies rely on a continuity of floral resources through the growing season to forage from to grow and reproduce. Around the Rocky Mountain Biological Laboratory, the wildflower season is extending while the number of low resource days are increasing. We poorly understand how bumble bee foraging choices and abundance will respond to this redistribution of floral resources, and to variation in floral resources more generally at appropriate spatial scales.
