I predict that bee abundance will decline with reduced floral resources and longer periods of resource shortages. However, bumble bee species may maintain their abundance under resource shortages if they are behaviourally plastic and expand the number of floral species that they visit. Additionally, I also plan to address how earlier life stages affect the production of reproductive bees late in the season, a fundamental but poorly understood relationship in natural areas. I am proposing to continue my observations of bumble bees and flowers throughout the entire flight period to address these questions that are fundamental to bumble bee population ecology and to predicting bee responses to environmental change.
ResearchPlanOrganisms: Bumble bees and the flowers they visit
Subject: Pollination

ResearchPlanTitle: Investigating the impact of climate change on forage plants
ResearchPlanAbstract: Mountains provide many important ecosystem services that benefit the economies and holistic well-being of the communities that dwell among these ecosystems . One clear link between the function of mountain ecosystems and human benefit derived from these ecological processes is the use of alpine meadows as grazing grounds for livestock as well as vital habitat for wildlife that draw hunters to Gunnison County for recreation. While numerous studies have shown that climate change will cause loss of many important forage species, we do not know how the nutritional quality of the plants that feed livestock and wildlife will be impacted by climate change. This research will use an existing climate change experiment that has been running for 6 years at RMBL to learn how warming and shifts in plant diversity will affect the quality of forage plants that support the livestock and hunting industries in Colorado.
Subject: Climate Change

ResearchPlanTitle: Priority Effects in Fungal Endophyte Communities
ResearchPlanAbstract: Priority effects, the process in which the order of the arrival of species shapes the composition of a local assemblage, can a be prominent mechanism for structuring communities but empirical tests have been restricted to simple, species-poor communities. Furthermore, predicting when priority effects are important in structuring communities requires examining the strength of priority effects across abiotic filters and biotic filters, such as interactions with macro-organisms. Fungal communities offer an ideal system to measure the strength of priority effects because the communities are hyperdiverse but also undergo strong biotic filtering by plant hosts. I propose to test, what is the relative importance of species richness, biotic filtering, and abiotic filtering on the strength of priority effects in fungal communities within plant roots? Using a combination of greenhouse and field experiments, I will expose seeds of big sagebrush and Thurberâ€™s fescue to soil conditioned by either plant species, and transplant the seedlings to new soil from either another plant individual of the same species or to a pot with soil from the other plant species. Furthermore, I will compare it in a series of increasingly diluted soils to determine if the species richness of fungi in the soil modifies the strength of priority effects. Finally, the field experiment will be implemented at two sites by RMBL to test if abiotic stress alters the strength of priority effects. I will determine if there are shifts in the fungal communities due to the treatments by extracting the DNA in the roots and soil within the pots, sequencing the fungi and conducting PERMANOVA models.
ResearchPlanOrganisms: Artemisia tridentata and Festuca thurberi (and their corresponding fungi)
Subject: Other

ResearchPlanTitle: Fish, insect, algae, and nutrient interactions along natural and human-altered environmental gradients
ResearchPlanAbstract: The nutritional quality of basal resources, such as aquatic algae and terrestrial plants, are an important determinant of food web structure and trophic dynamics in many ecosystems. Variation in resource quality along environmental gradients (i.e. nutrient availability, temperature, light availability) has the potential to affect consumer growth, mortality and fitness, thereby altering the productivity and taxonomic composition of consumer communities as well as their capacity to process energy and matter. Despite the complex nutritional requirements of animals, resource quality is frequently inferred from simple estimates of elemental mass-balance in trophic interactions, with an emphasis on carbon (C), nitrogen (N) and phosphorus (P). The corresponding framework of ecological stoichiometry theory has been frequently employed to predict the outcome of such interactions based on the magnitude of imbalances between the C:N:P of dietary supply and consumer demand. However, a growing body of evidence suggests that resource biochemical composition, in addition to elemental stoichiometry, may be an important indicator of resource quality in terrestrial and aquatic food webs. For example, polyunsaturated fatty acids have gained increasing attention as an indicator of nutritional quality and have been linked to increased growth rates and reproductive success across diverse animal taxa. In contrast to terrestrial plants, stream algae synthesize omega-3 fatty acids that are critical nutritional resources for fish, aquatic insects, as well as terrestrial consumers of aquatic insects, such as birds, spider, and rodents. In this study we will investigate how variation in basal resource fatty acid composition influences the trophic structure, and fatty acid content of stream food webs along a natural gradient in light availability. This research has direct application to a recreationally and economically important service provided by streams in Gunnison County and beyond. This study will also contribute to our understanding of how environmental changes, such as those related to climate change will affect native species and ecosystems.
Subject: Climate Change

ResearchPlanTitle: Examine the evolutionary ecology of multifaceted floral traits by measuring correlational selection for complex phenotypes
ResearchPlanAbstract: We have a skewed understanding of floral evolution because we lack floral scent micro and macro-evolution studies. Also, micro and macro-evolutionary questions of floral scents have lagged far behind functional ecology. This poses a real problem to our understanding of angiosperm local adaptation and diversification since we lack a clear picture of how important scents are for these processes, despite examples where scents are critical for particular plant-animal interactions. The Parachnowitsch lab has studied floral evolutionary ecology of Penstemon digitalis for over a decade, and their advances provide the foundations for this research project. The importance of scent for P. digitalis suggests studying floral scent in other Penstemon species, especially those with more typical pollination syndromes, will provide insight into its evolution. More recently, the lab has begun collecting floral scent profiles from the Penstemon genus (17 species in 2017, 14 species in 2018) with plans for further sampling in 2019 to help understand macro-evolutionary processes in the genus. These species’ scent profiles also aided in choosing a likely focal species, Penstemon strictus, the Rocky Mountain penstemon for this proposed experiment to examine the evolutionary ecology of multifaceted floral traits by measuring correlational selection for complex phenotypes. The project will be conducted as a part of my ongoing PhD program with the aim filling important gaps in understanding floral traits, their evolution, and interaction with pollinators..
ResearchPlanOrganisms: Penstemon strictus, the Rocky Mountain penstemon
Subject: Pollination

ResearchPlanTitle: Plant versus microbial control on soil carbon stocks and fluxes in a warming world
ResearchPlanAbstract: Understanding how terrestrial ecosystems will respond to future climates is key, particularly through long-term field experiments. At RMBL's warming meadows, scientists have the opportunity to address how plants and soils change as the atmosphere warms. Plant traits, or morphological characteristics, can tell us about plant function and potential effect within the ecosystem. Our group addresses how plant traits, and biodiversity of traits, change with changes in climate and associations to change in whole net ecosystem exchange of carbon and water.
Subject: Climate Change

ResearchPlanTitle: Life history tradeoffs of high elevation breeding sparrows
ResearchPlanAbstract: This study is a long-term investigation into the life histories (e.g., reproduction, behavioral ecology, age, sex) of mountain white-crowned sparrows (Zonotrichia leucophrys oriantha; MWCS) and Lincoln’s sparrows (Melospiza lincolnii; LISP). Lincoln’s sparrows are being included to supplement reproductive data given their highly similar nesting ecology to the MWCS. This study aims to elucidate the extent and the nature of life-history tradeoffs associated with endoparasite loads, elevation-based weather and climate patterns, habitat quality, and landscape context. Reproductive metrics of interest include nest success, clutch size, and number of young fledged. We are also interested in gaining insight of the breeding behaviors of MWCS, including nestling provisioning rates and incubation on-off bouts. This will be tested observationally using field sites at different elevations and of varying habitat structure. Methodologies include bird capture, measuring and banding as well as nest searching and monitoring and video camera recording during the nestling stage
Subject: Climate Change

ResearchPlanTitle: Forest Disturbance and Insect Herbivory
ResearchPlanAbstract: Forest disturbances are increasing in many biomes due to global environmental changes. However, many studies focus on the ecological effects of increasing temperatures and moisture while the effects of disturbances caused by human activities and climate change remain relatively poorly understood. So understanding and predicting forest ecosystem responses to disturbances is a key research priority. In this study the effects of drought conditions and severity in a temperate forest of Colorado, USA will be investigated. Disturbances in a forest ecosystem influence forest composition, structure and key functional processes which could have cascading impacts on the wider system. Measurements of insect herbivory provide insights into patterns of ecosystem change. Nutrients transferred into the soil via herbivory are comparable to the nutrients transferred via other important nutrient sources. In contrast to common theories, herbivory may increase nutrient fluxes of nitrogen and phosphorus even in unproductive ecosystems.
Subject: Climate Change

ResearchPlanTitle: Zinc transport mechanisms from alluvium into the upper Slate River
ResearchPlanAbstract: Hard rock mining in the upper Slate River watershed in north-central Gunnison Co, CO, has deposited a legacy of heavy metal contaminants that threaten ground- and surface water quality. Our analyses suggest that > 1,000 metric tons of zinc reside in shallow alluvial sediments along the Slate river between Nicholson Lake and Poverty Flat. These sediments can release heavy metals under oxidizing summer drought conditions, raising questions about impacts on ground- and surface water quality as advancing climate change causes warm summer soil temperatures to persist longer with greater moisture loss. These concerns are of practical significance, as the upper Slate River is being considered as a water supply for the town of Crested Butte and contributes about 7% of Gunnison River flow. In order for zinc to be released from alluvium to surface water, it must first be released to groundwater from sediments via biogeochemical processes. Subsequently, it must be transported out of alluvium into the river. However, groundwater-surface water exchange and its impact on zinc and heavy metals mobility have not been studied in mechanistic detail in the Slate River nor elsewhere in the Western U.S. This project will address the question, “Do upper Slate River alluvial sediments act as sources or sinks for heavy metal contaminants?” We will conduct a sampling project to investigate if biogeochemical and transport processes are coupled and causing zinc to be discharged from contaminated sediments to Slate river. The results from this project will be crucial to developing models to understand and simulate the movement of heavy metal contaminants in this important watershed, which serves as a model for numerous similar contaminated river systems in Colorado. This activity will further expand the size and connectivity of the RMBL and LBNL Watershed Function research networks by connecting USGS studies and planned LBNL studies in Redwell Basin and Oh-Be-Joyful Creek to floodplain and solute control dynamics in the Slate main stem, effectively creating a contiguous 10 km-long research domain extending from the town of Crested Butte up to the Red Well.
ResearchPlanOrganisms: N/A - this is a geochemistry proposal
Subject: Climate Change

ResearchPlanTitle: Paleo-ecological evaluation of fire and vegetation transformations in a western Colorado landscape
ResearchPlanAbstract: A major expected impact of ongoing and future climate change is ecological transformation, for example conversions from coniferous-dominated to deciduous-dominated forests. This project focuses on understanding the potential role of past ecological transformations in creating contemporary vegetation mosaics in western Colorado. The duration of aspen-dominated landscapes of this region have long been the subject of poorly informed debate within the land management and research communities, and which today remains unresolved. We will use paleoecological archives from lake-sediment records to reconstruct past vegetation change and fire history at a small network of sites in and around the Grand Mesa, Uncompahgre, and Gunnison (GMUG) National Forest. In comparison to existing paleoclimate records for the region and paleoclimate models, we will model the role of climate and disturbance in driving past ecological transformations, should they have occurred.
ResearchPlanOrganisms: Aspen, Gambel oak, Engelmann spruce, Douglas-fir, subalpine fir, ponderosa pine
Subject: Climate Change

ResearchPlanTitle: Behavioral responses of wildlife to recreational activity throughout a multi-use land area
ResearchPlanAbstract: Human recreational activities have the potential to impact wildlife. Through this research, we will investigate the behavioral responses of wildlife with respect to mountain biking. We will use camera traps to assess and compare wildlife occupancy on- and off-trails throughout a multi-use land area.
ResearchPlanOrganisms: Odocoileus hemionus, Alces alces, Cervus canadensis, Canis latrans, Vulpes vulpes
Subject: Other

ResearchPlanTitle: Can Immune Status or Parasites Influence a Marmot’s Frequency or Probability of Alarm Calling?
ResearchPlanAbstract: Animals emit alarm calls to alert others of the presence of a predator or to deter a predator. Whether or not an individual alarm calls is dependent on a number of external factors such as where an organisms is, how socially connected it is, and if others are near it. Additionally, internal factors such as stress can affect how an individual alarm calls. We asked if immune system activation or the presence of parasites are associated with the probability of a marmot to alarm call.
Subject: Long-Term

ResearchPlanTitle: WaRM Project; Below Ground Phenology; Carbon Mineralization
ResearchPlanAbstract: I will be looking at how 30 years of warming affects rates of carbon mineralization across soil depths at Almont in Gothic. There have been studies looking into carbon mineralization and soil depth; however, there are few studies that look at how carbon mineralization rates change with depth, let alone how warming affects that. This study will be based on a previous experiment that looks at the effects of warming, dominant species removal, and the combined effects of warming and dominant species removal meant to stimulate climate change. My study will reveal how climate change will alter below ground soil microbial processes.
Subject: Climate Change

ResearchPlanTitle: Does aphid colony size mediate ant competition for aphids?
ResearchPlanAbstract: Mutualisms are the species interaction in which both mutualist partner gain benefit from the relationship. Multiple-mutualist interactions can be benefit for species if they receive complementary benefits from all of their partners. Yet, it can also be a disadvantage if those partners provide less affective benefits in combination due to competition for mutualist partners. Ant-aphid mutualism is a food-for-protection interaction in which aphids produce honeydew to feed ants while ants provide protection from predators. Study on interaction of aphid, Aphis asclepiadis, with two species of ants, Formica rufa and Tapinoma sessile, shows that the ants presence associates with aphid colonies growth. Aphid colonies tended by F. rufa are observed to be 5x larger than colonies that tended by T. sessile. F. rufa also happens to be more aggressive than T. sessile. In this study, we will examine whether aphid colonies tended by F. rufa are larger because it is a better mutualist or because F. rufa competitively excludes T. sessile out of larger aphid colonies. We will do this by manipulating large and small aphid colonies on the plant, Ligusticum porteri , and observe which ants visit the colonies and how the colonies grow.
Subject: Other

ResearchPlanTitle: Resurvey of Bumblebee Distributions Across Elevational Gradients in Response to Climate Change
ResearchPlanAbstract: The impacts of climate change have altered organisms' geological and altitudinal distributions. One example is bumblebees in which their regular life cycles become asynchronous with the phenology of certain plants within certain elevations in subalpine communities. As a result, bumble bees previously not found in certain elevations may be spotted or overall community composition may be affected. With the previous resampling data from the years 1974, 2007, and 2014, bumblebee distribution and phenology data will be used to address the question: how does climate change affect bumblebee populations over time as well as their selected plants? In this project, I will capture bumblebees, place them in a photo booth which consists of two cylinders overlaid on top of each other with a small crevice for the bumblebee to sit in while I take a photo, transfer it over to a bee squeezer and mark its thorax with a dot of paint for resurvey purposes. The bumblebee will then be released. This method will allow for a successful survey of bumblebee populations as well as understanding whether bumblebees are the only pollinators affected by the phenology of the early snow melt plants. The overall aim of this project is to understand the long-term impact of climate change on pollination through spatial variance in bumblebee communities.
Subject: Climate Change

ResearchPlanTitle: Social Transmission in Yellow-Bellied Marmots
ResearchPlanAbstract: We are testing whether marmots have the capability to socially learn, despite their reduced sociality. We will use puzzle boxes and film individuals interacting in an attempt to acquire the bait inside. Social transmission in a lowly social species like marmots has significant implications on non-genetic cultural adaptability to new and changing surroundings.
Subject: Climate Change

ResearchPlanTitle: Effects of Pond Permanence on Avian Behaviors
ResearchPlanAbstract: As global temperatures rise as a result of global warming, aquatic ecosystems, such as alpine ponds, become more and more at risk of drying faster and at earlier times than normal. These changes in pond hydrology have the potential to not only drastically alter its aquatic ecosystems, but also the terrestrial and riparian ecosystems depending on the resource subsidies provided by the ponds. Vernal ponds are particularly vulnerable to these changes due to their size, therefore making the surrounding terrestrial ecosystems sensitive to the warming of the Earth as well. Through observing avian behaviors around both permanent and temporary ponds, our study strives to gain insight on how terrestrial predators react to the change of aquatic dynamics and hydrology. An increase in understanding of these causes and effects are important in building conservation efforts to the systems involved as global warming persists and grows in influence.
Subject: Climate Change

ResearchPlanTitle: How niche breadth changes with environmental perturbation: the impact of early snowmelt on subalpine pollinator specialization
ResearchPlanAbstract: With global climate change, we are seeing phenological changes across all systems. In the Colorado Rocky Mountains, earlier snowmelt and lower snowpack are expected to accelerate bloom time and cause a phenological mismatch between plants and their pollinators. To account for this mismatch, pollinators may change the plant species they interact with (likely increasing the number of interaction partners) and change their niche breadth to account for the difference in floral availability. I will study the impact of an environmental perturbation on plant-pollinator niche breadth, focusing on how niche breadth changes and how traits impact that change. I will perturb the system by inducing a phenological change (early snowmelt) that will accelerate bloom time by approximately two weeks, thus creating a phenological mismatch. I will sample plant-pollinator interactions and measure traits to look at whether trait-matching between plants and pollinators occur. I predict that bees will exhibit more generalist foraging in manipulated plots and that bee niche breadth will widen to include flowers available due to the phenological mismatch. I also predict that changes in niche breadth will correlate with species traits. The results of this study will help predict the outcomes of future climate change on plant-pollinator interactions, enabling us to better understand potential loss of species in this system.
Subject: Pollination

ResearchPlanTitle: Effects of Elevation and Pollinator-Mediated Selection on Flower Color Variation
ResearchPlanAbstract: Flower color has key fitness implications for plants, and is selected by through both biotic and abiotic factors. In one part of this experiment, I will look at how flower color changes within species at different parts of their altitudinal range. Previous work has revealed predictable shifts in overall community flower color composition at different elevations. The hypothesis is that as conditions change (for example, pollinators, UV exposure, temperature, etc) at different elevations, different pigments are selected for. However, there are several factors that could be behind these shifts in this area, such as community composition and historical effects. Thus, looking at this relationship within species will help to reveal whether natural selection is in fact responsible for the community level shifts. The other part of this experiment looks at how populations of different species are constrained within different pollinator visual spaces. Earlier research has shown that bee-pollinated species, although sometimes appearing quite varied in color to a human, are tightly constrained within bee vision. Our experiment will investigate if the same pattern holds in hummingbird-pollinated flowers—i.e. are these species constrained in bird vision, but not in bee vision? In addition to looking at bird-pollinated and bee-pollinated flowers, we will also look at species pollinated by both. Seeing how these species vary in color will shed light onto the question of whether having a greater number of weaker selective forces increases or limits variability.
Subject: Other

ResearchPlanTitle: The effect of water availability on pollinators and seed predators (Anthomyiidae) of Ipomopsis aggregata
ResearchPlanAbstract: Climate change is affecting the world in many ways from high temperatures, drought and high percentages of precipitation. Alpine plants are particularly vulnerable to climate change. Early snowmelt in these areas can cause a drought period before summer rains, leaving the plants stressed. This period of drought can lead to a decrease in the number and quality of flowers on the Ipomopsis plants, potentially leading to a reduction in pollinator visitation. In this study, we focus on Ipomopsis aggregata, and how its pollinators and seed predators are affected by water availability. We have six plots, of which half received an early snowmelt treatment. Each plot is split into four subplots, one will receive additional water, one has a rainout shelter that will cause drought-like conditions, and then two controls. I predict that the subplots with the rainout shelters will exhibit drought-like conditions and will have a lower amount of flowers and low amount of nectar, which will lead to fewer pollinators. In addition, I expect that these same plots will have fewer seed predators because the floral displays will be smaller and less attractive to the flies. The subplot with more water added will have a higher abundance of flowers, which will lead to more pollinator visitation but also more seed predators.
Subject: Climate Change

ResearchPlanTitle: Volatile organic compounds as signals for pollinators and seed predators, and their consistency across years.
ResearchPlanAbstract: Volatile organic compounds (VOCs) are emitted by every part of a plant and are believed to work as possible olfactory signals, drawing in pollinators and antagonists. This study was designed to address whether VOCs serve as a signal to pollinators, indicating the size of the nectar reward or aspects of floral morphology that influence access to the nectar. Seed predators could also use VOCs, and so this study also addresses whether they correlate with floral traits that can influence larval survival of seed predators. This part of the study will focus on three populations of Ipomopsis plants. Another part of the study will measure floral VOCs for six species in a community that was also studied in 2017 and 2018 to address the consistency of emission of VOCs across three years differing in environmental conditions including date of snowmelt.
ResearchPlanOrganisms: Ipomopsis Aggregata, Arenaria congesta, Achillea millefolium, Campanula rotundifolia, Eriogonum subalpinum, Galeum boreale, and Heterotheca villosa
Subject: Other

ResearchPlanTitle: Foraging preferences and their effect on growth for Trichoptera
ResearchPlanAbstract: It is well documented the sedge detritus lacks important nutrients that imperative for caddisfly development. These nutrients are polyunsaturated fatty acids (PUFAs) and phosphorus. The focus of our study is to understand if caddisfly larvae have a preference for detritus that is rich in either or both of these nutrients. Therefore, we propose three hypotheses: (1) Caddisfly larvae in a younger instar will prefer sedge that is phosphorus enriched, regardless of PUFA presence; (2) Caddisfly larvae in an older instar will prefer sedge that is colonized by biofilm (algae), regardless of phosphorus; (3) Positive growth in both young and old instars will correlate with instar’s preference to a specific treatment. We will feed sedge that’s incubated under four different conditions to the insects and monitor their preference and growth. Since our experiment is contained, we see little to no adverse effects.
Subject: Phenology

ResearchPlanTitle: Seasonal Progression of Algal Development and Quality in Streams that Vary in Timing of Springtime Peak Flow
ResearchPlanAbstract: Climate driven shifts in stream hydrology from early, rapid snowmelt may have implications for algae growing within high altitude montane streams. Peak flow scours the benthic layer clearing it of old algal growth and sediment, allowing for new algal development following peak flow. An earlier peak flow allows for a longer season for algae to accrue biomass, but the implications of a shift in peak flow for resource quality are unknown. Algae are crucial components of aquatic ecosystems because they are the basal food resource for animals, and algal nutrient uptake can dominate stream nutrient cycling. This study considers how variation in the timing of peak streamflow of different streams in the southern Rocky Mountains could impact the resource quality and development of algae. Algal samples from these streams will be analyzed for biomass, chlorophyll, community composition, and carbon to phosphorus ratios. Baetis bicaudatus, a grazing mayfly, will also be sampled as they can selectively feed on nutrient dense algae and therefore their growth, size at emergence, and body chemistry may better reflect variation among streams in algal resource quality than bulk algal samples. I hypothesize that with shorter and earlier peak flows, algae will (1) accrue more biomass, (2) have higher chlorophyll concentrations, and (3) have poorer elemental resource quality than algae in a stream with a later peak flow, more protracted snowmelt hydrograph. These hypotheses will be tested along six streams in the southwestern part of Colorado, USA. A change in algal resource quality at the foundation of stream foodwebs could not only have trophic consequences that affect macroinvertebrate populations and subsequently trout, but also could cause changes in nutrient cycling processes.
Subject: Climate Change

ResearchPlanTitle: Global Climate Change-Induced Mutualism Breakdown Among Legumes and their Soil Symbionts
ResearchPlanAbstract: Mutualistic interactions provide ecosystem services, enable survival, promote growth, increase fitness, and support nutrient cycling, and are key drivers of ecosystems success and function. While many studies have focused on the importance of mycorrhizal and rhizobial interactions in various systems, we show the importance of these interactions in a changing climate, depicted by an increasingly earlier snowmelt, and warmer, drier conditions. By using controlled plots which advance snowmelt by two weeks, we will understand how the root-mutualist structure of legumes changes (Lathyrus leucanthus, Vicia americana, Lupinus argenteus). These results will show how increasingly earlier snowmelt across the southern Rocky Mountains will affect the ability of these legumes to form mutualisms with soil microbial species. Changes in how many and which partners legumes associate with will alter the amount of nitrogen in the plant and local ecosystem and potentially change the quantity and quality of pollinator rewards.
ResearchPlanOrganisms: Lathyrus lanszwertii var. leucanthus, Vicia americana, Lupinus argenteus
Subject: Phenology

ResearchPlanInstitution: University of South Florida Saint Petersburg
ResearchPlanTitle: Surveying Historical Patterns of Vegetation Change and Phenology (1929-2019) in the Upper East River Valley Using RMBL’s Archival Herbarium Records
ResearchPlanAbstract: One of the ongoing challenges in studying the effects of global change on biodiversity is finding credible baseline data of prior conditions. The Rocky Mountain Biological Laboratory in Gothic, Colorado is located in a valley with an extended list of plant species and communities due to its various microclimates, sharp fluctuations of precipitation, and sudden changes in elevation. There have been many studies done in Gothic on changes in plant community composition, population distribution and changes in flower-timing, but the herbarium has been mainly used by researchers as a tool for properly identifying taxa. Herbarium data, as a novel tool, has the potential to assist biologists with evidence-based data when conducting strategic plans to trace vegetation distribution patterns and studies of long-term phenological changes in the East River Valley in Gothic, CO. With the data available in the RMBL’s herbarium online database potential study sites can be located, and target species lists can be generated from a long list of historical specimens (dating back to 1929) to conduct modern surveys, to make qualitative comparisons of species presence or absence, and to track any changes in plant communities. Here we present the use of archival herbarium data as a baseline for what could potentially be a long-term study of vegetation and phenological changes in alpine meadow and meadow wetland habitats.
Subject: Long-Term

ResearchPlanTitle: Consequences of Climate-Induced Range Shifts on Multiple Ecosystem Functions
ResearchPlanAbstract: My lab studies the effects of changing animal communities in the ponds of this valley. Specifically, we study caddisfly larvae, which are very prevalent in the ponds and play a notable role in the breakdown of dead plant material that falls into the water. Since we have observed different species of caddisflies moving upslope over the past 30 years, we want to know how new communities of caddisflies alter the ecosystem functioning of specific ponds, such as nutrient cycling. My project will involve mapping exactly where each species of caddisfly currently exists as well as how they have changed over the past few decades. This will help my lab by providing research directions, since I will be able to project exactly what kind of new communities will be forming in these ponds.
Subject: Climate Change

ResearchPlanTitle: Quantifying Nectar Resources in Bumble Bee Visited Plants
ResearchPlanAbstract: Native bumble bees play key roles in their ecosystems as pollinators, but very little is known about the floral resources on which they depend. Additionally, how those resources might be affected by conditions such as water availability, which are being altered under climate change, is poorly understood. To address this knowledge gap, I will quantify nectar resources for bumble bee visited plant species in subalpine meadows. Specifically, I will (1) examine variation in nectar resource production between species, (2) compare nectar resources across wet and dry meadow conditions, (3) examine variation in nectar resources between years. This research will clarify the relative contributions of plant species to the resource landscape available for bumble bees, and how this resource landscape may respond to variation in climatic conditions.
Subject: Pollination

ResearchPlanTitle: The Effects of Common Experimental Manipulations on Pollinator Activity and Pollination
ResearchPlanAbstract: Scientists often use experimental manipulations simply because there is precedent in other research and without considering the consequences and effectiveness of the manipulations in their own research. I will be studying two experimental manipulations that are commonly used at RMBL and in the world at large -- pollinator exclusion bags for studying pollination, and open-top chambers for studying climate warming -- and their effects on the pollination of Delphinium nuttallianum and Potentilla pulcherrima, two local wildflower species. By examining the effects that these manipulations have on pollinator community composition, pollination rate, and pollen deposition, I will be able to determine whether these manipulations are appropriate for RMBL's system, or if there are consequences for pollinators that have previously gone unnoticed. If the manipulations are appropriate, we would expect to see the pollinator-exclusion bags having no effect on the pollination of neighboring flowers and the open-top chambers having no effect on the pollination of flowers within the chamber.
Subject: Pollination

ResearchPlanTitle: How does flowering synchrony affect the reproductive success of three subalpine species?
ResearchPlanAbstract: Over the years, phenology data has suggested that flowering seasons are expanding. This could potentially impact how many plants are in bloom at the same time. If a plant blooms when many other plants are in bloom, they have many potential mates. Therefore, I predict that a plant will produce more fruits per flower if they bloom at the same time as many other plants of the same species. I will be examining this relationship in Delphinium nuttallianum (Nuttall’s larkspur), Lupinus argenteus (silvery lupine), and Erigeron speciosus (aspen fleabane). For each species, I will record the number of flowers open for each plant on a given day and I will examine how the bloom times overlap between individual plants. I will also record the number of fruits per flower for each plant. In addition, I will examine if the flowering seasons of these species have shifted using long-term phenology data.
ResearchPlanOrganisms: Delphinium nuttallianum, Lupinus argenteus, and Erigeron speciosus
Subject: Phenology

ResearchPlanTitle: Exploring mechanisms explaining coexistence patterns of Rhyacophila species (Trichoptera) in streams near the Rocky Mountain Biological Laboratory
ResearchPlanAbstract: Coexistence of closely related species can be explained by a number of biotic and abiotic factors. In Trichoptera (caddisflies), the patterns of coexistence of the species Rhyacophila in streams near the Rocky Mountain Biological Laboratory (RMBL) has been tracked for 43 years. This particular study is a continuation from previous student projects carried out in 2017, and 2018 to explore the mechanisms explaining patterns of coexistence of these caddisflies. In addition to coexistence patterns, data from previous studies include species preferences for streams of different altitude, size, water temperature, and the coverage of the nuisance diatom Didymosphenia geminata. The coverage of D. geminata varies among years (favored in low-flow years), and streams (favored in streams with lower levels of phosphorus). Previous studies considered those factors only at the scale of stream reaches, but microhabitat preferences within stream reaches by different species of Rhyacophila remain to be investigated. Another previously unexplored factor is resource partitioning of prey by these predatory caddisflies. Questions asked in this study will include: 1) Generally, do certain pairs of species coexist in stream reaches by partitioning microhabitats? 2) Specifically, do coexisting species of Rhyacophila prefer different current velocities, water depths, substrate particle sizes or coverage of Didymo? 3) Does partitioning of food (prey) resources explain coexistence of pairs of species of Rhyacophila? We will address those questions by continuing surveys in eight streams near RMBL, and adding measurements of microhabitat and diet preferences of coexisting Rhyacophila species.
Subject: Climate Change

ResearchPlanTitle: The impact of climate change on reproductive traits in Rocky Mountain plant communities: Differences in floral traits and phenology along an elevational gradient of transplanted communities
ResearchPlanAbstract: Alpine climates are adverse environments for plant communities, the most directly impactful aspects being scarcity of pollinators and abiotic factors like temperature and precipitation that influence resource allocation. As a result elevational gradients are dynamic environments that can be used to examine effects of climate on plant form, function, and diversity. The aim of this project is to assess the effects of temperature and precipitation on the floral traits and reproductive phenology of experimental transplanted communities along an elevational gradient. Traits measured will include flower length, petal length, diameter, and height of the highest flower. Data collection will occur along three sites off of Washington Gulch Road in Crested Butte, CO, each of which contains transplanted turfs from higher/lower on the mountain as well as both transplanted and untouched control plots. Analyses will be tested against a null hypothesis to see whether floral traits and phenology of the transplants differs significantly along an elevational gradient. Rejecting the null would indicate some degree of phenotypic plasticity in the floral traits and phenology of alpine plant communities along an elevational gradient, whereas the opposite would indicate genetic determinacy of these characteristics. As global patterns like climate change alter abiotic factors of environments worldwide, predicting the varying abilities of plant species and whole communities to adapt to new, adverse conditions will be key in understanding conservation and planning for the future. The transplant experiments are a novel manipulation that allows direct study of these key traits and provides applicable information for future actions.
Subject: Phenology

ResearchPlanTitle: The direct and indirect impacts of warming and species interaction on plant traits.
ResearchPlanAbstract: Alpine ecosystems support many ecosystems services that are at risk due to climate change. Climate change can impact ecosystems directly by warming and indirectly by causing a shift in plant species. Studies have shown that direct warming can increase the biomass of an ecosystem and yet different plant types respond in different ways. Functional traits of plants dictate the individuals plant’s response to environmental change. There is little research on how these plant functional traits can interactively affect the ecosystem’s function and which traits are driving ecosystem response. This study asks (1) How does warming directly alter plant functional traits? (2) How does removing the dominant species alter plant functional traits? (3) Will warming and species removal interact to alter plant traits at high and low elevations in similar ways? We will conduct this study at a high and low elevation site in the Colorado Rockies in four different treatment plots; ambient, warmed, dominant species removal, and warmed x species removal. We will measure the specific leaf area, plant height, stomatal density, and leaf C:N as metrics of plant functional traits. I hypothesize that: (1) warming will shift the individual and community-level traits to be more conservative and this effect will be stronger at the low elevation site. (2) Removing the dominant species will reduce overall biomass and lead to a larger breadth in traits as species fill in the space occupied by the dominant species and this effect will be larger at the low elevation site. (3) Warming will ameliorate the effects of species removal on plant traits.  My project will provide some of the first data on how experimental warming and species interactions influence plant traits in alpine ecosystems.
ResearchPlanOrganisms: Most common sub-alpine and alpine plant species in each plot.
Subject: Climate Change

ResearchPlanTitle: Exploration of pollinator communities across four subalpine plant species; Paul's Project: Linking changes in pollination to the population dynamics of flowering plants
ResearchPlanAbstract: Studies have shown that there have been pollinator declines occurring worldwide, and it is important to understand plant-pollinator interactions as thoroughly as possible, including which species are interacting with each other, to understand the possible consequences that may follow these declines. which prompts a number of problems considering their importance in plant reproduction. The primary objective of this study is to explore the variation in pollinator visitation rates and communities across four subalpine species that bloom sequentially throughout the summer growing season. This study will be conducted at the Rocky Mountain Biological Laboratory (RMBL) located at Gothic, Colorado. Timed pollinator observations of various patches of four subalpine plant species will be made as they flower between June and early August. This information will provide basic information on the type and frequency of visiting pollinators over time and across plants with their various shapes, blooming times, colors, and elevation. The secondary objective of this study is to create an understanding of how bags that are used to cover flowers to decrease pollination affect pollination studies. Observations will be made in the same way as ones previously mentioned of plots that have the same four plants with some flowers covered by bags. These plots are under the Iler+CaraDonna study looking the effect of pollinator declines on plant reproduction. This secondary objective is important for understanding how these widely used pollination bags may, or may not, have an effect on pollinators’ behavior to nearby, unbagged flowers.
ResearchPlanOrganisms: , Delphinium nuttallianum, Hydrophyllum fendleri, Erigeron speciousus and Potentilla pulcherrima, and visiting pollinators
Subject: Pollination

ResearchPlanTitle: Effects of weather and floral resource availability on foraging activity of cavity nesting bees (Osmia spp.)
ResearchPlanAbstract: NA
Subject: Climate Change

ResearchPlanTitle: Effects of Stridulation on Nicrophorus investigator’s Ability to Sequester Carrion
ResearchPlanAbstract: Burying beetles in the genus Nicrophorus require a small carcass, typically 16-50 grams, in order to reproduce. Once located, burial of the carcass may be achieved with either one beetle, or a beetle pair. After successful sequestration, the beetles then lay their eggs in their underground chamber and partake in biparental care. Burying beetle stridulation has been observed and documented when caring for their young, as well as among agonistic beetles competing for carrion. How stridulation may be used in order to facilitate cooperation during transportation of carrion, especially in situations where obstacles are present has yet to be thoroughly studied. This research aims to shed some light on how stridulation plays a role in Nicrophorus investigator’s ability to successfully sequester carrion.
Subject: Other

ResearchPlanTitle: Invasive Species Impacts on Soil Ecology and Biodiversity
ResearchPlanAbstract: Invasive species can alter ecosystems by outcompeting natives, altering biodiversity, and changing plant-soil feedbacks. Additionally, invasive species can be costly to stakeholders and landowners and incur to over $100 billion dollars annually in management costs. Linaria vulgaris, a non-native noxious weed from Europe and Asia, will be used as a study organism to better understand how invasive plant species impact biodiversity and soil ecology. We will also study if soil type is a limiting factor for Linaria vulgaris survival and growth by growing root cuttings and ramets in a controlled potted plant experiment.
Subject: Other

ResearchPlanTitle: Does road dust depress photosynthetic rates and water-use efficiency in Ipomopsis aggregata?
ResearchPlanAbstract: Assessing the physiological effects of road dust on wildflower species in subalpine meadows. Gothic is home to many wildflower species, many of which are subject to large amounts of dust that may affect their health and ability to reproduce or attract pollinators. With dust manipulation experiments, we will be able to see to what extent dust effects wildflowers such as Ipomopsis aggregata.
Subject: Other

ResearchPlanTitle: The effect of predation on ant-aphid mutualism
ResearchPlanAbstract: The effect of lygus bugs on the ant-aphid mutualism will be examined. Six sites of varying ant density from low to high will be used to observe the strength of the mutualism under the pressure of lygus bugs.
ResearchPlanOrganisms: Liguisticum porteri, ants, aphids, lygus bugs
Subject: Climate Change

ResearchPlanTitle: Observing pollinator trait variation in relation to niche breadth in seasons of high and low precipitation
ResearchPlanAbstract: Interactions between plants and pollinators are complex and a change to either can cause a significant impact on the other. Environmental extremes such as drought can alter plant-pollinator systems, such as changing the relative abundance of flower species, shifting species distribution, and decreasing floral resources (pollen and nectar). As a result of these changes due to drought, pollinator and particularly bees may be forced to change their foraging behavior. Bees’ foraging behavior is in part defined by their niche breadth, which is limited by multiple factors such as phenology of flowers, geography, and both the morphology of flowers and pollinators. Pollination events are only able to occur if the morphological traits of the pollinator and the flower “match” in such a way that the event is mutually beneficial; the pollinator needs to be able to receive nectar and come in contact with pollen. Trait matching is an essential component in defining pollinator niche breadths. In this project I will be examining the impact of a severe drought in 2018 on the foraging patterns and niche breadth of bee species in the area around Gothic, Colorado. I predict that because of the drought and resulting decrease or shift in floral resources, flower abundance, and flower species distribution, bee species will be forced to alter their foraging behavior and widen their niche breadth. As a result of this increase in generalist foraging behavior, bee traits and floral traits will match less well and less often during the drought year.
Subject: Pollination

ResearchPlanTitle: Lygus bug (Lygus spp.) omnivory’s impact on Ligusticum porteri plant quality and ant-aphid mutualism.
ResearchPlanAbstract: The herb Ligusticum porteri (also known as Oshá) is a food source for insects in Colorado’s East River Valley. Oshá is a food source for several kinds of insects, including aphids. Lygus bugs are omnivorous insects which eat Oshá as well as aphids. Past research has found that if lygus bug populations are high, aphid populations will be low and vice versa. The respective abundance of each insect seems to be linked to how early the snow melts in the late spring or early summer. In order to see how the abundance of lygus bugs impacts Oshá plants and aphids, I will enclose lygus bugs in mesh bags to allow them to feed on the plants for ~8 days and then remove the bags. After the removal of the bags, I will collect data on the quality of the plants, how many insects are on the plants in the days and weeks following bag removal, and how the addition of lygus bugs affected the system overall. As climate change worsens, snowmelt timing will change and so too will the relative abundances of these insects. Investigating how lygus bugs impact this system will hopefully indicate how these insects and plants will change in the future.
Subject: Other

ResearchPlanTitle: Effects of trails on small mammals communities
ResearchPlanAbstract: We will be studying the effects of recreational trails on small mammal communities. We will use a a new method using camera traps which will not require capturing any animals. The camera traps will allow us identify species and estimate the abundance of rodents at various distances from the trails. Our findings are important quantitative evidence that can allow managers to implement better policies of natural areas and ensure their persistence for both people and wildlife.
Subject: Climate Change

ResearchPlanTitle: Investigating the relationships between population, density, and herbivory of Thlaspi arvense in a common garden
ResearchPlanAbstract: Brassicaceae are an invasive family of mustard plants that use secondary defenses to deter herbivory with a class of chemicals called glucosinolates (Carlsson et. al, 2009; Keeler & Chew, 2008). Thlaspi arvense is a non-native member of the Brassicaceae family yet is still a target for herbivory. Studying the interaction of both T. arvense and herbivores assists in understanding the influences of what influences and a continued arms race of defense and attack (Rodman and Chew, 1980; Lee et. al, 2009). We will investigate how these two factors react to a change of density and an elevational gradient by measuring herbivory at similar phenological stages in a common garden in the Gothic townsite and in randomized field plots at sites of varying elevation. By manipulating density and seed source in the common garden, environmental factors are stabilized, and herbivory selection factors will become more prominent. We expect to find less herbivory per plant in denser populations and more herbivory in plants with seed sources from higher elevation will experience less herbivory.
Subject: Phenology

ResearchPlanTitle: Effects of Road Dust on the Pollination and Reproduction of Wildflowers
ResearchPlanAbstract: In order to explore this question, we will locate 30 pairs of flowering I. aggregate plants. We will simulate roadside dust levels with 5 puffs of sieved dust from a garden duster to one half of the plants, while the other half will receive a controlled 5 puffs of normal air from another garden duster. Treatment will be assigned at random within each pair. Flower buds on these plants will be capped with a piece of drinking straw for 21-29 hours to prevent pollinators from removing nectar. Then the nectar will be collected utilizing a 10-microliter micropipette, furthermore the concentration of the nectar will be measured using a refractometer.
Subject: Pollination

ResearchPlanTitle: Effects of avalanches on small mammal populations; a comparison using live traps and hair tube traps
ResearchPlanAbstract: Hair tubes will be placed out to collect hair from small mammals including deer mice, jumping mice and voles.
Subject: Climate Change

ResearchPlanTitle: Long-term bee phenology project
ResearchPlanAbstract: Insect pollinators are vital parts of natural and agricultural systems. There is a lack of long-term data on wild bee populations in North America, so standardized sampling protocols have been developed. The purpose of this study is to determine the effect of 10 years of long-term, repeated lethal sampling through the use of aerial netting and pan traps on wild bee abundance. Several single-sample sites will be sampled and compared to their phenologically similar repeated-sample sites. Then, statistical analyses will be utilized to compare bee abundance through the use of mixed models and repeated measures models.
Subject: Phenology

ResearchPlanTitle: Effects of blood parasites on incubation in Mountain White Crowned Sparrows
ResearchPlanAbstract: Blood parasite loads do not significantly influence body mass (Bennett 1988), yet metabolism efficiency is reduced in infected birds (Marzal 2004), suggesting that birds are foraging more often to counteract parasite presence. We hypothesize that infected MWCS females will be more food-stressed, causing an increase in off-bouts during incubation. Therefore, we suspect to observe MWCS with blood parasites to incubate less, and MWCS with no parasites to be incubating more. These extended off-bouts may cause longer incubation periods and decreased embryonic development, leading to changes in reproductive success in affected birds (Morton 2002). We plan to test this by trapping birds to create and analyze blood smears, and taking nest temperature data using data loggers to monitor off-bouts. This research can give insight on how birds are being effected by an increase in parasite vectors as temperatures warm in response to climate change. Our research includes disturbing nests which could potentially lead to nest failure, however we plan to combat this by spending little time at nests with several-day durations between visits. RMBL is a good study area for this research as it provides a temperature gradient between night and day that is significant enough to see strong incubation patterns with females. Additionally, Mountain White Crowned Sparrows exist here, and are a model species.
Subject: Climate Change

ResearchPlanTitle: Ecological role of Limnephilus picturatus in detritus dynamics
ResearchPlanAbstract: Caddisflies are the dominant detritivores in the ponds and wetlands near the Rocky Mountain Biological Laboratory, CO, and many other high elevation freshwaters. By processing detritus, caddisflies mobilize nutrients and energy that are not used by primary consumers which can play an important role in secondary production and nutrient cycling. Caddisflies are significant for these ecosystems because they are often oligotrophic and therefore limited by nutrients such as nitrogen and phosphorous. For example, previous studies have shown detritus processing by caddisflies has lead to stimulated algal growth. Historical data shows that certain species of caddisflies are shifting their range to higher elevations due to increasing temperatures. The long-term dataset at the Rocky Mountain Biological Laboratory has recorded detritus breakdown rates, chlorophyll-a concentration, caddisfly diet, and other measures for several species of caddisfly in this guild. However, data is missing for several species of caddisflies. My experiment will use these species of caddisflies in microcosms to measure their contribution to detritus breakdown, caddisfly biomass, and other factors while also adding to the historical dataset. I predict that detritus processing will be faster in microcosms with caddisflies than those with no caddisflies. Overall, my experiment will provide data on these species that we know little about and we will be able to use this data to create models that simulate real world conditions to see how caddisflies affect ecosystem functions.
ResearchPlanOrganisms: Caddisflies (Trichoptera), specifically Limnephilus externus, L. picturatus, and Asynarchus nigriculus.
Subject: Climate Change

ResearchPlanTitle: Identifying competitive exclusion of meadow species in sagebrush and bunchgrass dominated environments
ResearchPlanAbstract: Sagebrush and the bunchgrass Festuca thurberi often dominate montane and subalpine meadow environments in western Colorado. Systems dominated by these species create a unique competitive environment which affects which herbaceous meadow species can persist. Both taxa are expected to expand their range within montane and subalpine environments due to climate change, thus it is important to understand their impacts on meadow plant communities. In this study, presence and abundance of up to 25 different herbaceous meadow species will be recorded by sampling widely throughout the East River valley. A species distribution modelling approach will be used, relying on multiple years of data, in order to compare predicted presence and abundance of species against observations within systems dominated by sagebrush or bunchgrass. This study will lead to a greater understanding of the landscape of competitive interactions shaping the floral communities in the East River valley.
Subject: Climate Change

ResearchPlanTitle: Trap behavior of Zonotrichia leucophrys oriantha along an elevational gradient in the West-Elk Mountains
ResearchPlanAbstract: The Mountain White-Crowned Sparrow is a native, migratory species that resides in Gunnison County, CO, USA. Mountain White-Crowned Sparrows can serve as a model species because it lives and breeds across an elevational range, allowing for life-history differences in the population to be observed. Our hypothesis is based off of the Ideal Despotic Distribution theory, which states that individuals with a higher competitive ability are better able to obtain a higher quality of habitat and have a higher fitness. As a result, individuals with a lower competitive ability are pushed into less-ideal habitats and have lower fitness. As elevation increases, bird habitats become more fragmented and territories become smaller. Hence there is a negative correlation between elevation and resource availability. As it requires more energy for an individual to forage, provide for their young, and defend areas of territory, we hypothesize that lower-elevation birds will exhibit higher trap-activity levels than high-elevation birds.
Subject: Climate Change

ResearchPlanTitle: Anthocyanins in senescing leaves of Rocky Mountain Plants
ResearchPlanAbstract: Autumn color is a phenomenon of widespread interest, particularly the changes to red that involve the production of anthocyanin pigments just before the leaves die. My research at RMBL will add to existing data from eastern forests. The 150 or so species added to a previous 150 species will be subjected to statistical analysis, looking for influences on red coloration, including phylogeny, habitat and climate, and life history. These results will add to our understanding of autumn colors in Colorado, and in general.
Subject: Phenology

ResearchPlanTitle: Lupine scent project
ResearchPlanAbstract: Like color and shape, floral scent helps plants communicate with animals. But attraction via scent is not limited to pollinators, scent can also attract herbivores and, potentially, the natural enemies of these herbivores. Likewise, even while attracting some species, scent can repel others. Thus, floral scent plays many important roles in the ecology and reproductive biology of the plants which produce it. There is enormous variation in floral scent both between and within plant species, and this holds implications for variation in the interactions between individual plants and their environments. However, variation in scent within and among plant species remains poorly understood. Some populations of silvery lupine (Lupinus argenteus) have conspicuously strong scent, while others seem completely scentless. This variation appears to depend on elevation, with populations high in the alpine zone emitting strong scent, and lower montane and sub-alpine populations emitting little if any scent, and populations at intermediate elevations exhibiting a mixture of these traits. In 2017 and 2018 we analyzed lupine scent from one sub-alpine, one alpine, and one intermediate population near RMBL. We found that these populations showed strong differences in scent characteristics, and that, in the intermediate population, some individuals produce more alpine- or subalpine-like scent characteristics. We hope to conduct further studies to try to understand which factors are important for generation this variation, what the significance of this variation is for the plants and the animals that they interact with, and whether and how climate change may affect these plant traits and their impact on their communities.
Subject: Pollination

ResearchPlanTitle: Long-term studies of plant evolution and demography in an era of global change
ResearchPlanAbstract: I propose to continue long-term studies of how plants adapt to new environments with climate change. Species can persist through environmental change by migrating to new locations or by changes in traits that are adaptive under the new conditions. The latter process of “evolutionary rescue” is less well understood, primarily because of the difficulty of amassing the required data. I will capitalize on prior knowledge gained from 35 years at RMBL studying Ipomopsis plants (scarlet gilia and slendertube skyrocket) that make it uniquely possible to measure the parameters needed for prediction of evolutionary rescue in natural plant populations. The observed trend towards earlier snowmelt and associated droughts impacts these plant populations, but several heritable traits experience natural selection. I will continue to measure natural selection on vegetative and flower traits each year to determine the sensitivity of natural selection to snowmelt date and summer precipitation. These observational data will be supplemented by experimental manipulations of water. The traits range from physiological traits, such as water-use efficiency, that influence survival, to chemical compounds that give flowers a scent that influences pollinators and herbivores. The field data on selection will be combined with estimates of heritability to predict the pace of evolution and determine if it is rapid enough to allow populations to rebound despite the negative impacts of early snowmelt on survival and reproduction. The data will test several key points of general models for evolutionary rescue that apply to plants and animals from all kinds of habitats around the world.
ResearchPlanOrganisms: Ipomopsis aggregata and occasionally other plants
Subject: Long-Term

ResearchPlanTitle: The Role of Arbuscular Mycorrhizal Fungi in Linaria vulgaris Invasion
ResearchPlanAbstract: Commonly referred to as Yellow Toadflax, Linaria vulgaris (Plantaginaceae) is an invasive forb throughout North America. It is difficult to manage because it reproduces vegetatively, so that even small amounts of root tissue can germinate. Yellow Toadflax dominates plant communities in the Western U.S., whereas it is less pervasive in the Midwest. Invasive plants are often able to associate with mycorrhizal fungi outside of their native range in order to further invade. In other cases, invasive plants use harmful chemicals to reduce native plant association with AMF, giving them a competitive advantage. I hypothesize that Yellow Toadflax is successful in Colorado because it is able to associate with existing arbuscular mycorrhizal fungi (AMF) that allow it to better absorb nitrogen and phosphorous, whereas in Illinois prairies, AMF association does not provide the same advantages over native plants. I also hypothesize that Yellow Toadflax uses allelochemicals to disrupt AMF association with native plants. This study will take place in Gothic, Colorado in collaboration with Dr. Jennie Reithel and Dr. Becky Irwin and in Cook County, Illinois in the Forest Preserves of Cook County. Dr. Reithel and Dr. Irwin have performed a multi-year carbon and nitrogen manipulation study of meadows invaded with Yellow Toadflax. I will perform nutrient analyses of soil samples, Next Gen Sequencing of soil samples to determine mycorrhizal community composition, and biomass sampling of L. vulgaris tissue. I will also collect soil samples from invaded and uninvaded sites in both Colorado and Illinois for two greenhouse experiments. Greenhouse treatments will include nitrogen and phosphorous addition, active charcoal addition, and control treatments. This study will increase understanding of how invasive species manipulate soil biotic and abiotic communities in order to further invade and may provide management techniques for reducing Yellow Toadflax at RMBL.
Subject: Other

ResearchPlanTitle: The physiological drivers of plant community and ecosystem processes along elevational gradients
ResearchPlanAbstract: Elevational gradients provide a mosaic of microclimates/environments to study the impact of abiotic factors on plants and ecosystems. However, these data can be tricky to interpret due to the fact that many factors change together across the gradient. New advances in plant ecophysiological theory have led to the development of models that can be used to disentangle the effects of multiple drivers shaping plant responses to environmental gradients. Our project will use these models to explore the abiotic drivers of plant carbon and nutrient allocation to physiological processes along an elevational gradient. We will then explore the impacts of these processes on community dynamics (e.g., what species are found where and how well do they compete with others) and ecosystem processes (e.g., carbon and nutrient cycling). This will be done using a combination of field work and modeling. Our results will lead to greater mechanistic understanding of the underlying drivers of community and ecosystems processes along elevational gradients. This will ultimately lead to better predictions of how these processes might change under future conditions in montane ecosystems.
Subject: Climate Change

ResearchPlanTitle: Fungal Priority Effects
ResearchPlanAbstract: Priority effects, in which the order of arrival of species shapes the composition of a local species assemblage, can be a prominent mechanism for structuring communities. However, empirical tests have thus far been restricted to simple, species-poor communities. Understanding how priority effects scale with species richness is important for understanding their relevance in the diverse, complex communities that commonly occur in nature. Symbioses provide a tractable system for exploring the dependence of priority effects on species richness. In particular fungal endophytes are ideal since roots of an individual plant can harbor hundreds of species of fungi. In this study, we address the question: What is the relative importance of species richness in modifying the strength of priority effects for fungal community assembly?
Subject: Other

ResearchPlanTitle: Effect of advancing stream peak flow hydrology on stream biogeochemistry and primary productivity
ResearchPlanAbstract: Climate change is causing streams to reach their peak flows earlier due to advancing snowmelt timing and declining snowpack volume. My ongoing research aims to understand how this advancing flow phenology impacts stream nutrient cycling, primary producers, and grazing invertebrates. By studying seasonal patterns of nutrient uptake and algal accrual in streams that vary in timing of peak flow, I can use a space-for-time substitution to investigate how climate-driven advances in peak flow will alter this foundational ecosystem process and stream food webs.
Subject: Climate Change

ResearchPlanTitle: Novel Methods for Measuring River Discharge across Scale: Implications for Water and Environmental Management
ResearchPlanAbstract: River discharge integrates climate and watershed structure into a single metric with accurate discharge measurement vital to quantifying hydrologic response to perturbation. Low-order (small) tributary streamflows are important contributors of water (Jacobs 2011) and solutes (Alexander et al. 2007) to larger river systems; while river water and groundwater exchange along riparian corridors is a critical driver of carbon uptake and productivity in tributary systems to support biological integrity for the entire river network. The Colorado River Basin is emblematic of a system that relies on low-order stream networks to meet supply and sustain biodiversity. However, in-situ stream gauge networks in these systems are sparse or non-existent. The lack of tributary discharge data hinders our ability to quantify watershed sub-components that may have out-sized importance on water delivery or environmental health, while lack of data amplifies uncertainty in predicting hydrologic futures as a function of climate and land use change. We propose to validate efficient, non-contact methods of stream discharge measurement in the East River and explore scale-dependence of data assimilation on simulated results with an integrated hydrologic model.
Subject: Climate Change

ResearchPlanTitle: Consequences of the Helianthella quinquenervis inflorescence loss for plant growth, reproduction and ant-plant mutualisms.
ResearchPlanAbstract: Aspen sunflowers have been shown to use ants to protect themselves against seed-eating insects, where the plant feed the ants sugary nectar in return the ants deter the insects. In this study we are investigating how important the sugar nectar is for the ants. The answer to this question is especially important because climate change is resulting in an increased frequency of early season frosts that kill flower buds and thus reduce the amount of sugary nectar available to ants.
Subject: Climate Change

ResearchPlanTitle: Spatial variation in plant-pollinator interaction rewiring
ResearchPlanAbstract: Species interactions are fundamental components of community ecology. They describe how species function in their communities, and as such are critical to understanding how disturbances impact whole ecosystems. Therefore, it is important to understand how interactions change in response to ecological variation. My project will explore changes in plant-pollinator interactions across a spatial gradient, which varies in environmental context (i.e. temperature, soil moisture), biological compatibility (i.e. resource overlap, trait similarity), and community composition (i.e. species diversity, relative abundance). I will determine the relative importance of these drivers in influencing interaction patterns and explore the degree of variation that plant-pollinator interactions can withstand in each of these categories. This work will illustrate the multi-faceted considerations that must be included in pollinator conservation decisions in order to not only maintain insect population numbers but also conserve their functional role in providing pollination services.
Subject: Pollination

ResearchPlanTitle: Determinants of upper-elevation range limits in cavity-nesting bees
ResearchPlanAbstract: In recent decades, rapid warming has altered the environmental conditions experienced by many organisms. One of the most commonly documented biological responses to warming is range shifts, in which populations shift their distributions primarily towards higher latitudes and altitudes to track areas of climatically suitable habitat. Range shifts in bees may be of particular interest. Many aspects of bee life-histories, including their development, survival, and reproduction, are directly linked to temperature; yet bees are also indirectly affected by the availability of other factors such as floral resource abundance and nest-site availability, which may themselves be affected by temperature. I am proposing two field studies that investigate the potential for upslope range shifts in cavity-nesting bees by exploring the variables that determine their upper range limits. In the first study, I ask whether the potential for range shifts in cavity-nesting bees is limited by the lack of nesting cavities at high elevations where trees and dead wood (nesting substrates) may be scarce. In the second study, I ask whether the potential for range shifts in cavity-nesting bees is limited by the short duration of periods of favorable temperatures for offspring development at high-elevations. My proposed fieldwork will combine both observational and experimental techniques to address these questions.
Subject: Climate Change

ResearchPlanTitle: Phenology and Local Phylogeography of the Terrestrial Gartersnake (Thamnophis elegans)
ResearchPlanAbstract: This is an exploratory study to establish research on the phenology and local phylogeography of the Terrestrial Gartersnake (Thamnophis elegans). This is a relatively common, generalist species, therefore it may be able to provide some insight into how climate change has or may impact smaller snake species. I seek to collect data on range, sex, elevation, and genetic relatedness and establish a long-term study following this species as the climate changes.
Subject: Phenology

ResearchPlanTitle: Mapping Plant Phenology and Microclimates in the Upper Gunnison Watershed
ResearchPlanAbstract: Animals such as bees and other pollinators navigate complex landscapes as they forage for resources. Some parts of the landscape present richer resources than others, and those patches change over the course of the growing season and between years. Surprisingly, little is known about how the abundance and patchiness of these resources change over time, and how vulnerable they might be to habitat loss and climate change. This study uses imagery from drones, airplanes, and satellites to reconstruct the spatial pattern of nectar and pollen resources for pollinators, and uses detailed measurements of microclimate to understand how those resources change across the season and over longer spans of time.
Subject: Phenology

ResearchPlanTitle: BUMBLE BEE QUEEN FORAGING PLASTICITY AND REPRODUCTION IN RESPONSE TO RESOURCE AVAILABILITY
ResearchPlanAbstract: Bumble bee queens initiate new nests independently each spring, at which time these foundress queens carry out all tasks related to larval rearing and nest maintenance. This foundational stage of the bumble bee life cycle is thought to be particularly sensitive to environmental stressors such as diminishing or degraded floral resources, urbanization, pesticide use, and higher temperatures, which may help explain national and global declines in bumble bee populations. Yet, the colony founding stage and the factors that limit nesting success remain severely understudied. To examine the factors that limit reproduction in pre-worker foundress queens, I will combine RFID technology and colony monitoring to quantify foundress queen foraging behavior and reproductive output, respectively, and how they are impacted by artificially manipulated resource availability. An improved understanding of plasticity during this life stage may help predict bumble bee responses to a changing world.
Subject: Other

ResearchPlanTitle: Addressing the adaptive potential of within-generation and transgenerational plasticity due to herbivory in the perennial forb, Boechera stricta
ResearchPlanAbstract: Many plants can be "Phenotypic plastic" to adjust physical characters, or traits, within a generation to better perform in different environments (within-generation plasticity) or across generations (trans-generational plasticity). Insect herbivory has shaped entire communities, with the evolution of defense traits in plants and feeding strategies in insects. To this extent, rapidly occurring climate change is expected to result in increased insect herbivory and expansion into higher elevations that were previously insect limited as they become warmer. This shift will potentially result in plant communities becoming overrun by insects. Our work addresses two questions to understand if plant populations can rely on plasticity as a response to increased insect herbivory as a result of climate change: (1) Are insect herbivory defense traits in plants phenotypically plastic? (2) Does being plastic in defense traits result in a better chance of survival and creating more seeds? To answer these questions, we measured insect herbivory defense traits in populations from the species Boechera stricta from an elevational gradient for two generations. As a comparison, we also incorporate controlled applications of Bt insecticide. We propose that plants exposed to insect herbivory will have greater trait values for defense related traits and that populations from lower elevations, historically exposed to high amounts of herbivory, will have higher trait values for defense related traits than populations from higher elevations, where herbivory is less common. We also propose that exposure to herbivores in the first generation result in better protected plants in the second generation.
Subject: Climate Change

ResearchPlanTitle: Exploring the metabolic mechanisms underlying wild bumble bee foraging behaviors
ResearchPlanAbstract: Foraging specialization is defined as the preferential collection of one resource over another. Many organisms employ foraging specialization tactics to efficiently collect food resources. In the case of bumble bees, it has been well documented that some bees will specialize in collecting pollen whereas some will specialize in collecting nectar during a foraging trip. Additionally, bumble bees can consistently employ different tactics to collect the resource they are specializing in, such as nectar robbing behavior. Many studies have contributed to our understanding of the external, and to some degree, internal factors that can influence the aforementioned foraging states (i.e. pollen foraging, legitimate nectar foraging, nectar robbing). However, it is unknown whether any physiological mechanisms play a role in driving these behaviors.
