This study aims to examine whether there are any physiological mechanisms underlying bumble bee foraging states by using metabolomic approaches. Metabolomics is the study and assessment of metabolites and their interactions within endogenous biochemical processes, and provides a comprehensive assessment of an organism’s physiological state. The overall goal of this proposed research is to determine the physiological factors involved in bumble bee foraging behavior performance and the metabolic mechanisms involved in priming bees for pollen foraging, legitimate nectar foraging, and nectar robbing. Broadly, this project has important implications for understanding how individuals in a colony are organized into performing specific tasks and how the metabolome may influence complex behaviors.
Subject: Pollination

ResearchPlanTitle: Changes to predator and invertebrate populations alter connections of terrestrial and freshwater ecosystems
ResearchPlanAbstract: Terrestrial and aquatic ecosystems are connected by materials and organisms that move between perceived ecosystem boundaries. Terrestrial leaves and insects fall into freshwater ecosystems becoming food for various pond organisms. Freshwater insects emerge into terrestrial ecosystems becoming food for predators such as spiders and birds. Species within the freshwater ecosystems are experiencing shifts in their populations. There are naturally occurring shifts due to an organisms life history, such as salamander and caddisfly population densities fluctuating through time. There are also human induced shifts due to changing temperatures, such as certain caddisfly species moving up-slope. Regardless of the mechanism leading to the addition, loss, or change in numbers of a species, it could result in changes to the connections to terrestrial ecosystems (e.g. caddis emerging to be food for spiders and birds). To better understand how the movement of resources between land and water is driven by population changes, we will measure feeding rates of predators on caddisflies and insect emergence from ponds. This data will inform future work studying the intimate connections between ecosystems during a time of change.
Subject: Long-Term

ResearchPlanTitle: Microbial facilitation of exploitation in an alpine pollination mutualism: Are pollinator foraging decisions cued by microbial chemical signatures?
ResearchPlanAbstract: This summer, I will explore the ecology of cross-kingdom interactions between plants, pollinators, and the diverse microbiota that inhabit flowers. Recently, these nectar-inhabiting microbiota (NIM) have been identified as potentially significant mediators of plant-pollinator interactions, though microbial cues involved in pollinator foraging and ultimate impacts on plant fitness remain to be investigated. My research encompasses three major objectives. First, I will assess how different guilds of floral visitors influence communities of NIMs. By manipulating access to flowers to exclude legitimate visitors, primary nectar robbers, and/or secondary robbers, I will obtain and analyze nectar samples that include only the NIMs vectored by each guild type. From these samples, I will culture and isolate the most commonly associated NIMs for use in treatments in the following experiments. Second, I will experimentally test the effects of these microbiota on host phenotype. Third, I will investigate how floral visitors, both legitimate and illegitimate, respond to the presence of NIMs and potential phenotypic changes, as well as reproductive consequences for floral hosts.
ResearchPlanOrganisms: Corydalis caseana supsp. brandegii, Linaria vulgaris, Mertensia ciliata, Ipomopsis aggregata, Bombus appositus, Bombus occidentalis, Bombus spp., Selasphorus platycercus
Subject: Pollination

ResearchPlanTitle: Context Dependent Salamander Life History Responses to Climate Change
ResearchPlanAbstract: The proposed research will test the hypothesis that climatic variation is driving ecological changes that affect wildlife in high-elevation ecosystems. The study combines insights from 30 years of existing data with new field observations and experiments to test how extreme weather and environmental variables such as warming temperatures and reduced snowpack affect the phenology, life history, and thermal ecology of a keystone predator in a rapidly changing high-mountain environment. The research will explore the effects of past climatic variation on phenology (e.g., timing of reproduction and hibernation) and life history (e.g., body condition, survival, fecundity, longevity, etc.) using long-term demographic data. Statistical models will be used to evaluate relationships and links between population dynamics in salamanders that have polyphenic adult morphs (aquatic and terrestrial) that live in the same location but are subject to climate variation under these different environmental contexts. This research will compare temperature and water stress impacts of ongoing climate trends, which are crucial physiological considerations for amphibians that are sensitive to environmental temperatures and desiccation. These parameters will be studied under different environmental contexts (using biophysical models, and data logger-implanted salamanders as mobile temperature sensors) and under conditions of accelerated snowmelt (by combining salamander biophysical models and experimental manipulation of snowmelt date). Third, the research will investigate the thermal physiology of wild salamanders to assess sources of resilience to the changing thermal environment they are subjected to under climate change. Fourth, the environmental correlates of calling (as an indicator of breeding activity) and the timing of onset of spring breeding activity in a frog species will be investigated to provide baseline data on reproductive phenology shifts in response to climate change in a wide-ranging vertebrate.
ResearchPlanOrganisms: •	Ambystoma mavortium nebulosum (Arizona Tiger Salamander); Pseudacris maculata (Boreal Chorus Frog)
Subject: Climate Change

ResearchPlanInstitution: Faculty of Environmental Eart Science, Hokkaido University
ResearchPlanTitle: Comparisons of seasonal dynamics of flowering phenology, pollinator availability and pollination success at landscape scale along the elevational gradient
ResearchPlanAbstract: We aim to clarify the adaptive significance of flowering patterns of subalpine/alpine plant communities specific to the type of pollination, i.e., bee pollination, fly pollination, and mixed pollination. For this, we plan to use a three-step approach. 1) Quantification of seasonal activity of pollinators (visitation frequency and composition) and dynamics of flowering phenology at community scale along the elevational gradient from subalpine to alpine sites 2) Evaluation of seasonal activity and pollination efficiency of major pollinator groups (e.g., bumble bee, solitary bee, fly, hoverfly, hummingbird) 3) Clarification of the relationship between flowering time and pollination success of major plant species visited by different types of pollinators
Subject: Phenology

ResearchPlanTitle: Determining the abiotic drivers of solitary, ground-nesting bee phenology in the context of climate change
ResearchPlanAbstract: Solitary ground-nesting bees make up approximately 85% of the 20,000 bee species worldwide, yet little is known about how global change will affect them. One of the primary biological responses to climate change is a shift in the timing of an organism’s life events (e.g., flowering, migration, and emergence), also known as phenology. The timing of these events is critical for an organism’s growth, survival and reproduction. The proposed research aims to fill our knowledge gap of solitary ground-nesting bee phenology by combining an analysis of a long-term data set with observational and experimental field studies in a sensitive subalpine ecosystem. My research will improve our understanding of how an important, yet understudied, group of bees will respond to climate change.
Subject: Phenology

ResearchPlanTitle: Abiotic and biotic controls on chemical weathering rates and solute generation
ResearchPlanAbstract: Precipitation falling on mountainous watersheds is exposed to surface and subsurface processing, such as chemical weathering, before eventually leaving as streamflow. In turn, this processing is governed by a variety of abiotic and biotic interactions involving, e.g., the type of rock that governs geomorphology and mineralization and the type of vegetation that can generate acidity. The proposed work will focus on the role of vegetation as a means to influence water chemistry and quality. By employing a multi-scale approach, the project will address the following questions: 1) Does landscape-scale heterogeneity in vegetation, climate, and geology impart unique, spatially-variable signatures on soil production and chemical weathering rates? 2) What roles do the legacies of Pleistocene glaciation and Holocene geomorphic processes play in determining modern-day solute concentrations in surface waters? 3) Are physical erosion and chemical weathering rates linked at the watershed scale, and can these rates be predicted from watershed characteristics? These questions will be addressed in the physical and ecological setting of the East River watershed near Crested Butte, Colorado. The proposed technical approach will assess controls on weathering and solute generation at the soil profile, landform, and watershed scales. At the soil profile scale, soil production and chemical weathering rates will be quantified with cosmogenic nuclides and geochemical mass balance at sites that span biotic, climatic, and geologic gradients in order to isolate the key drivers of chemical weathering. At the landform scale, solute concentrations in surface waters will be used to assess whether surficial deposits generated by different geomorphic processes impart unique weathering signatures. At the watershed-scale, cosmogenic nuclides will be used to measure erosion rates. A series of reactive transport models will be constructed to place the field-based findings into a framework for making predictions regarding the roles that vegetation, climate, and geomorphology play in solute generation. The proposed research complements ongoing BER investments at the LBNL Watershed Science SFA Science Focus Area.
Subject: Climate Change

ResearchPlanTitle: Maternal Nutritional Stress and Its Effect on Philopatry in Golden Mantled Ground Squirrels
ResearchPlanAbstract: Stress is a physiological state experienced by all living organisms which can be passed across generations. The purpose of my study is to understand the consequences of maternal nutritional stress on daughter dispersal behavior (i.e. remain philopatric or disperse away from the natal home range). I address this in a population of golden mantled ground squirrels (GMGS), Callospermophilus lateralis, which has been studied for 30 years at Rocky Mountain Biological Research Laboratory in Gothic, Colorado. These hibernating mammals give birth to their young in burrows and offspring suckle from their mothers until emergence. During lactation, the stress hormone corticosterone can be transmitted from mother to offspring where it is eventually uptaken by developing hair follicles. By capturing and collecting hair samples from all mothers and daughters immediately upon emergence, stress data from the hair samples can be paired with philopatric/dispersal behavioral data to determine whether the nutritional stress of mothers determines if daughters remain philopatric or disperse after weaning. Sons tend to disperse regardless of circumstances whereas daughters sometimes remain philopatric to their natal home range. The ultimate goal of my thesis research is to gain insight into the role mother-daughter bonds play in shaping offspring behavior and fitness in light of environmental stress.
ResearchPlanOrganisms: Golden mantled ground squirrels (GMGS), Callospermophilus lateralis
Subject: Other

ResearchPlanTitle: Molecular evolution of Colias butterflies
ResearchPlanAbstract: Research on evolution by me and my research group has always included work at RMBL as an essential field component. For some time, we focused on mechanisms of maintenance of natural genetic variation at a small number of genes coding for three catalytic proteins, enzymes, embedded in energy-processing pathways central to all cellular life. We are now extending our approach to study natural variation in all the genes, hence their enzyme-catalyst protein products, making up an entire "module" of living organization: the intact pathway of energy processing known as glycolysis, together with its links to related processes. Initial data in hand argue for a wide range of evolutionary dynamics affecting genes of this "module" in wild insect populations. Our new work will probe the interactions between these insects and their environments which produce these diverse dynamics at different genes of this pathway. The results will extend basic understanding of how animals' adaptation to their environments works, and may also illuminate important problems of application to agriculture, medicine, and the genetics of conservation.
Subject: Other

ResearchPlanTitle: Mechanisms of Color Vision in Hummingbirds
ResearchPlanAbstract: Hummingbirds (family: Trochilidae) are an ideal study system for investigating relationships among visual physiology, behavior and cognition, and evolution. Hummingbirds are highly visual animals. They pollinate a great diversity of flowers and they have evolved a spectacular array of plumages, often characterized by iridescent patches. Despite the colorful world experienced by hummingbirds, relatively few details are known about their visual systems. We are performing color vision experiments on wild Broad-tailed Hummingbirds, the only resident breeding hummingbird species at RMBL. We are also investigating the ways in which Broad-tailed Hummingbirds use color in their courtship dive displays and foraging behavior. Finally, we are exploring the physiological and genetic/genomic mechanisms responsible for color vision in Broad-tailed Hummingbirds.
ResearchPlanOrganisms: Broad-tailed Hummingbirds and their preferred flowers
Subject: Other

ResearchPlanTitle: Advancing a Watershed Hydro-biogeochemical Theory: Linking Water Travel Time and Reactive Rates Under Changing Climate
ResearchPlanAbstract: Mountain watersheds are often regarded as the “water towers for humanity” (Viviroli et al. 2007). In western USA, mountain snow packs are estimated to supply about three-fourths of freshwater and more than 60 million people (Bales et al. 2006). They also represent the dominant-yet-vulnerable control on water availability. Here we choose Coal Creek, Colorado, a high-elevation (~ 2,700 – 3,700 m) mountainous catchment that has already seen > 5?C temperature increase in the past decades (based on SNOTEL measurements) and continued decline in snow fractions ( ~ 70% in 1980 to ~55% in 2018). We ask the overarching question of how and to what degree does a warming climate alter hydrological functioning and (biogeochemical and chemical weathering) reaction rates at the watershed scale? In particular, how does hydrological functioning (water storage, flow paths, and travel time) change responding to a warming climate? What are the corresponding alterations in biogeochemical and chemical weathering rates at the watershed scale? What is the general watershed-scale reaction rate law that causally links reaction rates to metrics of hydrological functioning that are determined by external hydroclimatic conditions and internal watershed structure characteristics? Using a combination of field measurements, transit time modeling, water fraction analysis, and process-based watershed hydro-biogeochemical modeling, we aim to develop a general rate law at the watershed scale, establishing a largely-unknown linkage between the extensively studied travel time theory and the recently developed young and new water fraction characteristics in hydrology to biogeochemical and weathering rates. Reaction rate laws are generally derived and parameterized in small scale field systems and well-mixed systems that have often been found non-applicable at the watershed scale. The Coal Creek watershed will serve as a model watershed to develop the general watershed-scale rate law, which will be further tested in a constellation of catchments within USA and across the globe that the PIs have involved in. These sites differ in the levels of snow dominance and geology, topography, and land cover conditions. This general law may be modified and expanded to ultimate compass a variety of environmental conditions. The proposed work will offer mechanistic understanding of how a warming climate alters water flow, storage, and travel time characteristics; and how and how much such alterations speed up reactions that drive the evolution of catchments and ultimately Earth surfaces. Although these aspects have been extensively studied within disciplinary boundaries, the inter-linkage is poorly understood and the hydro-biogeochemistry community is often puzzled by watershed process coupling, feedbacks, and emergent behaviors, all of which are important for projecting to the future. This work aims to unravel such linkage by integrating existing knowledge and approaches crossing hydrology and geochemistry boundaries, and to advance new fronts on climate change influences on water quantity and quality. The outcome of this work will advance our forecasting capabilities for water, mass, and energy in the rapidly changing planet. Notably, the developed general rate law will illustrate the first-order principle of hydro-biogeochemical process coupling. Ultimately, it will help develop forward projections to provide insight for adaptation, management, and prevention of water quantity and quality-related catastrophes. The proposed work continues our exploratory project on concentration discharge relationships at Coal Creek, CO. It will extend comprehensive data collection of soil, rocks, waters, and their isotope and chemistry, and model hydro-biogeochemical processes at the watershed scale. More importantly, this work will cast insights gained from Coal Creek to other sites that are impacted by a gradient of snow fractions to advance the theory of hydrological and biogeochemical coupling upon climate change influences. As far as we know there is no existing such studies yet at Coal Creek. It complements existing SBR LBNL SFA at the East River watershed.
Subject: Climate Change

ResearchPlanTitle: Biodiversity of aquatic and hyporheic insects in the Upper Gunnison Basin of Colorado.
ResearchPlanAbstract: Aquatic insects are the basis of stream, pond and riparian food webs. Understanding who lives in this habitat is key to interpreting the health of our aquatic habitats. This study works at increasing knowledge of our regional stream, pond and hyporheic insect populations. I also work on spiders in my free time :-)
Subject: Other

ResearchPlanTitle: Warming and Species Removal in Mountains (WaRM)
ResearchPlanAbstract: One of the fundamental challenges facing community and ecosystem ecologists is being able to predict ecosystem functions and services in a changing world. This is especially challenging because community- and ecosystem-level responses to environmental changes are affected by both the direct effects of changes in the abiotic environment and indirectly by changes in the traits of individual plants and by the structure of communities. While we have some understanding of how the responses of individual plants scale to ecosystem-level responses, we know much less about how community-level processes (e.g., species interactions, species replacement, species compensation) relate to ecosystem-level processes. Therefore, we (and others) argue that an urgent goal for research in global change ecology is to understand better the consequences of these suites of interactions in a changing world, and whether the community- and ecosystem-level responses to warming are contingent on background climate and vary consistently among disparate ecosystems. Here, we are manipulating warming and species interactions along gradients in mountains around the world.
Subject: Climate Change

ResearchPlanTitle: Watershed Function Science Focus Area (SFA)
ResearchPlanAbstract: Led by Berkeley Lab, the overarching objective of the Watershed Function Science Focus Area is to develop a fundamental understanding of watershed system functioning by addressing the question of how mountainous watersheds retain and release water, nutrients, and metals tied to climate disturbance over annual to decadal timescales. Perturbations of primary interest include those capable of inducing early snowmelt, such drought, warming, and dust/aerosol deposition. This work requires close coupling of field experimentation and observation (i.e., data gathering) with predictive numerical modeling. The work is focused on coupling (eco)hydrological processes with biogeochemical reactions occurring over the soil to bedrock continuum, which requires a wide diversity of infrastructure for sampling and monitoring. Significant gradients within the watershed include those pertaining to climate/elevation, land cover/vegetation, and geologic/bedrock type necessitating a broad distribution of sampling and monitoring locations spanning the four principle drainages. Addressing these gradients, the WFSFA has developed a novel, statistics-based approach that coarsely segregates the watershed into a network of five representative “functional units” or “functional zones” that account for variations in system characteristics, such as slope, aspect, topographic wetness index, predominant vegetation type, and geology. Field site development and data gathering within the watershed have been ongoing since May 2014, with work planned over the next 3+ years designed to assign functional behavior (e.g. diagnostic patterns water and solute export) to each of the five functional unit types.
Subject: Climate Change

ResearchPlanTitle: Ecohydrological controls on root and microbial respiration on Snodgrass Mountain in the East River watershed of Colorado
ResearchPlanAbstract: Belowground in the soil, microbes breakdown organic matter, releasing CO2. Plant roots produce CO2 also, via their metabolism. Our research seeks to understand how moisture inputs, such as snow and rain, influence the amount of CO2 produced belowground on Snodgrass Mountain in the East River watershed, near Crested Butte, Colorado. We will quantify the flux of CO2 from the soil to the atmosphere, and how plant and microbial sources of CO2 respond to the environment, across different elevations. We will work in the two main forest types in the East River watershed, spruce/fir and aspen. To do this, continuous measurements of soil CO2 concentrations, at multiple depths, will be combined with novel radiocarbon methods that will enable the separation of plant and microbial sources of CO2. At each site, these measurements will be linked to measurements of forest and snow phenology, microbial activity, and environmental factors such as air and soil temperature, soil moisture, and groundwater flow. Our work is motivated by our overarching hypothesis that quantifying belowground plant and microbial processes separately, and how they are influenced by snow and rain inputs, is necessary for understanding and predicting how the belowground East River watershed ecosystems will respond to changes in the environment.
Subject: Climate Change
